Thus it is said: ‘And because….’ This is said by way of a simile, and there is not an absolute similarity between a simile and the thing compared. Therefore, just as Buddhas arise only occasionally, wheel-turning monarchs do not arise in the same way. Even so, because of the difficulty of fulfilling the duties of a wheel-turning monarch, their arising is also rare. It should be understood that their rarity of sight is stated because of this common feature of rarity of arising. It is true that the quality accomplished through the power of the wheel-treasure is common to the wheel-turning monarch’s retinue, yet because it arises for his sake, it deserves to be said that ‘the wheel-turning monarch alone enjoys it by right of ownership.’ To show this, he says, ‘This is that…,’ and so on. Because the five, or even six, meanings mentioned are found in the other treasures too, it is said, ‘Similarly, the others….’ He is endowed with the elephant-, horse-, and counselor-treasures, by which his victory is unconquered; with the wheel-treasure as his retinue; and with the others as his instruments of enjoyment. The construction is: with the elephant-, horse-, jewel-, and woman-treasures as his instruments of enjoyment, and with the others as his retinue.

Catunnaṃ mahādīpānaṃ sirivibhavanti tattha laddhaṃ sirisampattiñceva bhogasampattiñca. Tādisamevāti “purebhattamevā”tiādinā vuttānubhāvameva. Yojanappamāṇaṃ padesaṃ byāpanena yojanappamāṇaṃ andhakāraṃ. Atidīghatādichabbidhadosaparivajjitaṃ.

‘The glory and wealth of the four great continents’ means the attainment of glory and the attainment of wealth obtained there. ‘Just like that’ means the very same power spoken of beginning with ‘even before the meal.’ By pervading a region a yojana in extent, it dispels darkness a yojana in extent. It is devoid of the six kinds of faults, such as being too long.

Sūrāti sattivanto, nibbhayāti atthoti āha “abhīrukā”ti. Aṅganti kāraṇaṃ. Yena kāraṇena “vīrā”ti vucceyyuṃ, taṃ vīraṅgaṃ. Tenāha “vīriyassetaṃ [M 2.0036] nāma”nti. Yāva cakkavāḷapabbatā cakkassa vattanato “cakkavāḷapabbataṃ sīmaṃ katvā ṭhitasamuddapariyanta”nti vuttaṃ. “Adaṇḍenā”ti imināva dhanadaṇḍassa, sarīradaṇḍassa ca akaraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. “Asatthenā”ti iminā pana senāya yujjhanassāti tadubhayaṃ dassetuṃ “ye katāparādhe”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vuttappakāranti sāgarapariyantaṃ.

‘Valiant’ means powerful; the meaning is fearless. Hence he says ‘not timid.’ ‘Mark’ means cause. The cause for which they would be called ‘heroes’ is the ‘mark of a hero.’ Therefore he says: ‘This is a name for energy.’ Because the wheel turns as far as the Cakkavāḷa mountain range, it is said, ‘ending at the ocean which stands having the Cakkavāḷa mountain range as its boundary.’ By ‘without the rod,’ the non-use of the rod of fines and the rod of physical punishment is stated. But by ‘without the sword,’ not fighting with an army is meant. To show both, it is said, ‘those who have committed an offense,’ and so on. ‘The manner described’ means ending at the ocean.

“Rañjanaṭṭhena rāgo, taṇhāyanaṭṭhena taṇhā”ti pavattiākārabhedena [P 2.0046] lobho eva dvidhā vutto[V 2.0032]. Tathā hissa dvidhāpi chadanaṭṭho ekantiko. Yathāha “andhatamaṃ tadā hoti, yaṃ rāgo sahate nara”nti, (netti. 11, 27) “taṇhāchadanachāditā”ti (udā. 64) ca. Iminā nayena dosādīnampi chadanaṭṭho vattabbo. Kilesaggahaṇena vicikicchādayo sesakilesā vuttā. Yasmā te sabbe pāpadhammā uppajjamānā sattasantānaṃ chādetvā pariyonandhitvā tiṭṭhanti kusalappavattiṃ nivārenti, tasmā te “chadanā, chadā”ti ca vuttā. Vivaṭṭacchadāti ca o-kārassa ā-kāraṃ katvā niddeso.

“Lust in the sense of dyeing, craving in the sense of thirsting”—thus greed is spoken of in two ways according to the difference in its mode of occurrence. For in both ways its nature is exclusively that of a covering. As it is said: “Then there is the deepest darkness, when lust overcomes a person,” and “covered by the covering of craving.” By this method, the covering nature of hatred and the others is also to be stated. By the term “defilements,” the remaining defilements such as doubt are mentioned. Because all those evil states, when they arise, cover and envelop the continuity of a being and stand preventing the occurrence of wholesome states, they are therefore called “coverings” (chadanā) and “covers” (chadā). And the expression “vivaṭṭacchadā” (uncovered coverings) is an explanation made by changing the “o” to an “ā”.

35. Tāsanti dvinnampi nipphattīnaṃ. Nimittabhūtānīti ñāpakakāraṇabhūtāni. Tathā hi lakkhīyati mahāpurisabhāvo etehīti lakkhaṇāni. Ṭhānagamanādīsu bhūmiyaṃ suṭṭhu samaṃ patiṭṭhitā pādā etassāti suppatiṭṭhitapādo. Taṃ panassa suppatiṭṭhitapādataṃ byatirekamukhena vibhāvetuṃ “yathā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha aggatalanti aggapādatalaṃ. Paṇhīti paṇhitalaṃ. Passanti pādatalassa dvīsu passesu ekekaṃ, ubhayameva vā pariyantaṃ passaṃ. “Assa panā”tiādi anvayato atthavibhāvanaṃ. Suvaṇṇapādukatalamiva ujukaṃ nikkhipiyamānaṃ. Ekappahārenevāti ekakkhaṇeyeva. Sakalaṃ pādatalaṃ bhūmiṃ phusati nikkhipane. Ekappahāreneva sakalaṃ pādatalaṃ bhūmito uṭṭhahatīti yojanā. Tasmā ayaṃ suppatiṭṭhitapādoti nigamanaṃ. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ anupubbaninnādiacchariyabbhutaṃ [P 2.0047] nissandaphalaṃ, taṃ parato lakkhaṇasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.201) āvibhavissatīti.

35. Tāsaṃ: this refers to both accomplishments. Being signs means being indicative causes. For the state of a Great Man is marked by these; hence they are called characteristics. His feet are well and evenly established on the ground when standing, walking, etc.; hence, he has well-established feet. To clarify this quality of having well-established feet by way of contrast, the words “just as,” etc., are stated. Herein, “aggatala” is the fore-sole. “Paṇhī” is the heel-sole. “Passa” is each of the two sides of the sole, or both edges. The words “but for him,” etc., are an explanation of the meaning in direct order. Like the sole of a golden sandal being placed down straight. “In a single placement” means in a single moment. When placing it down, the entire sole of the foot touches the ground. The connection is: in a single motion the entire sole of the foot lifts from the ground. Therefore, this is the conclusion: “he has well-established feet.” Whatever should be said here about the sequential, subtle, astonishing, and wonderful resultant fruit will become clear later in the commentary on the Lakkhaṇa Sutta.

Nābhi dissatīti lakkhaṇacakkassa nābhi parimaṇḍalasaṇṭhānā suparibyattā hutvā dissati, labbhatīti adhippāyo. Nābhiparicchinnāti tassaṃ nābhiyaṃ paricchinnā paricchedavasena ṭhitā. Nābhimukhaparikkhepapaṭṭoti pakaticakkassa [M 2.0037] akkhabbhāhatapariharaṇatthaṃ nābhimukhe ṭhapetabbaṃ parikkhepapaṭṭo, tappaṭicchanno idha adhippeto. Nemimaṇikāti nemiyaṃ āvalibhāvena ṭhitamaṇikālekhā. Sambahulavāroti bahuvidhalekhaṅgavibhāvanavāro. Sattīti āvudhasatti. Sirivacchoti siriaṅgā. Nandīti dakkhiṇāvattaṃ. Sovattikoti sovattiaṅgo. Vaṭaṃsakoti āveḷaṃ. Vaḍḍhamānakanti purimahādīsu dīpaṅkaṃ. Morahatthakoti morapiñchakalāpo, morapiñchapaṭisibbito vā bījanīviseso. Vāḷabījanīti cāmarivālaṃ. Siddhatthādi puṇṇaghaṭapuṇṇapātiyo. “Cakkavāḷo”ti vatvā tassa padhānāvayave dassetuṃ “himavā sineru…pe… sahassānī”ti vuttaṃ. “Cakkavattirañño parisaṃ upādāyā”ti idaṃ hatthiratanādīnampi tattha labbhamānabhāvadassanaṃ. Sabbotisattiādiko yathāvutto aṅgaviseso cakkalakkhaṇasseva parivāroti veditabbo.

“The navel is visible” means the navel of the wheel-mark is visible, being perfectly round in shape and very distinct; the intention is that it is obtainable. “Defined by the navel” means defined in that navel, established by way of a boundary. “The protective plate facing the navel” is the protective plate to be placed at the face of the navel of an ordinary wheel to prevent damage from the axle; here, what is covered by it is intended. “Jewels on the rim” are jewel-like lines situated in a row on the rim. “Many spokes” means the section distinguishing the many kinds of line-markings. “A spear” is a weapon-spear. “Sirivaccha” is the sirī-mark. “Nandī” is a right-coiling mark. “Sovattika” is the sovattika-mark. “Vaṭaṃsaka” is an ear-ornament. “Vaḍḍhamānaka” is a lamp-stand on the front banners, etc. “Morahatthaka” is a bunch of peacock feathers, or a special kind of fan sewn with peacock feathers. “Vāḷabījanī” is a chowrie. “Siddhattha,” etc., are full jars and full bowls. Having said “the Cakkavāḷa mountain range,” to show its principal components, “Himavā, Sineru… up to a thousand” is stated. “Including the retinue of a wheel-turning king”: this shows that the elephant-treasure and others are also obtainable there. All this—the spear and so on, the special features as described—should be understood as the retinue of the wheel-mark only.

“Āyatapaṇhī”ti [V 2.0033] idaṃ aññesaṃ paṇhito dīghataṃ sandhāya [P 2.0048] vuttaṃ, na pana atidīghatanti āha “paripuṇṇapaṇhī”ti. Yathā pana paṇhilakkhaṇaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ nāma hoti, taṃ byatirekamukhena dassetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Āraggenāti maṇḍalāya sikhāya. Vaṭṭetvāti yathā suvaṭṭaṃ hoti, evaṃ vaṭṭetvā. Rattakambalageṇḍukasadisāti rattakambalamayageṇḍukasadisā.

“Long-heeled”: this is said with reference to the length of the heels of others, but not that they are excessively long; thus it says “with full heels.” To show by way of contrast how the characteristic of the heel is called “full,” the words “just as,” etc., are stated. “With the point of an awl” means with a rounded point. “Having turned it” means having turned it so that it is well-rounded. “Like a ball of red wool” means like a ball made of red wool.

“Makkaṭassevā”ti dīghabhāvaṃ, samatañca sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Niyyāsatelenāti chattiritaniyyāsādiniyyāsasammissena telena, yaṃ “surabhiniyyāsa”ntipi vadanti. Niyyāsatelaggahaṇañcettha haritālavaṭṭiyā ghanasiniddhabhāvadassanatthaṃ.

“Like a monkey’s” refers to its length and evenness. “With resin-oil” means with oil mixed with resin, such as the resin of the chattiri tree and other resins, which they also call “fragrant resin.” And the mention of resin-oil here is for the purpose of showing the dense and smooth nature of the stick of orpiment.

Yathā satakkhattuṃ vihataṃ kappāsapaṭalaṃ sappimaṇḍe osāritaṃ ativiya mudu hoti, evaṃ mahāpurisassa hatthapādāti dassento “sappimaṇḍe”tiādimāha. Talunāti sukhumālā.

Just as a tuft of cotton carded a hundred times and dipped in the finest ghee becomes exceedingly soft, so too are the hands and feet of the Great Man—to show this, he says, “in the finest ghee,” and so on. “Tender” means delicate and soft.

Cammenāti aṅgulantaraveṭhitacammena. Paṭibaddhaaṅgulantaroti ekato sambaddhaaṅgulantaro na hoti. Ekappamāṇāti dīghato samānappamāṇā. Yavalakkhaṇanti abbhantarato aṅgulipabbe ṭhitaṃ yavalakkhaṇaṃ. Paṭivijjhitvāti taṃtaṃpabbānaṃ samānadesatāya aṅgulīnaṃ pasāritakālepi aññamaññaṃ vijjhitāni viya phusitvā tiṭṭhanti.

“With skin” means with skin wrapped between the fingers. “With connected spaces between the fingers” means the space between the fingers is not joined together. “Of one measure” means of equal measure in length. “The barley-mark” is the barley-mark situated on the inside of the finger-joint. “Pierced through”: because the respective joints are in the same position, even when the fingers are spread out, they remain touching one another as if pierced through.

Saṅkhā [M 2.0038] vuccanti gopphakā, uddhaṃ saṅkhā etesanti ussaṅkhā, pādā. Piṭṭhipādeti piṭṭhipādasamīpe. Tenāti piṭṭhipāde ṭhitagopphakabhāvena baddhā hontīti yojanā. Tayidaṃ “tenā”ti padaṃ uparipadadvayepi yojetabbaṃ [P 2.0049] “tena baddhabhāvena na yathāsukhaṃ parivaṭṭanti, tena yathāsukhaṃ naparivaṭṭanena gacchantānaṃ pādatalānipi na dissantī”ti. Uparīti piṭṭhipādato dvitiaṅgulimattaṃ uddhaṃ, “caturaṅgulamatta”nti ca vadanti. Nigūḷhāni ca honti, na aññesaṃ viya paññāyamānāni. Tenāti gopphakānaṃ upari patiṭṭhitabhāvena. Assāti mahāpurisassa. Satipi desantarappavattiyaṃ niccaloti dassanatthaṃ nābhiggahaṇaṃ. “Adhokāyova iñjatī”ti idaṃ purimapadassa kāraṇavacanaṃ. Yasmā adhokāyova iñjati, tasmā nābhito…pe… niccalo hoti. “Sukhena pādā parivaṭṭantī”ti idaṃ pana purimassa, pacchimassa ca kāraṇavacanaṃ. Yasmā sukhena pādā parivaṭṭanti, tasmā adhokāyova iñjati, yasmā sukhena pādā parivaṭṭanti, tasmā puratopi…pe… pacchatoyevāti.

“Saṅkhā” are called the ankles. “Ussaṅkhā” means “having ankles above,” referring to the feet. “On the top of the foot” means near the top of the foot. “By that”: the connection is that they are bound by the state of the ankles being situated on the top of the foot. This word “tena” should also be connected with the two words above: “because of that bound state, they do not turn as one pleases; because they do not turn as one pleases, the soles of the feet are not visible when walking.” “Above” means about two finger-breadths above the top of the foot; and some say “about four finger-breadths.” And they are concealed, not apparent like those of others. “By that” means by the state of being established above the ankles. “Of him” means of the Great Man. The mention of the navel is to show that he is motionless even when moving to another place. “Only the lower body moves”: this is a statement of the reason for the preceding phrase. Because only the lower body moves, therefore from the navel… (etc.)… he is motionless. But “the feet turn with ease” is a statement of the reason for both the preceding and the following. Because the feet turn with ease, therefore only the lower body moves; because the feet turn with ease, therefore in front… (etc.)… and behind.

Yasmā eṇimigassa samantato ekasadisamaṃsā anukkamena uddhaṃ thūlā jaṅghā honti, tathā [V 2.0034] mahāpurisassāpi, tasmā vuttaṃ “eṇimigasadisajaṅgho”ti. Paripuṇṇajaṅghoti samantato maṃsūpacayena paripuṇṇajaṅgho. Tenāha “na ekato”tiādi.

Because an eṇi-deer has shanks with evenly distributed flesh all around that gradually become thick upwards, and so too does the Great Man; therefore it is said, “with shanks like an eṇi-deer.” “With full shanks” means with shanks full all around from an accretion of flesh. Hence it is said, “not from one side,” and so on.

Etenāti “anonamanto”tiādivacanena, jāṇuphāsubhāvadīpanenāti attho. Avasesajanāti iminā lakkhaṇena rahitajanā. Khujjā vā honti heṭṭhimakāyato uparimakāyassa rassatāya, vāmanā vā uparimakāyato heṭṭhimakāyassa rassatāya, etena ṭhapetvā sammāsambuddhaṃ, cakkavattinañca itare sattā khujjapakkhikā, vāmanapakkhikā cāti dasseti.

“By this” means by the statement “without bending down,” etc.; the meaning is, by showing the ease with which he can touch his knees. “The remaining people” are people devoid of this characteristic. They are either hunchbacked, because of the shortness of the upper body in relation to the lower body, or dwarfish, because of the shortness of the lower body in relation to the upper body. By this he shows that, apart from a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha and a wheel-turning monarch, other beings belong to the party of the hunchbacked or the party of the dwarfish.

Kāmaṃ sabbāpi padumakaṇṇikā suvaṇṇavaṇṇāva, kañcanapadumakaṇṇikā pana pabhassarabhāvena tato sātisayāti [P 2.0050] āha “suvaṇṇapadumakaṇṇikasadisehī”ti. Ohitanti samohitaṃ antogadhaṃ. Tathābhūtaṃ pana taṃ tena channaṃ hotīti āha “paṭicchanna”nti.

Granted, all lotus pericarps are golden-colored, but the pericarp of a golden lotus surpasses them in radiance because of its luminosity; hence he says “like the pericarp of a golden lotus.” “Enclosed” means drawn in, retracted within. And since, being so, it is covered by that, he says “concealed.”

Suvaṇṇavaṇṇoti suvaṇṇavaṇṇavaṇṇoti ayamettha atthoti āha “jātihiṅgulakenā”tiādi, svāyamattho āvuttiñāyena ca veditabbo. Sarīrapariyāyo idha vaṇṇa-saddoti adhippāyo. Paṭhamavikappaṃ vatvā [M 2.0039] tathārūpāya pana ruḷhiyā abhāvaṃ manasi katvā vaṇṇadhātupariyāyameva vaṇṇa-saddaṃ gahetvā dutiyavikappo vutto. Tasmā padadvayenāpi suniddhantasuvaṇṇasadisachavivaṇṇoti vuttaṃ hoti.

“Golden-hued” means having a body of golden hue; this is the meaning here, he says, “like natural vermilion,” etc. This meaning should be understood by the principle of repetition. The intention here is that the word “vaṇṇa” is a synonym for body. Having stated the first alternative, but then, bearing in mind the absence of such a conventional usage, the second alternative is stated, taking the word “vaṇṇa” only as a synonym for the color-element. Therefore, by both words, it comes to be said that he has a skin-color like well-refined gold.

Rajoti sukhumarajo. Jallanti malīnabhāvāvaho reṇusañcayo. Tenāha “malaṃ vā”ti. Yadi vivattati, kathaṃ nhānādīnīti āha “hatthadhovanādīnī”tiādi.

“Raja” is fine dust. “Jalla” is an accumulation of fine particles that brings about a state of stain. Hence he says, “or a stain.” If it rolls off, how can there be bathing, etc.? He says, “washing the hands,” and so on.

Āvaṭṭapariyosāneti padakkhiṇāvaṭṭanavasena pavattassa āvaṭṭassa ante.

“At the end of the whorl” means at the end of the whorl that proceeds by way of a clockwise turning.

Brahmuno sarīraṃ purato vā pacchato vā anonamitvā ujukameva uggatanti āha “brahmā viya ujugatto”ti. Sā panāyaṃ ujugattatā avayavesu buddhippattesu daṭṭhabbā, na daharakāleti vuttaṃ “uggatadīghasarīro bhavissatī”ti. Itaresūti “khandhajāṇūsū”ti imesu dvīsu ṭhānesu namantā purato namantīti ānetvā sambandho. Passavaṅkāti dakkhiṇapassena vā vāmapassena vā vaṅkā. Sūlasadisāti potthakarūpakaraṇe ṭhapitasūlapādasadisā.

The body of a Brahmā does not bend forward or backward but rises up perfectly straight; hence it is said, 'straight-bodied like a Brahmā.' This straightness of body, however, should be seen in the limbs when they have reached full growth, not in childhood; thus it is said, 'he will have a towering and long body.' In the other cases, that is, in the 'shoulders and knees,' they bend forward; this is the connection. 'Bent at the side' means bent at the right or left side. 'Like a stake' means resembling the leg of a stake set up when making a manuscript model.

Hatthapiṭṭhiādivasena satta sarīrāvayavā ussadā upacitamaṃsā etassāti sattussado. Aṭṭhikoṭiyo [V 2.0035] paññāyantīti yojanā. Nigūḷhasirājālehīti lakkhaṇavacanametanti tena nigūḷhaaṭṭhikoṭīhītipi vuttameva hotīti. Hatthapiṭṭhādīhīti [P 2.0051] ettha ādi-saddena aṃsakūṭakhandhakūṭānaṃ saṅgahe siddhe taṃ ekadesena dassento “vaṭṭetvā…pe… khandhenā”ti āha. “Silārūpakaṃ viyā”tiādinā vā nigūḷhaaṃsakūṭatāpi vibhāvitā yevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

He is one with seven prominences (sattussado) because seven parts of his body, such as the backs of his hands, are prominent, with well-developed flesh. The connection is: 'The bone-ends are visible.' 'With hidden veins and sinews' is a term for the mark; by this it is also meant 'with hidden bone-ends.' In the phrase 'by the backs of the hands and so on,' the word 'and so on' is understood to include the shoulder blades and the collarbones. Illustrating this in part, he says: '...having made round... with the shoulder...' Alternatively, the hidden nature of the shoulder blades is also explained by the phrase 'like a stone image'; this should be understood.

Sīhassa pubbaddhaṃ sīhapubbaddhaṃ, paripuṇṇāvayavatāya sīhapubbaddhaṃ viya sakalo kāyo assāti sīhapubbaddhakāyo. Tenāha “sīhassa pubbaddhakāyo viya sabbo kāyo paripuṇṇo”ti. Sīhassevāti sīhassa viya. Dussaṇṭhitavisaṇṭhito na hotīti duṭṭhu saṇṭhito, virūpasaṇṭhito ca na hoti, tesaṃ tesaṃ avayavānaṃ ayuttabhāvena, virūpabhāvena ca saṇṭhiti upagato na hotīti attho. Saṇṭhantīti saṇṭhahanti. Dīghehīti aṅgulināsādīhi. Rassehīti gīvādīhi. Thūlehīti ūrubāhuādīhi[M 2.0040]. Kisehīti kesalomamajjhādīhi. Puthulehīti akkhihatthatalādīhi. Vaṭṭehīti jaṅghahatthādīhi.

The forepart of a lion is the 'lion's forepart.' Because his entire body is like a lion's forepart in its completeness of limbs, he has a 'lion-forepart body.' Hence it is said: 'Like a lion's forepart, his whole body is complete.' 'Of a lion' means 'like a lion.' He is not badly proportioned or misshapen, meaning he is not ill-proportioned, nor is he deformedly proportioned. The meaning is that he has not acquired a shape characterized by the unsuitability or ugliness of his various limbs. 'They are proportioned' means 'they are well-formed.' With long parts: such as fingers and nose. With short parts: such as the neck. With thick parts: such as the thighs and arms. With slender parts: such as the head hair, body hair, and waist. With broad parts: such as the eyes and palms. With round parts: such as the shanks and hands.

Satapuññalakkhaṇatāya nānācittena puññacittena cittito sañjātacittabhāvo “īdiso eva buddhānaṃ dhammakāyassa adhiṭṭhānaṃ bhavituṃ yutto”ti dasapāramīhi sajjito abhisaṅkhato, “dānacittena puññacittenā”ti vā pāṭho, dānavasena, sīlādivasena ca pavattapuññacittenāti attho.

Because it has the characteristic of a hundred merits, a state of mind has arisen, adorned by a meritorious mind of various kinds; furnished and prepared by the ten perfections, it is as if to say: 'Such a one is indeed fit to be the basis for the Dhamma-body of the Buddhas.' Alternatively, the reading is: 'with a mind of generosity, with a meritorious mind'; the meaning is, with a meritorious mind that has proceeded by way of generosity, and by way of virtue and so on.

Dvinnaṃ koṭṭānaṃ antaranti dvinnaṃ piṭṭhibāhānaṃ vemajjhaṃ piṭṭhimajjhassa uparibhāgo. Citaṃ paripuṇṇanti aninnabhāvena citaṃ, dvīhi koṭṭehi samatalatāya paripuṇṇaṃ. Uggammāti uggantvā, aninnaṃ samatalaṃ hutvāti adhippāyo. Tenāha “suvaṇṇaphalakaṃ viyā”ti.

'Between the two protuberances' means the space between the two shoulder blades, the upper part of the middle of the back. 'Filled up, complete' means filled up by being without a depression, complete by being level with the two protuberances. Uggammā means having risen up; the intention is having become level, without a depression. Therefore he said: 'like a golden plank.'

Nigrodho viya parimaṇḍaloti parimaṇḍalanigrodho viya [P 2.0052] parimaṇḍalo, “nigrodhaparimaṇḍalaparimaṇḍalo”ti vattabbe ekassa parimaṇḍala-saddassa lopaṃ katvā “nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo”ti vutto. Tenāha “samakkhandhasākho nigrodho”tiādi. Na hi sabbo nigrodho parimaṇḍaloti, parimaṇḍalasaddasannidhānena vā parimaṇḍalova nigrodho gayhatīti ekassa parimaṇḍalasaddassa lopena vināpi ayamattho labbhatīti āha “nigrodho viya parimaṇḍalo”ti. Yāvatako assāti yāvatakvassa o-kārassa va-kārādesaṃ katvā.

'Perfectly proportioned like a banyan tree' means he is perfectly proportioned like a perfectly proportioned banyan tree. When it should be said, 'nigrodhaparimaṇḍala-parimaṇḍalo,' one instance of the word 'parimaṇḍala' is elided, and it is said 'nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo.' Hence it is stated: 'a banyan tree with trunk and branches of equal measure,' and so on. For not every banyan tree is perfectly proportioned. Or, because of the proximity of the word 'parimaṇḍala,' only a perfectly proportioned banyan tree is to be understood. Therefore, even without the elision of one instance of the word 'parimaṇḍala,' this meaning is obtained. Thus it is said: 'perfectly proportioned like a banyan tree.' 'Yāvatako assa' becomes 'yāvatakvassa' by substituting 'va' for the letter 'o'.

Samavaṭṭitakkhandhoti samaṃ suvaṭṭitakkhandho. Koñcā viya dīghagalā, bakā viya vaṅkagalā[V 2.0036], varāhā viya puthulagalāti yojanā. Suvaṇṇāḷiṅgasadisoti suvaṇṇamayakhuddakamudiṅgasadiso.

'Evenly rounded shoulders' means his shoulders are evenly and well-rounded. The connection is: his neck is not long like a curlew's, nor crooked like a heron's, nor thick like a boar's. 'Like a golden drum' means like a small golden drum.

Rasaggasaggīti madhurādibhedaṃ rasaṃ gasanti anto pavesantīti rasaggasā rasaggasānaṃ aggā rasaggasaggā, tā etassa santīti rasaggasaggī. Tenāti ojāya apharaṇena hīnadhātukattā te bahvābādhā honti.

'One with supreme taste-conduits' (rasaggasaggī): The conduits that conduct tastes such as sweet, etc., by making them enter inside, are the 'taste-conduits' (rasaggasā). The best of these taste-conduits are the 'supreme taste-conduits' (rasaggasaggā). He possesses these, thus he is 'one with supreme taste-conduits.' 'By that' means: because the nutritive essence does not pervade, their constitution is deficient, and they are very sickly.

Hanūti sannissayadantādhārassa samaññā, taṃ bhagavato sīhassa hanu viya, tasmā bhagavā sīhahanu. Tattha yasmā buddhānaṃ rūpakāyassa, dhammakāyassa ca upamā nāma hīnūpamāva, natthi samānūpamā, kuto adhikūpamā, tasmā ayampi hīnūpamāti dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yasmā mahāpurisassa heṭṭhimānurūpavaseneva uparimampi saṇṭhitaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ [M 2.0041] “dvepi paripuṇṇānī”ti, tañca kho na sabbaso parimaṇḍalatāya, atha kho tibhāgāvasesamaṇḍalatāyāti āha “dvādasiyā pakkhassa candasadisānī”ti. Sallakkhetvāti attano lakkhaṇasatthānusārena [P 2.0053] upadhāretvā. Dantānaṃ uccanīcatā abbhantarabāhirapassavasenapi veditabbā, na aggavaseneva. Tenāha “ayapaṭṭakena chinnasaṅkhapaṭalaṃ viyā”ti. Ayapaṭṭakanti kakacaṃ adhippetaṃ. Samā bhavissanti, na visamā, samasaṇṭhānāti attho.

'Jaw' is the designation for the support on which the teeth rest. The Blessed One's jaw is like a lion's jaw; therefore the Blessed One is 'lion-jawed.' In this regard, because any comparison for the Buddhas' form-body or Dhamma-body is an inferior comparison—there is no equal comparison, still less a superior one—to show that this too is an inferior comparison, 'in this regard,' etc., was said. Because the Great Man's upper jaw is shaped in conformity with the lower one, it is said, 'both are complete.' And this is not by being completely round, but rather by being round with one-third remaining; thus he says, 'like the moon of the twelfth day of the fortnight.' 'Having discerned' means having investigated in accordance with one's own treatise on the marks. The evenness or unevenness of the teeth should be known by way of their inner and outer sides, not just by way of the tips. Hence it is said: 'like a sheet of conch cut with an iron plate.' 'Iron plate' here is intended to mean a saw. They will be even, not uneven; the meaning is of uniform shape.

Sātisayaṃ mududīghaputhulatādippakāraguṇā hutvā bhūtā jātāti pabhūtā, bha-kārassa ha-kāraṃ katvā pahūtā jivhā etassāti pahūtajivho.

Having become possessed of excellent qualities of such kinds as softness, length, and breadth, it is 'become, born' (bhūtā jātā), thus 'abundant' (pabhūtā). By changing the letter 'bh' to 'h', this becomes 'pahūtā.' He has an abundant (pahūtā) tongue (jivhā), therefore he is 'one with an abundant tongue' (pahūtajivho).

Vicchinditvā vicchinditvā pavattasaratāya chinnassarāpi. Anekākāratāya bhinnassarāpi. Kākassa viya amanuññasaratāya kākassarāpi. Apalibuddhattāti anupaddutavatthukattā, vatthūti ca akkharuppattiṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatoti ettha aṅgāni parato āgamissanti. Mañjughosoti madhurassaro.

Because their voice proceeds intermittently, some have a broken voice. Because it is of many kinds, some have a cracked voice. Because their voice is disagreeable like a crow's, some have a crow-like voice. 'Because it is unimpeded' means because its physical basis is unafflicted; and 'physical basis' should be understood as the place of articulation of the syllables. 'Endowed with eight factors': here the factors will be given below. 'Of lovely sound' means having a sweet voice.

Abhinīlanettoti adhikanīlanetto, adhikatā ca sātisayaṃ nīlabhāvena veditabbā, na nettanīlabhāvasseva adhikabhāvatoti āha “na sakalanīlanetto”tiādi. Pītalohitavaṇṇā setamaṇḍalagatarājivasena. Nīlasetakāḷavaṇṇā pana taṃtaṃmaṇḍalavaseneva veditabbā.

'With intensely blue eyes' means with exceedingly blue eyes. And this excellence should be understood as an excellent quality of the color blue, not as an excess of the blue part of the eye; hence it is said: 'not with the entire eye blue,' and so on. The yellow and red colors are by way of the streaks in the white circle. But the blue, white, and black colors should be understood as belonging to their respective circles.

“Cakkhubhaṇḍanti akkhidala”nti keci. “Akkhidalavaṭuma”nti aññe. Akkhidalehi pana [V 2.0037] saddhiṃ akkhibimbanti veditabbaṃ. Evañhi viniggatagambhīrajotanāpi yuttā hoti. “Adhippeta”nti iminā ayamettha adhippāyo ekadesena samudāyupalakkhaṇañāyenāti dasseti. Yasmā pakhuma-saddo loke akkhidalalomesu niruḷho, tenevāha “mudusiniddhanīlasukhumapakhumācitāni akkhīnī”ti.

Some say 'the eye-instrument' means the eyelid. Others say it means the rim of the eyelid. But it should be understood as the eyeball together with the eyelids. For in this way, the emission of deep radiance is also fitting. By the word 'intended,' he shows that the intention here is in accordance with the principle of indicating a whole by a part. Since the word 'pakhuma' (eyelash) is established in the world for the hairs of the eyelids, he therefore said: 'The eyes are endowed with soft, glossy, blue, and fine eyelashes.'

Kiñcāpi uṇṇā-saddo loke avisesato lomapariyāyo, idha pana lomavisesavācakoti āha “uṇṇā loma”nti. Nalāṭavemajjhe [P 2.0054] jātāti nalāṭamajjhagatā jātā. Odātatāya upamā, na mudutāya[M 2.0042]. Uṇṇā hi tatopi sātisayaṃ mudutarā. Tenāha“sappi maṇḍe”tiādi. Rajatapubbuḷakanti rajatamayatārakamāha.

Although in the world the word 'uṇṇā' is a synonym for hair in general, here it denotes a specific kind of hair; hence it is said, 'the uṇṇā is a hair.' 'Born in the very middle of the forehead' means born and situated in the middle of the forehead. The comparison is with respect to its whiteness, not its softness, for the uṇṇā is even more exceedingly soft than that. Therefore he said: 'like the cream of ghee,' etc. 'A silver bubble' means a silver star.

Dve atthavase paṭicca vuttanti yasmā buddhā, cakkavattino ca paripuṇṇanalāṭatāya, paripuṇṇasīsabimbatāya ca “uṇhīsasīsā”ti vuccanti, tasmā te dve atthavase paṭicca “uṇhīsasīso”ti idaṃ vuttaṃ. Idāni taṃ atthadvayaṃ mahāpurise suppatiṭṭhitanti “mahāpurisassa hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Saṇhatamatāya, suvaṇṇavaṇṇatāya, pabhassaratāya, paripuṇṇatāya ca rañño bandhauṇhīsapaṭṭo viya virocati. Kapisīsāti dvidhābhūtasīsā. Phalasīsāti phalitasīsā. Aṭṭhisīsāti maṃsassa abhāvato ativiya aṭṭhitāya, patanubhāvato vā taconaddhaaṭṭhimattasīsā. Tumbasīsāti lābusadisasīsā. Pabbhārasīsāti piṭṭhibhāgena olambamānasīsā. Purimanayenāti paripuṇṇanalāṭatāpakkhena. Uṇhīsaveṭhitasīso viyāti uṇhīsapaṭṭena veṭhitasīsapadeso viya. Uṇhīsaṃ viyāti chekena sippinā viracitauṇhīsamaṇḍalaṃ viya.

This was said with reference to two reasons: because Buddhas and wheel-turning monarchs are called 'those with a turban-like head' (uṇhīsasīsā) on account of their complete foreheads and their complete cranial globes, this was said, 'he has a turban-like head' (uṇhīsasīso), with reference to these two reasons. Now, to show that these two meanings are well-established in the Great Man, it is said: 'For the Great Man...,' etc. Because of its smoothness, golden color, radiance, and fullness, it shines like the turban-band bound on by a king. 'A monkey-head' (kapisīsa) means a head that is bifurcated. 'A split head' (phalasīsa) means a cloven head. 'A bony head' (aṭṭhisīsa) means a head that is extremely bony due to the absence of flesh, or a head that is mere bone covered with skin due to its thinness. 'A gourd-head' (tumbasīsa) means a head like a gourd. 'A sloping head' (pabbhārasīsa) means a head that slopes down at the back. 'By the former method' means on the side of having a complete forehead. 'Like one whose head is wrapped with a turban' means like the region of the head wrapped with a turban-band. 'Like a turban' means like a circular turban skillfully fashioned by a clever craftsman.

Vipassīsamaññāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Designation 'Vipassī'

37. Tassa vitthāroti tassa lakkhaṇapariggaṇhane nemittakānaṃ santappanassa vitthāro vitthārakathā. Gabbhokkantiyaṃ nimittabhūta supinapaṭiggāhakasantappane vuttoyeva. Niddosenāti khārikaloṇikādidosarahitena. Dhātiyoti thaññapāyikā dhātiyo. Tā hi dhāpenti thaññaṃ pāyentīti dhātiyo. “Tathā”ti iminā “saṭṭhi”nti padaṃ upasaṃharati[P 2.0055], sesāpīti nhāpikā, dhārikā, parihārikāti imā tividhā. Tāpi dahanti vidahanti nhānaṃ dahanti dhārentīti “dhātiyo” tveva vuccanti. Tattha dhāraṇaṃ urasā, ūrunā, hatthehi vā suciraṃ velaṃ sandhāraṇaṃ. Pariharaṇaṃ [V 2.0038] aññassa aṅkato attano aṅkaṃ, aññassa bāhuto attano bāhuṃ upasaṃharantehi haraṇaṃ sampāpanaṃ.

37. ‘Its detailed explanation’: this is the detailed account, the detailed discourse, on satisfying the interpreters of signs in their grasping of the characteristics. The satisfaction of those who accept dreams that have become signs at the time of the descent into the womb has already been stated. ‘Free from defects’ means devoid of defects such as alkaline salt. ‘Nurses’ refers to wet nurses. For they give suck, they make the child drink milk, thus they are called ‘nurses.’ By ‘Thus’ he connects the word ‘sixty.’ ‘The others’ are these three kinds: bath attendants, bearers, and attendants. They too are called ‘nurses’ because they give, arrange, give a bath, and bear. Therein, ‘bearing’ means holding for a very long time on the chest, on the thigh, or with the hands. ‘Attending’ refers to carrying and bringing from another’s lap to one’s own lap, or from another’s arm to one’s own arm.

38. Mañjussaroti saṇhassaro. Yo hi saṇho, so kharo na hotīti āha “akharassaro”ti. Vaggussaroti manorammassaro, manorammatā cassa cāturiyane puññayogatoti āha “chekanipuṇassaro”ti. Madhurassaroti sotasukhassaro, sotasukhatā cassa ativiya iṭṭhabhāvenāti āha “sātassaro”ti. Pemanīyassaroti [M 2.0043] piyāyitabbassaro, piyāyitabbatā cassa suṇantānaṃ attani bhattisamuppādanenāti āha “pemajanakassaro”ti. Karavīkassaroti. Karavīkasaddo yesaṃ sattānaṃ sotapathaṃ upagacchati, te attano sarasampattiyā pakatiṃ jahāpetvā avase karonto attano vase vatteti, evaṃ madhuroti dassento “tatrida”ntiādimāha. Tattha “karavīkasakuṇe”tiādi tassa sabhāvakathanaṃ. Laḷitanti pītivegasamuṭṭhitaṃ līḷaṃ. Chaḍḍetvāti “saṅkharaṇampi madhurasaddasavanantarāyakara”nti tiṇāni apanetvā. Anikkhipitvāti bhūmiyaṃ anikkhipitvā ākāsagatameva katvā. Anubaddhamigā vāḷamigehi. Tato maraṇabhayaṃ hitvā. Pakkhe pasāretvāti pakkhe yathāpasārite katvā apatantā tiṭṭhanti.

38. ‘A melodious voice’ means a soft voice. For what is soft is not harsh; hence it is said, ‘a non-harsh voice.’ ‘A pleasing voice’ means a charming voice, and its charm arises from skill and its connection with merit; hence it is said, ‘a skillful and expert voice.’ ‘A sweet voice’ means a voice pleasant to the ear, and its pleasantness comes from being extremely desirable; hence it is said, ‘an agreeable voice.’ ‘A lovable voice’ means a voice to be cherished, and its cherishability arises from generating devotion in its listeners; hence it is said, ‘a voice that generates affection.’ ‘A voice like the karavīka bird’: when the sound of the karavīka bird reaches the ears of beings, by the perfection of its own sound it makes them abandon their normal state and, bringing them under its control, makes them subject to its power. To show that it is thus sweet, it is said, ‘in this regard,’ etc. Therein, ‘the karavīka bird,’ etc., is a statement of its nature. ‘Playful’ means the graceful play arisen from a surge of joy. ‘Having cleared away’: having removed the grass, thinking, ‘Even rustling is an obstacle to hearing the sweet sound.’ ‘Not placing’: not placing it on the ground but keeping it just in the air. ‘Deer pursued’: by beasts of prey. Then, having abandoned the fear of death. ‘Spreading their wings’: having spread their wings out, they stand without falling.

Suvaṇṇapañjaraṃ vissajjesi yojanappamāṇe ākāse attano āṇāya pavattanato. Tenāha “so rājāṇāyā”tiādi. Laḷiṃsūti laḷitaṃ kātuṃ ārabhiṃsu. Taṃ pītinti [P 2.0056] taṃ buddhaguṇārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ teneva nīhārena punappunaṃ pavattaṃ pītiṃ avijahitvā vikkhambhitakilesā therānaṃ santike laddhadhammassavanasappāyā upanissayasampattiyā paripakkañāṇatāya sattahi…pe… patiṭṭhāsi. Sattasatamattena orodhajanena saddhiṃ padasāva therānaṃ santikaṃ upagatattā “sattahi jaṅghasatehi saddhi”nti vuttaṃ. Tatoti karavīkasaddato. Satabhāgena…pe… veditabbo anekakappakoṭisatasambhūtapuññasambhārasamudāgatavatthusampattibhāvato.

‘He released a golden cage’: because it moved in the sky for the extent of a yojana by his own command. Therefore it is said, ‘by the king’s command,’ etc. ‘They played’ means they began to play. ‘That joy’: not abandoning that joy—the joy with the Buddha’s virtues as its object, the joy that arose again and again in that same manner—and having suppressed the defilements, having obtained the suitability for hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the elders, through the accomplishment of supporting conditions and the maturity of his knowledge, he was established in… and so on. Because he approached the elders on foot together with a retinue of seven hundred women of the harem, it was said, ‘with seven hundred shanks.’ ‘From that’: from the sound of the karavīka bird. ‘By a hundredth part… etc.’ … should be understood as being due to the state of possessing the material accomplishment that had come about from the accumulation of the store of merit produced over many hundreds of koṭis of aeons.

39. Kammavipākajanti sātisayasucaritakammanibbattaṃ pittasemharuhirādīhi apalibuddhaṃ dūrepi ārammaṇaṃ sampaṭicchanasamatthaṃ kammavipākena sahajātaṃ, kammassa vā vipākabhāvena jātaṃ pasādacakkhu. Duvidhañhi dibbacakkhuṃ kammamayaṃ, bhāvanāmayanti. Tatridaṃ kammamayanti āha “na bhāvanāmaya”nti. Bhāvanāmayaṃ pana bodhimūle uppajjissati. Ayaṃ “so”ti sallakkhaṇaṃ kāmaṃ manoviññāṇena hoti, cakkhuviññāṇena pana tassa tathā vibhāvitattā manoviññāṇassa tattha tathāpavattīti āha “yena nimittaṃ…pe… sakkotī”ti.

39. ‘Born of kamma-result’: this is the sensitive eye, which is produced by exceptionally good kamma, is unobstructed by bile, phlegm, blood, etc., is capable of receiving even distant objects, is co-nascent with kamma-result, or is born from kamma in the mode of its result. For the divine eye is of two kinds: that produced by kamma and that produced by development (bhāvanā). Herein, this one is produced by kamma; thus it is said, ‘not produced by development.’ The one produced by development, however, will arise at the foot of the Bodhi tree. This discernment of ‘he’ (so) occurs through mind-consciousness, but since that is so clearly distinguished by eye-consciousness, mind-consciousness proceeds there accordingly; hence it is said: ‘by which sign… he is able.’

40. Vacanatthoti [M 2.0044][V 2.0039] saddattho. Nimīlananti nimīlanadassanaṃ navisuddhaṃ, tathā ca akkhīni avivaṭāni nimīladassanassa na visuddhibhāvato. Tabbipariyāyato pana dassanaṃ visuddhaṃ, vivaṭañcāti āha “antarantarā”tiādi.

40. ‘The meaning of the word’ is the meaning of the term. ‘Closing’: seeing with closed eyes is not clear; and thus the eyes are not open, because seeing with closed eyes is not a state of clarity. But conversely, the seeing is clear and the eyes are open; thus it is said, ‘from time to time,’ etc.

41. Nī-iti – jānanatthaṃ dhātuṃ gahetvā āha “panayati jānātī”ti. Yato vuttaṃ “animittā na nāyare”ti (visuddhi. 1.174; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.20), “vidūbhi [P 2.0057] neyyaṃ naravarassā”ti (netti. saṅgahavāra) ca. Nī-iti pana pavattanatthaṃ dhātuṃ gahetvā “nayati pavattetī”ti. Appamatto ahosi tesu tesu kiccakaraṇīyesu.

41. The root Nī: taking the root in the sense of ‘to know,’ it is said, ‘he leads (panayati), he knows (jānāti).’ For it is said: ‘The signless are not led,’ and ‘The best of men is to be led by the wise.’ But taking the root Nī in the sense of ‘to cause to proceed,’ it is said, ‘he leads (nayati), he causes to proceed (pavatteti).’ He was heedful in regard to those various duties to be done.

42. Vassāvāso vassaṃ uttarapadalopena, tasmā vassaṃ, vasse vā, sannivāsaphāsutāya arahatīti vassiko, pāsādo. Māsā pana vasse utumhi bhavāti vassikā. Itaresūti hemantikaṃ gimhikanti imesu. Eseva nayoti uttarapadalopena niddesaṃ atidisati.

42. The term for the rains-residence, vassāvāso, becomes vassaṃ by elision of the final member of the compound. Therefore, vassaṃ or vasse. Because the palace is suitable for comfortable dwelling during the rains, it is called vassiko. But the months, because they occur in the rainy season, are called vassikā. ‘In the others’ refers to the winter and summer residences. ‘This is the method’ extends the explanation by elision of the final member.

Nātiucco hoti nātinīcoti gimhiko viya ucco, hemantiko viya nīco na hoti, atha kho tadubhayavemajjhalakkhaṇatāya nātiucco hoti, nātinīco. Assāti pāsādassa. Nātibahūnīti gimhikassa viya na atibahūni. Nātitanūnīti hemantikassa viya na khuddakāni, tanutarajālāni ca. Missakānevāti hemantike viya na uṇhaniyāneva, gimhike viya ca na sītaniyāneva, atha kho ubhayamissakāneva. Tanukānīti na puthulāni. Uṇhappavesanatthāyāti sūriyasantāpānuppavesāya. Bhittiniyūhānīti dakkhiṇapasse bhittīsu niyūhāni. Siniddhanti sinehavantaṃ, siniddhaggahaṇeneva cassa garukatāpi vuttā eva. Kaṭukasannissitanti tikaṭukādikaṭukadrabbūpasañhitaṃ. Udakayantānīti udakadhārāvissandayantāni. Yathā jalayantāni, evaṃ himayantānipi tattha karonti eva. Tasmā hemante viya himāni patantāniyeva hontīti ca veditabbaṃ.

‘It is not too high, not too low’: it is not high like the summer palace, nor low like the winter palace, but rather, having the characteristic of being midway between both, it is not too high, not too low. ‘Its’: of the palace. ‘Not too many’: not very many, like those of the summer palace. ‘Not too fine’: not small like those of the winter palace, nor with very fine latticework. ‘Mixed’: not only for warmth as in the winter palace, nor only for coolness as in the summer palace, but rather mixed for both. ‘Fine’: not thick. ‘For the entry of heat’: for the non-entry of the sun’s heat. ‘Wall projections’: projections on the walls on the southern side. ‘Smooth’: having oiliness. And by the inclusion of ‘smooth,’ its heaviness is also stated. ‘Combined with pungent substances’: mixed with pungent substances such as the three pungent spices. ‘Water machines’: machines that discharge streams of water. Just as there are water machines, so too they make ice machines there. Therefore, it should be understood that, as if in winter, flakes of ice are indeed falling.

Sabbaṭṭhānānipīti [P 2.0058] sabbāni paṭikiriyānhānabhojanakīḷāsañcaraṇādiṭṭhānānipi, na nivāsaṭṭhānāniyeva. Tenāha “dovārikāpī”tiādi. Tattha kāraṇamāha “rājā kirā”tiādi.

‘All places’ means all places for activities such as personal care, bathing, eating, playing, and walking about, not just the dwelling places. Hence it is said, ‘even the doorkeepers,’ etc. Therein the reason is stated: ‘the king, it is said,’ etc.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first recitation section is concluded.

Jiṇṇapurisavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Aged Man

44. Gopānasivaṅkanti [V 2.0040][M 2.0045] vaṅkagopānasī viya. Vaṅkānañhi vaṅkabhāvassa nidassanatthaṃ avaṅkagopānasīpi gayhati. Ābhoggavaṅkanti ādito paṭṭhāya abbhuggatāya kuṭilasarīratāya vaṅkaṃ. Tenāha “khandhe”tiādi. Daṇḍaparaṃ daṇḍaggahaṇaparaṃ ayanaṃ gamanaṃ etassāti daṇḍaparāyanaṃ, daṇḍo vā paraṃ āyanaṃ gamanakāraṇaṃ etassāti daṇḍaparāyanaṃ. Ṭhānādīsu daṇḍo gati avassayo etassa tena vinā appavattanatoti daṇḍagatikaṃ, gacchati etenāti vā gati, daṇḍo gati gamanakāraṇaṃ etassāti daṇḍagatikaṃ. Daṇḍapaṭisaraṇanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Jarāturanti jarāya kilantaṃ assavasaṃ. Yadā ratho purato hotīti dvedhāpathe sampatte purato gacchante balakāye tattha ekaṃ saṇṭhānaṃ āruḷho majjhe gacchanto bodhisattena āruḷho ratho itaraṃ saṇṭhānaṃ gacchanto yadā purato hoti. Pacchā balakāyoti tadā pacchā hoti sabbo balakāyo. Tādise okāseti tādise vuttappakāre maggappadese. Taṃ purisanti taṃ jiṇṇapurisaṃ. Suddhāvāsāti siddhatthādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ sāsane brahmacariyaṃ caritvā suddhāvāsabhūmiyaṃ nibbattabrahmāno. Te hi tadā tattha tiṭṭhanti. “Kiṃ [P 2.0059] paneso jiṇṇo nāmā”ti eso tayā vuccamāno kiṃ atthato, taṃ me niddhāretvā kathehīti dasseti. Aniddhāritasarūpattā hi tassa attano bodhisatto liṅgasabbanāmena taṃ vadanto “ki”nti āha. “Yathā kiṃ te jāta”nti dvayameva hi loke yebhuyyato jāyati itthī vā puriso vā, tathāpi taṃ liṅgasabbanāmena vuccati, evaṃ sampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. “Kiṃ vuttaṃ hotī”tiādi tassa aniddhāritasarūpataṃyeva vibhāveti.

44. Like a crooked roof-rafter; for to illustrate the crookedness of crooked things, even a straight roof-rafter is taken. 'Bent by bending' (ābhoggavaṅka) means bent from the start, with a crooked and stooped body. Hence it is said, 'on the shoulders,' etc. 'Reliant on a staff' (daṇḍaparāyana) means one whose movement is dependent on a staff. 'Moving with a staff' (daṇḍagatika) means one for whom a staff is his support and reliance. 'Supported by a staff' (daṇḍapaṭisaraṇa) is similar. 'Afflicted by old age' (jarātura) means wearied and powerless due to old age. 'When the chariot is in front': at a fork in the road, while the army went ahead, the Bodhisatta's chariot, going in the middle, took one path while another part of the procession took the other, and so was in front. 'The army behind': then the entire army was behind. 'In such a place' means in such a place on the road as described. 'That man' means that aged man. 'The Suddhāvāsā': these are Brahmās reborn in the Suddhāvāsa plane after practicing the holy life in the dispensations of three Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones. They were standing there then. 'But what, pray, is this aged one?': this means, 'This person you speak of, what is he? Explain it to me.' For, because his nature was undetermined to him, the Bodhisatta, addressing him with a general pronoun, asks, 'What?' This is like asking, 'What is born to you?'; for though beings are generally born male or female, one asks with a general pronoun. This should be understood similarly. 'What is said?' etc., further clarifies his undetermined nature.

“Tena hī”tiādi “ayañca jiṇṇabhāvo sabbasādhāraṇattā mayhampi upari āpattito evā”ti mahāsattassa saṃvijjanākāravibhāvanaṃ. Rathaṃ sāretīti sārathi. Kīḷāvihāratthaṃ uyyuttā yanti upagacchanti etanti uyyānaṃ. Alanti paṭikkhepavacanaṃ. Nāmāti garahaṇe nipāto “kathañhināmā”tiādīsu (pārā. 39, 42, 87, 88, 90, 166, 170; pāci. 1, 13, 36) viya. Jātiyā ādīnavadassanatthaṃ taṃmūlassa ummūlanaṃ viya hotīti, tassa ca avassitabhāvato “jātiyā mūlaṃ [M 2.0046] khaṇanto nisīdī”ti āha. Siddhe hi kāraṇe phalaṃ siddhameva hotīti. Pīḷaṃ janetvā antotudanavasena sabbapaṭhamaṃ hadayaṃ anupavissa ṭhitattā paṭhamena sallena hadaye viddho viya nisīdīti yojanā.

'Therefore,' etc., is the Great Being's explanation of the way he was stirred, thinking: 'Since this state of old age is common to all, it will inevitably befall me too.' He who directs the chariot (rathaṃ sāreti) is a charioteer (sārathi). A park (uyyāna) is so called because they go (yanti) there, intent (uyyuttā) on sport and recreation. 'Enough!' is a word of rejection. 'Indeed' (nāma) is a particle used in reproach, as in instances such as 'how indeed?' To show the danger in birth, it is like uprooting its root; and because of its inevitability, he said, 'he sat down digging up the root of birth.' For when the cause is established, the result is surely established. The meaning is that he sat as if pierced in the heart by the first dart, because it generated affliction and, by way of an internal goad, was the very first thing to enter and remain in his heart.

Byādhipurisavaṇṇanā

The Description of the Sick Man

47. Pubbe [V 2.0041] vuttanayenevāti “suddhāvāsā kirā”tiādinā pubbe vutteneva nayena. Ābādhikanti ābādhavantaṃ. Dukkhitanti sañjātadukkhaṃ. Ajātanti ajātabhāvo, nibbānaṃ vā.

47. 'In the same way as said before' means in the manner previously stated, beginning with 'The Suddhāvāsa devas, it seems….' 'Afflicted' (ābādhika) means one who is ill. 'In pain' (dukkhita) means one in whom suffering has arisen. 'The unborn' (ajāta) means the state of not being born, or Nibbāna.

Kālakatapurisavaṇṇanā

The Description of the Deceased Man

50. Bhantanettakuppalādi vividhaṃ katvā lātabbato vilāto, vayhaṃ, sivikā cāti āha “vilātanti sivika”nti. Sivikāya diṭṭhapubbattā mahāsatto citakapañjaraṃ “sivika”nti āha. Ito paṭigatanti ito bhavato apagataṃ[P 2.0060]. Katakālanti pariyosāpitajīvanakālaṃ. Tenāha “yattaka”ntiādi.

50. Because it is to be carried having been variously decorated with things like turned water-lilies, it is called a vilāta, a vayha, and a sivikā (palanquin). Thus it is said: 'A vilāta is a sivikā.' Because the Great Being had seen a palanquin before, he called the frame of the funeral pyre a 'palanquin.' 'Gone from here' means gone away from this existence. 'His time is done' means his life-span is completed. Therefore, it is said, 'as much as,' etc.

Pabbajitavaṇṇanā

The Description of the Renunciant

53. Dhammaṃ caratīti dhammacaraṇo, tassa bhāvo dhammacaraṇabhāvoti dhammacariyameva vadati. Evaṃ ekekassa padassāti yathā “sādhudhammacariyāti pabbajito”ti yojanā, evaṃ “sādhusamacariyāti pabbajito”tiādinā ekekassa padassa yojanā veditabbā. Sabbānīti “sādhudhammacariyā”tiādīsu āgatāni sabbāni dhammasamakusalapuññapadāni. Dasakusalakammapathavevacanānīti dānādīni dasakusaladhammapariyāyapadāni.

53. 'One who practices the Dhamma' (dhammaṃ carati) is a practitioner of the Dhamma (dhammacaraṇo); his state is the state of practicing the Dhamma, which is simply righteous conduct (dhammacariyā). Thus for each term: just as the connection is 'a renunciant is one of good righteous conduct,' so the connection for each term should be understood, such as 'a renunciant is one of good peaceful conduct,' etc. 'All' refers to all the terms for righteous conduct, peaceful conduct, wholesome action, and meritorious action that appear in phrases like 'good righteous conduct,' etc. These are synonyms for the ten courses of wholesome action, that is, terms pertaining to the ten wholesome states, such as generosity, etc.

Bodhisattapabbajjāvaṇṇanā

The Description of the Bodhisatta's Going Forth

54. Pabbajitassa dhammiṃ kathaṃ sutvāti sambandho. Aññañca saṅgītianāruḷhaṃ tena tadā vuttaṃ dhammiṃ kathanti yojanā. “Vaṃsovā”ti padattayena dhammatā esāti dasseti. Cirassaṃ cirassaṃ passanti dīghāyukabhāvato. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “bahūnaṃ vassānaṃ…pe… accayenā”ti. Tenevāti na cirassaṃ diṭṭhabhāveneva. Acirakālantarikameva pubbakālakiriyaṃ dassento “jiṇṇañca disvā…pe… pabbajitañca disvā, tasmā ahaṃ pabbajitomhi rājā”ti āha [M 2.0047] yathā “nhatvā vatthaṃ paridahitvā gandhaṃ vilimpitvā mālaṃ piḷandhitvā bhutto”ti.

54. The connection is with 'having heard the Dhamma talk of one who has gone forth.' And the meaning is that 'Dhamma talk' refers to other things spoken by him at that time that were not included in the recitation. With the three words 'or green bamboo,' he shows: 'This is the nature of things.' They see it only after a very long time because they are long-lived. For so it is said: 'After many years... after the passing of….' 'Therefore' means because it had not been seen for a long time. Showing that the previous action occurred after only a short interval, he says: 'Having seen the aged... and having seen the renunciant, therefore I have gone forth, O king,' just as one might say: 'Having bathed, put on clothes, applied perfume, worn a garland, he ate.'

Mahājanakāyaanupabbajjāvaṇṇanā

The Description of the Great Multitude's Going Forth in His Wake

55. “Kasmā [V 2.0042] panetthā”tiādinā tesaṃ caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ mahāsatte saṃbhattataṃ, saṃvegabahulatañca dasseti, yato sutaṭṭhāneyeva ṭhatvā ñātimittādīsu kiñci anāmantetvā mattavaravāraṇo viya ayomayabandhanaṃ ghanabandhanaṃ chinditvā pabbajjaṃ upagacchiṃsu.

55. "But why here?"—by this and so forth, it shows their devotion to the Great Being and the abundance of spiritual urgency for those eighty-four thousand beings, since, standing right where they had heard, without even addressing any relatives or friends, they went forth, like a lordly elephant in rut breaking iron bonds and strong fetters.

Cattāro māse cārikaṃ cari na tāva ñāṇassa paripākaṃ gatattā.

For four months I wandered on tour, as my knowledge had not yet reached maturity.

Yadā pana ñāṇaṃ paripākaṃ gataṃ, taṃ dassento “ayaṃ panā”tiādimāha. Sabbeva ime pabbajitā mama gamanaṃ [P 2.0061] jānissanti, jānantā ca maṃ anubandhissantīti adhippāyo. Sannisīvesūti sannisinnesu. Saṇatevāti saṇati viya saddaṃ karoti viya.

When knowledge had fully matured, showing this, he said, "Now this..." and so on. His intention was: "All these renunciants will know of my departure, and knowing this, they will follow me." "Among those seated together" means among those who were seated. "Saṇateva" means: as if it makes a sound.

Avivekārāmānanti anabhirativivekānaṃ. Ayaṃ kāloti ayaṃ tesaṃ pabbajitānaṃ mama gamanassa ajānanakālo. Nikkhamitvāti paṇṇasālāya niggantvā, mahābhinikkhamanaṃ pana pageva nikkhanto. Pāramitānubhāvena uṭṭhitaṃ upari devatāhi dibbapaccattharaṇehi supaññattampi mahāsattassa puññānubhāvena siddhattā tena paññattaṃ viya hotīti vuttaṃ “pallaṅkaṃ paññapetvā”ti. “Kāmaṃ taco ca nhāru ca, aṭṭhi ca avasissatū”tiādi (ma. ni. 2.184; saṃ. ni. 2.22, 237; a. ni. 2.5; 8.13; mahāni. 17, 196) nayappavattaṃ caturaṅgavīriyaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā. Vūpakāsanti vivekavāsaṃ.

"Of those delighting in non-seclusion" means of those not delighting in seclusion. "This is the time" means this is the time when those who have gone forth do not know of my departure. "Having gone out" means having gone out from the leaf hut; however, as for the Great Renunciation, he had already gone forth previously. Through the power of his perfections, a seat arose, and even though it was well-prepared above by deities with divine coverings, because it was accomplished by the power of the Great Being's merit, it was as if prepared by him; thus it is said, "having prepared a seat." Having resolved upon the fourfold effort according to the method that begins, "Willingly, let only skin, sinews, and bones remain..." etc. "Seclusion" means dwelling in seclusion.

Aññenevāti yattha mahāpuriso tadā viharati, tato aññeneva disābhāgena. Kāmaṃ bodhimaṇḍo jambudīpassa majjhe nābhiṭṭhāniyo, tadā pana brahāraññe vivitte yogīnaṃ paṭisallānasāruppo hutvā tiṭṭhati, tadañño pana jambudīpappadeso yebhuyyena bahujano ākiṇṇamanusso iddho phīto ahosi. Tena te taṃ taṃ janapadadesaṃ uddissa gatā “anto jambudīpābhimukhā cārikaṃ pakkantā”ti vuttā anto jambudīpābhimukhā, na himavantādipabbatābhimukhāti attho.

"Elsewhere" means in a direction other than that where the great being was dwelling at that time. Granted, the Bodhimaṇḍa is the central navel-point in the middle of Jambudīpa, yet at that time, it stood in the great forest, secluded and suitable for the seclusion of yogis. But another region of Jambudīpa was, for the most part, crowded with many people, thronged with men, prosperous, and flourishing. Therefore, they set out toward those various regions, and it is said, "They departed on a journey toward the interior of Jambudīpa"—meaning toward the interior of Jambudīpa, not toward the Himalayas or other mountains.

Bodhisattaabhinivesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Bodhisatta's Resolve

57. Kāmaṃ [M 2.0048] bhagavā buddho hutvā sattasattāhāni tattheva vasi, sabbapaṭhamaṃ pana visākhapuṇṇamaṃ [V 2.0043] sandhāya “ekarattivāsaṃ upagatassā”ti vuttaṃ. Rahogatassāti raho janavivittaṃ ṭhānaṃ upagatassa, tena gaṇasaṅgaṇikābhāvena mahāsattassa kāyavivekamāha. Paṭisallīnassāti [P 2.0062] nānārammaṇacārato cittassa nivattiyā pati sammadeva nilīnassa tattha avisaṭacittassa, tena cittasaṅgaṇikābhāvenassa pubbabhāgiyaṃ cittavivekamāha. Dukkhanti jātiādimūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ. Kāmaṃ cutūpapātāpi jātimaraṇāni eva, maraṇajātiyova “jāyati mīyatī”ti pana vatvā “cavati upapajjatī”ti vacanaṃ na ekabhavapariyāpannānaṃ nesaṃ gahaṇaṃ, atha kho nānābhavapariyāpannānaṃ ekajjhaṃ gahaṇanti dassento āha “idaṃ dvayaṃ…pe… vutta”nti. Kasmā pana lokassa kicchāpattiparivitakkane “jarāmaraṇassā”ti jarāmaraṇavasena niyamanaṃ katanti āha “yasmā”tiādi. Jarāmaraṇameva upaṭṭhāti āditoti adhippāyo. Abhiniviṭṭhassāti āraddhassa. Paṭiccasamuppādamukhena vipassanārambhe tassa jarāmaraṇato paṭṭhāya abhiniveso aggato yāva mūlaṃ otaraṇaṃ viyāti āha “bhavaggato otarantassa viyā”ti.

57. The Blessed One, having become a Buddha, indeed stayed there for seven weeks. However, regarding the very first full moon of Visākha, it is said, "He had undertaken a single night's dwelling." "Secluded" means having gone to a place remote from people. Thus, by the absence of association with crowds, it refers to the physical seclusion of the Great Being. "Withdrawn" means the mind, having turned away from wandering among various objects, is rightly settled there, without distraction. Thus, by the absence of mental association, it refers to the preliminary mental seclusion. "Suffering" refers to suffering rooted in birth and so forth. Although passing away and reappearing are also birth and death, saying "one is born, one dies" refers to a single existence, but saying "one passes away, one is reborn" does not indicate that they are confined to a single existence. Instead, it shows the gathering of those pertaining to multiple existences; hence it is said, "this pair... is spoken of." But why, when considering the world's plight, is it specified in terms of aging and death? It is explained: "Because..." Aging and death alone appear first—this is the intended meaning. "Intent" means one who is determined. When beginning insight through dependent origination, his intent, starting from aging and death, penetrates downwards to the root, as if descending from the summit of existence. Hence, it is said, "as if descending from the summit of existence."

Upāyamanasikārāti upāyena manasikaraṇato manasikārassa pavattanato. Idāni taṃ upāyamanasikārapariyāyaṃ yonisomanasikāraṃ sarūpato, pavattiākārato ca dassetuṃ “aniccādīni hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yonisomanasikāro nāma hotīti yāthāvato manasikārabhāvato. Aniccādīnīti ādi-saddena dukkhānattaasubhādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Ayanti “etadahosī”ti evaṃ vutto “kimhi nu kho satī”tiādinayappavatto manasikāro. Tesaṃ aññataroti tesu aniccādimanasikāresu aññataro eko. Ko pana soti? Aniccamanasikārova, tattha kāraṇamāha “udayabbayānupassanāvasena pavattattā”ti. Yañhi uppajjati ceva cavati ca, taṃ aniccaṃ udayavayaparicchinnattā addhuvanti katvā. Tassa pana tabbhāvadassanaṃ yāthāvamanasikāratāya yonisomanasikāro[P 2.0063]. Ito yonisomanasikārāti hetumhi nissakkavacananti tassa iminā “upāyamanasikārenā”ti hetumhi karaṇavacanena atthamāha. Samāgamo ahosīti [M 2.0049] yāthāvato paṭivijjhanavasena saṅgamo ahosi. Kiṃ pana tanti kiṃ pana taṃ jarāmaraṇakāraṇanti āha “jātī”ti. “Jātiyā kho”tiādīsu ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – kimhi nu kho sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hoti, kiṃ paccayā jarāmaraṇa”nti jarāmaraṇakāraṇaṃ pariggaṇhantassa bodhisattassa “yasmiṃ sati yaṃ hoti, asati ca na hoti, taṃ tassa kāraṇa”nti evaṃ abyabhicārikāraṇapariggaṇhane “jātiyā kho sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hoti, jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa”nti yā jarāmaraṇassa kāraṇapariggāhikā paññā uppajjati, tāya uppajjantiyā samāgamo ahosīti. Sabbapadānīti “kimhi nu kho sati jāti hotī”tiādinā āgatāni jātiādīni viññāṇapariyosānāni nava padāni.

"Attention to means" means "because of paying attention by means, and because of the arising of attention." Now, to show that method of attention to means—wise attention—both in terms of its essence and the manner of arising, it is said, "such as impermanence, etc." Wise attention is so called because it is the state of paying attention as it truly is. "Impermanence, etc."—by the word "etc.," suffering, not-self, unattractiveness, and so on are included. "This" refers to the attention, expressed as "This occurred to me," which proceeds according to the method "When what exists...?" "Among them, any one" means any single one among those attentions to impermanence, etc. But which one? It is the attention to impermanence alone. There, the reason is stated: "because it arises through the contemplation of arising and passing away." For whatever arises and ceases is impermanent, being defined by arising and passing away, thus unstable. Seeing its being in that way is wise attention, as it is paying attention accurately. "From this wise attention"—this is an ablative expression indicating the cause. Here, the meaning is conveyed by the instrumental case, "by means of attention to means" as the cause. "An encounter occurred"—an encounter took place through penetrating it as it truly is. "But what is that?"—but what is the cause of aging and death? It is said, "birth." In the passage, "when there is birth," etc., the condensed meaning is: "When what exists does aging and death occur? What is the condition for aging and death?" For the Bodhisatta, who comprehends the cause of aging and death, it is: "When this exists, that arises; when this does not exist, that does not arise—this is its cause." Thus, in comprehending the unfailing cause, "when there is birth, aging and death exist; aging and death are conditioned by birth"—the wisdom that identifies the cause of aging and death arises. When it arises, an encounter occurs. "All the terms"—the nine terms, from "when what exists does birth occur?" up to consciousness as the end, that are mentioned.

Dvādasapadike [V 2.0044] paṭiccasamuppāde idha yāni dve padāni aggahitāni, tesaṃ aggahaṇe kāraṇaṃ pucchitvā vissajjetukāmo tesaṃ gahetabbākāraṃ tāva dassento “ettha panā”tiādimāha. Paccakkhabhūtaṃ paccuppannabhavaṃ paṭhamaṃ gahetvā tadanantaraṃ anāgataṃ “dutiya”nti gahaṇe atīto tatiyo hotīti āha “avijjā saṅkhārā hi atīto bhavo”ti. Nanu cettha anāgatassāpi bhavassa gahaṇaṃ na sambhavati paccuppannavasena abhinivesassa jotitattāti? Saccametaṃ, kāraṇe pana gahite phalaṃ gahitameva hotīti tathā vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Api cettha anāgatopi addhā atthato saṅgahito eva, yato parato “nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatana”ntiādinā anāgataddhasaṅgahikā desanā pavattā. Tehīti avijjāsaṅkhārehi ārammaṇabhūtehi. Na ghaṭiyati na sambajjhati. Mahāpuriso hi paccuppannavasena abhiniviṭṭhoti aghaṭane kāraṇamāha. Adiṭṭhehīti anavabuddhehi, itthambhūtalakkhaṇe cetaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ. Sati anubodhe paṭivedhena bhavitabbanti āha “na [P 2.0064] sakkā buddhena bhavitu”nti. Imināti mahāsattena. Teti avijjāsaṅkhārā. Bhavaupādānataṇhāvasenevāti bhavaupādānataṇhādassanavaseneva. Diṭṭhā taṃsabhāvataṃsahagatehi tehi samānayogakkhamattā. Visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.570) kathitāva, tasmā na idha kathetabbāti adhippāyo.

In the twelve-linked dependent origination, regarding the two links that are not grasped here—wishing to ask and answer the reason for their not being grasped, he first shows the manner in which they are to be grasped, saying, "But here," etc. Taking the directly perceived present existence first, and then the future as "the second," the past becomes the third; thus he says, "For ignorance and formations are the past existence." Is it not so that the grasping of the future existence is also not possible, since the resolve is shown to be with respect to the present? This is true, but it should be understood that when the cause is grasped, the result is thereby grasped as well; thus it is stated. Moreover, here the future time is also included in meaning, since further on the teaching proceeds by including the future, such as in "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases," etc. "By these" means by ignorance and formations, which serve as the object. "It does not connect" means it is not related. He states the reason for the non-connection: "For the great being is intent on the present." "By the unseen" means by what is not comprehended; this is an instrumental case indicating a characteristic. He says, "it is not possible to become a Buddha," because if there is to be an awakening, it must be through penetration. "By this" means by the great being. "Those" means ignorance and formations. "By way of existence, clinging, and craving" means by way of seeing existence, clinging, and craving. They are seen, as they are of a similar nature, are associated with them, and are subject to the same bondage. As already explained in the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhi. 2.570), therefore, it need not be discussed here—this is the intention.

58. Paccayatoti hetuto, saṅkhāratoti attho. “Kimhi nu kho sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hotī”tiādinā hi hetuparamparāvasena phalaparamparāya vuccamānāya [M 2.0050] “kimhi nu kho sati viññāṇaṃ hotī”ti vicāraṇāya “saṅkhāre kho sati viññāṇaṃ hotī”ti viññāṇassa visesakāraṇabhūte saṅkhāre aggahite tato viññāṇaṃ paṭinivattati nāma, na sabbapaccayato. Tenevāha “nāmarūpe kho sati viññāṇaṃ hotī”ti (dī. ni. 2.58), nāmampi cettha sahajātādivaseneva paccayabhūtaṃ adhippetaṃ, na kammūpanissayavasena paccuppannavasena abhinivisassa jotitattā. Ārammaṇatoti avijjāsaṅkhārasaṅkhātaārammaṇato, atītabhavasaṅkhātaārammaṇato vā. Atītaddhapariyāpannā hi avijjāsaṅkhārā. Yato paṭinivattamānaṃ viññāṇaṃ atītabhavatopi paṭinivattati nāma. Ubhayampīti paṭisandhiviññāṇampi vipassanāviññāṇampi. Nāmarūpaṃ nātikkamatīti paccayabhūtaṃ, ārammaṇabhūtañca nāmarūpaṃ nātikkamati tena vinā avattanato. Tenāha “nāmarūpato paraṃ na gacchatī”ti.

58. “From a condition” means from a cause; “from formations” is the meaning. For when, in the passage beginning “When what exists does aging-and-death occur?,” the sequence of results is stated by way of the sequence of causes, through the inquiry, “When what exists does consciousness occur?,” if formations—the specific cause for consciousness—are not grasped, consciousness is said to turn back from that, but not from all its conditions. Therefore it is said: “When name-and-form exists, consciousness occurs” (DN 14/ii.58). Here, “name” is also intended as a condition by way of co-nascence and so on, not by way of kamma as decisive support, because it is present adherence that is being illuminated. From an object: from the object designated as ignorance-and-formations, or from the object designated as past existence, for ignorance-and-formations pertain to the past. When consciousness turns back from that, it is said to turn back even from past existence. Both: this refers to both rebirth-linking consciousness and insight consciousness. It does not transcend name-and-form: it does not transcend name-and-form, which is its condition and its object, because it does not proceed without it. Therefore, it is said, “It does not go beyond name-and-form.”

Viññāṇe nāmarūpassa paccaye honteti viññāṇe nāmassa, rūpassa, nāmarūpassa ca paccaye honte. Nāmarūpe ca viññāṇassa paccaye honteti tathā nāme, rūpe, nāmarūpe ca viññāṇassa [V 2.0045] paccaye honteti catuvokāraekavokārapañcavokārabhavavasena yathārahaṃ yojanā veditabbā, dvīsupi aññamaññapaccayesu hontesūti pana pañcavokārabhavavaseneva. Ettakenāti evaṃ viññāṇa nāmarūpānaṃ [P 2.0065] aññamaññaṃ upatthambhanavasena pavattiyā. Jāyetha vā…pe… upapajjetha vāti “satto jāyati…pe… upapajjati vā”ti samaññā hoti viññāṇanāmarūpavinimuttassa sattapaññattiyā upādānabhūtassa dhammassa abhāvato. Tenāha “ito hī”tiādi. Etadevāti viññāṇaṃ, nāmarūpanti etaṃ dvayameva.

When consciousness is a condition for name-and-form: this means when consciousness is a condition for name, for form, and for name-and-form. And when name-and-form is a condition for consciousness: this means when name, form, and name-and-form are conditions for consciousness. Here the application should be understood as appropriate for the four-constituent, one-constituent, and five-constituent planes of existence; but when the two are mutually conditions for each other, this is only by way of the five-constituent plane of existence. Thus far: this refers to the occurrence of consciousness and name-and-form by way of their mutual support. One might be born… or… one might arise: this is a designation, “a being is born… or… arises,” because there is no phenomenon serving as the basis for the concept of a ‘being’ that is apart from consciousness and name-and-form. Therefore he said: “From this…” and so on. This very thing: it is just this pair, that is, consciousness and name-and-form.

Pañca padānīti “jāyetha vā”tiādīni pañca padāni. Nanu tattha paṭhamatatiyehi catutthapañcamāni atthato abhinnānīti āha “saddhiṃ aparāparaṃ cutipaṭisandhīhī”ti. Puna taṃ ettāvatāti vuttamatthanti yo “ettāvatā”ti padena pubbe vutto, tameva yathāvuttamatthaṃ “yadida”ntiādinā niyyātento nidassento puna vatvā. Anulomapaccayākāravasenāti paccayadhammadassanapubbakaṃ paccayuppannadhammadassanavasena. Paccayadhammānañhi attano paccayuppannassa [M 2.0051] paccayabhāvo idappaccayatā paccayākāro, so ca “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādinā vutto. Saṃsārappavattiyā anulomanato anulomapaccayākāro. Jātiādikaṃ sabbaṃ vaṭṭadukkhaṃ cittena samihitena kataṃ samūhavasena gahetvā pāḷiyaṃ “dukkhakkhandhassā”ti vuttanti āha “jāti…pe… dukkharāsissā”ti.

The five terms: these are the five terms beginning with “one might be born.” But are not the fourth and fifth terms identical in meaning with the first and third? To this he says: “together with successive deaths and rebirth-linkings.” Again, having stated with the phrase “that is,” etc., the same meaning that was previously expressed by the word “thus far,” he hands it over and points it out. By way of the forward order of conditional relations: this is by way of seeing conditionally arisen phenomena preceded by seeing the conditioning phenomena. For the conditionality of conditioning phenomena towards their own conditionally arisen phenomena is specific conditionality, the mode of condition, and this is stated in the passage beginning “with ignorance as condition, formations come to be.” It is the forward order of conditional relations because it conforms to the process of saṃsāra. Having taken all the suffering of the round beginning with birth—produced by a striving mind—as a whole, it is said in the Pāḷi “of this mass of suffering.” Thus he says: “birth… of this mass of suffering.”

59. Dukkhakkhandhassa anekavāraṃ samudayadassanavasena viññāṇassa pavattattā “samudayo samudayo”ti āmeḍitavacanaṃ avoca. Atha vā “evaṃ samudayo hotī”ti idaṃ na kevalaṃ nibbattinidassanapadaṃ, atha kho paṭiccasamuppāda-saddo viya samuppādamukhena idha samudaya-saddo nibbattimukhena paccayattaṃ vadati. Viññāṇādayo bhavantā idha paccayadhammā niddiṭṭhā, te sāmaññarūpena byāpanicchāvasena gaṇhanto “samudayo samudayo”ti āha, evañca katvā yaṃ vakkhati “imasmiṃ sati [P 2.0066] idaṃ hotīti paccayasañjānanamattaṃ kathita”nti, (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.59) taṃ samatthitaṃ hoti. Yadi evaṃ “udayadassanapaññā vesā”ti idaṃ kathanti? Nāyaṃ doso paccayato udayadassanamukhena nibbattilakkhaṇadassanassa sambhavato. Dassanaṭṭhena cakkhūti samudayassa paccakkhato dassanabhāvena cakkhu viyāti cakkhu. Ñātakaraṇaṭṭhenāti yathā samudayo sammadeva ñāto hoti avabuddho, evaṃ karaṇaṭṭhena. Pajānanaṭṭhenāti “viññāṇāditaṃtaṃpaccayuppattiyā etassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hotī”ti pakārato jānanaṭṭhena. Nibbijjhitvā paṭivijjhitvā uppannaṭṭhenāti anibbijjhitvā pubbe udayadassanapaññāya paṭipakkhadhamme nibbijjhitvā “ayaṃ samudayo”ti paccayato, khaṇato ca, sarūpato paṭivijjhitvā [V 2.0046] uppannabhāvena, nibbijjhanaṭṭhena paṭivijjhanaṭṭhena vijjāti vuttaṃ hoti. Obhāsaṭṭhenāti samudayasabhāvapaṭicchādanakassa mohandhakārassa ca kilesandhakārassa ca vidhamanavasena avabhāsakabhāvena.

59. Because consciousness occurs by way of seeing the arising of the mass of suffering many times, he spoke the repetitive statement, “Arising, arising.” Or, the statement “thus is the arising” is not merely a term indicating production; rather, just as the term “dependent origination” speaks of conditionality through the mode of co-arising, so here the term “arising” speaks of it through the mode of production. Here consciousness and so on are the conditioning phenomena that are indicated. Taking them in a general sense by way of designation, he said, “Arising, arising.” And by doing so, what he will say—“merely the recognition of conditions as ‘when this exists, that comes to be’ is stated”—is supported. If so, why is it said: “This is the wisdom of seeing arising”? There is no fault in this, because it is possible to see the characteristic of production by way of seeing the arising from conditions. Eye (cakkhu) in the sense of seeing: it is like an eye in that it sees the arising directly. Knowledge (ñāṇa) in the sense of causing to know: in the sense that it causes the arising to be rightly known and understood. Wisdom (paññā) in the sense of discerning: in the sense of knowing in detail that “the arising of this mass of suffering is due to the production of these respective conditions beginning with consciousness.” Knowledge (vijjā) in the sense of having arisen by becoming dispassionate and by penetrating: because it arises having become dispassionate towards the opposing states—with which one was not dispassionate before—through the wisdom of seeing arising, and having penetrated “this is the arising” from the standpoint of condition, moment, and intrinsic nature, it is called knowledge (vijjā) in the sense of becoming dispassionate and penetrating. Light (āloka) in the sense of illumination: in that it illuminates by dispelling the darkness of delusion and the darkness of the defilements, which conceal the nature of arising.

Idāni yathāvuttamatthaṃ paṭipāṭiyā vibhāvetuṃ “yathāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha cakkhuṃ udapādīti pāḷiyaṃ paduddhāro. Kathaṃ udapādīti ceti āha “dassanaṭṭhenā”ti. “Samudayassa paccakkhato dassanabhāvenāti vutto vāyamattho. Iminā nayena sesapadesupi attho veditabbo. Cakkhudhammoti cakkhūti pāḷidhammo. Dassanaṭṭho atthoti dassanasabhāvo tena [M 2.0052] pakāsetabbo attho. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Ettakehi padehīti imehi pañcahi padehi. “Kiṃ kathita”nti piṇḍatthaṃ pucchati. Paccayasañjānanamattanti viññāṇādīnaṃ paccayadhammānaṃ nāmarūpādipaccayuppannassa paccayasabhāvasañjānanamattaṃ kathitaṃ avisesato paccayasabhāvasallakkhaṇassa jotitattā. Saṅkhārānaṃ sammadeva [P 2.0067] udayadassanassa jotitattā “vīthipaṭipannā taruṇavipassanā kathitā”ti ca vuttaṃ.

Now, to explain the aforesaid meaning in due order, the passage beginning “as he said” was stated. Therein, “the eye arose” is an extraction of the term from the Pāḷi. If it is asked, “How did it arise?,” he says: “in the sense of seeing.” The meaning stated is: “in that it sees the arising directly.” The meaning of the remaining terms should be understood in the same way. The term “eye”: “eye” is the term from the Pāḷi. The meaning “in the sense of seeing”: this is the nature of seeing, the meaning to be explained by it. The same method applies to the rest. By these terms: by these five terms. “What has been stated?” he asks for the summary meaning. Merely the recognition of conditions: merely the recognition of the conditional nature of conditioning phenomena such as consciousness for conditionally arisen phenomena such as name-and-form is stated, because the characteristic mark of the conditional nature in general has been illuminated. And because the correct seeing of the arising of formations is illuminated, it is also said: “Tender insight that has entered upon the path has been described.”

61. Attanā adhigatattā āsannapaccakkhatāya “aya”nti vuttaṃ, ariyamaggādīnaṃ magganaṭṭhena maggoti. Pubbabhāgavipassanā hesā. Tenāha “bodhāyā”ti. Bodhapadassa bhāvasādhanataṃ sandhāyāha “catusaccabujjhanatthāyā”ti. Pariññāpahānabhāvanābhisamayā yāvadeva sacchikiriyābhisamayatthā nibbānādhigamatthattā brahmacariyavāsassāti vuttaṃ “nibbānabujjhanatthāya eva vā”ti. “Nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukha”nti (ma. ni. 2.215, 217; dha. pa. 204) hi vuttaṃ. Bujjhatīti cattāri ariyasaccāni ekapaṭivedhena paṭivijjhati, tena bodha-saddassa kattusādhanattamāha. Paccattapadehīti paṭhamāvibhattidīpakehi padehi. Nibbānameva kathitaṃ viññāṇādi nirujjhati etthāti katvā. Anibbattinirodhanti sabbaso paccayanirodhena anuppādanirodhaṃ accantanirodhaṃ.

61. Because it is attained by oneself and because of its immediate directness, it is called “this.” It is a path (magga) in the sense of seeking (maggana) the noble path and so on. This is preliminary insight. Hence he says: “for awakening.” Referring to the fact that the word ‘bodha’ is a noun of state, he says: “for the sake of awakening to the four truths.” Because the living of the holy life is for the purpose of attaining Nibbāna, which is for the sake of the breakthrough of realization by way of the breakthroughs of full understanding, abandonment, and development, it is said: “or for the sake of awakening to Nibbāna itself.” For it is said: “Nibbāna is the supreme happiness” (MN 75/i.508; Dhp 204). One awakens: one penetrates the four noble truths with a single penetration. Thereby he shows that the word ‘bodha’ is a noun of agency. By terms in the subjective case: by terms indicating the nominative case. Nibbāna itself is described, because consciousness, etc., cease in it. Cessation without production: the cessation of non-arising, the final cessation, through the complete cessation of conditions.

62. Sabbeheva etehi padehīti “cakkhū”tiādīhi pañcahi padehi. Nirodhasañjānanamattamevāti “nirodho nirodhoti kho”tiādinā nirodhassa sañjānanamattameva kathitaṃ pubbārambhabhāvato, na tassa paṭivijjhanavasena paccakkhato dassanaṃ ariyamaggassa anadhigatattā. Saṅkhārānaṃ sammadeva nirodhadassanaṃ nāma sikhāppattāya vipassanāya vasena icchitabbanti “vuṭṭhānagāminī balavavipassanā kathitā”ti ca vuttaṃ.

62. By all these terms: by the five terms beginning with “eye.” Merely the recognition of cessation: only the mere recognition of cessation is stated, as in “cessation, cessation,” because it is a preliminary stage, not a direct seeing of it by way of penetration, since the noble path has not been attained. The seeing of the cessation of formations in the right way is intended by way of the insight that has reached its peak. Therefore it is also said: “Powerful insight leading to emergence has been described.”

63. Viditvāti [V 2.0047] pubbabhāgiyena ñāṇena jānitvā. Tato aparabhāgeti vuttanayena paccayanirodhajānanato pacchābhāge. Upādānassa paccayabhūtesūti catubbidhassapi upādānassa ārammaṇapaccayādinā paccayabhūtesu, upādāniyesūti attho[P 2.0068]. Vahantoti pavattento. Idanti “aparena samayenā”tiādi vacanaṃ. Kasmā vuttanti “yāya paṭipattiyā sabbepi mahābodhisattā carimabhave bodhāya paṭipajjanti, vipassanāya mahābodhisattena tatheva paṭipanna”nti kathetukamyatāvasena pucchāvacanaṃ. Tenāha [M 2.0053] “sabbeyeva hī”tiādi. Tattha puttassa jātadivase mahābhinikkhamanaṃ, padhānānuyogo ca dhammatāvasena veditabbo, itaraṃ itikattabbatāvasena. Tatthāpi cirakālaparibhāvanāya laddhāsevanāya mahākaruṇāya sañcoditamānasattā “kicchaṃ vatāyaṃ loko āpanno”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.57; saṃ. ni. 2.4, 10) saṃsāradukkhato mocetuṃ icchitassa sattalokassa kicchāpattidassanamukhena jarāmaraṇato paṭṭhāya paccayākārasammasanampi dhammatāva. Tathā attādhīnatāya, kenaci anupakhatattā, asecanakasukhavihāratāya, catutthajjhānikatāya ca ānāpānakammaṭṭhānānuyogo. Pañcasu khandhesu abhinivisitvāti viññāṇanāmarūpādipariyāyena gahitesu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu vipassanābhinivesavasena abhinivisitvā paṭipattiṃ ārabhitvā. Anukkamanti anu anu gāmitabbato paṭipajjitabbato “anukkama”nti laddhanāmaṃ anupubbapaṭipattiṃ. Katvāti paṭipajjitvā.

63. “Having known” means knowing with preliminary knowledge. Then, “in the latter part” refers to the subsequent stage after knowing the cessation of conditions in the manner described. “In what are conditions for clinging” means in what are conditions by way of object-condition, etc., for the fourfold clinging; the meaning is, in the things that can be clung to. “Carrying on” means continuing. “This” refers to the statement beginning with “at a later time.” Why was it said? It is a question posed out of the desire to explain that “by the practice through which all great bodhisattas proceed in their final existence toward enlightenment, the great bodhisatta likewise practiced insight.” Therefore, it is said, “all indeed,” etc. Therein, the great renunciation on the day of his son’s birth and the pursuit of striving should be understood as due to natural law, while the rest is to be taken as a matter of custom.
