Moreover, due to long cultivation, a mind stirred by great compassion, having acquired familiarity, thinking, “Alas, this world has fallen into suffering,” and so forth (Dī. Ni. 2.57; Saṃ. Ni. 2.4, 10), the contemplation of the causal pattern starting from aging and death, through seeing the world’s suffering, arises naturally from the desire to liberate the world of beings from the suffering of saṃsāra. Similarly, the practice of mindfulness of breathing is due to self-mastery, being undisturbed by anyone, dwelling in unadulterated bliss, and having attained the fourth jhāna. ‘Having applied himself to the five aggregates’ means having applied himself to the five aggregates of clinging, taken in terms of consciousness, name-and-form, etc., by way of the penetration of insight, and then undertaking the practice. “Gradually” refers to the sequential practice, so named because it is to be undertaken step by step. “Having done” means having practiced.

Iti rūpanti ettha dutiyo iti-saddo nidassanattho, tena paṭhamo iti-saddo sarūpassa, parimāṇassa ca bodhako anekatthattā nipātānaṃ,āvuttiādivasena vāyamattho veditabbo. Antogadhāvadhāraṇañca vākyaṃ dassento “idaṃ rūpaṃ, ettakaṃ rūpaṃ, ito uddhaṃ rūpaṃ natthī”tiādimāha[P 2.0069]. Tattha “ruppanasabhāva”nti iminā sāmaññato rūpassa sabhāvo dassito, “bhūtupādāyabheda”ntiādinā visesato, tadubhayenapi “idaṃ rūpa”nti padassa attho niddiṭṭho. Tattha lakkhaṇaṃ nāma tassa tassa rūpavisesassa anaññasādhāraṇo sabhāvo. Raso tasseva attano phalaṃ pati paccayabhāvo. Paccupaṭṭhānaṃ tassa paramatthato vijjamānattā yāthāvato ñāṇassa gocarabhāvo. Padaṭṭhānaṃ āsannakāraṇaṃ, tenassa paccayāyattavuttitā dassitā. “Anavasesarūpapariggaho”ti iminā pana “ettakaṃ rūpaṃ, ito uddhaṃ” rūpaṃ natthīti padadvayassāpi attho niddiṭṭho rūpassa sabbaso pariyādānavasena niyāmanato. “Iti rūpassa samudayo”ti ettha pana iti-saddo “iti kho bhikkhave sappaṭibhayo bālo”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.124; a. ni. 3.1) viya pakāratthoti āha “itīti eva”nti.

“Iti rūpaṃ”: here the second ‘iti’ indicates example, while the first ‘iti’ conveys form and limitation, due to the multiple meanings of particles—or its meaning should be understood as emphasis through repetition, etc. The sentence, indicating inclusion and exclusion, demonstrates: ‘This is form, this much is form, beyond this there is no form,’ and so on. Here, ‘the nature of being afflicted’ shows the general characteristic of form, while ‘the differentiation based on the derived and primary elements’ reveals its specific aspects. Through both, the meaning of the term ‘this form’ is indicated. In this context, characteristic (lakkhaṇa) refers to the unique, non-common nature of each particular form. Function (rasa) is its own effect, its conditionality in relation to its result. Manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) is its being the object of knowledge as it truly exists in the ultimate sense. Proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) is the immediate cause, showing its dependent origination. ‘Comprehending form without remainder’—this indicates the meaning of the two phrases ‘this much is form’ and ‘beyond this there is no form,’ by complete restriction through the entire extent of form. ‘Thus is the arising of form’: here, the word ‘iti’ conveys manner, as in passages like ‘Thus, monks, the fool is full of fear’ (MN 3.124; AN 3.1), hence it is said, ‘iti means thus.’

Avijjāsamudayāti [V 2.0048] avijjāya uppādā, atthibhāvāti attho. Nirodhanirodhī hi uppādo atthibhāvavācakopi hoti, tasmā purimabhavasiddhāya [M 2.0054] avijjāya sati imasmiṃ bhave rūpasamudayo, rūpassa uppādo hotīti attho. “Taṇhāsamudayā”tiādīsupi eseva nayo. Āhārasamudayāti ettha pana pavattipaccayesu kabaḷīkārāhārassa balavatāya so eva gahito. Tasmiṃ pana gahite pavattipaccayatāsāmaññena utucittāni gahitāneva hontīti catusamuṭṭhānikarūpassa paccayato udayadassanaṃ vibhāvitamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Nibbattilakkhaṇa”ntiādinā kālavasena udayadassanamāha. Tattha nibbattilakkhaṇanti rūpassa uppādasaṅkhātaṃ saṅkhatalakkhaṇaṃ. Passantopīti na kevalaṃ paccayasamudayameva, atha kho khaṇato udayaṃ passantopi. Addhāvasena hi paṭhamaṃ udayaṃ passitvā ṭhito puna santativasena disvā anukkamena khaṇavasena passati. Avijjānirodhā rūpanirodhoti aggamaggena [P 2.0070] avijjāya anuppādanirodhato anāgatassa rūpassa anuppādanirodho hoti paccayābhāve abhāvato. Taṇhānirodhā kammanirodhoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Āhāranirodhāti pavattipaccayassa kabaḷīkārāhārassa abhāvena. Rūpanirodhoti taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpassa abhāvo hoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. “Vipariṇāmalakkhaṇa”nti bhaṅgakālavasena hetaṃ vayadassanaṃ, tasmā taṃ addhāvasena paṭhamaṃ passitvā puna santativasena disvā anukkamena khaṇavasena passati. Ayañca nayo pākatikavipassakavasena vutto, bodhisattānaṃ panetaṃ natthi. Esa nayo udayadassanepi.

‘From the arising of ignorance’ means from the production of ignorance, that is, its existence (atthibhāva). For arising (uppāda), which is the opposite of cessation, also signifies existence (atthibhāva). Therefore, when ignorance established in a previous existence is present, in this existence, the arising of form occurs—this is the meaning. The same principle applies to “from the arising of craving,” etc. “From the arising of nutriment”—here, among the conditions for continuity, physical food is emphasized due to its strength. However, when this is taken, conditions of season and mind are also included by the general nature of being continuity conditions. Thus, the discernment of arising from the conditions of the fourfold-originated form should be seen as clearly explained. “By the characteristic of production,” etc., refers to seeing arising in terms of time. Here, “the characteristic of production” means the conditioned characteristic of form, designated as its arising. “One who sees” does not merely see the arising of conditions but also sees the arising moment by moment. For first, one sees arising in terms of duration (addhā), then, having become stabilized, sees it in terms of continuity, and gradually perceives it moment by moment. “From the cessation of ignorance, there is cessation of form”—this means that through the non-arising cessation of ignorance by the highest path, the non-arising cessation of future form occurs due to the absence of conditions. The same principle applies to “from the cessation of craving, there is cessation of kamma.” “From the cessation of nutriment”—here, due to the absence of the continuity condition, physical food, there is cessation of the form originating from it. The rest follows the same method as described. “By the characteristic of dissolution”—this refers to seeing cessation in terms of the time of dissolution. Therefore, one first sees it in terms of duration (addhā), then in terms of continuity, and gradually perceives it moment by moment. This method is explained from the perspective of ordinary insight meditators, but it does not apply to bodhisattas. This principle applies to the discernment of arising as well.

“Iti vedanā”tiādīsupi heṭṭhā rūpe vuttanayānusārena attho veditabbo. Tenāha “ayaṃ vedanā, ettakā vedanā”tiādi. Tattha vedayita…pe… sabhāvanti ettha “vedayitasabhāvaṃ…pe… vijānanasabhāva”nti paccekaṃ sabhāva- saddo yojetabbo. Vedayitasabhāvanti anubhavanasabhāvaṃ. Sañjānanasabhāvanti “nīlaṃ pīta”ntiādinā ārammaṇassa sallakkhaṇasabhāvaṃ. Abhisaṅkharaṇasabhāvanti āyūhanasabhāvaṃ. Vijānanasabhāvanti ārammaṇassa upaladdhisabhāvaṃ. Sukhādīti ādi-saddena dukkhasomanassadomanassupekkhāvedanānaṃ saṅgaho rūpasaññādīti ādi-saddena saddasaññādīnaṃ, phassādīti ādi-saddena cetanā vitakkādīnaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīnanti ādi-saddena sabbesaṃ lokiyaviññāṇānaṃ saṅgaho. Yathā ca viññāṇe, esa nayo vedanādīsupi. Tesanti [M 2.0055] “samudayo”ti vuttadhammānaṃ. Tīsu khandhesūti vedanāsaññāsaṅkhārakkhandhesu. “Phuṭṭho vedeti, phuṭṭho sañjānāti, phuṭṭho cetetī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.93) vacanato [P 2.0071] “phassasamudayā”ti vattabbaṃ. “Nāmarūpapaccayāpi viññāṇa”nti (vibha. 246; dī. ni. 2.97) vacanato viññāṇakkhandhe “nāmarūpasamudayā”ti vattabbaṃ. Tesaṃ yevāti [V 2.0049] tīsu khandhesu “phassassa viññāṇakkhandhe nāmarūpassā”ti phassanāmarūpānaṃyeva vasena atthaṅgamapadampi yojetabbaṃ, avijjādayo pana rūpe vuttasadisā evāti adhippāyo.

"Thus feeling," etc.—here, the meaning should be understood according to the method explained earlier regarding form. Therefore it is said, "This is feeling, so much feeling," and so on. Here, regarding "the nature of feeling"...up to..."the nature of knowing," the word "nature" should be connected to each term separately: the nature of feeling, the nature of perceiving, the nature of forming, and the nature of knowing. "The nature of feeling" means the nature of experiencing. "The nature of perceiving" means the nature of marking an object with a characteristic, such as "blue, yellow," etc. "The nature of forming" means the nature of constructing. "The nature of knowing" means the nature of apprehending an object. "Pleasure, etc."—the word "etc." includes painful, joyful, sorrowful, and equanimous feeling. "Perception of form, etc."—the word "etc." includes perception of sound, etc. "Contact, etc."—the word "etc." includes volition, thought, etc. "Eye-consciousness, etc."—the word "etc." includes all mundane consciousnesses. And as with consciousness, so also with feeling, etc. "Of these" refers to the phenomena mentioned as "origination." "In the three aggregates" means in the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations. Because it is said, "Touched, one feels; touched, one perceives; touched, one intends" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.93), it should be stated, "from the origination of contact." Because it is said, "Dependent on name-and-form is consciousness" (Vibhaṅga 246; Dīgha Nikāya 2.97), regarding the aggregate of consciousness, it should be stated, "from the origination of name-and-form." "Of these very," in the three aggregates, "of contact," and in the aggregate of consciousness, "of name-and-form," the term for cessation should be connected only in relation to contact and name-and-form; but ignorance, etc., are to be understood similarly as stated regarding form—this is the intention.

Samapaññāsalakkhaṇavasenāti paccayato vīsati khaṇato pañcāti pañcavīsatiyā udayalakkhaṇānaṃ, paccayato vīsati khaṇato pañcāti pañcavīsatiyā eva vayalakkhaṇānaṃ cāti samapaññāsāya udayavayalakkhaṇānaṃ vasena. Tattha pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ udayo lakkhīyati etehīti lakkhaṇānīti vuccanti avijjādisamudayoti, tathā tesaṃ anuppādanirodho lakkhīyati etehīti lakkhaṇānīti vuccanti avijjādīnaṃ accantanirodho. Nibbattivipariṇāmalakkhaṇāni pana saṅkhatalakkhaṇamevāti. Evaṃ etāni samapaññāsalakkhaṇāni sarūpato veditabbāni. Yathānukkamena vaḍḍhiteti yathāvuttaudayabbayañāṇe tikkhe sūre pasanne hutvā vahante tato paraṃ vattabbānaṃ bhaṅgañāṇādīnaṃ uppattipaṭipāṭiyā buddhippatte paramukkaṃsagate vipassanāñāṇe. Pageva hi chattiṃsakoṭisatasahassamukhena pavattena sabbaññutaññāṇānucchavikena mahāvajirañāṇasaṅkhātena sammasanañāṇena sambhatānubhāvaṃ gabbhaṃ gaṇhantaṃ paripākaṃ gacchantaṃ paṭipadāvisuddhiñāṇaṃ aparimitakāle sambhatāya paññāpāramiyā ānubhāvena ukkaṃsapāramippattaṃ anukkamena vuṭṭhānagāminibhāvaṃ upagantvā yadā ariyamaggena ghaṭeti, tadā ariyamaggacittaṃ sabbakilesehi maggapaṭipāṭiyā vimuccati[P 2.0072], vimuccantañca tathā vimuccati, yathā sabbañeyyāvaraṇappahānaṃ hoti. Yaṃ kilesānaṃ “savāsanappahāna”nti vuccati, tayidaṃ pahānaṃ atthato anuppattinirodhoti āha “anuppādanirodhenā”ti. Āsavasaṅkhātehi kilesehīti bhavato ābhavaggaṃ, dhammato āgotrabhuṃ savanato pavattanato āsavasaññitehi rāgo, diṭṭhi, mohoti imehi kilesehi. Lakkhaṇavacanañcetaṃ, pāḷiyaṃ yadidaṃ “āsavehī”ti, tadekaṭṭhatāya pana sabbehipi [M 2.0056] kilesehi sabbehipi pāpadhammehi cittaṃ vimuccati. Aggahetvāti tesaṃ kilesānaṃ lesamattampi aggahetvā.

By way of the fifty characteristics: twenty-five arising characteristics (twenty by way of condition, five by way of moment), and similarly twenty-five passing away characteristics (twenty by way of condition, five by way of moment), thus by way of the fifty arising and passing away characteristics. Herein, the arising of the five aggregates is marked by these; hence they are called characteristics—namely, the origin of ignorance and so on. Similarly, their cessation through non-arising is marked by these; hence they are called characteristics—namely, the complete cessation of ignorance and so on. However, the characteristics of production and change are merely characteristics of the conditioned. Thus, these fifty characteristics should be understood in their own nature. As it develops sequentially: when the aforementioned knowledge of arising and passing away, having become sharp, valiant, and clear, proceeds, then subsequently, by the sequence of the arising of the knowledge of dissolution and so on, which are to be spoken of later, the insight knowledge reaches its peak, having attained the highest excellence. Indeed, when the knowledge of the purification of the path, which has taken on the embryo of power accumulated by the knowledge of comprehension, called the great diamond-knowledge, which proceeds through 360,000,000 ways and is suitable for omniscience, goes to maturity, having attained the highest perfection by the power of the perfection of wisdom accumulated over immeasurable time, and having gradually reached the state leading to emergence, when it connects with the noble path, then the noble path consciousness is liberated from all defilements in the sequence of the path. And being liberated, it is liberated in such a way that there is the abandoning of all coverings of what is to be known. That which is called 'abandonment of defilements with their latent tendencies' (savāsanappahāna), this abandonment is in essence cessation through non-arising; therefore it is said 'by cessation through non-arising.' By the defilements called taints (āsavas)—so called because they flow and proceed from existence up to the highest existence, and from phenomena up to the change of lineage—namely, lust, wrong view, and delusion. And this is a characteristic term, as in the Pāli phrase 'by the taints.' But because they are all of one meaning, the mind is liberated from all defilements and all evil states. Without taking up even the slightest trace of those defilements.

Maggakkhaṇe vimuccati nāma taṃtaṃmaggavajjhakilesehi phalakkhaṇe vimuttaṃ nāma. Maggakkhaṇe vā vimuttañceva vimuccati cāti uparimaggakkhaṇe heṭṭhimamaggavajjhehi vimuttañceva yathāsakaṃ pahātabbehi vimuccati ca. Phalakkhaṇe vimuttamevāti sabbasmimpi phalakkhaṇe vimuttameva, na vimuccati nāma.

At the moment of the path, one is said to be 'being liberated' (vimuccati)—that is, from the defilements to be abandoned by that particular path. At the moment of fruition, one is said to be 'liberated' (vimutta). Or, at the moment of the path, one is both 'liberated' and 'being liberated'—that is, at the moment of a higher path, one is both liberated from the defilements abandoned by the lower paths and is also being liberated from what should be abandoned by their respective paths. At the moment of fruition, one is simply 'liberated'—that is, in every moment of fruition, one is only liberated, not said to be 'being liberated'.

Sabbabandhanāti orambhāgiyuddhambhāgiyasaṅgahitā sabbasmāpi bhavasaññojanā, vippamutto visesato pakārehi mutto. Suvikasitacittasantānoti sātisayaṃ ñāṇarasmisamphassena suṭṭhu sammadeva [V 2.0050] samphullacittasantāno. “Cattāri maggañāṇānī”tiādi yehi ñāṇehi suvikasitacittasantāno, tesaṃ ekadesena dassanaṃ. Nippadesato dassanaṃ pana parato āgamissati, tasmā tattheva tāni vibhajissāma. Sakale ca buddhaguṇeti atītaṃse appaṭihatañāṇādike sabbepi buddhaguṇe. Yadā hi lokanātho aggamaggaṃ adhigacchati, tadā sabbe guṇe hatthagate karoti nāma. Tato paraṃ “hatthagate katvā ṭhito”ti vuccati.

"From all bonds"—this includes both the lower and higher fetters, all the fetters of existence; he is fully liberated, freed in a special way. "With a well-developed mind-stream"—his mind-stream is thoroughly and perfectly blossoming through the radiant touch of wisdom. "The four knowledges of the path," etc.—these show a portion of the knowledges by which his mind-stream is well-developed. The full explanation will come later, so we will analyze them there. "And all the Buddha’s qualities"—this refers to all the Buddha’s qualities, such as his unimpeded knowledge of the past. For when the Lord of the World attains the supreme path, he makes all qualities as if held in his hand. After that, it is said, "having made them as if held in his hand, he stands."

“Paripuṇṇasaṅkappo”ti vatvā paripuṇṇasaṅkappatāparidīpanaṃ udānaṃ dassetuṃ “anekajātisaṃsāra”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ādito dvinnaṃ gāthānamattho heṭṭhā brahmajālanidānavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) vutto eva. Parato [P 2.0073] pana ayoghanahatassāti ayo haññati etenāti ayoghanaṃ, kammārānaṃ ayokūṭaṃ, ayomuṭṭhi ca, tena ayoghanena hatassa pahatassa. Eva-saddo cettha nipātamattaṃ. Jalato jātavedasoti jalayamānassa aggissa, anādare vā etaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Anupubbūpasantassāti anukkamena upasantassa vikkhambhantassa niruddhassa. Yathā na ñāyate gatīti yathā tassa gati na ñāyati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ayomuṭṭhikūṭādinā pahatattā ayoghanena hatassa pahatassa ayogatassa, kaṃsabhājanādigatassa vā jalamānassa aggissa anukkamena upasantassa dasasu disāsu na katthaci gati paññāyati paccayanirodhena appaṭisandhikaniruddhattāti. Evaṃ sammāvimuttānanti sammā hetunā ñāyena tadaṅgavikkhambhanavimuttipubbaṅgamāya [M 2.0057] samucchedavimuttiyā ariyamaggena catūhipi upādānehi, āsavehi ca muttattā sammā vimuttānaṃ, tato eva kāmabandhanasaṅkhātaṃ kāmoghabhavoghādibhedaṃ avasiṭṭhaoghañca taritvā ṭhitattā kāmabandhoghatārīnaṃ suṭṭhu paṭipassambhitasabbakilesavipphanditattā kilesābhisaṅkhāravātehi akampanīyatāya acalaṃ nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ saṅkhārūpasamaṃ sukhaṃ pattānaṃ adhigatānaṃ khīṇāsavānaṃ gati devamanussādibhedāsu gatīsu “ayaṃ nāmā”ti paññāpetabbatāya abhāvato paññāpetuṃ natthi na upalabbhati, yathāvuttajātavedo viya apaññattikabhāvameva te gacchantīti attho. Evaṃ manasi karontoti “evaṃ anekajātisaṃsāra”ntiādinā (dha. pa. 153) attano katakiccattaṃ manasi karonto bodhipallaṅke nisinnova virocitthāti yojanā.

Having said, 'one with perfect resolve,' to illustrate the meaning of perfect resolve, the inspired utterance beginning with 'Through the round of many births I have wandered' was spoken. Therein, the meaning of the first two verses has already been explained in the commentary on the introduction to the Brahmajāla Sutta (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1, the account of the First Great Council). Furthermore, regarding 'struck by an iron hammer' (ayoghanahatassa): 'ayoghana' is that by which iron is struck, namely, the blacksmith's iron hammer or iron mallet. Thus, 'ayoghanahatassa' means 'of that which is struck or beaten by that iron hammer.' Here, the word 'eva' is merely a particle. Regarding 'of the blazing fire' (jalato jātavedaso): this refers to the fire that is blazing; or this is a genitive of disregard. 'Gradually subsided' (anupubbūpasantassa) means gradually calmed, suppressed, ceased. 'As its destination is not known' (yathā na ñāyate gati) means just as its destination is not known. This is what is said: of the blazing fire—struck by an iron hammer, mallet, or the like, beaten by an iron hammer, or gone into a bronze vessel, etc.—which has gradually subsided, its destination is not discerned in any of the ten directions; due to the cessation of its fuel, it has ceased without potential for renewal. Thus, 'of those rightly liberated' (sammāvimuttānaṃ): of those rightly liberated by the noble path, which is the liberation by eradication, preceded by liberation by substitution and by suppression, and who are freed from the four kinds of clinging and the taints. And for that very reason, 'of those who have crossed the flood of sensual bonds' (kāmabandhoghatārīnaṃ) refers to those who, having crossed the flood called sensual bondage—that is, the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, and the remaining floods—stand firm. Because all agitation of the defilements is perfectly stilled, and because they are unshaken by the winds of defilements and volitional formations, they have attained the unshakable bliss called Nibbāna, the stilling of formations. For those who have reached this, the arahants with taints destroyed, their destination among the various destinies of gods or humans cannot be designated; it is not found, because there is no means of designating them as 'this one here.' Just as the aforementioned fire, they go to a state beyond designation. This is the meaning. 'Reflecting thus' (evaṃ manasi karonto): the connection is that, reflecting on the fulfillment of his own task with the words 'Through the round of many births I have wandered,' etc. (Dhp. 153), he shone forth, seated right there on the seat of enlightenment.

Dutiyabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the second recitation division is complete.

Brahmayācanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Account of Brahmā's Request

64. Yannūnāti [P 2.0074][V 2.0051] parivitakkanatthe nipāto, ahanti bhagavā attānaṃ niddisatīti āha “yadi panāha”nti. “Aṭṭhame sattāhe”tiādi yathā amhākaṃ bhagavā abhisambuddho hutvā vimuttisukhapaṭisaṃvedanādivasena sattasu sattāhesu paṭipajji, tato parañca dhammagambhīratāpaccavekkhaṇādivasena, evameva sabbepi sammāsambuddhā abhisambuddhakāle paṭipajjiṃsu, te ca sattāhādayo tatheva vavatthapīyantīti ayaṃ sabbesampi buddhānaṃ dhammatā. Tasmā vipassī bhagavā abhisambuddhakāle tathā paṭipajjīti dassetuṃ āraddhaṃ. Tattha “aṭṭhame sattāhe”ti idaṃ sattamasattāhato paraṃ, sattāhato orime ca pavattāya paṭipattiyā vasena vuttaṃ, na pallaṅkasattāhassa viya aṭṭhamassa nāma sattāhassa vavatthitassa labbhamānattā. Anantaroti “adhigato kho myāyaṃ dhammo”tiādiko vitakko (dī. ni. 2.67; ma. ni. 1.281; 2.337; saṃ. ni. 1.172; mahāva. 7, 8).

64. The particle 'yannūna' is in the sense of reflection. The Blessed One refers to himself with 'ahaṃ' (I), saying, 'What if I…' The phrase 'in the eighth week' and so on means that just as our Blessed One, having become fully enlightened, spent seven weeks engaged in experiencing the bliss of liberation and so forth, and thereafter reflected on the profundity of the Dhamma and other matters, so too did all the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones follow the same course at the time of their full enlightenment. And those seven weeks and so on were similarly determined. This is the natural law for all Buddhas. Therefore, this is begun to show that the Blessed One Vipassī also followed that course at the time of his full enlightenment. In this context, 'in the eighth week' is stated with reference to the practice that occurred after the seventh week and within the week that followed, not because an eighth week is designated and obtainable by name like the week of sitting at the foot of the tree. 'Immediately' refers to the thought, 'This Dhamma has been attained by me,' and so on (Dī. Ni. 2.67; Ma. Ni. 1.281; 2.337; Saṃ. Ni. 1.172; Mahāva. 7, 8).

Paṭividdhoti sayambhuñāṇena “idaṃ dukkha”ntiādinā paṭimukhaṃ paṭivijjhanavasena pavatto, yathābhūtaṃ avabuddhoti attho. Dhammoti catusaccadhammo tabbinimuttassa [M 2.0058] paṭivijjhitabbadhammassa abhāvato. Gambhīroti mahāsamuddo viya makasatuṇḍasūciyā aññatra samupacitaparipakkañāṇasambhārehi aññesaṃ ñāṇena alabbhaneyyappatiṭṭho. Tenāha “uttānabhāvapaṭikkhepavacanameta”nti. Alabbhaneyyappatiṭṭho ogāhituṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya sarūpato visesato ca passituṃ na sakkāti āha “gambhīrattāva duddaso”ti. Dukkhena daṭṭhabboti kicchena kenaci kadācideva daṭṭhabbo. Yaṃ pana daṭṭhumeva na sakkā, tassa ogāhetvā anu anu bujjhane kathā eva natthīti āha “duddasattāva duranubodho”ti. Dukkhena avabujjhitabbo avabodhassa dukkarabhāvato. Imasmiṃ ṭhāne “taṃ kiṃ maññatha bhikkhave dukkarataraṃ vā durabhisambhavataraṃ vā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1115) suttapadaṃ [P 2.0075] vattabbaṃ. Santārammaṇatāya vā santo. Nibbutasabbapariḷāhatāya nibbuto. Padhānabhāvaṃ nītoti vā paṇīto. Atittikaraṭṭhena atappako sādurasabhojanaṃ viya. Ettha ca nirodhasaccaṃ santaṃ ārammaṇanti santārammaṇaṃ, maggasaccaṃ santaṃ, santārammaṇañcāti santārammaṇaṃ anupasantasabhāvānaṃ kilesānaṃ, saṅkhārānañca abhāvato santo nibbutasabbapariḷāhattā nibbuto, santapaṇītabhāveneva tadatthāya asecanakatāya atappakatā daṭṭhabbā. Tenāha “idaṃ dvayaṃ lokuttarameva sandhāya vutta”nti. Uttamañāṇassa visayattā na takkena avacaritabbo, tato eva nipuṇañāṇagocaratāya, saṇhasukhumasabhāvattā ca nipuṇo. Bālānaṃ avisayattā paṇḍitehi eva veditabboti paṇḍitavedanīyo. Ālīyanti abhiramitabbaṭṭhena [V 2.0052] sevīyantīti ālayā, pañca kāmaguṇā. Ālayanti abhiramaṇavasena sevantīti ālayā, taṇhāvicaritāni. Ālayaratāti ālayaniratā. Suṭṭhu muditā ativiya muditā anukkaṇṭhanato. Ramatīti ratiṃ vindati kīḷati laḷati. Ime sattā yathā kāmaguṇe, evaṃ rāgampi assādenti abhinandanti yevāti vuttaṃ “duvidhampī”tiādi.

“Penetrated” (paṭividdho) means that it has come about by way of direct, face-to-face penetration with self-arisen knowledge through phrases like “this is suffering,” meaning it is understood as it truly is. The Dhamma refers to the Four Noble Truths, because there is no penetrable phenomenon apart from them. “Profound” (gambhīro) means its ground is unobtainable by the knowledge of others—like the great ocean by a mosquito’s proboscis—except by those with an accumulated and fully matured store of wisdom. Therefore, it is said, “This is a statement rejecting superficiality.” Because its ground is unobtainable, it cannot be plunged into, nor can it be seen in its essence and details; therefore it is said, “Because it is profound, it is hard to see.” “Hard to see” (duddaso) means it is to be seen with difficulty, only occasionally by someone with effort. But if something cannot be seen at all, there is no question of gradually awakening to it by plunging into it. Therefore, it is said, “Because it is hard to see, it is hard to comprehend.” “Hard to comprehend” (duranubodho) means it is to be comprehended with difficulty due to the arduous nature of understanding. In this context, the sutta passage “What do you think, bhikkhus, which is more difficult, more challenging to fully awaken to?” (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1115) should be cited. Or, “peaceful” (santo) because it has peace as its object. “Extinguished” (nibbuto) because all fevers are extinguished. Or, “excellent” (paṇīto) because it has been brought to a state of preeminence. ‘Unsating’ (atappako) in the sense that one never has enough of it, like delicious food. Here, the truth of cessation is a peaceful object, thus it has a “peaceful object” (santārammaṇaṃ); and the truth of the path is peaceful and has a peaceful object, thus it has a “peaceful object.” Because of the absence of defilements and formations, which are unpeaceful in nature, it is “peaceful” (santo); because all fevers are extinguished, it is “extinguished” (nibbuto). Its unsating nature should be understood from its being inherently delightful (asecanaka) for that purpose, due to its peaceful and excellent nature. Therefore, it is said, “These two are spoken of with reference only to the supramundane.” Not to be fathomed by reasoning because it is the domain of supreme knowledge. For that very reason, and because of its refined and subtle nature, it is “subtle” (nipuṇo), being the domain of subtle knowledge. Not being the domain of fools, it is to be known only by the wise—thus, it is called “to be known by the wise” (paṇḍitavedanīyo). “They cling” (ālīyanti) means they are indulged in and resorted to in the sense of being delighted in; thus, the five strands of sensual pleasure are called “attachments” (ālayā). “They are attached” (ālayanti) means they resort to them by way of delighting in; thus, the wanderings of craving are called “attachments” (ālayā). “Delighting in attachments” (ālayaratā) means devoted to attachments. “Thoroughly delighted” (suṭṭhu muditā) means exceedingly delighted, without dissatisfaction. “They rejoice” (ramati) means they find enjoyment, play, and revel. These beings, just as they savor sensual pleasures, so too they relish and delight in craving. Thus, it is said, “both kinds” and so forth.

Ṭhānaṃ sandhāyāti ṭhāna-saddaṃ sandhāya. Atthato pana “ṭhāna”nti ca paṭiccasamuppādo eva adhippeto. Tiṭṭhati ettha phalaṃ tadāyattavuttitāyāti ṭhānaṃ, saṅkhārādīnaṃ paccayabhūtā avijjādayo. Imesaṃ saṅkhārādīnaṃ paccayāti idappaccayā, avijjādayova. Idappaccayā eva idappaccayatā yathā devo eva devatā[P 2.0076], idappaccayānaṃ vā avijjādīnaṃ attano phalaṃ paṭicca paccayabhāvo [M 2.0059] uppādanasamatthatā idappaccayatā, tena paramatthapaccayalakkhaṇo paṭiccasamuppādo dassito hoti. Paṭicca samuppajjati phalaṃ etasmāti paṭiccasamuppādo. Padadvayenāpi dhammānaṃ paccayaṭṭho eva vibhāvito. Tenāha “saṅkhārādipaccayānaṃ avijjādīnametaṃ adhivacana”nti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāsu (visuddhi. 2.570) vuttanayena veditabbo.

“Referring to a basis” (ṭhānaṃ sandhāya) means referring to the word “ṭhāna.” In meaning, however, “ṭhāna” is intended as dependent origination itself. It is called “ṭhāna” because the fruit stands (tiṭṭhati) there, its existence being dependent on it—that is, ignorance and other factors that are conditions for formations and so on. Idappaccayā means 'conditions for these,' that is, for formations and so on, which are ignorance and the rest. Idappaccayatā (specific conditionality) is simply idappaccayā (these conditions), just as devatā (divinity) is simply deva (a god). Alternatively, idappaccayatā is the state of being a condition, the capacity to produce, of ignorance and other factors—which are conditions—in relation to their own fruit. By this, dependent origination is shown to have the characteristic of a condition in the ultimate sense. “Dependent origination” (paṭiccasamuppādo) is that from which a fruit arises in dependence. Through both terms, the meaning of phenomena as conditions is clarified. Therefore, it is said: “This is a designation for ignorance and other factors that are conditions for formations and so on.” This is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the commentaries on the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhi. 2.570).

Sabbasaṅkhārasamathotiādi sabbanti sabbasaṅkhārasamathādipadābhidheyyaṃ sabbaṃ, atthato nibbānameva. Idāni tassa nibbānabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “yasmā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tanti nibbānaṃ. Āgammāti paṭicca ariyamaggassa ārammaṇapaccayahetu. Sammantīti appaṭisandhikūpasamavasena sammanti. Tathā santā ca savisesaṃ upasantā nāma hontīti āha “vūpasammantī”ti, etena sabbe saṅkhārā sammanti etthāti sabbasaṅkhārasamatho, nibbānanti dasseti. Sabbasaṅkhāravisaṃyutte hi nibbāne sabbasaṅkhāravūpasamapariyāyo ñāyāgato yevāti. Sesepadesupi eseva nayo. Upadhīyati ettha dukkhanti upadhi, khandhādayo. Paṭinissaṭṭhāti samucchedavasena pariccattā honti. Sabbā taṇhāti aṭṭhasatappabhedā sabbāpi taṇhā. Sabbe kilesarāgāti kāmarāgarūparāgādibhedā sabbepi kilesabhūtā rāgā, sabbepi vā kilesā idha kilesarāgāti veditabbā, na lobhavisesā eva cittassa viparītabhāvāpādanato. Yathāha “rattampi cittaṃ vipariṇataṃ, duṭṭhampi cittaṃ vipariṇataṃ, mūḷhampi cittaṃ vipariṇata”nti (pārā. 271) virajjantīti [P 2.0077] attano sabhāvaṃ vijahanti. Sabbaṃ dukkhanti jarāmaraṇādibhedaṃ sabbaṃ vaṭṭadukkhaṃ. Bhavena bhavanti tena tena bhavena bhavantaraṃ. Bhavanikantibhāvena saṃsibbati, phalena vā saddhiṃ kammaṃ sataṇhasseva āyatiṃ punabbhavabhāvato. Tato vānato nikkhantaṃ tattha tassa sabbaso abhāvato. Ciranisajjācirabhāsanehi piṭṭhiāgilāyanatālugalasosādivasena kāyakilamatho ceva kāyavihesā [V 2.0053] ca veditabbā. Sā ca kho desanāya atthaṃ ajānantānaṃ, appaṭipajjantānañca vasena, jānantānaṃ, pana paṭipajjantānañca desanāya kāyaparissamopi satthu aparissamova. Tenāha bhagavā “na ca maṃ dhammādhikaraṇaṃ vihesesī”ti (udā. 10). Tathā hi vuttaṃ “yā ajānantānaṃ desanā nāma, so mama kilamatho assā”ti. Ubhayanti cittakilamatho, cittavihesā [M 2.0060] cāti ubhayaṃ petaṃ buddhānaṃ natthi, bodhimūleyeva samucchinnattā.

“The pacification of all formations” and so on—here, “all” refers to everything denoted by terms like “the pacification of all formations,” but in essence, it is Nibbāna itself. Now, to reveal its nature as Nibbāna, it is said, “Because indeed…” “That” (taṃ) refers to Nibbāna. “Relying on” (āgamma) means depending on the Noble Path, as an object-condition. “They subside” (sammanti) means they subside by way of cessation that does not lead to rebirth. Similarly, those that are peaceful are specifically called “fully pacified” (vūpasammantī), hence it is said, “they cease completely.” By this, it is shown that Nibbāna is “the pacification of all formations” (sabbasaṅkhārasamatho), where all formations subside. For in Nibbāna, which is disconnected from all formations, the cessation of all formations is naturally evident. The same applies to the remaining terms. “Upadhi” means that suffering is placed here, referring to the aggregates and so on. “Utterly abandoned” (paṭinissaṭṭhā) means they are given up by way of complete eradication. “All craving” (sabbā taṇhā) means all craving in its one hundred and eight forms. “All defilements of lust” (sabbe kilesarāgā) includes sensual lust, form lust, and so on—all defilements that are forms of lust, or alternatively, all defilements should be understood here as “defilements of lust,” not merely as specific instances of greed, because they cause the mind to become perverted. As it is said: “The mind, even when lustful, becomes perverted; the mind, even when hateful, becomes perverted; the mind, even when deluded, becomes perverted” (Pārā. 271). “They fade away” (virajjanti) means they abandon their own nature. “All suffering” (sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ) refers to every kind of suffering in the cycle of existence, such as aging and death. By existence they come to be (bhavanti), from this or that existence to another existence. It continues through delight in existence, or because kamma, together with craving, leads to a future state of renewed existence along with its fruit. “Having gone beyond that” (tato vānato nikkhantaṃ) means having gone out of that craving, because there is no trace of it there whatsoever. Bodily fatigue and bodily distress should be understood as arising from prolonged sitting and prolonged speaking, such as back pain and dryness of the palate and throat. However, that teaching involves physical exhaustion for the Teacher only in relation to those who do not understand the meaning and do not practice; for those who understand and practice, even the physical exertion of teaching is no exhaustion for the Teacher. Therefore, the Blessed One said, “And no matter concerning the Dhamma caused me distress” (Udā. 10). For so it is said: “That teaching which is for those who do not understand, that would be fatigue for me.” “Both” (ubhayaṃ) refers to mental fatigue and mental distress—both of these are absent for the Buddhas, having been eradicated at the foot of the Bodhi tree.

65. Anubrūhanaṃ sampiṇḍanaṃ. Soti “apissū”ti nipāto. Vipassinti paṭi-saddayogena sāmiatthe upayogavacananti āha “vipassissā”ti. Vuddhippattā acchariyā vā anacchariyā. Vuddhiatthopi hi akāro hoti yathā“asekkhā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. tikamātikāya 11). Kappānaṃ cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni satasahassañca sadevakassa lokassa dhammasaṃvibhāgakaraṇatthameva pāramiyo [P 2.0078] pūretvā idāni samadhigatadhammarājassa tattha appossukkatāpattidīpanatā, gāthātthassa acchariyatā, tassa vuddhippatti cāti veditabbā. Atthadvārena hi gāthānaṃ anacchariyatā. Gocarā ahesunti upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Upaṭṭhānañca vitakketabbatāvāti āha “parivitakkayitabbataṃ pāpuṇiṃsū”ti.

65. “Strengthening” (anubrūhanaṃ) is compacting (sampiṇḍanaṃ). The particle so means “assuredly” (apissu). The word vipassi is a term used in the sense of pre-eminence due to its connection with the word paṭi; thus it is said, vipassissā (I shall see). The verses are marvelous or unmarvelous depending on whether they have attained growth. For the prefix a- can also have the meaning of growth, as in asekhā dhammā (states of one beyond training). Having fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand more, solely for the purpose of distributing the Dhamma to the world with its gods, for him who has now attained the status of a Dhamma King, the wondrous nature of the verse’s meaning and its attainment of growth should be understood as indicating the attainment of a state of lack of eagerness. For by way of their literal meaning, the verses are not marvelous. “They were within range” (gocarā ahesuṃ) means they arose (upaṭṭhahiṃsu). And since their arising is a matter to be reflected upon, it is said, “they reached a state fit for reflection.”

Yadi sukhāpaṭipadāva kathaṃ kicchatāti āha “pāramīpūraṇakāle”tiādi. Evamādīni duppariccajāni dentassa. Ha-iti vā byattanti etasmiṃ atthe nipāto, “ekaṃsatthe”ti keci. Ha byattaṃ, ekaṃsena vā alaṃ nippayojanaṃ evaṃ kicchena adhigatassa dhammassa desetunti yojanā. Halanti “ala”nti iminā samānatthaṃ padaṃ “halanti vadāmī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.172) viya. Rāgadosaphuṭṭhehīti phuṭṭhavisena viya sappena rāgena, dosena ca samphuṭṭhehi abhibhūtehi. Rāgadosānugatehīti rāgadosehi anubandhehi.

If the practice is pleasant, how is it difficult? He says, “At the time of fulfilling the perfections,” and so on, for one giving such things that are hard to give up. Ha is a particle in the sense of byatta (clearly); some say it is in the sense of ekaṃsa (certainly). The construal is: “Clearly (ha), or certainly, enough (alaṃ)! It is useless (nippayojanaṃ) to teach the Dhamma attained with such difficulty.” Halan is a word with the same meaning as alaṃ, as in such phrases as “I say halan” (Saṃ. Ni. Ṭī. 1.172). “By those touched by lust and hatred” means by those overwhelmed by lust and hatred, as if by a snake whose venom has been activated. “By those who follow lust and hatred” means by those who are pursued by lust and hatred.

Niccādīnanti niccaggāhādīnaṃ. Evaṃ gatanti evaṃ pavattaṃ aniccādiākārena pavattaṃ. “Catusaccadhamma”nti idaṃ aniccādīsu, saccesu ca yathālābhavasena gahetabbaṃ. Evaṃ gatanti vā evaṃ “anicca”ntiādinā abhinivisitvā mayā, aññehi ca sammāsambuddhehi gataṃ, ñātaṃ paṭividdhanti attho. Kāmarāgena, bhavarāgena ca rattā nīvaraṇehi nivutacittatāya, diṭṭhirāgena rattā viparītābhinivesena na dakkhanti yāthāvato imaṃ dhammaṃ nappaṭivijjhissanti. Evaṃ gāhāpetunti “anicca”ntiādinā sabhāvena yāthāvato dhamme [P 2.0079] jānāpetuṃ. Rāgadosaparetatāpi nesaṃ sammūḷhabhāvenevāti āha “tamokhandhena āvuṭā”ti.

“Of permanence, etc.” (niccādīnaṃ) refers to the grasping of permanence, etc. “Gone thus” (evaṃ gataṃ) means that which has proceeded thus, that which has proceeded in the manner of impermanence, etc. The term “the Dhamma of the Four Truths” should be understood as referring to impermanence, etc., and to the truths, as is appropriate. Alternatively, “gone thus” means: gone to, known, and penetrated by me and by other Perfectly Enlightened Ones by way of adhering to “impermanent,” and so on. Those impassioned by sensual lust and lust for existence, their minds being veiled by the hindrances, and those impassioned by lust for views through perverse adherence, will not see this Dhamma as it truly is; they will not penetrate it. “To cause to grasp thus” (evaṃ gāhāpetuṃ) means to cause them to know the Dhamma as it truly is, in its own nature as “impermanent,” and so on. Because their being overcome by lust and hatred is due to their state of utter delusion, he said, “they are shrouded by a mass of darkness.”

Dhammadesanāya [V 2.0054] appossukkatāpattiyā kāraṇaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “kasmā panā”tiādinā sayameva codanaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tattha yathāyaṃ idāni dhammadesanāya [M 2.0061] appossukkatāpatti sabbabuddhānaṃ āciṇṇasamāciṇṇadhammatāvasena, sabbabodhisattānaṃ ādito “kiṃ me aññātavesenā”tiādinā (bu. vaṃ. 2.99) mahābhinīhāre attano cittassa samussāhanaṃ āciṇṇasamāciṇṇadhammatā vāti āha “kiṃ me”tiādi. Tattha aññātavesenāti sadevakaṃ lokaṃ unnādento buddho ahutvā kevalaṃ buddhānaṃ sāvakabhāvūpagamanavasena aññātarūpena. Tividhaṃ kāraṇaṃ appossukkatāpattiyā paṭipakkhassa balavabhāvo, dhammassa paramagambhīratā, tattha ca bhagavato sātisayaṃ gāravanti taṃ dassetuṃ “tassa hī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha paṭipakkhā nāma rāgādayo kilesā sammāpaṭipattiyā antarāyakarattā. Tesaṃ balavabhāvato ciraparibhāvanāya sattasantānato dubbisodhiyatāya te satte mattahatthino viya dubbalaṃ purisaṃ ajjhottharitvā anayabyasanaṃ āpādentā anekasatayojanāyāmavitthāraṃ sunicitaṃ ghanasannivesaṃ kaṇṭakaduggampi adhisenti. Dūrappabheda ducchejjatāhi dubbisodhiyataṃ pana dassetuṃ “athassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ca anto āmaṭṭhatāya kañjikapuṇṇalābu ciraparivāsikatāya takkabharitacāṭi snehatintadubbalabhāvena vasātelapītapilotikā; telamissitatāya añjanamakkhitahatthā dubbisodhanīyā vuttā. Hīnūpamā [P 2.0080] cetā rūpappabandhabhāvato, acirakālikattā ca malīnatāya, kilesasaṃkileso eva pana dubbisodhanīyataro anādikālikattā, anusayitattā ca. Tenāha “atisaṃkiliṭṭhā”ti. Yathā ca dubbisodhanīyatāya evaṃ gambhīraduddasaduranubodhānampi vuttaupamā hīnūpamāva.

To explain the reason for the inclination towards inaction regarding teaching the Dhamma, he himself raises the question, beginning with, 'But why?'. Here, just as this present inclination towards inaction regarding teaching the Dhamma is in accordance with the customary and habitual nature of all Buddhas, so too for all Bodhisattas from the beginning, the rousing of their own minds in the great aspiration, as stated in the phrase, 'What is the use to me of an unknown guise?' (Bu.va. 2.99), is a customary and habitual nature. Thus, he says, 'What is the use to me?', and so on. Therein, 'in an unknown guise' means not as a Buddha who makes the world with its devas resound, but merely in the form of an unknown person by way of attaining the state of a disciple of the Buddhas. There are three reasons for the inclination towards inaction: the strength of the opposition, the extreme profundity of the Dhamma, and the Blessed One's exceeding reverence for it. To show this, the passage beginning 'For him...' is introduced. Therein, the opposition refers to the defilements such as lust, because they are obstacles to right practice. Due to their strength, their long-standing cultivation in the mental continuum of beings, and their difficulty to purify, they overwhelm a weak person like a maddened elephant, leading them to ruin and disaster, and they dominate even a thorny, impassable fortress, well-established and densely packed, hundreds of leagues in length and breadth. Furthermore, to show the difficulty of purification due to being hard to break apart and difficult to sever, the passage beginning 'And for him...' is stated. Therein, a gourd full of rice gruel due to being smeared inside; a pot full of buttermilk due to being kept for a long time; a rag that has absorbed fat and oil due to being soaked and weakened by grease; and a hand smeared with ointment due to being mixed with oil—these are said to be difficult to cleanse. These are inferior similes because they are a continuity of material form and because their stain is not long-lasting. But the defilement of corruptions is even more difficult to purify because it is beginningless and because it is latent. Therefore, he says, 'they are exceedingly defiled.' And just as for the difficulty of purification, so too for the profound, hard-to-see, and difficult-to-understand nature of the Dhamma, the similes given are inferior.

Gambhīropi dhammo paṭipakkhavidhamanena supākaṭo bhaveyya, paṭipakkhavidhamanaṃ pana sammāpaṭipattipaṭibaddhaṃ, sā saddhammasavanādhīnā, taṃ satthari, dhamme ca pasādāyattaṃ. So visesato loke sambhāvanīyassa garukātabbassa abhipatthanāhetukoti panāḷikāya sattānaṃ dhammasampaṭipattiyā brahmayācanādinimittanti taṃ dassento “apicā”tiādimāha.

Even the profound Dhamma would become very clear through the dispelling of the opposition; but the dispelling of the opposition is connected with right practice, that practice is dependent on listening to the good Dhamma, and that listening depends on confidence in the Teacher and the Dhamma. That confidence is especially a cause for the aspiration for what is to be esteemed and respected in the world. Thus, by this line of reasoning, Brahma's request and so on are a sign for the beings' right attainment of the Dhamma. To show this, he says, 'Moreover,' and so on.

66. “Aññataro”ti appaññāto viya kiñcāpi vuttaṃ, atha kho pākaṭo paññātoti dassetuṃ “imasmiṃ cakkavāḷe jeṭṭhakamahābrahmā”ti vuttaṃ. Mahābrahmabhavane jeṭṭhakamahābrahmā. So hi sakko viya [M 2.0062] kāmadevaloke, brahmaloke ca pākaṭo paññāto. Upakkilesabhūtaṃ appaṃ rāgādirajaṃ etassāti apparajaṃ, apparajaṃ akkhi paññācakkhu yesaṃ te taṃsabhāvāti katvā apparajakkhajātikāti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “paññāmaye”tiādimāha. Appaṃ rāgādirajaṃ yesaṃ te taṃsabhāvā apparajakkhajātikāti evamettha attho veditabbo. Assavanatāti “sayaṃ [V 2.0055] abhiññā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.28, 405; ma. ni. 1.154, 444) viya karaṇe paccattavacananti āha “assavanatāyā”ti. Dasapuññakiriyavatthuvasenāti dānādidasavidhavimuttiparipācanīyapuññakiriyavatthūnaṃ vasena. Tenāha “katādhikārā”tiādi. Papañcasūdaniyaṃ pana “dvādasapuññakiriyavasenā”ti [P 2.0081] (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.282) vuttaṃ, taṃ dānādīsu saraṇagamanaparahitapariṇāmanadvaya pakkhipanavasena vuttaṃ.

66. Although 'a certain one' is said as if referring to someone unknown, to show that he is in fact well-known and recognized, it is stated, 'the chief Great Brahmā in this world-system.' The chief Great Brahmā is in the realm of the Great Brahmās. For he, like Sakka in the world of the sense-sphere devas, is well-known and recognized in the Brahmā world. 'With little dust' means having little of the dust of defilement, such as lust. To show this meaning—that those whose eye is the eye of wisdom with little dust, being of such a nature, are 'of a nature with little dust in the eye'—he says, beginning with, 'consisting of wisdom.' Here the meaning should be understood thus: those who have little of the dust of lust and so on, being of such a nature, are of a nature with little dust in the eye. The word 'assavanatā' (from not hearing) is a term in the ablative with an instrumental sense, like in 'sayaṃ abhiññā' (by direct knowledge), and so on. Thus, he says, 'assavanatāya' (through not hearing). 'By means of the ten bases of meritorious action' means by means of the ten bases of meritorious action, such as giving, which bring about the maturing of liberation. Therefore, he says, beginning with, 'having made an aspiration.' In the Papañcasūdanī, however, it is said, 'by means of the twelve meritorious actions' (M-a 2.282), and that is said by including the two—taking refuge and the dedication for the welfare of others—with giving and so on.

69. Garuṭṭhāniyesu gāravavasena garukarapatthanā ajjhesanā, sāpi atthato patthanā evāti vuttaṃ “yācana”nti. Padesavisayañāṇadassanaṃ hutvā buddhānaṃyeva āveṇikabhāvato idaṃ ñāṇadvayaṃ “buddhacakkhū”ti vuccatīti āha “imesañhi dvinnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ buddhacakkhūti nāma”nti. Tiṇṇaṃ maggañāṇānanti heṭṭhimānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ maggañāṇānaṃ “dhammacakkhū”ti nāmaṃ, catusaccadhammadassananti katvā dassanamattabhāvato. Yato tāni ñāṇāni vijjūpamābhāvena vuttāni, aggamaggañāṇaṃ pana ñāṇakiccassa sikhāppattiyā dassanamattaṃ na hotīti “dhammacakkhū”ti na vuccatīti. Yato taṃ vajirūpamābhāvena vuttaṃ. Vuttanayenevāti “apparajakkhajātikā”ti ettha vuttanayeneva. Yasmā mandakilesā “apparajakkhā”ti vuttā, tasmā bahalakilesā “mahārajakkhā”ti veditabbā. Paṭipakkhavidhamanasamatthatāya tikkhāni sūrāni visadāni, vuttavipariyāyena mudūni. Saddhādayo ākārāti saddahanādippakāre vadati. Sundarāti kalyāṇā. Sammohavinodaniyaṃ pana “yesaṃ āsayādayo koṭṭhāsā sundarā, te svākārā”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 814) vuttaṃ, taṃ imāya atthavaṇṇanāya aññadatthu saṃsandati [P 2.0082] sametīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yato saddhāsampadādivasena ajjhāsayassa sundaratāti, tabbipariyāyato asundaratāti. Kāraṇaṃ nāma paccayākāro, saccāni vā. Paralokanti samparāyaṃ. Taṃ dukkhāvahaṃ vajjaṃ viya bhayato passitabbanti vuttaṃ “paralokañceva vajjañca bhayato passantī”ti. Sampattibhavato vā aññattā vipattibhavo “paraloko”ti vuttaṃ “para…pe… passantī”ti.

69. An entreaty is a respectful request made with reverence to those in a position of respect; since that too is in meaning just a request, it is called 'a petition.' Because the two knowledges concerning the domain of individuals are unique to the Buddhas, they are called the 'Buddha-eye.' Thus, he says, 'Indeed, these two knowledges are named the Buddha-eye.' Of the path-knowledges, the lower three are named the 'Dhamma-eye,' because it is a seeing of the Dhamma of the Four Truths, and because it is a mere seeing. For those knowledges are said to be like lightning. But the knowledge of the highest path, because it reaches the pinnacle of the function of knowledge, is not a mere seeing; thus, it is not called the 'Dhamma-eye.' For it is said to be like a diamond. 'In the way already stated' means in the way stated here in the phrase 'of a nature with little dust in the eye.' Since those with slight defilements are called 'those with little dust,' therefore those with thick defilements should be known as 'those with much dust.' They are sharp, courageous, and clear due to their ability to dispel the opposition; by the reverse of what was said, they are dull. 'Qualities such as faith' refers to the modes such as believing. 'Beautiful' means wholesome. In the Sammohavinodanī it is said, 'Those whose parts, such as inclination, are beautiful, they are of good qualities' (Vibh-a 814). It should be seen that this certainly corresponds and agrees with this explanation of the meaning. For through the perfection of faith and so on, the inclination is beautiful; and through its opposite, it is not beautiful. 'Cause' means the mode of condition, or the truths. 'The other world' means the future life. It should be seen with fear, like a fault that brings suffering; thus it is said, 'they see the other world and a fault with fear.' Or, because a state of ruin is different from a state of prosperity, it is called 'the other world'; thus it is said, 'they see the other... and so on.'

Ayaṃ [M 2.0063] panettha pāḷīti ettha “apparajakkhā”dipadānaṃ atthavibhāvane ayaṃ tassa tathābhāvasādhakapāḷi. Saddhādīnañhi vimuttiparipācakadhammānaṃ balavabhāvo tappaṭipakkhānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ dubbalabhāveneva hoti, tesañca balavabhāvo saddhādīnaṃ dubbalabhāvenāti vimuttiparipācakadhammānaṃ savisesaṃ atthitānatthitāvasena “apparajakkhā mahārajakkhā”ti ādayo pāḷiyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.111) vibhajitvā dassitā. Iti saddhādīnaṃ vasena pañca apparajakkhā, asaddhiyādīnaṃ vasena pañca mahārajakkhā. Evaṃ tikkhindriyamudindriyādayoti vibhāvitā paññāsa puggalā. Saddhādīnaṃ pana antarabhedena anekabhedā veditabbā. Khandhādayo eva [V 2.0056] lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena loko, sampattibhavabhūto loko sampattibhavaloko, sugatisaṅkhāto upapattibhavo, sampatti sambhavati etenāti sampattisambhavaloko sugatisaṃvattaniyo kammabhavo. Duggatisaṅkhātaupapattibhavaduggatisaṃvattaniyakammabhavā vipattibhavalokavipattisambhavalokā.

Herein, 'this is the Pāḷi' means: in explaining the meaning of the terms 'with little dust,' etc., this is the Pāḷi that establishes their being so. For the strength of faith and other qualities that ripen liberation comes about precisely through the weakness of their opposing evil states, and the strength of those evil states comes about through the weakness of faith and other qualities. Thus, in the Pāḷi (Paṭi. Ma. 1.111), terms such as 'those with little dust' and 'those with much dust' are distinguished and shown according to the specific presence or absence of qualities that ripen liberation. Thus, there are five types of individuals with little dust based on faith and other qualities, and five types of individuals with much dust based on lack of faith and other qualities. In this way, fifty individuals are distinguished, such as those with keen faculties and those with dull faculties. However, faith and other qualities should be understood as having many internal distinctions. The aggregates and so forth are 'the world' in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating. The world that is a state of attainment-existence is the 'world of attainment-existence.' The rebirth-existence designated as a good destination, and the kamma-existence that conduces to a good destination—from which attainment arises—is the 'world of the arising of attainment.' The rebirth-existence designated as a bad destination and the kamma-existence that conduces to a bad destination are the 'world of decline-existence' and the 'world of the arising of decline.'

Puna ekakadukādivasena lokaṃ vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “eko loko”tiādi vuttaṃ. Āhārādayo hi lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena lokoti. Tattha “eko loko sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā”ti (dī. ni. 3.303; a. ni. 10.27, 28; paṭi. ma. 1.2, 112, 208) yāyaṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānāya kathāya sabbasaṅkhārānaṃ paccayāyattavuttitā vuttā, tāya sabbo saṅkhāraloko eko ekavidho pakārantarassābhāvato. “Dve lokā”tiādīsupi iminā [P 2.0083] nayena attho veditabbo. Nāmaggahaṇena cettha nibbānassa aggahaṇaṃ tassa alokasabhāvattā. Nanu ca “āhāraṭṭhitikā”ti ettha paccayāyattavuttitāya maggaphalānampi lokatā āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati pariññeyyānaṃ dukkhasaccadhammānaṃ “idha loko”ti adhippetattā. Atha vā na lujjati na palujjatīti yo gahito, tathā na hoti, so lokoti taṃgahaṇarahitānaṃ lokuttarānaṃ natthi lokatā. Upādānānaṃ ārammaṇabhūtā khandhā upādānakkhandhā. Anurodhādivatthubhūtā lābhādayo aṭṭha lokadhammā. Dasāyatanānīti dasa rūpāyatanāni vivaṭṭajjhāsayassa adhippetattā. Tassa ca sabbaṃ tebhūmakakammaṃ garahitabbaṃ, vajjitabbañca hutvā upaṭṭhātīti vuttaṃ “sabbe abhisaṅkhārā vajjaṃ, sabbe bhavagāmikammā vajja”nti. Yesaṃ [M 2.0064] puggalānaṃ saddhādayo mandā, te idha “assaddhā”tiādinā vuttā. Na pana sabbena sabbaṃ saddhādīnaṃ abhāvatoti apparajakkhadukādīsu pañcasu dukesu ekekasmiṃ dasa dasa katvā “paññāsāya ākārehi imāni pañcindriyāni jānātī”ti vuttaṃ. Atha vā anvayato, byatirekato ca saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ paropariyattaṃ jānātīti katvā tathā vuttaṃ. Ettha ca apparajakkhādivasena āvajjantassa bhagavato te sattā puñjapuñjāva hutvā upaṭṭhahanti, na ekekā.

Again, in order to show the world divided into single, double, and so forth, it is said, 'One world,' and so on. For nutriment and so forth are indeed 'the world' in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating. Therein, the statement 'One world: all beings subsist on nutriment' (Dī. Ni. 3.303; A. Ni. 10.27, 28; Paṭi. Ma. 1.2, 112, 208), which is a discourse based on individuals, states that the existence of all conditioned things is dependent on conditions. By this, the entire world of conditioned things is one, of a single kind, since there is no other kind of nature. The meaning of 'two worlds,' etc., should also be understood in this way. Here, the mention of 'name' does not include Nibbāna, as it is not of the nature of the world. But does not the phrase 'subsist on nutriment' imply that even the path and fruition attain the nature of the world due to their dependence on conditions? No, it does not, because 'here is the world' is intended to refer to the truths of suffering, which are to be fully understood. Alternatively, that which is taken as 'does not break apart, does not decay' is not so; therefore, it is the world. Thus, the supramundane, which is devoid of such grasping, does not have the nature of the world. The aggregates that are the objects of clinging are the clinging-aggregates. The eight worldly conditions—gain, loss, and so forth—are the basis for attachment and aversion. The ten sense-bases refer to the ten material sense-bases, as they are intended for one with the inclination towards the cessation of the round of rebirth. And all kamma pertaining to the three realms is to be censured and avoided, as it is said, 'All volitional formations are a fault; all kamma leading to renewed existence is a fault.' Those individuals whose faith and other qualities are weak are here described by terms such as 'faithless.' However, it is not the case that they entirely lack faith and other qualities; for in the five pairs beginning with 'those with little dust,' in each pair, with ten each, it is said, 'He knows these five faculties in fifty ways.' Alternatively, it is said that he knows the higher and lower states of the faculties of faith, etc., by way of inclusion and exclusion. Here, when the Blessed One reflects on beings in terms of those with little dust and so on, those beings appear to the Blessed One in masses, not individually.

Uppalāni ettha santīti uppalinī, gacchopi jalāsayopi, idha pana jalāsayo adhippetoti āha “uppalavane”ti. Yāni udakassa anto nimuggāneva hutvā pusanti vaḍḍhanti, tāni antonimuggaposīnī. Dīpitānīti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pakāsitāni, idheva vā “aññānipī”tiādinā dīpitāni. Ugghaṭitaññūti ugghaṭanaṃ nāma ñāṇugghaṭanaṃ, ñāṇe ugghaṭitamatte eva jānātīti attho. Vipañcitaṃ [P 2.0084] vitthāramevamatthaṃ jānātīti vipañcitaññū. Uddesādīhi netabboti neyyo. Saha udāhaṭavelāyāti udāhāre dhammassa uddese udāhaṭamatte eva. Dhammābhisamayoti catusaccadhammassa ñāṇena saddhiṃ abhisamayo. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”tiādinā [V 2.0057] nayena saṅkhittena mātikāya dīpiyamānāya desanānusārena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhituṃ samattho “puggalo ugghaṭitaññū”ti vuccati. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ saṅkhittena mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā vitthārena atthe vibhajiyamāne arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ samattho “puggalo vipañcitaññū”ti vuccati. Uddesatoti uddesahetu, uddisantassa, uddisāpentassa vāti attho. Paripucchatoti atthaṃ paripucchantassa. Anupubbena dhammābhisamayo hotīti anukkamena arahattappatto hoti. Na tāya jātiyā dhammābhisamayo hotīti tena attabhāvena maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā antamaso jhānaṃ vā vipassanaṃ vā nibbattetuṃ na sakkoti. Ayaṃ vuccati puggalo padaparamoti ayaṃ puggalo byañjanapadameva paramaṃ assāti “padaparamo”ti vuccati.

'Uppalinī' is a place where lotuses are found; it can be a bush or a body of water. Here, however, a body of water is intended, hence it is said 'in the lotus pond' (uppalavane). Those that grow and flourish while remaining submerged within the water are called 'nourished while submerged' (antonimuggaposīnī). 'Dīpitāni' (illuminated) means 'explained' in the commentary, or here, 'illuminated' by phrases such as 'and others as well.' 'Ugghaṭitaññū' (one who understands upon unveiling) means that 'unveiling' is the unveiling of knowledge; the meaning is that one understands just by the mere unveiling of knowledge. 'Vipañcitaññū' (one who understands upon elaboration) means one who understands the meaning when it is elaborated in detail. 'Neyyo' (one to be led) means one who is to be led by way of exposition and so forth. 'Saha udāhaṭavelāya' (at the moment of utterance) means just at the moment the Dhamma is uttered in exposition. 'Dhammābhisamaya' (realization of the Dhamma) means the realization of the Dhamma of the Four Truths together with knowledge. 'This is called' means that this person, who is capable of attaining arahantship by directing his knowledge in accordance with the teaching, which is briefly presented by way of an outline (mātikā) such as 'the four foundations of mindfulness,' is called 'a person who understands upon unveiling.' 'This is called' means that this person, who is capable of attaining arahantship when the outline is briefly presented and the meaning is elaborated in detail, is called 'a person who understands upon elaboration.' 'Uddesato' (by way of exposition) means for the sake of exposition, for one who expounds, or for one who causes others to expound. 'Paripucchato' (by way of questioning) means for one who fully inquires into the meaning. 'Gradual realization of the Dhamma occurs' means that one attains arahantship progressively. 'Not by that birth does realization of the Dhamma occur' means that by that existence, one is incapable of producing even the path, fruit, jhāna, or insight. 'This person is called 'padaparama' (one for whom the letter is supreme)' means that this person for whom the mere letter (byañjana) is supreme is called 'padaparama.'

Yeti ye duvidhe puggale sandhāya vuttaṃ vibhaṅge kammāvaraṇenāti pañcavidhena ānantariyakammena. Vipākāvaraṇenāti ahetukapaṭisandhiyā. Yasmā duhetukānampi ariyamaggapaṭivedho natthi, tasmā duhetukapaṭisandhipi [M 2.0065] “vipākāvaraṇamevā”ti veditabbā. Kilesāvaraṇenāti niyatamicchādiṭṭhiyā. Assaddhāti buddhādīsu saddhā rahitā. Acchandikāti kattukamyatākusalacchandarahitā, uttarakurukā manussā acchandikaṭṭhānaṃ paviṭṭhā. Duppaññāti bhavaṅgapaññāya parihīnā, bhavaṅgapaññāya pana paripuṇṇāyapi yassa bhavaṅgaṃ lokuttarassa paccayo na hoti, sopi duppañño eva nāma. Abhabbā niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattanti [P 2.0085] kusalesu dhammesu sammattaniyāmasaṅkhātaṃ ariyamaggaṃ okkamituṃ adhigantuṃ abhabbā. “Na kammāvaraṇenā”tiādīni vuttavipariyāyena veditabbāni.

'Ye' (those) refers to the two types of individuals mentioned in the Vibhaṅga. 'Kammāvaraṇena' (by the hindrance of kamma) means by the fivefold heinous kamma (ānantariyakamma). 'Vipākāvaraṇena' (by the hindrance of result) means by rootless rebirth-linking (ahetukapaṭisandhi). Since even for those with two roots (duhetuka) there is no penetration of the Noble Path, therefore rebirth-linking with two roots should also be understood as 'a hindrance of result.' 'Kilesāvaraṇena' (by the hindrance of defilement) means by fixed wrong view (niyatamicchādiṭṭhi). 'Assaddhā' (faithless) means devoid of faith in the Buddha and so forth. 'Acchandikā' (without desire) means devoid of wholesome desire to act; the humans of Uttarakuru are said to have entered the state of being without desire. 'Duppaññā' (of little wisdom) means deficient in the wisdom of the life-continuum (bhavaṅgapaññā). However, even if one is fully endowed with the wisdom of the life-continuum, if one's life-continuum does not serve as a condition for the supramundane, such a person is still called 'of little wisdom.' 'Abhabbā niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattaṃ' (incapable of entering the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states) means they are incapable of entering or attaining the Noble Path, which is designated as the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states. Phrases such as 'not by the hindrance of kamma' should be understood in the opposite sense of what has been stated.

“Rāgacaritā”tiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ paramatthadīpaniyaṃ [paramatthamañjūsāyaṃ visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāyanti bhavitabbaṃ –

What should be said regarding 'those of lustful character' and so forth is to be understood according to the method stated in the Paramatthadīpanī [which should be understood as the Visuddhimagga commentary called the Paramatthamañjūsā].

“Sā esā paramatthānaṃ, tattha tattha yathārahaṃ;

Nidhānato paramattha-mañjūsā nāma nāmato”ti. (visuddhimaggamahāṭīkāya nigamane sayameva vuttattā)] visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayena veditabbaṃ;

'This, being a repository of the highest meanings, here and there as is appropriate, is by name called the Casket of the Highest Meaning (Paramatthamañjūsā).' (As it is said by the work itself in the conclusion of the Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā)] it should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary on the Visuddhimagga.

70. Ārabbhāti attano adhippetassa atthassa bhagavato jānāpanaṃ uddissāti attho. Selo pabbato ucco hoti thiro ca, na paṃsupabbato, missakapabbato vāti āha “sele yathā pabbatamuddhanī”ti. Dhammamayaṃ pāsādanti lokuttaradhammamāha. So hi pabbatasadiso ca hoti sabbadhamme atikkamma abbhuggataṭṭhena pāsādasadiso ca, paññāpariyāyo vā idha dhamma-saddo[V 2.0058]. Sā hi abbhuggataṭṭhena pāsādoti abhidhamme (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 16) niddiṭṭhā. Tathā cāha –

70. 'Ārabbha' means with the aim of making known to the Blessed One one's intended purpose. The mountain Sela is high and firm, not a mere heap of dust or a mixed mountain; hence it is said, 'as on a mountain peak.' 'A palace made of Dhamma' refers to the supramundane Dhamma. For it is like a mountain in that it surpasses all phenomena, and like a palace in that it is elevated. Alternatively, the word 'Dhamma' here is a designation for wisdom. For in the Abhidhamma it is described as a 'palace' due to its elevated nature. And thus it is said:

“Paññāpāsādamāruyha, asoko sokiniṃ pajaṃ;

Pabbataṭṭhova bhūmaṭṭhe, dhīro bāle avekkhatī”ti. (dha. pa. 28);

Having ascended the palace of wisdom, the sorrowless one surveys the sorrowing people; as one on a mountain peak surveys those on the ground, so the wise one surveys the foolish. (Dhp. 28)

“Yathā hī”tiādīsu yathā pabbate ṭhatvā rattandhakāre heṭṭhā olokentassa purisassa khette kedārapāḷikuṭiyo, tattha sayitamanussā ca na paññāyanti anujjalabhāvato. Kuṭikāsu pana aggijālā paññāyati ujjalabhāvato evaṃ dhammapāsādamāruyha sattalokaṃ olokayato bhagavato ñāṇassa āpāthaṃ nāgacchanti akatakalyāṇā sattā ñāṇagginā anujjalabhāvato, anuḷārabhāvato ca rattiṃ khittā sarā [M 2.0066] viya honti. Katakalyāṇā pana bhabbapuggalā dūre ṭhitāpi bhagavato ñāṇassa āpāthaṃ āgacchanti paripakkañāṇaggitāya [P 2.0086] samujjalabhāvato, uḷārasantānatāya himavantapabbato viya cāti evaṃ yojanā veditabbā.

In such phrases as 'Just as,' the meaning is as follows. Just as for a person standing on a mountain in the darkness of night and looking down, the fields, the ridges between the rice paddies, and the huts, and the people sleeping there, are not discerned due to their lack of brilliance, but the flames of fires in the huts are discerned due to their brilliance; similarly, when the Blessed One, having ascended the palace of the Dhamma, surveys the world of beings, those beings who have not performed wholesome deeds do not come within the range of his knowledge, because they are not illumined by the fire of knowledge and because they are not great, being like arrows shot at night. But those worthy individuals who have performed wholesome deeds, even if they are far away, do come within the range of the Blessed One’s knowledge, because they are resplendent with the fully matured fire of knowledge and because their mental continuities are lofty, like the Himalaya mountain. This is how the connection should be understood.

Uṭṭhehīti tvaṃ dhammadesanāya appossukkatāsaṅkhātasaṅkocāpattito kilāsubhāvato uṭṭhaha. Vīriyavantatāyāti sātisaya catubbidhasammappadhānavīriyavantatāya. Vīrassa hi bhāvo, kammaṃ vā vīriyaṃ. Kilesamārassa viya maccumārassapi āyatiṃ asambhavato “maccukilesamārāna”nti vuttaṃ. Abhisaṅkhāramāravijayassa aggahaṇaṃ kilesamāravijayeneva tabbijayassa jotitabhāvato. Vāhanasamatthatāyāti saṃsāramahākantārato nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ khemappadesaṃ sampāpanasamatthatāya.

“Arise!”: You should rise from the state of weariness that comes from the fault of diffidence, which is called a lack of enthusiasm for teaching the Dhamma. “With energy”: with the excellent energy of the fourfold right exertion. For the state or the action of a hero is energy. Since for the Māra of defilements, just as for the Māra of death, there is no future arising, it is said, 'of the Māra of death and the Māra of defilements.' The conquest of the Māra of formations is not mentioned because its conquest is illuminated by the conquest of the Māra of defilements. “Capable of bearing the burden”: capable of leading beings from the great wilderness of saṃsāra to the safe region known as Nibbāna.

71. “Apārutaṃ tesaṃ amatassa dvāra”nti keci paṭhanti. Nibbānassa dvāraṃ pavisanamaggo vivaritvā ṭhapito mahākaruṇūpanissayena sayambhuñāṇena adhigatattā. Saddhaṃ pamuñcantūti saddhaṃ pavedentu, attano saddahanākāraṃ upaṭṭhāpentūti attho. Sukhena akicchena pavattanīyatāya suppavattitaṃ. Na bhāsiṃ na bhāsissāmīti cintesi.

71. Some recite, “The door to the Deathless is open for them.” The door to Nibbāna, the path of entry, has been opened and set in place through the supporting condition of great compassion, because it was attained by self-arisen knowledge. “Let them release their faith” means let them declare their faith, let them establish their own way of believing. Because it can be set in motion easily and without difficulty, it is well set in motion. “I have not spoken, nor will I speak,” he thought.

Aggasāvakayugavaṇṇanā

The Description of the Pair of Chief Disciples

73. Sallapitvāti “vippasannāni kho te āvuso indriyānī”tiādinā (mahāva. 60) ālāpasallāpaṃ katvā. Tañhissa aparabhāge satthu santikaṃ upasaṅkamanassa paccayo ahosi.

73. “Having conversed”: having engaged in conversation with words such as, “Friend, your faculties are serene” (Mahāvagga 60). This became the reason for his approaching the Teacher later on.

75-6. Anupubbiṃ [V 2.0059] kathanti anupubbiyā anupubbaṃ kathetabbaṃ kathaṃ. Kā pana sāti? Dānādikathā. Tattha dānakathā tāva pacurajanesu pavattiyā sabbasādhāraṇattā, sukarattā, sīle patiṭṭhānassa upāyabhāvato ca ādito kathitā. Pariccāgasīlo hi puggalo pariggahavatthūsu [P 2.0087] nissaṅgabhāvato sukheneva sīlāni samādiyati, tattha ca suppatiṭṭhito hoti. Sīlena dāyakapaṭiggāhakavisuddhito parānuggahaṃ vatvā parapīḷānivattivacanato, kiriyadhammaṃ vatvā akiriyadhammavacanato, bhogasampattihetuṃ [M 2.0067] vatvā bhavasampattihetuvacanato ca dānakathānantaraṃ sīlakathā kathitā, tañce dānasīlaṃ vaṭṭanissitaṃ, ayaṃ bhavasampatti tassa phalanti dassanatthaṃ, imehi ca dānasīlamayehi paṇītapaṇītatarādibhedabhinnehi puññakiriyavatthūhi etā cātumahārājikādīsu paṇītapaṇītatarādibhedabhinnā aparimeyyā dibbabhogabhavasampattiyo hontīti dassanatthaṃ tadanantaraṃ saggakathaṃ. Vatvā ayaṃ saggo rāgādīhi upakkiliṭṭho, sabbadā anupakkiliṭṭho ariyamaggoti dassanatthaṃ saggānantaraṃ maggakathā kathetabbā. Maggañca kathentena tadadhigamupāyadassanatthaṃ saggapariyāpannāpi, pageva itare sabbepi kāmā nāma bahvādīnavā, aniccā adhuvā, vipariṇāmadhammāti kāmānaṃ ādīnavo, hīnā, gammā, pothujjanikā, anariyā, anatthasañhitāti tesaṃ okāro lāmakabhāvo, sabbepi bhavā kilesānaṃ vatthubhūtāti tattha saṃkileso, sabbaso kilesavippamuttaṃ nibbānanti nekkhamme ānisaṃso ca kathetabboti ayamattho maggantīti ettha iti-saddena ādiatthajotakena bodhitoti veditabbaṃ.

75-6. “Gradual talk” means a talk that should be given gradually, step-by-step. And what is that? It is the talk on generosity and so forth. Therein, the talk on generosity is given first because it is common to all people, easy to practice, and is a means for establishing oneself in virtue. For a person of charitable disposition, being unattached to possessions, easily undertakes the moral precepts and becomes well-established in them. After the talk on generosity, the talk on virtue is given, because it speaks of purifying the donor and recipient through virtue, of helping others after having spoken of refraining from harming others, of a dhamma of inaction after having spoken of a dhamma of action, and of the cause of prosperous existences after having spoken of the cause of wealth. To show that if that generosity and virtue are dependent on the round of existence, this prosperous existence is their fruit, and to show that through these meritorious actions—differentiated into refined, more refined, and so on—immeasurable divine enjoyments and prosperous states of existence arise in the realms of the Four Great Kings and so on, the talk on heaven is given next. After that, to show that this heaven is defiled by lust and so on, whereas the noble path is always undefiled, the talk on the path should be given after the talk on heaven. And when speaking of the path, in order to show the means for its attainment, one should speak of the danger in sensual pleasures—that all sensual pleasures, even those in heaven, let alone others, are full of dangers, impermanent, unstable, and subject to change; their inferiority and baseness—that they are low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and not connected with the goal; the defilement of all states of existence, as they are the basis for defilements; and the benefit in renunciation—that Nibbāna is complete freedom from the defilements. It should be understood that this entire meaning is indicated in the word 'path' by the particle 'iti', which here signifies 'and so forth'.

Sukhānaṃ nidānanti diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ, samparāyikānaṃ, nibbānapaṭisaṃyuttānañcāti sabbesampi sukhānaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Yañhi kiñci loke bhogasukhaṃ nāma, taṃ sabbaṃ dānanidānanti pākaṭo yamattho. Yaṃ pana taṃ [P 2.0088] jhānavipassanāmaggaphalanibbānapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ sukhaṃ, tassāpi dānaṃ upanissayapaccayo hotiyeva. Sampattīnaṃ mūlanti yā imā loke padesarajjaṃ sirissariyaṃ sattaratanasamujjalacakkavattisampadāti evaṃpabhedā mānusikā sampattiyo, yā ca cātumahārājikacātumahārājādibhedā dibbasampattiyo, yā vā panaññāpi sampattiyo, tāsaṃ sabbāsaṃ idaṃ dānaṃ nāma mūlaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Bhogānanti bhuñjitabbaṭṭhena “bhogo”ti laddhanāmānaṃ manāpiyarūpādīnaṃ, tannissayānañca upabhogasukhānaṃ. Avassayaṭṭhena patiṭṭhā. Visamagatassāti byasanappattassa. Tāṇanti rakkhā tato paripālanato. Leṇanti byasanehi paripāciyamānassa olīyanapadeso. Gatīti gantabbaṭṭhānaṃ. Parāyaṇanti paṭisaraṇaṃ. Avassayoti vinipatituṃ adento nissayo. Ārammaṇanti olubbhārammaṇaṃ.

'The source of happiness' means the cause of all happiness: that experienced in this very life, that in the next life, and that connected with Nibbāna. For it is a manifest fact that whatever happiness from wealth exists in the world, all of it has generosity as its source. Moreover, for that happiness connected with jhāna, insight, path, fruition, and Nibbāna, generosity is indeed a supporting condition. 'The root of attainments' means that this generosity is the root, the cause, of all attainments, whether they be human attainments of different kinds, such as regional kingship, supreme sovereignty, or the splendor of a wheel-turning monarch resplendent with the seven treasures; or divine attainments of different kinds, such as that of the Four Great Kings; or any other attainments. 'Of wealth' means of pleasant forms and so on, which have received the name 'wealth' (bhoga) in the sense of 'to be enjoyed,' and of the pleasures of enjoyment dependent on them. 'A foundation' is in the sense of a support. 'For one who has gone amiss' means for one who has met with misfortune. 'Protection' means guarding and preserving from that. 'A refuge' is a place of shelter for one being tormented by calamities. 'A destination' is a place to go. 'A final resort' is a sanctuary. 'A support' is a basis that prevents one from falling. 'An object' is an object to be held on to.

Ratanamayasīhāsanasadisanti sabbaratanamayasattaṅgamahāsīhāsanasadisaṃ mahagghaṃ hutvā sabbaso vinipatituṃ [V 2.0060] appadānato. Mahāpathavisadisaṃ gatagataṭṭhāne [M 2.0068] patiṭṭhāya labhāpanato. Ālambanarajjusadisanti yathā dubbalassa purisassa ālambanarajju uttiṭṭhato, tiṭṭhato ca upatthambho, evaṃ dānaṃ sattānaṃ sampattibhave uppattiyā, ṭhitiyā ca paccayabhāvato. Dukkhanittharaṇaṭṭhenāti duggatidukkhanittharaṇaṭṭhena. Samassāsanaṭṭhenāti [P 2.0089] lobhamacchariyādipaṭisattupaddavato sammadeva assāsanaṭṭhena. Bhayaparittāṇaṭṭhenāti dāliddiyabhayato paripālanaṭṭhena. Maccheramalādīhīti maccheralobhadosaissāvicikicchādiṭṭhi ādicittamalehi. Anupalittaṭṭhenāti anupakkiliṭṭhatāya. Tesanti maccheramalādikacavarānaṃ. Etehi eva durāsadaṭṭhena. Asantāsanaṭṭhenāti anabhibhavanīyatāya santāsābhāvena. Yo hi dāyako dānapati, so sampatipi kutoci na bhāyati, pageva āyatiṃ. Dhammasīsena puggalo vutto. Balavantaṭṭhenāti mahābalavatāya. Dāyako hi dānapati sampati pakkhabalena balavā hoti, āyatiṃ pana kāyabalādīhipi. Abhimaṅgalasammataṭṭhenāti “vaḍḍhikāraṇa”nti abhisammatabhāvena. Vipattibhavato sampattibhavūpanayanaṃ khemantabhūmisampāpanaṃ, bhavasaṅgāmato yogakkhemasampāpanañca khemantabhūmisampāpanaṭṭho.

It is like a throne made of jewels: like a great lion throne made of all the seven kinds of jewels, being extremely valuable, because it does not allow one to fall into complete ruin. Like the great earth, it provides a foundation for all who come and go, enabling them to gain support and stability. Like a supporting rope for a weak person, just as a rope helps a feeble man to stand and remain steady, so too does generosity serve as a condition for beings to arise in fortunate states and to remain there. By the meaning of crossing over suffering—it is the means to cross over the suffering of miserable states. By the meaning of consolation—it properly consoles one from the afflictions of adversaries such as greed and stinginess. By the meaning of protection from fear—it safeguards one from the fear of poverty. By ‘from the stains of miserliness, etc.’ is meant being unpolluted by the mental defilements such as miserliness, greed, hatred, envy, doubt, wrong views, and so forth. By ‘difficult to approach’ is meant that it is indeed difficult to approach by these very impurities. By the meaning of being unshakable—it is invincible, without agitation. For a donor, a giver of gifts, does not fear anything even in the present, let alone in the future. A person is referred to as the foremost in the Dhamma. By the meaning of being powerful—it signifies great strength. A donor, a giver of gifts, becomes powerful in the present through the strength of his support, and in the future, also through physical strength and other means. By the meaning of being esteemed as supremely auspicious—it is regarded as a cause of growth. Leading from a state of ruin to a state of prosperity, attaining the state of security; and from the battle of existence, attaining security from the bonds (yogakkhema)—this is the meaning of attaining the state of security.

Idāni dānaṃ vaṭṭagatā ukkaṃsappattā sampattiyo viya vivaṭṭagatāpi tā sampādetīti bodhicariyabhāvenapi dānaguṇe dassetuṃ “dānañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sakkamārabrahmasampattiyo attahitāya eva, cakkavattisampatti pana attahitāya, parahitāya cāti dassetuṃ sā tāsaṃ parato vuttā, etā lokiyā, imā pana lokuttarāti dassetuṃ tato paraṃ “sāvakapāramīñāṇa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāpi ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭhatarukkaṭṭhatamāti dassetuṃ kamena ñāṇattayaṃ vuttaṃ. Tesaṃ pana dānassa paccayabhāvo heṭṭhā vutto eva. Etenevassa brahmasampattiyāpi paccayabhāvo dīpitoti veditabbo.

Now, to show the qualities of giving even in the aspect of conduct conducive to enlightenment, it is said, “for giving indeed,” and so on, meaning that giving produces attainments even for those who have gone beyond the round of rebirth, just as it produces attainments for those who have reached prosperity in the round. Here, the attainments of Sakka, Māra, and Brahmā are solely for one’s own welfare, whereas the attainment of a wheel-turning monarch is for one’s own welfare and the welfare of others; to show this, the latter is stated after those. To show that these are mundane, while the following are supramundane, “the knowledge of the disciples’ perfection” and so on is stated after that. There also, to show the successively higher, even higher, and highest, the threefold knowledge is stated in order. However, their conditionality on giving has already been mentioned below. By this very fact, it should be understood that giving is also indicated as a condition for the attainment of Brahmā.

Dānañca nāma dakkhiṇeyyesu hitajjhāsayena vā pūjanajjhāsayena vā attano santakassa paresaṃ pariccajanaṃ, tasmā dāyako sattesu ekantahitajjhāsayo purisapuggalo, so “paresaṃ hiṃsati, paresaṃ vā santakaṃ haratī”ti aṭṭhānametanti āha “dānaṃ dadanto sīlaṃ samādātuṃ sakkotī”ti. Sīlasadiso alaṅkāro natthīti akittimaṃ hutvā sabbakālaṃ sobhāvisesāvahattā. Sīlapupphasadisaṃ pupphaṃ natthīti etthāpi [M 2.0069] eseva nayo. Sīlagandhasadiso gandho natthīti ettha “candanaṃ [P 2.0090] tagaraṃ vāpī”tiādikā (dha. pa. 55) gāthā, “gandho isīnaṃ ciradikkhitānaṃ, kāyā cuto gacchati mālutenā”tiādikā (jā. 2.17.55) ca vattabbā[V 2.0061]. Sīlañhi sattānaṃ ābharaṇañceva alaṅkāro ca gandhavilepanañca parassa dassanīyabhāvāvahañca. Tenāha “sīlālaṅkārena hī”tiādi.

Giving, indeed, is the relinquishing of one’s own possessions to those worthy of offerings, with the intention of benefiting them or honoring them.
