Therefore, the donor is a person whose sole intention is the welfare of beings. It is impossible that such a one would harm others or take what belongs to others. Hence, it is said, “One who gives a gift is able to undertake virtue.” There is no ornament equal to virtue—being genuine, it brings exceptional beauty at all times. There is no flower like the flower of virtue—here too, the same principle applies. There is no fragrance equal to the fragrance of virtue. Here, the verse beginning, “Sandalwood, tagara…” (Dhammapada 55) and the verse, “The fragrance of the long-ordained ascetics, wafts from their bodies on the wind…” (Jātaka 2.17.55) should be mentioned. For virtue is both the adornment and the ornament of beings, as well as their fragrant ointment, and it brings about a state of being pleasing to others. Therefore, it is said, “Indeed, with the ornament of virtue…” and so on.

“Ayaṃ saggo labbhatī”ti idaṃ majjhimehi chandādīhi āraddhaṃ sīlaṃ sandhāyāha. Tenāha sakko devarājā –

“This heaven is attainable”—this is said in reference to virtue undertaken with middling zeal and so forth. Thus spoke Sakka, the king of the gods:

“Hīnena brahmacariyena, khattiye upapajjati;

Majjhimena ca devattaṃ, uttamena visujjhatī”ti. (jā. 2.22.429);

“By an inferior holy life, one is reborn among nobles; by a middling one, as a deity; by the highest, one is purified.”

Iṭṭhoti sukho, kantoti kamanīyo, manāpoti manavaḍḍhanako, taṃ panassa iṭṭhādibhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “niccamettha kīḷā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Niccanti sabbakālaṃ kīḷāti kāmūpasaṃhitā sukhavihārā. Sampattiyoti bhogasampattiyo. Dibbanti dibbabhavaṃ devalokapariyāpannaṃ. Sukhanti kāyikaṃ, cetasikañca sukhaṃ. Dibbasampattinti dibbabhavaṃ āyusampattiṃ, vaṇṇayasaissariyasampattiṃ, rūpādisampattiñca. Evamādīti ādi-saddena yāmādīhi anubhavitabbaṃ dibbasampattiṃ vadati.

‘Pleasant’ means agreeable; ‘charming’ means desirable; ‘agreeable’ means heart-pleasing. To show its nature as pleasant and so on, it is said, ‘Always here is sport,’ and so forth. ‘Always’ means at all times. ‘Sport’ refers to pleasant abiding associated with sensual pleasures. ‘Prosperity’ means prosperity in possessions. ‘Divine’ pertains to divine existence, belonging to the realm of the gods. ‘Pleasure’ is both bodily and mental happiness. ‘Divine prosperity’ refers to divine existence, prosperity in lifespan, beauty, fame, dominion, and prosperity in form and so forth. ‘And so on’—by the word ‘and so on,’ it refers to divine prosperity to be experienced by the Yāma devas and others.

Appassādāti nirassādā paṇḍitehi yathābhūtaṃ passantehi tattha assādetabbatābhāvato. Bahudukkhāti mahādukkhā sampati, āyatiñca vipuladukkhānubandhattā. Bahupāyāsāti anekavidhaparissayā. Etthāti kāmesu. Bhiyyoti bahuṃ. Dosoti aniccatādinā, appassādatādinā ca dūsitabhāvo, yato te viññūnaṃ cittaṃ nārādhenti. Atha vā ādīnaṃ vāti pavattatīti ādīnavo, paramakapaṇatā, tathā [P 2.0091] ca kāmā yathābhūtaṃ paccavekkhantānaṃ paccupatiṭṭhanti. Lāmakabhāvoti nihīnabhāvo aseṭṭhehi sevitabbattā, seṭṭhehi na sevitabbattā ca. Saṃkilissananti vibādhetabbatā upatāpetabbatā. Nekkhamme ānisaṃsanti ettha yattakā kāmesu ādīnavā, tappaṭipakkhato tattakā nekkhamme ānisaṃsā. Api ca “nekkhammaṃ nāmetaṃ asambādhaṃ asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ, nikkhantaṃ kāmehi, nikkhantaṃ kāmasaññāya, nikkhantaṃ kāmavitakkehi, nikkhantaṃ kāmapariḷāhehi, nikkhantaṃ byāpādato”tiādinā [M 2.0070] (sārattha. ṭī. 3.26 mahāvagge) nayena nekkhamme ānisaṃse pakāsesi, pabbajjāya, jhānādīsu ca guṇe vibhāvesi vaṇṇesi.

‘Of little pleasure’ means of no pleasure, as the wise who see things as they truly are find no delight there. ‘Of much suffering’ means of great suffering in the present and because it is accompanied by abundant suffering in the future. ‘Full of distress’ means fraught with many kinds of trouble. ‘Herein’ refers to sensual pleasures. ‘More’ means much. ‘Fault’ refers to their being tainted by impermanence and so forth, and by their lack of true pleasure, which is why they do not please the minds of the discerning. Alternatively, ‘danger’ (ādīnava) means that which proceeds bringing misery (ādīnaṃ vāti); it is utter wretchedness. Thus, sensual pleasures appear to those who examine them as they truly are. ‘Lowly nature’ means inferiority, being fit to be pursued only by the base and not by the noble. ‘Defilement’ means being liable to be harassed and tormented. As for ‘the benefits of renunciation,’ the benefits of renunciation are as many as there are dangers in sensual pleasures, being the opposite of those dangers. Moreover, he described the benefits of renunciation in this way: ‘Renunciation is called unconfined, undefiled, the escape from sensual pleasures, the escape from perceptions of sensuality, the escape from thoughts of sensuality, the escape from the fever of sensuality, the escape from ill will,’ and so forth (Sāratthappakāsinī-ṭīkā 3.26, Mahāvagga). He also revealed and praised the virtues of going forth, and the qualities of jhāna and other attainments.

Vuttanayanti ettha yaṃ avuttanayaṃ “kallacitte”tiādi, tattha kallacitteti kammaniyacitte, heṭṭhā [V 2.0062] pavattitadesanāya assaddhiyādīnaṃ cittadosānaṃ vigatattā uparidesanāya bhājanabhāvūpagamanena kammakkhamacitteti attho. Assaddhiyādayo hi yasmā cittassa rogabhūtā tadā te vigatā, tasmā arogacitteti attho. Diṭṭhimānādikilesavigamanena muducitte. Kāmacchandādivigamena vinīvaraṇacitte. Sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ uḷārapītipāmojjayogena udaggacitte. Tattha saddhāsampattiyā pasannacitte. Yadā ca bhagavā aññāsīti sambandho. Atha vā kallacitteti kāmacchandavigamena arogacitte. Muducitteti byāpādavigamena mettāvasena akathinacitte. Vinīvaraṇacitteti uddhaccakukkuccavigamena vikkhepassa vigatattā tena apihitacitte. Udaggacitteti thinamiddhavigamena [P 2.0092] sampaggahitavasena alīnacitte. Pasannacitteti vicikicchāvigamena sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ adhimuttacitte, evampettha attho veditabbo.

Herein, regarding the stated method, that which is the unstated method is ‘with a ready mind’ and so forth. Therein, ‘with a ready mind’ refers to a mind fit for work. Because the mental defects of lack of faith and so forth have been removed by the preceding teaching, making one a worthy vessel for the higher teaching, it means a mind capable of undertaking the task. For since lack of faith and the like are indeed diseases of the mind, and these have been removed, the meaning is ‘a healthy mind.’ ‘With a pliant mind’ means with a mind that is softened by the removal of defilements such as wrong views and conceit. ‘With an unobstructed mind’ means with a mind that has the hindrances removed, such as sensual desire and so forth. ‘With an uplifted mind’ means with a mind uplifted through abundant joy and gladness in the right practice. Here, ‘with a confident mind’ refers to being clear due to the attainment of faith. And when the Blessed One knew—this is the connection. Alternatively, ‘with a ready mind’ means a healthy mind free from sensual desire. ‘With a pliant mind’ means a mind not hardened, imbued with loving-kindness, free from ill will. ‘With an unobstructed mind’ means a mind from which restlessness and remorse have been removed, free from distraction, and thus unhindered. ‘With an uplifted mind’ means a mind free from sloth and torpor, firm and not sluggish, being well-grasped. ‘With a confident mind’ means a mind free from doubt, resolved in right practice. Thus, the meaning here should be understood in this way.

“Seyyathāpī”tiādinā upamāvasena nesaṃ saṃkilesappahānaṃ, ariyamagguppādañca dasseti. Apagatakāḷakanti vigatakāḷakaṃ. Sammadevāti suṭṭhu eva. Rajananti nīlapītādiraṅgajātaṃ. Paṭiggaṇheyyāti gaṇheyya pabhassaraṃ bhaveyya. Tasmiṃyeva āsaneti tissameva nisajjāyaṃ, etena nesaṃ lahuvipassakatā, tikkhapaññatā, sukhapaṭipadākhippābhiññatā ca dassitā hoti. Virajanti apāyagamanīyarāgarajādīnaṃ vigamena virajaṃ. Anavasesadiṭṭhivicikicchāmalāpagamanena vītamalaṃ. Paṭhamamaggavajjhakilesarajābhāvena vā virajaṃ. Pañcavidhadussīlyamalāpagamanena vītamalaṃ. Dhammacakkhunti brahmāyusutte (ma. ni. 2.383) heṭṭhimā tayo maggā vuttā, cūḷarāhulovāde (ma. ni. 3.416) āsavakkhayo, idha pana sotāpattimaggo adhippeto. “Yaṃ kiñci samudayadhammaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhamma”nti tassa uppattiākāradassananti. Nanu ca maggañāṇaṃ asaṅkhatadhammārammaṇaṃ, na saṅkhatadhammārammaṇanti? Saccametaṃ. Yasmā taṃ nirodhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā kiccavasena sabbasaṅkhataṃ paṭivijjhantaṃ uppajjati, tasmā tathā vuttaṃ.

By 'Just as,' and so forth, he shows the abandoning of their defilements and the arising of the noble path by way of simile. ‘Free from darkness’ means devoid of darkness. ‘Rightly’ means truly well. ‘Dust’ refers to the stains born from blue, yellow, and other colors. ‘Would receive’ means it would take it and become radiant. ‘In that very seat’ refers to that very sitting—by this, their swift insight, sharp wisdom, and the easy practice leading to quick realization are shown. ‘Stainless’ means stainless through the removal of the dust of passion and so forth that leads to the lower realms. ‘Free from taints’ means devoid of the taints of wrong views and doubt without remainder. Alternatively, ‘stainless’ refers to the absence of the dust of defilements that are abandoned by the first path. ‘Free from impurities’ means rid of the five kinds of immoral impurities. ‘The eye of Dhamma’—in the Brahmāyu Sutta (MN 91), the lower three paths are mentioned; in the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta (MN 147), the destruction of the taints is spoken of. Here, however, the stream-entry path is intended. ‘Whatever is of a nature to arise, all that is of a nature to cease’—this is the seeing of its mode of arising. But does not path-knowledge have the unconditioned as its object, not the conditioned? This is true. Because it arises by taking cessation as its object and, by way of its function, penetrates all conditioned phenomena, it is said thus.

“Suddhaṃ vattha”nti nidassitaupamāyaṃ idaṃ upamāsaṃsandanaṃ vatthaṃ viya cittaṃ, vatthassa āgantukamalehi kiliṭṭhabhāvo viya cittassa rāgādimalehi saṃkiliṭṭhabhāvo[M 2.0071], dhovanasilā viya anupubbikathā, udakaṃ viya saddhā, udake temetvā ūsagomayachārikābharehi kāḷakapadese samucchinditvā vatthassa dhovanapayogo [P 2.0093] viya saddhāsinehena temetvā temetvā satisamādhipaññāhi dose sithilī katvā sutādividhinā cittassa sodhane vīriyārambho, tena payogena vatthe nānākāḷakāpagamo viya vīriyārambhena kilesavikkhambhanaṃ, raṅgajātaṃ viya ariyamaggo, tena suddhassa vatthassa pabhassarabhāvo viya vikkhambhitakilesassa cittassa maggena pariyodapananti. “Diṭṭhadhammā”ti [V 2.0063] vatvā dassanaṃ nāma ñāṇadassanato aññampi atthīti taṃ nivattanatthaṃ “pattadhammā”ti vuttaṃ. Patti ca ñāṇasampattito aññampi vijjatīti tato visesadassanatthaṃ “viditadhammā”ti vuttaṃ. Sā pana viditadhammatā dhammesu ekadesenāpi hotīti nippadesato viditabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “pariyogāḷhadhammā”ti vuttaṃ, tena nesaṃ saccābhisambodhiṃyeva vibhāveti. Maggañāṇañhi ekābhisamayavasena pariññādikiccaṃ sādhentaṃ nippadesatova catusaccadhammaṃ samantato ogāhantaṃ paṭivijjhatīti. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

‘Pure cloth’ is the simile presented here. This is the application of the simile: the mind is like the cloth; the defilement of the cloth by adventitious stains is like the defilement of the mind by stains such as lust and so forth; the washing stone is like the gradual teaching; water is like faith; the effort of washing the cloth by wetting it in water and then rubbing it with alkaline earth, cow-dung, and ashes to remove the dark stains is like the arousing of energy to purify the mind by repeatedly moistening it with the moisture of faith and then loosening the faults with mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom through the method of listening and so forth; the removal of various dark stains from the cloth by that effort is like the suppression of defilements by the arousing of energy; the dye is like the noble path; the radiant state of the purified cloth is like the cleansing by the path of the mind whose defilements have been suppressed. Having said ‘seen the Dhamma,’ to exclude any other kind of seeing apart from knowledge-seeing, it is said ‘attained the Dhamma.’ Since attainment also exists apart from the attainment of knowledge, to show the distinction, it is said ‘understood the Dhamma.’ As that state of understanding the Dhamma might occur only partially regarding the Dhamma, to show complete understanding without remainder, it is said ‘deeply penetrated the Dhamma.’ By this, he reveals their very awakening to the truths. For the knowledge of the path, while fulfilling the tasks such as full understanding through a single realization, penetrates and discerns the Four Noble Truths from all sides and without omission. The rest is as explained previously.

77. Cīvaradānādīnīti cīvarādiparikkhāradānaṃ sandhāyāha. Yo hi cīvarādike aṭṭha parikkhāre, pattacīvarameva vā sotāpannādiariyassa, puthujjanasseva vā sīlasampannassa datvā “idaṃ parikkhāradānaṃ anāgate ehibhikkhubhāvāya paccayo hotū”ti patthanaṃ paṭṭhapesi, tassa ca sati adhikārasampattiyaṃ buddhānaṃ sammukhībhāve iddhimayaparikkhāralābhāya saṃvattatīti veditabbaṃ. Vassasatikattherā viya ākappasampannāti adhippāyo.

77. ‘Gifts such as robes, and so forth’ refers to giving requisites such as robes and so forth. For one who gives the eight requisites beginning with robes—or just the bowl and robes—to a noble one such as a stream-enterer, or even to a virtuous worldling, and then establishes the aspiration, ‘May this gift of requisites become a condition for attaining the state of an ehi-bhikkhu in the future,’ it should be understood that when the supporting conditions are fulfilled in the presence of the Buddhas, it conduces to the attainment of requisites created by psychic power. The meaning is that he will be endowed with dignified deportment like the Elder of a Hundred Years.

Sandassesīti suṭṭhu paccakkhaṃ katvā dassesi. Idhalokatthanti idhalokabhūtaṃ khandhapañcakasaṅkhātamatthaṃ. Paralokatthanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Dassesīti sāmaññalakkhaṇato, salakkhaṇato ca dassesi. Tenāha “anicca”ntiādi. Tattha hutvā abhāvato aniccanti dassesi. Udayabbayapaṭipīḷanato dukkhanti dassesi. Avasavattanato anattāti dassesi. Ime ruppanādilakkhaṇā pañcakkhandhāti rāsaṭṭhena khandhe dassesi. Ime cakkhādisabhāvā [P 2.0094] nissattanijjīvaṭṭhena aṭṭhārasa dhātuyoti dassesi. Imāni cakkhādisabhāvāneva dvārārammaṇabhūtāni dvādasa āyatanānīti dassesi. Ime [M 2.0072] avijjādayo jarāmaraṇapariyosānā dvādasa paccayadhammā paṭiccasamuppādoti dassesi. Rūpakkhandhassa heṭṭhā vuttanayena paccayato cattāri, khaṇato ekanti imāni pañca lakkhaṇāni dassesi. Tathāti iminā “pañca lakkhaṇānī”ti padaṃ ākaḍḍhati. Dassentoti iti-saddo nidassanattho, evanti attho. Nirayanti aṭṭhamahānirayasoḷasaussadanirayappabhedaṃ sabbaso nirayaṃ dassesi. Tiracchānayoninti apadadvipadacatuppadabahuppadādibhedaṃ migapasupakkhisarīsapādivibhāgaṃ nānāvidhaṃ tiracchānalokaṃ. Pettivisayanti khuppipāsikavantāsikaparadattūpajīvinijjhāmataṇhikādibhedabhinnaṃ nānāvidhaṃ petasattalokaṃ. Asurakāyanti kālakañcikāsuranikāyaṃ. Evaṃ tāva duggatibhūtaṃ paralokatthaṃ vatvā idāni sugatibhūtaṃ vattuṃ “tiṇṇaṃ kusalānaṃ vipāka”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Vehapphale subhakiṇṇeyeva saṅgahetvā asaññīsu, arūpīsu ca sampattiyā dassetabbāya abhāvato duviññeyyatāya “navannaṃ brahmalokāna”ntveva vuttaṃ.

‘He demonstrated’ (sandassesi) means he demonstrated by making it thoroughly evident, as if directly perceived. ‘The substance of this world’ (idhalokattha) means the substance designated as the five aggregates, which constitute this world. ‘The substance of the next world’ (paralokattha)—here too, the same method applies. ‘He demonstrated’ (dassesi)—he demonstrated both in terms of general characteristics and specific characteristics. Therefore, he said, ‘impermanent,’ and so forth. Therein, he demonstrated impermanence due to its non-existence after having come into being. He demonstrated suffering due to the oppression of arising and vanishing. He demonstrated non-self due to its not being subject to control. These five aggregates, characterized by affliction and so forth, he demonstrated as aggregates in the sense of a heap. These eighteen elements, being the natures of the eye and so forth, he demonstrated in the sense of being without a living being and without a soul. These twelve sense bases, being precisely the natures of the eye and so forth, and serving as doors and objects, he demonstrated. These twelve conditional factors, beginning with ignorance and ending with aging-and-death, he demonstrated as dependent origination. For the form aggregate, he demonstrated these five characteristics: four from the perspective of condition, according to the method stated previously, and one from the perspective of moment. By ‘thus’ (tathā), he draws in the phrase ‘five characteristics.’ ‘Showing’ (dassento)—the word ‘iti’ here is for the purpose of illustration, meaning ‘thus.’ ‘Hell’ (niraya)—he demonstrated all hells, including the eight great hells and the sixteen secondary hells, with their various divisions. ‘The animal realm’ (tiracchānayoni)—he demonstrated the various kinds of animal worlds, divided into footless, two-footed, four-footed, and many-footed creatures, such as beasts, livestock, birds, reptiles, and so forth. ‘The realm of ghosts’ (pettivisaya)—he demonstrated the various kinds of ghostly beings, differentiated as those tormented by hunger and thirst, those who live on vomit, those who subsist on what is given by others, and those consumed by craving. ‘The host of demons’ (asurakāya)—the host of Kālakañjika demons. Having thus spoken of the next world as a state of woe, he now speaks of it as a state of happiness, saying, ‘the result of three wholesome deeds,’ and so forth. The Vehapphala realm is included within the Subhakiṇṇa realm; and because there is no attainment to be shown in the non-percipient and formless realms, and because they are difficult to understand, it is simply said, ‘the nine Brahmā worlds.’

Gaṇhāpesīti [V 2.0064] te dhamme samādinne kārāpesi.

‘Caused to take up’ (gaṇhāpesi)—he caused them to undertake those teachings.

Samuttejanaṃ nāma samādinnadhammānaṃ yathā anupakārakā dhammā parihāyanti, pahīyanti ca, upakārakā dhammā parivaḍḍhanti, visujjhanti ca, tathā nesaṃ ussāhuppādananti āha “abbhussāhesī”ti. Yathā pana taṃ ussāhuppādanaṃ hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “idhalokatthañcevā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tāsetvā tāsetvāti paribyattabhāvāpādanena tejetvā tejetvā. Adhigataṃ viya katvāti yesaṃ katheti, tehi tamatthaṃ paccakkhato anubhuyyamānaṃ viya katvā. Veneyyānañhi buddhehi pakāsiyamāno [P 2.0095] attho paccakkhatopi pākaṭataro hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Tathā hi bhagavā evaṃ thomīyati –

‘Arousing’ (samuttejana) means generating enthusiasm in those who have undertaken the teachings, so that unhelpful qualities decline and are abandoned, and helpful qualities increase and become purified—thus it is said, ‘he aroused’ (abbhussāhesi). To illustrate how such arousal occurs, it is stated, ‘for the welfare in this world,’ and so forth. ‘By repeatedly making them skilled’ (tāsetvā tāsetvā) means by repeatedly sharpening and energizing them, bringing them to a state of complete clarity. ‘Making it as if attained’ (adhigataṃ viya katvā) means making that meaning appear as if directly experienced by those to whom he speaks. Indeed, for those capable of being guided, the meaning explained by the Buddhas appears even clearer than direct perception. Thus, the Blessed One is praised in this way:

“Ādittopi ayaṃ loko, ekādasahi aggibhi;

Na tathā yāti saṃvegaṃ, sammohapaliguṇṭhito.

“Though this world is ablaze with eleven fires, one shrouded in delusion does not feel such urgency.

Sutvādīnavasaññuttaṃ, yathā vācaṃ mahesino;

Paccakkhatopi buddhānaṃ, vacanaṃ suṭṭhu pākaṭa”nti.

Having heard the word of the Great Sage concerning danger, the word of the Buddhas is much clearer even than direct perception.”

Tenāha “dvattiṃsakammakāraṇapañcavīsatimahābhayappabhedañhī”tiādi. Dvattiṃsakammakāraṇāni “hatthampi chindantī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.178) dukkhakkhandhasutte āgatanayena [M 2.0073] veditabbāni. Pañcavīsatimahābhayāni “jātibhayaṃ jarābhayaṃ byādhibhayaṃ maraṇabhaya”ntiādinā (cūḷani. 123) tattha tattha sutte āgatanayena veditabbāni. Āghātanabhaṇḍikā adhikuṭṭanakaḷiṅgaraṃ, yaṃ “accādhāna”ntipi vuccati.

Therefore, he said, ‘for it includes the thirty-two grounds for punishment and the twenty-five kinds of great fear,’ and so forth. The thirty-two grounds for punishment should be understood according to the method that comes in the Dukkhakkhandha Sutta (MN 13), beginning with ‘they cut off his hands.’ The twenty-five great fears should be understood according to the method that comes in various suttas, beginning with ‘the fear of birth, the fear of aging, the fear of sickness, the fear of death’ (Cnd 123). An ‘execution block’ (āghātanabhaṇḍikā) is a log for excessive beating, which is also called ‘overloading’.

Paṭiladdhaguṇena codesīti “taṃtaṃguṇādhigamena ayampi tumhehi paṭiladdho, ānisaṃso ayampī”ti paccakkhato dassento “kiṃ ito pubbe evarūpaṃ atthī”ti codento viya ahosi. Tenāha “mahānisaṃsaṃ katvā kathesī”ti.

‘He exhorted by means of the attained quality’ (paṭiladdhaguṇena codesi) means that by showing directly, ‘This too has been attained by you through the acquisition of such and such qualities, and this benefit as well,’ he was as if challenging, ‘Was there anything like this before?’ Therefore, it is said, ‘He spoke having made it of great benefit.’

Tappaccayañca kilamathanti saṅkhārapavattihetukaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sattasantāne uppajjanakaparissamaṃ saṃvighātaṃ vihesaṃ. Idhāti heṭṭhā paṭhamamaggādhigamatthāya kathāya. Sabbasaṅkhārūpasamabhāvato santaṃ. Atittikaraparamasukhatāya paṇītaṃ. Sakalasaṃsārabyasanato tāyanatthena [V 2.0065] tāṇaṃ. Tato nibbindahadayānaṃ nilīyanaṭṭhānatāya leṇaṃ. Ādi-saddena gatipaṭisaraṇaṃ paramassāsoti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho.

‘And fatigue due to that cause’ (tappaccayañca kilamathaṃ) means the exhaustion, disturbance, and affliction arising in each being’s continuum, caused by the proceeding of formations. ‘Here’ (idha) refers to the discourse below for the attainment of the first path. It is peaceful because it is the subsiding of all formations. It is sublime on account of the supreme bliss that is never wearisome. It is a shelter (tāṇa) in the sense of protecting from the entire disaster of saṃsāra. For those whose hearts are disenchanted, it is a cave (leṇa) in the sense of being a place of hiding. By the word ‘etc.’ (ādi-saddena), such terms as destination, refuge, and supreme consolation are included.

Mahājanakāyapabbajjāvaṇṇanā

An Account of the Going Forth of the Great Multitude

80. Saṅghappahonakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ abhāvā “saṅghassa aparipuṇṇattā”ti vuttaṃ. Dve aggasāvakā eva hi tadā ahesuṃ.

80. Because there was an absence of monks sufficient for a Saṅgha, it was said, ‘because the Saṅgha was incomplete.’ For at that time, there were only the two chief disciples.

Cārikāanujānanavaṇṇanā

An Account of the Permission for Wandering

86. “Kadā [P 2.0096] udapādī”ti pucchaṃ “sambodhito”tiādinā saṅkhepato vissajjetvā puna taṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “bhagavā kirā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pitu saṅgahaṃ karonto vihāsi sambodhito “satta saṃvaccharāni satta māse satta divase”ti ānetvā sambandho, tañca kho veneyyānaṃ tadā abhāvato. Kilañjehi bahi chādāpetvā, vatthehi anto paṭicchādāpetvā, upari ca vatthehi chādāpetvā, tassa heṭṭhā suvaṇṇa…pe… vitānaṃ kārāpetvā. Mālāvacchaketi pupphamālāhi vacchākārena veṭhite. Gandhantareti cāṭibharitagandhassa antare. Pupphānīti cāṭiādibharitāni jalajapupphāni ceva caṅkotakādibharitāni thalajapupphāni ca.

86. To the question, ‘When did it arise?’, having answered briefly with ‘from enlightenment,’ and so on, it was then said, ‘The Blessed One, it is said…,’ and so on, to show this in detail. The connection is made by bringing in the phrase ‘seven years, seven months, and seven days’ from his enlightenment, during which he dwelt showing kindness to his father; and this was because at that time there were no receptive beings. Having had the outside covered with mats, the inside covered with cloth, and the top also covered with cloth, and having had a golden… canopy made beneath it. ‘With garlands like calves’ (mālāvacchake) means encircled with flower garlands in the shape of a calf. ‘Amidst perfumes’ (gandhantare) means amidst a vessel filled with perfume. ‘Flowers’ (pupphāni) means water-born flowers filling vessels and so on, and land-born flowers, such as caṅkotaka, filling baskets and so on.

Kāmañcāyaṃ [M 2.0074] rājā buddhapitā, tathāpi buddhā nāma lokagaruno, na te kenaci vase vattetabbā, atha kho te eva pare attano vase vattenti, tasmā rājā “nāhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ demī”ti āha.

Although this king is the Buddha's father, nevertheless, Buddhas are the teachers of the world; they are not to be brought under anyone's power, but rather they themselves bring others under their power. Therefore, the king said, 'I will not give the Saṅgha of monks.'

Dānamukhanti dānakaraṇūpāyaṃ, dānavattanti attho. Na dāni me anuññātāti idāni me dānaṃ na anuññātā, no na anujānantīti attho.

‘The entrance to giving’ (dānamukhaṃ) means the means of giving; the meaning is the practice of giving. ‘Now it is not permitted to me’ means ‘Now giving is not permitted to me’; the meaning is not that they do not permit it.

Paritassanajīvitanti dukkhajīvikā dāliddiyanti attho.

‘A life of agitation’ (paritassanajīvitaṃ) means a painful livelihood; the meaning is poverty.

Sabbesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pahosīti bhagavato aṭṭhasaṭṭhi ca bhikkhusatasahassānaṃ bhāgato dātuṃ pahosi, na sabbesaṃ pariyattabhāvena. Tenāha “senāpatipi attano deyyadhammaṃ adāsī”ti. Jeṭṭhikaṭṭhāneti jeṭṭhikadeviṭṭhāne.

‘It was sufficient for all the monks’ means that he was able to give a share to the Blessed One and sixty-eight hundred-thousand monks, but not in a way that was sufficient for all. Therefore, it is said, ‘The commander-in-chief also gave his own gift.’ ‘In the position of the eldest’ (jeṭṭhikaṭṭhāne) means in the position of the chief queen.

Tatheva [V 2.0066] katvāti carapurise ṭhapetvā. Sucinti suddhaṃ. Paṇītanti uḷāraṃ, bhāvanapuṃsakañcetaṃ “ekamanta”ntiādīsu (pārā. 2) viya. Bhañjitvāti madditvā, pīḷetvāti [P 2.0097] attho. Jātisappikhīrādīhiyevāti antojātasappikhīrādīhiyeva, amhākameva gāviādito gahitasappiādīhiyevāti attho.

‘Having done so in the same way’ means after stationing spies. ‘Pure’ (suciṃ) means clean. ‘Excellent’ (paṇītaṃ) means superior, and this is a neuter of state, like in ‘to one side’ (ekamantaṃ) and so on (Pārā. 2). ‘Having broken’ (bhañjitvā) means having crushed; the meaning is having pressed. ‘Only with genuine ghee, milk, etc.’ (jātisappikhīrādīhiyeva) means only with home-produced ghee, milk, etc.; the meaning is only with ghee and so on taken from our own cows, etc.

90. Parāpavādaṃ, parāpakāraṃ, sītuṇhādibhedañca guṇāparādhaṃ khamati sahati adhivāsetīti khanti. Sā pana yasmā sīlādīnaṃ paṭipakkhadhamme savisesaṃ tapati santapati vidhamatīti paramaṃ uttamaṃ tapo. Tenāha “adhivāsanakhanti nāma paramaṃ tapo”ti. “Adhivāsanakhantī”ti iminā dhammanijjhānakkhantito viseseti. Titikkhanaṃ khamanaṃ titikkhā.Akkharacintakā hi khamāyaṃ titikkhā-saddaṃ vaṇṇenti. Tenevāha “khantiyā eva vevacana”ntiādi. Sabbākārenāti santapaṇītanipuṇasivakhemādinā sabbappakārena. So pabbajito nāma na hoti pabbājitabbadhammassa apabbājanato. Tasseva tatiyapadassa vevacanaṃ anatthantarattā.

90. Patience (khanti) is to bear, endure, and tolerate another’s blame, another’s harm, the variations of cold and heat, and offenses against virtue. And since it especially burns, torments, and dispels the states that are opposed to virtue and so on, it is the supreme, the highest austerity (tapo). Therefore it is said, ‘Patient forbearance is the highest austerity.’ By this phrase ‘patient forbearance,’ it is distinguished from the patience of reflecting on the Dhamma. Forbearance (titikkhā) is tolerating, being patient. For etymologists explain the word ‘forbearance’ (titikkhā) in the sense of patience (khamā). Therefore it is said, ‘It is just a synonym for patience,’ and so on. ‘In every way’ means in all ways: as peaceful, sublime, subtle, safe, secure, and so on. He is not a renunciant (pabbajito) because he has not renounced what is to be renounced. The third term is a synonym for this, as it has no different meaning.

“Na hī”tiādinā taṃ evatthaṃ vivarati. Uttamatthena paramanti vuccati para-saddassa seṭṭhavācakattā, “puggalaparoparaññū”tiādīsu (a. ni. 7.68; netti. 118) viya. Paranti aññaṃ. Idāni para-saddaṃ aññapariyāyameva gahetvā atthaṃ dassetuṃ “atha vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Malassāti pāpamalassa. Apabbājitattāti anīhaṭattā anirākatattā[M 2.0075]. Samitattāti nirodhitattā tesaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ. “Samitattā hi pāpānaṃ samaṇoti pavuccatī”ti hi vuttaṃ.

The passage beginning ‘For not…’ clarifies that very meaning. In the sense of ‘highest,’ it is called ‘supreme’ (paramaṃ), because the word ‘para’ denotes what is best, as in passages such as ‘one who knows the higher and lower among persons’ (AN 7.68; Netti 118). ‘Paraṃ’ means another. Now, taking the word ‘para’ only as a synonym for ‘other,’ the passage beginning ‘Or else…’ was stated to show the meaning. ‘Of stain’ (malassa) means of the stain of evil. ‘Because he has not renounced’ (apabbājitattā) means because he has not removed it, not cast it out. ‘Because they are stilled’ (samitattā) means because those evil states are suppressed. For it is said: ‘Because his evils are stilled (samita), he is called a “recluse” (samaṇa).’

Apica bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ pātimokkhaṃ uddisanto pātimokkhakathāya ca sīlapadhānattā sīlassa ca visesato doso paṭipakkhoti [P 2.0098] tassa niggaṇhanavidhiṃ dassetuṃ ādito “khantī paramaṃ tapo”ti āha, tena aniṭṭhassa paṭihananūpāyo vutto, titikkhāgahaṇena pana iṭṭhassa, tadubhayenapi uppannaṃ ratiṃ abhibhuyya viharatīti ayamattho dassitoti. Taṇhāvānassa vūpasamanato nibbānaṃ paramaṃ vadanti buddhā. Tattha khantiggahaṇena payogavipattiyā abhāvo dassito, titikkhāgahaṇena āsayavipattiyā abhāvo. Tathā khantiggahaṇena parāparādhasahatā, titikkhāgahaṇena paresu anaparajjhanā dassitā. Evaṃ kāraṇamukhena anvayato pātimokkhaṃ dassetvā idāni byatirekato taṃ dassetuṃ “na hī”tiādi vuttaṃ, tena yathā sattānaṃ jīvitā voropanaṃ, pāṇileḍḍudaṇḍādīhi vibādhanañca “parūpaghāto, paraviheṭhana”nti vuccati, evaṃ tesaṃ mūlasāpateyyāvaharaṇaṃ, dāraparāmasanaṃ, visaṃvādanaṃ, aññamaññabhedanaṃ, pharusavacanena mammaghaṭṭanaṃ, niratthakavippalāpo[V 2.0067], parasantakagijjhanaṃ, ucchedavindanaṃ, micchābhinivesanañcaupaghāto, viheṭhanañca hotīti yassa kassaci akusalassa kammapathassa, kammassa ca karaṇena pabbajito, samaṇo ca na hotīti dasseti.

Furthermore, when the Blessed One was reciting the Pātimokkha to the monks, because the discourse on the Pātimokkha has virtue as its chief subject, and because aversion is specifically the opponent of virtue, to show the method for restraining it, he said at the outset, ‘Patience is the highest austerity.’ By this, the method for repelling the undesirable was stated; by the inclusion of forbearance, the method for repelling the desirable was stated. By both, this meaning is shown: that one dwells having overcome the delight that has arisen. The Buddhas say that Nibbāna is supreme because it is the calming of the sewing of craving. Here, by the inclusion of patience, the absence of failure in application is shown; by the inclusion of forbearance, the absence of failure in disposition is shown. Likewise, by the inclusion of patience, the enduring of others’ offenses is shown; by the inclusion of forbearance, not offending others is shown. Having thus shown the Pātimokkha positively through its causes, now to show it negatively, the passage beginning ‘For not…’ was stated. By this it is shown that just as depriving beings of life and injuring them with one’s fists, with clods, with sticks, and so on is called ‘harming others, harassing others,’ so too the taking of their essential property, intercourse with their wives, deceiving them, causing division between them, striking at their vitals with harsh speech, useless chatter, coveting others’ property, finding annihilationism, and wrong adherence are also harm and harassment. By the doing of any unwholesome course of action or deed whatsoever, one is not a renunciant and not a recluse.

Sabbākusalassāti sabbassāpi dvādasākusalacittuppādasaṅgahitassa sāvajjadhammassa. Karaṇaṃ nāma tassa attano santāne uppādananti tappaṭikkhepato akaraṇaṃ “anuppādana”nti vuttaṃ. “Kusalassā”ti idaṃ “etaṃ buddhāna sāsana”nti vakkhamānattā ariyamaggadhamme, tesañca sambhārabhūte tebhūmakakusaladhamme sambodhetīti āha “catubhūmakakusalassā”ti. Upasampadāti upasampādanaṃ, taṃ pana tassa samadhigamoti āha “paṭilābho”ti. Cittajotananti cittassa pabhassarabhāvakaraṇaṃ sabbaso parisodhanaṃ. Yasmā [P 2.0099] aggamaggasamaṅgino cittaṃ sabbaso pariyodapīyati nāma, aggaphalakkhaṇe pana pariyodapitaṃ hoti puna pariyodapetabbatāya abhāvato, iti pariniṭṭhitapariyodapanataṃ sandhāyāha “taṃ pana arahattena hotī”ti. Sabbapāpaṃ pahāya tadaṅgādivasenevāti adhippāyo. “Sīlasaṃvarenā”ti hi iminā tebhūmakassāpi saṅgahe itarappahānānampi saṅgaho hotīti, evañca katvā sabbaggahaṇaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti[M 2.0076]. Samathavipassanāhīti lokiyalokuttarāhi samathavipassanāhi. Sampādetvāti nipphādetvā. Sampādanañcettha hetubhūtāhi phalabhūtassa sahajātāhipi, pageva purimasiddhāhīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Of all that is unwholesome' refers to all blameworthy phenomena included in the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness. 'Doing' means the arising of those states in one's own continuity, and its rejection, non-doing, is called 'non-arising.' 'Of the wholesome' here refers to the phenomena of the noble path, as it is said, 'This is the teaching of the Buddhas,' and also includes the wholesome phenomena of the three planes that serve as its requisites. Thus, it is called 'the wholesome of the four planes.' 'Accomplishment' means attainment, and here it refers to the acquisition of that state. 'Purification of the mind' means making the mind radiant, its thorough cleansing. For the mind of one endowed with the supreme path is indeed thoroughly purified, but at the moment of the supreme fruition, it is purified, there being no need for it to be purified again. Hence, referring to this state of completed purification, it is said, 'That is achieved through Arahantship.' The intention here is to abandon all evil by way of abandonment by substitution and so on. For by 'restraint by virtue,' with the inclusion of the wholesome of the three planes, the other types of abandonment are also included. Thus, the use of the word 'all' is justified. 'Through serenity and insight' refers to both mundane and supramundane serenity and insight. 'Having accomplished' means bringing to fulfillment. Here, accomplishment is to be understood as being by those that have become causes, by those co-nascent with what has become the fruit, and even more so by those previously perfected.

Kassacīti hīnādīsu kassaci sattassa kassaci upavādassa, tena davakamyatāyapi upavadanaṃ paṭikkhipati. Upaghātassa akaraṇanti etthāpi “kassacī”ti ānetvā sambandho. Kāyenāti ca nidassanamattametaṃ manasāpi paresaṃ anatthacintanādivasena upaghātakaraṇassa vajjetabbattā. Kāyenāti vā ettha arūpakāyassāpi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo, na copanakāyakarajakāyānameva. Pa atimokkhanti pakārato ativiya sīlesu mukhyabhūtaṃ. “Atipamokkha”nti tameva padaṃ upasaggabyattayena vadati. Evaṃ bhedato padavaṇṇanaṃ katvā tatvato vadati “uttamasīla”nti. “Pāti vā”tiādinā pālanato rakkhaṇato ativiya mokkhanato ativiya mocanato pātimokkhanti dasseti. “Pāpā ati mokkhetīti atimokkho”ti nimittassa kattubhāvena upacaritabbato. Yo vā nanti yo vā puggalo naṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ pāti [P 2.0100] samādiyitvā avikopento rakkhati, taṃ “pātī”ti laddhanāmaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarasīle ṭhitaṃ mokkhetīti pātimokkhanti ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato pana pātimokkhapadassa attho visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (visuddhi. ṭī. 1.14) vuttanayena veditabbo.

'To anyone'—in the context of lowly beings and so on, to any being, in regard to any reproach—thereby he rejects reproach even out of a desire for playfulness. The non-committing of harm—here too, 'to anyone' is brought in and connected. 'With the body'—this is merely an illustration, for harming others by way of thinking of their disadvantage and so on, even with the mind, should be avoided. Or 'with the body'—here, the inclusion of the formless body should also be understood, not just the physical body and the body born of action. 'Pātimokkha' means that which is exceedingly the foremost among virtues in its mode. 'Atipamokkha'—that very word speaks of it with a change of prefix. Thus, having given an etymological explanation of the word, he states its essence as 'the highest virtue.' By 'pāti vā' and so on, he shows it is 'pātimokkha' because it protects, because it guards, because it exceedingly releases, because it exceedingly liberates. 'From evil, it exceedingly releases, thus atimokkha'—this should be understood figuratively, with the sign being treated as the agent. Or, whatever person undertakes that Pātimokkha restraint virtue and guards it without breaking—it releases that person, who is thus called a 'protector' and is established in the Pātimokkha restraint virtue; hence 'pātimokkha.' This is the summary here; in detail, however, the meaning of the word Pātimokkha should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary to the Visuddhimagga (Vism-ṭīkā 1.14).

Mattaññutāti [V 2.0068] bhojane mattaññutā, sā pana visesato paccayasannissitasīlavasena gahetabbāti āha “paṭiggahaṇaparibhogavasena pamāṇaññutā”ti. Ājīvapārisuddhisīlavasenāpi gayhamāne “pariyesanavissajjanavasenā”tipi vattabbaṃ. Saṅghaṭṭanavirahitanti janasaṅghaṭṭanavirahitaṃ, nirajanasambādhaṃ vivittanti attho. Catupaccayasantoso dīpito paccayasantosatāsāmaññena itaradvayassāpi lakkhaṇahāranayena jotitabhāvato. “Aṭṭhasamāpattivasibhāvāyā”ti iminā payojanadassanavasena yadatthaṃ vivittasenāsanasevanaṃ icchitaṃ, so adhicittānuyogo vutto. Aṭṭha samāpattiyo cettha vipassanāya pādakabhūtā adhippetā, na yā kācīti sakalassāpi adhicittānuyogassa jotitabhāvo veditabbo.

'Moderation' means moderation in food; but that should especially be understood by way of the virtue dependent on the requisites; thus, he says, 'knowing the measure by way of receiving and consuming.' When taken by way of the virtue of purity of livelihood, it should also be said 'by way of seeking and giving up.' 'Free from crowding' means free from the crowding of people, meaning secluded, without the throng of people. Contentment with the four requisites is explained, because the nature of the other two is also illuminated by way of applying the characteristic, through the generality of contentment with requisites. 'For the sake of mastery over the eight attainments'—by this, showing the purpose for which the frequenting of secluded lodgings is desired, the application to the higher mind is stated. Here, the eight attainments are intended as the foundation for insight, not just any attainments; thus, it should be understood that the entire application to the higher mind is illuminated.

Devatārocanavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Deities' Announcement.

91. Ettāvatāti [M 2.0077] ettakena suttapadesena. Tatthāpi ca iminā…pe… kathanena suppaṭividdhabhāvaṃ pakāsetvāti yojanā. Ca-saddo byatirekattho, tena idāni vuccamānatthaṃ ullaṅgeti. Ekamidāhanti ekaṃ ahaṃ. Idaṃ-saddo nipātamattaṃ. Ādi-saddena “bhikkhave samaya”nti evamādi pāṭho saṅgahito. Ahaṃ bhikkhave ekaṃ samayanti evaṃ pettha padayojanā.

91. 'Ettāvatā' means by this much, by this portion of the Sutta. Here too, by this... explanation, its thorough penetration is revealed—this is the construction. The word 'ca' conveys the sense of exclusion; thus, it transcends the meaning now being stated. 'Ekamidāhaṃ' means 'one I.' The word 'idaṃ' is merely a particle. The word 'ādi' includes passages such as 'Bhikkhus, at one time' and so on. 'Ahaṃ bhikkhave ekaṃ samayaṃ' is the phrasing of the words here.

Subhagavaneti subhagattā subhagaṃ, sundarasirikattā[P 2.0101], sundarakāmattā vāti attho. Subhagañhi taṃ sirisampattiyā, sundare cettha kāme manussā patthenti. Bahujanakantatāyapi taṃ subhagaṃ. Vanayatīti vanaṃ, attasampattiyā attani sinehaṃ uppādetīti attho. Vanute iti vā vanaṃ, attasampattiyā eva “maṃ paribhuñjathā”ti satte yācati viyāti attho. Subhagañca taṃ vanañcāti subhagavanaṃ, tasmiṃ subhagavane. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃpana kiṃ iminā papañcenāti “evaṃ nāmake vane”ti vuttaṃ. Kāmaṃ sālarukkhopi “sālo”ti vuccati, yo koci rukkhopi vanappati jeṭṭhakarukkhopi. Idha pana pacchimo eva adhippetoti āha “vanappatijeṭṭhakassa mūle”ti. Mūlasamugghātavasenāti anusayasamucchindanavasena.

'In Subhagavana' means: it is 'subhaga' (delightful) because of its good fortune, its beautiful splendor, or its beautiful desires. For it is delightful due to its wealth of splendor, and people there long for beautiful pleasures. It is also delightful because it is pleasing to many people. 'It entreats (vanayati), thus it is a forest (vana)'; the meaning is: due to its own prosperity, it generates affection for itself. Or, 'it asks (vanute), thus it is a forest (vana)'; the meaning is: due to its own prosperity, it seems to ask beings, 'Enjoy me.' It is both delightful (subhaga) and a forest (vana), thus 'Subhagavana'; in that Subhagavana. In the commentary, however, it is asked, 'Why this elaboration?' and stated, 'in a forest with such a name.' Indeed, a sāla tree is called 'sāla,' as is any tree, or the chief tree of the forest. Here, however, only the last is intended; thus he said: 'at the root of the chief tree of the forest.' 'By way of uprooting the root' means by way of eradicating the underlying tendencies.

Na vihāyantīti akuppadhammatāya na vijahanti. “Na kañci sattaṃ tapantīti atappā”ti idaṃ tesu tassā samaññāya niruḷhatāya vuttaṃ, aññathā sabbepi suddhāvāsā na kañci sattaṃ tapantīti atappā nāma siyuṃ. “Na vihāyantī”tiādinibbacanesupi eseva nayo. Sundaradassanāti dassanīyāti ayamatthoti āha “abhirūpā”tiādi. Sundarametesaṃ dassananti [V 2.0069] sobhanametesaṃ cakkhunā dassanaṃ, viññāṇena dassanaṃ pīti attho. Sabbe heva…pe… jeṭṭhā pañcavokārabhave tato visiṭṭhānaṃ abhāvato.

'Na vihāyantī' means they do not fall away due to their unshakeable nature. 'Na kañci sattaṃ tapantīti atappā'—this is said because that designation, 'the Untormenting,' is established in reference to them, meaning 'they do not torment any being.' Otherwise, all the Pure Abodes could be called 'Atappā' since they do not torment any being. The same principle applies to the explanations of 'Na vihāyantī' and so on. 'Sundaradassanā' means pleasing to see—this is the meaning, as stated: 'beautiful' and so on. 'Sundarametesaṃ dassanaṃ' means their appearance is splendid; their seeing with the eye, and also their seeing with consciousness, is delightful—this is the meaning. Indeed, all... are the foremost in the five-constituent existence, since there is none more distinguished than them.

Sattannaṃ buddhānaṃ vasenāti sattannaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ apadānavasena. Avihehi ajjhiṭṭhena ekena avihābrahmunā kathitā tehi sabbehi kathitā nāma hontīti vuttaṃ “tathā avihehī”ti. Eseva nayo sesesupi. Tenāha bhagavā “devatā maṃ etadavocu”nti. Yaṃ pana pāḷiyaṃ “anekāni devatāsatānī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ [P 2.0102] pacchā attano sāsane [M 2.0078] visesaṃ adhigantvā tattha uppannānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Anusandhidvayampīti dhammadhātupadānusandhi, devatārocanapadānusandhīti duvidhaṃ anusandhiṃ. Niyyātentoti nigamento. Yaṃ panettha atthato avibhattaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

'By way of the seven Buddhas' means by way of the accounts of the seven Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones. When spoken by one Aviha brahmā at the request of the Aviha gods, it is as if spoken by all of them; thus it is said 'so by the Aviha gods.' This is the same method in the remaining cases. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'The deities told me this.' However, what is stated in the Pāḷi text as 'many hundreds of deities' was all said with reference to those who later attained distinction in his Dispensation and were reborn there. 'Both connections' means the two kinds of connection: the connection with the term 'dhammadhātu' and the connection with the term 'the Deities' Announcement.' 'Concluding' means bringing it to a conclusion. Whatever herein is not analyzed in terms of meaning, that is easily understood.

Mahāpadānasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

Elucidation of the Hidden Meanings in the Exposition of the Great Discourse on the Lineage.

2. Mahānidānasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Exposition of the Great Discourse on Causation.

Nidānavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Introduction.

95. Janapadinoti [P 2.0103][V 2.0070][M 2.0079] janapadavanto, janapadassa vā issarasāmino rājakumārā gottavasena kurū nāma. Tesaṃ nivāso yadi eko janapado, kathaṃ bahuvacananti āha “ruḷhisaddenā”ti. Akkharacintakā hi īdisesu ṭhānesu yutte viya īdisaliṅgavacanāni icchanti. Ayamettha ruḷhi yathā aññatthāpi “aṅgesu viharati, mallesu viharatī”ti ca. Tabbisesanepi janapadasadde jātisadde ekavacanameva. Aṭṭhakathācariyā panāti pana-saddo visesatthajotano, tena “puthuatthavisayatāya evetaṃ puthuvacana”nti “bahuke panā”tiādinā vakkhamānaṃ visesaṃ joteti. Sutvāti mandhātumahārājassa ānubhāvadassanānusārena paramparānugataṃ kathaṃ sutvā. Anusaṃyāyantenāti anuvicarantena. Etesaṃ ṭhānanti candimasūriyamukhena cātumahārājikabhavanamāha. Tenāha “tattha agamāsī”tiādi. Soti mandhātumahārājā. Tanti cātumahārājikarajjaṃ. Gahetvāti sampaṭicchitvā. Puna pucchi pariṇāyakaratanaṃ.

95. 'Janapadino' means 'possessing a country,' or the princes who are lords and masters of a country, called the Kurus by lineage. If their dwelling is one country, how is it in the plural? He said, 'by conventional usage.' For grammarians, in such cases, desire such gender and number forms as are appropriate. This is the convention here, just as elsewhere, 'he dwells among the Aṅgas, he dwells among the Mallās.' Even when it is a qualifier for them, the words 'janapada' and 'jāti' are only in the singular. 'The commentary teachers, however'—the word 'pana' (however) indicates a special meaning; thereby it illuminates the special point to be stated later with 'because of the diversity of meanings, this is in the plural,' and 'but many,' etc. 'Having heard' means having heard a story passed down through tradition in accordance with the display of the majesty of King Mandhātu. 'Anusaṃyāyantena' means 'investigating.' 'The place of these' refers to the realm of the Four Great Kings, by way of the moon and sun. Therefore, he said, 'there he went,' etc. 'He' is King Mandhātu. 'That' is the kingdom of the Four Great Kings. 'Having taken' means 'having accepted.' Again, he asked about the jewel of the advisor.

Dovārikabhūmiyaṃ tiṭṭhanti sudhammāya devasabhāya, devapurassa ca catūsu dvāresu ārakkhāya adhigatattā. “Dibbarukkhasahassapaṭimaṇḍita”nti [P 2.0104] idaṃ “cittalatāvana”ntiādīsupi yojetabbaṃ.

They stand in the role of gatekeepers for the Sudhammā divine assembly hall, having been appointed to guard the four gates of the divine city. 'Adorned with a thousand celestial trees'—this should also be connected with 'the Cittalatā Grove,' and so on.

Pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāsīti bhassitvā pathaviyā āsannaṭṭhāne aṭṭhāsi. Na hi cakkaratanaṃ bhūmiyaṃ patati, tathāṭhitañca nacirasseva antaradhāyi tenattabhāvena cakkavattiissariyassa abhāvato. “Cirataraṃ kālaṃ ṭhatvā”ti apare. Rājā ekakova agamāsi attano ānubhāvena. Manussabhāvoti manussagandhasarīranissandādimanussabhāvo. Pāturahosīti devaloke pavattivipākadāyino aparāpariyāya vedanīyassa kammassa katokāsattā sabbadā soḷasavassuddesikatā mālāmilāyanādi dibbabhāvo pāturahosi. Tadā manussānaṃ asaṅkheyyāyukatāya [V 2.0071] sakkarajjaṃ kāretvā. “Kiṃ me iminā upaddharajjenā”ti atricchatāya atittova. Manussaloke utuno kakkhaḷatāya vātātapena phuṭṭhagatto kālamakāsi.

Having slipped, it stood in a place near the earth. For the wheel-treasure does not fall to the ground; and having stood thus, it soon disappeared because of the absence of the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch in that existence. 'Having stood for a very long time,' say others. The king went all alone by his own power. 'Human state' means the human state characterized by human scent, bodily secretions, and so on. 'He appeared' means: because in the deva world an opportunity was made for kamma that gives its result in a subsequent existence and is to be experienced in a later period, the divine state appeared, characterized by always appearing as sixteen years old, having unfading garlands, and so on. At that time, when humans had an incalculable lifespan, having ruled as Sakka, and thinking, 'What is this half-kingdom to me?', he remained unsatisfied due to excessive greed. In the human world, due to the harshness of the climate, his body being afflicted by wind and heat, he passed away.

Avayavesu [M 2.0080] siddho viseso samudāyassa visesako hotīti ekampi raṭṭhaṃ bahuvacanena vohariyati.

A distinction established among the parts becomes a distinguisher of the whole; thus, even a single kingdom is referred to in the plural.

Da-kārena atthaṃ vaṇṇayanti niruttinayena. Kammāsoti kammāsapādo vuccati uttarapadalopena yathā “rūpabhavo rūpa”nti. Kathaṃ pana so “kammāsapādo”ti vuccatīti āha “tassa kirā”tiādi. Damitoti ettha kīdisaṃ damanaṃ adhippetanti āha “porisādabhāvato paṭisedhito”ti. “Ime pana therāti majjhimabhāṇakā”ti keci. Apare pana “aṭṭhakathācariyā”ti, “dīghabhāṇakā”ti vadanti. Ubhayathāpi cūḷakammāsadammaṃ sandhāya tathā vadanti. Yakkhiniputto hi kammāsapādo alīnasattukumārakāle (cariyā. 2.75) bodhisattena tattha damito. Sutasomakāle (jā. 2.21.371) pana bārāṇasirājā porisādabhāvapaṭisedhanena yattha damito, taṃ mahākammāsadammaṃ nāma. “Putto”ti vatvā “atrajo”ti vacanaṃ orasaputtabhāvadassanatthaṃ.

They explain the meaning by means of the letter 'da' according to the etymological method. 'Kammāso' is called 'Kammāsapāda' through the elision of the final part, just as 'rūpabhavo' becomes 'rūpa.' But how is he called 'Kammāsapāda'? He says, 'of him, indeed,' etc. As for 'damito' (tamed), what kind of taming is intended here? He says, 'prevented from the state of being a man-eater.' Some say, 'But these elders are the reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya.' Others, however, say, 'the commentary teachers,' or 'the reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya.' In both cases, they speak thus with reference to the Lesser Taming of Kammāsa. For Kammāsapāda, the son of the yakkhiṇī, was tamed there by the Bodhisatta when he was Prince Alīnasattu. But in the time of Sutasoma, where the king of Bārāṇasī was tamed by being prevented from the state of being a man-eater, that is called the Greater Taming of Kammāsa. Having said 'son,' the word 'atrajo' (one's own offspring) is for the purpose of showing he was an heir born of the breast.

Yehi āvasitappadeso “kururaṭṭha”nti nāmaṃ labhi, te uttarakuruto āgatamanussā tattha rakkhitaniyāmeneva pañca sīlāni rakkhiṃsu. Tesaṃ diṭṭhānugatiyā pacchimajanatāti so desadhammavasena avicchedato pavattamāno kuruvattadhammoti [P 2.0105] paññāyittha. Ayañca attho kurudhammajātakena dīpetabbo. So aparabhāge paṭhamaṃ yattha saṃkiliṭṭho jāto, taṃ dassetuṃ “kururaṭṭhavāsīna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Yattha bhagavato vasanokāsabhūto koci vihāro na hoti, tattha kevalaṃ gocaragāmakittanaṃ nidānakathāya pakati yathā taṃ sakkesu viharati devadahaṃ nāma sakyānaṃ nigamoti imamatthaṃ dassento “avasanokāsato”tiādimāha.

The region inhabited by them received the name 'Kururaṭṭha.' Those people who came from Uttarakuru observed the five precepts there as if by a protected rule. Following their example, that which proceeded unbrokenly for later generations due to the custom of the land came to be known as the 'Kuruvattadhamma.' And this meaning should be illustrated by the Kurudhamma Jātaka. To show where he was first born defiled in a later part, it is said, 'of the inhabitants of Kururaṭṭha,' and so forth. Where there is no monastery that is a place for the Blessed One to dwell, the mere mention of the alms-resort village is the custom in the introductory story, just as in 'he dwells among the Sakyans, in a market town of the Sakyans named Devadaha.' To show this meaning, he said, 'from the absence of a dwelling place,' and so on.

“Āyasmā”ti vā “devānaṃ piyā”ti vā “tatra bhava”nti vā piyasamudāhāro esoti āha “āyasmāti piyavacanameta”nti. Tayidaṃ piyavacanaṃ garugāravavasena vuccatīti āha “gāravavacanameta”nti.

'Venerable,' or 'dear to the gods,' or 'your honor'—this is an endearing expression. Therefore, he said, '“Venerable” is an endearing expression.' This endearing expression is spoken out of respect and reverence; thus he said, 'It is an expression of reverence.'

Atidūraaccāsannavajjanena nātidūranāccāsannaṃ nāma gahitaṃ, taṃ pana avakaṃsato ubhinnaṃ pasāritahatthānaṃ [V 2.0072] saṅghaṭṭanena veditabbaṃ. Cakkhunā cakkhuṃ āhacca daṭṭhabbaṃ hoti, tenāpi agāravameva kataṃ hoti. Gīvaṃ parivattetvāti parivattanavasena gīvaṃ pasāretvā.

'Not too far, not too close' is understood by avoiding what is too far and too close. This, however, should be known by the touching of two outstretched hands from a lowered position. One should see by meeting eye with eye; even by this, disrespect is committed. 'Having turned the neck' means stretching out the neck by way of turning.

Kulasaṅgahatthāyāti [M 2.0081] kulānuddayatāvasena kulānaṃ anuggaṇhanatthāya sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ nikkhipanto viya bhikkhapaṭiggaṇhanena tesaṃ mahato puññābhisandassa jananena. Paṭisammajjitvāti antevāsikehi sammajjanaṭṭhānaṃ sakkaccakāritāya puna sammajjitvā. Tikkhattunti “ādito paṭṭhāya anta”ntiādinā vuttacaturākārūpasañhite tayo vāre, tenassa dvādasakkhattuṃ sammasitabhāvamāha.

'For the sake of supporting families' means: for the purpose of assisting families out of compassion for them, by generating for them a great flow of merit through the acceptance of alms, like one depositing a bundle worth a thousand. 'Having swept again' means: having swept again because the place for sweeping had been carefully prepared by the resident pupils. 'Three times' means three times combined with the four aspects described beginning with 'from the beginning to the end,' thereby stating that it was swept twelve times in all.

Amhākaṃ bhagavato gambhīrabhāveneva kathitattā sesabuddhehipi evameva kathitoti dhammanvaye ṭhatvā vuttaṃ “sabbabuddhehi…pe… kathito”ti. Sālindanti saparibhaṇḍaṃ. “Sineruṃ ukkhipanto viyā”ti [P 2.0106] iminā tādisāya desanāya sudukkarabhāvamāha. Suttameva “suttantakatha”nti āha dhammakkhandhabhāvato. Yathā vinayapaṇṇattibhūmantarasamayantarānaṃ vijānanaṃ anaññasādhāraṇaṃ sabbaññutañāṇasseva visayo, evaṃ antadvayavinimuttassa kārakavedakarahitassa paccayākārassa vibhajanaṃ pīti dassetuṃ “buddhānañhī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha ṭhānānīti kāraṇāni. Gajjitaṃ mahantaṃ hotīti taṃ desetabbasseva anekavidhatāya, duviññeyyatāya ca nānānayehi pavattamānaṃ desanāgajjitaṃ mahantaṃ vipulaṃ, bahubhedañca hoti. Ñāṇaṃ anupavisatīti tato eva desanāñāṇaṃ desetabbadhamme vibhāgaso kurumānaṃ anu anu pavisati, tena anupavissa ṭhitaṃ viya hotīti attho. Buddhañāṇassa mahantabhāvo paññāyatīti evaṃvidhassa nāma dhammassa desakaṃ, paṭivedhakañcāti buddhānaṃ desanāñāṇassa, paṭivedhañāṇassa ca uḷārabhāvo pākaṭo hoti. Ettha ca kiñcāpi “sabbaṃ vacīkammaṃ buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇapubbaṅgamaṃ ñāṇānuparivatta”nti (mahāni. 69, 169; cūḷani. 85; paṭi. ma. 3.5; netti. 14) vacanato sabbāpi bhagavato desanā ñāṇarahitā natthi, sīhasamānavuttitāya sabbattha samānappavatti. Desetabbavasena pana desanā visesato ñāṇena anupaviṭṭhā, gambhīratarā ca hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kathaṃ pana vinayapaññattiṃ patvā desanā tilakkhaṇabbhāhatā suññatapaṭisaṃyuttā hotīti? Tatthāpi sannisinnaparisāya ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ pavattamānā desanā saṅkhārānaṃ aniccatādivibhāvanaṃ, sabbadhammānaṃ attattaniyatābhāvappakāsanañca hoti. Tenevāha “anekapariyāyena [P 2.0107] dhammiṃ kathaṃ katvā”tiādi.

Because our Blessed One spoke with profundity, it is said that all other Buddhas also spoke in the same way. Thus, standing in the lineage of the Dhamma, it is said: 'All Buddhas... have spoken.' `Sālinda` means together with its appurtenances. The phrase 'like lifting Mount Sineru' illustrates how difficult such a teaching is to deliver. The term `suttantakathā` refers to the discourse itself, as it constitutes a portion of the Dhamma. Just as the understanding of the distinctions of Vinaya ordinances, grounds, and times is uniquely the domain of omniscient knowledge, so too is the analysis of conditioned genesis, which is free from the two extremes and devoid of a doer and an experiencer. To demonstrate this, the passage beginning 'for the Buddhas' is introduced. Here, `ṭhānāni` means causes. `The roar is great` signifies that because of the manifold nature of what is to be taught and its difficulty of comprehension, the roar of the teaching, unfolding in many ways, is great, vast, and of many kinds. `Knowledge enters into it` means that the knowledge of teaching, making a division of the Dhamma to be taught, penetrates it again and again. Thus, it is as if knowledge remains dwelling within it. The greatness of a Buddha’s knowledge is made known: as the teacher and penetrator of such a Dhamma, the sublime nature of the Buddhas' teaching knowledge and penetrative knowledge becomes manifest. And here, although it is said, 'All verbal action of the Blessed Buddha is preceded by knowledge and revolves around knowledge' (Mahāni. 69, 169; Cūḷani. 85; Paṭi. Ma. 3.5; Netti. 14), meaning that none of the Blessed One’s teachings are devoid of knowledge, and due to his lion-like conduct, it proceeds uniformly everywhere, it should be understood that the teaching, in terms of what is to be taught, is especially permeated by knowledge and is even more profound. But how does the teaching, upon reaching disciplinary rules, become stamped with the three characteristics and associated with emptiness? Here too, the teaching, proceeding in accordance with the disposition of the assembled audience, involves the analysis of formations as impermanent, etc., and declares the absence of selfhood and what belongs to a self in all phenomena. Hence it is said: 'Having delivered a discourse on the Dhamma in many ways...' and so on.

Āpajjāti [M 2.0082] patvā yathā ñāṇakoñcanādaṃ vissajjeti, evaṃ pāpuṇitvā.

`Āpajjati` means 'having reached'; just as one releases the heron's cry of knowledge, so it means 'having attained.'

Pamāṇātikkameti [V 2.0073] aparimāṇatthe “yāvañcidaṃ tena bhagavatā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.4) viya. Aparimeyyabhāvajotano hi ayaṃ yāva-saddo. Tenāha “atigambhīro attho”ti. Avabhāsatīti ñāyati upaṭṭhāti. Ñāṇassa tathā upaṭṭhānañhi sandhāya “dissatī”ti vuttaṃ. Nanu esa paṭiccasamuppādo ekantagambhīrova, tattha kasmā gambhīrāvabhāsatā jotitāti? Saccametaṃ, ekantagambhīratādassanatthameva panassa gambhīrāvabhāsaggahaṇaṃ. Tasmā aññattha labbhamānaṃ catukoṭikaṃ byatirekamukhena nidassetvā taṃ evassa ekantagambhīrataṃ vibhāvetuṃ “ekañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Etaṃ natthīti agambhīro, agambhīrāvabhāso cāti etaṃ dvayaṃ natthi, tena yathādassite catukoṭike pacchimā eka koṭi labbhatīti dasseti. Tenāha “ayañhī”tiādi.

`Pamāṇātikkameti` means 'goes beyond measure' in the sense of being immeasurable, as in phrases like 'as far as this was spoken by the Blessed One' (Dī. Ni. 1.4). For this word `yāva` illuminates the state of being immeasurable. Hence it is said, 'The meaning is exceedingly profound.' `Avabhāsati` means 'it is known, it presents itself.' The phrase 'it is seen' is used with reference to the manifestation of knowledge in this way. Now, is not this dependent origination entirely profound? Why then is its profound appearance illuminated? Indeed, it is so. The mention of its profound appearance is solely for the purpose of revealing its absolute profundity. Therefore, having shown elsewhere the fourfold logical alternative (catukoṭika) through the method of exclusion, it is stated beginning with 'for one thing' to clarify that very absolute profundity. 'This does not exist' means it is not profound, and there is no appearance of profundity—these two do not exist. Thus, he shows that in the fourfold alternative as presented, the last alternative is obtained. Hence it is said, beginning with 'for this.'

Yehi gambhīrabhāvehi paṭiccasamuppādo “gambhīro”ti vuccati, te catūhi upamāhi ulliṅgento “bhavaggaggahaṇāyā”tiādimāha. Yathā bhavaggaṃ hatthaṃ pasāretvā gahetuṃ na sakkā dūrabhāvato, evaṃ saṅkhārādīnaṃ avijjādipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho pākatikañāṇena gahetuṃ na sakkā. Yathā sineruṃ bhinditvā miñjaṃ pabbatarasaṃ pākatikapurisena nīharituṃ na sakkā, evaṃ paṭiccasamuppādagate dhammatthādike pākatikañāṇena bhinditvā vibhajja paṭivijjhanavasena jānituṃ na sakkā. Yathā mahāsamuddaṃ pākatikapurisassa bāhudvayena padhārituṃ na sakkā, evaṃ vepullaṭṭhena mahāsamuddasadisaṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṃ pākatikañāṇena desanāvasena padhārituṃ na sakkā. Yathā mahāpathaviṃ parivattetvā [P 2.0108] pākatikapurisassa pathavojaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkā, evaṃ “itthaṃ avijjādayo saṅkhārādīnaṃ paccayā hontī”ti tesaṃ paccayabhāvo pākatikañāṇena nīharitvā gahetuṃ na sakkāti. Evaṃ catubbidhagambhīratāvasena catasso upamā yojetabbā. Pākatikañāṇavasena cāyamatthayojanā katā diṭṭhasaccānaṃ tattha paṭivedhasabhāvato, tathāpi yasmā sāvakānaṃ, paccekabuddhānañca tattha sappadesameva ñāṇaṃ, buddhānaṃyeva nippadesaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “buddhavisayaṃ pañha”ntiādi.

The states of profundity by which dependent origination is called 'profound' are indicated with four similes, beginning with 'for grasping the peak of existence.' Just as one cannot grasp the peak of existence by stretching out a hand, due to its distance, so too the fact that formations and so on have arisen and come about from ignorance and so on as conditions cannot be grasped by ordinary knowledge. Just as an ordinary person cannot split Mount Sineru and extract its marrow, the essence of the mountain, so too the principles and meanings contained in dependent origination cannot be known by way of penetration through ordinary knowledge, by analyzing and dividing them. Just as an ordinary person cannot fathom the great ocean with their two arms, so too dependent origination, which is like the great ocean in its vastness, cannot be fathomed by ordinary knowledge by way of teaching. Just as an ordinary person cannot overturn the great earth and extract its essential property, so too the causal relationship—that 'in this way, ignorance and other factors are conditions for formations and so on'—cannot be extracted and grasped by ordinary knowledge. Thus, these four similes should be applied by way of the fourfold profundity. This explanation is given from the standpoint of ordinary knowledge, for those who have seen the truths are by nature able to penetrate it. However, since the knowledge of disciples and Paccekabuddhas in this matter is only partial, while only that of the Buddhas is complete, it is said: 'The question falls within the Buddha’s domain,' and so on.

Ussādentoti [M 2.0083] paññāya ukkaṃsento, uggaṇhantoti attho. Apasādentoti nibbhacchanto, niggaṇhantoti attho.

`Ussādento` means 'extolling with wisdom,' or 'praising.' `Apasādento` means 'rebuking,' or 'censuring.'

Ussādanāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on Extolling

Tenāti mahāpaññābhāvena. Tatthāti therassa satipi uttānabhāve, paṭiccasamuppādassaaññesaṃ [V 2.0074] gambhīrabhāve. Subhojanarasapuṭṭhassāti sundarena bhojanarasena positassa. Katayogassāti nibaddhapayogena kataparicayassa. Mallapāsāṇanti mallehi mahabbaleheva ukkhipitabbapāsāṇaṃ. Kuhiṃ imassa bhāriyaṭṭhānanti kasmiṃ passe imassa pāsāṇassa garutarappadesoti tassa sallahukabhāvaṃ dīpento vadati.

‘Therefore’ (tena) means by reason of great wisdom. ‘There’ (tattha) means: although for the elder the matter was clear, for others dependent origination was profound. ‘Nourished with the taste of good food’ (subhojanarasapuṭṭhassa) means nourished by excellent food flavors. ‘Of one who has made effort’ (katayogassa) means one who has become familiar through constant application. ‘A wrestler’s stone’ (mallapāsāṇaṃ) means a stone that must be lifted even by wrestlers of great strength. ‘Where is the heavy part of this?’ (kuhiṃ imassa bhāriyaṭṭhānaṃ) means ‘on which side is the heavier area of this stone?’—thus he speaks, indicating its lightness.

Timirapiṅgaleneva dīpenti tassa mahāvipphārabhāvato. Tenāha “tassa kirā”tiādi. Pakkuthatīti pakkuthantaṃ viya parivattati parito vivattati. Lakkhaṇavacanañhetaṃ. Piṭṭhiyaṃ sakalinapadakāpiṭṭhaṃ. Kāyūpapannassāti mahatā kāyena upetassa, mahākāyassāti attho.

They illuminate even with a dark and tawny flame because of his great radiance. Therefore it is said, ‘Indeed, his…’ and so on. ‘Pakkuthati’ means it turns around, revolving all around as if boiling. This is a descriptive term. `Piṭṭhiyaṃ` (on the back) means the back of the entire sole of the foot. ‘Kāyūpapannassa’ means endowed with a great body; that is the meaning of ‘of a great body’.

Piñchavaṭṭīti piñchakalāpo. Supaṇṇavātanti nāgaggahaṇādīsu pakkhapapphoṭanavasena uppajjanakavātaṃ.

‘Piñchavaṭṭī’ means a bundle of tail-feathers. ‘Supaṇṇa-wind’ (supaṇṇavātaṃ) means the wind that arises from the flapping of its wings when seizing serpents and the like.

Pubbūpanissayasampattikathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Discourse on the Attainment of a Supportive Previous Condition

“Pubbūpanissayasampattiyā”tiādinā uddiṭṭhakāraṇāni vitthārato vivarituṃ “ito kirā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha itoti ito kappato[P 2.0109]. Satasahassimeti satasahassame. Haṃsāvatī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi jātanagaraṃ. Dhurapattānīti bāhirapattāni, yāni dīghatamāni.

To explain in detail the causes stated by ‘by the attainment of a supportive previous condition’ (pubbūpanissayasampattiyā) and so on, ‘Indeed, from this’ (ito kira) and so on was said. Herein, ‘from this’ (ito) means from this aeon. ‘A hundred thousand’ (satasahassime) means the hundred-thousandth. There was a city named Haṃsāvatī, the city of his birth. ‘Dhurapattānī’ means the outer leaves, which are the longest.

Kaniṭṭhabhātāti vemātikabhātā kaniṭṭho yathā amhākaṃ bhagavato nandatthero. Buddhānañhi sahodarā bhātaro nāma na honti. Kathaṃ jeṭṭhā tāva na uppajjanti, kaniṭṭhānaṃ pana asambhavo eva. Bhoganti vibhavaṃ. Upasantoti corajanitasaṅkhobhavūpasamena upasanto janapado.

‘Younger brother’ (kaniṭṭhabhātā) means a younger half-brother, like the Venerable Nanda, our Blessed One’s younger brother. For Buddhas do not have full brothers. How so? Elder ones, for a start, are not born; as for younger ones, there is simply no possibility. ‘Wealth’ (bhogaṃ) means riches. ‘Pacified’ (upasanto) means a country pacified by the calming of the disturbance caused by thieves.

Dve sāṭake nivāsetvāti sāṭakadvayameva attano kāyaparihārikaṃ katvā itaraṃ sabbasambhāraṃ attato mocetvā.

‘Having put on two robes’ (dve sāṭake nivāsetvā) means having made just the pair of robes one’s own body covering, and having relinquished all other possessions from oneself.

Pattaggahaṇatthanti antopakkhittauṇhabhojanattā aparāparaṃ hatthe parivattentassa pattaggahaṇatthaṃ. Uttarisāṭakanti attano uttarisāṭakaṃ. Etāni [M 2.0084] pākaṭaṭṭhānānīti etāni yathāvuttāni bhagavato desanāya pākaṭāni therassa puññakaraṇaṭṭhānāni.

‘For the purpose of holding the bowl’ (pattaggahaṇatthaṃ) means for the purpose of holding the bowl, as one turns it over repeatedly in the hand due to the hot food placed inside. ‘Upper robe’ (uttarisāṭakaṃ) means one’s own upper robe. ‘These are the evident places’ (etāni pākaṭaṭṭhānāni) means these, as stated, are the evident places of merit-making for the elder according to the Blessed One’s teaching.

Paṭisandhiṃ [V 2.0075] gahetvāti amhākaṃ mahābodhisattassa paṭisandhiggahaṇadivase eva paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā.

‘Having taken rebirth’ (paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā) means having taken rebirth on the very day of our Great Bodhisatta’s conception.

Titthavāsādivaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Dwellings of Sectarians and So Forth

Uggahaṇaṃ pāḷiyā uggaṇhanaṃ. Savanaṃ atthasavanaṃ. Paripucchanaṃ gaṇṭhiṭṭhānesu atthaparipucchanaṃ. Dhāraṇaṃ pāḷiyāpi pāḷiatthassapi citte ṭhapanaṃ. Sabbañcetaṃ idha paṭiccasamuppādavasena veditabbaṃ.

‘Learning’ (uggahaṇaṃ) means learning the Pāli texts. ‘Listening’ (savanaṃ) means listening to the meaning. ‘Questioning’ (paripucchanaṃ) means inquiring about the meaning in places where there are difficulties. ‘Retention’ (dhāraṇaṃ) means fixing both the Pāli texts and their meanings in the mind. And all this should be understood here in terms of Dependent Origination.

Sotāpannānañca…pe... upaṭṭhātitattha sammohaviddhaṃsanena “yaṃ kiñci samudayadhammaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhamma”nti (dī. ni. 1.298; saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 16; cūḷani. 4, 7, 8) attapaccakkhavasena upaṭṭhānato. Nāmarūpaparicchedoti saha paccayena nāmarūpassa paricchijja avabodho.

For stream-enterers [...] by the dispelling of delusion there, through the personal realization of ‘Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease’ (DN I 298; SN V 1081; Vin Mv 16; Cūḷani 4, 7, 8). ‘The delimitation of name-and-form’ (nāmarūpapariccheda) means the clear understanding of name-and-form by distinguishing it together with its conditions.

Paṭiccasamuppādagambhīratāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Profundity of Dependent Origination

“Atthagambhīratāyā”tiādinā saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ [P 2.0110] “tatthā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Jātipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭhoti jātipaccayato sambhūtaṃ hutvā sahitassa attano paccayānurūpassa jarāmaraṇassa uddhaṃ uddhaṃ āgatabhāvo, anupavattatthoti attho. Atha vā sambhūtaṭṭho ca samudāgataṭṭho ca sambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho. “Na jātito jarāmaraṇaṃ na hoti,” na ca jātiṃ vinā “aññato hotī”ti hi jātipaccayasambhūtaṭṭho vutto, itthañca jātito samudāgacchatīti jātipaccayasamudāgataṭṭho, yā yā jāti yathā yathā paccayo hoti, tadanurūpapātubhāvoti attho. So anupacitakusalasambhārānaṃ ñāṇassa tattha appatiṭṭhatāya agādhaṭṭhena gambhīro. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

To explain the meaning stated concisely by ‘due to the profundity of meaning’ and so on, the passage beginning ‘herein’ and so on is begun. ‘The state of having arisen and come together from the condition of birth’ (jātipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭha) means the state of aging-and-death having arisen from the condition of birth, and its subsequent repeated occurrence in accordance with its own condition, upward and upward; this is the meaning of uninterrupted existence. Alternatively, the state of having arisen and the state of having come together constitute the state of having arisen and come together. For it is said that ‘aging-and-death does not occur without birth,’ nor does it arise ‘from elsewhere’ apart from birth—thus, the state of having arisen from the condition of birth is stated. And in this way, it comes together from birth—thus, the state of having come together through the condition of birth means a manifestation in accordance with whatever birth, in whatever way, serves as a condition; this is the meaning. For those who have not accumulated the provisions of the wholesome, knowledge does not take hold there; thus, it is profound due to its unfathomable depth. The same principle applies to the remaining terms.

Avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ paccayaṭṭhoti yenākārena yadavatthā avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo hoti. Yena hi pavattiākārena, yāya ca avatthāya avatthitā avijjā tesaṃ tesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo hoti, tadubhayassapi duravabodhanīyato avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ navahi ākārehi paccayaṭṭho [M 2.0085] anupacitakusalasambhārānaṃ ñāṇassa tattha appatiṭṭhatāya agādhaṭṭhena gambhīro. Esa nayo sesapadesupi.

‘The conditionality of formations by ignorance’ (avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ paccayaṭṭha) means the manner and the state in which ignorance is a condition for formations. Indeed, in whatever manner of occurring and in whatever state ignorance is established, it becomes a condition for those various formations. Because both of these aspects are difficult to understand, the state of ignorance being a condition for formations in nine ways is profound due to its unfathomable nature, since knowledge does not become established there for those who have not accumulated the provisions of the wholesome. The same principle applies to the remaining terms.

Katthaci [V 2.0076] anulomato desīyati, katthaci paṭilomatoti idha pana paccayuppādā paccayuppannuppādasaṅkhāto anulomo, paccayanirodhā paccayuppannanirodhasaṅkhāto ca paṭilomo adhippeto. Ādito pana paṭṭhāya antagamanaṃ anulomo, antato ca ādigamanaṃ paṭilomoti adhippeto. Ādito paṭṭhāya anulomadesanāya, antato paṭṭhāya paṭilomadesanāya ca tisandhi catusaṅkhepo. “Ime bhikkhave cattāro āhārā kiṃ nidānā”tiādikāya (saṃ. ni. 2.11) ca vemajjhato paṭṭhāya paṭilomadesanāya, “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā”tiādikāya (saṃ. ni. 2.43, 45) anulomadesanāya ca dvisandhi tisaṅkhepo. “Saṃyojaniyesu [P 2.0111] bhikkhave dhammesu assādānupassino viharato taṇhā pavaḍḍhati, taṇhāpaccayā upādāna”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.53, 57) ekasandhi dvisaṅkhepo. Ekaṅgo hi paṭiccasamuppādo desito. Labbhateva hi so “tatra bhikkhave sutavā ariyasāvako paṭiccasamuppādaṃyeva sādhukaṃ yoniso manasi karoti ‘iti imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti…pe… nirujjhatī’ti. Sukhavedaniyaṃ bhikkhave phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhavedanā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.62) imassa suttassa vasena veditabbo. Iti tena tena kāraṇena tathā tathā pavattetabbattā paṭiccasamuppādo desanāya gambhīro. Tenāha “ayaṃ desanāgambhīratā”ti. Na hi tattha sabbaññutañāṇato aññaṃ ñāṇaṃ patiṭṭhaṃ labhati.

In some places it is taught in the forward order, in some places in the reverse order. Here, however, the forward order (anuloma) is intended as the arising of the conditioned from the condition, and the reverse order (paṭiloma) as the cessation of the conditioned from the cessation of the condition. From the beginning to the end is intended as the forward order, and from the end back to the beginning as the reverse order. By means of the teaching in the forward order starting from the beginning, and the teaching in the reverse order starting from the end, there are three connections and four summaries. And by means of the teaching in the reverse order starting from the middle, as in ‘Monks, what is the source of these four nutriments?’ (SN 12.11), and the teaching in the forward order, as in ‘Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; from contact as condition, feeling arises’ (SN 12.43, 45), there are two connections and three summaries. In passages like ‘Monks, when one dwells contemplating gratification in things that fetter, craving increases; from craving as condition, clinging arises’ (SN 12.53, 57), there is one connection and two summaries. Indeed, Dependent Origination is taught as a single limb. For it can be understood through this discourse: ‘Therein, monks, a learned noble disciple carefully and wisely attends to Dependent Origination itself: “When this exists, that comes to be… when this ceases, that ceases.”’ And also: ‘Monks, dependent on a contact that is felt as pleasant, pleasant feeling arises’ (SN 12.62). Thus, because Dependent Origination must be expounded in various ways for various reasons, it is profound in its teaching. Therefore it is said, ‘This is the profundity of the teaching.’ Indeed, no other knowledge finds a footing there apart from the knowledge of omniscience.

“Avijjāya panā”tiādīsu jānanalakkhaṇassa ñāṇassa paṭipakkhabhūto avijjāya aññāṇaṭṭho. Ārammaṇassa paccakkhakaraṇena dassanabhūtassa paṭipakkhabhūto adassanaṭṭho. Yenesā attano sabhāvena dukkhādīnaṃ yāthāvasarasaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ na deti chādetvā pariyonandhitvā tiṭṭhati, so tassā saccāsampaṭivedhaṭṭho. Abhisaṅkharaṇaṃ saṃvidhānaṃ, pakappananti attho. Āyūhanaṃ sampiṇḍanaṃ, sampayuttadhammānaṃ attano kiccānurūpatāya rāsīkaraṇanti attho. Apuññābhisaṅkhārekadeso sarāgo. Añño virāgo. Rāgassa vā appaṭipakkhabhāvato rāgappavaḍḍhako, rāguppattipaccayo [M 2.0086] ca sabbopi apuññābhisaṅkhāro sarāgo. Itaro tabbidūrabhāvato virāgo. “Dīgharattaṃ hetaṃ bhikkhave assutavato puthujjanassa ajjhositaṃ mamāyitaṃ parāmaṭṭhaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti” (saṃ. ni. 2.61) attaparāmāsassa [P 2.0112] viññāṇaṃ visesato vatthu vuttanti viññāṇassa suññataṭṭho gambhīro. Attā vijānāti saṃsaratīti sabyāpāratāsaṅkantiabhinivesabalavatāya abyāpāraasaṅkantipaṭisandhipātubhāvaṭṭhā ca gambhīrā. Nāmarūpassa paṭisandhikkhaṇe ekatova uppādo ekuppādo, pavattiyaṃ visuṃ visuṃ yathārahaṃ ekuppādo. Nāmassa rūpena, rūpassa ca nāmena asampayogato vinibbhogo nāmassa nāmena[V 2.0077], rūpassa ca rūpena ekaccassa ekaccena avinibbhogo (nāmassa nāmena avinibbhogo vibha. mūlaṭī. 242) yojetabbo. Ekuppādekanirodhehi avinibbhoge adhippete so rūpassa ca ekakalāpapavattino rūpena labbhatīti. Atha vā ekacatuvokārabhavesu nāmarūpānaṃ asahavattanato aññamaññaṃ vinibbhogo, pañcavokārabhave sahavattanato avinibbhogo ca veditabbo.

In the phrase ‘By ignorance,’ and so on, the meaning of ignorance is ‘not knowing,’ which is the opposite of knowledge, whose characteristic is knowing. Its meaning is ‘not seeing,’ which is the opposite of the ‘seeing’ that consists in directly apprehending an object. Because it does not allow the true nature of suffering, etc., to be penetrated as it really is, but instead stands concealing and enveloping it, its meaning is the ‘non-penetration of the truths.’ ‘Forming’ (abhisaṅkharaṇa) means preparing, arranging, or contriving. ‘Accumulating’ (āyūhana) means amassing, the meaning being the gathering of associated states into a mass in accordance with their respective functions. A portion of demeritorious formations is accompanied by lust; another is without lust. Or, because it does not oppose lust but rather increases it, and because every demeritorious formation is a condition for the arising of lust, it is accompanied by lust. The other, being far removed from that, is without lust. ‘For a long time, monks, this has been clung to, made mine, and adhered to by the uninstructed ordinary person: “This is mine, this I am, this is my self”’ (Saṃyutta Nikāya II, 61). Because consciousness is specifically said to be the basis for self-grasping, the meaning of the emptiness of consciousness is profound. The ideas ‘the self knows,’ ‘it transmigrates,’ are profound due to the strength of adherence to the views of agency and transmigration, and because of the state of the manifestation of rebirth-linking without an agent and without transmigration. At the moment of rebirth-linking, the simultaneous arising of name-and-form is a single arising. During the course of existence, they arise separately, each appropriately, as a single arising. Due to the non-conjunction of name with form, and of form with name, there is separation; the non-separation of one from another should be applied in the case of name with name, and form with form (the non-separation of name from name is to be construed thus, Vibhaṅga Mūlaṭīkā 242). When non-separation is intended in terms of single arising and single cessation, this is found for form with form in the case of that which occurs in a single material group. Alternatively, in the one-constituent and four-constituent existences, since name-and-form do not occur together, there is mutual separation; in the five-constituent existence, because they occur together, there is non-separation. This should be understood.

Nāmassa ārammaṇābhimukhaṃ namanaṃ namanaṭṭho. Rūpassa virodhipaccayasamavāye visadisuppatti ruppanaṭṭho. Indriyapaccayabhāvo adhipatiyaṭṭho. “Lokopeso, dvārāpesā, khettaṃ peta”nti vuttalokādiattho cakkhādīsu pañcasu yojetabbo. Manāyatanassa pana lujjanato, manosamphassādīnaṃ dvārakhettabhāvato ca ete atthā veditabbā. Āpāthagatānaṃ rūpādīnaṃ pakāsanayogyatālakkhaṇaṃ obhāsanaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ visayibhāvo, manāyatanassa vijānanaṃ. Saṅghaṭṭanaṭṭho visesato cakkhusamphassādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ, itare channampi yojetabbā.
