Phusanañca phassassa sabhāvo. Saṅghaṭṭanaṃ raso, itare upaṭṭhānākārā. Ārammaṇarasānubhavanaṭṭho rasavasena vutto, vedayitaṭṭho lakkhaṇavasena. Sukhadukkhama ajjhattabhāvo [P 2.0113] yathākkamaṃ tissannaṃ vedanānaṃ sabhāvavasena vutto. “Attā vedayatī”ti abhinivesassa balavabhāvato nijjīvaṭṭho vedanāya gambhīro. Nijjīvāya vā vedanāya vedayitaṃ nijjīvavedayitaṃ, so eva atthoti nijjīvavedayitaṭṭho.

The bending of name towards its object is the meaning of 'bending' (namana). The arising of what is dissimilar in the assemblage of opposing conditions is the meaning of 'being affected' (ruppana). The state of being a condition by way of predominance is the meaning of 'predominance' (adhipatiya). The meanings of 'world,' 'door,' and 'field' as stated—'this is the world, this is the door, this is the field'—should be applied to the five sense faculties beginning with the eye. For the mind-base, however, these meanings should be understood from its perishing, and from its being the door and field for mind-contact and so on. The characteristic of suitability for manifesting forms, etc., that have come into range is the illumination of the eye, etc., and their being an object; for the mind-base, it is cognizing. The meaning of 'striking' applies especially to the five beginning with eye-contact, but it should also be applied to the other six. Touching is the intrinsic nature of contact. Striking is its function, while the others are its manifestations. The meaning of 'experiencing the taste of the object' is stated by way of function; the meaning of 'feeling' is stated by way of characteristic. The internal nature of pleasure, pain, and neutrality, in due order, is stated as the intrinsic nature of the three feelings. Because the adherence to the view 'The self feels' is strong, the meaning of feeling as 'lifeless' is profound. Or, the feeling of what is lifeless is 'lifeless feeling'—that very meaning is the meaning of 'lifeless feeling.'

Sappītikataṇhāya [M 2.0087] abhinanditaṭṭho. Balavatarataṇhāya gilitvā pariniṭṭhāpanaṃ ajjhosānaṭṭho. Itare pana jeṭṭhabhāvaosāraṇasamuddaduratikkamaapāripūrivasena veditabbā. Ādānaggahaṇābhinivesaṭṭhā catunnampi upādānānaṃ samānā, parāmāsaṭṭho diṭṭhupādānādīnameva, tathā duratikkamaṭṭho. “Diṭṭhikantāro”ti (dha. sa. 392) hi vacanato diṭṭhīnaṃ duratikkamatā. Daḷhaggahaṇattā vā catunnampi duratikkamaṭṭho yojetabbo. Yonigatiṭhitinivāsesukhipananti samāse bhummavacanassa alopo daṭṭhabbo. Evañhi tena āyūhanābhisaṅkharaṇapadānaṃ samāso hoti. Yathā tathā jāyanaṃ jātiattho. Tassā pana sannipātato jāyanaṃ sañjātiattho. Mātukucchiṃ okkamitvā viya jāyanaṃ okkantiattho. So jātito nibbattanaṃ nibbattiattho. Kevalaṃ pātubhavanaṃ pātubhāvaṭṭho.

The meaning of 'delighting' is craving accompanied by joy. The meaning of 'adhering' is swallowing and bringing to completion by means of a stronger craving. The others, however, should be understood by way of being foremost, drawing in, being a vast ocean, being hard to cross, and being incomplete. The meanings of taking up, grasping, and adhering are common to all four kinds of clinging. The meaning of misapprehension is only for view-clinging and the like; so too is the meaning of being hard to cross. For, according to the saying, 'the wilderness of views' (Dhammasaṅgaṇi 392), is the difficulty of crossing views. Or, due to firm grasping, the meaning of being hard to cross should also be connected with all four kinds of clinging. In the compound 'yonigatiṭhitinivāsesukhipana,' the non-elision of the locative plural ending should be seen. For thus by that, there is a compound of the terms 'striving' and 'accumulating.' Birth in any way whatsoever is the meaning of 'birth' (jāti). But birth from their conjunction is the meaning of 'conception' (sañjāti). Birth as a descent, as into a mother's womb, is the meaning of 'descent' (okkanti). The production from that birth is the meaning of 'arising' (nibbatti). Mere appearance is the meaning of 'manifestation' (pātubhāva).

Jarāmaraṇaṅgaṃ maraṇappadhānanti tassa maraṇaṭṭhā eva khayādayo gambhīrāti dassitā. Uppannauppannānañhi navanavānaṃ khayena kamena khaṇḍiccādiparipakkapavattiyaṃ loke jarāvohāroti[V 2.0078]. Khayaṭṭho vā jarāya vuttoti daṭṭhabbo. Navabhāvāpagamo hi “khayo”ti [P 2.0114] vattuṃ yuttoti vipariṇāmaṭṭho dvinnampi vasena yojetabbo, santativasena vā jarāya khayavayabhāvā, sammutikhaṇikavasena maraṇassa bhedavipariṇāmaṭṭhā yojetabbā. Avijjādīnaṃ sabhāvo paṭivijjhīyatīti paṭivedho. Vuttañhetaṃ nidānakathāyaṃ “tesaṃ tesaṃ vā tattha tattha vuttadhammānaṃ paṭivijjhitabbo salakkhaṇasaṅkhāto aviparītasabhāvo paṭivedho”ti. (Dī. ni. aṭṭha. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā; abhi. aṭṭha. nidānakathā) so hi avijjādīnaṃ sabhāvo maggañāṇeneva asammohapaṭivedhavasena paṭivijjhitabbato aññāṇassa alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhatāya agādhaṭṭhena gambhīro. Sā sabbāpīti sā yathāvuttā saṅkhepato catubbidhā vitthārato anekappabhedā sabbāpi paṭiccasamuppādassa gambhīratā therassa uttānakā viya upaṭṭhāsi catūhi aṅgehi samannāgatattā. Udāhu aññesampīti “mayhaṃ tāva esa paṭiccasamuppādo uttānako hutvā upaṭṭhāti, kiṃ nu kho aññesampi evaṃ uttānako hutvā upaṭṭhātī”ti mā evaṃ avaca mayāva dinnanaye catusaccakammaṭṭhānavidhimhi ṭhatvā.

The factor of aging-and-death is primarily death, showing that its meanings, such as decay, are profound. For in the world, the term 'aging' is used to describe the gradual process of maturing into broken teeth and so on, through the decay of each newly arisen phenomenon. It should be understood that the meaning of aging is decay. For the departure of newness is fit to be called 'decay'; thus the meaning of transformation should be applied to both aging and death. By way of continuity, there are the states of decay and passing away for aging; by way of the conventional and the momentary, the meanings of breaking up and transformation should be applied for death. Penetration (paṭivedha) is so called because the intrinsic nature of ignorance and other factors is penetrated. As stated in the introductory discourse: 'Penetration is the unperverted intrinsic nature, designated as the specific characteristic, which is to be penetrated, of those various dhammas mentioned in those various places.' For the intrinsic nature of ignorance and other factors is profound with a fathomless meaning, since it is to be penetrated only by the knowledge of the path by way of non-deluded penetration, and since it provides no obtainable footing for ignorance. All of it—that is, all the profundity of dependent origination, which is fourfold in brief and of manifold divisions in detail—appeared to the elder as if it were shallow, because he was endowed with four factors. Or perhaps for others too—'For me, this dependent origination appears as if shallow. I wonder, does it also appear as if shallow for others?' Do not speak thus, while standing in the method I have given, in the procedure of the meditation subject of the Four Truths.

Apasādanāvaṇṇanā

Exposition on Disparagement

Oḷārikanti [M 2.0088] vatthuvītikkamasamatthatāvasena thūlaṃ. Kāmaṃ kāmarāgapaṭighāyeva atthato kāmarāgapaṭighasaṃyojanāni, kāmarāgapaṭighānusayā ca, tathāpi aññoyeva saṃyojanaṭṭho bandhanabhāvato, añño anusayanaṭṭho appahīnabhāvena santāne thāmagamananti katvā, iti kiccavisesavisiṭṭhabhede gahetvā “cattāro kilese”ti ca vuttaṃ. Eseva nayo itaresupi. Aṇusahagateti aṇusabhāvaṃ upagate. Tabbhāvattho hi ayaṃ sahagata-saddo “nandirāgasahagatā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.400; ma. ni. 1.91, 133, 460; 3.374; saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 14; vibha. 203; paṭi. ma. 1.34; 2.30) viya.

Grossness (oḷārika) is coarse in the sense of being capable of transgressing the object. Although sensual desire and aversion are, in essence, the fetters of sensual desire and aversion, and the underlying tendencies of sensual desire and aversion, nevertheless, the meaning of 'fetter' is distinct because of its binding nature, and the meaning of 'underlying tendency' is distinct because it remains with strength in the continuum, not yet abandoned. Thus, having taken them as distinguished by specific functions, it is said, 'four defilements.' The same principle applies to the others as well. 'Accompanied by the subtle' (aṇusahagata) means having attained a subtle nature. For here, the word 'accompanied' (sahagata) signifies the state of being that, just as in instances such as 'accompanied by delight and lust' (Dīgha Nikāya 2.400; Majjhima Nikāya 1.91, 133, 460; 3.374; Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1081; Mahāvagga 14; Vibhaṅga 203; Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.34; 2.30) and so forth.

Yathā uparimaggādhigamanavasena saccasampaṭivedho [P 2.0115] paccayākārapaṭivedhavasena, evaṃ sāvakabodhipaccekabodhisammāsambodhiadhigamanavasenapi saccasampaṭivedho paccayākārapaṭivedhavasenevāti dassetuṃ “kasmā cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sabbathāvāti sabbappakāreneva kiñcipi pakāraṃ asesetvāti attho. Ye katābhinīhārānaṃ mahābodhisattānaṃ vīriyassa ukkaṭṭhamajjhimamudutāvasena bodhisambhārasambharaṇe kālabhedā icchitā, te dassento “cattāri, aṭṭha, soḷasa vā asaṅkhyeyyānī”ti āha, svāyamattho cariyāpiṭakavaṇṇanāya gahetabbo. Sāvako padesañāṇe [V 2.0079] ṭhitoti sāvako hutvā sekkhabhāvato tatthāpi padesañāṇe ṭhito. Buddhānaṃ kathāya “taṃ tathāgato abhisametī”tiādikāya paccanīkaṃ hoti. Anaññasādhāraṇassa hi vasena buddhānaṃ sīhanādo, na aññasādhāraṇassa.

Just as the thorough penetration of the truths by way of attaining the higher paths is through the penetration of the mode of conditions, so too the thorough penetration of the truths by way of attaining the enlightenment of disciples, solitary Buddhas, or perfectly self-enlightened Buddhas is through the penetration of the mode of conditions. To show this, it is said, 'And for what reason?' and so on. 'In every way' (sabbathā) means in every possible manner, without omitting any manner whatsoever. To show the divisions of time desired for accumulating the requisites for enlightenment according to the strong, moderate, or mild effort of great bodhisattvas who have made their resolution, he said, 'four, eight, or sixteen incalculables.' This meaning should be taken from the commentary on the Cariyāpiṭaka. 'A disciple is established in partial knowledge' means that, being a disciple, due to being a trainee, he is established in partial knowledge even there. This is contrary to the discourse of the Buddhas, such as, 'The Tathāgata fully understands that.' For the lion's roar of the Buddhas is based on what is not common to others, not on what is common.

“Vāyamantassevā”ti iminā visesato ñāṇasambhārasambharaṇaṃ paññāpāramitāpūraṇaṃ vadati. Tassa ca sabbampi puññaṃ upanissayo.

By 'of one who is striving,' this specifically refers to the accumulation of the requisites for knowledge and the fulfillment of the perfection of wisdom. And all merit serves as a supporting condition for that.

“Esa devamanussānaṃ, sabbakāmadado nidhi;

Yaṃ yadevābhipatthenti, sabbametena labbhatī”ti. (khu. pā. 8.10) –

This is a treasure for gods and humans, a bestower of all desires; whatever they long for, all is obtained by this. (Khu. Pā. 8.10)

Hi vuttaṃ. Tasmā mahābodhisattānaṃ sabbesampi puññasambhāro yāvadeva ñāṇasambhārattho sammāsambodhisamadhigamasamatthattāti āha “paccayākāraṃ [M 2.0089] …pe… natthī”ti. Idāni paccayākārapaṭivedhasseva vā mahānubhāvatādassanamukhena paṭiccasamuppādasseva paramagambhīrataṃ dassetuṃ “avijjā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Navahi ākārehīti uppādādīhi navahi ākārehi. Avijjā hi saṅkhārānaṃ uppādo hutvā paccayo hoti, pavattaṃ hutvā nimittaṃ, āyūhanaṃ, saṃyogo, palibodho, samudayo, hetu, paccayo hutvā paccayo hoti. Evaṃ saṅkhārādayo viññāṇādīnaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāmagge “kathaṃ [P 2.0116] paccayapariggahe paññā dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ? Avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ uppādaṭṭhiti ca pavattaṭṭhiti ca nimittaṭṭhiti ca āyūhanaṭṭhiti ca saññogaṭṭhiti ca palibodhaṭṭhiti ca samudayaṭṭhiti ca hetuṭṭhiti ca paccayaṭṭhiti ca imehi navahākārehi avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā paccayasamuppannā”tiādi (paṭi. ma. 1.45).

It has been said. Therefore, for all great bodhisattvas, the accumulation of merit is solely for the purpose of the accumulation of wisdom, enabling the attainment of perfect self-enlightenment. Hence, it is stated: 'The mode of conditions... there is not.' Now, to reveal the profound depth of dependent origination itself—either through the penetration of the mode of conditions or through a demonstration of its great power—the words 'ignorance,' etc., are used. 'By nine modes' means by the nine modes such as origination. For ignorance, being the origination of formations, becomes a condition; being their occurrence, it is a sign, an accumulation, a connection, an obstruction, an origin, a cause, and being a condition, it is a condition. Similarly, formations and so on are for consciousness and so on. This is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: 'How is wisdom in the discernment of conditions the knowledge of the stability of phenomena? Ignorance is a condition for formations by these nine modes: the state of origination, the state of occurrence, the state of being a sign, the state of accumulation, the state of connection, the state of obstruction, the state of being an origin, the state of being a cause, and the state of being a condition. Thus, formations are dependently arisen from ignorance as condition.' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.45), and so on.

Tattha navahākārehīti navahi paccayabhāvūpagamanākārehi. Uppajjati etasmā phalanti uppādo, phaluppattiyā kāraṇabhāvo. Sati ca avijjāya saṅkhārā uppajjanti, nāsati, tasmā avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ uppādo hutvā paccayo hoti. Tathā avijjāya sati saṅkhārā pavattanti, nīyanti ca. Yathā ca bhavādīsu khipanti, evaṃ tesaṃ avijjā paccayo hoti. Tathā āyūhanti phaluppattiyā ghaṭenti, saṃyujjanti attano phalena. Yasmiṃ santāne sayaṃ uppannā, taṃ palibundhanti. Paccayantarasamavāye udayanti uppajjanti. Hinoti ca saṅkhārānaṃ kāraṇabhāvaṃ gacchati. Paṭicca avijjaṃ saṅkhārā ayanti pavattantīti evaṃ avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ kāraṇabhāvūpagamanavisesā uppādādayo veditabbā. Tattha tathā saṅkhārādīnaṃ viññāṇādīsu uppādaṭṭhitiādīsupi. Tiṭṭhati etenāti ṭhiti, kāraṇaṃ. Uppādo eva ṭhiti uppādaṭṭhiti[V 2.0080]. Eseva nayo sesesupi. “Paccayo hotī”ti idaṃ idha lokanāthena tadā paccayapariggahassa āraddhabhāvadassanaṃ. So ca ārambho ñāyāruḷho “yathā ca purimehi mahābodhisattehi bodhimūle pavattito, tatheva ca pavattito”ti. Acchariyavegābhihatā dasasahassilokadhātu saṅkampi sampakampīti dassento “diṭṭhamattevā”tiādimāha.

Here, navahākārehi (by nine modes) means by nine ways of undertaking the state of a condition. Uppāda (origination) means 'arises from this,' being the causal state for the origination of the fruit. When ignorance exists, formations arise; when it does not, they do not. Thus, ignorance, by being the origination, becomes a condition for formations. Likewise, when ignorance exists, formations proceed and are led. Just as they cast into existences and so on, so ignorance is a condition for them. Thus they strive, exert themselves for the origination of the fruit, and are connected with their own fruit. They bind the continuity in which they themselves arise. They come into existence and arise in the conjunction of other conditions. And it impels, that is, it assumes the causal state of formations. Because formations proceed dependent on ignorance, thus the specific modes in which ignorance undertakes the causal state of formations—such as origination, etc.—should be understood. Similarly, the origination, persistence, etc., of formations and so on in consciousness and so on should be understood there as well. Ṭhiti (persistence) means 'it persists by this,' being the cause. Origination itself is persistence—origination-persistence. The same principle applies to the rest. By 'is a condition'—here, the Lord of the World shows the commencement of the discernment of conditions at that time. And that commencement accords with reason: 'Just as it was enacted by the previous great bodhisattvas at the root of enlightenment, so too was it enacted here.' Showing that the ten-thousandfold world-system trembled and shook, struck by the force of astonishment, he said, 'As soon as it was seen,' and so on.

Etassa dhammassāti etassa paṭiccasamuppādasaññitassa [P 2.0117] dhammassa. So pana yasmā atthato hetupabhavānaṃ hetu. Tenāha “etassa paccayadhammassā”ti, jātiādīnaṃ jarāmaraṇādipaccayatāyāti attho. Nāmarūpaparicchedo, tassa ca paccayapariggaho na paṭhamābhinivesamattena hoti[M 2.0090], atha kho tattha aparāparaṃ ñāṇuppattisaññitena anu anu bujjhanena, tadubhayābhāvaṃ pana dassento “ñātapariññāvasena ananubujjhanā”ti āha. Niccasaññādīnaṃ pajahanavasena vattamānā vipassanā dhamme ca paṭivijjhantī eva nāma hoti paṭipakkhavikkhambhanena tikkhavisadabhāvāpattito, tadadhiṭṭhānabhūtā ca tīraṇapariññā, ariyamaggo ca pariññāpahānābhisamayavasena pavattiyā tīraṇapahānapariññāsaṅgaho cāti tadubhayapaṭivedhābhāvaṃ dassento “tīraṇa…pe… appaṭivijjhanā”ti āha. Tantaṃ vuccati vatthavīnanatthaṃ tantavāyehi daṇḍake āsañjitvā pasāritasuttapaṭṭī tanīyatīti katvā. Taṃ pana suttasantānākulatāya nidassanabhāvena ākulameva gahitanti āha “tantaṃ viya ākulakajātā”ti. Saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “yathā nāmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Samānetunti pubbena paraṃ samaṃ katvā ānetuṃ, avisamaṃ ujuṃ kātunti attho. Tantameva vā ākulaṃ tantākulaṃ, tantākulaṃ viya jātā bhūtāti tantākulajātā. Majjhimaṃ paṭipadaṃ anupagantvā antadvayapatanena paccayākāre khalitā ākulā byākulā honti. Teneva antadvayapatanena taṃtaṃdiṭṭhigāhavasena paribbhamantā ujukaṃ dhammaṭṭhiti kathaṃ paṭipajjituṃ na jānanti. Tenāha “na sakkonti taṃ paccayākāraṃ ujuṃ kātu”nti. Dve bodhisatteti paccekabodhisattamahābodhisatte. Attano dhammatāyāti attano sabhāvena, paropadesena vināti attho. Tattha tattha guḷakajātanti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne jātaguḷakampi gaṇṭhīti [P 2.0118] suttagaṇṭhi. Tato eva gaṇṭhibaddhaṃ baddhagaṇṭhikaṃ. Paccayesu pakkhalitvāti aniccadukkhānattādisabhāvesu paccayadhammesu niccādiggāhavasena pakkhalitvā. Paccaye ujuṃ kātuṃ asakkontāti tasseva niccādiggāhassa avissajjanato paccayadhammanimittaṃ attano dassanaṃ ujuṃ kātuṃ asakkontā idaṃsaccābhinivesakāyaganthavasena gaṇṭhikajātā hontīti āha “dvāsaṭṭhi…pe… gaṇṭhibaddhā”ti. Ye hi keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā sassatadiṭṭhiādidiṭṭhiyo nissitā allīnā.

Etassa dhammassā (of this Dhamma) refers to the Dhamma known as dependent origination. But because it is, in essence, the cause of things that arise from a cause, therefore, it is said, 'of this conditioned Dhamma,' meaning that birth and so on are conditions for aging and death and so on. The delineation of name-and-form and the discernment of its condition do not occur merely through an initial inclination, but rather through repeated awakening there, known as the arising of knowledge, bit by bit. Showing the absence of both, it is said, 'not awakening by way of knowing and full understanding.' Insight, proceeding by abandoning perceptions of permanence and so on, is indeed called 'penetrating phenomena' because it attains sharp clarity by overcoming opposition through suppression. Its foundation is the full understanding by judgment, and the noble path, because it proceeds by way of full understanding, abandoning, and realization, is comprised of the full understanding by judgment and by abandoning. Showing the absence of penetrating both, it is said, 'not penetrating by judgment...' Tanta (thread) is so called because a strip of threads, attached to a loom and stretched out by weavers for the purpose of weaving cloth, is extended. But because it is taken as a tangle, representing the continuity of threads, it is said to be 'tangled like a thread.' To explain in detail the meaning stated briefly, it is said, 'Just as...' Samānetuṃ (to make equal) means to bring the later equal to the former, making it straight and not uneven. Or, the tangled thread itself is tantākula (thread-tangled), meaning it has become tangled like a thread. Not approaching the middle way, by falling into the two extremes, they become confused and perplexed about the causal mode. Therefore, wandering while grasping at various views due to falling into the two extremes, they do not know how to practice the straight Dhamma-state. Therefore, it is said, 'They are not able to make that causal mode straight.' Dve bodhisatte (the two Bodhisattas) refers to the Paccekabodhisatta (Solitary Buddha) and the Mahābodhisatta (Great Bodhisatta). Attano dhammatāyāti (by their own nature) means by their own inherent quality, without another's instruction. Tattha tattha guḷakajāta (knots are formed here and there) means a knot of thread (suttagaṇṭhi) that has formed in various places. Therefore, it is called gaṇṭhibaddha (bound by knots) or baddhagaṇṭhika (having knots tied). Paccayesu pakkhalitvā (stumbling over conditions) means stumbling over conditioned phenomena, which have the nature of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, by grasping at permanence and so on. Paccaye ujuṃ kātuṃ asakkontā (unable to make conditions straight) means, due to not relinquishing that grasping at permanence and so on, they are unable to straighten their own view of the sign of conditioned phenomena. Thus, they become knotted by way of the bodily knot of adherence to 'this is truth.' Therefore, it is said, 'Sixty-two... bound by knots.' Indeed, whatever ascetics or brahmins rely on and cling to views of eternalism and so on.

Vinanato [V 2.0081] “kulā”ti itthiliṅgavasena laddhanāmassa tantavāyassa gaṇṭhikaṃ nāma ākulabhāvena aggato vā mūlato vā duviññeyyāyeva khalitatantasuttanti āha “kulāgaṇṭhikaṃ vuccati pesakārakañjiyasutta”nti. Sakuṇikāti kulāvakasakuṇikā. Sā hi rukkhasākhāsu olambanakulāvakā [M 2.0091] hoti. Tañhi sā kulāvakaṃ tato tato tiṇahīrādike ānetvā tathā vinandhati, yathā tesaṃ pesakārakañjiyasuttaṃ viya aggena vā aggaṃ mūlena vā mūlaṃ samānetuṃ vivecetuṃ vā na sakkā. Tenāha “yathā hī”tiādi. Tadubhayampīti “kulāgaṇṭhika”nti vuttaṃ kañjiyasuttaṃ, kulāvakañca. Purimanayenevāti “evameva sattā”tiādinā pubbe vuttanayeneva.

Because of entanglement, the term 'kulā,' a feminine noun, refers to the weaver's knot, which is a tangled thread that is difficult to discern from either end or root due to its confused state. Thus, it is said, 'kulā-gaṇṭhika is called the weaver's tangled thread (pesakārakañjiyasutta).' 'Sakuṇikā' means a nest-making bird (kulāvakasakuṇikā). Indeed, it is a bird that makes a hanging nest (kulāvaka) on tree branches. It weaves that nest by bringing grass, fibers, and such from various places, in such a way that, like the weaver's tangled thread, it is impossible to bring end to end or root to root, or to disentangle them. Therefore, it is said, 'just as,' etc. 'Both of these' refers to the tangled thread (kañjiyasutta) called 'kulā-gaṇṭhika,' and the nest (kulāvaka). 'By the former way' means by the way previously stated, beginning with 'just so, beings,' etc.

Kāmaṃ muñjapabbajatiṇāni yathājātānipi dīghabhāvena patitvā araññaṭṭhāne aññamaññaṃ vinandhitvā ākulabyākulāni hutvā tiṭṭhanti, tāni pana na tathā [P 2.0119] dubbiveciyāni, yathā rajjubhūtānīti dassetuṃ “yathā tānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

Though muñja grass, pabbaja grass, and other grasses, even as they naturally grow, having fallen due to their length in a forest area, become intertwined and entangled with one another, standing in a confused and disordered state, yet they are not as difficult to disentangle as when they have become ropes—to illustrate this, 'just as those,' etc., is stated. The rest here follows the same method as stated below.

Apāyāti avaḍḍhitā, sukhena, sukhahetunā vā virahitāti attho. Dukkhassa gatibhāvatoti āpāyikassa dukkhassa pavattiṭṭhānabhāvato. Sukhasamussayatoti abbhudayato. Vinipatitattāti virūpaṃ nipatitattā yathā tenattabhāvena sukhasamussayo na hoti, evaṃ nipatitattā. Itaroti saṃsāro. Nanu “apāya”ntiādinā vuttopi saṃsāro evāti? Saccametaṃ, nirayādīnaṃ pana adhimattadukkhabhāvadassanatthaṃ apāyādiggahaṇaṃ. Gobalībaddañāyenāyamattho veditabbo. Khandhānañca paṭipāṭīti pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ hetuphalabhāvena aparāparaṃ pavatti. Abbocchinnaṃ vattamānāti avicchedena pavattamānā. Taṃ sabbampīti taṃ “apāya”ntiādinā vuttaṃ sabbaṃ apāyadukkhañceva vaṭṭadukkhañca. “Mahāsamudde vātukkhittanāvā viyā”ti idaṃ paribbhamaṭṭhānassa mahantadassanatthañceva paribbhamanassa anavaṭṭhitatādassanatthañca “upamāya. Yantesu yuttagoṇo viyā”ti idaṃ pana avasabhāvadassanatthañceva duppamokkhabhāvadassanatthañcāti veditabbaṃ.

'Apāya' means 'devoid of growth,' or 'devoid of happiness or the cause of happiness.' It is so called because it is the destination of suffering, being the place where the suffering of those in miserable states occurs. It is a state devoid of an accumulation of happiness, that is, of prosperity. 'Vinipatitattā' means 'because of having fallen into a distorted state,' such that, through that state of being, an accumulation of happiness does not occur; thus, because of having fallen in such a way. 'The other' refers to saṃsāra. But is not saṃsāra itself implied by terms like 'apāya,' etc.? Indeed, it is. However, the mention of 'apāya' and similar terms is to show the extreme suffering of hell and other such states. This meaning should be understood by the maxim of the cattle and the oxen. 'And the sequence of aggregates' refers to the successive occurrence of the five aggregates as cause and effect. 'Uninterruptedly occurring' means proceeding without cessation. 'All that' refers to everything stated by terms like 'apāya,' etc.—both the suffering of the miserable states and the suffering of the cycle of existence. The simile 'like a boat tossed by winds in the great ocean' is to illustrate the vastness of the sphere of wandering and the instability of that wandering. The simile 'like an ox yoked to a machine' should be understood as illustrating both the lack of autonomy and the difficulty of release.

Paṭiccasamuppādavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of Dependent Origination

Iminā tāvāti ettha tāva-saddo kamattho, tena “tantākulakajātā”ti padassa anusandhi parato āvibhavissatīti dīpeti. Atthi idappaccayāti ettha ayaṃ paccayoti idappaccayo, tasmā idappaccayā, imasmā paccayāti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “imasmā nāma paccayā jarāmaraṇa”nti [V 2.0082] evaṃ vattabbo atthi nu kho jarāmaraṇassa paccayoti. Tenāha [M 2.0092] “atthi nu kho…pe… bhaveyyā”ti. Ettha hi “kiṃ paccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ? Jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa”nti upari jātisaddapaccayasaddasamānādhikaraṇena [P 2.0120] kiṃ-saddena idaṃ-saddassa samānādhikaraṇatādassanato kammadhārayasamāsatā idappaccayasaddassa yujjati. Na hettha “imassa paccayā idappaccayā”ti jarāmaraṇassa, aññassa vā paccayato jarāmaraṇasambhavapucchā sambhavati viññātabhāvato, asambhavato ca, jarāmaraṇassa pana paccayapucchā sambhavati. Paccayasaddasamānādhikaraṇatāyañca idaṃ-saddassa “imasmā paccayā”ti paccayapucchā yujjati.

Here, in 'iminā tāva,' the word 'tāva' indicates a sequence, showing that the connection to the phrase 'tantākulakajātā' will become clear later. In 'atthi idappaccayā,' 'ayaṃ paccayo' (this condition) is 'idappaccayo'; therefore, 'idappaccayā' means 'imasmā paccayā' (from this condition). This is said to mean: 'Is there indeed a condition for aging-and-death, such that one could say, "from this specific condition comes aging-and-death"?' Therefore, it is said, 'Is there indeed... should be...' Here, the status of 'idappaccaya' as a karmadhāraya (determinative) compound is justified because the word 'idaṃ' is shown to have the same case as the word 'kiṃ' in the subsequent passage 'What is the condition for aging-and-death? Birth is the condition for aging-and-death,' where 'jāti' and 'paccaya' also have the same case. For here, a question about the possibility of aging-and-death arising from a condition of aging-and-death ('imassa paccayā idappaccayā') or from another condition is not possible, either because it is already understood or because it is impossible; rather, the question about the condition for aging-and-death itself is possible. And because the word 'idaṃ' has the same case as the word 'paccaya,' the question 'from this condition' ('imasmā paccayā') is justified as a question about the condition.

Sā pana samānādhikaraṇatā yadipi aññapadatthasamāsepi labbhati, aññapadatthavacanicchābhāvato panettha kammadhārayasamāso veditabbo. Sāmivacanasamāsapakkhe pana nattheva samānādhikaraṇatāsambhavoti. Nanu ca “idappaccayatā paṭiccasamuppādo”ti ettha idappaccaya-saddo sāmivacanasamāso icchitoti? Saccaṃ icchito ujukameva tattha paṭiccasamuppādavacanicchāti katvā, idha pana kevalaṃ jarāmaraṇassa paccayaparipucchā adhippetā, tasmā yathā tattha idaṃ-saddassa paṭiccasamuppādavisesanatā, idha ca “pucchitabbapaccayatthatā sambhavati, tathā tattha, idha ca samāsakappanā veditabbā. Kasmā pana tattha kammadhārayasamāso na icchitoti? Hetuppabhavānaṃ hetu paṭiccasamuppādoti imassa atthassa kammadhārayasamāse asambhavatoti imassa, attano paccayānurūpassa anurūpo paccayo idappaccayoti etassa ca atthassa icchitattā. Yo panettha idaṃ-saddena gahito attho, so “atthi idappaccayā jarāmaraṇa”nti jarāmaraṇaggahaṇeneva gahitoti idaṃ-saddo paṭiccasamuppādato pariccajanato aññassa asambhavato paccaye [P 2.0121] avatiṭṭhati, tenettha kammadhārayasamāso. Tattha pana idaṃ-saddassa tato pariccajanakāraṇaṃ natthīti sāmivacanasamāso eva icchito. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃpana yasmā jarāmaraṇādīnaṃ paccayapucchāmukhenāyaṃ paṭiccasamuppādadesanā āraddhā, paṭiccasamuppādo ca nāma atthato hetuppabhavānaṃ hetūti vutto vāyamattho, tasmā “imassa jarāmaraṇassa paccayo”ti evamatthavaṇṇanā katā.

Although this same co-referentiality is also found in a relative compound (bahubbīhi), here it should be understood as a karmadhāraya (determinative) compound, due to the absence of an intention to express the meaning of another word. In the case of a sāmivacana (genitive) compound, however, co-referentiality is entirely impossible. Now, is it not the case that in the phrase 'idappaccayatā paṭiccasamuppādo,' the word 'idappaccaya' is intended as a sāmivacana (genitive) compound? Indeed, it is so intended, because there the intention is to express the term 'paṭiccasamuppāda' directly. Here, however, the inquiry is solely about the condition for aging and death. Therefore, the formation of the compound should be understood in each case according to how it is possible: there, the word 'idaṃ' serves to specify 'paṭiccasamuppāda,' while here, it serves the purpose of the condition to be inquired about. But why is a karmadhāraya compound not intended there? Because a karmadhāraya compound is impossible for the meaning 'paṭiccasamuppāda is the cause of what arises from causes,' and because the intended meaning is 'idappaccaya is a condition appropriate to that which corresponds to its own condition.' Here, the meaning conveyed by the word 'idaṃ' is already conveyed by the mention of 'aging-and-death' in the phrase 'atthi idappaccayā jarāmaraṇa.' Therefore, since it is not possible for the word 'idaṃ' to refer to anything else—having excluded 'paṭiccasamuppāda'—it must refer to 'condition.' Hence, here it is a karmadhāraya compound. There, however, since there is no reason for the word 'idaṃ' to exclude that, the sāmivacana (genitive) compound is indeed intended. Furthermore, in the commentary, because this teaching on dependent origination is introduced through an inquiry into the conditions for aging and death, etc., and because dependent origination is, in essence, said to be the cause of what arises from causes, the explanation of the meaning was given as 'the condition of this aging and death.'

Paṇḍitenāti ekaṃsabyākaraṇīyādipañhāvisesajānanasamatthāya paññāya samannāgatena. Tameva hissa paṇḍiccaṃ dassetuṃ “yathā”tiādi vuttaṃ[M 2.0093]. Yādisassa jīvassa diṭṭhigatiko sarīrato anaññattaṃ pucchati “taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīra”nti, so evaṃ paramatthato nupalabbhati, kathaṃ tassa vañjhātanayassa viya dīgharassatā sarīrato aññatā vā anaññatā vā byākātabbā siyā, tasmāssa pañhassa ṭhapanīyatā veditabbā. Tuṇhībhāvo nāmesa pucchato anādaro vihesā [V 2.0083] viya hotīti “abyākatameta”nti pakārantaramāha. Evaṃ abyākaraṇakāraṇaṃ ñātukāmassa kathetabbaṃ hoti, kathite ca jānantassa pamādopi evaṃ siyā, kathanavidhi pana “yādisassā”tiādinā dassito eva. Evaṃ appaṭipajjitvāti evaṃ ṭhapanīyapañhe viya tuṇhībhāvādiṃ anāpajjitvā eva. “Appaṭipajjitvā”ti vacanaṃ nidassanamattametaṃ. “Kiṃ sabbaṃ anicca”nti vutte “kiṃ saṅkhataṃ sandhāya pucchasi, udāhu asaṅkhata”nti paṭipucchitvā byākātabbaṃ hoti “kiṃ khandhapañcakaṃ pariññeyya”nti puṭṭhe “atthi tattha pariññeyyaṃ, atthi na pariññeyya”nti vibhajja byākātabbaṃ hoti, evaṃ appaṭipajjitvāti ca ayamettha attho icchitoti. Pubbe yassa paccayassa atthitāmattaṃ [P 2.0122] coditanti atthitāmattaṃ vissajjitaṃ. Pucchāsabhāgena hi vissajjananti. Idāni tasseva sarūpapucchā karīyatīti “puna ki”nti vuttaṃ. Idhāpi “yathā”tiādi sabbaṃ ānetvā vattabbaṃ.

'By a wise one' means endowed with wisdom capable of understanding the different kinds of questions, such as those requiring a categorical answer. To demonstrate that very wisdom, 'as follows,' etc., is stated. When one who holds the view that the soul is not different from the body asks, 'Is the soul the same as the body?'—such a soul is not found in an ultimate sense. How then could its otherness or non-otherness from the body be declared, any more than the longness or shortness of a barren woman’s son? Therefore, this question should be understood as one to be set aside. For silence shows disregard for the questioner and can be like harassment; hence, another way is stated: 'this is unanswered.' The reason for not answering should be told to one who wishes to know. And when it is told, heedlessness might arise in one who understands; the method of explaining, however, has already been shown with 'for such a one,' etc. 'Not having thus proceeded' means not resorting to silence or other such means, as one would for a question to be set aside. The statement 'not having thus proceeded' is merely illustrative. When asked, 'Is everything impermanent?' one should answer after counter-questioning, 'Are you asking with reference to the conditioned or the unconditioned?' If asked, 'Should the five aggregates be fully understood?' one should answer analytically: 'Therein, some should be fully understood, and some should not.' This is the intended meaning here of 'not having thus proceeded.' Previously, only the mere existence of a condition was questioned, and so its mere existence was answered. For the answer corresponds to the nature of the question. Now, a question about its very nature is posed—hence, 'again, what?' is said. Here too, 'as follows,' etc., should all be brought in and stated.

“Esa nayo sabbapadesū”ti atidesavasena ussukkaṃ katvā “nāmarūpapaccayā”tiādinā tattha apavādo āraddho. Yasmā dassetukāmo, tasmā idaṃ vuttanti yojanā. Channaṃ vipākasamphassānaṃyeva gahaṇaṃ hoti viññāṇādi vedanāpariyosānā vipākavidhīti katvā anekesu suttapadesu, (ma. ni. 3.126; udā. 1) abhidhamme (vibha. 225) ca yebhuyyena tesaṃyeva gahaṇassa niruḷhattā. Idhāti imasmiṃ sutte. Ca-saddo byatirekattho, tenettha “gahitampī”tiādinā vuccamānaṃyeva visesaṃ joteti. Paccayabhāvo nāma paccayuppannāpekkho tena vinā tassa asambhavato. Tasmā saḷāyatanappaccayāti “saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso”ti iminā padenāti yojanā. Avayavena vā samudāyopalakkhaṇametaṃ “saḷāyatanapaccayā”ti, tasmā “saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso”ti iminā padenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Gahitampīti chabbidhaṃ vipākaphassampi. Aggahitampīti avipākaphassampi kusalākusalakiriyāphassampi. Paccayuppannavisesaṃ dassetukāmoti [M 2.0094] yojanā. Na cettha paccayuppannova upādinno icchito, atha kho paccayopi upādinno icchitoti ajjhattikāyatanasseva saḷāyatanaggahaṇena gahaṇanti katvā vuttaṃ “saḷāyatanato…pe… dassetukāmo”ti. Na hi phassassa cakkhādisaḷāyatanameva paccayo, atha kho “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso”tiādi (ma. ni. 3.421, 425, 426; saṃ. ni. 2.44, 45; 2.4.60; kathā. 465, 467) vacanato rūpāyatanādirūpañca cakkhuviññāṇādināmañca paccayo, tasmā imaṃ cakkhādisaḷāyatanato atirittaṃ [P 2.0123] āvajjanādi viya sādhāraṇaṃ ahutvā, tassa tassa phassassa sādhāraṇatāya aññaṃ visesapaccayaṃ pi-saddena avisiṭṭhaṃ sādhāraṇapaccayaṃ pidassetukāmo bhagavā, “nāmarūpapaccayā [V 2.0084] phasso”ti idaṃ vuttanti yojanā. Abhidhammabhājanīyepi imameva paccayaṃ sandhāya “nāmarūpapaccayā phasso”ti vuttanti tadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 243) “paccayavisesadassanatthañceva mahānidānadesanāsaṅgahatthañcā”ti atthavaṇṇanā katā. Paccayānanti jātiādīnaṃ paccayadhammānaṃ. Nidānaṃ kathitanti jarāmaraṇādikassa nidānattaṃ kathitaṃ ekaṃsiko paccayabhāvo kathito. Tañhi tesaṃ paccayabhāve abyabhicārīti dassetuṃ “iti kho paneta”ntiādinā upari desanā pavattā. Nijjaṭeti nijjālake. Niggumbeti nikkhepe. Padadvayenāpi ākulābhāvameva dasseti, tasmā anākulaṃ abyākulaṃ mahantaṃ paccayanidānamettha kathitanti mahānidānaṃ suttaṃ aññathābhāvassa abhāvato.

“This is the method in all instances.” Thus, having made an effort by way of extension, an exception is introduced with “dependent on name-and-form,” and so on. The connection is that this is said because he wishes to show this. Only the six resultant contacts are included, because the process of result consists of consciousness and so forth, ending with feeling, and because their inclusion is generally established in many passages of the suttas (Majjhima Nikāya 3.126; Udāna 1) and in the Abhidhamma (Vibhaṅga 225). “Here” means in this sutta. The particle “ca” has a contrastive sense; thus, it highlights the very distinction stated by “even what is included,” and so on. The state of being a condition is relative to what is conditioned, for without the latter, the former cannot exist. Therefore, the connection is with the phrase “dependent on the six sense bases, contact.” Alternatively, “dependent on the six sense bases” is an indication of the whole by a part; therefore, it is said to be connected with the phrase “dependent on the six sense bases, contact.” “Even what is included” means the sixfold resultant contact. “Even what is not included” means non-resultant contact, that is, wholesome, unwholesome, and functional contact. The connection is that he wishes to show the distinction in what is conditioned. Here, it is not that only the conditioned is intended to be taken up, but rather the condition is also intended to be taken up. Thus, taking the inclusion of the six sense bases as referring only to the internal sense bases, it is said, “from the six sense bases… wishing to show.” For the six sense bases such as the eye are not the sole condition for contact. Rather, as stated in passages such as “dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact” (Majjhima Nikāya 3.421, 425, 426; Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.44, 45; 2.4.60; Kathāvatthu 465, 467), the form base, etc., which are form, and eye-consciousness, etc., which are name, are also conditions. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to show another specific condition in addition to this sixfold sense base—one that is not a general condition like adverting, etc., but is specific to each respective contact—and also, with the particle 'pi', to indicate the undifferentiated general condition, said, “dependent on name-and-form, contact.” This is the connection. Even in the Abhidhamma analysis, it is with reference to this very condition that it is said, “dependent on name-and-form, contact,” and in its commentary (Vibhaṅga Aṭṭhakathā 243) the meaning is explained as: “for the purpose of showing the distinction of conditions and for the purpose of including the Great Discourse on Causation.” “Of conditions” means of the conditional phenomena such as birth, etc. “The source is spoken of” means that the status of aging-and-death, etc., as a source is spoken of; a definite state of conditionality is spoken of. To show that this is unfailing in their being conditions, the teaching above proceeds with “thus indeed,” and so on. “He disentangles” means he makes it free from tangles. “He clears” means he makes it free from thickets. By this pair of words, he shows the absence of confusion. Therefore, because a great source of conditions, unconfused and unbewildering, is taught herein, it is the Mahānidāna Sutta, due to the absence of its being otherwise.

98. Tesaṃ tesaṃ paccayānanti tesaṃ tesaṃ jātiādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ. Yasmā paccayabhāvo nāma tehi tehi paccayehi anūnādhikeheva tassa tassa phalassa sambhavato tatho taccho, tappakāro vā sāmaggiupagatesu paccayesu muhuttampi tatho nibbattanadhammānaṃ asambhavābhāvato. Avitatho avisaṃvādanako visaṃvādanākāravirahito aññadhammapaccayehi aññadhammānuppattito. “Anaññathā”ti vuccati aññathābhāvassa abhāvato. Tasmā “tathaṃ avitathaṃ anaññathaṃ paccayabhāvaṃ dassetu”nti vuttaṃ. Pariyāyati [P 2.0124] attano phalaṃ pariggahetvā vattatīti pariyāyo, hetūti āha “pariyāyenāti kāraṇenā”ti. Sabbena sabbanti devattādinā [M 2.0095] sabbabhāvena sabbā jāti. Sabbathā sabbanti tatthāpi cātumahārājikādisabbākārena sabbā, nipātadvayametaṃ, nipātañca abyayaṃ, tañca sabbaliṅgavibhattivacanesu ekākārameva hotīti pāḷiyaṃ “sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabba”nti vuttaṃ. Atthavacane pana tassa tassa jātisaddāpekkhāya itthiatthavuttitaṃ dassetuṃ “sabbākārena sabbā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Imināva nayenāti iminā jātivāre vutteneva nayena. Devādīsūti ādi-saddena gandhabbayakkhādike pāḷiyaṃ (dī. ni. 2.98) āgate, tadantarabhede ca saṅgaṇhāti.

98. “Of those various conditions” means of the various conditions such as birth, etc. For the state of being a condition is true and real, since a given result arises from its specific conditions, neither deficient nor excessive. Or, it is of such a nature because when the conditions have come together, it is impossible for phenomena that are to arise from them not to arise even for a moment. It is unfailing and non-deceptive, free from any deceptive character, because a different phenomenon does not arise from the conditions for another phenomenon. It is called “not otherwise” because of the absence of otherness. Therefore, it is said, “to show the state of being a condition as true, unfailing, and not otherwise.” It is a 'way' (pariyāya) because it proceeds by encompassing its own result; this means 'cause,' hence he says, “‘by way of’ means ‘by the cause.’” “All in every way” (sabbena sabbaṃ) means all birth in every mode of being, such as that of a god. “In every manner, all” (sabbathā sabbaṃ) means all, in every way, such as in the realm of the Four Great Kings. These two are particles. A particle is indeclinable and remains the same in all genders, cases, and numbers; thus, in the Pāli, it is said, “sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ.” However, in the explanation of the meaning, to show its usage in the feminine sense with reference to the word 'birth' (jāti), it is said, “all (sabbā) in every way (sabbākārena),” and so on. “By this very method” means by the method explained in this section on birth. “Among gods, etc.”: the word “etc.” includes the gandhabbas, yakkhas, and so on, that are mentioned in the Pāli (Dīgha Nikāya 2.98), and it also includes their subdivisions.

Idha nikkhittaatthavibhajanattheti imasmiṃ “kassaci kimhicī”ti aniyamato uddesavasena vuttatthassa niddisanatthe jotetabbe nipāto, tadatthajotanaṃ nipātapadanti attho. Tassāti tassa padassa. Teti dhammadesanāya sampadānabhūtaṃ theraṃ vadati. Seyyathidanti vā te katameti ceti attho. Ye hi “kassacī”ti, “kimhicī”ti ca aniyamato vutto attho, te katameti. Kathetukamyatāpucchā hesā. Devabhāvāyāti devabhāvatthaṃ. Khandhajātīti khandhapātubhāvo, yathā khandhesu uppannesu “devā”ti samaññā hoti, tathā tesaṃ uppādoti attho. Tenāha “yāyā”ti āha. Sabbapadesūti “gandhabbānaṃ gandhabbatthāyā”tiādīsu sabbesu jātiniddesapadesu[V 2.0085], bhavādipadesu ca. Yena hi nayena sace hi jātīti ayamatthayojanā katā, jātiniddesapadesova “bhavo”tiādinā bhavādipadesupi so kātabboti. Devāti upapattidevā cātumahārājikato paṭṭhāya yāva bhavaggā dibbanti kāmaguṇādīhi kīḷanti laḷanti viharanti jotantīti katvā. Gandhaṃ abbanti paribhuñjantīti gandhabbā, dhataraṭṭhassa [P 2.0125] mahārājassa parivārabhūtā. Yajanti vessavaṇasakkādike pūjentīti yakkhā, tena tena vā paṇidhikammādinā yajitabbā pūjetabbāti yakkhā, vessavaṇassa mahārājassa parivārabhūtā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “amanussā”ti avisesena vuttaṃ. Bhūtāti kumbhaṇḍā, virūḷhakassa mahārājassa parivārabhūtā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “ye keci nibbattasattā”ti avisesena vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhipakkhā bhamaratuppaḷādayo. Cammapakkhā jatusiṅgālādayo. Lomapakkhā haṃsamorādayo. Sarīsapā ahivicchikasatapadiādayo.

Here, for the purpose of analyzing the meaning set down: a particle is to be illuminated for the purpose of specifying a meaning that was stated indeterminately by way of a summary statement as “of anyone” or “in anything.” The meaning is that a particle is a word that illuminates that meaning. “Of that” (tassa) means of that word. “To you” (te) refers to the Elder who is the recipient of the Dhamma teaching. The meaning of seyyathidaṃ is “which are they?” The meanings stated indeterminately as “of anyone” and “in anything”—which are they? This is a question prompted by the desire to speak. “For the state of a god” (devabhāvāya) means for the purpose of the state of a god. “Birth of aggregates” (khandhajāti) means the manifestation of aggregates; the meaning is that when the aggregates have arisen in such a way that the designation “god” occurs, that is their arising. Therefore, he said, “whatever” (yā yā). “In all passages” means in all passages specifying birth, such as “of gandhabbas, for the state of a gandhabba,” and so on, and also in the passages on becoming, etc. For by whatever method this application of meaning has been made for the passage specifying birth, that same application should be made for the passages on becoming, etc., beginning with “becoming.” “Gods” (devā) means gods by rebirth, from the Cātumahārājika realm up to the peak of existence, so called because they sport (dibbanti), play, enjoy, dwell, and shine with sensual pleasures. “They enjoy (abbanti) scent (gandhaṃ)” means they consume it; thus they are “gandhabbas,” the attendants of the great king Dhataraṭṭha. “They worship (yajanti)” means they pay homage to Vessavaṇa, Sakka, and so on; thus they are “yakkhas.” Or, “they are to be worshipped (yajitabbā)” and paid homage to with some vow or act of aspiration; thus they are “yakkhas,” the attendants of the great king Vessavaṇa. In the commentary, however, they are spoken of generally as “non-human beings.” “Spirits” (bhūtā) means kumbhaṇḍas, the attendants of the great king Virūḷhaka. In the commentary, however, they are spoken of generally as “any beings that have come to exist.” “Bone-winged” are bees, beetles, and the like. “Skin-winged” are bats, flying foxes, and the like. “Hair-winged” are swans, peacocks, and the like. “Crawling creatures” (sarīsapā) are snakes, scorpions, centipedes, and the like.

“Tesaṃ [M 2.0096] tesa”nti idaṃ na yevāpanakaniddeso viya avuttasaṅgahatthaṃ vacanaṃ, atha kho ayevāpanakaniddeso viya vuttasaṅgahatthanti. Ādi-saddeneva ca āmeḍitattho saṅgayhatīti āha “tesaṃ tesaṃ devagandhabbādīna”nti. Tadattāyāti taṃbhāvāya, yathārūpesu khandhesu pavattamānesu “devā gandhabbā”ti lokasamaññā hoti, tathārūpatāyāti attho. Tenāha “devagandhabbādibhāvāyā”ti. “Nirodho, vigamo”ti ca paṭiladdhattālābhassa bhāvo vuccati, idha pana accantābhāvo adhippeto “sabbaso jātiyā asatī”ti avatvā “jātinirodhā”ti vuttattāti āha “abhāvāti attho”ti.

“This phrase ‘for each of them’ is not a statement meant to include what is unsaid, like an exhaustive enumeration, but rather it is a statement meant to include what is said, like a non-exhaustive enumeration. And the meaning of repetition is understood by the word ‘etcetera’ itself; hence it is said, ‘for each of the devas, gandhabbas, etc.’ ‘For that state’ means for that mode of being; that is, the meaning is for that particular form, in which, when such aggregates are occurring, the worldly convention ‘devas, gandhabbas’ arises. Therefore, it is said, ‘for the state of being devas, gandhabbas, etc.’ ‘Cessation, disappearance’ refers to the state of one who has acquired an existence. Here, however, absolute non-existence is intended; because instead of saying ‘birth being entirely non-existent,’ it is said ‘from the cessation of birth,’ hence it is stated, ‘the meaning is non-existence.’”

Phalatthāya hinotīti yathā phalaṃ tato nibbattati, evaṃ hinoti pavattati, tassa hetubhāvaṃ upagacchatīti attho. Idaṃ gaṇhatha nanti “idaṃ me phalaṃ, gaṇhatha na”nti evaṃ appeti viya niyyāteti viya. “Esa nayo”ti avisesaṃ atidisitvā visesamattassa atthaṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Nanu cāyaṃ jāti parinipphannā, saṅkhatabhāvā ca na hoti vikārabhāvato, tathā jarāmaraṇaṃ, tassa kathaṃ sā hetu hotīti codanaṃ sandhāyāha [P 2.0126] “jarāmaraṇassa hī”tiādi. Tabbhāve bhāvo, tadabhāve ca abhāvo jarāmaraṇassa jātiyā upanissayatā.

It leads to the fruit, meaning just as the fruit arises from that, so it proceeds, attaining the state of being its cause. ‘Take this,’ as if saying, ‘This is my fruit, take it, is it not?’ thus it bestows or offers. Having generally extended the principle without distinction, to show the meaning of a specific instance, it is said, ‘Moreover,’ etc. But is not this birth already fully accomplished? And being a conditioned phenomenon, it is not subject to alteration. Similarly, aging and death—how can that be its cause? Intending to address this objection, he said, ‘For aging and death,’ etc. When that exists, this exists; and when that does not exist, this does not exist—this is the dependence of aging and death on birth as its decisive support.

99. Okāsapariggahoti pavattiṭṭhānapariggaho. Upapattibhave yujjati upapattikkhandhānaṃ yathāvuttaṭṭhānato aññattha anuppajjanato. Idha panāti imasmiṃ sutte “kāmabhavo”tiādinā āgate imasmiṃ ṭhāne. Kammabhave yujjati kāmabhavādijotanā visesato tassa jātiyā paccayabhāvatoti. Tenāha “so hi jātiyā upanissayakoṭiyāva paccayo”ti. Nanu ca upapattibhavopi [V 2.0086] jātiyā upanissayavasena paccayo hotīti? Saccaṃ hoti, so pana na tathā padhānabhūto, kammabhavo pana padhānabhūto paccayo janakabhāvatoti. “So hi jātiyā”tiādi vuttaṃ kāmabhavūpagaṃ kammaṃ kāmabhavo. Esa nayo rūpārūpabhavesupi. Okāsapariggahova kato“kimhicī”ti iminā sattapariggahassa katattā.

99. ‘Determination of location’ means the determination of the place of occurrence. It applies to rebirth-existence, because the rebirth-aggregates do not arise elsewhere than in their specified place. But here, in this sutta, in this context introduced by phrases such as ‘sensual existence’ and so forth, it applies to kamma-existence, because the manifestation of sensual existence, etc., is specifically a condition for that birth. Therefore, it is said, ‘For it is indeed a condition in the category of decisive support for birth.’ But is not rebirth-existence also a condition for birth by way of decisive support? It is true, but it is not as primary, whereas kamma-existence is a primary condition because of its generative nature. The statement beginning ‘For it is indeed for birth…’ is made. Kamma leading to sensual existence is sensual existence. The same method applies to form and formless existences as well. The determination of location has been made by this word ‘in what?’, because the determination of a being has already been made.

100. Tiṇṇampi kammabhavānanti kāmakammabhavādīnaṃ tiṇṇampi kammabhavānaṃ. Tiṇṇañca upapattibhavānanti kāmupapattibhavādīnaṃ tiṇṇañca upapattibhavānaṃ. Tathā [M 2.0097] sesānipīti diṭṭhupādānādīni sesupādānānipi tiṇṇampi kammabhavānaṃ, tiṇṇañca upapattibhavānaṃ paccayoti attho. Itīti evaṃ vuttanayena. Dvādasa kammabhavā dvādasa upapattibhavāti catuvīsatibhavā veditabbā. Yasmā kammabhavassa paccayabhāvamukheneva upādānaṃ upapattibhavassa paccayo nāma hoti, na aññathā, tasmā upādānaṃ kammabhavassa ujukameva paccayabhāvoti āha “nippariyāyenettha dvādasa kammabhavā labbhantī”ti. Tesanti kammabhavānaṃ. Sahajātakoṭiyāti akusalassa kammabhavassa sahajātaṃ upādānaṃ sahajātakoṭiyā, itaraṃ anantarūpanissayādivasena upanissayakoṭiyā, kusalassa kammabhavassa pana [P 2.0127] upanissayakoṭiyāva paccayo. Ettha ca yathā aññamaññanissayasampayuttaatthiavigatādipaccayānaṃ sahajātapaccayena ekasaṅgahataṃ dassetuṃ “sahajātakoṭiyā”ti vuttaṃ, evaṃ ārammaṇūpanissayaanantarūpanissayapakatūpanissayānaṃ ekajjhaṃ gahaṇavasena “upanissayakoṭiyā”ti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

100. “Of the three kamma-existences” refers to the three kamma-existences, such as kamma-existence in the sensual sphere. “And of the three rebirth-existences” refers to the three rebirth-existences, such as rebirth-existence in the sensual sphere. “Similarly, the rest” means that the remaining clingings, such as clinging to views and so forth, are also conditions for the three kamma-existences and the three rebirth-existences. This is the meaning. “Thus” means in the manner explained. Twelve kamma-existences and twelve rebirth-existences should be understood as twenty-four existences. Because clinging becomes a condition for rebirth-existence only through being a condition for kamma-existence, and not otherwise, clinging is directly a condition for kamma-existence; therefore it is said, “Here, the twelve kamma-existences are obtained directly.” “Of these” refers to the kamma-existences. “In the category of co-arising” means that for unwholesome kamma-existence, co-arisen clinging is in the category of co-arising; the other kinds of clinging are in the category of decisive support by way of contiguity-decisive-support and so forth. For wholesome kamma-existence, however, it is a condition only in the category of decisive support. Here, to show the inclusion of conditions such as mutuality, dependence, association, presence, and non-disappearance under the co-arising condition, the phrase “in the category of co-arising” is used. Similarly, it should be understood that the phrase “in the category of decisive support” is used to indicate the collective inclusion of object-decisive-support, contiguity-decisive-support, and natural-decisive-support.

101. Upādānassāti ettha kāmupādānassa taṇhā upanissayakoṭiyāva paccayo, sesupādānānaṃ sahajātakoṭiyāpi upanissayakoṭiyāpi viññāṇādi ca vedanāpariyosānā vipākavidhīti katvā.

101. Regarding clinging, here craving is a condition for sensual clinging only in the category of decisive support. For the remaining clingings, it is a condition both in the category of co-arising and in the category of decisive support, this being because consciousness and so forth, ending with feeling, are the process of resultants.

102. Yadidaṃ vedanāti ettha vipākavedanāti tameva tāva upanissayakoṭiyā paccayo itarakoṭiyā asambhavato. Aññāti kusalākusalakiriyavedanā. Aññathāpīti sahajātakoṭiyāpi.

102. As for “that is, feeling,” here it refers to resultant feeling; that alone is a condition in the category of decisive support, since the other category is impossible. “Other” refers to wholesome, unwholesome, and functional feelings. “In another way” also means in the category of co-arising.

103. Ettāvatāti jarāmaraṇādīnaṃ paccayaparamparādassanavasena pavattāya ettakāya desanāya. Purimataṇhanti purimabhavasiddhaṃ taṇhaṃ. “Esa paccayo taṇhāya, yadidaṃ vedanā”ti vatvā tadanantaraṃ “phassapaccayā vedanāti iti kho panetaṃ vutta”ntiādinā vedanāya paccayabhūtassa phassassa uddharaṇaṃ aññesu suttesu āgatanayena paṭiccasamuppādassa desanāmaggo[V 2.0087], taṃ pana anotaritvā samudācārataṇhādassanamukheneva taṇhāmūlakadhamme desento āciṇṇadesanāmaggato okkamanto viya, tañca desanaṃ passato appavattanti pasayha balakkārena desento viya ca hotīti āha “idānī”tiādi. Dve taṇhāti idhādhippetataṇhā eva [M 2.0098] dvidhā bhindanto āha. Esanataṇhāti bhogānaṃ pariyesanavasena pavattataṇhā. Esitataṇhāti pariyiṭṭhesu bhogesu uppajjamānataṇhā. Samudācārataṇhāyāti pariyuṭṭhānavasena pavattataṇhāya. Duvidhāpesā vedanaṃ paṭicca taṇhā [P 2.0128] nāma vedanāpaccayā ca appaṭiladdhānaṃ bhogānaṃ paṭilābhāya pariyesanā, laddhesu ca tesupātabyatāpattiādi hotīti.

103. “Thus far” refers to the extent of the teaching that has proceeded by way of showing the sequence of conditions for aging-and-death and so forth. “Former craving” means the craving established in a previous existence. After stating, “This is the condition for craving, that is, feeling,” the usual path of teaching dependent origination, as it comes in other suttas, is to extract contact as the condition for feeling, with statements such as “Contact is the condition for feeling.” But without descending into that, by teaching the phenomena rooted in craving by way of showing manifest craving, it is as if he deviates from the customary path of teaching. And for one who sees that teaching as not proceeding, it is as if he teaches forcefully, by compulsion. Therefore, it is said, “Now,” and so forth. “Two cravings”: he speaks dividing the craving intended here into two. “Craving for seeking” is the craving that proceeds by way of seeking possessions. “Craving for what is sought” is the craving that arises regarding possessions already sought. “By manifest craving” means by craving that proceeds by way of obsession. This craving, although twofold, is called ‘craving conditioned by feeling.’ And with feeling as its condition, there is both the seeking for the acquisition of unattained possessions and, when they are obtained, the occurrence of distress and so forth.

Paritassanavasena pariyesati etāyāti pariyesanā. Āsayato, payogato ca pariyesanā tathāpavatto cittuppādo. Tenāha “taṇhāya sati hotī”ti. Rūpādiārammaṇapaṭilābhoti savatthukānaṃ rūpādiārammaṇānaṃ gavesanavasena, pavattiyaṃ pana apariyiṭṭhaṃyeva labbhati, tampi atthato pariyesanāya laddhameva nāma tathārūpassa kammassa pubbekatattā eva labbhanato. Tenāha “so hi pariyesanāya sati hotī”ti. Sukhavinicchayanti sukhaṃ visesato nicchinotīti sukhavinicchayo, sukhaṃ sabhāvato, samudayato, atthaṅgamanato, nissaraṇato ca yāthāvato jānitvā pavattañāṇaṃ, taṃ sukhavinicchayaṃ. Jaññāti jāneyya. “Subhasukha”ntiādikaṃ ārammaṇe abhūtākāraṃ vividhaṃ ninnabhāvena nicchinoti āropetīti vinicchayo. Assādānupassanataṇhādiṭṭhiyāpi evameva vinicchayabhāvo veditabbo. Imasmiṃ pana sutte vitakkoyeva āgatoti yojanā. Imasmiṃ pana sutteti sakkapañhasutte. (Dī. ni. 2.358) tattha hi “chando kho, devānaṃ inda, vitakkanidāno”ti āgataṃ. Idhāti imasmiṃ mahānidānasutte. “Vitakkeneva vinicchinātī”ti etena “vinicchīyati etenāti vinicchayo”ti vinicchaya-saddassa karaṇasādhanamāha. “Ettaka”ntiādi vinicchayanākāradassanaṃ.

One searches by way of agitation; therefore, it is searching. Searching, from the perspective of intention and application, is a mind-state that proceeds in that way. Therefore, it is said, 'When there is craving, there is searching.' The acquisition of objects such as forms means by way of seeking objects such as forms that have a basis. However, in the course of existence, even what is not sought is obtained, and that too is in essence obtained by searching, because it is obtained due to such kamma having been done previously. Therefore, it is said, 'For when there is searching, there is gain.' The discernment of pleasure means that one discerns pleasure specifically; this is the discernment of pleasure. It is the knowledge that proceeds from truly knowing pleasure in terms of its nature, its origin, its cessation, and the escape from it; that is the discernment of pleasure. Jaññā means one should know. Regarding 'beautiful and pleasant' and so forth, it discerns and superimposes various unreal characteristics on the object by way of inclination; this is called discernment. Similarly, the nature of discernment should be understood in the context of craving and wrong views through the contemplation of gratification. In this sutta, however, only thought is mentioned; this is the interpretation. 'In this sutta' refers to the Sakkapañha Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 2.358). For there it is said, 'Desire, O Lord of Devas, is rooted in thought.' 'Here' means in this Mahānidāna Sutta. By 'one discerns only through thought,' he states the instrumental derivation of the word 'vinicchaya' as 'that by which one discerns is discernment.' 'This much' and so forth shows the mode of discernment.

Chandanaṭṭhena chando, evaṃ rañjanaṭṭhena rāgo, svāyaṃ anāsevanatāya mando hutvā pavatto idhādhippetoti āha “dubbalarāgassādhivacana”nti. Ajjhosānanti taṇhādiṭṭhivasena abhinivisanaṃ. “Mayhaṃ [P 2.0129] ida”nti hi taṇhāgāho yebhuyyena attaggāhasannissayova hoti. Tenāha “ahaṃ mama”nti, “balavasanniṭṭhāna”nti ca tesaṃ gāhānaṃ thirabhāvappattimāha. Taṇhādiṭṭhivasena pariggahakaraṇanti “ahaṃ mama”nti balavasanniṭṭhānavasena abhiniviṭṭhassa [M 2.0099] attattaniyaggāhavatthuno aññāsādhāraṇaṃ viya katvā pariggahetvā ṭhānaṃ, tathāpavatto lobhasahagatacittuppādo. Attanā pariggahitassa vatthuno yassa vasena parehi sādhāraṇabhāvassa asahamāno [V 2.0088] hoti puggalo, so dhammo asahanatā. Evaṃ vacanatthaṃ vadanti niruttinayena. Saddalakkhaṇe pana yassa dhammassa vasena macchariyayogato puggalo maccharo, tassa bhāvo, kammaṃ vā macchariyaṃ, macchero dhammo. Macchariyassa balavabhāvato ādarena rakkhaṇaṃ ārakkhoti āha “dvāra…pe… suṭṭhu rakkhaṇa”nti. Attano phalaṃ karotīti karaṇaṃ, yaṃ kiñci kāraṇaṃ, adhikaṃ karaṇanti adhikaraṇaṃ, visesakāraṇaṃ. Visesakāraṇañca bhogānaṃ ārakkhadaṇḍādānādianatthasambhavassāti vuttaṃ “ārakkhādhikaraṇa”ntiādi. Paranisedhanatthanti māraṇādinā paresaṃ vibādhanatthaṃ. Ādīyati etenāti ādānaṃ, daṇḍassa ādānaṃ daṇḍādānaṃ, abhibhavitvā paraviheṭhanacittuppādo. Satthādānepi eseva nayo. Hatthaparāmāsādivasena kāyena kātabbakalaho kāyakalaho. Mammaghaṭṭanādivasena vācāya kātabbakalaho vācākalaho. Virujjhanavasena virūpaṃ gaṇhāti etenāti viggaho. Viruddhaṃ vadati etenāti vivādo. Tuvaṃ tuvanti agāravavacanasahacaraṇato tuvaṃ tuvaṃ, sabbete tathāpavattā dosasahagatacittuppādā veditabbā. Tenāha bhagavā “aneke pāpakā akusalā dhammā sambhavantī”ti (dī. ni. 2.104).

By the meaning of delighting, it is desire; similarly, by the meaning of coloring, it is lust. This lust, having become weak due to non-cultivation, is what is intended here; therefore he says, 'a synonym for weak lust.' Adherence (`ajjhosāna`) means clinging by way of craving and wrong view. For indeed, the grasping of craving, 'This is mine,' mostly relies on the grasping of self. Therefore, he says, 'I, mine,' and 'firmly established,' indicating the attainment of firmness by these graspings. The act of taking possession by way of craving and wrong view means the state of taking possession of an object grasped as self and what belongs to self, which is adhered to by way of firm establishment as 'I, mine,' as if it were not common to others; such is the arising of a mind accompanied by greed. That quality by which a person, regarding an object taken possession of by oneself, becomes unable to bear its being common to others, that quality is the inability to bear sharing. Thus, they explain the meaning of the word according to the method of etymology. In terms of the characteristic of the word, however, miserliness is the state or action of that quality by which a person is miserly due to the connection with miserliness; it is a miserly quality. Because of the strong nature of miserliness, guarding with care is protection; therefore, he says, 'guarding... thoroughly guarding.' That which produces its own result is a cause (`karaṇaṃ`); this means any cause (`kāraṇaṃ`). A superior cause (`adhikaṃ karaṇaṃ`) is a primary cause (`adhikaraṇaṃ`), a special cause. And it is said that 'protection as the primary cause' and so forth refers to the special cause for the arising of misfortunes such as those related to guarding wealth, taking up a rod, and so forth. The purpose of obstructing others means for the purpose of harming others by killing and so forth. That by which one takes is taking. The taking of a rod is rod-taking; it is a mind-state of overpowering and harming others. The same method applies to taking up weapons as well. A quarrel to be done by the body, by way of striking with the hand and so forth, is a bodily quarrel. A quarrel to be done by speech, by way of striking at vital points and so forth, is a verbal quarrel. That by which one seizes in a distorted manner by way of opposition is contention. That by which one speaks in opposition is dispute. 'You, you' is so-called due to being associated with disrespectful speech. All these should be understood as mind-states accompanied by aversion that proceed in that way. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'Many evil, unwholesome states arise' (Dīgha Nikāya 2.104).

112. Desanaṃ nivattesīti “taṇhaṃ paṭicca pariyesanā”tiādinā anulomanayena pavattitaṃ desanaṃ paṭilomanayena [P 2.0130] puna “ārakkhādhikaraṇa”nti ārabhanto nivattesi. Pañcakāmaguṇikarāgavasenāti ārammaṇabhūtā pañca kāmaguṇā etassa atthīti pañcakāmaguṇiko, tattha rañjanavasena abhiramaṇavasena pavattarāgo, tassa vasena uppannā rañjanavasena taṇhāyanavasena pavattā rūpāditaṇhāva kāmesu taṇhāti kāmataṇhā. Bhavati atthi sabbakālaṃ tiṭṭhatīti pavattā bhavadiṭṭhi uttarapadalopena bhavo, taṃsahagatā taṇhā bhavataṇhā. Vibhavati vinassati ucchijjatīti pavattā vibhavadiṭṭhi vibhavo uttarapadalopena, taṃsahagatā taṇhā vibhavataṇhāti āha “sassatadiṭṭhī”tiādi. Ime dve dhammāti [M 2.0100] “esa paccayo upādānassa, yadidaṃ taṇhā”ti (dī. ni. 2.101) evaṃ vuttā vaṭṭamūlataṇhā ca “taṇhaṃ paṭicca pariyesanā”ti (dī. ni. 2.103) evaṃ vuttā samudācārataṇhā cāti ime dve dhammā. Vaṭṭamūlasamudācāravasenāti vaṭṭamūlavasena ceva samudācāravasena ca. Dvīhi koṭṭhāsehīti dvīhi bhāgehi. Dvīhi avayavehi samosaranti nibbattanavasena samaṃ vattanti itoti samosaraṇaṃ, paccayo, ekaṃ samosaraṇaṃ etāsanti ekasamosaraṇā. Kena pana ekasamosaraṇāti āha “vedanāyā”ti. Dvepi hi taṇhā vedanāpaccayā evāti. Tenāha “vedanāpaccayena ekapaccayā”ti. Tato tato osaritvā āgantvā samavasanaṭṭhānaṃ osaraṇa samosaraṇaṃ. Vedanāya [V 2.0089] samaṃ saha ekasmiṃ ārammaṇe osaraṇakapavattanakā vedanā samosaraṇāti āha “idaṃ sahajātasamosaraṇaṃ nāmā”ti.

112. He turned back the teaching means he reversed the teaching that began with 'dependent on craving, there is seeking' and proceeded in direct order, starting anew in reverse order with 'protection as the primary cause.' Regarding 'by way of passion for the five strands of sensual pleasure': One for whom the five strands of sensual pleasure exist as objects is a `pañcakāmaguṇiko`. The passion that proceeds by way of delighting and enjoying in them; due to that passion, the craving for forms and so on, which proceeds by way of delighting and longing, arises. This craving for sensual pleasures is 'sensual craving' (`kāmataṇhā`). The view of existence (`bhavadiṭṭhi`), which proceeds as 'it becomes, it exists, it stands for all time,' is called 'existence' (`bhava`) by dropping the latter part of the compound; the craving associated with it is craving for existence (`bhavataṇhā`). The view of non-existence (`vibhavadiṭṭhi`), which proceeds as 'it ceases to be, it is destroyed, it is annihilated,' is called 'non-existence' (`vibhava`) by dropping the latter part of the compound; the craving associated with it is craving for non-existence (`vibhavataṇhā`). Hence, it is said, 'the eternalist view,' etc. 'These two phenomena' are the root-craving of the cycle of existence, as stated: 'This is the condition for clinging, namely, craving' (Dī. Ni. 2.101), and the craving of habitual behavior, as stated: 'Dependent on craving, there is seeking' (Dī. Ni. 2.103). The phrase 'by way of the root of the cycle and habitual behavior' means both by way of the root of the cycle and by way of habitual behavior. The phrase 'with two parts' means with two divisions. They converge with two parts; this means they proceed together by way of arising. Hence, convergence is a condition. They have a single convergence, thus they are 'single-convergent.' But by what are they 'single-convergent'? It is said: 'By feeling.' For both cravings are indeed conditioned by feeling. Therefore, it is said: 'By the condition of feeling, they have a single condition.' Having descended and arrived from here and there, the place of settling down together is descent and convergence. Because they cause descent and proceeding upon a single object equally and together with feeling, this is convergence with feeling. Hence, it is said: 'This is called co-arisen convergence.'

113. Sabbeti uppattidvāravasena bhinditvā vuttā savipākaphassā eva viññāṇādi vedanāpariyosānā vipākavithīti [P 2.0131] katvā. Paṭiccasamuppādakathā nāma vaṭṭakathāti āha “ṭhapetvā cattāro lokuttaravipākaphasse”ti. Bahudhāti bahuppakārena. Ayañhi pañcadvāre cakkhupasādādivatthukānaṃ pañcannaṃ vedanānaṃ cakkhusamphassādiko phasso sahajātaaññamaññanissayavipākaāhārasampayuttaatthiavigatavasena aṭṭhadhā paccayo hoti. Sesānaṃ pana ekekasmiṃ dvāre sampaṭicchanasantīraṇatadārammaṇavasena pavattānaṃ kāmāvacaravipākavedanānaṃ cakkhusamphassādiko phasso upanissayavasena ekadhāva paccayo hoti. Manodvārepi tadārammaṇavasena pavattānaṃ kāmāvacaravipākavedanānaṃ sahajātamanosamphasso tatheva aṭṭhadhā paccayo hoti, tathā paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutivasena pavattānaṃ tebhūmakavipākavedanānaṃ. Yā pana tā manodvāre tadārammaṇavasena pavattā kāmāvacaravedanā, tāsaṃ manodvārāvajjanasampayutto manosamphasso upanissayavasena ekadhāva paccayo hotīti evaṃ phasso bahudhā vedanāya paccayo hotīti veditabbaṃ.

113. All these are stated having been divided by way of the door of arising, because the resultant process consists of only resultant contacts, beginning with consciousness and ending with feeling. Because the exposition of dependent origination is an exposition of the round, he said, 'excluding the four supramundane resultant contacts.' 'In many ways' means in numerous modes. For in the five doors, contact beginning with eye-contact becomes an eightfold condition for the five feelings that have eye-sensitivity, etc., as their basis, by way of conascence, mutual dependence, support, result, nutriment, association, presence, and non-disappearance. For the rest, however, in each door, contact beginning with eye-contact becomes a single condition by way of decisive support for the sense-sphere resultant feelings that arise by way of receiving, investigating, and registering. In the mind-door, too, the conascent mental contact becomes an eightfold condition in the same way for the sense-sphere resultant feelings that arise by way of registering, and likewise for the three-realm resultant feelings that arise as rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death. As for those sense-sphere feelings that arise in the mind-door by way of registering, the mental contact associated with mind-door adverting becomes a single condition by way of decisive support. Thus, it should be understood that contact is a condition for feeling in many ways.

114. Vedanādīnanti vedanāsaññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇānaṃ. Asadisabhāvāti anubhavanasañjānanābhisaṅkharaṇavijānanabhāvā. Te hi aññamaññavidhurena vedayitādirūpena ākiriyanti paññāyantīti ākārāti vuccanti. Teyevāti [M 2.0101] vedanādīnaṃ te eva vedayitādiākārā. Sādhukaṃ dassiyamānāti sakkaccaṃ paccakkhato viya pakāsiyamānā. Taṃ taṃ līnamatthaṃ gamentīti “arūpaṭṭho ārammaṇābhimukhanamanaṭṭho”ti evamādikaṃ taṃ taṃ līnaṃ apākaṭamatthaṃ gamenti ñāpentīti liṅgāni. Tassa tassa sañjānanahetutoti tassa tassa arūpaṭṭhādikassa sallakkhaṇassa kāraṇattā. Nimīyanti anumīyanti etehīti nimittāni. Tathā tathā arūpabhāvādippakārena, vedayitādippakārena ca uddisitabbato kathetabbato uddesā. Tasmāti “asadisabhāvā”tiādinā vuttamevatthaṃ kāraṇabhāvena paccāmasati. Yasmā vedanādīnaṃ aññamaññaasadisabhāvā yathāvuttenatthena ākārādayo, tasmā ayaṃ idāni vuccamāno ettha pāḷipade attho.

114. 'Beginning with feeling' refers to feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. 'Dissimilar in nature' means the nature of experiencing, perceiving, forming, and cognizing. These are distinguished from each other by their distinct modes of experiencing, etc., and thus are called 'characteristics' (ākārā). They themselves are the characteristics of experiencing, etc., of feeling, etc. 'Being well shown' means being carefully revealed as if directly seen. 'They reveal that hidden meaning' means they make known that subtle, unclear meaning, such as 'the state of being formless,' 'the state of bending towards the object,' etc.; thus, they are 'indicators' (liṅgāni). 'As the cause of perceiving that' means because they are the cause for discerning that individual characteristic of the state of being formless, etc. They are inferred by these; hence, they are 'marks' (nimittāni). Because they are to be pointed out and spoken of in such and such a way—by way of the state of being formless, etc., and by way of experiencing, etc.—they are 'designations' (uddesā). 'Therefore'—he reflects upon the very meaning stated by 'dissimilar in nature,' etc., as the reason. Because the characteristics, etc., of feeling, etc., are dissimilar in nature from each other in the aforesaid sense, therefore this is the meaning of the Pāli term here which is now being stated.

Nāmasamūhassāti ārammaṇābhimukhaṃ namanaṭṭhena “nāma”nti laddhasamaññassa [P 2.0132] vedanādicatukkhandhasaṅkhātassa arūpadhammapuñjassa. Paññattīti “nāmakāyo arūpakalāpo arūpino [V 2.0090] khandhā”tiādikā paññāpanā hoti. Cetanāpadhānattā saṅkhārakkhandhadhammānaṃ “saṅkhārānaṃ cetanākāre”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tathā hi suttantabhājanīye saṅkhārakkhandhavibhajane “yā cetanā sañcetanā sañcetayitatta”nti (vibha. 249 abhidhammabhājanīye) cetanāva niddiṭṭhā. Asatīti asantesu. Vacanavipallāsena hi evaṃ vuttaṃ. Cattāro khandhe vatthuṃ katvāti vedanā saññā cittaṃ cetanādayoti ime catukkhandhasaññite nissayapaccayabhūte dhamme vatthuṃ katvā. Ayañca nayo pañcadvārepi sambhavatīti “manodvāre”ti visesitaṃ. Adhivacanasamphassavevacanoti adhivacanamukhena paññattimukhena gahetabbattā “adhivacanasamphasso”ti laddhanāmo. Soti manosamphasso. Pañcavokāre ca hadayavatthuṃ nissāya labbhanato rūpakāye paññāyateva, ayaṃ pana nayo idha na icchito vedanādipaṭikkhepavasena asambhavapariyāyassa jotitattāti “pañcapasāde vatthuṃ katvā uppajjeyyā”ti attho vutto. Na hi vedanāsannissayena vinā pañcapasāde vatthuṃ katvā manosamphassassa sambhavo atthi. Uppattiṭṭhāne asati anuppattiṭṭhānato phalassa uppatti nāma kadācipi natthīti imamatthaṃ yathādhigatassa atthassa nidassanavasena dassento “ambarukkhe”tiādimāha[M 2.0102]. Rūpakāyatoti kevalaṃ rūpakāyato. Tassāti manosamphassassa.

'Of the group of name' refers to the collection of immaterial phenomena, known as the four aggregates beginning with feeling, which is designated as 'name' because of its characteristic of bending towards the object. 'Designation' is the description such as 'the body of name, the group of the immaterial, the immaterial aggregates,' and so on. Because volition is predominant among the phenomena of the formations aggregate, it is said, 'of formations in the mode of volition,' and so on. Indeed, in the analysis of the formations aggregate in the Suttanta classification, only volition is specified: 'Whatever volition, intending, or act of intending there is' (Vibh. 249, in the Abhidhamma classification). 'When non-existent' means when they are absent. This is stated due to a reversal of case-ending. 'Having made the four aggregates the basis' means having made as basis these phenomena which serve as the support condition, designated as the four aggregates: feeling, perception, consciousness, and volition, etc. And since this method is also possible in the five doors, 'in the mind-door' is specified. 'Designation-contact' is so named because it is to be apprehended by way of a term, by way of a concept. That is mind-contact. In the five-constituent existence, since it is obtained dependent on the heart-basis, it is indeed manifest in the material body. However, this method is not intended here, because an impossible case is illuminated by way of the rejection of feeling, etc. The meaning stated is: 'It would arise having made the five sense faculties the basis.' For without dependence on feeling, there is no possibility of mind-contact arising having made the five sense faculties the basis. To illustrate this meaning in accordance with the meaning as it has been grasped, showing that where there is no place of arising, the arising of a fruit from a non-arising place never occurs, he said, 'a sky-tree,' etc. 'From the material body alone' means solely from the material body. 'Of that' refers to mind-contact.

Virodhipaccayasannipāte vibhūtatarā visadisuppatti, tasmiṃ vā sati attano santāne vijjamānasseva visadisuppattihetubhāvo ruppanākāro. So eva ruppanākāro vatthusappaṭighādikaṃ taṃ taṃ līnamatthaṃ gametīti liṅgaṃ. Tassa tassa sañjānanahetuto nimittaṃ. Tathā tathā uddisitabbato uddesoti evamettha ākārādayo atthato [P 2.0133] veditabbā. Vatthārammaṇānaṃ aññamaññapaṭihananaṃ paṭigho, tato paṭighato jāto paṭighasamphasso. Tenāha “sappaṭigha”ntiādi. Nāmakāyatoti kevalaṃ nāmakāyato. Tassāti paṭighasamphassassa. Sesaṃ paṭhamapañhe vuttanayameva.

In the conjunction of opposing conditions, a dissimilar arising becomes more manifest; or, when that exists, the mode of alteration is the state of being a cause for the dissimilar arising of what is already present in one's own continuity. That very mode of alteration makes known a particular subtle meaning, such as the impingement of the base, etc.; thus, it is an indicator (liṅga). Because it is the cause for perceiving this or that, it is a mark (nimitta). Because it is to be pointed out in such and such a way, it is a designation (uddesa). Thus, in this context, the characteristics, etc., should be understood according to their meaning. The mutual striking of base and object is impingement; born from that impingement is impingement-contact. Hence, he said, 'with impingement,' and so on. 'From the name-body alone' means solely from the name-body. 'Of that' refers to impingement-contact. The rest is in the same way as stated in the first question.

Ubhayavasenāti nāmakāyo rūpakāyoti ubhayasannissayassa adhivacanasamphasso paṭighasamphassoti ubhayasamphassassa vasena.

'By way of both' means by way of the dual dependence on the name-body and the form-body, and by way of both contacts, namely, designation-contact and impingement-contact.

Visuṃ visuṃ paccayaṃ dassetvāti byatirekamukhena paccekaṃ nāmakāyarūpakāyasaññitaṃ paccayaṃ dassetvā. Tesanti phassānaṃ. Avisesatoti visesaṃ akatvā sāmaññato. Dassetunti byatirekamukheneva dassetuṃ. Eseva hetūti esa chasupi dvāresu pavatto nāmarūpasaṅkhāto hetu yathārahaṃ dvinnampi phassānaṃ. Idāni taṃ yathārahaṃ pavattiṃ vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “cakkhudvārādīsu hī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'Having shown the condition separately' means having shown individually, by way of exclusion, the condition termed name-body and form-body. 'Of these' means of the contacts. 'Without distinction' means without making a distinction, generally. 'To show' means to show by way of exclusion. 'This is the cause' means this cause, termed name-and-form, which occurs in the six doors, is the cause for both contacts, as is appropriate. Now, to show that occurrence as is appropriate by analyzing it, it is said, 'For in the eye-door, etc.'

Sampayuttakā [V 2.0091] khandhāti phassena sampayuttā vedanādayo khandhā. Āvajjanassāpi sampayuttakkhandhaggahaṇenevettha gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ tadavinābhāvato. Parato manosamphassepi eseva nayo. Pañcavidhopīti cakkhusamphassādivasena pañcavidhopi. So phassoti paṭighasamphasso. Bahudhāti bahuppakārena. Tathā hi vipākanāmaṃ vipākassa anekabhedassa manosamphassassa sahajātaaññamaññanissayavipākasampayuttaatthiavigatavasena sattadhā paccayo hoti. Yaṃ panettha āhārakiccaṃ, taṃ āhārapaccayavasena. Yaṃ indriyakiccaṃ, taṃ indriyapaccayavasena paccayo hoti. Avipākaṃ pana nāmaṃ avipākassa manosamphassassa ṭhapetvā vipākapaccayaṃ itaresaṃ vasena paccayo hoti. Rūpaṃ pana cakkhāyatanādibhedaṃ cakkhusamphassādikassa pañcavidhassa phassassa nissayapurejātaindriyavippayuttaatthiavigatavasena [P 2.0134][M 2.0103] chadhā paccayo hoti. Rūpāyatanādibhedaṃ tassa pañcavidhassa ārammaṇapurejātaatthiavigatavasena catudhā paccayo hoti.
