Manosamphassassa pana tāni rūpāyatanādīni, dhammārammaṇañca tathā ca ārammaṇapaccayamatteneva paccayo hoti. Vatthurūpaṃ pana manosamphassassa nissayapurejātavippayuttaatthiavigatavasena pañcadhā paccayo hoti. Evaṃ nāmarūpaṃ assa phassassa bahudhā paccayo hotīti veditabbaṃ.

The associated aggregates are the aggregates of feeling and so forth that are associated with contact. Herein, by the term 'associated aggregates,' the inclusion of the aggregates associated with mind-door adverting should also be understood, as they are inseparable. The same principle applies later to mental contact. The term 'fivefold' refers to the five kinds of contact, such as eye-contact and so forth. That contact is contact with impingement. The term 'in many ways' means in various ways. For example, resultant mentality, due to its various divisions, serves as a condition for resultant mental contact in seven ways: through co-nascence, mutuality, dependence, result, association, presence, and non-disappearance. Whatever herein has the function of nutriment is a condition by way of the nutriment condition. Whatever has the function of a faculty is a condition by way of the faculty condition. Non-resultant mentality, however, serves as a condition for non-resultant mental contact through the remaining conditions, excluding the result condition. Form, such as the eye-base and so forth, serves as a condition for the fivefold contact, such as eye-contact, in six ways: through dependence, pre-nascence, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. Form, such as the visible-object base and so forth, serves as a condition for that fivefold contact in four ways: through object, pre-nascence, presence, and non-disappearance. For mental contact, however, those forms such as the visible-object base, as well as the mental object, are a condition merely by way of the object condition. The physical base, however, serves as a condition for mental contact in five ways: through dependence, pre-nascence, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. Thus, it should be understood that name-and-form serves as a condition for this contact in many ways.

115. Paṭhamuppattiyaṃ viññāṇaṃ nāmarūpassa visesapaccayoti imamatthaṃ byatirekamukhena dassetuṃ pāḷiyaṃ “mātukucchimhi na okkamissathā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Gabbhaseyyakapaṭisandhi hi bāhirato mātukucchiṃ okkamantassa viya hontīpi atthato yathāpaccayaṃ khandhānaṃ tattha paṭhamuppattiyeva. Tenāha “pavisitvā…pe… na vattissathā”ti. Suddhanti kevalaṃ viññāṇena amissitaṃ virahitaṃ. “Avasesa”nti idaṃ nāmāpekkhaṃ, tasmā avasesaṃ nāmarūpanti imaṃ viññāṇaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesaṃ nāmarūpaṃ vāti attho. Paṭisandhivasena okkantanti paṭisandhiggahaṇavasena, mātukucchiṃ okkamantassa vā paṭhamāvayavabhāvena otiṇṇaṃ. Vokkamissathāti santativicchedaṃ vināsaṃ upagamissatha, taṃ pana maraṇaṃ nāma hotīti āha “cutivasenā”ti. Assāti viññāṇassa, tañca kho viññāṇasāmaññavasena vuttaṃ. Tenāha “tasseva cittassa nirodhenā”ti, paṭisandhicittasseva nirodhenāti attho. Tatoti paṭisandhicittato. Paṭisandhicittassa, tato dutiyatatiyacittānaṃ vā nirodhena cuti na hotīti vuttamatthaṃ yuttito vibhāvetuṃ “paṭisandhicittena hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Etasmiṃ antareti etasmiṃ soḷasacittakkhaṇe kāle. Antarāyo natthīti ettha dārakassa tāva maraṇantarāyo mā hotu tadā cuticittassa asambhavato, mātu pana kathaṃ tadā maraṇantarāyābhāvoti? Taṃ taṃ kālaṃ anatikkamitvā [V 2.0092] tadantareyeva [P 2.0135] cavanadhammāya gabbhaggahaṇasseva asambhavato. Tenāha “ayañhi anokāso nāmā”ti, cutiyāti adhippāyo.

115. In the first arising, consciousness is the specific condition for name-and-form. To explain this meaning through the method of exclusion, the Pāli text states, 'If consciousness were not to enter the mother’s womb,' and so forth. For rebirth-linking in the womb, though appearing as if entering the mother’s womb from outside, is in reality just the first arising of the aggregates there according to conditions. Therefore, it is said, 'Having entered... you shall not continue.' The term 'pure' means merely, unmixed with consciousness, and devoid. The term 'the remainder' refers to name; thus, 'the remainder is name-and-form' means that apart from this consciousness, the remainder is name-and-form. The term 'entered by way of rebirth-linking' means entered in the manner of grasping rebirth-linking, or descended as the initial element in the mother’s womb. The term 'you shall perish' means you will meet with discontinuity, destruction. But that is called death; hence it is said, 'by way of passing away.' The term 'of that' refers to consciousness, and this is stated in a general sense regarding consciousness. Therefore, it is said, 'with the cessation of that very consciousness,' meaning with the cessation of just the rebirth-linking consciousness. The term 'from that' means from the rebirth-linking consciousness. The meaning conveyed is that death does not occur with the cessation of the second or third consciousnesses following the rebirth-linking consciousness; to clarify this logically, it is said, 'because of the rebirth-linking consciousness,' and so forth. The term 'during this interval' means during this period of sixteen mind-moments. The phrase 'there is no danger' means that for the child, there is no danger of death in that interval, since the death-consciousness cannot arise at that time. But how can there be no danger of death for the mother then? Because without passing beyond that time, conception cannot occur during that interval, as the embryo is liable to perish. Therefore, it is said, 'for this is not the occasion,' with reference to death.

Paṭisandhicittena saddhiṃ samuṭṭhitarūpānīti okkantikkhaṇe uppannakammajarūpāni vadati. Tāni hi nippariyāyato paṭisandhicittena saddhiṃ samuṭṭhitarūpāni nāma, na utusamuṭṭhānāni paṭisandhicittassa uppādato pacchā samuṭṭhitattā. Cittajāhārajānaṃ [M 2.0104] pana tadā asambhavo eva. Yāni paṭisandhicittena saddhiṃ samuṭṭhitarūpāni, tāni tividhāni tassa uppādakkhaṇe samuṭṭhitāni, ṭhitikkhaṇe samuṭṭhitāni, bhaṅgakkhaṇe samuṭṭhitānīti. Tesu uppādakkhaṇe samuṭṭhitāni sattarasamassa bhavaṅgassa uppādakkhaṇe nirujjhanti, ṭhitikkhaṇe samuṭṭhitāni ṭhitikkhaṇe nirujjhanti, bhaṅgakkhaṇe samuṭṭhitāni bhaṅgakkhaṇe nirujjhanti. Tattha “bhañjamāno dhammo bhañjamānassa dhammassa paccayo hotī”ti na sakkā vattuṃ, uppāde, pana ṭhitiyañca na na sakkāti “sattarasamassa bhavaṅgassa uppādakkhaṇe, ṭhitikkhaṇe ca dharantānaṃ vasena tassa paccayampi dātuṃ na sakkontī”ti vuttaṃ. Rūpakāyūpatthambhitasseva hi nāmakāyassa pañcavokāre pavattīti. Tehi rūpadhammehi tassa cittassa balavataraṃ sandhāyāha “sattarasamassa…pe… pavatti pavattatī”ti. Paveṇī ghaṭiyatīti aṭṭhacattālīsakammajassa [P 2.0136] rūpapaveṇī sambandhā hutvā pavattati. Paṭhamañhi paṭisandhicittaṃ, tato yāva soḷasamaṃ bhavaṅgacittaṃ, tesu ekekassa uppādaṭhitibhaṅgavasena tayo tayo khaṇā. Tattha ekekassa cittassa tīsu tīsu khaṇesu samatiṃsa samatiṃsa kammajarūpāni uppajjanti. Iti soḷasatikā aṭṭhacattālīsaṃ honti. Esa nayo tato paresupi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “aṭṭhacattālīsakammajassa rūpapaveṇī sambandhā hutvā pavattatī”ti. Sace pana na sakkontīti paṭisandhicittena saddhiṃ samuṭṭhitarūpāni sattarasamassa bhavaṅgassa paccayaṃ dātuṃ sace na sakkonti. Yadi hi paṭisandhicittato sattarasamaṃ cuticittaṃ siyā, paṭisandhicittassa ṭhitibhaṅgakkhaṇesupi kammajarūpaṃ na uppajjeyya, pageva bhavaṅgacittakkhaṇesu. Tathā sati nattheva tassa cittassa paccayalābhoti pavatti nappavattati, paveṇī na ghaṭiyateva, aññadatthu vicchijjati. Tenāha “vokkamatiti nāma hotī”tiādi.

The material phenomena that arise together with the rebirth-linking consciousness refers to the kamma-produced material phenomena that have arisen at the moment of conception. Indeed, they are, in the ultimate sense, the material phenomena that arise together with the rebirth-linking consciousness, not those produced by temperature, because the latter arise after the arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness. Moreover, at that time, there is absolutely no possibility of those born of mind or nutriment. The material phenomena that arise together with the rebirth-linking consciousness are of three kinds: those that arise at its arising moment, those that arise at its static moment, and those that arise at its dissolution moment. Among these, those that arise at the arising moment cease at the arising moment of the seventeenth life-continuum; those that arise at the static moment cease at its static moment; and those that arise at the dissolution moment cease at its dissolution moment. Here, it cannot be said that 'a vanishing phenomenon is a condition for a vanishing phenomenon,' but it can indeed be said regarding the arising and static moments. Therefore, it is stated: 'They cannot serve as a condition for the seventeenth life-continuum at its arising and static moments because they are ceasing.' For the mental body exists in the five-aggregate existence only when supported by the material body. Referring to the strengthening of that consciousness by those material phenomena, it is said, 'The seventeenth... and so forth... the continuity proceeds.' The term 'the lineage is connected' means that the lineage of forty-eightfold kamma-produced material phenomena continues in connection. First, there is the rebirth-linking consciousness, then up to the sixteenth life-continuum consciousness. For each of these, there are three moments: arising, static, and dissolution. In each of these three moments of every consciousness, thirty kamma-produced material phenomena arise. Thus, sixteen times three makes forty-eight. This is the method, and the same applies thereafter. Therefore, it is said: 'The lineage of forty-eightfold kamma-produced material phenomena continues in connection.' But if they cannot—if the material phenomena arising together with the rebirth-linking consciousness cannot serve as a condition for the seventeenth life-continuum—if the seventeenth consciousness after the rebirth-linking consciousness were the death-consciousness, then no kamma-produced material phenomena would arise even at the static and dissolution moments of the rebirth-linking consciousness, let alone during the moments of the life-continuum consciousness. In such a case, that consciousness would not obtain a condition at all, and the continuity would not proceed; the lineage would not connect, but would instead be cut off. Hence, it is said: 'There is what is called 'separation,'' and so forth.

Itthattāyāti itthaṃpakāratāya. Yādiso gabbhaseyyakassa attabhāvo, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tassa ca pañcakkhandhā anūnā eva hontīti āha “evaṃ paripuṇṇapañcakkhandhabhāvāyā”ti. Upacchijjissathāti santānavicchedena vicchindeyya. Suddhaṃ nāmarūpamevāti viññāṇavirahitaṃ kevalaṃ nāmarūpameva. Avayavānaṃ pāripūri vuḍḍhi. Thirabhāvappatti virūḷhi. Mahallakabhāvappatti vepullaṃ. Tāni [V 2.0093] ca yathākkamaṃ paṭhamādivayavasena hontīti vuttaṃ “paṭhamavayavasenā”tiādi. Vā-saddo aniyamattho, tena vassasahassadvayādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

The term 'in such a way' means in such a manner. This is said with reference to the kind of existence of one lying in the womb. And his five aggregates are indeed complete; hence it is said, 'thus, for the state of complete five aggregates.' The term 'it would be cut off' means it would be severed by the interruption of the continuity. The term 'merely name-and-form' means only name-and-form, devoid of consciousness. Growth is the fulfillment of the parts. Development is the attainment of stability. Flourishing is the attainment of greatness. And these occur in sequence according to the initial and subsequent stages, as stated by 'through the first stage,' and so forth. The word 'vā' indicates indefiniteness; thus, the inclusion of two thousand years and so forth should be understood.

Viññāṇamevāti [M 2.0105] niyamavacanaṃ, ito bāhirakappitassa attano, issarādīnañca paṭikkhepapadaṃ, na avijjādiphassādipaṭikkhepapadaṃ paṭiyogīnivattanapadattā avadhāraṇassa. Tenāha “eseva hetū”tiādi. Ayañca nayo heṭṭhāpi sabbapadesu yathārahaṃ vattabbo. Idāni viññāṇameva nāmarūpassa padhānakāraṇanti imamatthaṃ opammavasena vibhāvetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Paccekaṃ viya samuditassāpi nāmarūpassa viññāṇena vinā attakiccāsamatthataṃ dassetuṃ “tvaṃ nāmarūpaṃ nāmā”ti ekajjhaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Purecāriketi pubbaṅgameva. Viññāṇañhi [P 2.0137] sahajātadhammānaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā “manopubbaṅgamā dhammā”ti. (Dha. pa. 1; netti. 90, 92; peṭako. 13, 83) bahudhāti anekappakārena paccayo hoti.

The term 'consciousness alone' (viññāṇameva) is a definitive statement, a term for rejecting a fabricated self, gods, and so forth from outside, but not a term for rejecting ignorance, contact, and so forth, since the determination serves to negate the opposing factors. Hence it is said, 'This is the cause' (eseva hetu), and so forth. This method should be applied appropriately to all passages below as well. Now, to explain the meaning that consciousness alone is the principal cause of name-and-form, it is illustrated with a simile: 'Just as...' (yathā hi), and so forth. To show that name-and-form, even when taken as a whole, is incapable of performing its function without consciousness—just as when taken individually—it is taken together and stated: 'You are name-and-form' (tvaṃ nāmarūpaṃ nāma). The term 'preceding' (purecārika) means simply 'forerunner'. For consciousness is the forerunner of co-arisen phenomena. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'Mind is the forerunner of all things' (Dhp. 1; Netti. 90, 92; Peṭ. 13, 83). The term 'in many ways' (bahudhā) means it is a condition in various ways.

Kathaṃ? Vipākanāmassa hi paṭisandhiyaṃ aññaṃ vā viññāṇaṃ sahajātaaññamaññanissayavipākaāhāraindriyasampayuttaatthiavigatapaccayehi navadhā paccayo hoti. Vatthurūpassa paṭisandhiyaṃ sahajātaaññamaññanissayavipākaāhāraindriyavippayuttaatthiavigatapaccayehi navadhā paccayo hoti. Ṭhapetvā pana vatthurūpaṃ sesarūpassa imesu navasu aññamaññapaccayaṃ apanetvā sesehi aṭṭhahi paccayehi paccayo hoti. Abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇaṃ pana asaññasattarūpassa, pañcavokāre vā kammajassa suttantikapariyāyato upanissayavasena ekadhāva paccayo hoti. Avasesañhi paṭhamabhavaṅgato pabhuti sabbampi viññāṇaṃ tassa nāmarūpassa yathārahaṃ paccayo hotīti veditabbaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato pana paccayanaye dassiyamāne sabbāpi mahāpakaraṇakathā ānetabbā hotīti na vitthāritā. Kathaṃ panetaṃ paccetabbaṃ “paṭisandhināmarūpaṃ viññāṇapaccayā hotī”ti? Suttato, yuttito ca. Pāḷiyañhi “cittānuparivattino dhammā”tiādinā (dha. sa. mātikā 62) nayena bahudhā vedanādīnaṃ viññāṇapaccayatā āgatā. Yuttito pana idha cittajena rūpena diṭṭhena adiṭṭhassāpi rūpassa viññāṇaṃ paccayo hotīti viññāyati. Cittehi pasanne, appasanne vā tadanurūpāni rūpāni uppajjamānāni diṭṭhāni, diṭṭhena ca adiṭṭhassa anumānaṃ hotīti. Iminā idha “diṭṭhena cittajarūpena adiṭṭhassāpi paṭisandhirūpassa viññāṇaṃ paccayo hotī”ti paccetabbametaṃ[P 2.0138]. Kammasamuṭṭhānassāpi hi rūpassa cittasamuṭṭhānassa viya viññāṇapaccayatā paṭṭhāne āgatāti.

How? For resultant mentality at rebirth-linking, consciousness is a condition in nine ways: as conascence, mutuality, support, result, nutriment, faculty, association, presence, and non-disappearance. For the physical base at rebirth-linking, consciousness is a condition in nine ways: as conascence, mutuality, support, result, nutriment, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. But for the remaining materiality, excluding the physical base, consciousness is a condition in eight ways, omitting mutuality from these nine. Volitional consciousness, for the materiality of non-percipient beings or for the kamma-born materiality in the five-constituent existence, is a condition in one way, as decisive support according to the Suttanta method. For the rest, from the first life-continuum onwards, all consciousness is a condition for that name-and-form as is appropriate. This is the summary here. In detail, however, all the discussions from the Great Treatise should be brought in when explaining the conditional relations, but they are not elaborated here. How then should this be understood: "Rebirth-linking name-and-form arises dependent on consciousness"? By the Suttas and by reasoning. For in the Pāli canon, through passages like "mental states that follow the mind" (Dhs. Mātikā 62), the dependence of feeling and so forth on consciousness is stated in many ways. By reasoning, here it is understood that consciousness is a condition even for unseen materiality, by inference from the seen mind-produced materiality. When the mind is clear or unclear, corresponding forms are seen to arise, and from the seen, the unseen can be inferred. Thus, here it should be understood that consciousness is a condition for the unseen rebirth-linking materiality, by inference from the seen mind-produced materiality. For even kamma-produced materiality, like mind-produced materiality, is stated in the Paṭṭhāna to have consciousness as a condition.

116. Idha [V 2.0094][M 2.0106] samudaya-saddo samudāya-saddo viya samūhapariyāyoti āha “dukkharāsisambhavo”ti. Ekakoti asahāyo rājaparisārahito. Passeyyāma te rājabhāvaṃ amhehi vināti adhippāyo. Yathārahaṃ parisaṃ rañjetīti hi rājā. Atthatoti atthasiddhito avadantampi vadati viya. “Hadayavatthu”nti imināva tannissayopi gahito vāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ānantariyabhāvato nissayanissayopi “nissayo” tveva vuccatīti. Paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ nāma bhaveyyāsi, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatīti attho. Tenāha “passeyyāmā”tiādi. Bahudhāti anekadhā paccayo hoti. Kathaṃ? Nāmaṃ tāva paṭisandhiyaṃ sahajātaaññamaññanissayavipākasampayuttaatthiavigatapaccayehi sattadhā viññāṇassa paccayo hotīti. Kiñci panettha hetupaccayena, kiñci āhārapaccayenāti evaṃ aññathāpi paccayo hoti. Avipākaṃ pana nāmaṃ yathāvuttesu paccayesu ṭhapetvā vipākapaccayaṃ itarehi chahi paccayehi paccayo hoti. Kiñci panettha hetupaccayena, kiñci āhārapaccayenāti aññathāpi paccayo hoti, tañca kho pavattiyaṃyeva, na paṭisandhiyaṃ. Rūpato pana hadayavatthu paṭisandhiyaṃ viññāṇassa sahajātaaññamaññanissayavippayuttaatthi avigatapaccayehi chadhāva paccayo hoti. Pavattiyaṃ pana sahajātaaññamaññapaccayavajjitehi pañcahi purejātapaccayena saha teheva paccayehi paccayo hoti. Cakkhāyatanādibhedaṃ pana pañcavidhampi rūpaṃ yathākkamaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādibhedassa viññāṇassa nissayapurejātaindriyavippayuttaatthiavigatapaccayehi paccayo hotīti evaṃ nāmarūpaṃ viññāṇassa bahudhā paccayo hotīti veditabbaṃ.

116. Here, the term 'samudaya' (origin) is used in the sense of accumulation, like the word 'samudāya,' as it is said: 'the arising of the mass of suffering.' 'Alone' (ekako) means without companions, deprived of a royal assembly. 'We would see your kingship without us' is the intended meaning. For a king is so called because he delights his assembly appropriately. 'Atthato' (in meaning) implies that even what is unsaid is as if said, due to the accomplishment of the meaning. By 'hadayavatthu' (heart-base), it should be understood that what is dependent on it is also included. Due to the state of immediacy, that which is dependent on the support is also called 'nissaya' (support). 'You might be rebirth-linking consciousness' means that it is not possible for it to exist (independently). Hence, it is said: 'We would see,' etc. 'In many ways' means it is a condition in manifold ways. How? First, mentality (nāma) is a condition for consciousness in seven ways at rebirth-linking: through co-nascence, mutuality, support, result, association, presence, and non-disappearance conditions. Here, some are conditioned by the root-condition, some by the nutriment-condition, and so on, in other ways as well. However, non-resultant mentality, leaving out the result-condition, is a condition in the remaining six ways. Some are conditioned by the root-condition, some by the nutriment-condition, and so on, in other ways as well; but this applies only during the course of life, not at rebirth-linking. As for materiality (rūpa), the heart-base is a condition for consciousness at rebirth-linking in six ways: through co-nascence, mutuality, support, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance conditions. During the course of life, however, it is a condition by means of five conditions: the previously mentioned ones, excluding co-nascence and mutuality, but including the pre-nascence condition. The fivefold materiality—such as the eye-base, etc.—is a condition for the corresponding types of consciousness (e.g., eye-consciousness) through dependence, pre-nascence, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance conditions, respectively. Thus, it should be understood that mentality-materiality is a condition for consciousness in many ways.

Yvāyamanukkamena viññāṇassa nāmarūpaṃ, paṭisandhināmarūpassa[P 2.0139], ca viññāṇaṃ pati paccayabhāvo, so kadāci viññāṇassa sātisayo, kadāci nāmarūpassa, kadāci ubhinnaṃ sadisoti tividhopi so “ettāvatā”ti padena ekajjhaṃ gahitoti dassento “viññāṇe…pe… pavattesū”ti vatvā puna yamidampi viññāṇaṃ nāmarūpasaññitānaṃ pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ aññamaññanissayena pavattānaṃ ettakena sabbā saṃsāravaṭṭappavattīti imamatthaṃ dassento “ettakena…pe… paṭisandhiyo”ti āha. Tattha ettakenāti ettakeneva, na ito aññena kenaci kārakavedakasabhāvena attanā, issarādinā vāti attho. Antogadhāvadhāraṇañhetaṃ padaṃ.

This sequential conditionality, wherein name-and-form is a condition for consciousness, and consciousness is a condition for rebirth-linking name-and-form, is sometimes predominant on the side of consciousness, sometimes on the side of name-and-form, and sometimes equally balanced between both. Thus, showing that all three types are included under the term 'to this extent,' having stated, 'With consciousness... and so on... in those that have come to be,' he then says 'By this much... and so on... rebirth-linkings,' thereby demonstrating that the entire process of the round of existence proceeds by this much, namely, by this consciousness which proceeds through the mutual dependence of the five aggregates designated as name-and-form. Here, 'by this much' means by just this much alone, not by any other agent or experiencer with the nature of a self, a creator, or the like. This word implies an internal limitation.

Vacanamattameva [M 2.0107] adhikiccāti dāsādīsu sirivaḍḍhakādi-saddā viya atathattā vacanamattameva adhikāraṃ katvā pavattassa. Tenāha “atthaṃ adisvā”ti. Vohārassāti voharaṇamattassa. Pathoti pavattimaggo pavattiyā visayo. Yasmā saraṇakiriyāvasena puggalo “sato”ti vuccati, sampajānanakiriyāvasena “sampajāno”ti, tasmā vuttaṃ “kāraṇāpadesavasenā”ti. Kāraṇaṃ [V 2.0095] niddhāretvā utti niruttīti. Ekameva atthaṃ “paṇḍito”tiādinā pakārato ñāpanato “paññattī”ti vadanti. So eva hi “paṇḍito”ti ca “byatto”ti ca “medhāvī”ti ca paññāpīyatīti. Paṇḍiccappakārato pana paṇḍito, veyyattiyappakārato byattoti paññāpīyatīti evaṃ pakārato paññāpanato paññatti. Yasmā idha adhivacananiruttipaññattipadāni samānatthāni. Sabbañca vacanaṃ adhivacanādibhāvaṃ bhajati, tasmā kesuci vacanavisesesu visesena pavattehi adhivacanādisaddehi sabbāni vacanāni paññattiatthappakāsanasāmaññena vuttānīti iminā adhippāyena ayamatthayojanā katāti veditabbā.

'Merely the word is the primary concern,' as with words like 'Sirivaḍḍhaka' used for slaves, which, being not so in reality, function by making the mere word the basis. Hence it is said, 'not seeing the meaning.' 'Of conventional usage' means merely the act of using convention. 'The path' refers to the way of proceeding, the domain of what proceeds. Because a person is called 'mindful' (sato) by way of the act of remembering and 'clearly comprehending' (sampajāno) by way of the act of clear comprehension, therefore it is said, 'by way of assigning a reason.' An utterance (utti) after having determined the reason (kāraṇa) is an expression (nirutti). A single meaning is called a 'designation' (paññatti) because it is made known through various modes, such as 'wise' (paṇḍito) and so forth. For indeed, the same person is designated as 'wise' (paṇḍito), 'skilled' (byatto), and 'intelligent' (medhāvī). He is designated as 'wise' from the mode of wisdom (paṇḍicca), and as 'skilled' from the mode of skill (veyyattiya). Thus, a designation (paññatti) is the making known through such modes. Because here, the terms 'appellation' (adhivacana), 'expression' (nirutti), and 'designation' (paññatti) have the same meaning. And since all speech partakes of the nature of appellation and the like, therefore, all words are spoken of by the terms 'appellation' and so forth—which are used specifically in certain specific instances of speech—by way of the common characteristic of revealing the meaning of a concept. It should be understood that this explanation of the meaning is given with this intention.

Atha vā adhi-saddo uparibhāve, upari vacanaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Kassa upari? Pakāsetabbassa atthassāti pākaṭo yamattho. Adhīnaṃ vā vacanaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Kena adhīnaṃ? Atthena. Tathā taṃtaṃatthappakāsena [P 2.0140] nicchitaṃ, niyataṃ vā vacanaṃ nirutti. Pathavīdhātupurisāditaṃtaṃpakārena ñāpanato paññattīti evaṃ adhivacanādipadānaṃ sabbavacanesu pavatti veditabbā, aññathā sirivaḍḍhakadhanavaḍḍhakappakārānameva niruttitā, “paṇḍito viyatto”ti evaṃ pakārānameva ekameva atthaṃ tena tena pakārena ñāpentānaṃ paññattitā ca āpajjeyyāti. Evaṃ tīhipi nāmehi vuttassa vohārassa pavattimaggopi saha viññāṇena nāmarūpanti ettāvatāva icchitabbo. Tenāha “itī”tiādi. Paññāya avacaritabbanti paññāya pavattitabbaṃ, ñeyyanti attho. Tenāha “jānitabba”nti. Vaṭṭanti kilesavaṭṭaṃ, kammavaṭṭaṃ, vipākavaṭṭanti tividhampi vaṭṭaṃ. Vattatīti pavattati. Tayidaṃ “jāyethā”tiādinā pañcahi padehi vuttassa atthassa nigamanavasena vuttaṃ. Ādi-saddena itthītipurisātiādīnampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Nāmapaññattatthāyāti khandhādiphassādisattādiitthādināmassa paññāpanatthāya. Vatthupi ettāvatāva. Tenāha “khandhapañcakampi ettāvatāva paññāyatī”ti. Ettāvatā ettakena, saha viññāṇena nāmarūpappavattiyāti attho.

Alternatively, the prefix 'adhi-' is in the sense of 'above'; adhivacana is a statement about what is above. Above what? The meaning to be made clear, the meaning that is manifest. Or, adhivacana means a word dependent on something. Dependent on what? On the meaning. Thus, nirutti is a word determined, or fixed, by the clarification of this or that meaning. Paññatti (designation) is so called because it makes known in a particular way this or that thing, such as the earth element or a person. Thus, the application of terms like adhivacana should be understood in all expressions. Otherwise, the state of being nirutti would apply merely to expressions like 'Sirivaḍḍhaka' or 'Dhanavaḍḍhaka,' and the state of being paññatti would apply to phrases like 'wise and skilled' when conveying a single meaning through various expressions. Thus, the path of occurrence for what is expressed by these three names—along with consciousness, as nāmarūpa—should be accepted only to this extent. Therefore, it is said, 'Thus...' and so on. 'To be traversed by wisdom' means it should be proceeded with by wisdom; the meaning is 'to be known.' Hence, it is said, 'It should be known.' Vaṭṭa refers to the threefold cycle: the cycle of defilements, the cycle of kamma, and the cycle of results. It revolves; it proceeds. This is stated as a conclusion to the meaning expressed by the five terms beginning with 'jāyetha.' By the term 'ādi' (etc.), the inclusion of 'woman,' 'man,' and so on should also be understood. 'For the purpose of name-designation' means for the purpose of designating names such as aggregates, contact, beings, women, and so on. The basis is only to this extent. Therefore, it is said, 'The five aggregates are also designated only to this extent.' 'Only to this extent' means with this much—that is, with the occurrence of name-and-form along with consciousness.

Attapaññattivaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Designation of Self

117. Anusandhiyati [M 2.0108] etenāti anusandhi, heṭṭhā āgatadesanāya anusandhānavasena pavattā uparidesanā, sā paṭhamapadassa dassitā, idāni dutiyapadassa dassetabbāti tamatthaṃ dassento “iti bhagavā”tiādimāha. Rūpinti rūpavantaṃ. Parittanti na vipulaṃ, appakanti attho. Yasmā attā nāma koci paramatthato natthi. Kevalaṃ pana diṭṭhigatikānaṃ parikappitamattaṃ[V 2.0096], tasmā yattha nesaṃ attasaññā, yathā cassa rūpibhāvādiparikappanā hoti, taṃ dassento “yo”tiādimāha. Rūpiṃ parittanti attano upaṭṭhitakasiṇarūpavasena rūpiṃ, tassa avaḍḍhitabhāvena parittaṃ. Paññapeti nīlakasiṇādivasena nānākasiṇalābhī. Tanti attānaṃ[P 2.0141]. Anantanti kasiṇanimittassa appamāṇatāya paricchedassa anupaṭṭhānato antarahitaṃ. Ugghāṭetvāti bhāvanāya apanetvā. Nimittaphuṭṭhokāsanti tena kasiṇanimittena phuṭṭhappadesaṃ. Tesūti catūsu arūpakkhandhesu. Viññāṇamattamevāti “viññāṇamayo attā”ti evaṃvādī.

117. It is called 'connection' (anusandhi) because it connects; the subsequent teaching proceeds by way of connection with the preceding teaching. That has been shown for the first line; now it must be shown for the second. To show that meaning, he says, 'Thus the Blessed One,' and so on. 'Having form' (rūpiṃ) means possessing form. 'Limited' (parittaṃ) means not vast; the meaning is 'small.' Since there is ultimately no such thing as a self, but merely a concept imagined by those holding such views, he shows where their notion of self arises and how their conception of having form, etc., comes about by saying 'who' (yo) and so on. 'Having limited form' refers to one who has form by way of the established kasiṇa form, and it is limited because of its undeveloped state. 'Declares' (paññapeti) refers to one who has attained various kasiṇas, such as the blue kasiṇa. 'That' (taṃ) refers to the self. 'Infinite' (anantaṃ) means boundless due to the immeasurability of the kasiṇa sign, because a limit is not established. 'Having removed' (ugghāṭetvā) means having removed through meditation. 'The area touched by the sign' refers to the area contacted by that kasiṇa sign. 'In them' refers to the four formless aggregates. 'Consciousness alone' (viññāṇamattameva) refers to one who holds the view, 'The self is made of consciousness.'

118. “Etarahī”ti sāvadhāraṇamidaṃ padanti tadatthaṃ dassento “idānevā”ti vatvā avadhāraṇena nivattitamatthaṃ āha “na ito para”nti. Tattha tattheva sattā ucchijjantīti ucchedavādī, tenāha “ucchedavasenetaṃ vutta”nti. Bhāvinti sabbaṃ sadā bhāviṃ avinassanakaṃ. Tenāha “sassatavasenetaṃ vutta”nti. Atathāsabhāvanti yathā paravādī vadanti, na tathā sabhāvaṃ. Tathabhāvāyāti ucchedabhāvāya vā sassatabhāvāya vā. Aniyamavacanañhetaṃ vuttaṃ sāmaññajotanāvasena. Sampādessāmīti tathabhāvaṃ assa sampannaṃ katvā dassayissāmi, patiṭṭhāpessāmīti attho. Tathā hi vakkhati “sassatavādañca jānāpetvā”tiādi. (Dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.118) imināti “atathaṃ vā panā”tiādi vacanena, anucchedasabhāvampi samānaṃ sassatavādino mativasenāti adhippāyo. Upakappessāmīti upecca samatthayissāmi.

118. 'Now' is a term with emphasis; demonstrating that meaning, it says 'just now,' and by this emphasis states the meaning that is excluded: 'not beyond this.' 'Here, beings are annihilated right there'—this is the annihilationist. Therefore, it is said, 'This is stated from the perspective of annihilationism.' 'Existing' means everything is always existing, imperishable. Hence, it is said, 'This is stated from the perspective of eternalism.' 'A nature that is not so' refers to a nature that is not as others claim. 'For such a state' means either for the state of annihilation or for the state of eternalism. This is stated as an indeterminate statement, by way of general indication. 'I will establish' means 'I will make that state fully accomplished and demonstrate it'; that is the meaning. For it will be said, 'Having made known the doctrine of eternalism,' etc. By this statement—'or what is untrue,' etc.—the intention is that even what is of a non-annihilated nature is understood according to the eternalist’s view. 'I will bring it about' means 'I will approach and support.'

Evaṃ samānanti evaṃ bhūtaṃ samānaṃ. Rūpakasiṇajjhānaṃ rūpaṃ uttarapadalopena, adhigamanavasena taṃ etassa atthīti rūpīti āha “rūpinti rūpakasiṇalābhi”nti. Parittattānudiṭṭhīti ettha rūpī-saddopiāvuttiādinayena ānetvā vattabbo, rūpībhāvampi hi so diṭṭhigatiko parittabhāvaṃ viya [M 2.0109] attano abhinivissa ṭhitoti. Arūpinti etthāpi eseva nayo. “Pattapalāsabahulagacchasaṅkhepena ghanagahanajaṭāvitānā [P 2.0142] nātidīghasantānā valli, tabbiparītā latā”ti vadanti. Appahīnaṭṭhenāti maggena asamucchinnabhāvena. Kāraṇalābhe sati uppajjanārahatā anusayanaṭṭho.

'Thus being' means being in such a state. 'Rūpa' stands for 'form-kasiṇa jhāna' by elision of the latter part of the compound. Because he possesses that by way of attainment, he is 'rūpī'; thus it is said, ''Rūpī' means one who has attained the form-kasiṇa.' Regarding 'limited self-view,' here the word 'rūpī' should also be supplied by the method of repetition, etc., for that view-holder is established, having clung to the state of having form as his own, just as he clings to the state of being limited. In 'formless' too, this is the same method. They say: 'A valli is a creeper of not very long extension, with a dense, impenetrable, tangled canopy, in short, a bush with many leaves and branches; a latā is the opposite of that.' 'By the meaning of not being abandoned' means by the state of not being eradicated by the path. The meaning of latent tendency is the capability of arising when a cause is obtained.

Arūpakasiṇaṃ nāma kasiṇugghāṭiṃ ākāsaṃ, na paricchinnākāsakasiṇaṃ. “Ubhayampi arūpakasiṇamevā”ti keci. Arūpakkhandhagocaraṃ vāti vedanādayo arūpakkhandhā “attā”ti abhinivesassa gocaro etassāti arūpakkhandhagocaro, diṭṭhigatiko, taṃ arūpakkhandhagocaraṃ. Vā-saddo vuttavikappattho. Saddayojanā pana arūpaṃ arūpakkhandhā gocarabhūtā etassa atthīti arūpī, taṃ arūpiṃ. Lābhino cattāroti rūpakasiṇādilābhavasena taṃ taṃ diṭṭhivādaṃ sayameva parikappetvā [V 2.0097] taṃ ādāya paggayha paññāpanakā cattāro diṭṭhigatikā. Tesaṃ antevāsikāti tesaṃ lābhīnaṃ vādaṃ paccakkhato, paramparāya ca uggahetvā tatheva naṃ khamitvā rocetvā paññāpanakā cattāro. Takkikā cattāroti kasiṇajjhānassa alābhino kevalaṃ takkanavaseneva yathāvutte cattāro diṭṭhivāde sayameva abhinivissa paggayha ṭhitā cattāro. Tesaṃ antevāsikā pubbe vuttanayena veditabbā.

The formless kasiṇa is the space from the removal of the kasiṇa, not the limited-space kasiṇa. Some say, 'Both are indeed formless kasiṇas.' Or, 'having the formless aggregates as its object': the formless aggregates, such as feeling, are the object of his adherence to 'self'; thus he is 'one whose object is the formless aggregates,' a view-holder; that one whose object is the formless aggregates. The particle 'vā' has the meaning of the stated alternative. The word construction, however, is: the formless aggregates have become the object for him, thus he is 'arūpī' (formless); that 'arūpiṃ' (formless one). The four attainers: these are four view-holders who, by way of attaining the form kasiṇa and so on, themselves fabricate this or that doctrine of views, and having adopted it and upheld it, proclaim it. Their disciples: these are four who, having learned the doctrine of those attainers directly and through tradition, and having accepted and approved it just so, proclaim it. The four reasoners: these are four who, not having attained the kasiṇa jhāna, merely by way of reasoning, themselves cling to, uphold, and are established in the four doctrines of views as stated. Their disciples should be understood in the way previously stated.

Naattapaññattivaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Designation of Not-Self

119. Āraddhavipassakopīti samparāyikavipassakopi, tena balavavipassanāya ṭhitaṃ puggalaṃ dasseti. Na paññapeti eva abahussuto pīti adhippāyo. Tādiso hi vipassanāya ānubhāvo. Sāsanikopi jhānābhiññālābhī “na paññapetī”ti na vattabboti so idha na uddhaṭo. Idāni nesaṃ apaññāpane kāraṇaṃ dasseti “etesañhī”tiādinā. Icceva ñāṇaṃ hoti, na viparītaggāho tassa kāraṇassa dūrasamussāritattā. Arūpakkhandhā icceva ñāṇaṃ hotīti yojanā.

119. 'Even one who has begun insight' means even one with insight pertaining to the future; by this he indicates a person established in strong insight. The intention is that he does not designate, even if he is unlearned. For such is the power of insight. Even a follower of the teaching who has attained jhāna and higher knowledges cannot be said 'not to designate,' therefore he is not mentioned here. Now, the reason for their non-designation is shown by 'for these,' and so on. Knowledge arises just thus, not a wrong grasp, because the cause for that has been removed far away. The connection is: 'Knowledge arises just thus: "These are the formless aggregates."

Attasamanupassanāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Contemplation of Self

121. Diṭṭhivasena samanupassitvā, na ñāṇavasena. Sā ca samanupassanā atthato diṭṭhidassanavasena.

121. One contemplates by way of views, not by way of knowledge. And that contemplation is, in its meaning, a seeing by way of views.

“Vedanaṃ [M 2.0110] attato samanupassatī”ti evaṃ [P 2.0143] āgatā vedanākkhandhavatthukā sakkāyadiṭṭhi. Iṭṭhādibhedaṃ ārammaṇaṃ na paṭisaṃvedetīti appaṭisaṃvedanoti vedakabhāvapaṭikkhepamukhena sañjānanādibhāvopi paṭikkhitto hoti tadavinābhāvatoti āha “iminā rūpakkhandhavatthukā sakkāyadiṭṭhi kathitā”ti. “Attā me vediyatī”ti iminā appaṭisaṃvedanattaṃ paṭikkhipati. Tenāha “nopi appaṭisaṃvedano”ti. “Vedanādhammo”ti pana iminā “vedanā me attā”ti imaṃ vādaṃ paṭikkhipati. Vedanāsaṅkhāto dhammo etassa atthīti hi vedanādhammoti vedanāya samannāgatabhāvaṃ tassa paṭijānāti. Tenāha “etassa ca vedanādhammo avippayuttasabhāvo”ti. Saññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇakkhandhavatthukā sakkāyadiṭṭhi kathitāti ānetvā sambandho. “Vedanāsampayuttattā vediyatī”ti taṃsampayogato taṃkiccakatamāha yathā cetanāyogato cetano purisoti. Sabbesampi taṃ sārammaṇadhammānaṃ ārammaṇānubhavanaṃ labbhateva, tañca kho ekadesato phuṭṭhatāmattato[V 2.0098], vedanāya pana vissavitāya sāmibhāvena ārammaṇarasānubhavananti. Tassā vasena saññādayopi taṃsampayuttattā “vediyatī”ti vuccanti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ “ārammaṇarasānubhavanaṭṭhānaṃ patvā sesasampayuttadhammā ekadesamattakameva anubhavantī”ti, (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1 dhammuddesakathā) rājasūdanidassanena vāyamattho tattha vibhāvito eva. Etassāti saññādikkhandhattayassa. “Avippayuttasabhāvo”ti iminā avisaṃyogajanitaṃ kañci visesaṃ ṭhānaṃ dīpeti.

‘He regards feeling as self’—thus arises the identity view based on the feeling aggregate. ‘It is non-experiencing’ means that by rejecting the state of experiencing, the states of perceiving and so on are also rejected due to their inseparability. Hence, it is said, ‘By this, the identity view based on the form aggregate is explained.’ By ‘My self feels,’ the state of non-experiencing is rejected. Therefore, it is said, ‘Nor is it non-experiencing.’ But by ‘having the nature of feeling,’ this rejects the view that ‘feeling is my self.’ For ‘having the nature of feeling’ means that a phenomenon called feeling exists for it; thus, it acknowledges its being endowed with feeling. Hence, it is said, ‘And for this, the nature of feeling is inseparable.’ The identity view based on the aggregates of perception, formations, and consciousness has been explained—this is brought in and connected. ‘Because it is associated with feeling, it feels’—from that association, its function is stated, just as a person is called ‘intending’ due to association with intention. For all those phenomena that take an object, the experience of the object is indeed obtained, but only partially, merely as contact. Feeling, however, pervadingly and with mastery, experiences the flavor of the object. On account of this, perception and the others, being associated with it, are also said to ‘feel.’ As it is stated in the Aṭṭhasālinī: ‘Having reached the place of experiencing the flavor of the object, the remaining associated phenomena experience only a portion.’ This meaning is well illustrated there by the example of the royal cook. ‘For it’ refers to the triad of aggregates: perception, and so on. ‘Of inseparable nature’—this indicates a certain special condition not arising from disassociation.

122. Tatthāti tesu vāresu. Tīsu diṭṭhigatikesūti “vedanā me attā”ti, “appaṭisaṃvedano me attā”ti, “vedanādhammo me attā”ti ca evaṃvādesu [P 2.0144] tīsu diṭṭhigatikesu. Tissannaṃ vedanānaṃ bhinnasabhāvattā sukhaṃ vedanaṃ “attā”ti samanupassato dukkhaṃ, adukkhamasukhaṃ vā vedanaṃ “attā”ti samanupassanā na yuttā. Evaṃ sesadvaye pīti āha “yo yo yaṃ yaṃ vedanaṃ attāti samanupassatī”ti.

122. ‘Therein’ refers to those instances. ‘In the three speculative views’—that is, in the three speculative views with such doctrines as ‘feeling is my self,’ ‘my self is non-experiencing,’ or ‘my self has the nature of feeling.’ Due to the distinct nature of the three feelings, for one who regards pleasant feeling as ‘self,’ it is not fitting to regard painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as ‘self.’ Similarly with regard to the remaining two, it is said, ‘Whoever regards whichever feeling as self.’

123. “Hutvā abhāvato”ti iminā udayabbayavantatāya aniccāti dasseti, “tehi tehī”tiādinā anekakāraṇasaṅkhatattā saṅkhatāti. Taṃ taṃ paccayanti “indriyaṃ, ārammaṇaṃ, viññāṇaṃ, sukha, vedanīyo phasso”ti [M 2.0111] evaṃ ādikaṃ taṃ taṃ attano kāraṇaṃ paṭicca nissāya sammā sassatādibhāvassa, ucchedādibhāvassa ca abhāvena ñāyena samakāraṇena sadisakāraṇena anurūpakāraṇena uppannā. Khayasabhāvāti khayadhammā, vayasabhāvāti vayadhammā virajjanasabhāvāti virāgadhammā, nirujjhanasabhāvāti nirodhadhammā, catūhipi padehi vedanāya bhaṅgabhāvameva dasseti. Tenāha “khayoti…pe… khayadhammātiādi vutta”nti.

123. ‘Having come into being, it ceases to be,’ this shows impermanence through its nature of arising and passing away. ‘By those various ones’ indicates being conditioned, due to being formed by multiple causes. They arise depending on and relying on this and that particular cause, such as ‘sense faculty, object, consciousness, contact associated with pleasant feeling,’ in accordance with the principle of proper and appropriate causation, similar causation, and analogous causation, without a state of eternalism or annihilationism. ‘Having the nature of destruction’ means subject to destruction. ‘Having the nature of decay’ means subject to decay. ‘Having the nature of fading away’ means subject to fading away. ‘Having the nature of cessation’ means subject to cessation. These four terms all point to the perishable nature of feeling. Therefore, it is said: ‘Destruction...subject to destruction, etc.’

Vigatoti sabhāvavigamena vigato. Ekassevāti ekasseva diṭṭhigatikassa. Tīsupi kālesūti tissannaṃ vedanānaṃ pavattikālesu. Eso me attāti “eso sukhavedanāsabhāvo, dukkhaadukkhamasukhavedanāsabhāvo me attā”ti kiṃ pana hotī, ekasseva bhinnasabhāvataṃ anummattako kathaṃ paccetīti adhippāyena pucchati. Itaro evampi tassa na hoti yevāti dassento “kiṃ pana na bhavissatī”tiādimāha. Visesenāti sukhādivibhāgena. Sukhañca dukkhañcāti ettha ca-saddena adukkhamasukhaṃ saṅgaṇhāti, sukhasaṅgahameva vā tena kataṃ santasukhumabhāvato. Avisesenāti avibhāgena vedanāsāmaññena. Vokiṇṇanti sukhādibhedena vomissakaṃ. Taṃ tividhampi vedanaṃ esa [P 2.0145] diṭṭhigatiko ekajjhaṃ gahetvā attāti samanupassati. Ekakkhaṇe ca bahūnaṃ vedanānaṃ uppādo āpajjati avisesena vedanāsabhāvattā. Attano hi tasmiṃ [V 2.0099] sati sadā sabbavedanāpavattippasaṅgato diṭṭhigatiko agatiyā ekakkhaṇepi bahūnampi vedanānaṃ uppattiṃ paṭijāneyyāti tassa avasaraṃ adento “na ekakkhaṇe bahūnaṃ vedanānaṃ uppatti atthī”ti āha, paccakkhaviruddhametanti adhippāyo. Etena petaṃ nakkhamatīti etena viruddhattasādhanenapi sabbena sabbaṃ attano abhāvenapi paṇḍitānaṃ na ruccati, etaṃ dassanaṃ dhīrā nakkhamantīti attho.

‘Vigato’ means gone due to the departure of its own nature. ‘Ekasseva’ refers solely to one who holds a view. ‘Tīsupi kālesu’ means during the times of occurrence of the three feelings. ‘Eso me attā’—thinking, ‘This nature of pleasant feeling is my self, this nature of painful or neutral feeling is my self’—but how could one who is not mad believe in the divided nature of a single thing? The question is asked with this intention. The other, showing that this is not so for him, says, ‘But why would it not be?’ and so on. ‘Visesena’ means by distinction, such as pleasant, painful, etc. In ‘sukhañca dukkhañca,’ the word ‘ca’ includes the neutral feeling, or it is simply a collection of the pleasant, due to its peaceful and subtle nature. ‘Avisesena’ means without distinction, by feeling in general. ‘Vokiṇṇaṃ’ means mixed, with distinctions like pleasant, etc. This holder of a speculative view grasps this threefold feeling all together and regards it as self. Moreover, the arising of many feelings in a single moment would follow, because of the undifferentiated nature of feeling. For if the self existed, from the consequence that all feelings would be constantly occurring, the holder of the view, through a wrong course, would have to acknowledge the arising of many feelings even in a single moment. Not giving an opportunity for that, it is said, ‘There is no arising of many feelings in a single moment’—the intention being that this contradicts direct experience. ‘Etena petaṃ nakkhamati’—by this proof of contradiction, and also by the complete absence of a self, this is not approved of by the wise. The meaning is that the discerning do not tolerate this view.

124. Indriyabaddhepi rūpappabandhe vāyodhātuvipphāravasena kāci kiriyā nāma labbhatīti suddharūpakkhandhepi yattha kadāci vāyodhātuvipphāro labbhati, tameva nidassanabhāvena gaṇhanto “tālavaṇṭe vā vātapāne vā”ti āha. Vedanādhammesūti vedanādhammavantesu. “Ahamasmī”ti iminā tayopi khandhe ekajjhaṃ gahetvā ahaṃkārassa uppajjanākāro vuttoti. “Ayamahamasmī”ti pana iminā tattha ekaṃ ekaṃ gahetvā ahaṃkārassa uppajjanākāro vutto. Tenāha “ekadhammopī”tiādi[M 2.0112]. Tanti “ahamasmī”ti ahaṃkāruppattiṃ. Sā hi catukkhandhanirodhena anupalabbhamānasannissayā sasavisāṇatikhiṇatā viya na bhaveyyāvāti.

124. Even in a continuum of matter bound to the faculties, some activity is obtained by means of the agitation of the wind element. Thus, even in the mere aggregate of form, wherever the agitation of the wind element is occasionally found, taking that very thing as an example, it is said, ‘like a palm-leaf fan or a window.’ ‘In things with the nature of feeling’ means in things that possess the nature of feeling. By ‘I am,’ the mode of arising of the conceit ‘I am’ is stated by taking the three aggregates together. But by ‘This I am,’ the mode of arising of the conceit ‘I am’ is stated by taking each one of them. Therefore, it is said, ‘even a single thing,’ and so on. ‘That’ refers to the arising of the conceit ‘I am.’ For with the cessation of the four aggregates, it would not exist, as its basis would not be perceived, just like the sharpness of a rabbit’s horn.

Ettāvatāti “kittāvatā ca ānandā”tiādinā “tantākulakajātā”ti padassa anusandhidassanavasena pavattena ettakena desanādhammena. Kāmaṃ heṭṭhāpi vaṭṭakathāva kathitā, idha pana diṭṭhigatikassa vaṭṭato sīsukkhipanāsamatthatāvibhāvanavasena micchādiṭṭhiyā mahāsāvajjabhāvadīpaniyakathā pakāsitāti taṃ dassento “vaṭṭakathā kathitā”ti āha. Nanu vaṭṭamūlaṃ avijjā taṇhā, tā anāmasitvā tato aññathā kasmā idha vaṭṭakathā kathitāti āha “bhagavā [P 2.0146] hī”tiādi. Avijjāsīsenāti avijjaṃ uttamaṅgaṃ katvā, avijjāmukhenāti attho. Koṭi na paññāyatīti “asukassa nāma sammāsambuddhassa, cakkavattino vā kāle avijjā uppannā, na tato pubbe atthī”ti avijjāya ādi mariyādā appaṭihatassa mama sabbaññutaññāṇassāpi na paññāyati avijjamānattā evāti attho. Ayaṃ paccayo idappaccayo, tasmā idappaccayā, imasmā āsavādikāraṇāti attho. Bhavataṇhāyāti bhavasaṃyojanabhūtāya taṇhāya. Bhavadiṭṭhiyāti sassatadiṭṭhiyā. “Tattha tattha upapajjanto”ti iminā “ito ettha etto idhā”ti evaṃ apariyantaṃ aparāparuppattiṃ dasseti. Tenāha “mahāsamudde”tiādi.

'So far'—this refers to the extent explained by the teaching method, as seen in the continuity from phrases like "how far, Ānanda" up to "entangled like a ball of thread." Although the discussion of the cycle has already been explained below, here it is elaborated to highlight the grave danger of wrong view by demonstrating the inability of one holding such views to lift their head from the cycle, illustrating its great faultiness. 'Is not the root of the cycle ignorance and craving? Without addressing them, why else would the cycle be discussed here?' To clarify this, it is said, "the Blessed One, indeed..." 'With ignorance at the head'—means making ignorance the foremost, or through the doorway of ignorance. 'The end is not discerned'—this means that the beginning and limit of ignorance is not discerned even by my unopposed omniscient knowledge, because such a beginning or limit does not exist. For example, it cannot be said that 'ignorance arose in the time of such-and-such a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One or a wheel-turning monarch, and did not exist before that.' This condition is this-conditionality; therefore, from this-conditionality, from this cause of taints and so on, is the meaning. 'Craving for existence'—refers to craving that forms the fetter of existence. 'View of existence'—means eternalism. 'Being reborn here and there'—this shows endless, successive rebirths without limit, as in "from here to there, from there to here." Hence, it is said, "in the great ocean," etc.

126. Paccayākāramūḷhassāti bhūtakathanametaṃ, na visesanaṃ. Sabbopi hi diṭṭhigatiko paccayākāramūḷho evāti. Vivaṭṭaṃ kathentoti vaṭṭato vinimuttattā vivaṭṭaṃ, vimokkho, taṃ kathento[V 2.0100]. Kārakassāti satthuovādakārakassa, sammāpaṭipajjantassāti attho. Tenāha “satipaṭṭhānavihārino”ti. So hi vedanānupassanāya, dhammānupassanāya ca sammāpaṭipattiyā “neva vedanaṃ attānaṃ samanupassatī”tiādinā vattabbataṃ arahati. Tenāha “evarūpo hī”tiādi. Sabbadhammesūti sabbesu tebhūmakadhammesu. Te hi sammasanīyā. Na aññanti vedanāya aññaṃ saññādidhammaṃ attānaṃ na samanupassatīti. “Khandhalokādayo”ti rūpādidhammā eva vuccanti, tesaṃ samūhoti dassetuṃ “rūpādīsu dhammesū”ti vuttaṃ. Na upādiyati diṭṭhitaṇhāgāhavasena. “Seyyohamasmī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 4.108; mahāni. 21, 178; dha. sa. 1121; vibha. 832, 866) pavattamānamaññanāpi [M 2.0113] taṇhādiṭṭhimaññanā viya paritassanarūpā evāti āha “taṇhādiṭṭhimānaparitassanāyapī”ti.

126. 'Of one deluded about the structure of conditionality' is a statement of fact, not a qualification. For all those with wrong views are indeed deluded by the structure of conditionality. 'Teaching the un-rolling' means teaching that which, by being free from the cycle of existence, is the un-rolling, that is, liberation. 'Of the doer' refers to one who acts according to the Teacher's instruction, meaning one who practices rightly. Hence it is said, 'of one who dwells in the establishments of mindfulness.' For through proper practice of contemplation of feelings and contemplation of phenomena, he is worthy of being described by the statement, 'he does not regard feeling as self,' etc. Therefore, it is said, 'one of such kind,' etc. 'In all phenomena' refers to all phenomena of the three realms. For these are to be thoroughly comprehended. 'Not another' means he does not regard any other phenomenon, such as perception, etc., as self apart from feeling. 'The world of the aggregates, etc.' refers to phenomena such as form, etc.; to indicate that they are a collection, it is said, 'among phenomena such as form, etc.' He does not cling by way of the grip of views and craving. The conceit that arises in such ways as 'I am better,' etc., is also like conceit based on craving and views, being of the nature of agitation. Hence it is said, 'and of the agitation from craving, view, and conceit.'

Sā evaṃ diṭṭhīti sā arahato evaṃpakārā diṭṭhīti yo vadeyya[P 2.0147], tadakallaṃ, taṃ na yuttanti attho. Evamassa diṭṭhīti etthāpi evaṃpakārā assa arahato diṭṭhītiādinā yojetabbaṃ. Evañhi satīti yo vadeyya “hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā itissa diṭṭhī”ti, tassa ce vacanaṃ tathevāti attho. “Arahā na kiñci jānātī”ti vuttaṃ bhaveyya jānato tathā diṭṭhiyā abhāvato. Tenevāti tathā vattumayuttattā eva. Catunnampi nayānanti “hoti tathāgato”tiādinā āgatānaṃ catunnaṃ vārānaṃ. Ādito tīsu vāresu saṅkhipitvā pariyosānavāre vitthāritattā “avasāne ‘taṃ kissa hetū’tiādimāhā”ti vuttaṃ. “Ādito tīsu vāresu tatheva desanā pavattā, yathā pariyosānavāre, pāḷi pana saṅkhittā”ti keci.

'That is such a view'—if someone were to say that this is the Arahant’s view of such a kind, that would be improper; that is not fitting, is the meaning. 'Such is his view'—here too, it should be construed as 'such is the Arahant's view,' etc. 'This being so'—if someone were to say, 'His view is that "the Tathāgata exists after death,"' then his statement would indeed be so, is the meaning. 'The Arahant knows nothing' would be said, because one who knows has no such view. 'For that very reason'—precisely because it is unfitting to speak thus. 'Of the four methods'—refers to the four instances that come as 'the Tathāgata exists,' etc. In the first three instances, it is summarized, while in the final instance, it is elaborated; hence it is said, 'at the end, he stated, "for what reason," etc.' 'In the first three instances, the teaching proceeds in the same way as in the final instance, but the Pāli is abbreviated,' say some.

Vohāroti “satto itthī puriso”tiādinā, “khandhāāyatanānī”tiādinā, “phasso vedanā”tiādinā ca vohāritabbavohāro. Tassa pana vohārassa pavattiṭṭhānaṃ nāma saṅkhepato ime evāti āha “khandhā āyatanāni dhātuyo”ti. Yasmā nibbānaṃ pubbabhāge saṅkhārānaṃ nirodhabhāveneva paññāpiyati ca, tasmā tassāpi khandhamukhena avacaritabbatā labbhatīti “paññāya avacaritabbaṃ khandhapañcaka”nti vuttaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā “imasmiṃyeva byāmamatte kaḷevare sasaññimhi samanake lokañca paññapemi lokasamudayañca lokanirodhañca lokanirodhagāminiñca paṭipada”nti. (Saṃ. ni. 1.107; a. ni. 4.45) paññāvacaranti vā tebhūmakadhammānametaṃ gahaṇanti “khandhapañcaka”ntveva vuttaṃ, tasmā “yāvatā paññā”ti etthāpi lokiyapaññāya eva gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vaṭṭakathā hesāti. Tathā hi “yāvatā vaṭṭaṃ vaṭṭati” icceva vuttaṃ. Tenevāha “tantākulakapadasseva anusandhi dassito”ti. Yasmā bhagavā diṭṭhisīsenettha vaṭṭakathaṃ kathetvā yathānusandhināpi vaṭṭakathaṃ kathesi, tasmā “tantākulakapadasseva [V 2.0101][P 2.0148] anusandhi dassito”ti sāvadhāraṇaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Paṭiccasamuppādakathā panettha yāvadeva tassa gambhīrabhāvavibhāvanatthāya vitthāritā, vivaṭṭakathāpi samānā idha paccāmaṭṭhāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Designation' refers to the designation to be designated, such as 'a being, a woman, a man,' etc., or 'the aggregates, the sense bases,' etc., or 'contact, feeling,' etc. The basis for the occurrence of such designations, in brief, is precisely these; hence he said, 'the aggregates, the sense bases, the elements.' Because Nibbāna, in the preliminary stage, is made known precisely as the state of cessation of formations, it is therefore possible for it to be traversed by way of the aggregates. Hence it is said, 'the five aggregates are to be traversed by wisdom.' Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'In this very fathom-long body, with its perception and mind, I proclaim the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world.' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.107; Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.45). Alternatively, 'the domain of wisdom' refers to this grasping of phenomena pertaining to the three realms; hence it is simply called 'the five aggregates.' Therefore, in the phrase 'as far as wisdom,' this should be understood as referring only to mundane wisdom. 'This is a discourse on the cycle.' For it is said, 'as far as the cycle revolves.' Therefore, he said, 'the connection of the very phrase "entangled like a ball of thread" is shown.' Because the Blessed One first gave a discourse on the cycle here with view as the head and then explained the cycle according to the connection, the phrase 'the connection of the very phrase "entangled like a ball of thread" is shown' is stated with emphasis. The discourse on dependent origination here is expanded only for the purpose of revealing its profound nature. Although it is a discourse on the un-rolling, it should be understood here as being reconsidered.

Sattaviññāṇaṭṭhitivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Seven Stations of Consciousness

127. Gacchanto [M 2.0114] gacchantoti samathapaṭipattiyaṃ suppatiṭṭhito hutvā vipassanāgamanena, maggagamanena ca gacchanto gacchanto. Ubhohi bhāgehi muccanato ubhatobhāgavimutto nāma hoti. So “evaṃ asamanupassanto”ti vutto vipassanāyānikoti katvā “yo ca na samanupassatīti vutto so yasmā gacchanto gacchanto paññāvimutto nāma hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Heṭṭhā vuttānanti “kittāvatā ca, ānanda, attānaṃ na paññapento na paññāpetī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.119), “yato kho, ānanda, bhikkhu neva vedanaṃ attānaṃ samanupassatī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.125 ādayo) ca heṭṭhā pāḷiyaṃ āgatānaṃ dvinnaṃ puthujjanabhikkhūnaṃ. Nigamananti nissaraṇaṃ. Nāmanti paññāvimuttādināmaṃ.

127. 'Going and going'—being well-established in the practice of serenity, and going by way of insight and by way of the path, one goes and goes. By being freed from both parts, one is called 'liberated in both ways.' He who is called 'not regarding thus' is one whose vehicle is insight; therefore, it is said that 'he who does not regard' is called 'wisdom-liberated' because he goes and goes. 'Of those mentioned below'—refers to the two ordinary monks mentioned below in the Pāli text in passages such as, 'And to what extent, Ānanda, does one not declare oneself nor make oneself known?' (Dī. Ni. 2.119), and 'When, Ānanda, a bhikkhu does not regard feeling as self,' etc. (Dī. Ni. 2.125 ff.). 'Conclusion'—means escape. 'Name'—refers to a name such as 'wisdom-liberated,' etc.

Paṭisandhivasena vuttāti nānattakāyanānattasaññitāvisesavisiṭṭhapaṭisandhivasena vuttā satta viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo. Taṃtaṃsattanikāyaṃ pati nissayato hi nānattakāyāditā taṃpariyāpannapaṭisandhisamudāgatāti daṭṭhabbā tadabhinibbattakakammabhavassa tathā āyūhitattā. Catasso āgamissantīti rūpavedanāsaññāsaṅkhārakkhandhavasena catasso viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo āgamissanti “rūpupāyaṃ vā āvuso viññāṇaṃ tiṭṭhamānaṃ tiṭṭhatī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 3.311). Viññāṇapatiṭṭhānassāti paṭisandhiviññāṇassa etarahi [P 2.0149] patiṭṭhānakāraṇassa. Atthato vuttavisesavisiṭṭhā pañcavokāre rūpavedanāsaññāsaṅkhārakkhandhā, catuvokāre vedanādayo tayo khandhā veditabbā. Sattāvāsabhāvaṃ upādāya “dve ca āyatanānīti dve nivāsaṭṭhānānī”ti vuttaṃ. Nivāsaṭṭhānapariyāyopi āyatanasaddo hoti yathā “devāyatanadvaya”nti. Sabbanti viññāṇaṭṭhiti āyatanadvayanti sakalaṃ. Tasmā gahitaṃ tattha ekameva aggahetvāti adhippāyo. Pariyādānaṃ anavasesaggahaṇaṃ na gacchati vaṭṭaṃ viññāṇaṭṭhitiāyatanadvayānaṃ aññamaññaantogadhattā.

‘Spoken of by way of rebirth-linking’ means the seven stations of consciousness are spoken of by way of a rebirth-linking qualified by the distinction of diversity of bodies and diversity of perceptions. For the diversity of bodies, etc., in each class of beings, should be understood as dependent on that as a basis, since it arises from the rebirth-linking included therein, due to the kamma-becoming that generates it having been accumulated in that way. ‘Four will come’ means these four stations of consciousness will come, classified by way of the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and volitional formations, as stated: ‘Friends, consciousness persists when it has a basis in form,’ etc. (Dī. Ni. 3.311). ‘Of the basis for consciousness’ refers to the present cause for the establishment of rebirth-linking consciousness. In meaning, the aggregates qualified by the distinction spoken of are to be understood as: in the five-aggregate existence, the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and volitional formations; in the four-aggregate existence, the three aggregates beginning with feeling. With reference to their being abodes of beings, it is said: ‘And two bases,’ meaning two dwelling-places. The term ‘base’ is also a synonym for a dwelling-place, as in ‘the two divine abodes.’ ‘All’ refers to the entirety of the stations of consciousness and the two bases. Therefore, the meaning is that everything is included, not just one part. Complete inclusion is not reached, because the stations of consciousness and the two bases are mutually contained within one another.

Nidassanatthe nipāto, tasmā seyyathāpi manussāti yathā manussāti vuttaṃ hoti. Viseso hotiyeva satipi bāhirassa kārakassa abhede ajjhattikassa bhinnattā. Nānattaṃ kāye etesaṃ, nānatto [V 2.0102] vā kāyo etesanti nānattakāyā, iminā nayena sesapadesupi [M 2.0115] attho veditabbo. Nesanti manussānaṃ. Nānattā saññā etesaṃ atthīti nānattasaññino. Sukhasamussayato vinipāto etesaṃ atthīti vinipātikā satipi devabhāve dibbasampattiyā abhāvato, apāyesu vā gato natthi nipāto etesanti vinipātikā. Tenāha “catuapāyavinimuttā”ti. Dhammapadanti satipaṭṭhānādidhammakoṭṭhāsaṃ. Vijāniyāti sutamayena tāva ñāṇena vijānitvā. Tadanusārena yonisomanasikāraṃ paribrūhanto sīlavisuddhiādikaṃ sammāpaṭipattiṃ api paṭipajjema. Sā ca paṭipatti hitāya diṭṭhadhammikādisakalahitāya amhākaṃ siyā. Idāni tattha sīlapaṭipattiṃ tāva vibhāgena dassento “pāṇesu cā”ti gāthamāha.

The particle is for the purpose of illustration; therefore, ‘just as humans’ means ‘as humans.’ There is indeed a distinction, even when the external factor is the same, because the internal one is different. ‘Diversity is in their body,’ or ‘their body is diverse,’ thus they are ‘diverse-bodied.’ In this manner, the meaning should be understood in the remaining terms as well. ‘Of them’ means of humans. ‘They have diverse perceptions,’ thus they are ‘those with diverse perceptions.’ ‘For them there is a fall from an accumulation of pleasure,’ thus they are ‘those liable to fall’ (vinipātikā), since even though they are in a divine state, they lack divine attainment. Or, ‘for them, having gone to the woeful states, there is no fall,’ thus they are ‘those liable to fall.’ Hence he said, ‘freed from the four woeful states.’ ‘A teaching-phrase’ means a section of the Dhamma, such as the foundations of mindfulness, etc. ‘Having understood’ means having first understood with knowledge derived from learning. Then, developing appropriate attention in accordance with that, may we undertake the right practice, including the purification of virtue and so on. And may that practice be for our benefit, for all benefits such as those in the present life. Now, to show the practice of virtue there in detail, he speaks the verse beginning with ‘And toward beings.’

Brahmakāye paṭhamajjhānanibbatte brahmasamūhe, brahmanikāye vā bhavāti brahmakāyikā. Mahābrahmuno parisāya bhavāti brahmapārisajjā tassa paricārakaṭṭhāne ṭhitattā. Mahābrahmuno purohitaṭṭhāne ṭhitāti brahmapurohitā[P 2.0150]. Āyuvaṇṇādīhi mahanto brahmānoti mahābrahmuno. Satipi tesaṃ tividhānampi paṭhamena jhānena abhinibbattabhāve jhānassa pana pavattibhedena ayaṃ visesoti dassetuṃ “brahmapārisajjā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Parittenāti hīnena, sā cassa hīnatā chandādīnaṃ hīnatāya veditabbā, paṭiladdhamattaṃ vā hīnaṃ. Kappassāti asaṅkhyeyyakappassa. Hīnapaṇītānaṃ majjhe bhavattā majjhimena, sā cassa majjhimatā chandādīnaṃ majjhimatāya veditabbā, paṭilabhitvā nātisubhāvitaṃ vā majjhimaṃ. Upaḍḍhakappoti asaṅkhyeyyakappassa upaḍḍhakappo. Vipphārikataroti brahmapārisajjehi pamāṇato vipulataro, sabhāvato uḷārataro ca hoti. Sabhāvenapi hi uḷāratarova, taṃ panettha appamāṇaṃ. Tathā hi parittābhādīnaṃ, parittasubhādīnañca kāye satipi sabhāvavematte ekattavaseneva vavatthāpīyatīti “ekattakāyā” tveva vuccanti. Paṇītenāti ukkaṭṭhena, sā cassa ukkaṭṭhatā chandādīnaṃ ukkaṭṭhatāya veditabbā, subhāvitaṃ vā sammadeva vasibhāvaṃ pāpitaṃ paṇītaṃ padhānabhāvaṃ nītanti katvā, idhāpi kappo asaṅkhyeyyakappavaseneva veditabbo paripuṇṇassa mahākappassa asambhavato. Itīti evaṃ vuttappakārena. Teti “brahmakāyikā”ti vuttā tividhāpi brahmāno. Saññāya ekattāti tihetukabhāvena saññāya ekattasabhāvattā[M 2.0116]. Na hi tassā sampayuttadhammavasena aññopi koci bhedo atthi.

Those who are in the Brahmā group (Brahmakāya)—a multitude of Brahmās, or an assembly of Brahmās, born from the first jhāna—are called ‘of the Brahmā group’ (Brahmakāyikā). Those who are in the retinue of Mahābrahmā are ‘Brahmā’s Retinue’ (Brahmapārisajjā) because they stand in the position of his attendants. Those who stand in the position of Mahābrahmā’s ministers are ‘Brahmā’s Ministers’ (Brahmapurohitā). He is Mahābrahmā because he is a great Brahmā in terms of lifespan, appearance, and so on. Although these three types are all born through the first jhāna, to show that this distinction is based on the different modes of occurrence of the jhāna, it is said, ‘But Brahmā’s Retinue,’ and so on. ‘By the limited’ means by the inferior; and this inferiority should be understood as the inferiority of their aspiration and other qualities, or that what is merely attained is inferior. ‘Of an eon’ means of an incalculable eon. Because it is in the middle of the inferior and the superior, it is ‘by the middling’; and this middling quality should be understood as the middling nature of their aspiration and other qualities, or that what is attained is not very well-developed. ‘Half an eon’ means half of an incalculable eon. ‘More expansive’ means more extensive in measure than Brahmā’s Retinue and more exalted by nature. For even by nature they are more exalted, and that for them is immeasurable. Thus, in the case of beings such as those of Limited Radiance and Limited Glory, although there is a difference in the nature of their bodies, they are established simply by way of unity, and thus are called ‘of one body.’ ‘By the superior’ means by the excellent; and this excellence should be understood as the excellence of their aspiration and other qualities, or because what is well-developed has been properly brought to a state of mastery, it is superior, having been brought to a state of preeminence. Here too, an eon should be understood by way of an incalculable eon, since a full great eon is not possible. ‘Thus’ means in the manner spoken of. ‘They’ refers to the three types of Brahmās spoken of as ‘of the Brahmā group.’ ‘Unity of perception’ means that their perception is of a single nature due to being accompanied by three wholesome roots. For there is no other distinction in it based on associated mental states.

Evanti iminā nānattakāyaekattasaññinoti dasseti.

‘Thus’—by this he indicates ‘those with diverse bodies and unified perception.’

Daṇḍaukkāyāti daṇḍadīpikāya. Saratīti dhāvati viya. Vissaratīti vippakiṇṇā viya dhāvati[V 2.0103]. Dve kappāti dve mahākappā. Ito paresupi eseva nayo. Idhāti imasmiṃ sutte. Ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasena ābhassaraggahaṇeneva sabbepi te parittābhā, appamāṇābhāpi gahitā.

‘By a firebrand’ means by a torch. By ‘it moves’ is meant ‘as if it runs.’ By ‘it spreads out’ is meant ‘it runs as if scattered.’ ‘Two eons’ means two great eons. This same method applies in the subsequent cases as well. ‘Here’ means in this sutta. By way of the highest limit, through the inclusion of the Ābhassara realm, all those of limited radiance and immeasurable radiance are also included.

Sobhanā pabhā subhā, subhāya kiṇṇā subhākiṇṇāti vattabbe ā-kārassa rassattaṃ, antima-ṇa-kārassa ha-kārañca katvā “subhakiṇhā”ti vuttā, aṭṭhakathāyaṃpana niccalāya ekagghanāya pabhāya subhoti pariyāyavacananti [P 2.0151] “subhena okiṇṇā vikiṇṇā”ti attho vutto, etthāpi antima-ṇa-kārassa ha-kārakaraṇaṃ icchitabbameva. Na chijjitvā chijjitvā pabhā gacchati ekagghanattā. Catutthaviññāṇaṭṭhitimeva bhajanti kāyassa, saññāya ca ekarūpattā. Vipulasantasukhāyuvaṇṇādiphalattā vehapphalā. Etthāti viññāṇaṭṭhitiyaṃ.

A beautiful radiance is ‘glory’ (subhā). When it should be said ‘strewn with glory’ (subhāya kiṇṇā), which becomes subhākiṇṇā, the long ‘ā’ is shortened and the final ‘ṇ’ is made into ‘h,’ resulting in ‘subhakiṇhā.’ In the commentary, however, ‘subha’ is a synonym for steady, solid radiance, so the meaning given is ‘covered and strewn with glory.’ Here too, the change of the final ‘ṇ’ to ‘h’ is to be accepted. The radiance does not proceed by breaking up, due to its solidity. They partake only of the fourth station of consciousness, because their body and perception are of a single form. They are called ‘of Great Fruit’ (Vehapphalā) because they have the fruit of vast, peaceful bliss, lifespan, beauty, and so on. ‘Herein’ means in this station of consciousness.

Vivaṭṭapakkhe ṭhitā napunarāvattanato. “Na sabbakālikā”ti vatvā tameva asabbakālikattaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “kappasatasahassampī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Soḷasakappasahassaccayena uppannānaṃ suddhāvāsabrahmānaṃ parinibbāyanato, aññesañca tattha anuppajjanato buddhasuññe loke suññaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ hoti, tasmā suddhāvāsā na sabbakālikā, khandhāvāraṭṭhānasadisā honti suddhāvāsabhūmiyo. Iminā suttena suddhāvāsānaṃ sattāvāsabhāvadīpaneneva viññāṇaṭṭhitibhāvo dīpito, tasmā suddhāvāsāpi sattasu viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu catutthaviññāṇaṭṭhitiṃ navasu sattāvāsesu catutthasattāvāsaṃyeva bhajanti.

They stand on the side of the evolving eon, because they do not return again. Having stated, ‘They are not perpetual,’ to explain that very non-perpetuity, it is said, ‘Even for a hundred thousand eons,’ and so on. Because the Suddhāvāsa Brahmās who have arisen there attain final Nibbāna after the passing of sixteen thousand eons, and because others are not born there, that place becomes empty in a world devoid of a Buddha. Therefore, the Suddhāvāsa realms are not perpetual; the Suddhāvāsa planes are like temporary encampments. By this sutta, in showing that the Suddhāvāsa realms are abodes of beings, their status as a station of consciousness is also shown. Therefore, the Suddhāvāsa devas, among the seven stations of consciousness, partake only of the fourth station of consciousness, and among the nine abodes of beings, only of the fourth abode of beings.

Sukhumattāti saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvappattattā. Paribyattaviññāṇakiccābhāvato neva viññāṇaṃ, sabbaso aviññāṇaṃ na hotīti nāviññāṇaṃ, tasmā paripphuṭaviññāṇakiccavantīsu viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu avatvā.

‘Due to subtlety’ means because the remaining formations have attained a state of subtlety. Since there is no function of manifest consciousness, it is not consciousness; and since it is not entirely without consciousness, it is not non-consciousness. Thus it is called ‘neither-consciousness-nor-non-consciousness.’ Therefore, it is not spoken of among the stations of consciousness, which possess a clearly pervading function of consciousness.

128. Tañca viññāṇaṭṭhitinti paṭhamaṃ viññāṇaṭṭhitiṃ. Heṭṭhā vuttanayena sarūpato, manussādivibhāgato, saṅkhepato, “nāmañca rūpañcā”ti bhedato [M 2.0117] ca pajānāti. Tassā samudayañcāti tassā paṭhamāya viññāṇaṭṭhitiyā pañcavīsatividhaṃ samudayañca pajānāti. Atthaṅgamepi eseva nayo. Assādetabbato, assādato ca assādaṃ. Ayaṃ aniccādibhāvo ādīnavo. Chandarāgo vinīyati etena, ettha vāti chandarāgavinayo, saha maggena nibbānaṃ. Chandarāgappahānanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Mānadiṭṭhīnaṃ vasenāhanti vā, taṇhāvasena mamanti vā abhinandanāpi mānassa paritassanā viya daṭṭhabbā. Sabbatthāti sabbesu sesesu aṭṭhasupi vāresu[P 2.0152]. Tatthāti upari tīsu viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu dutiyāyatanesu. Tattha hi rūpaṃ natthi. Puna tatthāti paṭhamāyatane. Tattha hi eko rūpakkhandhova. Etthāti [V 2.0104] ca tameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tattha hi rūpassa kammasamuṭṭhānattā āhāravasena yojanā na sambhavati.

128. “And that station of consciousness” (tañca viññāṇaṭṭhitiṃ) refers to the first station of consciousness. He understands it in the manner stated below: by its own nature, by its division into humans and so on, briefly, and by the distinction of “name and form.” “And its origin” (tassā samudayañca)—he understands the twenty-fivefold origin of that first station of consciousness. The same method applies to its cessation. “Enjoyment” (assādaṃ) is so called from what is to be enjoyed (assādetabbato) and from enjoyment (assādato). This state of impermanence and so forth is the danger (ādīnava). Desire and lust are removed by this (etena) or herein (ettha), thus it is the removal of desire and lust (chandarāgavinayo), which is Nibbāna together with the path. “The abandoning of desire and lust” (chandarāgappahānaṃ)—here too, the same method applies. Or, by way of conceit and views as ‘I am,’ or by way of craving as ‘mine’—even delight (abhinandanā) should be seen as agitation (paritassanā), like conceit. “In all cases” (sabbattha) means in all the remaining eight instances. “There” (tattha) means in the two sense bases in the three higher stations of consciousness. For there, form does not exist. “Again, there” (puna tattha) means in the first base. For there, only the single aggregate of form exists. “And here” (ettha) is also stated with reference to that same one. For there, since form arises from kamma, a connection by way of nutriment is not possible.

Yato khoti ettha to-saddo dā-saddo viya kālavacano “yato kho, sāriputta, bhikkhusaṅgho”tiādīsu (pārā. 21) viyāti vuttaṃ “yadā kho”ti. Aggahetvāti kañcipi saṅkhāraṃ “etaṃ mamā”tiādinā aggahetvā. Paññāvimuttoti aṭṭhannaṃ vimokkhānaṃ anadhigatattā sātisayassa samādhibalassa abhāvato paññābaleneva vimutto. Tenāha “aṭṭha vimokkhe asacchikatvā paññābalenevā”tiādi. Appavattinti āyatiṃ appavattiṃ katvā. Pajānanto vimuttoti vā paññāvimutto, paṭhamajjhānaphassena vinā parijānanādippakārehi cattāri saccāni jānanto paṭivijjhanto tesaṃ kiccānaṃ matthakappattiyā niṭṭhitakiccatāya visesena muttoti vimutto. So paññāvimutto. Sukkhavipassakoti samathabhāvanāsinehābhāvena sukkhā lūkhā, asiniddhā vā vipassanā etassāti sukkhavipassako. Ṭhatvāti pādakakaraṇavasena ṭhatvā. Aññatarasminti ca aññataraaññatarasmiṃ, ekekasminti attho. Evañhissa pañcavidhatā siyā. “Na heva kho aṭṭha vimokkhe kāyena phusitvā viharatī”ti iminā sātisayassa samādhibalassa abhāvo dīpito. “Paññāya cassa disvā”tiādinā sātisayassa paññābalassa bhāvo. Paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā hontīti na āsavā paññāya passanti, dassanakāraṇā pana parikkhīṇā “disvā parikkhīṇā”ti vuttā. Dassanāyattaparikkhayattā eva hi dassanaṃ āsavānaṃ khayassa purimakiriyā hoti.

Here, in `yato kho`, the sound `to` is a temporal word like the sound `dā` (as in `yadā`), as in ‘When, Sāriputta, the community of monks...’ (Pārā. 21); thus it is said to mean ‘when indeed’ (yadā kho). By ‘not having grasped’ (aggahetvā) is meant not having grasped any formation with the thought, ‘This is mine,’ and so on. “Wisdom-liberated” (paññāvimutto) means that, due to not having attained the eight liberations and due to the absence of superior power of concentration, he is liberated solely by the power of wisdom. Therefore, it is said, “not having realized the eight liberations... by the power of wisdom alone,” and so on. By ‘non-occurrence’ (appavattiṃ) is meant having brought about non-occurrence in the future. Or, `paññāvimutto` means one who is liberated while understanding (`pajānanto vimutto`); that is, knowing and penetrating the four truths through such means as full understanding, etc., without the contact of the first jhāna, he is especially liberated by the completion of the task through reaching the culmination of their functions. He is wisdom-liberated. A dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassako) is one whose insight is dry (sukkhā), rough (lūkhā), or unmoistened (asiniddhā) due to the absence of the moisture of serenity meditation. By ‘standing’ (ṭhatvā) is meant standing by way of making it a foundation. And ‘in any one’ (aññatarasmiṃ) means in one or another, that is, in each individual one. Thus, it may be fivefold. By “Indeed, he does not dwell having contacted the eight liberations with the body,” the absence of superior power of concentration is shown. By “and for him, having seen with wisdom,” the presence of superior power of wisdom is shown. When it is said, “and for him, having seen with wisdom, the taints are destroyed,” it is not that the taints see with wisdom; rather, because they are destroyed for the reason of seeing, it is said they are “destroyed having seen.” For it is because their destruction is dependent on seeing that seeing is the preliminary action for the destruction of the taints.

Aṭṭhavimokkhavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Eight Liberations

129. Ekassa [M 2.0118] bhikkhunoti sattasu ariyapuggalesu ekassa bhikkhuno. Viññāṇaṭṭhitiādinā parijānanādivasappa vattaniggamanañca [P 2.0153] paññāvimuttanāmañca. Itarassāti ubhatobhāgavimuttassa. Ime sandhāya hi pubbe “dvinnaṃ bhikkhūna”nti vuttaṃ. Kenaṭṭhenāti kena sabhāvena. Sabhāvo hi ñāṇena yāthāvato araṇīyato ñātabbato “attho”ti vuccati, so eva ttha-kārassa ṭṭha-kāraṃ katvā “aṭṭho”ti vutto. Adhimuccanaṭṭhenāti adhikaṃ savisesaṃ muccanaṭṭhena, etena satipi sabbassāpi rūpāvacarajjhānassa vikkhambhanavasena paṭipakkhato vimuttabhāve yena bhāvanāvisesena taṃ jhānaṃ sātisayaṃ paṭipakkhato vimuccitvā pavattati, so bhāvanāviseso dīpito. Bhavati hi samānajātiyuttopi bhāvanāvisesena pavattiākāraviseso, yathā taṃ saddhāvimuttatā diṭṭhippattassa. Tathā paccanīkadhammehi suṭṭhu vimuttatāya[V 2.0105], evaṃ aniggahitabhāvena nirāsaṅkatāya abhirativasena suṭṭhu adhimuccanaṭṭhenapi vimokkho. Tenāha “ārammaṇe cā”tiādi. Ayaṃ panatthoti ayaṃ adhimuccanaṭṭho pacchime vimokkhe nirodhe natthi, kevalo vimuttaṭṭho eva tattha labbhati, taṃ sayameva parato vakkhati.

129. “Of one bhikkhu” refers to one bhikkhu among the seven noble individuals. This refers to the transcending of what has arisen by way of full understanding and so on, through the stations of consciousness and so forth, and to the designation ‘wisdom-liberated.’ “The other” refers to one liberated in both ways. It was with reference to these that it was previously said, “of two bhikkhus.” “In what sense?” means by what essential nature. For the essential nature, because it is to be known truly by knowledge, is called “meaning” (attha). That very thing, by changing the sound `ttha` to the sound `ṭṭha`, is called `aṭṭha`. “In the sense of conviction” means in the sense of being liberated exceptionally and distinctively. By this is shown that special development by which, even though all form-sphere jhānas are liberated from their opponents by way of suppression, that jhāna proceeds, having been exceptionally liberated from its opponents. For even among those of a similar class, there can be a distinction in the mode of occurrence due to a special development, as in the case of one liberated by faith in relation to one attained to view. Similarly, liberation (vimokkha) is also in the sense of strong conviction due to being well liberated from opposing states, thus being unsuppressed, free from anxiety, and by way of delight. Hence it is said: “in the object,” and so on. But this meaning, this sense of conviction, is not present in the final liberation, cessation. There, only the meaning of being liberated is found; that he himself will explain later.

Rūpīti yenāyaṃ sasantatipariyāpannena rūpena samannāgato, taṃ yassa jhānassa hetubhāvena visiṭṭhaṃ rūpaṃ hoti, yena visiṭṭhena rūpena “rūpī”ti vucceyya rūpī-saddassa atisayatthadīpanato, tadeva sasantatipariyāpannarūpavasena paṭiladdhaṃ jhānaṃ idha paramatthato rūpībhāvasādhakanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenāha “ajjhatta”ntiādi. Rūpajjhānaṃ rūpaṃ uttarapadalopena. Rūpānīti panettha purimapadalopo daṭṭhabbo. Tena vuttaṃ “nīlakasiṇādirūpānī”ti. Rūpe kasiṇarūpe saññā rūpasaññā, sā etassa atthīti rūpasaññī, saññāsīsena jhānaṃ vadati. Tappaṭikkhepena [P 2.0154] arūpasaññī. Tenāha “ajjhattaṃ na rūpasaññī”tiādi.

As for “one with form” (rūpī): that form included in one’s own continuum with which one is endowed, which becomes a distinguished form by being the cause of a certain jhāna, and by which distinguished form one would be called “one with form”—because this indicates the superlative meaning of the word `rūpī`—it is that very jhāna, acquired by means of the form included in one’s own continuum, that should be seen here as ultimately establishing the state of being one with form.
