Bahuvipākanti yaṃ mahāvipākaṃ paṇītaṃ, taṃ atulaṃ. Yaṃ panettha majjhimaṃ, taṃ hīnaṃ, ukkaṭṭhanti dvidhā bhinditvā dvīsu bhāgesu pakkhipitabbaṃ. Hīnattikavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva appabahuvipākataṃ niddhāretvā tassa vasena tulātulabhāvo veditabbo. Sambhavati etasmāti sambhavoti āha “sambhavassa hetubhūta”nti. Niyakajjhattaratoti sasantānadhammesu vipassanāvasena, gocarāsevanāya ca nirato. Savipākaṃ samānaṃ pavattivipākamattadāyikammaṃ savipākaṭṭhena sambhavaṃ. Na ca taṃ kāmādibhavābhisaṅkhārakanti tato visesanatthaṃ “sambhava”nti vatvā “bhavasaṅkhāra”nti vuttaṃ. Ossajjīti ariyamaggena avassajji[V 2.0138]. Kavacaṃ viya attabhāvaṃ pariyonandhitvā ṭhitaṃ attani sambhūtattā attasambhavaṃ kilesañca abhindīti kilesabhedasahabhāvikammossajjanaṃ dassento tadubhayassa kāraṇaṃ avoca “ajjhattarato samāhito”ti.

Tulīyati (is weighed) means tulanti (they weigh). To show that the word tula is an instrument of action, the word tulita (weighed) is used. It is limited due to its lack of great power. Thus, because it is fragmented all around, it is called 'limited' (paritta). Due to the suppression of opposing forces, its long continuity, and its abundant results, it is neither balanced nor limited. For the reasons previously stated without distinction when the 'great' (mahaggata) was called 'immeasurable' (atula), those same reasons are found to an even greater extent in the formless realm compared to the form realm; hence it is said, 'The formless realm is immeasurable,' while the other is called 'balanced.' Among the three types of kamma, that which has minor results—that which produces weak, inferior results—is 'balanced' (tula). That which has abundant results—that which has great, excellent results—is 'immeasurable' (atula). As for what is intermediate here, it should be divided into two parts, inferior and superior, and placed within the two groups. Following the method stated in the explanation of the inferior triad, the state of being balanced or immeasurable should be understood by determining the lesser and greater results. Sambhava means 'it originates from this'; thus, it is said, 'being the cause of arising.' Niyakajjhattarato (delighting inwardly) means being devoted to the phenomena within one’s own continuum by way of insight, and to the cultivation of one’s meditation object. Kamma that is accompanied by results, giving only the result of its process, is 'arising' (sambhava) by virtue of being result-bearing. And it is not the volitional formations leading to existence in the sensual realm, etc.; therefore, to specify this distinction, after calling it 'arising', it is referred to as 'formations of existence' (bhavasaṅkhāra). Ossajji (he relinquished) means he relinquished through the noble path. Showing the relinquishing of kamma, which is accompanied by the breaking of defilement—the defilement called 'self-arisen' (attasambhava) because it arises within the self, and which stands enveloping the individual existence like armor—he stated the cause for both: 'inwardly delighted and composed.'

Tīrentoti “uppādo bhayaṃ, anuppādo khema”ntiādinā vīmaṃsanto. “Tulento tīrento”tiādinā saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “pañcakkhandhā”ti ādiṃ vatvā bhavasaṅkhārassa avassajjanākāraṃ sarūpato dassesi. “Eva”ntiādinā pana udānavaṇṇanāyaṃ ādito vuttamatthaṃ nigamanavasena dassesi.

Tīrento (investigating) means scrutinizing with such thoughts as: 'arising is fearful, non-arising is security,' and so forth. To show in detail the meaning briefly stated as 'weighing, investigating,' and so on, he began with 'the five aggregates,' showing the manner of relinquishing the formations of existence in their true nature. And by 'Thus,' and so on, in the explanation of the utterance, he showed the meaning stated from the beginning by way of conclusion.

Mahābhūmicālavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Great Earth-Trembling

171. Yanti karaṇe vā adhikaraṇe vā paccattavacananti adhippāyena āha “yena samayena, yasmiṃ vā samaye”ti. Ukkhepakavātāti [P 2.0199] udakasandhārakavātaṃ upacchinditvā ṭhitaṭṭhānato khepakavātā. “Saṭṭhi…pe… bahala”nti idaṃ tassa vātassa ubbedhappamāṇameva gahetvā vuttaṃ, āyāmavitthārato pana dasasahassacakkavāḷappamāṇampi udakasandhārakavātaṃ upacchindatiyeva. Ākāseti pubbe vātena patiṭṭhitokāse. Puna vātoti ukkhepakavāte tathākatvā vigate udakasandhārakavāto puna ābandhitvā [M 2.0155] gaṇhāti yathā taṃ udakaṃ na bhassati, evaṃ utthambhentaṃ ābandhanavitānavasena bandhitvā gaṇhāti. Tato udakaṃ uggacchatīti tato ābandhitvā gahaṇato tena vātena utthambhitaṃ udakaṃ uggacchati upari gacchati. Hotiyevāti antarantarā hotiyeva. Bahalabhāvenāti mahāpathaviyā mahantabhāvena. Sakalā hi mahāpathavī tadā oggacchati, uggacchati ca, tasmā kampanaṃ na paññāyati.

171. With the intention that 'yan' is a singular case ending in the instrumental or locative sense, it is said: 'at the time when, or in which time'. 'Ukkhepakavātā' (uplifting winds) means the winds that throw up from the place where they stand after having cut off the water-supporting wind. 'Sixty... up to... thick' is said taking only the measure of that wind's height, but in length and breadth it cuts off the water-supporting wind even to the extent of ten thousand world-systems. 'In space' (ākāse) means in the space previously established by the wind. 'Again, the wind' means: when the uplifting wind, having acted thus, has departed, the water-supporting wind again binds and seizes the water so that it does not fall; it binds and seizes it, supporting it by binding it like a canopy. 'Then the water rises' means that from that binding and seizing, the water, supported by that wind, rises upward. 'It is indeed' means it occurs intermittently. 'Due to its thickness' means because of the great massiveness of the great earth. For at that time, the entire great earth both sinks and rises, and thus the shaking is not discernible.

Ijjhanassāti icchitatthasijjhanassa. Anubhavitabbassaissariyasampattiādikassa. Parittāti paṭiladdhamattā nātisubhāvitā. Tathā ca bhāvanā balavatī na hotīti āha “dubbalā”ti. Saññāsīsena hi bhāvanā vuttā. Appamāṇāti paguṇā subhāvitā. Sā hi thirā daḷhatarā hotīti āha “balavā”ti. “Parittā pathavīsaññā, appamāṇā āposaññā”ti desanāmattameva, āposaññāya pana subhāvitāya pathavīkampo sukheneva ijjhatīti ayamettha adhippāyo veditabbo. Saṃvejento dibbasampattiyā pamattaṃ sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ. Vīmaṃsanto vā tāvadeva samadhigataṃ attano iddhibalaṃ. Mahāmoggallānattherassa pāsādakampanaṃ pākaṭanti taṃ anāmasitvā saṅgharakkhitasāmaṇerassa pāsādakampanaṃ dassetuṃ “so kirāyasmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pūtimisso [V 2.0139] gandho etassāti pūtigandho, tena pūtigandheneva [P 2.0200] adhigatamātukucchisambhavaṃ viya gandheneva sīsena, ativiya dārako evāti attho.

Of success (ijjhanassa) means of the accomplishment of a desired aim. It refers to that which is to be experienced, such as the attainment of sovereignty and wealth. 'Limited (parittā)' means just obtained, not very well developed. And thus, because the development is not strong, it is said to be 'weak'. Indeed, development (bhāvanā) is spoken of with perception (saññā) as its head. 'Immeasurable (appamāṇā)' means proficient, well-developed. For that is firm and stronger, hence it is said to be 'strong'. 'Limited is the earth perception, immeasurable is the water perception'—this is merely a statement. However, with the water perception well-developed, the earth-trembling is easily accomplished; this meaning should be understood here. Arousing a sense of urgency in Sakka, the king of the devas, who was heedless due to divine prosperity. Or, examining his own psychic power that he had just then attained. To show the shaking of the mansion by the novice Saṅgharakkhita, without alluding to the well-known shaking of the mansion by the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, it is said, 'that venerable one,' etc. 'He has a foul smell' (pūtigandho) means his smell is mixed with putridity. By that foul smell alone, like one just born from a mother's womb, with smell as his main characteristic, he is exceedingly like a child—this is the meaning.

Ācariyanti ācariyūpadesaṃ. Iddhābhisaṅkhāro nāma iddhividhappaṭipakkhādībhāvena icchitabbo, so ca upāye kosallassa attanā na sammā uggahitattā na tāva sikkhitoti āha “asikkhitvāva yuddhaṃ paviṭṭhosī”ti. “Pilavanta”nti iminā sakalameva pāsādavatthuṃ udakaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhātabbapāsādova tattha pilavatīti dasseti. Adhiṭṭhānakkamaṃ pana upamāya dassento “tāta…pe… jānāhī”ti āha. Tattha kapallakapūvanti āsittakapūvaṃ, taṃ pacantā kapāle paṭhamaṃ kiñci piṭṭhaṃ ṭhapetvā anukkamena vaḍḍhetvā antantena paricchindanti pūvaṃ samantato paricchinnaṃ katvā ṭhapenti, evaṃ “āpokasiṇavasena ‘pāsādena patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ udakaṃ hotū’ti adhiṭṭhahanto samantato pāsādassa yāva pariyantā yathā udakaṃ hoti, tathā adhiṭṭhātabba”nti upamāya upadisati.

'The teacher' (ācariyaṃ) means the teacher's instruction. The volitional formation of psychic power (iddhābhisaṅkhāro) should be desired because it is the counteraction to obstacles to the varieties of psychic power, and so on. And because he himself has not properly grasped the skill in the means, he has not yet trained; thus it is said, 'You have entered the battle without having trained'. By the word 'pilavantaṃ' (floating), it indicates that having made the entire palace-base into water, the palace to be resolved upon itself floats there. To illustrate the sequence of resolution by way of an analogy, he says, 'Dear one... understand'. Here, 'kapallakapūva' refers to a poured cake. While baking it, they first place a little dough on the potsherd, then gradually expand it and define it at the very edge, thus setting the cake down with its perimeter delimited all around. Similarly, by the method of the water kasiṇa, one should resolve, 'Let the place where the palace stands become water,' in such a way that the water extends all around the palace up to its boundaries. This is taught by way of analogy.

Mahāpadāne [M 2.0156] vuttamevāti “dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto tusitā kāyā cavitvā mātukucchiṃ okkamatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.18) vatvā “ayañca dasasahassī lokadhātu saṅkampati sampakampati sampavedhatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.18), tathā “dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto mātukucchimhā nikkhamatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.30) vatvā “ayañca dasasahassī lokadhātu saṅkampati sampakampati sampavedhatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.32) ca [P 2.0201] mahābodhisattassa gabbhokkantiyaṃ, abhijātiyañca dhammatāvasena mahāpadānepathavīkampassa vuttattā itaresupi catūsu ṭhānesu pathavīkampo dhammatāvasenevāti mahāpadāneatthato vuttaṃ evāti adhippāyo.

It is indeed stated in the Mahāpadāna: 'This is the nature of things, monks, that when the Bodhisatta passes away from the Tusita realm and enters his mother’s womb, this ten-thousandfold world-system trembles, quakes, and shakes.' (DN 14) And similarly, 'This is the nature of things, monks, that when the Bodhisatta emerges from his mother’s womb, this ten-thousandfold world-system trembles, quakes, and shakes.' (DN 14) Thus, since the earth-trembling at the great Bodhisatta's conception and birth is stated in the Mahāpadāna as being the nature of things, it is implied that in the other four instances too, the earth-trembling occurs as the nature of things. This is the intended meaning: that it is indeed stated in the Mahāpadāna in substance.

Idāni nesaṃ pathavīkampanaṃ kāraṇato, pavattiākārato ca vibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “iti imesū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dhātukopenāti ukkhepakadhātusaṅkhātāya vāyodhātuyā pakopena. Iddhānubhāvenāti ñāṇiddhiyā vā kammavipākajiddhiyā vā pabhāvena, tejenāti attho. Puññatejenāti puññānubhāvena, mahābodhisattassa puññabalenāti attho. Ñāṇatejenāti paṭivedhañāṇānubhāvena. Sādhukāradānavasenāti yathā anaññasādhāraṇena paṭivedhañāṇānubhāvena abhihatā mahāpathavī abhisambodhiyaṃ akampittha, evaṃ anaññasādhāraṇena desanāñāṇānubhāvena abhihatā mahāpathavī akampittha, taṃ panassā sādhukāradānaṃ viya hotīti “sādhukāradānavasenā”ti vuttaṃ.

Now, to show the distinction of these earth tremblings by way of cause and mode of occurrence, 'Thus, in these...' etc., was said. 'By disturbance of the elements' means by the disturbance of the wind element, reckoned as the uplifting element. 'By the power of psychic potency' means by the power of the psychic potency of knowledge or by the psychic potency resulting from karmic fruition; the meaning is, by its force. 'By the power of merit' means by the influence of merit, that is, by the power of the great Bodhisatta's merit. 'By the power of knowledge' means by the power of the knowledge of penetration. 'By way of giving approval' means just as the great earth, struck by the unique power of the knowledge of penetration at the complete enlightenment, trembled, even so, the great earth, struck by the unique power of the knowledge of the teaching, trembled. That, however, is like the giving of approval to him, therefore it is said, 'by way of giving approval'.

Yena [V 2.0140] pana bhagavā asītianubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍitadvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇa- (dī. ni. 2.33; 3.198; ma. ni. 2.385) vicitrarūpakāyo sabbākāraparisuddhasīlakkhandhādiguṇaratanasamiddhidhammakāyo puññamahattathāmamahattayasamahaāiddhimahattapaññāmahattānaṃ paramukkaṃsagato asamo asamasamo appaṭipuggalo arahaṃ sammāsambuddho attano attabhāvasaññitaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ kappaṃ vā kappāvasesaṃ vā ṭhapetuṃ samatthopi saṅkhatadhammaṃ paṭijigucchanākārappavattena ñāṇavisesena tiṇāyapi amaññamāno āyusaṅkhārossajjanavidhinā nirapekkho ossajji. Tadanubhāvābhihatā mahāpathavī āyusaṅkhārossajjane akampittha, taṃ panassā kāruññasabhāvasaṇṭhitā viya hotīti vuttaṃ “kāruññasabhāvenā”ti[M 2.0157]. Yasmā bhagavā parinibbānasamaye catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasaṅkhyā samāpattiyo [P 2.0202] samāpajji antarantarā phalasamāpattisamāpajjanena, tassa pubbabhāge sātisayaṃ tikkhaṃ sūraṃ vipassanāñāṇañca pavattesi, “yadatthañca mayā evaṃ sucirakālaṃ anaññasādhāraṇo paramukkaṃsagato ñāṇasambhāro sambhato, anuttaro ca vimokkho samadhigato, tassa vata me sikhāppattaphalabhūtā accantaniṭṭhā anupādisesanibbānadhātu ajja samijjhatī”ti bhiyyo ativiya somanassappattassa bhagavato pītivipphārādiguṇavipulatarānubhāvo parehi asādhāraṇañāṇātisayo udapādi, yassa samāpattibalasamupabrūhitassa ñāṇātisayassa ānubhāvaṃ sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ “dveme piṇḍapātā samasamaphalā samasamavipākā”tiādi (udā. 75), tasmā tassa ānubhāvena samabhihatā mahāpathavī akampittha. Taṃ panassā tassaṃ velāyaṃ ārodanākārappatti viya hotīti “aṭṭhamo ārodanenā”ti vuttaṃ.

By which the Blessed One, adorned with the eighty minor marks and the thirty-two major marks of a great man (Dī. Ni. 2.33; 3.198; Ma. Ni. 2.385), whose body was of diverse beauty, whose aggregate of virtues such as morality was utterly pure in every way, whose body of Dhamma was rich in qualities, who had reached the highest excellence in merit, power, majesty, supernormal powers, and wisdom, who was incomparable, matchless, without peer, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One—though capable of maintaining the five aggregates identified with his own being for an aeon or the remainder of an aeon—due to his knowledge characterized by revulsion toward conditioned things, relinquished it without attachment, not even valuing it as much as a blade of grass, by the method of abandoning the life-formation. Struck by the power of that, the great earth trembled at the relinquishment of the life-formation, and that was as if it were established in a compassionate nature for him—thus it is said, 'through the nature of compassion'. Because at the time of his final passing, the Blessed One entered attainments numbering twenty-four hundred-thousand koṭis, with intermittent entering into fruition attainment, and in the earlier part of that time, his insight knowledge was exceedingly sharp, keen, and valiant—'That accumulation of knowledge for which I have striven for so long, unique and supreme, has been gathered, the incomparable liberation has been realized. Truly, today, for me, the ultimate goal, the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining, the fruit reached at the peak, will be accomplished'—thus, for the Blessed One, who had attained even greater and more abundant joy, there arose a unique excellence of knowledge, not shared by others, with a more extensive power of qualities such as the diffusion of joy. It was with reference to the power of this excellence of knowledge, augmented by the power of his attainments, that it was said: 'These two alms-givings are equal in fruit, equal in result' (Udā. 75). Therefore, struck by that power, the great earth trembled. Yet at that time, it was as if it expressed lamentation—thus it is said, 'the eighth by lamentation'.

Idāni saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivaranto “mātukucchiṃ okkamante”tiādimāha. Ayaṃ panatthoti “sādhukāradānavasenā”tiādinā vutto attho. Pathavīdevatāya vasenāti ettha samuddadevatā viya mahāpathaviyā adhidevatā kira nāma atthi. Tādise kāraṇe sati tassā cittavasena ayaṃ mahāpathavī saṅkampati sampakampati sampavedhati, yathā vātavalāhakadevatānaṃ cittavasena vātā vāyanti, sītuṇhaabbhavassavalāhakadevatānaṃ cittavasena sītādayo bhavanti. Tathā hi visākhapuṇṇamāyaṃ abhisambodhiatthaṃ bodhirukkhamūle nisinnassa lokanāthassa antarāyakaraṇatthaṃ upaṭṭhitaṃ mārabalaṃ vidhamituṃ –

Now, explaining the meaning that was stated briefly, he said, 'when entering the mother's womb,' and so on. This is the meaning conveyed by 'by way of giving approval,' etc. 'By the will of the earth-deity'—here, just as there is a presiding deity over the ocean, so too, it is said, there exists a presiding deity of the great earth. When such a cause exists, this great earth trembles, shakes, and quakes by the will of that deity—just as winds blow by the will of the wind and cloud deities, and cold, heat, clouds, and rain occur by the will of the deities governing cold, heat, clouds and rain. For example, on the Visākha full-moon day, to dispel Māra's army that had appeared to create obstacles for the Lord of the World, who was seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree for the sake of enlightenment—

“Acetanāyaṃ [P 2.0203] pathavī, aviññāya sukhaṃ dukhaṃ;

Sāpi dānabalā mayhaṃ, sattakkhattuṃ pakampathā”ti. (cariyā. 1.124) –

'This earth is non-sentient, it does not know pleasure or pain; yet by the power of my giving, it trembled seven times.' (Cariyā. 1.124)

Vacanasamanantaraṃ [V 2.0141] mahāpathavī bhijjitvā saparisaṃ māraṃ parivattesi. Etanti sādhukāradānādi. Yadipi natthi acetanattā, dhammatāvasena pana vuttanayena siyāti sakkā vattuṃ. Dhammatā pana atthato dhammasabhāvo, so puññadhammassa vā ñāṇadhammassa vā ānubhāvasabhāvoti. Tayidaṃ sabbaṃ vicāritameva, evañca katvā –

Immediately after the utterance, the great earth split open and overturned Māra together with his retinue. This is the giving of approval and so forth. Although this approval does not exist due to the earth's non-sentience, it can be said to occur by way of natural law in the manner described. Natural law, in essence, is the inherent nature of phenomena, which is the powerful nature of meritorious qualities or knowledge. All this has already been considered, and having done so—

“Ime [M 2.0158] dhamme sammasato, sabhāvasarasalakkhaṇe;

Dhammatejena vasudhā, dasasahassī pakampathā”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 1.166);

"While thoroughly comprehending these phenomena in their own nature, essence, and characteristics, through the power of the Dhamma, the ten-thousandfold earth trembled." (Bu. vaṃ. 1.166);

Ādi vacanañca samatthitaṃ hoti.

And the initial statement is thus supported.

Niddiṭṭhanidassananti niddiṭṭhassa atthassa niyyātanaṃ, nigamananti attho. Ettāvatāti pathavīkampādiuppādajananena ceva pathavīkampassa bhagavato hetunidassanena ca. “Addhā ajja bhagavatā āyusaṅkhāro ossaṭṭho”ti sallakkhesi pārisesañāyena. Evañhi tadā thero tamatthaṃ vīmaṃseyya nāyaṃ bhūmikampo dhātuppakopahetuko tassa apaññāyamānarūpattā, bāhirakopi isi evaṃ mahānubhāvo buddhakāle natthi, sāsanikopi satthu anārocetvā evaṃ karonto nāma natthi, sesānaṃ pañcannaṃ idāni asambhavo, evaṃ bhūmikampo cāyaṃ mahābhiṃsanako salomahaṃso ahosi, tasmā pārisesato āha “ajja bhagavatā āyusaṅkhāro ossaṭṭhoti sallakkhesī”ti.

Niddiṭṭhanidassana means the conveying of the indicated meaning; it means the conclusion. Ettāvatā means by the generation of the earthquake and so forth, and by the Blessed One's indication of the cause of the earthquake. "Surely today the Blessed One has relinquished his life-formation," he inferred by the method of elimination. For at that time the elder would have investigated that matter thus: this earthquake is not caused by the disturbance of the elements, since its nature is not discernible; nor is there any external ascetic of such great power during the Buddha's time; nor is there any disciple within the Dispensation who would act thus without informing the Teacher; and the remaining five causes are now impossible. Thus, this earthquake was most terrifying and hair-raising. Therefore, by the method of elimination, he inferred, "Today the Blessed One has relinquished his life-formation."

Aṭṭhaparisavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Eight Assemblies

172. Okāsaṃ adatvāti “tiṭṭhatu bhante bhagavā kappa”ntiādi (dī. ni. 2.178) nayappavattāya therassa āyācanāya avasaraṃ adatvā. Aññānipi aṭṭhakāni sampiṇḍento hetuaṭṭhakato aññāni parisābhibhāyatanavimokkhavasena [P 2.0204] tīṇi aṭṭhakāni saṅgahetvā dassento “aṭṭha kho imā”tiādimāha. “Āyasmato ānandassa sokuppattiṃ pariharanto vikkhepaṃ karonto”ti keci sahasā bhaṇite balavasoko uppajjeyyāti.

172. ‘Without giving an opportunity’ means not granting a chance for the elder’s request, which proceeds by way of 'Please, venerable sir, may the Blessed One remain for an aeon' (Dī. Ni. 2.178), and so forth. Summarizing also other sets of eight, showing three sets of eight—other than the set of eight causes—by way of the assemblies, the spheres of mastery, and the liberations, he spoke thus, 'These eight...' and so forth. Some say this was done 'while avoiding the arising of sorrow for Venerable Ānanda, causing a distraction,' lest strong sorrow should arise if it were said suddenly.

Samāgantabbato, samāgacchatīti vā samāgamo, parisā. Bimbisārapamukho samāgamo bimbisārasamāgamo. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo. Bimbisāra…pe… samāgamādisadisaṃ khattiyaparisanti yojanā. Aññesu cakkavāḷesupi labbhateyeva satthu khattiyaparisādiupasaṅkamanaṃ. Ādito tehi saddhiṃ satthu bhāsanaṃ ālāpo. Kathanapaṭikathanaṃ sallāpo. Dhammupasañhitā pucchā paṭipucchā [V 2.0142] dhammasākacchā. Saṇṭhānaṃ paṭicca kathanaṃ saṇṭhānapariyāyattā [M 2.0159] vaṇṇa-saddassa “mahantaṃ hatthirājavaṇṇaṃ abhinimminitvā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.138) viya. “Tesa”nti padaṃ ubhayapadāpekkhaṃ “tesampi lakkhaṇasaṇṭhānaṃ viya satthu sarīrasaṇṭhānaṃ, tesaṃ kevalaṃ paññāyati evā”ti. Nāpi āmukkamaṇikuṇḍalo bhagavā hotīti yojanā. Chinnassarāti dvidhābhūtassarā. Gaggarassarāti jajjaritassarā. Bhāsantaranti tesaṃ sattānaṃ bhāsato aññaṃ bhāsaṃ. Vīmaṃsāti cintanā. “Kimatthaṃ…pe… desetī”ti idaṃ nanu attānaṃ jānāpetvā dhamme kathite tesaṃ sātisayo pasādo hotīti iminā adhippāyena vuttaṃ? Yesaṃ attānaṃ ajānāpetvāva dhamme kathite pasādo hoti, na jānāpetvā, tādise sandhāya satthā tathā karoti. Tattha payojanamāha “vāsanatthāyā”ti. Evaṃ sutopīti evaṃ aviññātadesako aviññātāgamanopi suto dhammo attano dhammasudhammatāyeva anāgate paccayo hoti suṇantassa.

A `samāgama` is so called because it 'should be approached' or because it 'approaches'; hence, it is an assembly. The assembly headed by Bimbisāra is the Bimbisāra assembly. The same method applies to the other two. The connection is: 'the khattiya assembly, which is like the Bimbisāra... assembly, and so on.' In other world-systems as well, the Teacher’s approaching the assemblies of khattiyas and so forth is indeed found. From the beginning, the Teacher’s speaking with them is `ālāpa` (conversation). Speaking and counter-speaking is `sallāpa` (dialogue). A question and counter-question connected with the Dhamma is `dhammasākacchā` (Dhamma discussion). The word `vaṇṇa` is a synonym for `saṇṭhāna` (appearance), as in 'having created a great elephant-king’s appearance' (Saṃ. Ni. 1.138), and so forth. The word 'tesaṃ' refers to both parties, thus: 'The Teacher's bodily form appears to them just like their own characteristic form; it is evident only to them.' The connection is: 'Nor is the Blessed One one who wears jewels and earrings.' `Chinnassara` means a voice that has become twofold. `Gaggarassara` means a rough, grating voice. `Bhāsantara` means a language other than that spoken by those beings. `Vīmaṃsā` means reflection. Was not this, 'For what purpose... does he teach?', said with this intention: 'When the Dhamma is taught after he has made himself known, their confidence becomes exceptional'? With reference to those for whom confidence arises when the Dhamma is taught without making himself known, not after making himself known, the Teacher acts thus. Therein, he states the purpose: 'for the sake of habituation.' `Evaṃ sutopi` means: even when the Dhamma is heard thus from one whose country is unknown and whose coming is unknown, it becomes a condition in the future for the one who hears, precisely because of the Dhamma's own nature as good Dhamma.

“Ānandā”tiādiko saṅgītianāruḷho pāḷidhammo eva tathā dassito. Esa nayo ito paresupi evarūpesu ṭhānesu.

The Pāli Dhamma beginning with 'Ānanda,' and so forth, which is not included in the recitations, is itself shown thus. This method applies to similar instances hereafter as well.

Aṭṭhaabhibhāyatanavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Eight Bases of Mastery

173. Abhibhavatīti [P 2.0205] abhibhu, parikammaṃ, ñāṇaṃ vā. Abhibhu āyatanaṃ etassāti abhibhāyatanaṃ, jhānaṃ. Abhibhavitabbaṃ vā ārammaṇasaṅkhātaṃ āyatanaṃ etassāti abhibhāyatanaṃ. Ārammaṇābhibhavanato abhibhu ca taṃ āyatanañca yogino sukhavisesānaṃ adhiṭṭhānabhāvato, manāyatanadhammāyatanabhāvato vātipi sasampayuttaṃ jhānaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ. Tenāha “abhibhavanakāraṇānī”tiādi. Tāni hīti abhibhāyatanasaññitāni jhānāni. “Puggalassa ñāṇuttariyatāyā”ti idaṃ ubhayatthāpi yojetabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Paṭipakkhabhāvena paccanīkadhamme abhibhavanti puggalassa ñāṇuttariyatāya ārammaṇāni abhibhavanti. Ñāṇabaleneva hi ārammaṇābhibhavanaṃ viya paṭipakkhābhibhavo pīti.

173. `Abhibhu` means 'one who overcomes'; it is preliminary work or knowledge. Its sphere is mastery, therefore it is an `abhibhāyatana`; this is jhāna. Or, its sphere, designated as the object, is to be mastered, therefore it is an `abhibhāyatana`. Because it overcomes the object, it is mastery (`abhibhu`), and because that sphere is a basis for the yogi's special bliss, or because it is the mind-sphere and the dhamma-sphere, the jhāna together with its associated states is an `abhibhāyatana`. Therefore it is said, 'the causes of overcoming,' and so forth. For these are the jhānas designated as the bases of mastery. The phrase 'for the superiority of a person's knowledge' should be applied in both contexts. How? By way of opposition, they overcome opposing states; for the superiority of a person's knowledge, they overcome objects. For by the power of knowledge alone, just as there is the overcoming of objects, so too is there the overcoming of opposition.

Parikammavasena ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī, na appanāvasena. Na hi paṭibhāganimittārammaṇā appanā ajjhattavisayā sambhavati, taṃ pana ajjhattaparikammavasena laddhaṃ [M 2.0160] kasiṇanimittaṃ avisuddhameva hoti, na bahiddhāparikammavasena laddhaṃ viya visuddhaṃ.

By way of preliminary work, one is a perceiver of form internally, not by way of absorption. For absorption with the counterpart sign as its object is not possible with an internal object; but that kasiṇa sign obtained by way of internal preliminary work is indeed impure, not pure like that obtained by way of external preliminary work.

Parittānīti [V 2.0143] yathāladdhāni suppasarāvamattāni. Tenāha “avaḍḍhitānī”ti. Parittavasenevāti vaṇṇavasena ābhoge vijjamānepi parittavaseneva idaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ vuttaṃ. Parittatā hettha abhibhavanassa kāraṇaṃ. Vaṇṇābhoge satipi asatipi abhibhāyatanabhāvanā nāma tikkhapaññasseva sambhavati, na itarassāti āha “ñāṇuttariko puggalo”ti. Abhibhavitvā samāpajjatīti ettha abhibhavanaṃ, samāpajjanañca upacārajjhānādhigamasamanantarameva appanājhānuppādananti āha “saha nimittuppādenevettha appanaṃ pāpetī”ti. Saha nimittuppādenāti ca appanāparivāsābhāvassa lakkhaṇaṃ vacanametaṃ. Yo “khippābhiñño”ti vuccati, tatopi ñāṇuttarasseva abhibhāyatanabhāvanā. Etthāti etasmiṃ nimitte. Appanaṃ pāpetīti bhāvanaṃ appanaṃ neti.

`Parittāni` means as obtained, the size of a small bowl. Therefore, it is said, 'unexpanded.' `Parittavaseneva` means: even though there is attention by way of color, this base of mastery is spoken of in terms of the limited. Here, limitedness is the cause of mastery. Whether there is attention to color or not, the development of the base of mastery is possible only for one of sharp wisdom, not for others. Hence, it is said, 'a person superior in knowledge.' `Abhibhavitvā samāpajjati` means: here, mastering and attaining is the production of absorption-jhāna immediately after achieving access concentration. Therefore, it is said, 'here, one reaches absorption simultaneously with the arising of the sign.' The phrase 'simultaneously with the arising of the sign' is a statement indicating the absence of a preparatory period for absorption. The development of the base of mastery is for one who is even more superior in knowledge than one who is called 'swift in direct knowledge.' `Ettha` means in this sign. `Appanaṃ pāpeti` means leading the development to absorption.

Ettha [P 2.0206] ca keci “uppanne upacārajjhāne taṃ ārabbha ye heṭṭhimantena dve tayo javanavārā pavattanti, te upacārajjhānapakkhikā eva, tadanantarañca bhavaṅgaparivāsena, upacārāsevanāya ca vinā appanā hoti, saha nimittuppādeneva appanaṃ pāpetī”ti vadanti, taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ. Na hi parivāsitaparikammena appanāvāro icchito, nāpi mahaggatappamāṇajjhānesu viya upacārajjhāne ekantato paccavekkhaṇā icchitabbā, tasmā upacārajjhānādhigamanato paraṃ katipayabhavaṅgacittāvasāne appanaṃ pāpuṇanto “saha nimittuppādenevettha appanaṃ pāpetī”ti vutto. Saha nimittuppādenevāti ca adhippāyikamidaṃ vacanaṃ, na nītatthaṃ, adhippāyo vuttanayeneva veditabbo, na antosamāpattiyaṃ tadā tathārūpassa ābhogassa asambhavato. Samāpattito vuṭṭhitassa ābhogo pubbabhāgabhāvanāyavasena jhānakkhaṇe pavattaṃ abhibhavanākāraṃ gahetvā pavattoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Abhidhammaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “iminā tassa pubbābhogo kathito”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 204) vuttaṃ. Antosamāpattiyaṃ tathā ābhogābhāve kasmā “jhānasaññāyapī”ti vuttanti āha “abhibhavana…pe… atthī”ti.

Here, some say: 'When access concentration has arisen, taking that as object, at least two or three javana-courses occur which belong to the side of access concentration. Immediately after, without a preparatory period of bhavaṅga or cultivation of access, absorption occurs. One reaches absorption simultaneously with the arising of the sign.' This is merely their opinion. For an absorption course with a preparatory preliminary work is not intended, nor should reviewing be absolutely expected in access concentration as it is in the sublime and immeasurable jhānas. Therefore, one who reaches absorption at the end of a few bhavaṅga-cittas after attaining access concentration is said to 'reach absorption here simultaneously with the arising of the sign.' And the phrase 'simultaneously with the arising of the sign' is a statement of intention, not of explicit meaning. The intention should be understood according to the method stated, because at that time, during the attainment, such attention is impossible. It should be understood that the attention of one who has arisen from attainment proceeds by grasping the mode of overcoming that occurred at the moment of jhāna, by way of the preliminary-part development. In the Abhidhamma commentary, however, it is said, 'By this, his previous attention is explained' (DhsA. 204). If there is no such attention during the attainment, why is it said, 'even in the perception of jhāna...'? It is replied, 'Because there is overcoming... and so forth...'

Vaḍḍhitappamāṇānīti [M 2.0161] vipulappamāṇānīti attho, na ekaṅguladvaṅgulādivasena vaḍḍhiṃ pāpitānīti tathā vaḍḍhanassevettha asambhavato. Tenāha “mahantānī”ti. Bhattavaḍḍhitakanti bhuñjanabhājanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā dinnabhattaṃ, ekāsane purisena bhuñjitabbabhattato upaḍḍhabhattanti attho.

`Vaḍḍhitappamāṇāni` means 'of extensive measure,' not 'brought to an increase by way of one or two inches,' as such an increase is impossible here. Hence it is said, 'mahantāni' (great). `Bhattavaḍḍhitaka` means food given after enlarging the eating vessel; the meaning is half the food that can be eaten by a person in one sitting.

Rūpe saññā rūpasaññā, sā assa atthīti rūpasaññī, na rūpasaññī arūpasaññī, saññāsīsena jhānaṃ vadati. Rūpasaññāya anuppādanaṃ evettha alābhitā.

Perception in regard to form is `rūpasaññā`. One for whom that exists is a `rūpasaññī` (perceiver of form). One who is not a perceiver of form is an `arūpasaññī` (perceiver of the formless). He speaks of jhāna with perception as the chief factor. Here, the non-production of form-perception itself is the non-attainment.

Bahiddhāva [P 2.0207][V 2.0144] uppannanti bahiddhā vatthusmiṃyeva uppannaṃ. Abhidhamme pana “ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni…pe… appamāṇāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānī”ti (dha. sa. 220) evaṃ catunnaṃ abhibhāyatanānaṃ āgatattā abhidhammaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 204) “kasmā pana ‘yathā suttante ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittānītiādi vuttaṃ, evaṃ avatvā idha catūsupi abhibhāyatanesu ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññitāva vuttā’ti codanaṃ katvā ‘ajjhattarūpānaṃ anabhibhavanīyato’ti kāraṇaṃ vatvā, tattha vā hi idha vā bahiddhā rūpāneva abhibhavitabbāni, tasmā tāni niyamato vattabbānīti tatrāpi idhāpi vuttāni. ‘Ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī’ti idaṃ pana satthu desanāvilāsamattamevā”ti vuttaṃ. Ettha ca vaṇṇābhogarahitāni, sahitāni ca sabbāni parittāni “parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānī”ti vuttāni, tathā appamāṇāni “appamāṇāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānī”ti. Atthi hi so pariyāyo parittāni abhibhuyya tāni ce kadāci vaṇṇavasena ābhujitāni honti, suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni abhibhuyyāti. Pariyāyakathā hi suttantadesanāti. Abhidhamme (dha. sa. 222) pana nippariyāyadesanattā vaṇṇābhogarahitāni visuṃ vuttāni, tathā sahitāni. Atthi hi ubhayattha abhibhavanavisesoti. Tathā idha pariyāyadesanattā vimokkhānampi abhibhavanapariyāyo atthīti “ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī”tiādinā paṭhamadutiyaabhibhāyatanesu paṭhamavimokkho, tatiyacatutthaabhibhāyatanesu dutiyavimokkho, vaṇṇābhibhāyatanesu tatiyavimokkho ca abhibhavanappavattito saṅgahito. Abhidhamme pana nippariyāyadesanattā vimokkhābhibhāyatanāni asaṅkarato dassetuṃ vimokkhe vajjetvā abhibhāyatanāni kathitāni[P 2.0208]; sabbāni ca vimokkhakiccāni jhānāni vimokkhadesanāyaṃ vuttāni. Tadetaṃ [M 2.0162] “ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī”ti āgatassa abhibhāyatanadvayassa abhidhamme abhibhāyatanesu avacanato “rūpī rūpāni passatī”tiādīnañca sabbavimokkhakiccasādhāraṇavacanabhāvato vavatthānaṃ katanti viññāyati. “Ajjhattarūpānaṃ anabhibhavanīyato”ti idaṃ katthacipi “ajjhattaṃ rūpāni passatī”ti avatvā sabbattha yaṃ vuttaṃ “bahiddhā rūpāni passatī”ti, tassa kāraṇavacanaṃ, tena yaṃ aññahetukaṃ, taṃ tena hetunā vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana desanāvilāsahetukaṃ ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññitāya eva abhidhamme (dha. sa. 223) vacanaṃ, na tassa aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ maggitabbanti dasseti. Ajjhattarūpānaṃ anabhibhavanīyatā ca tesaṃ bahiddhā rūpānaṃ viya abhūtattā. Desanāvilāso ca yathāvuttavavatthānavasena veditabbo veneyyajjhāsayavasena vijjamānapariyāyakathābhāvato. “Suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānī”ti eteneva siddhattā na nīlādi abhibhāyatanāni vattabbānīti ce? Taṃ na, nīlādīsu katādhikārānaṃ nīlādibhāvasseva abhibhavanakāraṇattā. Na hi tesaṃ parisuddhāparisuddhavaṇṇānaṃ [V 2.0145] parittatā, appamāṇatā vā abhibhavanakāraṇaṃ, atha kho nīlādibhāvo evāti. Etesu ca parittādikasiṇarūpesu yaṃ yaṃ caritassa imāni abhibhāyatanāni ijjhanti, taṃ dassetuṃ “imesu panā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

‘Externally arisen’ means arisen in an external object. However, in the Abhidhamma, it is stated: ‘Internally percipient of formlessness, one sees external forms as limited, fair or foul… or as unlimited, fair or foul’ (Dhs. 220). Since this appears in the context of the four bases of mastery, the Abhidhamma commentary (Dhs. Aṭṭha. 204) explains: ‘But why, without stating as in the Suttas—“perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms as limited,” etc.—is it here said that in all four bases of mastery, one is internally percipient of formlessness?’ Having raised this objection, it is answered: ‘Because internal forms cannot be mastered.’ For whether there or here, it is the external forms that must be mastered. Therefore, those must be invariably stated, and so they are stated both there and here. ‘Perceiving forms internally’ is merely an embellishment of the Teacher’s instruction. Here, all limited forms, both devoid of color-aspects and possessing them, are called ‘limited, fair or foul,’ and similarly, unlimited forms are called ‘unlimited, fair or foul.’ For there is this method: having mastered the limited forms, if they are sometimes apprehended in terms of color, then the fair and foul are mastered. For the Sutta teaching is a figurative discourse. In the Abhidhamma (Dhs. 222), however, because the teaching is non-figurative, forms devoid of color-aspects are stated separately, as are those possessing them, for there is a distinction in the manner of mastery in both cases. Similarly, here, because the teaching is figurative, the mode of mastery applies also to the liberations. Thus, in the first and second bases of mastery, the first liberation is included; in the third and fourth, the second liberation; and in the color-bases of mastery, the third liberation—all due to the process of mastery. In the Abhidhamma, however, because the teaching is non-figurative, the bases of mastery and liberations are shown without confusion, the bases of mastery being spoken of, omitting the liberations. And all the jhānas that perform the function of liberation are stated in the discourse on the liberations. Thus, it is understood that a distinction is made due to the non-mention in the Abhidhamma's section on bases of mastery of the two bases of mastery that come with 'perceiving forms internally,' and due to the fact that statements like 'one with form sees forms,' etc., are general statements for all functions of liberation. This phrase ‘because internal forms cannot be mastered’ is the reason why, without stating ‘one sees internal forms’ anywhere, it is everywhere said, ‘one sees external forms.’ Thus, whatever is due to another cause is stated for that cause. As for the statement in the Abhidhamma (Dhs. 223) that one is internally percipient of formlessness—this is due to the embellishment of the teaching, and no other reason need be sought. The unmasterability of internal forms is because they are not actual, unlike external forms. The embellishment of the teaching should be understood in accordance with the distinction stated above, based on the dispositions of those to be trained, because figurative discourses exist. If one asks, ‘Does ‘fair or foul’ imply that the blue and so forth bases of mastery are not to be stated?’ The answer is: No, because for those who have made blue and so forth their sphere, it is the nature of blueness itself that is the cause of mastery. For it is not the limited or unlimited nature of pure or impure colors that causes mastery, but the nature of blueness, etc., itself. And among these limited and so forth kasiṇa forms, to show which bases of mastery are successful for which temperament, it is said: ‘But in these…’ etc.

Sabbasaṅgāhakavasenāti sakalanīlavaṇṇanīlanidassananīlanibhāsānaṃ sādhāraṇavasena. Vaṇṇavasenāti sabhāvavaṇṇavasena. Nidassanavasenāti passitabbatāvasena cakkhuviññāṇādiviññāṇavīthiyā gahetabbatāvasena. Obhāsavasenāti sappabhāsatāya avabhāsanavasena. Umāpupphanti atasipupphaṃ. Nīlameva hoti vaṇṇasaṅkarābhāvato. Bārāṇasisambhavanti bārāṇasiyaṃ samuṭṭhitaṃ.

‘By all-inclusive means’ refers to the common way of all blue hues, blue appearances, and blue radiances. ‘By color means’ refers to its inherent color. ‘By appearance means’ refers to its being seen, and its being grasped through the cognitive process of eye-consciousness and other consciousness processes. ‘By radiance means’ refers to its shining forth due to its luminosity. ‘Flax flower’ refers to the atasi flower. It is purely blue due to the absence of color mixture. ‘Originating in Bārāṇasī’ means it originated in Bārāṇasī.

Ekaccassa ito bāhirakassa appamāṇaṃ ativitthāritaṃ kasiṇanimittaṃ [P 2.0209] olokentassa bhayaṃ uppajjeyya “kiṃ nu kho idaṃ sakalaṃ lokaṃ abhibhavitvā ajjhottharitvā gaṇhātī”ti, tathāgatassa pana tādisaṃ bhayaṃ vā sārajjaṃ vā natthīti abhītabhāvadassanatthameva ānītāni.

For some outsider, upon seeing an immeasurably vast kasiṇa sign, fear might arise, thinking, ‘What is this that overwhelms and covers the entire world?’ But the Tathāgata has no such fear or agitation. These are brought forth solely to demonstrate his state of fearlessness.

Aṭṭhavimokkhavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Eight Liberations

174. Uttānatthāyeva [M 2.0163] heṭṭhā atthato vibhattattā. Ekaccassa vimokkhoti ghosopi bhayāvaho vaṭṭābhiratabhāvato, tathāgatassa pana vimokkhe upasampajja viharatopi taṃ natthīti abhītabhāvadassanatthameva ānītāni.

174. Its meaning is clear because it has been analyzed in detail below. For some, even the sound of ‘liberation’ is frightening due to their delight in the cycle of existence. But for the Tathāgata, even when dwelling having entered upon liberation, that fear does not exist. Therefore, these are brought forth solely to show his state of fearlessness.

Ānandayācanakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Story of Ānanda's Entreaty

178. Bodhīti sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. Tañhi “catumaggañāṇapaṭivedha”ntveva vuttaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇappaṭivedhassa taṃmūlakattā. Evaṃ vuttabhāvanti “ākaṅkhamāno ānanda tathāgato kappaṃ vā tiṭṭheyyā”ti (dī. ni. 2.166) evaṃ vuttabhāvaṃ.

178. Enlightenment (bodhi) is omniscient knowledge. For it is said to be 'the penetration of the knowledge of the four paths,' because the penetration of omniscient knowledge has that as its root. The meaning of 'thus stated' is the fact that it was stated, 'Ānanda, if the Tathāgata wished, he could remain for an eon' (Dī. Ni. 2.166).

179. Tampi oḷārikanimittaṃ kataṃ tassa mārena pariyuṭṭhitacetaso na paṭividdhaṃ na sallakkhitaṃ.

179. That gross sign was made, but it was not penetrated, not discerned by him, whose mind was assailed by Māra.

183. Ādikehīti evamādīhi mittāmaccasuhajjāhi. Piyāyitabbato piyehi. Manavaḍḍhanato [V 2.0146] manāpehi. Jātiyāti jātianurūpagamanena. Nānābhāvo visuṃbhāvo asambaddhabhāvo. Maraṇena vinābhāvoti cutiyā tenattabhāvena apunarāvattanato vippayogo. Bhavena aññathābhāvoti bhavantaraggahaṇena purimākārato aññākāratā “kāmāvacarasatto rūpāvacaro hotī”tiādinā, tatthāpi “manusso devo hotī”tiādināpi yojetabbo. Kutettha labbhāti kuto kuhiṃ kismiṃ nāma ṭhāne ettha etasmiṃ khandhappavatte “yaṃ taṃ jātaṃ…pe… mā palujjī”ti laddhuṃ sakkā. Na sakkā eva tādisassa kāraṇassa abhāvatoti āha “netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti. Evaṃ acchariyabbhutadhammaṃ tathāgatassāpi sarīraṃ, kimaṅgaṃ pana aññesanti adhippāyo. “Paccāvamissatī”ti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ [P 2.0210] vijjati satiṃ sūpaṭṭhitaṃ katvā ñāṇena paricchinditvā āyusaṅkhārānaṃ ossaṭṭhattā, buddhakiccassa ca pariyosāpitattā. Na hettha māsattayato paraṃ buddhaveneyyā labbhantīti.

183. Ādikehi (by others, etc.): this means by friends, ministers, well-wishers, and so forth. Piyehi (by the dear): so called because they are to be cherished (piyāyitabbato). Manāpehi (by the pleasing): so called because they increase affection (manavaḍḍhanato). Jātiyā (by birth): this means by proceeding in accordance with birth. Nānābhāvo (diversity) means separateness (visuṃbhāvo), a state of disconnection (asambaddhabhāvo). Maraṇena vinābhāvo (separation by death): this means separation (vippayogo) due to passing away (cutiyā), and due to not returning in that very state of being. Bhavena aññathābhāvo (transformation by existence): this means a change from the previous form by taking another existence, such as 'a being in the sense-sphere becomes one in the form-sphere,' and similarly, 'a human becomes a deva' should also be connected there. Kutettha labbhā (where can this be found?): this means, in what place, where, in what spot, in this stream of aggregates, can it be obtained that 'what is born... should not perish'? It is indeed impossible, due to the absence of such a cause; hence it is said, 'This condition does not exist.' The intention is: thus, even the Tathāgata's body is a marvelous and wonderful phenomenon; how much more so others? Paccāvamissati (will return): this condition does not exist, for with mindfulness well-established and having discerned with knowledge, the life-formations have been relinquished, and the Buddha's task has been completed. For here, beyond three months, no more beings to be trained by the Buddha are to be found.

184. Sāsanassa ciraṭṭhiti nāma sasambhārehi ariyamaggadhammehi kevalehīti āha “sabbaṃ lokiyalokuttaravaseneva kathita”nti lokiyāhi [M 2.0164] sīlasamādhipaññāhi vinā lokuttaradhammasamadhigamassa asambhavato.

184. The long duration of the Dispensation is said to be solely by means of the noble path-factors together with their requisites. It is said, 'Everything is spoken of in terms of the mundane and the supramundane,' since without mundane virtue, concentration, and wisdom, the attainment of supramundane qualities is impossible.

Tatiyabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the third recitation section is finished.

Nāgāpalokitavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Elephant-Gaze

186. Nāgāpalokitanti nāgassa viya apalokitaṃ, hatthināgassa apalokanasadisaṃ apalokananti attho. Āhaccāti phusitvā. Aṅkusakalaggāni viyāti aṅkusakāni viya aññamaññasmiṃ laggāni āsattāni hutvā ṭhitāni. Ekābaddhānīti aññamaññaṃ ekato ābaddhāni. Tasmāti gīvaṭṭhīnaṃ ekagghanānaṃ viya ekābaddhabhāvena, na kevalaṃ gīvaṭṭhīnaṃyeva, atha kho sabbānipi tāni buddhānaṃ ṭhapetvā bāhusandhiādikā dvādasa mahāsandhiyo, aṅgulisandhiyo ca itarasandhīsu ekābaddhāni hutvā ṭhitāni, yato nesaṃ pakatihatthīnaṃ koṭisahassabalappamāṇaṃ kāyabalaṃ hoti. Vesālinagarābhimukhaṃ akāsi kaṇṭakaparivattane viya kapilanagarābhimukhaṃ. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ taṃ nāgāpalokitaṃ nāma jātaṃ? Tadajjhāsayaṃ upādāya. Bhagavā [V 2.0147] hi nāgāpalokitavaseneva apaloketukāmo jāto, puññānubhāvena panassa patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ parivatti, tena taṃ “nāgāpalokitaṃ” tveva vuccati.

186. By 'nāgāpalokita' is meant a gaze like that of an elephant, a gaze resembling the gaze of a royal elephant; that is the meaning. By 'having touched' (āhacca) is meant having touched (phusitvā). By 'like goad-hooks' (aṅkusakalaggāni viya) is meant like goad-hooks (aṅkusakāni viya), stuck together and clinging to one another. By 'bound together' (ekābaddhāni) is meant bound to one another as one. By 'therefore' (tasmā) — just as the neck bones are like a single mass, being bound together; not only the neck bones, but indeed all those bones of the Buddhas—except for the twelve major joints, such as the shoulder joints, and the finger joints—are bound together as one with the other joints and remain so. Hence, their bodily strength is of the measure of the strength of a thousand crores of ordinary elephants. He turned to face the city of Vesālī, as he had turned to face Kapilavatthu, like the turning of a thorny plant. If so, how did it come to be called 'nāgāpalokita'? Based on his inclination. For the Blessed One desired to gaze in the manner of an elephant, but due to the power of his merit, the place where he stood turned around; therefore it is called 'nāgāpalokita'.

“Idaṃ pacchimakaṃ ānanda tathāgatassa [P 2.0211] vesāliyā dassana”nti nayidaṃ vesāliyā apalokanassa kāraṇavacanaṃ anekantikattā, bhūtakathanamattaṃ panetaṃ. Maggasodhanavasena taṃ dassetvā aññadevettha apalokanakāraṇaṃ dassetukāmo “nanu cā”tiādimāha. Taṃ taṃ sabbaṃ pacchimadassanameva anukkamena kusināraṃ gantvā parinibbātukāmatāya tato tato nikkhantattā. “Anacchariyattā”ti iminā yathāvuttaṃ anekantikattaṃ pariharati, tayidaṃ sodhanamattaṃ. Idaṃ panettha aviparītaṃ kāraṇanti dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Na hi bhagavā sāpekkho vesāliṃ apalokesi, “idaṃ pana me gamanaṃ apunarāgamana”nti dassanamukhena bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya apalokesi. Tenāha “apica vesālirājāno”tiādi.

The statement, 'This is the last sight, Ananda, that the Tathāgata will have of Vesālī,' is not a statement giving the reason for looking back at Vesālī, as it is not definitive, but is merely a statement of fact. Having shown that by way of purifying the path, he wishes to indicate another reason for looking back, saying, 'Surely,' and so on. All of that is indeed the final sight, as he gradually departed from there to go to Kusinārā with the intention of attaining final Nibbāna. By 'because it is not astonishing' (anacchariyattā), he refutes the indefiniteness as previously explained, and this is merely a clarification. To show that this is indeed the correct reason here, 'moreover' (apicā) and so on, was stated. For the Blessed One did not look back at Vesālī with attachment, but rather, by way of showing, 'This journey of mine is a non-return,' he looked back for the welfare and happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world. Therefore, he says, 'Moreover, the kings of Vesālī,' and so on.

Antakaroti [M 2.0165] sakalavaṭṭadukkhassa sakasantāne, parasantāne ca vināsakaro abhāvakaro. Buddhacakkhudhammacakkhudibbacakkhumaṃsacakkhusamantacakkhusaṅkhātehi pañcahi cakkhūhi cakkhumā. Savāsanānaṃ kilesānaṃ samucchinnattā sātisayaṃ kilesaparinibbānena parinibbuto.

By 'he makes an end' (antakaro) — he is the destroyer and annihilator of all the suffering of the round of rebirths in his own continuity and in others' continuities. He is possessed of vision (cakkhumā) by means of the five eyes, namely, the Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, the divine eye, the fleshly eye, and the all-seeing eye. He is fully extinguished (parinibbuto) because of the complete cutting off of defilements together with their latent tendencies, through the surpassing quenching of defilements.

Catumahāpadesavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Four Great References

187. Mahāokāseti mahante okāse. Mahantāni dhammassa patiṭṭhāpanaṭṭhānāni. Yesu patiṭṭhāpito dhammo nicchīyati asandehato, kāni pana tāni? Āgamanavisiṭṭhāni suttotaraṇādīni. Dutiyavikappe apadisantīti apadesā, “sammukhā metaṃ āvuso bhagavato suta”ntiādinā kenaci ābhatassa “dhammo”ti vinicchinane kāraṇaṃ. Kiṃ pana tanti? Tassa yathābhatassa suttotaraṇādi eva. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ cattāroti? Yasmā dhammassa dve samparāyā satthā, sāvakā ca, tesu ca sāvakā saṅghagaṇapuggalavasena tividhā[P 2.0212], evaṃ “tumhākaṃ mayā yaṃ dhammo paṭiggahito”ti apadisitabbānaṃ bhedena cattāro. Tenāha “sammukhā me taṃ āvuso bhagavato suta”ntiādi. Tathā ca vuttaṃ nettiyaṃ “cattāro mahāpadesā buddhāpadeso saṅghāpadeso sambahulattherāpadeso ekattherāpadeso. Ime cattāro mahāpadesā”ti (netti. 18) buddho apadeso etassāti buddhāpadeso. Esa nayo sesesupi. Tenāha “buddhādayo…pe… mahākāraṇānī”ti.

187. ‘In the great open space’ (mahāokāseti) means in a vast open space. ‘Great foundations’ (mahantāni dhammassa patiṭṭhāpanaṭṭhānāni) are the great grounds for establishing the Dhamma, where the Dhamma, once established, is ascertained without doubt. What are they? They are the distinguished traditions, such as the handing down of the suttas. In the second interpretation, they are called ‘references’ (apadesa) because they refer (apadisanti), being the reason for discerning what is called ‘Dhamma’ when something is brought forth by someone, such as, ‘Friends, I heard this in the presence of the Blessed One.’ But what is the textual tradition (tanti)? It is simply the handing down of the suttas pertaining to what was brought forth. If so, how are there four? Because the Dhamma has two resorts (samparāya): the Teacher and the disciples. And among the disciples, they are threefold: in terms of the Saṅgha, a group, and an individual. Thus, there are four by the division of those to whom one may refer, saying, ‘The Dhamma that I received from you.’ Therefore, it is said, ‘Friends, I heard this in the presence of the Blessed One,’ and so on. And so it is stated in the Netti: ‘The four great references are the Buddha-reference, the Saṅgha-reference, the reference of many elders, and the reference of a single elder. These are the four great references.’ The Buddha is a reference for this—thus, the Buddha-reference. The same principle applies to the rest. Therefore, it is said, ‘Beginning with the Buddha… these are the great reasons.’

188. Neva [V 2.0148] abhinanditabbanti na sampaṭicchitabbaṃ. Ganthassa sampaṭicchanaṃ nāma savananti āha “na sotabba”nti. Padabyañjanānīti padāni ca byañjanāni ca, atthapadāni, byañjanapadāni cāti attho. Pajjati attho etehīti padāni, akkharādīni byañjanapadāni. Pajjitabbato padāni, saṅkāsanādīni atthapadāni. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃpana “‘padasaṅkhātāni byañjanānī’ti byañjanapadāneva vuttānī”ti keci, taṃ na, atthaṃ byañjentīti byañjanāni, byañjanapadāni, tehi byañjitabbato byañjanāni, atthapadānīti ubhayasaṅgahato. Imasmiṃ ṭhāneti tenābhatasuttassa imasmiṃ padese. Pāḷi vuttāti kevalo pāḷidhammo pavatto. Attho vuttoti pāḷiyā attho pavatto niddiṭṭho. Anusandhi kathitoti yathāraddhadesanāya, upari desanāya ca anusandhānaṃ kathitaṃ sambandho kathito[M 2.0166]. Pubbāparaṃ kathitanti pubbenāparaṃ avirujjhanañceva visesādhānañca kathitaṃ pakāsitaṃ. Evaṃ pāḷidhammādīni sammadeva sallakkhetvā gahaṇaṃ sādhukaṃ uggahaṇanti āha “suṭṭhu gahetvā”ti. Sutte otāretabbānīti [P 2.0213] ñāṇena sutte ogāhetvā tāretabbāni, taṃ pana ogāhetvā taraṇaṃ tattha otaraṇaṃ anuppavesanaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ “sutte otāretabbānī”ti. Saṃsandetvā dassanaṃ sandassananti āha “vinaye saṃsandetabbānī”ti.

188. ‘Neither should one delight in it’ (neva abhinanditabbaṃ) means it should not be accepted. ‘The acceptance of a text’ (ganthassa sampaṭicchanaṃ) is called listening—thus it is said, ‘should not be listened to.’ ‘Words and expressions’ (padabyañjanāni) means both words (padāni) and expressions (byañjanāni), that is, words of meaning (atthapadāni) and words of expression (byañjanapadāni). ‘Words’ (padāni) are so called because meaning is reached through them; words of expression are letters and so on. ‘Words’ (padāni) are so called because they are to be understood; words of meaning are explanations and so on. However, some say in the commentary that ‘expressions counted as words’ refers only to ‘words of expression,’ but that is not so, because it encompasses both. For ‘expressions’ (byañjanāni) can mean ‘words of expression’ (byañjanapadāni) because they express meaning, and they can also mean ‘words of meaning’ (atthapadāni) because meaning is to be expressed by them. ‘In this place’ (imasmiṃ ṭhāne) means in this part of the discourse that has been brought forth. ‘The Pāḷi has been spoken’ (Pāḷi vuttā) means only the Dhamma in the Pāḷi language has been set forth. ‘The meaning has been spoken’ (Attho vutto) means the meaning of the Pāḷi has been set forth and explained. ‘The connection has been stated’ (Anusandhi kathito) means the connection has been explained, the relation has been stated, both with the teaching as it began and with the subsequent teaching. ‘The sequence has been stated’ (Pubbāparaṃ kathitaṃ) means both the non-contradiction of what follows with what precedes and the adding of specifics have been explained and clarified. Thus, having properly discerned the Dhamma in the Pāḷi and so forth, one should grasp it well—thus it is said, ‘having grasped it thoroughly.’ ‘Should be made to enter the discourses’ (Sutte otāretabbāni) means one should immerse them in the suttas with knowledge and carry the analysis through. That immersion and carrying through is an entering into, a thorough penetration; thus it is said, ‘should be made to enter the discourses.’ Showing by comparing (Saṃsandetvā dassanaṃ) is comparison (sandassanaṃ)—thus it is said, ‘should be compared with the Vinaya.’

Kiṃ pana taṃ suttaṃ, ko vā vinayoti vicāraṇāya ācariyānaṃ matibhedamukhena tamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “ettha cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vinayoti vibhaṅgapāṭhamāha. So hi mātikāsaññitassa suttassa atthasūcanato “sutta”nti vattabbataṃ arahati. Vividhanayattā, visiṭṭhanayattā ca vinayo, khandhakapāṭho. Evanti evaṃ suttavinayesu pariggayhamānesu vinayapiṭakampi na pariyādīyati parivārapāḷiyā asaṅgahitattā. Suttantābhidhammapiṭakāni vā suttaṃ atthasūcanādiatthasambhavato. Evampīti “suttantābhidhammapiṭakāni suttaṃ, vinayapiṭakaṃ vinayo”ti evaṃ suttavinayavibhāge vuccamānepi. Na tāva pariyādīyantīti na tāva anavasesato pariggayhanti, kasmāti āha “asuttanāmakañhī”tiādi. Yasmā “sutta”nti imaṃ nāmaṃ anāropetvā saṅgītampi jātakādibuddhavacanaṃ atthi, tasmā vuttanayena tīṇi piṭakāni na pariyādiṇṇānīti. Suttanipātaudānaitivuttakādīni dīghanikāyādayo viya suttanāmaṃ āropetvā asaṅgītānīti adhippāye panettha jātakādīhi saddhiṃ tānipi gahitāni. Buddhavaṃsacariyāpiṭakānaṃ panettha aggahaṇe kāraṇaṃ maggitabbaṃ, kiṃ vā tena magganena? Sabbopāyaṃ vaṇṇanānayo theravādaṃ dassanamukhena paṭikkhitto evāti.

But what is that Sutta, or what is the Vinaya? To explain that meaning through the differing opinions of the teachers, it is said, ‘Here too,’ and so forth. The Vinaya is said to be the Vibhaṅga text. For it deserves to be called ‘Sutta’ because it indicates the meaning of the Sutta designated as Mātikā. Due to its diverse and distinguished methods, the Vinaya is the Khandhaka text. Thus, when the Sutta and Vinaya are understood in this way, the Vinaya Piṭaka is not fully encompassed, because the Parivāra Pāḷi is not included. Or, the Suttanta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas are the Sutta, due to the possibility of meanings such as indicating the meaning. Even so, when the division of Sutta and Vinaya is spoken of as ‘the Suttanta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas are the Sutta, and the Vinaya Piṭaka is the Vinaya,’ they are not yet fully encompassed. Why? It is said, ‘because indeed there are those not named “Sutta.”’ Because there is also the Buddha’s word, such as the Jātaka, which has been recited without being given this name ‘Sutta,’ therefore, in the manner stated, the three Piṭakas are not completely included. The Suttanipāta, Udāna, Itivuttaka, and others, unlike the Dīghanikāya and so on, were not recited with the name ‘Sutta’ affixed; in this sense, they are included here along with the Jātaka and others. Regarding the non-inclusion of the Buddhavaṃsa and Cariyāpiṭaka here, a reason should be sought. Or what is the use of seeking it? This entire method of explanation is rejected by way of presenting the Theravāda view.

Atthīti kiṃ atthi, asuttanāmakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ natthi evāti dasseti. Tathā hi nidānavaṇṇanāyaṃ [V 2.0149] (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā; sārattha. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) amhehi vuttaṃ [P 2.0214] “suttanti sāmaññavidhi, visesavidhayo pare”ti. Taṃ sabbaṃ paṭikkhipitvā “suttanti vinayo”tiādinā vuttaṃ saṃvaṇṇanānayaṃ “nāyamattho idhādhippeto”ti paṭisodhetvā. Vineti etena kileseti vinayo, kilesavinayanūpāyo, so eva ca naṃ karotīti kāraṇanti āha “vinayo pana kāraṇa”nti.

‘Is there?’ What is there? He shows that there is in fact no Buddha-word not named ‘Sutta.’ For thus it was said by us in the commentary on the introduction (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1. Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā; Sārattha. Ṭī. 1. Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā), ‘Sutta means a general rule; the others are specific rules.’ Rejecting all of that, and having corrected the method of explanation stated as ‘Sutta means Vinaya,’ etc., with the words ‘This meaning is not intended here,’ he says, ‘One tames defilements by this, thus it is Vinaya; it is the means for taming defilements, and because it itself does this, it is the cause.’ Hence it is said, ‘But Vinaya is the cause.’

Dhammeti [M 2.0167] pariyattidhamme. Sarāgāyāti sarāgabhāvāya kāmarāgabhavarāgaparibrūhanāya. Saññogāyāti bhavasaṃyojanāya. Ācayāyāti vaṭṭassa vaḍḍhanatthāya. Mahicchatāyāti mahicchabhāvāya. Asantuṭṭhiyāti asantuṭṭhibhāvāya. Saṅgaṇikāyāti kilesasaṅgaṇagaṇasaṅgaṇavihārāya. Kosajjāyāti kusītabhāvāya. Dubbharatāyāti dupposatāya. Virāgāyāti sakalavaṭṭato virajjanatthāya. Visaññogāyāti kāmabhavādīhi visaṃyujjanatthāya. Apacayāyāti sabbassāpi vaṭṭassa apacayanāya, nibbānāyāti attho. Appicchatāyāti paccayappicchatādivasena sabbaso icchāpagamāya. Santuṭṭhiyāti dvādasavidhasantuṭṭhibhāvāya. Pavivekāyāti pavivittabhāvāya, kāyavivekāditadaṅgavivekādivivekasiddhiyā. Vīriyārambhāyāti kāyikassa ceva, cetasikassa ca vīriyassa paggahaṇatthāya. Subharatāyāti sukhaposanatthāya. Evaṃ yo pariyattidhammo uggahaṇadhāraṇaparipucchāmanasikāravasena yoniso paṭipajjantassa sarāgādibhāvaparivajjanassa kāraṇaṃ hutvā virāgādibhāvāya saṃvattati, ekaṃsato eso dhammo. Eso vinayo, sammadeva [P 2.0215] apāyādīsu apatanavasena dhāraṇato, kilesānaṃ vinayanato, satthu sammāsambuddhassa ovādānusiṭṭhibhāvato etaṃ satthusāsananti dhāreyyāsi jāneyyāsi, avabujjheyyāsīti attho. Catusaccassa sūcanaṃ suttanti āha “sutteti tepiṭake buddhavacane”ti. Tepiṭakañhi buddhavacanaṃ saccavinimuttaṃ natthi. Rāgādivinayanakāraṇaṃ tathāgatena suttapadena pakāsitanti āha “vinayeti etasmiṃ rāgādivinayakāraṇe”ti.

‘Dhamma’ means the Dhamma of learning. ‘For passion’ means for the state of passion, for the strengthening of sensual passion and the passion for existence. ‘For bondage’ means for the fetter of existence. ‘For accumulation’ means for the growth of the cycle of existence. ‘For great desire’ means for the state of great desire. ‘For discontent’ means for the state of discontent. ‘For socializing’ means for dwelling in the company of defilements and the company of groups. ‘For laziness’ means for the state of laziness. ‘For being hard to sustain’ means for being difficult to nourish. ‘For dispassion’ means for the purpose of detachment from the entire cycle of existence. ‘For disjunction’ means for the purpose of being disjoined from sensual desires, existence, and so on. ‘For reduction’ means for the decrease of the entire cycle of existence; the meaning is for Nibbāna. ‘For fewness of desires’ means for the complete abandonment of desires in terms of fewness of desires regarding requisites, etc. ‘For contentment’ means for the state of twelvefold contentment. ‘For seclusion’ means for the state of solitude, for the accomplishment of seclusion, such as bodily seclusion and seclusion by way of its factors. ‘For the arousal of energy’ means for the exertion of both bodily and mental energy. ‘For being easy to sustain’ means for the purpose of being easy to nourish. Thus, the Dhamma of learning, when practiced wisely by one through study, retention, questioning, and reflection, becomes a cause for avoiding states of passion and so on, leading to states of dispassion and so on—this Dhamma is unambiguously so. This is the Vinaya, because it rightly holds one from falling into states of woe and so on, because it tames defilements, and because it is the advice and instruction of the Teacher, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. You should hold, know, and understand this as the Teacher’s dispensation. The indication of the four truths is Sutta. He says: ‘in the Sutta’ means in the Tipiṭaka, the Buddha’s word. For the Tipiṭaka, the Buddha’s word, is not devoid of the truths. The cause for taming lust and so on was declared by the Tathāgata with the term Sutta. He says: ‘in the Vinaya’ means in this cause for taming lust and so on.

Sutte osaraṇañcettha tepiṭake buddhavacane pariyāpannatāvaseneva veditabbaṃ, na aññathāti āha “suttapaṭipāṭiyā katthaci anāgantvā”ti. Challiṃ uṭṭhapetvāti arogassa mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato upakkamena challiyā sakalikāya, papaṭikāya vā uṭṭhapanaṃ viya arogassa sāsanadhammassa tiṭṭhato byañjanamattena tappariyāpannaṃ viya hutvā challisadisaṃ pubbāparaviruddhatādidosaṃ uṭṭhapetvā paridīpetvā, tādisāni pana ekaṃsato guḷhavessantarādipariyāpannāni hontīti āha “guḷhavessantara…pe…paññāyantīti attho”ti[V 2.0150]. Rāgādivinayeti rāgādīnaṃ vinayanatthe. Tadākāratāya na paññāyamānāni na dissamānāni chaḍḍetabbāni vajjitabbāni na gahetabbāni. Sabbatthāti sabbavāresu.

And here, entering into the Sutta should be understood only by way of its inclusion in the Buddha’s words of the Tipiṭaka, and not otherwise, he said, ‘without occurring anywhere in the sequence of suttas.’ ‘Having raised a bark fragment’ means just as one might remove a bark fragment, a flake, or a sliver of bark from a healthy, standing tree by effort, so too, while the teaching of the Sāsana-Dhamma stands unafflicted, one seemingly raises and clearly illuminates a fault resembling a bark fragment—a contradiction between earlier and later statements—being as if included by mere expression. However, such things are unambiguously included in the Guḷha Vessantara and so forth—thus he said, ‘the Guḷha Vessantara… are understood,’ this is the meaning. ‘In the taming of lust, etc.’ means in the meaning of taming lust, etc. ‘Not appearing in that manner’—those that are not apparent or visible are to be discarded, avoided, and not taken up. ‘In all cases’ means in all instances.

Imasmiṃ [M 2.0168] pana ṭhāneti imasmiṃ mahāpadesaniddesaṭṭhāne. “Sutte cattāro mahāpadesā”tiādinā vuttampi avuttena saddhiṃ gahetvā pakiṇṇakakathāya mātikaṃ uddisati. Ñātuṃ [P 2.0216] icchito attho pañho, tassa vissajjanāni pañhābyākaraṇāni, atthasūcanādiatthena suttaṃ, pāḷi, taṃ suttaṃ anulometi anukūletīti suttānulomaṃ, mahāpadeso. Ācariyā vadanti saṃvaṇṇenti pāḷiṃ etenāti ācariyavādo aṭṭhakathā. Tassa tassa therassa attano eva mati adhippāyoti attanomati. Dhammavinicchaye patteti dhamme vinicchinitabbe upaṭṭhite. Imeti anantaraṃ vuttā cattāro mahāpadesā. Pamīyati dhammo paricchijjati vinicchīyati etenāti pamāṇaṃ. Tenāha “yaṃ ettha sametī”tiādi. Itaranti mahāpadesesu asamentaṃ. Puna itaranti akappiyaṃ anulomentaṃ kappiyaṃ paṭibāhantaṃ sandhāyāha.

‘In this place’ means in this section explaining the great authorities. Taking what is stated, such as ‘The four great authorities in the Sutta,’ along with what is unstated, he recites the matrix in the miscellaneous discussion. The meaning one wishes to know is a question; its answers are the explanations of questions. The Sutta, the Pāli text, is so called because it indicates the meaning, etc. That which conforms to the Sutta, which is in agreement with it, is Sutta-conformity, a great authority. ‘The teachers speak, they comment on the Pāli by this’—thus, the teachers' statement is the commentary. ‘The opinion, the intention, of each elder is his own’—thus, it is one's own view. ‘When it comes to the discernment of the Dhamma’ means when a Dhamma to be discerned is present. ‘These’ refers to the four great authorities stated immediately after. ‘The Dhamma is measured, defined, discerned by this’—thus, it is the standard. Therefore, he said, ‘That which agrees here,’ and so on. ‘The other’ refers to what does not agree with the great authorities. Again, ‘the other’ refers to that which approves the improper and rejects the proper.

Ekaṃseneva byākātabbo vissajjetabboti ekaṃsabyākaraṇīyo. Vibhajjāti pucchitamatthaṃ avadhāraṇādibhedena vibhajitvā. Paṭipucchāti pucchantaṃ puggalaṃ paṭipucchitvā. Ṭhapanīyoti tidhāpi avissajjanīyattā ṭhapanīyo byākaraṇaṃ akatvā ṭhapetabbo. “Cakkhuṃ anicca”nti pañhe uttarapadāvadhāraṇaṃ sandhāya “ekaṃseneva byākātabba”nti vuttaṃ niccatāya lesassāpi tattha abhāvato. Purimapadāvadhāraṇe pana vibhajjabyākaraṇīyatā cakkhusotesu visesatthasāmaññatthānaṃ asādhāraṇabhāvato. Dvinnaṃ tesaṃ sadisatācodanā paṭipucchanamukheneva byākaraṇīyā paṭikkhepavasena, anuññātavasena ca vissajjitabbatoti āha “yathā cakkhu, tathā sotaṃ…pe… ayaṃ paṭipucchābyākaraṇīyo pañho”ti. Taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīranti jīvasarīrānaṃ anaññatāpañho. Yassa yena anaññatācoditā, so eva paramatthato [P 2.0217] nupalabbhatīti vañjhātanayassa matteyyatākittanasadisoti abyākātabbatāya ṭhapanīyo vuttoti. Imāni cattāri pañhabyākaraṇāni pamāṇaṃ teneva nayena tesaṃ pañhānaṃ byākātabbato.

It should be answered categorically, it should be replied—this is a question to be answered categorically. To be analyzed means dividing the asked meaning by distinctions such as determination, etc. To be cross-questioned means cross-questioning the person who asks. To be set aside means it is to be set aside without giving an answer, because it is not to be answered in any of the three ways. In the question, “Is the eye impermanent?” the determination of the latter word is intended, hence it is said, “It should be answered categorically,” because there is not even a trace of permanence there. But in the determination of the former word, it requires an analytical answer because the eye and the ear have specific and general meanings that are not shared. The assertion of similarity between the two is to be answered by means of cross-questioning, by way of rejection and by way of affirmation. Thus it is said, “As with the eye, so with the ear… this is a question to be answered by cross-questioning.” The question, “Is the soul the same as the body?” is a question about the identity of soul and body. When identity is asserted between one thing and another, that very thing is ultimately not found; this is like proclaiming the maternity of a barren woman's son. Therefore, it is said that it is to be set aside as unanswerable. These four ways of answering questions are the standard, for those questions should be answered by that very method.

Vinayamahāpadeso kappiyānulomavidhānato nippariyāyato anulomakappiyaṃ nāma, mahāpadesabhāvena pana taṃsadisatāya suttantamahāpadesesupi “anulomakappiya”nti ayaṃ aṭṭhakathāvohāro. Yadipi tattha tattha bhagavatā pavattitapakiṇṇakadesanāva aṭṭhakathā, sā pana dhammasaṅgāhakehi paṭhamaṃ tīṇi piṭakāni saṅgāyitvā tassa atthavaṇṇanānurūpeneva [M 2.0169] vācanāmaggaṃ āropitattā “ācariyavādo”ti vuccati ācariyā vadanti saṃvaṇṇenti pāḷiṃ etenāti. Tenāha [V 2.0151] “ācariyavādo nāma aṭṭhakathā”ti. Tisso saṅgītiyo āruḷho eva ca buddhavacanassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanābhūto kathāmaggo mahindattherena tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ ābhato pacchā tambapaṇṇiyehi mahātherehi sīhaḷabhāsāya ṭhapito nikāyantaraladdhisaṅkarapariharaṇatthaṃ. Attanomati nāma theravādo. Nayaggāhenāti suttādito labbhamānanayaggahaṇena. Anubuddhiyāti suttādīniyeva anugatabuddhiyā. Attano paṭibhānanti attano eva tassa atthassa vuttanayena upaṭṭhānaṃ, yathāupaṭṭhitā atthā eva tathā vuttā. Samentameva gahetabbanti yathā suttena saṃsandati, evaṃ mahāpadesato atthā uddharitabbāti dasseti. Pamādapāṭhavasena ācariyavādassa kadāci pāḷiyā asaṃsandanāpi siyā, so na gahetabboti dassento āha “ācariyavādopi suttena samentoyeva gahetabbo”ti. Sabbadubbalā puggalassa sayaṃ paṭibhānabhāvato. Tathā ca sāpi gahetabbā, kīdisī? Suttena samentā yevāti yojanā. Tāsūti tīsu saṅgītīsu. “Āgatameva pamāṇa”nti iminā mahākassapādīhi saṅgītameva “sutta”nti idhādhippetanti tadaññassa [P 2.0218] suttabhāvameva paṭikkhipati. Tadatthā eva hi tisso saṅgītiyo. Tatthāti gārayhasutte. Na ceva sutte osaranti, na ca vinaye sandissantīti veditabbāni tassa asuttabhāvato tena “anulomakappiyaṃ suttena samentameva gahetabba”nti vuttaṃ evatthaṃ nigamanavasena nidasseti. Sabbattha “na itara”nti vacanaṃ tattha tattha gahitāvadhāraṇaphaladassanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The Vinaya Great Authority is called “conformable and allowable” because it directly prescribes what is allowable. However, due to its nature as a great authority, this commentarial usage of “conformable and allowable” also applies to the Suttanta Great Authorities due to their similarity. Although the miscellaneous teachings given by the Blessed One here and there are the commentary, yet because the compilers of the Dhamma first recited the three Piṭakas and then established the method of exposition in accordance with their meaning, it is called “the teachers' doctrine”—because the teachers explain and comment upon the Pāli by this. Hence it is said, “The teachers' doctrine is the commentary.” The path of discourse, which serves as the explanation of the meaning of the Buddha’s word and was established in the three recitations, was brought to the island of Tambapaṇṇi by the elder Mahinda. Later, the great elders of Tambapaṇṇi established it in the Sinhalese language to avoid the confusion arising from the doctrines of other schools. “One's own opinion” means the Theravāda. “By grasping the method” means by adopting the method derived from the suttas and so forth. “By following understanding” means by intelligence that follows from the suttas and the like. “One's own inspiration” refers to the presentation of that meaning in the stated way, as it appears—thus the meanings are spoken as they appear. “It should be taken only when consistent” shows that the meaning should be drawn out from the great authorities in such a way that it corresponds with the sutta. Sometimes, due to negligence in reading, the teachers' doctrine may not align with the Pāli; that should not be accepted. To indicate this, it is said, “Even the teachers' doctrine should be taken only when consistent with the sutta.” An individual’s own inspiration is the weakest of all. And even that should be accepted—but of what kind? The explanation is: “Only when consistent with the sutta.” “Among them” means among the three recitations. By “What has come down is the standard,” it is here intended that only what was recited by Mahākassapa and others in the councils is “sutta,” thereby rejecting the status of anything else as sutta. Indeed, the three recitations were for that very purpose. “Here” refers to a blameworthy sutta. It should be understood that they neither conform to the sutta nor are found in the Vinaya—this shows their non-sutta nature. Therefore, it is said, “What is conformable and allowable should be taken only when consistent with the sutta,” thus indicating the conclusion of the meaning here. Everywhere, the statement “not the other” should be seen as showing the result of the determination accepted in each case.

Kammāraputtacundavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Cunda, the Smith's Son

189. Sūkaramaddavanti vanavarāhassa mudumaṃsaṃ. Yasmā cundo ariyasāvako sotāpanno, aññe ca bhagavato, bhikkhusaṅghassa ca āhāraṃ paṭiyādentā anavajjameva paṭiyādenti, tasmā vuttaṃ “pavattamaṃsa”nti. Taṃ kirāti “nātitaruṇassā”tiādinā vuttavisesaṃ. Tathā hi taṃ “mudu ceva siniddhañcā”ti vuttaṃ. Mudumaṃsabhāvato hi abhisaṅkharaṇavisesena ca “maddava”nti vuttaṃ. Ojaṃ pakkhipiṃsu “ayaṃ bhagavato pacchimako āhāro”ti puññavisesāpekkhāya, taṃ pana tathāpakkhittadibbojatāya garutaraṃ jātaṃ.

189. “Sūkaramaddava” means the tender meat of a wild boar. Because Cunda, a noble disciple and stream-enterer, and others preparing food for the Blessed One and the community of monks did so faultlessly, it is called “readily available meat.” That, it is said, refers to the special kind mentioned by “not too young,” etc. Indeed, it was described as “tender and succulent.” Due to its tender nature and special preparation, it is called “maddava.” They infused it with nutritive essence, thinking, “This is the Blessed One’s last meal,” out of a desire for special merit. However, because of the divine nutritive essence thus infused, it became harder to digest.

Aññe [M 2.0170] yaṃ dujjīraṃ, taṃ ajānantā “kassaci adatvā vināsita”nti upavadeyyunti parūpavādamocanatthaṃ bhagavā “nāhaṃ ta”ntiādinā sīhanādaṃ nadati.

Others, not knowing that it was hard to digest, might have accused them, saying, “They destroyed it without giving it to anyone.” To dispel such blame from others, the Blessed One roared the lion's roar, saying, “I do not see…,” etc.

190. Kathaṃ panāyaṃ sīhanādo nanu taṃ bhagavatopi sammāpariṇāmaṃ na gatanti? Nayidaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, yasmā “sammadeva taṃ bhagavato pariṇāmaṃ gata”nti vattuṃ arahati tappaccayā uppannassa [V 2.0152] vikārassa abhāvato, aññapaccayassa ca vikārassa mudubhāvaṃ āpāditattā. Tenāha “na pana bhuttappaccayā”tiādi. Na hi bhagavā, aññe vā pana khīṇāsavā navavedanuppādanavasena āhāraṃ paribhuñjanti aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatameva katvā āhārassa upabhuñjanato. Yadi evaṃ kasmā pāḷiyaṃ “bhattaṃ bhuttāvissa kharo ābādho uppajjī”tiādi vuttaṃ? Taṃ bhojanuttarakālaṃ [P 2.0219] uppannattā vuttaṃ. “Na pana bhuttapaccayā”ti vutto vāyamattho aṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Katupacitassa laddhokāsassa kammassa vasena balavatipi roge uppanne garusiniddhabhojanappaccayā vedanāniggaho jāto, tenāha “yadi hī”tiādi. Patthitaṭṭhāneti icchitaṭṭhāne, icchā cassa tattha gantvā vinetabbaveneyyāpekkhā daṭṭhabbā. Gāthāyampi “suta”nti iminā sutamattaṃ, paresaṃ vacanamattametaṃ, na pana bhojanappaccayā ābādhaṃ phusi dhīroti dasseti.

190. But how is this a lion’s roar? Surely, was it not that the food was not properly digested by the Blessed One? This should not be seen in this way, for it is proper to say that it was indeed rightly digested by the Blessed One, since no disorder arose from that cause, and a disorder from another cause was rendered mild. Therefore, it is said, “Not, however, because of eating,” and so on. For neither the Blessed One nor other Arahants consume food in a way that produces new feelings; rather, they partake of food having made it endowed with the eight factors. If so, why is it stated in the Pāli text, “Having eaten the meal, a severe illness arose,” and so on? That is said because it arose after the meal. This meaning, “Not, however, because of eating,” is stated in the commentary. When, by the force of karma previously accumulated and finding an opportunity, a strong illness arose, the suppression of the feeling occurred because of the heavy, rich food; therefore, it is said, “If indeed,” and so on. ‘At a desired place’ means at a wished-for place, and his wish should be seen as being in consideration of those to be trained by going there. In the verse also, by ‘heard,’ it is shown that this is merely what is heard, merely the words of others, and that the wise one was not afflicted by illness because of the food.

Pānīyāharaṇavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Bringing of Water

191. Pasannabhāvena udakassa acchabhāvo veditabboti āha “acchodakāti pasannodakā”ti. Sādurasattā sātatāti āha “madhurodakā”ti. Tanukameva salilaṃ visesato sītalaṃ, na bahalanti āha “tanusītalasalilā”ti. Nikkaddamāti setabhāvassa kāraṇamāha. Paṅkacikkhallādivasena hi udakassa vivaṇṇatā, sabhāvato pana taṃ setavaṇṇaṃ evāti.

191. By 'purity,' the clarity of the water should be understood; thus it is said: 'clear water means pure water.' Because of its pleasant taste and continuous nature, it is said: 'sweet water.' The water is indeed thin and especially cool, not thick; thus it is said: 'thin, cool water.' 'Free from mud' states the reason for its whiteness. For water becomes discolored due to mud, mire, etc., but by nature it is indeed white in color.

Pukkusamallaputtavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Account of Pukkusa, the Malla's Son

192. Dhuravāteti paṭimukhavāte. Dīghapiṅgaloti dīgho hutvā piṅgalacakkhuko. Piṅgalakkhiko hi so “āḷāro”ti paññāyittha. Evarūpanti dakkhati karissati bhavissatīti īdisaṃ. Īdisesūti yatra yaṃcāti evarūpanipātasaddayuttaṭṭhānesu.

192. 'In a headwind' means 'against the wind.' 'Tall and tawny-eyed' means 'being tall, with tawny eyes.' Indeed, he was known as 'Āḷāra' because he had tawny eyes. 'Of such a kind' means 'of this sort,' referring to what one will see, do, or become. 'In such cases' refers to places connected with such particles as 'yatra' and 'yaṃ ca'.

193. Vicarantiyo [M 2.0171] meghagabbhato niccharantiyo viya hontīti vuttaṃ “niccharantīsūti vicarantīsū”ti. Navavidhāyāti navappakārāya. Navasu hi pakāresu ekavidhāpi asani tappariyāpannatāya “navavidhā” tveva vuccati. Īdisī hi esā ruḷhi aṭṭhavimokkhapattipi samaññā viya. Asaññaṃ karoti, yo tassā saddena[P 2.0220], tejasā ca ajjhotthaṭo. Ekaṃ cakkanti ekaṃ maṇḍalaṃ. Saṅkāraṃ tīrentī paricchijjantī viya dassetīti saterā.
