Gaggarāyamānāti gaggarātisaddaṃ karontī, anuravadassanañhetaṃ. Kapisīsāti kapisīsākāravatī. Macchavilolikāti [V 2.0153] udake paripphandamānamaccho viya viluḷitākārā. Kukkuṭasadisāti pasāritapakkhakukkuṭākārā. Naṅgalassa kassanakāle kassakānaṃ hatthena gahetabbaṭṭhāne maṇikā hoti, taṃ upādāya naṅgalaṃ “daṇḍamaṇikā”ti vuccati, tasmā daṇḍamaṇikākārā daṇḍamaṇikā. Tenāha “naṅgalasadisā”ti. Deve vassantepi sajotibhūtatāya udakena atemetabbato mahāsani “sukkhāsanī”ti vuttā. Tenāha “patitaṭṭhānaṃ samugghāṭetī”ti.

193. Because they wander as if emerging from the womb of a cloud, it is said: 'niccharantīsu' means 'vicarantīsu'. 'Of nine kinds' means of nine types. Indeed, although lightning is of one kind among nine types, because it is included therein, it is called 'ninefold'. This is indeed such a conventional usage, like the designation for one who has attained the eight liberations. It renders senseless one who is overwhelmed by its sound and its power. 'One wheel' means one circle. 'Saterā' means that which appears as if cutting through and severing a rubbish heap. 'Roaring' means making a rumbling sound; this is to show its reverberation. 'Kapisīsā' means having the shape of a monkey’s head. 'Macchavilolikā' means having a twisting shape like a fish writhing in water. 'Kukkuṭasadisā' means having the shape of a rooster with spread wings. At the time of plowing, there is a knob at the part of the plow to be held by the farmers' hands; on account of this, the plow is called 'daṇḍamaṇikā'. Therefore, 'daṇḍamaṇikā' means having the shape of a daṇḍamaṇikā. Hence it is said: 'like a plow'. Even when the sky rains, because it is fiery and cannot be soaked by water, the great lightning is called 'dry lightning'. Hence it is said: 'it tears up the place where it strikes'.

Bhusāgāraketi bhusamaye agārake. Tattha kira mahantaṃ palālapuñjaṃ abbhantarato palālaṃ nikkaḍḍhitvā sālāsadisaṃ pabbajitānaṃ vasanayoggaṭṭhānaṃ kataṃ, tadā bhagavā tattha vasi, taṃ pana khalamaṇḍalaṃ sālāsadisanti āha “khalasālāya”nti. Etthāti hetumhi bhummavacananti āha “etasmiṃ kāraṇe”ti, asanipātena channaṃ janānaṃ hatakāraṇeti attho. So tvaṃ bhanteti ayameva vā pāṭho.

'In the Bhusāgāraka' means in a house at the time of much straw. There, it is said, from a large pile of straw, the straw was pulled out from the inside and a place suitable for renunciants to live, resembling a hall, was made. At that time, the Blessed One stayed there. That threshing floor, resembling a hall, is what is meant by 'in the threshing-hall'. 'Ettha' is a locative used in the sense of cause; thus it is said 'for this reason', meaning, for the reason that six people were killed by a lightning strike. 'So tvaṃ bhante' is an alternative reading.

194. Siṅgī nāma kira uttamaṃ ativiya pabhassaraṃ buddhānaṃ chavivaṇṇobhāsaṃ devalokato āgatasuvaṇṇaṃ. Tenevāha “siṅgīsuvaṇṇavaṇṇa”nti. “Kiṃ pana thero taṃ gaṇhī”ti sayameva pucchaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā tattha kāraṇaṃ dassento “kiñcāpī”tiādimāha. Teneva kāraṇenāti upaṭṭhākaṭṭhānassa matthakappatti, paresaṃ [P 2.0221] vacanokāsapacchedanaṃ, tena vatthena satthu pūjanaṃ, satthu ajjhāsayānuvattananti iminā teneva yathāvuttena catubbidhena kāraṇena.

194. Siṅgī, it is said, is the name for the finest gold, exceedingly radiant, with a lustre like the complexion of the Buddhas, which comes from the deva world. Hence it is said: 'the color of siṅgī gold'. Raising the question himself, 'But did the elder take it?', he then shows the reason, beginning with 'kiñcāpi'. 'For that very reason' means: for that same fourfold reason as stated, namely: reaching the pinnacle of the position of attendant, cutting off others' opportunity to speak, honoring the Teacher with that cloth, and acting in accordance with the Teacher's intention.

195. Thero ca tāvadeva taṃ siṅgīvaṇṇaṃ maṭṭhadussaṃ bhagavato upanāmesi “paṭiggaṇhatu me bhante bhagavā imaṃ maṭṭhadussaṃ, taṃ mamassa dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti. Paṭiggahesi bhagavā, paṭiggahetvāva naṃ paribhuñji[M 2.0172]. Tena vuttaṃ “bhagavāpi tato ekaṃ nivāsesi, ekaṃ pārupī”ti. Tāvadeva kira taṃ bhikkhū ovaṭṭikaraṇamattena tunnakammaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā therassa upanesuṃ, thero bhagavato upanāmesi. Hataccikaṃ viyāti paṭihatappabhaṃ, viya-saddo nipātamattaṃ. Bhagavato hi sarīrappabhāhi abhibhuyyamānā tassa vatthayugassa pabhassaratā nāhosi. Antantenevāti anto anto eva, abbhantarato evāti attho. Tenāha “bahipanassa pabhā natthī”ti.

195. Then the elder immediately offered that siṅgī-colored soft cloth to the Blessed One, saying, 'Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept this soft cloth from me; may this be for my long-term welfare and happiness.' The Blessed One accepted it, and having accepted it, he used it. Therefore, it is said: 'The Blessed One then wore one as an undergarment and one as an upper robe.' At that very moment, it is said, the monks, having completed the sewing work merely by making a hem, presented it to the elder, and the elder offered it to the Blessed One. 'Hataccikaṃ viya' means its radiance was subdued; the word 'viya' is merely a particle. For the radiance of that pair of cloths did not appear, being overwhelmed by the radiance of the Blessed One’s body. 'Antanteneva' means only inside, only within; that is, only on the inside. Hence it is said: 'There was no radiance on its outside'.

“Pasannarūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpetī”ti etenetassa āhārassa bhuttappaccayā na so rogoti ayamattho dīpito. Dvīsu kālesu evaṃ hoti dvinnaṃ nibbānadhātūnaṃ samadhigamasamayabhāvato. Upavattane antarena yamakasālānanti ettha vattabbaṃ parato āgamissati.

By 'it produces a clear appearance', the meaning is shown that that illness was not caused by the food he had eaten. This occurs at two times, because they are the occasions for the attainment of the two Nibbāna-elements. Regarding 'in Upavattana, between the twin sāla trees', what is to be said on this will come later.

196. Sabbaṃ [V 2.0154] suvaṇṇavaṇṇameva ahosi ativiya parisuddhāya pabhassarāya ekagghanāya bhagavato sarīrappabhāya nirantaraṃ abhibhūtattā.

196. Everything appeared as if made of gold, because it was continuously overwhelmed by the exceedingly pure, radiant, and uniform radiance of the Blessed One’s body.

Dhammeti pariyattidhamme. Pavattāti pāvacanabhāvena desetā. Puratova nisīdi ovādappaṭikaraṇabhāvato.

'Dhammaṃ' means the scriptural teaching. 'Pavattā' means an expounder, in the sense of the Teaching. He sat right in front because it was an occasion for receiving advice and instruction.

197. Dānānisaṃsasaṅkhātā [P 2.0222] lābhāti vaṇṇadānabaladānādibhedā dānassa ānisaṃsasaññitā diṭṭhadhammikā, samparāyikā ca lābhā icchitabbā. Te alābhāti te sabbe tuyhaṃ alābhā, lābhā eva na honti. Diṭṭheva dhamme paccakkhabhūte imasmiṃyeva attabhāve bhavā diṭṭhadhammikā. Samparetabbato pecca gantabbato “samparāyo”ti laddhanāme paraloke bhavā samparāyikā. Diṭṭhadhammikā ca samparāyikā ca diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikā. Dānānisaṃsasaṅkhātā lābhāti dānānisaṃsabhūtā lābhā. Sabbathā samameva hutvā samaṃ phalaṃ etesaṃ na ekadesenāti samasamaphalā. Piṇḍapātāti tabbisayaṃ dānamayaṃ puññamāha.

197. 'Gains known as the benefits of giving' means: the immediate and future gains, designated as the benefits of giving—differentiated as the gift of beauty, the gift of strength, and so on—which are to be desired. 'Te alābhā' means all those are non-gains for you; they are not gains at all. 'Diṭṭhadhammikā' are those that exist in this very life, in this very existence which is directly visible in the present. 'Samparāyikā' are those that exist in the next world, which has gained the name 'samparāya' because it is to be gone to, to be reached after death. 'Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikā' means both immediate and future. 'Gains known as the benefits of giving' means gains that constitute the benefits of giving. 'Samasamaphalā' means having equal fruit, because their fruit is entirely equal in every way, not just in part. 'Piṇḍapātā' refers to the merit consisting of giving related to that.

Yadi khettavasena nesaṃ samaphalatā adhippetā, satipi ekasantānabhāve puthujjanaarahantabhāvasiddhaṃ nanu tesaṃ khettaṃ visiṭṭhanti dassetuṃ “nanu cā”tiādimāha. Parinibbānasamatāyāti kilesaparinibbānakhandhaparinibbānabhāvena parinibbānasamatāya. “Paribhuñjitvā parinibbuto”ti etena [M 2.0173] yathā paṇītapiṇḍapātaparibhogūpatthambhitarūpakāyasannissayo dhammakāyo sukheneva kilese pariccaji, bhojanasappāyasaṃsiddhiyā evaṃ sukheneva khandhe pariccajīti evaṃ kilesapariccāgassa, khandhapariccāgassa ca sukhasiddhinimittatāya ubhinnaṃ piṇḍapātānaṃ samaphalatā jotitā. “Piṇḍapātasīsena ca piṇḍapātadānaṃ jotita”nti vutto vāyamattho. Yathā hi sujātāya “imaṃ āhāraṃ nissāya mayhaṃ devatāya vaṇṇasukhabalādiguṇā sammadeva sampajjeyyu”nti uḷāro ajjhāsayo tadā ahosi, evaṃ cundassapi kammāraputtassa “imaṃ āhāraṃ nissāya bhagavato vaṇṇasukhabalādiguṇā sammadeva sampajjeyyu”nti uḷāro ajjhāsayoti evampi nesaṃ ubhinnaṃ samaphalatā veditabbā. Satipi catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasamāpattīnaṃ devasikaṃ vaḷañjanasamāpattibhāve yathā pana abhisambujjhanadivase abhinavavipassanaṃ paṭṭhapento rūpasattakādi (visuddhi. ṭī. 2.707 vitthāro) vasena cuddasahākārehi [P 2.0223] sannetvā mahāvipassanāmukhena tā samāpattiyo samāpajji, evaṃ parinibbānadivasepi sabbā tā samāpajjīti evaṃ samāpattisamatāyapi tesaṃ samaphalatā. Cundassa tāva anussaraṇaṃ uḷārataraṃ hotu bhagavato dinnabhāvena aññathattābhāvato, sujātāya pana [V 2.0155] kathaṃ devatāya dinnanti? Evaṃsaññibhāvatoti āha “sujātā cā”tiādi. Aparabhāgeti abhisambodhito aparabhāge. Puna aparabhāgeti parinibbānato parato. Dhammasīsanti dhammānaṃ matthakabhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ. Me gahitanti mama vasena gahitaṃ. Tenāha “mayhaṃ kirā”tiādi.

If their equal fruitfulness is intended in terms of the field, then even in the case of a single continuum, since the state of an ordinary person and an Arahant is established, to show that their field is superior, he says, beginning with 'Is it not so?' (nanu ca). `By the equality of final Nibbāna` means by the equality of final Nibbāna through the final Nibbāna of defilements and the final Nibbāna of aggregates. By `having partaken, he attained final Nibbāna`, it is shown that just as the Dhamma-body, supported by the physical body sustained by partaking of excellent almsfood, easily relinquished defilements, and by the perfection of suitable food, easily relinquished the aggregates, so too, the equal fruitfulness of both alms-offerings is illuminated by being a sign of the easy accomplishment of relinquishing defilements and relinquishing aggregates. `The gift of alms is illuminated by the foremost alms-offering`—this is the intended meaning. Just as Sujātā at that time had the noble aspiration, 'By means of this food, may the qualities of beauty, happiness, strength, and so on, arise perfectly for my deity,' so too, Cunda the blacksmith’s son had the noble aspiration, 'By means of this food, may the qualities of beauty, happiness, strength, and so on, arise perfectly for the Blessed One.' Thus, the equal fruitfulness of both should be understood in this way as well. Furthermore, even though there were daily attainments amounting to twenty-four hundred thousand crores, just as on the day of his full awakening, while establishing fresh insight, he entered those attainments through fourteen modes by way of the sevenfold contemplation of form and so on (the details are in Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā 2.707), by means of the great insight, so too, on the day of his final Nibbāna, he entered all those attainments; thus, their equal fruitfulness is also due to the equality of attainments. For Cunda, the recollection is more sublime because it was given to the Blessed One and because of its unalterable nature. But how is it for Sujātā, since it was given to a deity? Because she had such a perception, he says, beginning with `Sujātā too`. `In the later part` means in the part after full awakening. `Again, in the later part` means after the final Nibbāna. `The head of the Dhamma` means Nibbāna, which is the pinnacle of dhammas. `Taken by me` means taken by my power. Therefore, he says, beginning with `For me, indeed`.

Adhipatibhāvo ādhipateyyanti āha “jeṭṭhabhāvasaṃvattaniyaka”nti.

`The state of being a chief` is `overlordship`. He says: `that which conduces to the condition of being the eldest`.

Saṃvareti sīlasaṃvare. Veranti pāṇātipātādipañcavidhaṃ veraṃ. Tañhi veridhammabhāvato, verahetutāya ca “vera”nti vuccati. Kosallaṃ vuccati ñāṇaṃ, tena yutto kusaloti āha “kusalo pana ñāṇasampanno”ti. Ñāṇasampadā nāma ñāṇapāripūrī, sā ca aggamaggavasena veditabbā, aggamaggo ca niravasesato kilese pajahatīti āha “ariyamaggena…pe… jahātī”ti. Imaṃ pāpakaṃ jahitvāti dānena tāva lobhamacchariyādipāpakaṃ, sīlena pāṇātipātādipāpakaṃ jahitvā tadaṅgavasena pahāya tato samathavipassanādhammehi vikkhambhanavasena, tato maggapaṭipāṭiyā samucchedavasena anavasesaṃ pāpakaṃ pahāya. Tathā [M 2.0174] pahīnattā eva rāgādīnaṃ khayā kilesanibbānena sabbaso kilesavūpasamena nibbuto parinibbutoti saupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā desanāya kūṭaṃ gaṇhanto “iti cundassa…pe… sampassamāno udānaṃ udānesī”ti.

`In restraint` means in the restraint of morality. `Enmity` means the fivefold enmity, such as killing living beings. For it has the nature of enmity and is the cause of enmity, and is therefore called 'enmity.' Skill is called knowledge; one endowed with that is called 'skilled,' hence it is said, 'a skilled one is endowed with knowledge.' The endowment of knowledge is the perfection of knowledge, and that should be understood in terms of the highest path; and the highest path abandons defilements without remainder, hence it is said, 'by the noble path... he abandons.' `Having abandoned this evil` means: having first abandoned evil such as greed and stinginess by means of giving, and evil such as killing living beings by means of morality—abandoning them by substitution of opposites; then by the qualities of serenity and insight, by way of suppression; and then, by the sequence of the path, by way of eradication, abandoning evil completely without remainder. Thus, because of having been so abandoned, through the destruction of lust and so on, through the Nibbāna of defilements, by the complete pacification of all defilements, he is extinguished, fully extinguished. Grasping the pinnacle of this teaching on the Nibbāna element with residue, he said: "thus, Cunda... clearly seeing, uttered this inspired utterance."

Catutthabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the fourth section for recitation is finished.

Yamakasālavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Twin Sāla Trees

198. Evaṃ [P 2.0224] taṃ kusinārāyaṃ hotīti yathā anurādhapurassa thūpārāmo dakkhiṇapacchimadisāyaṃ, evaṃ taṃ uyyānaṃ kusinārāya dakkhiṇapacchimadisāyaṃ hoti. Tasmāti yasmā nagaraṃ pavisitukāmā uyyānato upecca vattanti gacchanti etenāti “upavattana”nti vuccati, taṃ sālapantibhāvena ṭhitaṃ sālavanaṃ. Antarenāti vemajjhe. Tassa kira mañcakassāti tattha paññapiyamānassa tassa mañcakassa. Tatrāpi…pe… eko pādabhāgassa, tasmā “antarena yamakasālāna”nti vuttaṃ. Saṃsibbitvāti aññamaññaāsattaviṭapasākhatāya saṃsibbitvā viya. “Ṭhitasākhā”tipi vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Yaṃ pana pāḷiyaṃ “uttarasīsakaṃ mañcakaṃ [V 2.0156] paññapehī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ pacchimadassanaṃ daṭṭhuṃ āgatānaṃ devatānaṃ daṭṭhuṃ yogyatāvasena vuttaṃ. Keci pana “uttaradisāvilokanamukhaṃ pubbadisāsīsakaṃ katvā mañcakaṃ paññapehīti attho”ti vadanti, taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ.

198. Thus, it was in Kusinārā—just as the Thūpārāma is to the southwest of Anurādhapura, so was that park to the southwest of Kusinārā. `Therefore` means because those who wished to enter the city approached and proceeded from the park, it is called 'Upavattana.' It was a sāla grove, standing as a row of sāla trees. `Between` means in the very middle. `Of that very couch` means of that couch being prepared there. Even there... one part was for the feet, hence it is said, 'between the Twin Sāla Trees.' `Intertwined` means as if intertwined due to the branches and foliage clinging to one another. 'Standing branches' is also mentioned in the commentary. However, in the Pāli text, it is said, 'prepare the couch with the head to the north,' which was spoken for the sake of suitability for the deities who came to see the final sight. Some, however, say, 'the meaning is to prepare the couch facing the northern direction with the head to the east,' but that is merely their opinion.

Ete nāgānamuttamāti ete gottato gocariādināmakā hatthināgesu balena seṭṭhatamā. Majjhimaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.148) pana keci hatthino ito aññathā āgatā, so pana nesaṃ nāmamattakato bhedo daṭṭhabbo.

`These are the best of nāgas` means these, named according to their lineage, range, and so on, are the foremost among elephant nāgas in strength. In the Majjhima commentary, however, some elephants are described differently, but this should be seen as merely a difference in name.

Paribhuttakālato paṭṭhāya…pe… parikkhayaṃ gataṃ, “na pana paribhuttappaccayā”ti heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva attho daṭṭhabbo. Caṅgavāreti ūmiyaṃ. Katokāsassa kammassa vasena yathāsamuṭṭhito rogo ārogyaṃ abhimaddatīti katvā etamatthaṃ dassento “viyā”ti vuttaṃ. Yasmā bhagavā heṭṭhā vuttanayena [P 2.0225] kappaṃ, kappāvasesaṃ vā ṭhātuṃ samattho eva, tattakaṃ kālaṃ [M 2.0175] ṭhāne payojanābhāvato āyusaṅkhāre ossajjitvā tādisassa kammassa okāsaṃ adāsi, tasmā etamatthaṃ dassento “viyā”tipi vattuṃ yujjatiyeva.

From the time it was consumed... until it was exhausted, the meaning of 'but not because of being consumed' should be understood in the same way as stated below. `Caṅgavāre` means in a wave. To illustrate this meaning, 'like' is said, because an illness arising due to a deed that has found its opportunity crushes health. Because the Blessed One, as explained below, was indeed capable of lasting for an aeon or the remainder of an aeon, but relinquished the life-sustaining formations and gave an opportunity to such a deed since there was no need to remain for that long, therefore it is indeed fitting to say 'like' to illustrate this meaning.

Kusalaṃ kātabbaṃ maññissanti “evaṃ mahapphalaṃ, evaṃ mahānisaṃsaṃ, mahānubhāvañca taṃ kusala”nti.

They will think, 'Merit should be done, for that merit is of such great fruit, such great benefit, and great power.'

Ekassāpi sattassa vaṭṭadukkhavūpasamo buddhānaṃ garutaro hutvā upaṭṭhāti atidullabhabhāvato, tasmā “aparampi passatī”tiādi vuttaṃ, svāyamattho māgaṇḍiyasuttena (su. ni. 841) dīpetabbo.

The pacification of the suffering of the round for even a single being is presented to the Buddhas as more important, owing to its extreme rarity. Therefore, it is said, 'He sees even another,' and so on. This meaning should be illustrated by the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta (Snp 4.9).

Tatiyaṃ pana kāraṇaṃ sattānaṃ uppajjanakaanatthapariharaṇanti taṃ dassento puna “aparampi passatī”tiādimāha.

Furthermore, the third reason is the avoidance of harm arising for beings. To show this, he again says, 'He sees even another...'

Sīhaseyyanti. Ettha sayanaṃ seyyā, sīhassa viya seyyā sīhaseyyā, taṃ sīhaseyyaṃ. Atha vā sīhaseyyanti seṭṭhaseyyaṃ, yadidaṃ atthadvayaṃ parato āgamissati.

`The lion's posture.` Here, lying down is `seyyā`; a posture like a lion's is `sīhaseyyā`, that is, the lion's posture. Alternatively, `sīhaseyyā` means the superior posture. These two meanings will be forthcoming.

“Vāmena passena sentī”ti evaṃ vuttā kāmabhogiseyyā, dakkhiṇapassena sayāno nāma natthi dakkhiṇahatthassa sarīraggahaṇādiyogakkhamato, purisavasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ.

The posture of one who enjoys sensual pleasures is described thus: 'they lie on the left side.' There is no such thing as lying on the right side, because the right hand is suitable for tasks such as grasping the body. And this is stated from the perspective of a man.

Ekena [V 2.0157] passena sayituṃ na sakkonti dukkhuppattito.

They are not able to lie on one side due to the arising of suffering.

Ayaṃ sīhaseyyāti ayaṃ evaṃ vuttā sīhaseyyā. “Tejussadattā”ti iminā sīhassa abhīrubhāvaṃ dasseti. Bhīrukā hi sesamigā attano āsayaṃ pavisitvā santāsapubbakaṃ yathā tathā sayanti, sīho pana abhīrubhāvato satokārī bhikkhu viya satiṃ upaṭṭhāpetvāva sayati. Tenāha “purimapāde”tiādi. Dakkhiṇe purimapāde vāmassa purimapādassa ṭhapanavasena dve purimapāde ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapetvā. Pacchimapādeti dve pacchimapāde. Vuttanayeneva idhāpi ekasmiṃ ṭhāne pādaṭṭhapanaṃ veditabbaṃ, ṭhitokāsasallakkhaṇaṃ abhīrubhāveneva. “Sīsaṃ pana ukkhipitvā”tiādinā vuttā sīhakiriyā anutrāsapabujjhanaṃ [P 2.0226] viya abhīrubhāvasiddhā dhammatāvasenevāti veditabbā. Sīhavijambhitavijambhanaṃ ativelaṃ ekākārena ṭhapitānaṃ sarīrāvayavānaṃ gamanādikiriyāsu yogyabhāvāpādanatthaṃ. Tikkhattuṃ sīhanādanadanaṃ appesakkhamigajātapariharaṇatthaṃ.

This is the lion's posture; thus it is called the lion's posture. 'Tejussadattā' indicates the lion's fearlessness. For other timid animals, having entered their lairs, lie down in any which way, preceded by terror; but the lion, on account of its fearlessness, lies down having established mindfulness, like a mindful monk. Therefore it is said, 'with the forefeet,' and so on. Having placed the two forefeet in one place by placing the left forefoot on the right forefoot. The hind feet means the two hind feet. Here too, the placing of the feet in one place should be understood in the way stated; the marking of the place where it lies is due to its fearlessness. The lion's action stated by 'having lifted its head,' and so on, like awakening without alarm, should be understood as being by way of its nature, accomplished through fearlessness. The lion's stretching is for the purpose of making the limbs of the body, which have been kept in one posture for a very long time, fit for actions such as walking. The roaring of the lion's roar three times is for the purpose of driving away the kinds of animals of little power.

Seti [M 2.0176] abyāvaṭabhāvena pavattati etthāti seyyā, catutthajjhānameva seyyā catutthajjhānaseyyā. Kiṃ pana taṃ catutthajjhānanti? Ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ, tato hi vuṭṭhahitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā bhagavā anukkamena aggamaggaṃ adhigantvā tathāgato jātoti. “Tayidaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ nāma, na seyyā, tathāpi yasmā ‘catutthajjhānā vuṭṭhahitvā samanantarā bhagavā parinibbāyī’ti (dī. ni. 2.219) vakkhati, tasmā lokiyacatutthajjhānasamāpatti eva tathāgataseyyā”ti keci, evaṃ sati parinibbānakālikāva tathāgataseyyāti āpajjati, na ca bhagavā lokiyacatutthajjhānasamāpajjanabahulo vihāsi. Aggaphalavasena pavattaṃ panettha catutthajjhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tattha yathā sattānaṃ niddupagamanalakkhaṇā seyyā bhavaṅgacittavasena hoti, sā ca nesaṃ paṭhamajātisamanvayā yebhuyyavuttikā, evaṃ bhagavato ariyajātisamanvayaṃ yebhuyyavuttikaṃ aggaphalabhūtaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ “tathāgataseyyā”ti veditabbaṃ. Sīhaseyyā nāma seṭṭhaseyyāti āha “uttamaseyyā”ti.

One lies down (seti) herein, it proceeds in a state of non-busyness; thus it is a posture (seyyā). The fourth jhāna itself is the posture, the fourth jhāna posture. But what is that fourth jhāna? The fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing. For, having emerged from that, the Blessed One developed insight and gradually attained the supreme path, thus becoming the Tathāgata. Some say: 'This is a basis, not a posture. Yet, because it will be said, “Having emerged from the fourth jhāna, the Blessed One immediately attained final Nibbāna,” therefore the attainment of the mundane fourth jhāna is the Tathāgata’s posture.' If this were so, it would follow that the Tathāgata's posture is only at the time of final Nibbāna; but the Blessed One did not dwell frequently attaining the mundane fourth jhāna. Here, the fourth jhāna should be understood as that which occurs by way of the supreme fruit. Just as for beings, the posture characterized by falling asleep occurs by way of the life-continuum consciousness, and that for them is generally connected with their first birth, so too for the Blessed One, the fourth jhāna which is connected with the noble birth, generally occurs as the supreme fruit, and should be understood as the 'Tathāgata’s posture.' The lion’s posture is the foremost posture; therefore it is said, 'the highest posture.'

Natthi etissā uṭṭhānanti anuṭṭhānā, seyyā, taṃ anuṭṭhānaseyyaṃ. “Ito uṭṭhahissāmī”ti manasikārassa abhāvato “uṭṭhānasaññaṃ manasi karitvā”ti na vuttaṃ. Etthāti etasmiṃ anuṭṭhānaseyyupagamane. Kāyavasena anuṭṭhānaṃ, na cittavasena, cittavasena ca anuṭṭhānaṃ nāma niddupagamananti [P 2.0227] tadabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “niddāvasenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bhavaṅgassāti niddupagamanalakkhaṇassa bhavaṅgassa.

There is no rising from it, thus it is a non-rising posture; that is the non-rising posture. Because of the absence of the mental act, 'I will rise from this,' it is not said, 'having brought to mind the perception of rising.' 'Herein' means in this undertaking of the non-rising posture. The non-rising is by way of the body, not by way of the mind; and non-rising by way of the mind is called falling asleep. To show the absence of that, it is said, 'by way of sleep,' and so on. 'Of the bhavaṅga' means of the bhavaṅga which is characterized by falling asleep.

Sabbapāliphullāti [V 2.0158] sabbatthakameva vikasanavasena phullā, na ekadesavikasanavasena. Tenāha “sabbe samantato pupphitā”ti. Ekacchannāti samphullapupphehi ekākārena sabbattheva chāditā. Ullokapadumānīti heṭṭhā olokentāni viya tiṭṭhanapadumāni. Morapiñchakalāpo viya pañcavaṇṇapupphasañchāditattā.

'Fully blossomed' means blossomed completely in every way, not by way of partial blossoming. Therefore, it is said, 'all fully blossomed all around.' 'Single-canopied' means covered entirely everywhere in a uniform manner by fully blossomed flowers. 'Looking-down lotuses' means lotuses standing as if looking downward. Like a peacock's tail-feather plume, because of being covered with flowers of five colors.

Nandapokkharaṇīsambhavānīti nandapokkharaṇītīrasambhavāni. Mahātumbamattanti āḷhakamattaṃ. Paviṭṭhānīti khittāni. Sarīrameva okirantīti sarīrameva ajjhokiranti.

'Born from Nanda's lotus pond' means born from the bank of Nanda's lotus pond. 'As large as a great gourd' means an āḷhaka in measure. 'Entered' means thrown. 'Sprinkling the body' means completely covering the body.

Devatānaṃ [M 2.0177] upakappanacandanacuṇṇānīti saṭṭhipi paññāsampi yojanāni vāyanakasetavaṇṇacandanacuṇṇāni. Dibbagandhajālacuṇṇānīti dibbagandhadibbacuṇṇāni. Haritālaañjanacuṇṇādīnipi dibbāni paramasugandhāni evāti veditabbāni. Tenevāha “sabbadibbagandhavāsavikatiyo”ti.

'Sandalwood powder prepared for the deities' means sandalwood powders, sixty or even fifty yojanas in extent, white in color like woven cloth. 'Powders of a net of divine fragrances' means divine fragrances and divine powders. Powders of yellow orpiment, collyrium, and so on, should also be understood as divine and supremely fragrant. Therefore it is said, 'all varieties of divine fragrances and perfumes.'

Ekacakkavāḷe sannipatitvā antalikkhe vajjanti mahābhinikkhamanakāle viya.

Having assembled in a single world-system, they resound in the sky, as at the time of the Great Renunciation.

Tāti devatā. Ganthamānā vāti mālaṃ racantiyo eva. Apariniṭṭhitā vāti yathādhippāyaṃ pariyositā eva. Hatthena hatthanti attano hatthena parassa hatthaṃ. Gīvāya gīvanti kaṇṭhagāhavasena attano gīvāya parassa gīvaṃ. Gahetvāti āmasitvā. Mahāyaso mahāyasoti āmeḍitavasena aññamaññaṃ ālāpavacanaṃ.

'They' means the deities. 'While weaving' means simply fashioning a garland. 'Unfinished' means completed as intended. 'Hand to hand' means one's own hand to another's hand. 'Neck to neck' means, by way of seizing the neck, one's own neck to another's neck. 'Having seized' means having touched. 'O great glory, great glory' is a mutual address by way of repetition.

199. Mahantaṃ ussāhanti tathāgatassa pūjāsakkāravasena pavattiyamānaṃ mahantaṃ ussāhaṃ disvā.

199. 'A great effort' refers to seeing the great effort proceeding by way of honor and veneration for the Tathāgata.

Sāyeva [P 2.0228] pana paṭipadāti pubbabhāgapaṭipadā eva. Anucchavikattāti adhigantabbassa navavidhalokuttaradhammassa anurūpattā.

'But that very practice' means the preliminary practice. 'Due to its suitability' means due to its fitness for the ninefold supramundane Dhamma that is to be attained.

Sīlanti cārittasīlamāha. Ācārapaññattīti cārittasīlaṃ. Yāva gotrabhutoti yāva gotrabhuñāṇaṃ, tāva pavattetabbā samathavipassanā sammāpaṭipadā. Idāni taṃ sammāpaṭipadaṃ byatirekato, anvayato ca vibhāvetuṃ “tasmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Jinakāḷasuttanti jinamahāvaḍḍhakinā ṭhapitaṃ vajjetabbagahetabbadhammasandassanakāḷasuttaṃ sikkhāpadamariyādaṃ, upāsakopāsikāvāresu [V 2.0159] “gandhapūjaṃ mālāpūjaṃ karotī”ti vacanaṃ cārittasīlapakkhe ṭhapetvā karaṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, tena bhikkhubhikkhunīnampi tathākaraṇaṃ anuññātamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Conduct' means morality of practice. 'The regulation of behavior' means morality of practice. 'Until the state of change-of-lineage' means until the change-of-lineage knowledge; up to that point, the right practice of serenity and insight should be developed. Now, to explain that right practice both by way of contrast and in accordance, the passage beginning with 'therefore' was stated. 'The Jina's measuring line' means the disciplinary rule, the standard of training, established by the Jina, the great carpenter, which shows qualities to be avoided and qualities to be adopted. In the cases of laymen and laywomen, the statement 'performs perfume offerings and garland offerings' was stated in reference to the performance, having placed it on the side of morality of practice. Therefore, it should be understood that monks and nuns are also permitted to do so.

Ayañhīti dhammānudhammapaṭipadaṃ sandhāya vadati.

'This indeed' he speaks, referring to the practice in accordance with the Dhamma.

Upavāṇattheravaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Elder Upavāṇa

200. Apanesīti ṭhitappadesato yathā apagacchati, evamakāsi, na pana nibbhacchi. Tenāha “ānando”tiādi. Vuttasadisā vāti samacittapariyāyadesanāyaṃ (a. ni. 2.37) vuttasadisā eva. Āvārentoti chādento.

200. 'He removed him' means he acted in such a way that he departed from his standing place, but he did not rebuke him. Therefore, it is said, 'Ānanda,' and so on. 'Similar to what was said' means just as it was said in the discourse on the topic of a balanced mind (Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.37). 'Obstructing' means covering.

Yasmā [M 2.0178] kassapassabuddhassa cetiye ārakkhadevatā ahosi, tasmā therova tejussado, na aññe arahantoti ānetvā yojanā.

Because he was the guardian deity at the shrine of the Buddha Kassapa, therefore the elder alone possessed such radiant power, not other arahants—this is the connection to be made.

Idāni āgamanato paṭṭhāya tamatthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “vipassimhi kira sammāsambuddhe”tiādi āraddhaṃ. “Cātumahārājikā devatā”ti idaṃ gobalībaddañāyena gahetabbaṃ bhummadevatādīnampi tappariyāpannattā. Tesaṃ manussānaṃ.

Now, from the arrival onwards, to explain that matter in detail, the passage beginning with 'In the time of the Fully Enlightened One Vipassī' was begun. 'The deities of the Four Great Kings'—this should be understood by the maxim of the ox and bullock, as earth deities and others are also included under that category. Of those humans.

Tatthāti kassapassa bhagavato cetiye.

'There' means at the shrine of the Blessed One Kassapa.

201. Adhivāsentīti rocenti.

201. 'They consent' means they approve.

Chinnapāto viya chinnapāto, taṃ chinnapātaṃ, [P 2.0229] bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso yaṃ. Āvaṭṭantīti abhimukhabhāvena vaṭṭanti. Yattha patitā, tato katipayaratanaṭṭhānaṃ vaṭṭanavaseneva gantvā puna yathāpatitameva ṭhānaṃ vaṭṭanavasena āgacchanti. Tenāha “āvaṭṭantiyo patitaṭṭhānameva āgacchantī”ti. Vivaṭṭantīti yattha patitā, tato vinivaṭṭanti. Tenāha “patitaṭṭhānato parabhāgaṃ vaṭṭamānā gacchantī”ti. Purato vaṭṭanaṃ āvaṭṭanaṃ, itaraṃ tividhampi vivaṭṭananti dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Devatā dhāretuṃ na sakkoti udakaṃ viya osīdanato. Tenāha “tatthā”tiādi. Tatthāti pakatipathaviyaṃ. Devatā osīdanti dhātūnaṃ saṇhasukhumālabhāvato. Pathaviyaṃ [V 2.0160] pathaviṃ māpesunti pakatipathaviyaṃ attano sarīraṃ dhāretuṃ samatthaṃ iddhānubhāvena pathaviṃ māpesuṃ.

‘Like a broken bowl’ means that broken bowl; this is a designation in the neuter gender by way of construal. ‘They revolve’ means they revolve towards something. Where they fall, from there, after going a distance of a few ratanas by the force of revolving, they return to the very place they fell by the force of revolving. Therefore, it is said, ‘those that revolve come back to the place where they fell.’ ‘They turn away’ means from where they fell, they turn away. Therefore, it is said, ‘revolving, they go from the place of falling to another part.’ Revolving forward is ‘revolving towards’; to show that the other three kinds are ‘turning away,’ the passage beginning with ‘moreover’ was stated. The deities cannot hold themselves up, because of sinking like water. Therefore, it is said, ‘there,’ and so on. ‘There’ means on the natural earth. The deities sink because their elements are fine, subtle, and tender. ‘On the earth, they created an earth’ means that on the natural earth, by the power of their psychic ability, they created an earth capable of supporting their own bodies.

Kāmaṃ domanasse asatipi ekacco rāgo hotiyeva, rāge pana asati domanassassa asambhavo evāti tadekaṭṭhabhāvatoti āha “vītarāgāti pahīnadomanassā”ti. Silāthambhasadisā iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu nibbikāratāya.

Although when sorrow is absent, some lust may still arise, when lust is absent, the arising of sorrow is impossible—thus, because they have one meaning, he said, ‘Free from lust means with sorrow abandoned.’ Like a stone pillar, due to being unchangeable in the face of the agreeable and disagreeable.

Catusaṃvejanīyaṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Four Places Inspiring Spiritual Urgency

202. Apāragaṅgāyāti gaṅgāya orambhāge. “Saṅkārachaḍḍakasammajjaniyo gahetvā”tiādi attano attano vasanaṭṭhāne vattakaraṇākāradassanaṃ. “Evaṃ dvīsu kālesū”tiādi nidassanatthaṃ paccāmasanaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā adhigataṃ.

202. ‘On the near side of the Ganges’ means on this bank of the Ganges. The passage beginning with ‘Taking up brooms for removing rubbish’ shows the manner of performing the duties in one’s own dwelling place. The passage beginning with ‘Thus at the two times’ is a repetition for the purpose of illustration; that was understood below.

Kammasādhano [M 2.0179] sambhāvanattho bhāvanīya-saddoti āha “manasā bhāvite sambhāvite”ti. Dutiyavikappe pana bhāvanaṃ, vaḍḍhanañca paṭipakkhapahānatoti āha “ye vā”tiādi.

The word ‘bhāvanīya’ is an agent of action and has the meaning of possibility; thus he said, ‘to be cultivated, to be developed in the mind.’ In the second alternative, however, cultivation and growth are by means of abandoning opposing factors; thus he said, ‘or those,’ and so on.

Buddhādīsu tīsu vatthūsu pasannacittassa, na kammaphalasaddhāmattena. Sā cassa saddhāsampadā evaṃ [P 2.0230] veditabbāti phalena hetuṃ dassento “vattasampannassā”ti āha. Saṃvego nāma sahottappañāṇaṃ, abhijātiṭṭhānādīnipi tassa uppattihetūni bhavantīti āha “saṃvegajanakānī”ti.

Of one whose mind is pleased regarding the three objects—the Buddha and so on—not merely through belief in the fruit of kamma. And this accomplishment in faith should be understood thus: showing the cause by the result, he said, ‘of one endowed with duties.’ Awe (saṃvega) is knowledge together with moral dread; he said that even things such as noble birth are causes for its arising, as in ‘generating awe.’

Cetiyapūjanatthaṃ cārikā cetiyacārikā. Sagge patiṭṭhahissantiyeva buddhaguṇārammaṇāya kusalacetanāya saggasaṃvattaniyabhāvato.

A journey for the purpose of honoring shrines is a shrine pilgrimage. They will surely be established in heaven, because a wholesome intention that has the qualities of the Buddha as its object is conducive to heaven.

Ānandapucchākathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Discourse of Ānanda's Question

203. Etthāti mātugāme. Ayaṃ uttamā paṭipatti, yadidaṃ adassanaṃ, dassanamūlakattā tappaccayānaṃ sabbānatthānaṃ. Lobhoti kāmarāgo. Cittacalanā paṭipattiantarāyakaro cittakkhobho. Murumurāpetvāti saaṭṭhikaṃ katvā khādane anuravadassanaṃ. Aparimitaṃ kālaṃ dukkhānubhavanaṃ aparicchinnadukkhānubhavanaṃ. Vissāsoti visaṅgo ghaṭṭanābhāvo. Otāroti tattha cittassa [V 2.0161] anuppaveso. Asihatthena verīpurisena, pisācenāpi khāditukāmena. Āsīdeti akkamanādivasena bādheyya. Assāti mātugāmassa. Pabbajitehi kattabbakammanti āmisapaṭiggahaṇādi pabbajitehi kātabbaṃ kammaṃ. Satīti vā kāyagatāsati upaṭṭhāpetabbā.

203. ‘Here’ means in regard to women. This is the highest practice, namely, not seeing, because seeing is the root of all misfortunes that are dependent on it. ‘Lust’ means sensual desire. ‘Wavering of mind’ is a disturbance of mind that is an obstacle to practice. ‘Making a crunching sound’ means making an accompanying sound when eating something with bones. ‘Experiencing suffering for an immeasurable time’ means experiencing uninterrupted suffering. ‘Familiarity’ means non-attachment, an absence of friction. ‘Opportunity’ means the entering of the mind therein. ‘With a sword in hand’ means by an enemy with a sword in hand, or even by a demon wishing to devour. ‘One might assail’ means one might harm by way of assault and so forth. ‘Of her’ means of a woman. ‘An action to be done by renunciants’ means an action to be done by renunciants, such as accepting material things. Or ‘mindfulness’: mindfulness directed to the body should be established.

204. Atantibaddhāti abhāravahā. Pesitacittāti nibbānaṃ pati pesitacittā.

204. ‘Not bound by a thread’ means not carrying a burden. ‘With mind dispatched’ means with mind dispatched towards Nibbāna.

205. Vihatenāti kappāsavihananadhanunā pabbajaṭānaṃ vijaṭanavasena hatena. Tenāha “supothitenā”ti, asaṅkaraṇavasena suṭṭhu pothitenāti attho, dassanīyasaṃvejanīyaṭṭhānakittanena ca vasanaṭṭhānaṃ kathitaṃ.

205. ‘By the carded’ means struck by a cotton-carder's bow in the manner of disentangling the matted hair of ascetics. Therefore, it is said ‘well-beaten,’ meaning well-beaten in a way that does not cause entanglement. And by the mention of places that are worth seeing and that inspire spiritual urgency, a dwelling place is spoken of.

Ānandaacchariyadhammavaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Marvellous Qualities of Ānanda

207. Theraṃ adisvā āmantesīti tattha adisvā āvajjanto therassa ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ, pavattiñca ñatvā āmantesi.

207. ‘He addressed the elder without seeing him’: here, ‘without seeing’ means that, reflecting on the elder's location and knowing his situation, he addressed him.

Kāyakammassa [P 2.0231][M 2.0180] hitabhāvo hitajjhāsayena pavattitattāti āha “hitavuddhiyā katenā”ti. Sukhabhāvo kāyikadukkhābhāvo, cetasikasukhabhāvo cetasikasukhasamuṭṭhitattā cāti vuttaṃ “sukhasomanasseneva katenā”ti. Āvirahovibhāgato advayabhāvato advayenāti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “yathā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Satthu khettabhāvasampattiyā, therassa ajjhāsayasampattiyā ca “ettakamida”nti pamāṇaṃ gahetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya pamāṇavirahitattā tassa kammassāti āha “cakkavāḷampī”tiādi.

The bodily action is beneficial because it proceeds from a beneficial intention—thus it is said, ‘done for welfare and growth.’ The state of happiness is the absence of bodily suffering, and the state of mental happiness is because it arises from mental joy—thus it is said, ‘done with pleasure and joy.’ To show this meaning—that it is non-dual because it is without duality and without distinction between the manifest and the concealed—the passage beginning with ‘just as’ was stated. Due to the Teacher's attainment of the state of a field of merit and the elder's attainment of intention, and because it is impossible to grasp the measure of that action, saying ‘it is this much,’ that action is without measure; thus it is said, ‘even the entire world-system,’ and so on.

Evaṃ pavattitenāti evaṃ odissakamettābhāvanāya vasena pavattitena. Vivaṭṭūpanissayabhūtaṃ kataṃ upacitaṃ puññaṃ etenāti katapuñño, arahattādhigamāya katādhikāroti attho. Tenāha “abhinīhārasampannosīti dassetī”ti.

‘Thus proceeded’ means thus proceeded by way of cultivating loving-kindness directed towards specific beings. ‘One who has made merit’ means one by whom merit has been made and accumulated, which has become a supporting condition for turning away from rebirth; the meaning is one who has made a resolution for the attainment of arahantship. Therefore, it shows, ‘You are accomplished in aspiration.’

208. Katthaci saṅkucitaṃ hutvā ṭhitaṃ mahāpathaviṃ pattharanto viya, paṭisaṃhaṭaṃ hutvā ṭhitaṃ ākāsaṃ vitthārento viya, catusaṭṭhādhikayojanasatasahassubbedhaṃ cakkavāḷagiriṃ adho osārento viya, aṭṭhasaṭṭhādhikasahassayojanasatasahassubbedhaṃ sineruṃ ukkhipento viya, satayojanāyāmavitthāraṃ mahājambuṃ khandhe gahetvā cālento viyāti pañca hi upamā hi therassa guṇakathā [V 2.0162] mahantabhāvadassanatthañceva aññesaṃ dukkaṭabhāvadassanatthañca āgatāva. Eteneva cāti ca-saddena “ahaṃ etarahi arahaṃ sammāsambuddho” (dī. ni. 2.4), “sadevakasmiṃ lokasmiṃ natthi me paṭipuggalo”ti (ma. ni. 1.285; 2.341; mahāva. 11; kathā. 405; mi. pa. 5.11) ca evaṃ ādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Byattoti [P 2.0232] khandhakosallādisaṅkhātena veyyattiyena samannāgato. Medhāvīti medhāsaṅkhātāya sammābhāvitāya paññāya samannāgato.

208. As if spreading out the great earth that had become contracted; as if expanding the sky that had become withdrawn; as if lowering the Cakkavāḷa mountain range, which is 100,064 yojanas high; as if lifting up Mount Sineru, which is 101,068 yojanas high; as if taking the great Jambu tree, one hundred yojanas in length and breadth, on his shoulder and shaking it—these five similes are given to show the greatness of the elder’s virtues and to show how difficult they are for others to accomplish. And by this word ‘and’ (ca), the inclusion of such passages as, “I am now the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One,” and, “In the world with its gods, there is no counterpart to me,” should be understood. ‘Competent’ means endowed with the skill known as expertise in the aggregates and so on. ‘Wise’ means endowed with well-cultivated wisdom, known as intelligence.

209. Paṭisanthāradhammanti pakaticārittavasena vuttaṃ, upagatānaṃ pana bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīnañca pucchāvissajjanavasena ceva cittarucivasena ca yathākālaṃ dhammaṃ desetiyeva, upāsakopāsikānaṃ pana upanisinnakathāvasena.

209. ‘The practice of friendly welcome’ is spoken of in terms of natural conduct. But for monks and nuns who have approached, he indeed teaches the Dhamma at the appropriate time, both by way of answering questions and according to their inclinations. For laymen and laywomen, however, it is by way of talks given while they are sitting near.

Mahāsudassanasuttadesanāvaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Teaching of the Mahāsudassana Sutta

210. Khuddaka-saddo [M 2.0181] patirūpavācī, ka-saddo appatthoti āha “khuddakanagaraketi nagarapatirūpake sambādhe khuddakanagarake”ti. Dhuparavisālasaṇṭhānatāya taṃ “ujjaṅgalanagaraka”nti vuttanti āha “visamanagarake”ti. Aññesaṃ mahānagarānaṃ ekadesappamāṇatāya sākhāsadise. Ettha ca “khuddakanagarake”ti iminā tassa nagarassa appakabhāvo vutto, “ujjaṅgalanagarake”ti iminā bhūmivipattiyā nihīnabhāvo, “sākhānagarake”ti iminā appadhānabhāvo. Sārappattāti vibhavasārādinā sāramahattaṃ pattā.

210. The word `khuddaka` speaks of resemblance, while the suffix `-ka` has the meaning of smallness; thus it is said: ‘in a small townlet’ means in a small, congested town that resembles a city. Because it has a shape that is spread out like a wisp of smoke, it is called an `ujjaṅgalanagaraka`; this means ‘an uneven town.’ Being the size of one part of other great cities, it is like a branch town. Here, ‘in a small townlet’ indicates the smallness of that town; ‘an uneven townlet’ indicates its inferiority due to the poor quality of the land; and ‘a branch townlet’ indicates its lack of importance. ‘Having attained the essence’ means having attained the greatness of essence through the essence of prosperity and so on.

Kahāpaṇasakaṭanti ettha “dvikumbhaṃ sakaṭaṃ. Kumbho pana dasambaṇo”ti vadanti. Dve pavisantīti dve kahāpaṇasakaṭāni dve āyavasena pavisanti.

"Kahāpaṇasakaṭa": here, they say, "a cart is two kumbhas. A kumbha, however, is ten ambaṇas." "Dve pavisanti": two carts carrying kahāpaṇas enter, two by way of income.

Subhikkhāti sulabhāhārā, sundarāhārā ca. Tenāha “khajjabhojjasampannā”ti. Saddaṃ karonteti ravasārinā tuṭṭhabhāvena koñcanādaṃ karonte. Avivittāti asuññā, kadāci ratho paṭhamaṃ gacchati, taṃ añño anubandhanto gacchati, kadāci dutiyaṃ vuttaratho paṭhamaṃ gacchati, itaro taṃ anubandhati evaṃ aññamaññaṃ anubandhamānā. Etthāti kusāvatīnagare. Tassa mahantabhāvato ceva iddhādibhāvato ca niccaṃ payojitāneva bheriādīni tūriyāni, samma [P 2.0233] sammāti vā aññamaññaṃ piyālāpasaddo samma-saddo. Kaṃsatāḷādisabbatāḷāvacarasaddo tāḷa-saddo, kūṭabheri-saddo kumbhathūṇasaddo.

"Subhikkhā": having easily obtainable and fine food. Hence, it is said, "endowed with hard and soft food." "Saddaṃ karonte": making a koñca-sound with a joyful disposition, resounding. "Avivittā": not empty; sometimes one chariot goes first, another following it; sometimes the second-mentioned chariot goes first, the other following it—thus, they follow one another. "Ettha": in the city of Kusāvatī. Because of its greatness and its state of power, musical instruments such as drums were always played. "Samma sammā" or the sound of mutual affectionate speech is the "samma-sound". The sound of bronze cymbals and all other percussion instruments is the "tāḷa-sound"; the sound of kettle drums is the "kūṭabheri-sound"; the sound of pot-shaped drums is the "kumbhathūṇa-sound".

Evarūpā [V 2.0163] saddā honti kacavarākiṇṇavīthitāya, araññe kandamūlapaṇṇādiggahaṇāya, tattha dukkhajīvikatāya cāti yathākkamaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Idha na evaṃ ahosi devaloke viya sabbaso paripuṇṇasampattikatāya.

Such sounds exist due to streets being strewn with rubbish, due to gathering roots, tubers, leaves, and so forth in the forest, and due to a difficult livelihood there; this should be connected in sequence. Here, it was not so; it was like a heavenly realm due to its state of completely fulfilled prosperity.

Mahantaṃ kolāhalanti saddhāsampannānaṃ devatānaṃ, upāsakānañca vasena purato purato mahatī ugghosanā hoti. Tattha bhagavantaṃ uddissa katassa vihārassa abhāvato, bhikkhusaṅghassa ca mahantabhāvato te āgantvā…pe… pesesi. Pesento ca “kathañhi nāma bhagavā pacchime kāle attano pavattiṃ amhākaṃ nārocesi, nesaṃ domanassaṃ mā ahosī”ti “ajja kho vāseṭṭhā”tiādinā sāsanaṃ pesesi.

"Mahantaṃ kolāhalaṃ": a great proclamation occurs further and further ahead on account of the faithful deities and lay devotees. There, due to the absence of a monastery made for the Blessed One and due to the greatness of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, they came and... he sent a message. And while sending it, thinking, "How is it that the Blessed One did not inform us of his state in his final time? Let them not have sorrow," he sent the message beginning with, "Today, Vāseṭṭhā..."

Mallānaṃ vandanāvaṇṇanā

The description of the Mallas' homage.

211. Aghaṃ [M 2.0182] dukkhaṃ āventi pakāsentīti aghāvino, pākaṭībhūtadukkhāti āha “uppannadukkhā”ti. Ñātisālohitabhāvena kulaṃ parivattati etthāti kulaparivattaṃ. Taṃ taṃkulīnabhāgena ṭhito sattanikāyo “kulaparivattaso”ti vuttanti āha “kulaparivatta”nti. Te pana taṃtaṃkulaparivattaparicchinnā mallarājāno tasmiṃ nagare vīthiādisabhāgena vasantīti vuttaṃ “vīthisabhāgena ceva racchāsabhāgena cā”ti.

211. Because they reveal and make manifest misery and suffering, they are called "aghāvino"; because their suffering has become manifest, he said, "those for whom suffering has arisen." "Kulaparivattaṃ" is that wherein the family revolves by reason of kinship and blood-relationship. Because the group of beings established according to their respective family lineage is referred to as "kulaparivattaso" (by family group), he said "kulaparivatta". However, those Malla kings, defined by their respective family groups, dwell in that city in sections by street and road; thus it is said: "by way of street-sections and by way of road-sections."

Subhaddaparibbājakavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Description of the Story of Subhadda the Wanderer.

212. Kaṅkhā eva kaṅkhādhammo. Ekato vāti bhūmiṃ avibhajitvā sādhāraṇatova. Bījato ca aggaṃ gahetvā āhāraṃ sampādetvā dānaṃ bījaggaṃ. Gabbhakāleti gabbhadhāraṇato paraṃ khīraggahaṇakāle. Tenāha “gabbhaṃ phāletvā khīraṃ niharitvā”tiādi. Puthukakāleti sassānaṃ nātipakke puthukayogyaphalakāle. Lāyanagganti pakkassa sassassa lavane lavanārambhe dānaṃ adāsi. Lunassa [P 2.0234] sassassa veṇivasena bandhitvā ṭhapanaṃ veṇikaraṇaṃ. Tassa ārambhe dānaṃ veṇaggaṃ. Veṇiyo pana ekato katvā rāsikaraṇaṃ kalāpo. Tattha aggadānaṃ kalāpaggaṃ. Kalāpato nīharitvā maddane aggadānaṃ khalaggaṃ. Madditaṃ ophuṇitvā dhaññassa rāsikaraṇe aggadānaṃ khalabhaṇḍaggaṃ. Dhaññassa khalato koṭṭhe pakkhipane aggadānaṃ koṭṭhaggaṃ. Uddharitvāti koṭṭhato uddharitvā.

212. Doubt itself is the state of doubt. "Ekato vā" means commonly, without dividing the land. Taking the best portion from the seed and preparing food, the gift is "bījagga" (the best of the seed). "Gabbhakāle" refers to the time after conception, at the time of drawing milk; hence it is said: "having split the womb and drawn out the milk," etc. "Puthukakāle" is the time when crops are not yet fully ripe but suitable for being eaten green. "Lāyanagga" refers to the gift given at the beginning of harvesting ripe crops. Tying harvested crops into bundles is "veṇikaraṇa". The gift given at the start of this is "veṇagga". Bundles brought together are a "kalāpa". The best gift given there is "kalāpagga". Taking crops from the bundles, the best gift given during threshing is "khalagga". After threshing, the best gift given when heaping up the winnowed grain is "khalabhaṇḍagga". The best gift given when putting the grain from the threshing floor into the granary is "koṭṭhagga". "Uddharitvā" means having taken it out from the granary.

“Nava [V 2.0164] aggadānāni adāsī”ti iminā “kathaṃ nu kho ahaṃ satthu santike aggatova mucceyya”nti aggaggadānavasena vivaṭṭūpanissayassa kusalassa katūpacitattā, ñāṇassa ca tathā paripākaṃ gatattā aggadhammadesanāya tassa bhājanabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tenāha “imaṃ aggadhammaṃ tassa desessāmī”tiādi. Ohīyitvā saṅkocaṃ āpajjitvā.

By this, "He gave nine foremost gifts," it shows his state of being a vessel for the teaching of the foremost Dhamma. This is because, with the thought, "How might I be liberated in the foremost way in the Teacher's presence?", he had performed and accumulated wholesome action—which is a supporting condition for turning away from rebirth—by way of giving the foremost of gifts, and because his wisdom had likewise reached maturity. Hence, it is said: "I will teach him this foremost Dhamma," etc. "Ohīyitvā": having fallen back, having become contracted.

213. Aññātukāmova na sandiṭṭhiṃ parāmāsī. Abbhaññiṃsūti sandehajātassa pucchāvacananti katvā jāniṃsūti atthamāha. Tenāha pāḷiyaṃ “sabbeva na abbhaññiṃsū”ti. Nesanti pūraṇādīnaṃ. Sā paṭiññāti “karoto kho mahārāja kārayato”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.166) paṭiññātā, sabbaññupaṭiññā [M 2.0183] eva vā. Niyyānikāti sappāṭihāriyā, tesaṃ vā siddhantasaṅkhātā paṭiññā vaṭṭato nissaraṇaṭṭhena niyyānikāti. Sāsanassa sampattiyā tesaṃ sabbaññutaṃ, tabbipariyāyato ca asabbaññutaṃ gacchatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenāha “tasmā”tiādi. Atthābhāvatoti subhaddassa sādhetabbaatthābhāvato. Okāsābhāvatoti tathā vitthāritaṃ katvā dhammaṃ desetuṃ avasarābhāvato. Idāni tameva okāsābhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “paṭhamayāmasmi”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

213. Merely wishing to know, he did not grasp his own view. Regarding "abbhaññiṃsu", taking it as a question-and-answer for one in whom doubt has arisen, he states the meaning as "jāniṃsu" (they knew). Therefore, it is said in the Pāli text: "they all did not fully know." "Nesaṃ" refers to Pūraṇa and others. That declaration is the one declared by saying, "O great king, for the doer and the instigator..." (Dī. Ni. 1.166), or it is simply a declaration of omniscience. "Niyyānika" means leading out, either because it is miraculous, or because their declaration, known as their established doctrine, leads out in the sense of escape from the round of existence. It should be understood that their omniscience is determined by the success of their teaching, and their lack of omniscience by the opposite. Therefore, it is said: "Thus..." "Due to the absence of purpose" means because there was no purpose to be accomplished by Subhadda. "Due to the lack of opportunity" means because there was no occasion to teach the Dhamma in such detail. Now, to show that very lack of opportunity, it is said: "In the first watch..." and so on.

214. Yesaṃ [P 2.0235] samaṇabhāvakarānaṃ dhammānaṃ sampādanena samaṇo, te pana ukkaṭṭhaniddesena ariyamaggadhammāti catumaggasaṃsiddhiyā pāḷiyaṃ cattāro samaṇā vuttāti te bāhirasamaye sabbena sabbaṃ natthīti dassento “paṭhamo sotāpannasamaṇo”tiādimāha. Purimadesanāyāti “yasmiñca kho, subhadda, dhammavinaye”tiādinā vuttāya desanāya. Byatirekato, anvayato ca adhippeto attho vibhāvīyatīti paṭhamanayopettha “purimadesanāyā”ti padena saṅgahito vāti daṭṭhabbo. Attano sāsanaṃ niyamento āha “imasmiṃ kho”ti yojanā. Āraddhavipassakehīti samādhikammikavipassakehi, sikhāppattavipassake sandhāya vuttaṃ, na paṭṭhapitavipassane. Apare pana “bāhirakasamaye vipassanārambhassa ganthopi natthevāti avisesavacanameta”nti vadanti. Adhigataṭṭhānanti adhigatassa kāraṇaṃ, tadatthaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadanti attho, yena sotāpattimaggo adhigato, na uparimaggo, so sotāpattimagge ṭhito akuppadhammatāya tassa, tattha vā siddhito ṭhitapubbo bhūtapubbagatiyāti sotāpattimaggaṭṭho sotāpanno, na sesaariyā bhūmantaruppattito. Sotāpanno hi attanā adhigataṭṭhānaṃ sotāpattimaggaṃ aññassa kathetvā sotāpattimaggaṭṭhaṃ kareyya, na aṭṭhamako asambhavato. Esa nayo sesamaggaṭṭhesūti etthāpi imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Paguṇaṃ kammaṭṭhānanti attano paguṇaṃ vipassanākammaṭṭhānaṃ, eteneva “avisesavacana”nti vādo paṭikkhittoti daṭṭhabbo.

214. One is a monastic by fulfilling the qualities that make one a monastic. But those qualities, in the highest sense, are the qualities of the noble path. Thus, because the four monastics are mentioned in the Pāli due to the accomplishment of the four paths, he said, "The first is the stream-enterer monastic," and so on, to show that they are completely non-existent in outside schools. By "the earlier teaching" is meant the teaching stated as, "In whatever Dhamma and Discipline, Subhadda," etc. It should be understood that the intended meaning is clarified here by way of exclusion and inclusion, and that the first method is also included by the word "purimadesanāya". Defining his own Dispensation, he says, "In this..."; this is the connection. "Those who have undertaken insight" refers to those practicing insight with concentration as their vehicle; it is said with reference to those who have reached the peak of insight, not those who have just established insight. Others, however, say, "In outside schools, there is not even a text on the beginning of insight, so this is a general statement." "The attained state" means the cause of attainment, that is, the preliminary practice for it, by which the stream-entry path is attained, not the higher paths. Such a one, established in the stream-entry path due to its unshakable nature, or one who has previously been established there by its accomplishment, is a stream-enterer established in the stream-entry path—not the other noble ones, due to rebirth in other realms. For a stream-enterer, having personally attained the stream-entry path, could explain that state to another and establish them in the stream-entry path, but not make them an eighth person, as that is impossible. This is the method, and the meaning should be understood in this same way regarding those established in the other paths. "A familiar meditation subject" means one's own familiar insight meditation subject; by this, the claim that "it is a general statement" should be seen as refuted.

Sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ [V 2.0165] adhippetaṃ. Tañhi sabbañeyyadhammāvabodhane “kusalaṃ chekaṃ nipuṇa”nti vuccati tattha [P 2.0236] asaṅgaappaṭihataṃ pavattatīti katvā. Samadhikāni [M 2.0184] ekena vassena. Ñāyanti etena catusaccadhammaṃ yāthāvato paṭivijjhantīti ñāyo, lokuttaramaggoti āha “ariyamaggadhammassā”ti. Padissati etena ariyamaggo paccakkhato dissatīti padeso, vipassanāti vuttaṃ “padese vipassanāmagge”ti. Samaṇopīti ettha pi-saddo “padesavattī”ti etthāpi ānetvā sambandhitabboti āha “padesavatti…pe… natthīti vuttaṃ hotī”ti.

The omniscient knowledge is intended. For it is called 'skillful, sharp, and subtle' in comprehending all knowable things, because it operates therein without attachment or obstruction. It is more by one year. They know—through this, the four noble truths are penetrated as they truly are—thus it is called ñāya, the supramundane path; hence he said, 'of the noble path of the Dhamma.' It is seen—through this, the noble path is directly seen—thus it is called padesa; insight is what is meant, as it is said: 'in the padesa which is the path of insight.' Regarding 'even an ascetic,' here the particle pi (even) should be brought over and connected also with 'one who dwells in the padesa,' thus he says: 'one who dwells in the padesa... it is said there is none.'

215. Soti tathāvutto antevāsī. Tenāti ācariyena. Attano ṭhāne ṭhapito hoti parapabbājanādīsu niyuttattā.

215. He is the disciple thus spoken of. By 'tena' is meant 'by the teacher.' He is established in his own position because he is appointed to tasks such as giving the going forth to others.

Sakkhisāvakoti paccakkhasāvako, sammukhasāvakoti attho. Bhagavati dharamāneti dharamānassa bhagavato santike. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo. Sabbopi soti sabbo so tividhopi. Ayaṃ pana arahattaṃ patto, tasmā paripuṇṇagatāya matthakappatto pacchimo sakkhisāvakoti.

An 'eyewitness disciple' means a direct disciple, that is, a disciple in his presence. 'While the Blessed One was living' means in the vicinity of the Blessed One during his lifetime. This same principle applies to the other two as well. 'All of them' means all three types. But this one has attained arahantship; therefore, having reached the summit through complete attainment, he is the last eyewitness disciple.

Pañcamabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the fifth recitation division is concluded.

Tathāgatapacchimavācāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Tathāgata's Final Utterance

216. Tanti bhikkhusaṅghassa ovādakaṅgaṃ dassetuṃ…pe… vuttaṃ dhammasaṅgāhakehīti adhippāyo. Suttābhidhammasaṅgahitassa dhammassa atisajjanaṃ sambodhanaṃ desanā, tasseva pakārato ñāpanaṃ veneyyasantāne ṭhapanaṃ paññāpananti “dhammopi desito ceva [P 2.0237] paññatto cā”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā vinayatantisaṅgahitassa kāyavācānaṃ vinayanato “vinayo”ti laddhādhivacanassa atthassa atisajjanaṃ sambodhanaṃ desanā, tasseva pakārato ñāpanaṃ asaṅkarato ṭhapanaṃ paññāpananti “vinayopi desito ceva paññatto cā”ti vuttaṃ. Adhisīlasikkhāniddesabhāvena sāsanassa mūlabhūtattā vinayo paṭhamaṃ sikkhitabboti taṃ tāva ayamuddesaṃ sarūpato dassento “mayā hi vo”tiādimāha. Tattha sattāpattikkhandhavasenāti sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ avītikkamanīyatāvasena[V 2.0166]. Satthukiccaṃ sādhessati “idaṃ vo kattabbaṃ, idaṃ vo na kattabba”nti kattabbākattabbassa vibhāgena anusāsanato.

216. 'That' is to show the advisory function for the community of bhikkhus... this is the meaning as stated by the compilers of the Dhamma. The expounding, addressing, and teaching of the Dhamma collected in the Suttas and Abhidhamma is the 'teaching'; making it known in detail and establishing it in the minds of those to be trained is the 'declaration'—thus it is said, 'The Dhamma has been both taught and declared.' Similarly, the expounding, addressing, and teaching of that which has obtained the designation 'Vinaya' because it disciplines body and speech, collected in the Vinaya scripture, is the 'teaching'; making it known in detail and establishing it without confusion is the 'declaration'—thus it is said, 'The Vinaya has been both taught and declared.' Because the Vinaya, being the foundation of the Teaching by way of its exposition of the training in higher virtue, must be studied first, he now gives this summary, showing its nature, by saying, 'For by me to you…' Herein, 'by way of the seven categories of offenses' means by way of the non-transgressibility of the seven categories of offenses. 'It will fulfill the Teacher’s task' by instructing through the distinction between what should and should not be done.

Tena [M 2.0185] tenākārenāti tena tena veneyyānaṃ ajjhāsayānurūpena pakārena. Ime dhammeti ime sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhamme. Tappadhānattā suttantadesanāya “suttantapiṭakaṃ desita”nti vuttaṃ. Satthukiccaṃ sādhessati taṃtaṃcariyānurūpaṃ sammāpaṭipattiyā anusāsanato. Kusalākusalābyākatavasena nava hetū. “Satta phassā”tiādi sattaviññāṇadhātusampayogavasena vuttaṃ. Dhammānulome tikapaṭṭhānādayo cha, tathā dhammapaccanīye, dhammānulomapaccanīye, dhammapaccanīyānulometi catuvīsati samantapaṭṭhānāni etassāti catuvīsatisamantapaṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ pana paccayānulomādivasena vibhajiyamānaṃ aparimāṇanayaṃ evāti āha “anantanayamahāpaṭṭhānapaṭimaṇḍita”nti. Satthukiccaṃ sādhessatīti khandhādivibhāgena ñāyamānaṃ catusaccasambodhāvahattā satthārā sammāsambuddhena kātabbakiccaṃ nipphādessati.

'In this or that manner' means in a way suitable to the inclinations of those to be trained. 'These teachings' refers to these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Because of their prominence in the teaching of the discourses, it is said, 'The Sutta Piṭaka has been taught.' 'It will fulfill the Teacher’s task' by instructing in proper practice suitable to each individual’s conduct. There are nine roots in terms of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. 'Seven contacts,' and so on, are stated in connection with the seven consciousness elements. In the Conforming method, there are six sub-methods, such as the Tika-Paṭṭhāna; likewise in the Opposing, Conforming-Opposing, and Opposing-Conforming methods—thus there are twenty-four comprehensive conditional relations. Since this, when analyzed by way of the conditional sequence and so on, has infinite methods, it is said to be 'adorned with the Great Paṭṭhāna of infinite methods.' 'It will fulfill the Teacher’s task' means that, being understood through the analysis of the aggregates and so on, it accomplishes the task to be done by the Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One, because it leads to the full understanding of the four truths.

Ovadissanti anusāsissanti ovādānusāsanīkiccanipphādanato.

They instruct and train, fulfilling the task of instruction and training.

Cārittanti samudācārā, navesu piyālāpaṃ vuḍḍhesu [P 2.0238] gāravālāpanti attho. Tenāha “bhanteti vā āyasmāti vā”ti. Gāravavacanaṃ hetaṃ yadidaṃ bhanteti vā āyasmāti vā, loke pana “tatra bhava”nti, “devānaṃ piyā”ti ca gāravavacanameva.

'Conduct' refers to proper behavior—that is, speaking affectionately to junior monks and respectfully to the elders; this is the meaning. Hence it is said, 'Bhante' or 'Āyasmā.' This is indeed a term of respect, namely 'Bhante' or 'Āyasmā'; but in the world, 'tatra bhava' and 'devānaṃ piyā' are also terms of respect.

“Ākaṅkhamāno samūhanatū”ti vutte “na ākaṅkhamāno na samūhanatū”tipi vuttameva hotīti āha “vikappavacaneneva ṭhapesī”ti. Balanti ñāṇabalaṃ. Yadi asamūhananaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, tadeva ca icchitaṃ, atha kasmā bhagavā “ākaṅkhamāno samūhanatū”ti avocāti? Tathārūpapuggalajjhāsayavasena. Santi hi keci khuddānukhuddakāni sikkhāpadāni samādāya saṃvattituṃ anicchantā, tesaṃ tathā avuccamāne bhagavati vighāto uppajjeyya, taṃ tesaṃ bhavissati dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya, tathā pana vutte tesaṃ vighāto na uppajjeyya “amhākaṃ evāyaṃ doso, yato amhesu eva keci samūhananaṃ na icchantī”ti. Keci “sakalassa pana sāsanassa saṅghāyattabhāvakaraṇatthaṃ tathā vutta”nti vadanti. Yañca kiñci satthārā sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, taṃ samaṇā sakyaputtiyā sirasā sampaṭicchitvā jīvitaṃ viya rakkhanti. Tathā hi te “khuddānukhuddakāni sikkhāpadāni ākaṅkhamāno saṅgho samūhanatū”ti [M 2.0186] vuttepi na samūhaniṃsu, aññadatthu “purato viya tassa accayepi rakkhiṃsu evā”ti satthusāsanassa[V 2.0167], saṅghassa ca mahantabhāvadassanatthampi tathā vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hi āyasmā ānando, aññepi vā bhikkhū “katamaṃ pana bhante khuddakaṃ, katamaṃ anukhuddaka”nti na pucchiṃsu samūhanajjhāsayasseva abhāvato.

When it is said, 'If one wishes, let them abolish,' it is also as good as saying, 'If one does not wish, let them not abolish.' Thus, it is said, 'He established it by way of an alternative statement.' 'Strength' means the strength of wisdom. If non-abolition is seen and desired, then why did the Blessed One say, 'If one wishes, let them abolish'? It is due to the disposition of such individuals. For there are some who do not wish to undertake training in the minor and lesser rules. If it were not spoken thus by the Blessed One, distress might arise in them; that would be to their long-term harm and suffering. But if spoken thus, distress would not arise in them, thinking, 'This is our own shortcoming, since some among us do not wish to abolish.' Some say, 'It was said to make the entire dispensation dependent on the Sangha.' Whatever rule the Teacher has laid down, the Sakyan ascetics accept it wholeheartedly and guard it as if it were their life. Thus, even when told, 'If the Sangha wishes, let it abolish the minor and lesser rules,' they did not abolish them. Instead, they guarded them even after his passing just as they did before. This should be seen as showing the greatness of the Teacher’s dispensation and the Sangha. For indeed, the Venerable Ānanda, and other bhikkhus, did not ask, 'Which, venerable sir, is minor, and which is lesser?' because they had no inclination to abolish them.

Na taṃ evaṃ gahetabbanti “nāgasenatthero khuddānukhuddakaṃ jānātī”tiādinā vuttaṃ taṃ nesaṃ vacanaṃ iminā vuttākārena na gahetabbaṃ adhippāyassa aviditattā. Idāni taṃ adhippāyaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “nāgasenatthero [P 2.0239] hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yasmā nāgasenatthero (milindapañhe abhejjavagge vitthāro) paresaṃ vādapathopacchedanatthaṃ saṅgītikāle dhammasaṅgāhakamahātherehi gahitakoṭṭhāsesu ca antimakoṭṭhāsameva gahetvā milindarājānaṃ paññāpesi. Mahākassapatthero pana ekasikkhāpadampi asamūhanitukāmatāya tathā kammavācaṃ sāveti, tasmā taṃ tesaṃ vacanaṃ tathā na gahetabbaṃ.

It should not be taken in this way, thinking, 'The Elder Nāgasena knows the minor and the lesser rules.' Their statement should not be taken in this manner because the intended meaning is not understood. Now, to clarify that intention, it is said, 'For the Elder Nāgasena,' etc. Because the Elder Nāgasena (as detailed extensively in the Abhejjavagga of the Milindapañha), in order to cut off the path of argument for others, took only the final portion of the established points taken by the great elders who compiled the Dhamma at the Council, and instructed King Milinda. But the Elder Mahākassapa, desiring not to abolish even a single training rule, recited the formal act in that way. Therefore, their statement should not be taken in that manner.

217. Dveḷhakanti dvidhāgāho, anekaṃsaggāhoti attho. Vimatīti saṃsayāpatti. Tenāha “vinicchituṃ asamatthatā”ti. Taṃ vo vadāmīti taṃ saṃsayavantaṃ bhikkhuṃ sandhāya vo tumhe vadāmi.

217. 'Doubt' (dveḷhaka) means a twofold grasping, that is, an indecisive grasping. 'Perplexity' (vimati) means falling into doubt. Hence, it is said: 'inability to decide.' 'That I tell you' means: referring to that doubtful bhikkhu, I speak to you (plural).

Nikkaṅkhabhāvapaccakkhakaraṇañāṇaṃ yevāti buddhādīsu tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ nikkaṅkhabhāvassa paccakkhakāriyābhāvato tamatthaṃ paṭivijjhitvā ṭhitaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇameva. Ettha etasmiṃ atthe.

It is precisely the knowledge that makes the state of doubtlessness directly evident. This is because for those bhikkhus there was no way of making their state of doubtlessness regarding the Buddha and so on directly evident; rather, it was the omniscient knowledge itself that stood, having penetrated that matter. 'Here' means in this context.

218. Appamajjanaṃ appamādo, so pana atthato ñāṇūpasañhitā sati. Yasmā tattha satiyā byāpāro sātisayo, tasmā “satiavippavāsenā”ti vuttaṃ. Appamādapadeyeva pakkhipitvā adāsi taṃ atthato, tassa sakalassa buddhavacanassa saṅgaṇhanato ca.

218. 'Non-negligence' is heedfulness, which, in essence, is mindfulness associated with knowledge. Since the activity of mindfulness is especially prominent therein, it is said: 'through the non-abandonment of mindfulness.' It is included within the very term 'heedfulness,' and thus given as its meaning, because it encompasses all the Buddha's teachings.

Parinibbutakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on Complete Unbinding

219. Jhānādīsu, citte ca paramukkaṃsagatavasībhāvatāya “ettake kāle ettakā samāpattiyo samāpajjitvā parinibbāyissāmī”ti kālaparicchedaṃ katvā samāpatti samāpajjanaṃ “parinibbānaparikamma”nti adhippetaṃ. Theroti anuruddhatthero.

219. Regarding the jhānas and so forth, and due to the mastery over the mind having reached the highest excellence, determining the time by thinking, 'After attaining such-and-such meditative states for such-and-such a period, I will attain final Nibbāna,' and then entering those attainments is what is meant by 'preparation for final Nibbāna.' 'The elder' refers to the Elder Anuruddha.

Ayampi [M 2.0187] cāti yathāvuttapañcasaṭṭhiyā jhānānaṃ samāpannabhāvakathāpi saṅkhepakathā eva, kasmā[V 2.0168]? Yasmā bhagavā tadāpi devasikaṃ vaḷañjanasamāpattiyo sabbāpi aparihāpetvā samāpajji evāti dassento “nibbānapuraṃ pavisanto”tiādimāha.

This too—that is, the account of having attained the sixty-five jhānas as stated—is just a summary explanation. Why? Because the Blessed One, even then, entered all the daily customary attainments without abandoning any; showing this, it is said, 'entering the city of Nibbāna,' and so forth.

Imāni dvepi samanantarāneva paccavekkhaṇāyapi yebhuyyenānantariyakatāya jhānapakkhikabhāvato, yasmā [P 2.0240] bhavaṅgacittaṃ sabbapacchimaṃ, tato bhavato cavanato “cutī”ti vuccati, tasmā na kevalaṃ ayameva bhagavā, atha kho sabbepi sattā bhavaṅgacitteneva cavantīti dassetuṃ “ye hi kecī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

These two also, being immediate and for the most part without interval even for reflection, pertain to the jhāna side. Since the life-continuum consciousness is the very last, and its falling away from existence is called 'passing away,' therefore, to show that not only this Blessed One, but indeed all beings pass away with the life-continuum consciousness, it is said: 'Whatever beings,' and so forth.

220. Paṭibhāgapuggalavirahitoti sīlādiguṇehi asadisatāya sadisapuggalarahito.

220. 'Devoid of a counterpart' means being without a similar person due to being incomparable in qualities such as virtue and so forth.

221. Saṅkhārā vūpasamanti etthāti vūpasamoti evaṃsaṅkhātaṃ ñātaṃ kathitaṃ nibbānaṃ.

221. Because 'formations are stilled herein,' it is called 'the stilling'; thus is Nibbāna designated, known, and spoken of.

222. Yanti paccatte upayogavacananti āha “yo kālaṃ akarī”ti.

222. 'They go' is a term of individual application, as when it is said, 'who made his time' (i.e., passed away).

Suvikasitenevāti pītisomanassayogato suṭṭhu vikasitena muditena. Vedanaṃ adhivāsesi abhāvasamudayo kato suṭṭhu pariññātattā. Anāvaraṇavimokkho sabbaso nibbutabhāvato.

'With well-blossomed' means thoroughly blossomed and gladdened due to the connection with rapture and joy. 'He endured the feeling' means that its arising and passing away were made to be thoroughly understood. 'The unobstructed liberation' is so called because of the state of being completely extinguished.

223. Ākaronti attano phalāni samānākāre karontīti ākārā, kāraṇāni. Sabbākāravarūpeteti sabbehi ākāravarehi uttamakāraṇehi sīlādiguṇehi samannāgateti attho.

223. 'Modes' (ākārā) are so called because they make their own fruits in a similar manner; they are causes. 'Endowed with all excellent modes' means endowed with all excellent modes, which are supreme causes, that is, with qualities such as virtue and so forth.

225. Kathaṃbhūtāti kīdisābhūtā.

225. 'Of what sort?' means of what kind or nature.

Cullakaddhānanti parittaṃ kālaṃ dvattināḍikāmattaṃ velaṃ.

'A short period' means a brief time, a period of about two or three nāḷikas.

Buddhasarīrapūjāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Veneration of the Buddha’s Bodily Relics

227. Kaṃsatāḷādi tāḷaṃ avacarati etthāti “tāḷāvacara”nti vuccati ātatāditūriyabhaṇḍaṃ. Tenāha “sabbaṃ tūriyabhaṇḍa”nti.

227. Because rhythm, such as that of cymbals and so forth, is employed herein, it is called 'tāḷāvacara,' which refers to musical instruments such as those with stretched hide. Hence, it is said, 'all musical instruments.'

Dakkhiṇadisābhāgenevāti [V 2.0169][M 2.0188] aññena disābhāgena anāharitvā yamakasālānaṃ ṭhānato dakkhiṇadisābhāgeneva, tatopi dakkhiṇadisābhāgaṃ haritvā netvā.

'By the southern direction only' means not bringing it from any other direction, but only from the southern side of the place of the twin sāl trees, and from there, carrying and taking it to the southern part.

Jetavanasadiseti sāvatthiyā jetavanasadise ṭhāne, “jetavanasadise ṭhāne”tipi pāṭho.

'In a place like Jetavana' means in a place similar to Jetavana in Sāvatthī. There is also the reading, 'in a place similar to Jetavana.'

228. Pasādhanamaṅgalasālāyāti [P 2.0241] abhisekakāle alaṅkaraṇamaṅgalasālāya.

228. 'In the hall for auspicious adornment' means in the hall for auspicious decoration at the time of the consecration ceremony.

229. Devadāniyoti tassa corassa nāmaṃ.

229. 'Devadāniya' is the name of that thief.

Mahākassapattheravatthuvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Story of the Elder Mahākassapa

231. Pāvāyāti pāvā nagarato. Āvajjanapaṭibaddhattā jānanassa anāvajjitattā satthu parinibbānaṃ ajānanto “dasabalaṃ passissāmī”ti thero cintesi, satthu sarīre vā satthusaññaṃ uppādento tathā cintesi. Tenevāha “atha bhagavantaṃ ukkhipitvā”ti. “Dhuvaṃ parinibbuto bhavissatī”ti cintesi pārisesañāyena. Jānantopi thero ājīvakaṃ pucchiyeva, pucchane pana kāraṇaṃ sayameva pakāsetuṃ “kiṃ panā”tiādi āraddhaṃ.

231. 'From Pāvā' means from the city of Pāvā. Because his knowing was bound by absorption and not turned outwards, the elder, not knowing of the Teacher's final Nibbāna, thought, 'I will see the Ten-Powered One'; or he thought thus while arousing the perception of the Teacher in the Teacher's body. By way of inference, he thought, 'Surely, he must have attained final Nibbāna.' Although knowing this, the elder still asked the Ājīvaka; but the reason for asking is introduced by 'But what...' and so forth, in order to reveal it himself.

Ajja sattāhaparinibbutoti ajja divasato paṭilomato sattame ahani parinibbuto.

'Having attained final Nibbāna seven days ago' means that counting backwards from today, he attained final Nibbāna on the seventh day.

232. Nāḷiyā vāpakenāti nāḷiyā ceva thavikāya ca.

232. 'With a tube or a bag' means with both a tube and a bag.

Mañjuketi mañjubhāṇine madhurassare. Paṭibhāneyyaketi paṭibhānavante. Bhuñjitvā pātabbayāgūti paṭhamaṃ bhuñjitvā pivitabbayāgu.

'Sweetly-speaking' means one who speaks sweetly, with a melodious voice. 'Eloquent' means one who possesses eloquence. 'Gruel to be drunk after having eaten' means gruel to be drunk after having first eaten.

Tassāti subhaddassa vuḍḍhapabbajitassa.

'His' refers to Subhadda, the one ordained in old age.

Ārādhitasāsaneti samāhitasāsane. Alanti samattho. Pāpoti pāpapuggalo. Osakkāpetunti hāpetuṃ antaradhāpetuṃ.

'In the accomplished teaching' means in the well-established Dispensation. 'Able' means capable. 'The evil one' means an evil person. 'To make it retreat' means to cause it to decline, to make it disappear.

Pañhavārāti pañhā viya vissajjanāni “yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ [V 2.0170] hotī”tiādinā, (dha. sa. 1.1) “yasmiṃ samaye rūpūpapattiyā maggaṃ bhāvetī”tiādinā [P 2.0242][M 2.0189] (dha. sa. 1.251) ca pavattāni ekaṃ dve bhūmantarāni. Mūle naṭṭhe pisācasadisā bhavissāmāti yathā rukkhe adhivattho pisāco tassa sākhāparivāre naṭṭhe khandhaṃ nissāya vasati, khandhe naṭṭhe mūlaṃ nissāya vasati, mūle pana naṭṭhe anissayova hoti, tathā bhavissāmāti attho. Atha vā mūle naṭṭheti pisācena kira rukkhagacchādīnaṃ kañcideva mūlaṃ chinditvā attano puttassa dinnaṃ, yāva taṃ tassa hatthato na vigacchati, tāva so taṃ padesaṃ adissamānarūpo vicarati. Yadā pana tasmiṃ kenaci acchinnabhāvena vā sativippavāsavasena vā naṭṭhe manussānampi dissamānarūpo vicarati, taṃ sandhāyāha “mūle naṭṭhe pisācasadisā bhavissāmā”ti.

'Question sections' means answers that proceed like questions, such as 'At the time when a wholesome mind pertaining to the sense-sphere has arisen...' (Dhs 1), and 'At the time when one develops the path for rebirth in the form realm...' (Dhs 257), which are separated by one or two intervening sections. 'If the root is destroyed, we will be like demons' means: just as a demon dwelling in a tree, when its branches and foliage are destroyed, lives depending on the trunk; when the trunk is destroyed, it lives depending on the root; but when the root is destroyed, it becomes without support—such is the meaning. Alternatively, regarding 'when the root is destroyed': it is said that a demon cut off a certain root of a tree or the like and gave it to its child. As long as that root did not leave the child’s hand, the demon wandered invisibly in that area. But when that root was lost, either by being snatched away by someone or through a lapse of mindfulness, the demon then wandered in a form visible even to humans. Referring to this, it is said, 'If the root is destroyed, we will be like demons.'

Maṃ kāyasakkhiṃ katvāti taṃ paṭipadaṃ kāyena sacchikatavantaṃ tasmā tassā desanāya sakkhibhūtaṃ maṃ katvā. Paṭicchāpesi taṃ paṭicchāpanaṃ kassapasuttena dīpetabbaṃ.

'Having made me a personal witness' means having made me one who has realized that practice with the body, and who has therefore become a witness to that teaching. He concealed it. That concealment should be clarified by means of the Kassapa Sutta.

233. Candanaghaṭikābāhullato candanacitakā.

233. Because of an abundance of sandalwood logs, it was a sandalwood pyre.

Taṃ sutvāti taṃ āyasmatā anuruddhattherena vuttaṃ devatānaṃ adhippāyaṃ sutvā.

'Having heard that' means having heard that intention of the deities, which was spoken by the venerable Elder Anuruddha.

234. Dasikatantaṃ vāti paliveṭhitaahatakāsikavatthānaṃ dasaṭhānena tantumattampi vā. Dārukkhandhaṃ vāti candanādicitakadārukkhandhaṃ vā.

234. 'Or a thread from a fringe' means even just a thread from ten sections of new, wrapped Benares cloth. 'Or a log of wood' means a log of wood for the pyre, such as sandalwood and so forth.

235. Samudāyesu pavattavohārānaṃ avayavesu dissanato sarīrassa avayavabhūtāni aṭṭhīni “sarīrānī”ti vuttāni.

235. Because they are seen among the parts in conventional expressions that occur with respect to aggregates, the bones, being parts of the body, are called 'sarīrāni'.

Na vippakiriṃsūti sarūpeneva ṭhitāti attho. “Sesā vippakiriṃsū”ti vatvā yathā pana tā vippakiṇṇā ahesuṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

They did not scatter, meaning they remained in their own form. Having said, "The rest scattered," to show how they scattered, "there" and so on is said.

Udakadhārā nikkhamitvā nibbāpesunti devatānubhāvena. Evaṃ mahatiyo bahū udakadhārā kimatthāyāti āha [P 2.0243] “bhagavato citako mahanto”ti. Mahā hi so vīsaratanasatiko. Aṭṭhadantakehīti naṅgalehi aṭṭheva hi nesaṃ dantasadisāni potthāni honti, tasmā “aṭṭhadantakānī”ti vuccati.

Streams of water came forth and extinguished it by the power of the deities. Why so many great streams of water? It is said, "The Blessed One's pyre was large." For it was indeed large, being one hundred and twenty cubits.
