"With eight-toothed ones"—with plows, for indeed they have eight protuberances similar to teeth; therefore they are called "eight-toothed."

Dhammakathāva [V 2.0171][M 2.0190] pamāṇanti ativiya acchariyabbhutabhāvato passantānaṃ, suṇantānañca sātisayaṃ pasādāvahabhāvato, savisesaṃ buddhānubhāvadīpanato. Parinibbutassa hi buddhassa bhagavato evarūpo ānubhāvoti taṃ pavattiṃ kathentānaṃ dhammakathikānaṃ attano ñāṇabalānurūpaṃ pavattiyamānā dhammakathā evettha pamāṇaṃ vaṇṇetabbassa atthassa mahāvisayattā, tasmā vaṇṇanābhūmi nāmesāti adhippāyo. Catujjātiyagandhaparibhaṇḍaṃ kāretvāti tagarakuṅkumayavanapupphatamālapattāni pisitvā katagandhena paribhaṇḍaṃ kāretvā. Khacitvāti tattha tattha olambanavasena racetvā, gandhavatthūni gahetvā ganthitamālā gandhadāmāni ratanāvaḷiyo ratanadāmāni. Bahikilañjaparikkhepassa, antosāṇiparikkhepassa karaṇena sāṇikilañjaparikkhepaṃ kāretvā. Vātaggāhiniyo paṭākā vātapaṭākā. Sarabharūpapādako pallaṅko sarabhamayapallaṅko, tasmiṃ sarabhamayapallaṅke.

"The Dhamma talk is the measure" means because of its exceedingly marvelous and astonishing nature for those who see it, and because it brings extraordinary faith to those who hear it, and because it illuminates the special power of the Buddha. For such is the power of the Blessed Buddha who has attained final Nibbāna—thus, for Dhamma preachers narrating that event, the Dhamma talk itself, proceeding in accordance with their own power of knowledge, is the measure here, due to the vast scope of the meaning to be described. Therefore, the intention is that this is called the ground of praise. "Having prepared a fourfold assortment of fragrant substances" means having ground tagara, saffron, yavanapuppha, and tamāla leaves, and having made an adorned bundle with the resulting fragrance. "Decorating" means arranging them here and there as hanging ornaments, taking fragrant items, making tied garlands, fragrant strings, jeweled festoons, and jeweled strands. Having made an outer enclosure of reed mats and an inner enclosure of cloth, thus preparing a combined enclosure of cloth and reed mats. "Wind-catching banners" means wind flags. "A couch with legs shaped like Sarabha beasts" means a couch made of Sarabha beasts, on that couch made of Sarabha beasts.

Sattihatthā purisā sattiyo taṃsahacaraṇato yathā “kuntā pacarantī”ti, tehi samantato rakkhāpanaṃ pañcakaraṇanti āha “sattihatthehi purisehi parikkhipāpetvā”ti. Dhanūhīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Sannāhagavacchikaṃ viya katvā nirantarāvaṭṭhitaārakkhasannāhena gavacchijālaṃ viya katvā.

"Men with spears in hand" (sattihatthā purisā): [this is like when] one says 'spears are moving' because of their association with the men. Thus, it is said 'having surrounded with men holding spears' (sattihatthehi purisehi parikkhipāpetvā) to indicate guarding on all sides by them, a five-fold action. The same principle applies to 'with bows'. Having made it like an armored window, that is, having made it like a lattice window with a continuous, established guard of armor.

Sādhukīḷitanti [P 2.0244] saparahitaṃ sādhanaṭṭhena sādhū, tesaṃ kīḷitaṃ uḷārapuññapasavanato, samparāyikatthāvirodhikaṃ kīḷāvihāranti attho.

"Well-played indeed" (sādhukīḷitaṃ) means that the virtuous (sādhū) are those who accomplish their own and others' welfare, and their play is the accumulation of great merit, a sporting and recreation that does not contradict the goal of the future—such is the meaning.

Sarīradhātuvibhajanavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Distribution of the Relics

236. Imināva niyāmenāti yena nīhārena mahātale nisinno kañci parihāraṃ akatvā kevalaṃ iminā niyāmeneva. Supinakoti dussupinako. Dukūladupaṭṭaṃ nivāsetvāti dve dukūlavatthāni ekajjhaṃ katvā nivāsetvā. Evañhi tāni sokasamappitassāpi abhassitvā tiṭṭhanti.

236. By this very method: by which means, sitting on the bare ground, without making any special arrangement, simply by this very method. Supinako: a bad dream. Dukūladupaṭṭaṃ nivāsetvā: having worn two garments of fine cloth together. For thus, even for one overcome by sorrow, they remain without falling off.

Abhisekasiñcakoti rajjābhiseke abhisekamaṅgalasiñcako uttamamaṅgalabhāvato. Visaññī jāto yathā taṃ bhagavato guṇavisesāmatarasaññutāya avaṭṭhitapemo pothujjanikasaddhāya patiṭṭhitapasādo katūpakāratāya sañjanitacittamaddavo.

The sprinkler of consecration means the auspicious sprinkler at a royal consecration, it being the highest auspicious rite. He became unconscious, as it were, being one whose affection was made firm by perceiving the nectar of the Blessed One's special qualities, whose confidence was established on the faith of an ordinary person, and whose tenderness of mind was generated by the good that had been done for him.

Suvaṇṇabimbisakavaṇṇanti [V 2.0172][M 2.0191] suviracita apassenasadisaṃ.

Suvaṇṇabimbisakavaṇṇaṃ: well-made, resembling a backrest.

Kasmā panettha pāveyyakā pāḷiyaṃ sabbapacchato gahitā, kiṃ te kusinārāya āsannatarāpi sabbapacchato uṭṭhitā? Āma, sabbapacchato uṭṭhitāti dassetuṃ “tattha pāveyyakā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Why here are the Pāveyyakas mentioned last of all in the Pāli text? Even though they were closer to Kusinārā, did they set out last of all? Yes, to show that they set out last of all, 'there, the Pāveyyakas' and so on was stated.

Dhātupāsanatthanti satthu dhātūnaṃ payirupāsanāya. Nesaṃ pakkhā ahesuṃ “ñāyena tesaṃ santakā dhātuyo”ti.

Dhātupāsanatthaṃ: for the purpose of revering the Teacher's relics. Their side was: 'The relics rightfully belong to them.'

237. Doṇagajjitaṃ nāma avoca satthu avatthattayūpasaṃhitaṃ. Etadatthameva hi bhagavā maggaṃ gacchanto “pacchato āgacchanto doṇo brāhmaṇo yāva me padavaḷañjaṃ passati, tāva mā vigacchatū”ti adhiṭṭhāya aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisīdi. Doṇopi kho [P 2.0245] brāhmaṇo “imāni sadevake loke aggapuggalassa padānī”ti sallakkhento padānusārena satthu santikaṃ upagacchi, satthāpissa dhammaṃ desesi, tenapi so bhagavati niviṭṭhasaddho ahosi. Etadavoca, kiṃ avocāti āha “suṇantu…pe… avocā”ti.

237. The Teacher spoke what is called the Doṇagajjita, connected with the threefold occasion. For this very purpose, the Blessed One, while walking the path, resolved, 'Until the brahmin Doṇa, coming behind me, sees my footprint, may it not disappear,' and sat down at the foot of a certain tree. The brahmin Doṇa, reflecting, 'These are the footprints of the foremost person in the world with its devas,' followed the footprints and approached the Teacher. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma, and he too became firmly devoted to the Blessed One. This he said, what did he say? He said, 'Listen...'

Kāyena ekasannipātā vācāya ekavacanā abhinnavacanā evaṃ samaggā hotha. Tassa panidaṃ kāraṇanti āha “sammodamānā”ti. Tenāha “cittenāpi aññamaññaṃ sammodamānā hothā”ti.

Be assembled together in body, speaking with one and unbroken voice—thus be in concord. The reason for this is stated: 'Agreeing.' Therefore, it is said, 'Agree with each other even in mind.'

238. Tato tato samāgatasaṅghānanti tato tato attano vasanaṭṭhānato samāgantvā sannipatitabhāvena samāgatasaṅghānaṃ. Tathā samāpatitasamūhabhāvena samāgatagaṇānaṃ. Vacanasampaṭicchanena paṭissuṇitvā.

238. Tato tato samāgatasaṅghānaṃ: of the Sanghas assembled from here and there, by way of having assembled and convened from their respective dwelling places here and there. Likewise, of the groups assembled by way of having gathered as a multitude. Vacanasampaṭicchanena: having accepted the words.

Dhātuthūpapūjāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Worship of Relic Stupas

239. Yakkhaggāho devatāveso. Khipitakaṃ dhātukkhobhaṃ uppādetvā khipitakarogo. Arocako āhārassa aruccanarogo.

239. Yakkhaggāho: possession by a spirit, possession by a deity. Khipitakaṃ: the sneezing sickness, caused by a disturbance of the bodily elements. Arocako: lack of appetite, the sickness of disinclination for food.

Sattamadivaseti [V 2.0173] sattavassasattamāsato parato sattame divase. Balānurūpenāti vibhavabalānurūpena.

Sattamadivase: on the seventh day after seven years and seven months. Balānurūpena: according to one's wealth and power.

Pacchā saṅgītikārakāti dutiyaṃ tatiyaṃ saṅgītikārakā. Dhātūnaṃ antarāyaṃ disvāti tattha tattha cetiye yathāpatiṭṭhāpitabhāveneva ṭhitānaṃ [M 2.0192] dhātūnaṃ micchādiṭṭhikānaṃ vasena antarāyaṃ disvā, mahādhātunidhānena sammadeva rakkhitānaṃ anāgate asokena dhammaraññā tato uddharitvā vitthāritabhāve kate sadevakassa lokassa hitasukhāvahabhāvañca disvāti adhippāyo. Paricaraṇamattamevāti gahetvā paricaritabbadhātumattameva. Rājūnaṃ hatthe ṭhapetvā, na cetiyesu. Tathā hi pacchā asokamahārājā cetiyesu dhātūnaṃ na labhati.

Pacchā saṅgītikārakā: the compilers of the second and third councils. Dhātūnaṃ antarāyaṃ disvā: seeing the danger to the relics—seeing the danger from those with wrong views to the relics which were established in various shrines just as they had been originally enshrined, and seeing also that the great treasury of relics, properly protected, would in the future be taken out from there by King Asoka Dhammarājā and spread widely, bringing welfare and happiness to the world with its devas—this is the meaning. Paricaraṇamattameva: only the measure of relics suitable for taking and honoring. They were placed in the hands of kings, not in shrines. Thus, later, King Asoka the Great did not find the relics in the shrines.

Purimaṃ [P 2.0246] purimaṃ katassa gaṇhanayogyaṃ pacchimaṃ pacchimaṃ kārento aṭṭha aṭṭha haricandanādimaye karaṇḍe ca thūpe ca kāresi. Lohitacandanamayādīsupi eseva nayo. Maṇikaraṇḍesūti lohitaṅkamasāragallaphalikamaye ṭhapetvā avasesamaṇivicittakesu karaṇḍesu.

Making each successive one suitable for receiving the one made before it, he had eight caskets and eight stupas made of yellow sandalwood and so on. The same method applies to those made of red sandalwood and so on. Maṇikaraṇḍesu: in the remaining caskets variegated with jewels, having placed them in those made of ruby, coral, and crystal.

Thūpārāmacetiyappamāṇanti devānaṃpiyatissamahārājena kāritacetiyappamāṇaṃ.

The measure of the Thūpārāma Cetiya means the measure of the cetiya built by the great king Devānampiyatissa.

Mālā mā milāyantūti “yāva asoko dhammarājā bahi cetiyāni kāretuṃ ito dhātuyo uddharissati, tāva mālā mā milāyantū”ti adhiṭṭhahitvā. Āviñchanarajjuyanti aggaḷāviñchanarajjuyaṃ. Kuñcikamuddikanti dvāravivaraṇatthaṃ kuñcikañceva muddikañca.

Mālā mā milāyantū: having resolved, 'Until King Asoka Dhammarājā takes out the relics from here to build cetiyas outside, may the garlands not wither.' Āviñchanarajjuyaṃ: on the bolt-pulling rope. Kuñcikamuddikaṃ: both the key and the seal, for opening the door.

Vāḷasaṅghātayantanti kukkulaṃ paṭibhayadassanaṃ aññamaññapaṭibaddhagamanāditāya saṅghāṭitarūpakayantaṃ yojesi. Tenāha “kaṭṭharūpakānī”tiādi. Āṇiyā bandhitvāti anekakaṭṭharūpavicittayantaṃ attano devānubhāvena ekāya eva āṇiyā bandhitvā vissakammo devalokameva gato. “Samantato”tiādi pana tasmiṃ dhātunidāne ajātasattuno kiccavisesānuṭṭhānadassanaṃ.

Vāḷasaṅghātayantaṃ: he devised a terrifying mechanism of connected figures, terrifying to behold, by means of their interconnected movement, etc. Hence it is said, 'wooden figures,' etc. Āṇiyā bandhitvā: having bound the intricate mechanism of many wooden figures with just one pin by his divine power, Vissakamma went to the deva world. 'Samantato' and so on shows Ajātasattu’s failure to perform the specific duties related to that relic deposit.

“Asukaṭṭhāne nāma dhātunidhāna”nti raññā pucchite “tasmiṃ sannipāte visesalābhino nāhesu”nti keci. “Attānaṃ nigūhitvā tassa vuḍḍhatarassa vacanaṃ nissāya vīmaṃsanto jānissatīti na kathesu”nti apare. Yakkhadāsaketi upahārādividhinā devatāvesanake bhūtāviggāhake.

'At such and such a place is the relic deposit'—when asked by the king, some said, 'At that gathering we gained nothing special.' Others said, 'They concealed themselves, and relying on the elder's words, he would know by investigating, so they did not speak.' Yakkhadāsaka: one who causes divine possession and seizes spirits by means of offerings and the like.

Imaṃ [P 2.0247][V 2.0174] padanti “evametaṃ bhūtapubba”nti dutiyasaṅgītikārehi ṭhapitaṃ imaṃ padaṃ. Mahādhātunidhānampi tassa atthaṃ katvā tatiyasaṅgītikārāpi ṭhapayiṃsu.

Imaṃ padaṃ: this phrase, 'thus it was in the past,' was established by the compilers of the Second Council. The compilers of the Third Council also established it, having made its meaning the great relic deposit.

Mahāparinibbānasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

The Explanation of the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta Clarifying the Hidden Meaning.

4. Mahāsudassanasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on the Great King of Glory

Kusāvatīrājadhānīvaṇṇanā

Description of the Royal City of Kusāvatī

242. Sovaṇṇamayāti [P 2.0248][V 2.0175][M 2.0193] suvaṇṇamayā. Ayaṃ pākāroti sabbaratanamayo pākāro. Tayo tayoti anto ca tayo, bahi ca tayoti tayo tayo.

242. Sovaṇṇamayā means made of gold. This wall means a wall made entirely of jewels. Tayo tayo means three inside and three outside, thus three and three.

Esikatthambho indakhīlo nagarasobhano alaṅkāratthambho. Aṅgīyati ñāyati puthulabhāvo etenāti aṅgaṃ, parikkhepo. Tiporisaṃ aṅgaṃ etissāti tiporisaṅgā. Tenāha “tenā”tiādi. Tena pañcahatthappamāṇena tiporisena. Paṇṇaphalesupīti sabbaratanamayānaṃ tālānaṃ paṇṇaphalesupi. Eseva nayoti “paṇṇesu ekaṃ pattakaṃ sovaṇṇamayaṃ, ekaṃ rūpiyamayaṃ. Phalesupi eko lekhābhāvo sovaṇṇamayo, eko rūpiyamayo”tiādiko ayamattho atidiṭṭho. Pākārantareti dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ pākārānaṃ antare. Ekekā hutvā ṭhitā tālapanti.

The main pillar (esikatthambho) is the Indakhīla pillar, the ornamental pillar that beautifies the city. Aṅga means a part, an extent, because its breadth is known by it. Tiporisaṅgā means having a breadth of three porisas. Therefore it is said, 'by that,' etc. By that three porisas, which is a measure of five cubits. Even in leaves and fruits means even in the leaves and fruits of the palm trees made entirely of jewels. This is the method means this meaning, 'among the leaves, one leaf is made of gold, one of silver; and among the fruits, one decorative streak is made of gold, one of silver,' etc., is indicated. Between the ramparts means in the space between two ramparts. A row of palm trees stood, each one separate.

Chekoti paṭu suvisado, so cassa paṭubhāvo manosāroti āha “sundaro”ti. Rañjetunti rāgaṃ uppādetuṃ. Khamatevāti rocateva. Na bībhacchetīti na tajjeti, sotasukhabhāvato piyāyitabbo ca hoti. Kumbhathuṇadaddarikādi ekatalaṃ tūriyaṃ. Ubhayatalaṃ pākaṭameva. Sabbato pariyonaddhaṃ caturassaambaṇakaṃ, paṇavādi ca. Vaṃsādīti ādi-saddena saṅkhādikaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Sumucchitassāti suṭṭhu pariyattassa. Pamāṇeti nātidaḷhanātisithilatāsaṅkhāte majjhime mucchanappamāṇe[P 2.0249]. Hatthaṃ vā pādaṃ vā cāletvāti hatthalayapādalaye sajjetvā. Naccantāti sākhānaccaṃ naccantā.

Cheko means skillful and very clear; his skill is the essence of his mind, hence it is said 'beautiful'. Rañjetuṃ means to arouse passion. Khamateva means it is pleasing indeed, it is agreeable. Na bībhaccheti means it does not repel, it does not frighten, and it should be loved because it is pleasing to the ear. Kumbhathuṇadaddarikādi: single-faced instruments such as pot-drums, pillar-drums, and tambourines. Ubhayatalaṃ: double-faced instruments are well-known. Sabbato pariyonaddhaṃ: completely enclosed quadrangular drums, such as the paṇava, etc. Vaṃsādi: the term 'etc.' includes conches and the like. Sumucchitassa means well-tuned, well-arranged. Pamāṇe: the measure refers to the middle state of tuning, described as neither too tight nor too loose. Hatthaṃ vā pādaṃ vā cāletvā means arranging the hand rhythms and foot rhythms. Naccantā means dancing branch dances.

Cakkaratanavaṇṇanā

Description of the Wheel-Treasure

243. Uposathaṃ [V 2.0176] vuccati aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ sabbadivasesu gahaṭṭhehi rakkhitabbasīlaṃ, samādānavasena taṃ tassa atthīti uposathiko, tassa uposathikassa. Tenāha “samādinnauposathaṅgassā”ti. Tadāti tasmiṃ [M 2.0194] kāle. Kasmiṃ pana kāleti? Yasmiṃ kāle cakkavattibhāvasaṃvattaniyadānasīlādipuññasambhārasamudāgamasampanno pūritacakkavattivatto kāladīpadesavisesapaccājātiyā ceva kularūpabhogādhipateyyādiguṇavisesasampattiyā ca tadanurūpe attabhāve ṭhito hoti, tasmiṃ kāle. Tādise hi kāle cakkavattibhāvī purisaviseso yathāvuttaguṇasamannāgato rājā khattiyo muddhāvasitto visuddhasīlo anuposathaṃ satasahassavissajjanādinā sammāpaṭipattiṃ paṭipajjati, na yadā cakkaratanaṃ uppajjati, tadā eva. Ime ca visesā sabbacakkavattīnaṃ sādhāraṇavasena vuttā. Tenāha “pātova…pe… dhammatā”ti. Bodhisattānaṃ pana cakkavattibhāvāvahaguṇāpi cakkavattiguṇāpi sātisayāva honti.

243. Uposatha is said to be the eight-factored virtue to be observed by householders on all days; and one who possesses it by way of undertaking it is an uposathika, hence 'of the uposathika'. Therefore it is said, 'of one who has undertaken the Uposatha factors'. Tadā means at that time. But at what time? At the time when one, endowed with the accumulation of merit such as generosity and virtue conducive to the state of a wheel-turning monarch, fulfilling the duties of a wheel-turning king, stands in a suitable state of existence distinguished by excellence of time, place, specific rebirth, and qualities such as family, beauty, wealth, and sovereignty—at that time. For at such a time, a distinguished man destined to be a wheel-turning monarch, endowed with the aforementioned qualities—a consecrated Khattiya king of purified virtue—on the Uposatha day undertakes right conduct by generosity involving the distribution of a hundred thousand, and so forth, not only when the wheel-treasure appears. These distinctions are stated as common to all wheel-turning monarchs. Therefore it is said: 'In the morning...by nature'. However, for the Bodhisattas, the qualities that bring about wheel-turning sovereignty and the qualities of a wheel-turning monarch are even more surpassing.

Vuttappakārapuññakammapaccayanti cakkavattibhāvāvahadānadamasaṃyamādipuññakammahetukaṃ. Nīlamaṇisaṅghātasadisanti indanīlamaṇisañcayasamānaṃ. Dibbānubhāvayuttattāti dassaneyyatā, manuññaghosatā, ākāsagāmitā, obhāsavissajjanā, appaṭighātatā, rañño icchitatthanipphattikāraṇatāti evamādīhi dibbasadisehi ānubhāvehi samannāgatattā, etena dibbaṃ viyāti dibbanti dasseti. Na hi taṃ devalokapariyāpannaṃ. Sahassaṃ arā etassāti vā sahassāraṃ. Sabbehi ākārehīti sabbehi sundarehi paripuṇṇāvayave lakkhaṇasampanne cakke icchitabbehi ākārehi. Paripūranti paripuṇṇaṃ, sā cassā pāripūriṃ idāneva vitthāressati.

Vuttappakārapuññakammapaccaya means caused by meritorious deeds such as giving, self-control, and restraint, which lead to the state of a wheel-turning monarch. Nīlamaṇisaṅghātasadisa means resembling a collection of sapphire gems. Dibbānubhāvayutta means endowed with divine powers, because it is endowed with divine-like powers such as being pleasing to see, having a delightful sound, moving through the sky, emitting light, being unobstructed, and fulfilling the king's desires; by this it shows that it is divine, as it were. For it does not belong to the realm of gods. Sahassāraṃ means having a thousand spokes; or, it is so called because 'it has a thousand spokes'. Sabbehi ākārehi means in all desirable aspects of a wheel that is beautiful, complete in its parts, and endowed with auspicious marks. Paripūraṃ means complete; its completeness he will now elaborate.

Panāḷīti chiddaṃ. Suddhasiniddhadantapantiyā nibbivarāyāti [P 2.0250] adhippāyo. Tassā pana panāḷiyā samantato passassa rajatamayattā sārarajatamayā vuttā. Yasmā cassa cakkassa rathacakkassa viya antobhāvo nāma natthi, tasmā vuttaṃ “ubhosupi bāhirantesū”ti. Kataparikkhepā hoti panāḷīti yojanā. Nābhipanāḷiparikkhepapaṭṭesūti nābhiparikkhepapaṭṭe ceva nābhiyā panāḷiparikkhepapaṭṭe ca.

Panāḷī means an opening or hole. The intention is that the row of teeth is pure, glossy, and without gaps. That panāḷī is said to be made of solid silver because its sides are entirely made of silver. And since that wheel has no inner part, like a chariot wheel, therefore it is said 'on both outer edges'. The interpretation is: the panāḷī has a circumference. Nābhipanāḷiparikkhepapaṭṭesu means on the circumference band of the hub and on the circumference band of the hub's panāḷī.

Tesanti arānaṃ. Ghaṭakā nāma alaṅkārabhūtā khuddakapuṇṇaghaṭā. Tathā maṇikā nāma muttāvaḷikā. Paricchedalekhā tassa tassa paricchedadassanavasena ṭhitā paricchinnalekhā. Ādi-saddena [V 2.0177] mālākammādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Suvibhattānevāti aññamaññaṃ asaṃkiṇṇattā suṭṭhu vibhattāni.

Tesaṃ means of the spokes. Ghaṭakā are small ornamental full pots. Similarly, maṇikā are strings of pearls. Paricchedalekhā are distinct lines standing to show the divisions of each. The word 'ādi' includes garland-work and the like. Suvibhattāni means well-divided, being unmixed with one another.

“Surattā”tiādīsu [M 2.0195] surattaggahaṇena mahānāmavaṇṇataṃ paṭikkhipati, suddhaggahaṇena saṃṅkiliṭṭhataṃ, siniddhaggahaṇena lūkhataṃ. Kāmaṃ tassa cakkaratanassa nemimaṇḍalaṃ asandhikameva nibbattaṃ, sabbatthakameva pana kevalaṃ pavāḷavaṇṇena ca sobhatīti pakaticakkassa sandhiyuttaṭṭhāne surattasuvaṇṇapaṭṭādimayāhi vaṭṭaparicchedalekhāhi paññāyamānāhi sasandhikā viya dissantīti āha “sandhīsu panassā”tiādi.

In 'brightly colored,' etc., the term 'brightly colored' rejects the color of safflower dye, the term 'pure' rejects impurity, and the term 'glossy' rejects roughness. Although the rim of that wheel-jewel is indeed seamless, and it shines everywhere with a purely coral color, yet at the places where a natural wheel has joints, it appears as if it has joints due to the circular boundary lines manifested by bright red gold bands, etc. Hence, he said, 'at its joints, however,' etc.

Nemimaṇḍalapiṭṭhiyanti nemimaṇḍalassa piṭṭhipadese. Ākāsacāribhāvato hissa tattha vātaggāhī pavāḷadaṇḍo hoti. Dasannaṃ dasannaṃ arānaṃ antareti dasannaṃ dasannaṃ arānaṃ antare samīpe padese. Chiddamaṇḍalakhacitoti maṇḍalasaṇṭhānachiddavicitto. Sukusalasamannāhatassāti suṭṭhu kusalena sippinā pahatassa, vāditassāti attho. Vaggūti manoramo. Rajanīyoti suṇantānaṃ rāguppādako. Kamanīyoti kanto. Samosaritakusumadāmāti olambitasugandhakusumadāmā. Nemiparikkhepassāti [P 2.0251] nemipariyantaparikkhepassa. Nābhipanāḷiyā dvinnaṃ passānaṃ vasena “dvinnampi nābhipanāḷīna”nti vuttaṃ. Ekā eva hi sā panāḷi. Yehīti yehi dvīhi mukhehi. Puna yehīti yehi muttakalāpehi.

Nemimaṇḍalapiṭṭhiyaṃ means on the back of the rim-circle. Because it moves through the sky, it has a wind-catching coral-staff there. Dasannaṃ dasannaṃ arānaṃ antare means in the vicinity or area between every ten spokes. Chiddamaṇḍalakhacita means variegated with holes shaped like circles. Sukusalasamannāhatassa means well-struck by a skilled artisan, that is, played. Vaggū means delightful. Rajanīya means arousing passion in listeners. Kamanīya means lovely. Samosaritakusumadāmā means hung with fragrant flower garlands. Nemiparikkhepassa means of the circumference around the edge of the rim. Regarding the navel-tube, 'of both navel-tubes' is said with reference to the two sides, but in reality, there is only one tube. Yehi means by those two openings. Again, yehi means by those clusters of pearls.

Odhāpayamānanti sotuṃ avahitāni kurumānaṃ.

Odhāpayamānaṃ means making them attentive to listen.

Cando purato cakkaratanaṃ pacchāti evaṃ pubbāpariyena pubbāparabhāvena.

Cando purato cakkaratanaṃ pacchā means the moon in front and the wheel-treasure behind; thus in sequence, by the state of being front and back.

Antepurassāti anurādhapure rañño antepurassa. Uttarasīhapañjarasadiseti tadā rañño pāsāde tādisassa uttaradisāya sīhapañjarassa labbhamānattā vuttaṃ. Sukhena sakkāti kiñci anāruhitvā, sarīrañca anullaṅghitvā yathāṭhiteneva hatthena pupphamuṭṭhiyo khipitvā sukhena sakkā hoti pūjetuṃ.

Antepurassa means of the king's inner palace in Anurādhapura. Uttarasīhapañjarasadisa means like the northern lion window; it is said thus because at that time such a lion window, facing the northern direction, was to be found in the king's palace. Sukhena sakkā means it is easily possible to make offerings by throwing handfuls of flowers with the hand, without climbing up anything or stretching the body, just as one stands.

Nānāvirāgaratanappabhāsamujjalanti nānāvidhavicittavaṇṇaratanobhāsapabhassaraṃ. Ākāsaṃ abbhuggantvā pavatteti āgantvā ṭhitaṭṭhānato upari ākāsaṃ abbhuggantvā pavatte.

Nānāvirāgaratanappabhāsamujjalaṃ means shining with the radiance of various precious gems, dazzling with the light of diverse and varied-colored jewels. Ākāsaṃ abbhuggantvā pavatte means it rises into the sky and proceeds, having ascended into the sky from the place where it had arrived and stood.

244. Rājāyuttāti [V 2.0178] rañño kicce āyuttakapurisā.

244. Rājāyuttā means men engaged in the king's business.

Sineruṃ [M 2.0196] vāmapassena katvā tassa dhurataraṃ gacchanto “vāmapassena sineruṃ pahāyā”ti vuttaṃ.

Sineruṃ vāmapassena katvā tassa dhurataraṃ gacchanto means going far beyond Mount Sineru, having made it on his left side. Hence it is said, 'having left Mount Sineru on the left'.

Vinibbedhenāti tiriyaṃ vinivijjhanavasena. Sannivesakkhamoti khandhāvārasannivesayogyo. Sulabhāhārupakaraṇoti sukheneva laddhabbadhaññagorasadārutiṇādibhojanasādhano.

Vinibbedhena means by penetrating transversely. Sannivesakkhama means suitable for arranging a camp. Sulabhāhārupakaraṇa means having easily obtainable means for food such as grain, dairy products, wood, and grass.

Paracakkanti parassa rañño senā, āṇā vā.

Paracakkaṃ means the army of another king, or his command.

Āgamananandanoti āgamanena nandijanano. Gamanena socetīti gamanasocano. Upakappethāti uparūpari kappetha, saṃvidahatha upanethāti attho. Upaparikkhitvāti hetutopi sabhāvatopi phalatopi diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikādiādīnavatopi [P 2.0252] vīmaṃsitvā. Vibhāventi paññāya atthaṃ vibhūtaṃ karontīti vibhāvino, paññavanto. Anuyantāti anuvattakā, anuvattakabhāveneva, pana rañño ca mahānubhāvena te jigucchanavasena pāpato anoramantāpi ekacce ottappavasena oramantīti veditabbaṃ.

Āgamananandana means generating joy by arrival. Gamanasocana means causing grief by departure. Upakappetha means prepare again and again, arrange, bring near—this is the meaning. Upaparikkhitvā means having investigated through cause, inherent nature, result, and the dangers of consequences in this life, the next life, etc. Vibhāvino means those who make the meaning clear with wisdom; they are the wise. Anuyantā means followers, those who comply. However, it should be understood that due to the king's great influence, some, even if not refraining from evil out of aversion, do restrain themselves out of moral dread.

Ogacchamānanti osīdantaṃ. Yojanamattanti vitthārato yojanamattaṃ padesaṃ. Gambhīrabhāvena pana yathā bhūmi dissati, evaṃ ogacchati. Tenāha “mahāsamuddatala”ntiādi. Ante cakkaratanaṃ udakena senāya anajjhottharaṇatthaṃ. Puratthimo mahāsamuddo pariyanto etassāti puratthimamahāsamuddapariyanto, taṃ puratthimamahāsamuddapariyantaṃ, puratthimamahāsamuddaṃ pariyantaṃ katvāti attho.

Ogacchamānaṃ means receding. Yojanamattaṃ means an area extending a league in breadth. However, due to its depth, it recedes in such a way that the ground appears. Hence it is said, 'the surface of the great ocean,' etc. At the edge, the wheel-treasure is to prevent the water from overwhelming the army. Puratthimamahāsamuddapariyanto means 'that which has the eastern great ocean as its boundary'; the meaning is having made the eastern great ocean the limit.

Cāturantāyāti catusamuddantāya, puratthimadisādicatukoṭṭhāsantāya vā. Sobhayamānaṃ viyāti viya-saddo nipātamattaṃ. Attano acchariyaguṇehi sobhantameva hi taṃ tiṭṭhati. Pāḷiyampi hi “upasobhayamānaṃ” tveva vuttaṃ.

Cāturantāya means extending to the four oceans or to the limits of the four cardinal directions. Sobhayamānaṃ viya means 'as if adorning'; the word 'viya' is merely a particle. Indeed, it stands adorned by its own marvelous qualities. In the Pāli text itself, it is stated as 'upasobhayamānaṃ' (thoroughly adorning).

Hatthiratanavaṇṇanā

Description of the Elephant-Treasure

246. Haricandanādīhīti ādi-saddena catujjātiyagandhādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Āgamanaṃ cintethāti [V 2.0179] vadanti cakkavattivattassa pūritatāya paricitattā. Kāḷatilakādīnaṃ abhāvena visuddhasetasarīro. Sattapatiṭṭhoti bhūmiphusanakehi vāladhi, varaṅgaṃ, hatthoti imehi ca tīhi, catūhi pādehi cāti [M 2.0197] sattahi avayavehi patiṭṭhitattā sattapatiṭṭho. Sabbakaniṭṭhoti sabbehi chaddantakulahatthīhi hīno. Uposathakulā sabbajeṭṭhoti uposathakulato āgacchanto tattha sabbappadhāno āgacchatīti yojanā. Vuttanayenāti “mahādānaṃ datvā”tiādinā vuttena nayena. Cakkavattīnaṃ, cakkavattiputtānañca cakkavattiṃ uddissa cintayantānaṃ āgacchati. Apanetvāti attano ānubhāvena apanetvā. Gandhameva hi tassa itare hatthī na sahanti.

246. 'With yellow sandalwood, etc.'—the word 'etc.' includes the four kinds of fragrances, etc. 'Consider the arrival'—they say this because they are familiar with and have fulfilled the duty of a wheel-turning monarch. 'Pure white body'—because of the absence of black sesame-like spots, etc. 'Seven supports' means supported by seven parts: namely, the tail (touching the ground), the genital organ, the trunk, and the four feet—thus, by these seven limbs. 'Inferior to all' means lower than all Chaddanta lineage elephants. 'Foremost of the Uposatha lineage' means the most distinguished one coming from the Uposatha lineage comes—this is the connection. 'In the manner stated' means in the way described, such as 'having given a great gift,' etc. It comes to wheel-turning monarchs and the sons of wheel-turning monarchs who contemplate the wheel-turning monarch. 'Removing' means removing them by his own power—for other elephants cannot bear even his fragrance.

Gharadhenuvacchako viyāti ghare paricitadhenuyā tattheva [P 2.0253] jātasaṃvaddhavacchako viya. Sakalapathavinti sakalaṃ jambudīpasaññitaṃ pathaviṃ.

Gharadhenuvacchako viya means like a calf born and raised in the same house as a familiar cow.

Assaratanavaṇṇanā

Description of the Horse-Treasure

247. Sindhavakulatoti sindhavassājānīyakulato.

247. Sindhavakulato means from the lineage of Sindhu thoroughbred horses.

Maṇiratanavaṇṇanā

Description of the Jewel-Treasure

248. Sakaṭanābhisamapariṇāhanti pariṇāhato mahāsakaṭassa nābhiyā samappamāṇaṃ. Ubhosu antesūti heṭṭhā, upari cāti dvīsu antesu. Kaṇṇikapariyantatoti dvinnaṃ kañcanapadumānaṃ kaṇṇikāya pariyantato. Muttājālake ṭhapetvāti suvisuddhe muttamaye jālake patiṭṭhāpetvā. Aruṇuggamanavelā viyāti aruṇuggamanasīsena sūriyaudayakkhaṇaṃ upalakkheti.

248. Sakaṭanābhisamapariṇāhaṃ means equal in circumference to the hub of a great cart. Ubhosu antesu means at both ends, that is, at the lower and upper ends. Kaṇṇikapariyantato means from the edge of the pericarp, that is, from the boundary of the pericarps of the two golden lotuses. Muttājālake ṭhapetvā means having placed it on a net of pearls, that is, having established it upon a perfectly pure net made of pearls. Aruṇuggamanavelā viya means like the time of dawn's rising; it signifies the moment of sunrise by the 'head' of the dawn's arising.

Itthiratanavaṇṇanā

Description of the Woman-Treasure

249. “Itthiratanaṃ pātubhavatī”ti vatvā kutassā pātubhāvoti dassetuṃ “maddarājakulato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Maddaraṭṭhaṃ kira jambudīpe abhirūpānaṃ itthīnaṃ uppattiṭṭhānaṃ. Tathā hi “siñcayamahārājassa devī, vessantaramahārājassa devī, bhaddakāpilānī”ti evamādi itthiratanaṃ maddaraṭṭhe eva uppannaṃ. Puññānubhāvenāti cakkavattirañño puññatejena.

249. Having said, 'The woman-treasure appears,' to show from where her appearance originates, it is stated, 'from the Madda royal family,' and so on. The Madda country, it is said, is in Jambudīpa, a place of origin for beautiful women. Thus indeed, 'the queen of King Siñcaya, the queen of King Vessantara, Bhaddakāpilānī,' and so on—such woman-treasures arose in the Madda country alone. Puññānubhāvena means by the majestic power of the wheel-turning king's merit.

Saṇṭhānapāripūriyāti hatthapādādisarīrāvayavānaṃ susaṇṭhitāya. Avayavapāripūriyā hi samudāyapāripūrisiddhi[V 2.0180]. Rūpanti sarīraṃ “rūpaṃ tveva saṅkhaṃ gacchatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.306) viya. Dassanīyāti surūpabhāvena passitabbayuttā. Tenāha [M 2.0198] “dissamānāvā”tiādi. Somanassavasena cittaṃ pasādeti yoniso cintentānaṃ kammaphalasaddhāya vasena. Pasādāvahattāti kāraṇavacanena yathā pāsādikatāya vaṇṇapokkharatāsiddhi vuttā, evaṃ dassanīyatāya pāsādikatāsiddhi, abhirūpatāya ca dassanīyatāsiddhi vattabbāti nayaṃ dasseti. Paṭilomato vā vaṇṇapokkharatāya [P 2.0254] pāsādikatāsiddhi, pāsādikatāya dassanīyatāsiddhi, dassanīyatāya abhirūpatāsiddhi yojetabbā. Evaṃ sarīrasampattivasena abhirūpatādike dassetvā idāni sarīre dosābhāvavasenapi te dassetuṃ “abhirūpā vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yathā pamāṇayuttā, evaṃ ārohapariṇāhayogato ca pāsādikā nātidīghatādayo, evaṃ manussānaṃ dibbarūpatāsampattipīti “appattā dibbavaṇṇa”nti vuttaṃ.

'Completeness of form' means by the well-formedness of the body's limbs, such as hands and feet. For the completeness of the parts leads to the accomplishment of the completeness of the whole. 'Form' refers to the body, as in the phrase 'it is reckoned as form' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.306) and so on. 'Worthy of sight' means suitable to be seen due to having a beautiful appearance. Therefore, it is said, 'being seen,' etc. It gladdens the mind through joy for those who reflect wisely, by way of faith in the fruit of kamma. 'Because it brings delight' is a causal expression: just as the attainment of a beautiful complexion is said to be due to being delightful, so too the attainment of being delightful is said to be due to being worthy of sight, and the attainment of being worthy of sight is said to be due to being beautiful—this illustrates the method. Alternatively, in reverse order: the attainment of being delightful is to be connected with a beautiful complexion, the attainment of being worthy of sight with being delightful, and the attainment of being beautiful with being worthy of sight. Having thus shown beauty and the like by way of bodily perfection, now, to show these qualities also by way of the absence of defects in the body, it is said, 'or beautiful,' etc. Therein, just as they are endowed with proportion, so too they are delightful due to height and girth, not being excessively tall, etc., and since humans do not attain the perfection of divine form, it is said, 'not having attained divine complexion.'

Ārohasampatti vuttā ubbedhena pāsādikabhāvato. Pariṇāhasampatti vuttā kisathūladosābhāvato. Vaṇṇasampatti vuttā vivaṇṇatābhāvato. Kāyavipattiyāti sarīradosassa. Satavāravihatassāti sattakkhattuṃ vihatassa, “satavāravihatassā”ti ca idaṃ kappāsapicuvasena vuttaṃ, tūlapicuno pana vihananameva natthi. Kuṅkumatagaraturukkhayavanapupphāni catujjāti. “Tamālatagaraturukkhayavanapupphānī”ti apare.

The perfection of height is spoken of due to its pleasing appearance in elevation. The perfection of girth is spoken of due to the absence of the defect of being too thin or too stout. The perfection of complexion is spoken of due to the absence of discoloration. 'Bodily defect' means a flaw in the body. 'Struck a hundred times' means struck seven times; and this 'struck a hundred times' is said with regard to a ball of cotton, but for a ball of silk-cotton, there is no striking at all. Saffron, tagara, frankincense, and yavana flowers are the four kinds. Others say, 'tamāla, tagara, frankincense, and yavana flowers.'

Aggidaḍḍhā viyāti āsanagatena agginā daḍḍhā viya. Paṭhamamevāti rājānaṃ disvāpi kiccantarappasutā ahutvā kiccantarato paṭhamameva, dassanasamakālaṃ evāti attho. Rañño nisajjāya pacchā nipātanaṃ nisīdanaṃ sīlaṃ etissāti pacchānipātinī. Taṃ taṃ attanā rañño kātabbakiccaṃ “kiṃ karomī”ti pucchitabbatāya kiṃ karaṇaṃ paṭisāvetīti kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī.

'As if burned by fire' means as if burned by a fire that has taken hold. 'First indeed' means not being absorbed in other duties even upon seeing the king, but before any other duty, at the very moment of seeing; that is the meaning. She whose habit is to sit down after the king has sat down is a `pacchānipātinī`. She is a `kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī` (one who is responsive to commands) because she inquires, 'What shall I do?' regarding each and every duty to be done by her for the king, and thus reports what is to be done.

Mātugāmo nāma yebhuyyena saṭhajātiko, itthiratanassa pana taṃ natthīti dassetuṃ “svāssā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Women, as a rule, are generally of a deceitful nature. But to show that this is not so for the woman-jewel, 'she for him,' and so on is said.

Guṇāti rūpaguṇā ceva ācāraguṇā ca. Purimakammānubhāvenāti katassa purimakammassānubhāvena itthiratanassa [P 2.0255] tabbhāvasaṃvattaniyassa purimakammassa ānubhāvena. Cakkavattinopi parivārasampattisaṃvattaniyaṃ puññakammaṃ tādisassa phalavisesassa upanissayo hotiyeva. Tenāha “cakkavattino [M 2.0199] puññaṃ upanissāyā”ti, etena sesesupi saviññāṇakaratanesu attano [V 2.0181] kammavasena nibbattesupi tesaṃ tesaṃ visesānaṃ tadupanissayatā vibhāvitā evāti daṭṭhabbā. Pubbe ekadesavasena labbhamānā pāripūrī rañño cakkavattibhāvūpagamanato paṭṭhāya sabbākāraparipūrā jātā.

'Virtues' means virtues of beauty and also virtues of conduct. 'By the power of past deeds' means by the power of the past deeds done, specifically the past deeds that bring about the state of being a woman-jewel. Even the meritorious deed of a wheel-turning monarch, which brings about the perfection of his retinue, is indeed a support for such a special result. Therefore it is said, 'relying on the merit of the wheel-turning monarch,' and by this, it should be understood that, even for the other sentient jewels, although they arise by their own kamma, the fact that his merit is a support for their respective special qualities is indeed made clear. The completeness, previously obtained in a partial way, became fully complete in every way from the time the king attained the state of a wheel-turning monarch.

Gahapatiratanavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Householder Jewel

250. Pakatiyā vāti sabhāveneva cakkaratanapātubhāvato pubbepi. Yādisaṃ rañño cakkavattissa puññabalaṃ nissāya yathāvuttā cakkaratanānubhāvanibbatti, tādisaṃ etassa puññabalaṃ nissāya gahapatiratanassa kammavipākajaṃ dibbacakkhuṃ nibbattetīti āha “cakkaratanānubhāvasahita”nti. Kāraṇassa hi ekasantatipatitatāya, phalassa ca samānakālikatāya tathāvacanaṃ.

250. 'Or by nature' means by its very essence, even before the appearance of the Wheel-Jewel. Just as the arising of the power of the Wheel-Jewel as described occurs for the wheel-turning king by relying on the power of his merit, so too, by relying on the power of this one's merit, the divine eye, born from the result of kamma, arises for the Householder Jewel. Therefore, it is said, 'accompanied by the power of the Wheel-Jewel.' For because the cause falls into a single continuity and the fruit is simultaneous, the statement is made thus.

Pariṇāyakaratanavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Counselor Jewel

251. “Ayaṃ dhammo, ayaṃ adhammo”tiādinā kammassakatāvabodhanasaṅkhātassa paṇḍitabhāvassa atthitāya paṇḍito. Bāhusaccabyattiyā byatto. Sabhāvasiddhāya medhāsaṅkhātāya pakatipaññāya atthitāya medhāvī. Attano yāthāvabuddhamatthaṃ paresaṃ vibhāvetuṃ pakāsetuṃ samatthatāya vibhāvī. Vavatthapetunti nicchituṃ.

251. He is wise (`paṇḍito`) because of the existence of the state of wisdom, which consists of understanding the ownership of kamma, as in 'This is the Dhamma, this is not the Dhamma,' etc. He is skilled (`byatto`) due to his competence in extensive learning. He is intelligent (`medhāvī`) because of the existence of natural wisdom, which consists of innate intelligence. He is an elucidator (`vibhāvī`) because of his capability to make clear and explain to others the meaning as he has understood it. 'To determine' means to decide.

Catuiddhisamannāgatavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of Being Endowed with the Four Accomplishments

252. Vipaccanaṃ vipāko, vipāko eva vepāko yathā “vikatameva vekata”nti. Samaṃ nātisītanāccuṇhatāya avisamaṃ bhuttassa vepāko etissā atthīti samavepākinī, tāya samavepākiniyā.

252. Digestion is the result (`vipāko`); the result itself is `vepāko`, just as 'what is wrought' (`vikata`) is 'the work' (`vekata`). The digestion of what has been eaten is even (`samaṃ`), that is, not uneven, by being neither too cold nor too hot. She who possesses this is a `samavepākinī` (one with even digestion). By that `samavepākiniyā`.

Dhammapāsādapokkharaṇivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Lotus Pond of the Dhamma Palace

253. Janarāsiṃ kāretvā tena janarāsinā khaṇitvā na māpesi. Kiñcarahīti āha “rañño panā”tiādi. Tattha kāraṇaṃ parato āgamissati. Ekāya vedikāya parikkhittā pokkharaṇiyo[P 2.0256]. Pariveṇaparicchedapariyanteti ettha pariveṇaṃ nāma samantato vivaṭaṅgaṇabhūtaṃ pokkharaṇiyā [V 2.0182] tīraṃ, tassa paricchedabhūte pariyante ekāya vedikāya [M 2.0200] parikkhittā pokkharaṇiyo. Etadahosīti etaṃ “yaṃnūnāhaṃ imāsu pokkharaṇīsū”tiādikaṃ ahosīti. Sabbotukanti sabbesu utūsu pupphanakaṃ. Nānāvaṇṇauppalabījādīnīti rattanīlādinānāvaṇṇapupphena pupphanakauppalabījādīni. Jalajathalajamālanti jalajathalajapupphamālaṃ.

253. He did not have it created by having a crowd of people dig with that crowd. How then? He said, 'But for the king...' etc. The reason for this will come later. The lotus ponds were enclosed by a single railing. 'At the boundary defining the precinct': here, 'precinct' (`pariveṇa`) means the open courtyard area around the pond's edge; at the boundary that defines it, the lotus ponds were enclosed by a single railing. 'This occurred to him' means the thought, 'Suppose I were to...' and so on, occurred. 'All-seasonal' means flowering in every season. 'Seeds of lotuses of various colors, etc.' means seeds of lotuses, etc., that bloom with flowers of various colors like red and blue. 'Garlands of water-born and land-born' means garlands of aquatic and terrestrial flowers.

254. Paricāravasenāti taṅkhaṇikaparicāravasena, idañca paṭhamaṃ paṭṭhapitaniyāmeneva vuttaṃ, pacchā pana yānasayanādīni viya itthiyopi atthikānaṃ pariccattā eva. Tenāha “itthīhipī”tiādi. Pariccāgavasenāti nirapekkhapariccāgavasena. Dīyatīti dānaṃ, deyyavatthu. Taṃ aggīyati nissajjīyati etthāti dānaggaṃ, parivesanaṭṭhānaṃ. Tādisāni atthīti yādisāni rañño dānagge khomasukhumādīni vatthāni, tādisāni yesaṃ attano santakāni santi. Ohāyāti pahāya tattheva ṭhapetvā. Attho atthi yesaṃ teti atthikā. Evaṃ anatthikāpi daṭṭhabbā.

254. 'By way of attendance' means by way of momentary attendance. This was stated according to the rule established at first, but later, like vehicles and beds, women too were indeed relinquished to those in need. Therefore, it is said, 'even women,' etc. 'By way of relinquishment' means by way of relinquishment without attachment. What is given is a gift, an object to be given. That wherein it is offered and relinquished is a `dānagga` (place of giving), a place of distribution. 'There are such things' means: just as there are cloths like fine linen in the king's place of giving, so too there are those who possess such things as their own. 'Having left' means having abandoned, leaving it right there. Those who have a need are the needy. Similarly, the non-needy should also be understood.

255. Kalahasaddopīti pi-saddena dānādhippāyena gehato nīhataṃ puna gehaṃ pavesetuṃ na yuttanti imamatthaṃ samucceti. Tenāha “na kho etaṃ amhākaṃ patirūpa”ntiādi (dī. ni. 2.255).

255. 'Even the sound of quarreling'—with the word 'even,' it includes this meaning: that it is not proper to take back into the house what was taken out of the house with the intention of giving. Therefore, it is said, 'Indeed, this is not suitable for us,' etc. (Dīgha Nikāya 2.255).

257. Uṇhīsamatthaketi sikhāpariyantamatthake. Paricchedamatthaketi pāsādaṅgaṇaparicchedassa matthake.

257. 'At the top of the turban' means at the top, up to the topknot. 'At the top of the boundary' means at the top of the boundary of the palace courtyard.

258. Haratīti ativiya pabhassarabhāvena cakkhūni paṭiharantaṃ duddikkhatāya diṭṭhiyo harati apanentaṃ [P 2.0257] viya hoti. Taṃ pana haraṇaṃ nesaṃ paripphandanenāti āha “phandāpetī”ti.

258. 'It carries away' means that with its exceedingly radiant nature it repels the eyes; being difficult to see, it is as if it carries away and removes one's sight. That carrying away, however, is due to their (the eyes') trembling; therefore it is said, 'it causes them to tremble.'

Paṭhamabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the First Recitation Section is concluded.

Jhānasampattivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Accomplishment of Jhāna

260. Mahatiyā iddhiyāti mahantena icchitatthasamijjhanena. Tesaṃyeva icchiticchitatthānaṃ. “Anubhavitabbāna”nti [V 2.0183] iminā ānubhāva-saddassa kammasādhanataṃ dasseti. Pubbe sampannaṃ katvā deyyadhammapariccāgassa katabhāvaṃ dassento “sampattipariccāgassā”ti āha. Attānaṃ dameti etenāti damo.

260. 'Mahatiyā iddhiyā' means with great power, through the great fulfillment of desired objectives. This refers to those very desired objectives that were wished for. By 'anubhavitabbānaṃ,' he indicates the objective construction of the term 'ānubhāva.' Showing that the giving of a suitable gift was an act previously accomplished, he said, 'sampattipariccāgassā.' 'Damo' is that by which one tames oneself.

Bodhisattapubbayogavaṇṇanā

An Explanation of the Bodhisatta's Former Endeavors

Assāti [M 2.0201] mahāsudassanarañño. Eko theroti appaññāto nāmagottato aññataro puthujjano thero. Theraṃ disvāti aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisinnaṃ disvā. Kaṭṭhattharaṇanti kaṭṭhamayaṃ attharaṇaṃ, dāruphalakanti attho.

'Assa' refers to King Mahāsudassana. 'Eko thero' means an unknown elder, an ordinary person whose name and clan were unknown. 'Theraṃ disvā' means seeing an elder seated at the foot of a certain tree. 'Kaṭṭhattharaṇa' means a wooden spread, that is, a wooden plank.

Paribhogabhājananti pānīyaparibhojanīyādiparibhogayogyaṃ bhājanaṃ. Ārakaṇṭakanti sūcivijjhanakakaṇṭakaṃ. Pipphalikanti khuddakasatthakaṃ. Udakatumbakanti kuṇḍikaṃ.

'Paribhogabhājana' refers to a vessel suitable for use with drinkables, consumables, and so on. 'Ārakaṇṭaka' means a thorn for piercing like an awl. 'Pipphalika' means a small knife. 'Udakatumbaka' means a water pot.

Kūṭāgāradvāreyeva nivattesīti kūṭāgāraṃ paviṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya tesaṃ micchāvitakkānaṃ pavattiyā okāsaṃ nādāsi.

'Kūṭāgāradvāreyeva nivattesi' means that from the time he entered the gabled mansion, he gave no opportunity for those wrong thoughts to arise.

261. Kasiṇameva paññāyati mahāpurisassa tattha tattha katādhikārattā, tesañca padesānaṃ suparikammakatakasiṇasadisattā.

261. The kasiṇa alone is perceived by the Great Being due to his having made a foundation in various places, and because those areas resemble well-prepared kasiṇas.

262. Cattāri jhānānīti cattāri kasiṇajjhānāni. Kasiṇajjhānappamaññānaṃyeva vacanaṃ tāsaṃ tadā ādaragāravavasena nibbattitattā. Mahābodhisattānañhi arūpajjhānesu [P 2.0258] ādaro natthi, abhiññāpadaṭṭhānataṃ pana sandhāya tānipi nibbattenti, tasmā mahāsatto tāpasaparibbājakakāle yattake lokiyaguṇe nibbatteti, te sabbepi tadā nibbattesiyeva. Tenāha “mahāpuriso panā”tiādi.

262. 'Cattāri jhānāni' means the four kasiṇa-jhānas. This statement refers only to the kasiṇa-jhānas and the illimitables, as they arose at that time out of respect and reverence. For Great Bodhisattas, there is no interest in the formless jhānas, but they develop them with reference to their being a basis for the higher knowledges. Therefore, whatever worldly qualities the Great Being developed during the time he was an ascetic wanderer, he developed all of them at that time. Therefore it is said, 'the Great Being, however,' etc.

Caturāsītinagarasahassādivaṇṇanā

An Explanation of the Eighty-four Thousand Cities, and so forth

263. Abhiharitabbabhattanti upanetabbabhattaṃ.

263. 'Abhiharitabbabhatta' means food that should be brought.

264. Nibaddhavattanti pubbe upanibaddhaṃ pākavattaṃ.

264. 'Nibaddhavatta' means a previously assigned cooking duty.

Subhaddādeviupasaṅkamanavaṇṇanā

An Explanation of Queen Subhaddā's Approach

265. Āvaṭṭetvāti [V 2.0184] ativisitvā. Yaṃ yaṃ rañño icchitaṃ dānūpakaraṇañceva bhogūpakaraṇañca, tassa tassa tatheva samiddhabhāvaṃ vitthavati.

265. 'Āvaṭṭetvā' means having excelled. She described in detail the abundance of whatever requisites for giving and articles of enjoyment the king desired.

266. Sace pana rājā jīvite chandaṃ janeyya, ito parampi ciraṃ kālaṃ tiṭṭheyya mahiddhiko mahānubhāvoti evaṃ mahajjhāsayā devī bhogesu, jīvite ca rājānaṃ sāpekkhaṃ kātuṃ vāyami. Tena vuttaṃ “mā [M 2.0202] heva kho rājā”tiādi. Tenevāha “tassa kālaṅkiriyaṃ anicchamānā”tiādi. Chandaṃ janehīti ettha chanda-saddo taṇhāpariyāyoti āha “pemaṃ uppādehī”ti. Apekkhati ārammaṇaṃ etāya na vissajjetīti apekkhā, taṇhā.

266. With the great intention, "If the king were to generate a desire for life, he might remain for a long time hereafter, powerful and majestic," the queen strove to make the king attached to both enjoyments and life. Therefore, it is said: "May the king not..." and so on. Hence it is stated: "Not desiring his death..." and so on. Regarding "generate a desire," here the word "chanda" is a synonym for craving, as he says: "arouse affection." Apekkhā is that by which one is attached to an object and does not let it go; it is craving.

267. Garahitāti ettha kehi garahitā, kasmā ca garahitāti antolīnaṃ codanaṃ vissajjento “buddhehī”tiādimāha, tena viññugarahitattā, duggatisaṃvattaniyato ca sāpekkhakālakiriyā parivajjetabbāti dasseti.

267. Regarding 'Garahitā' (blamed): answering the implicit question, "By whom is it blamed, and why is it blamed?" he says, "by the Buddhas," and so forth. By this, he shows that because it is blamed by the wise and leads to a bad destination, death with attachment should be avoided.

268. Ekamantaṃ gantvāti rañño cakkhupathaṃ vijahitvā.

268. 'Ekamantaṃ gantvā' means having left the king's field of vision.

Brahmalokūpagamanavaṇṇanā

An Explanation of Attaining the Brahma World

269. Soṇassāti koḷivīsassa soṇassa. Ekā bhattapātīti ekaṃ bhattavaḍḍhitakaṃ. Tādisaṃ bhattanti tathārūpaṃ garuṃ madhuraṃ siniddhaṃ bhattaṃ. Bhuttānanti bhuttavantānaṃ.

269. 'Soṇassa' means of Soṇa of the Koḷivīsa clan. 'Ekā bhattapātī' means one serving of food. 'Tādisaṃ bhattaṃ' means such food that is heavy, sweet, and rich. 'Bhuttānaṃ' means of those who have eaten.

271. Dāsamanussāti dāsā ceva āyuttakamanussā ca.

271. 'Dāsamanussā' means slaves and employed persons.

Idāni yathāvuttāya rañño mahāsudassanassa bhogasampattiyā kammasarikkhataṃ uddharanto “etāni panā”tiādimāha, taṃ suviññeyyameva.

Now, drawing out the correspondence with kamma for the prosperity of King Mahāsudassana as previously stated, he said, "etāni pana," and so forth. That is easily understood.

272. Ādito [P 2.0259] paṭṭhāyāti samudāgamanato paṭṭhāya. Yattha taṃ puññaṃ āyūhitaṃ, yato sā sampatti nibbattā, tato tatiyattabhāvato pabhuti. Mahāsudassanassa jātakadesanā hi tadā samudāgamanato paṭṭhāya bhagavatā desitāti. Paṃsvāgārakīḷaṃ viyāti yathā nāma dārakā paṃsūhi vāpigehabhojanādīni [V 2.0185] dassentā yathāruci kīḷitvā gamanakāle sabbaṃ taṃ vidhaṃsentā gacchanti, evameva bhagavā mahāsudassanakāle attanā anubhūtaṃ dibbasampattisadisaṃ acinteyyānubhāvasampattiṃ vitthārato dassetvā puna attano desanaṃ ādīnavanissaraṇadassanavasena vivaṭṭābhimukhaṃ viparivattento “sabbā sā sampatti aniccatāya vipariṇatā vidhaṃsitā”ti dassento “passānandā”tiādimāha. Vipariṇatāti vipariṇāmaṃ sabhāvavigamaṃ gatā. Tenāha “pakativijahanenā”tiādi. Pakatīti sabhāvadhammānaṃ udayavayaparicchinno [M 2.0203] kakkhaḷaphusanādisabhāvo, so bhaṅgakkhaṇato paṭṭhāya jahito, pariccajanto sabbaso nattheva. Tenāha “nibbutapadīpo viya apaññattikabhāvaṃ gatā”ti.

272. 'Ādito paṭṭhāya' means starting from its arising. That is, from the third existence onwards, where that merit was accumulated and from which that prosperity was produced. The teaching of the Mahāsudassana Jātaka was indeed taught by the Blessed One from that arising onwards. 'Paṃsvāgārakīḷaṃ viya' means like playing with a sand house: just as children, making representations of reservoirs, houses, food, and so on out of sand, play as they please and then, when it is time to go, destroy it all and leave, even so the Blessed One, having displayed in detail the inconceivable and powerful prosperity similar to divine prosperity that he himself experienced during the time of Mahāsudassana, then turned his teaching towards Nibbāna by way of showing the danger and the escape, demonstrating that "all that prosperity, due to impermanence, has changed and been destroyed," and says, "See, Ānanda..." 'Vipariṇatā' means it has gone to alteration, to the disappearance of its nature. Therefore, he says, "by abandoning its original nature," and so forth. 'Pakati' means the intrinsic nature of phenomena, defined by arising and passing away, such as the nature of hardness, contact, and so on. From the moment of dissolution, it is abandoned; being completely relinquished, it is not at all. Therefore, he says, "like an extinguished lamp, it has gone to a state of being unmanifest."

Ettāvatāti ādito paṭṭhāya pavattena ettakena desanāmaggena. Anekāni vassakoṭisatasahassāniyeva ubbedho etissāti anekavassakoṭisatasahassubbedhā. Aniccalakkhaṇaṃ ādāyāti taṃ sampattigataṃ aniccalakkhaṇaṃ desanāya gahetvā vibhāvetvā. Yathā nisseṇimuccane tādisaṃ satahatthubbedhaṃ rukkhaṃ pakatipurisena ārohituṃ na sakkā, evaṃ aniccatāvibhāvanena tassā sampattiyā apekkhānisseṇimuccane [P 2.0260] kenaci ārohituṃ na sakkāti āha “aniccalakkhaṇaṃ ādāya nisseṇiṃ muñcanto viyā”ti. Tenevāti yathāvuttakāraṇeneva, ādito sātisayaṃ kāmesu assādaṃ dassetvāpi upari nesaṃ “passānandā”tiādinā ādīnavaṃ, okāraṃ, saṃkilesaṃ, nekkhamme ānisaṃsañca vibhāvetvā desanāya niṭṭhāpitattā. Pubbeti atītakāle. Vasabharājāti vasabhanāmako sīhaḷamahārājā.

'Ettāvatā' means by this much of the teaching path that has proceeded from the beginning. 'Anekavassakoṭisatasahassubbedhā' means that its height is indeed many hundreds of thousands of crores of years. 'Aniccalakkhaṇaṃ ādāya' means having grasped and explained, by way of the teaching, that characteristic of impermanence pertaining to that prosperity. Just as it is impossible for an ordinary person to climb a tree a hundred cubits high without a ladder, so too, through the explanation of impermanence, when the ladder of attachment to that prosperity is removed, it is impossible for anyone to ascend; thus it is said, 'Taking up the characteristic of impermanence like releasing a ladder.' 'Teneva' means for the reason just stated: because, having first shown the exceeding delight in sensual pleasures, the teaching was concluded by subsequently analyzing, through the words 'See, Ānanda,' etc., their danger, fault, and defilement, and the benefit in renunciation. 'Pubbe' means in past times. 'Vasabharājā' means the great king of Sri Lanka named Vasabha.

Udakapupphuḷādayoti ādi-saddena tiṇagge ussāvabinduādike saṅgaṇhāti.

'Udakapupphuḷādayo' (water bubbles, etc.): by the word 'etc.,' he includes dewdrops on the tips of grass and the like.

Mahāsudassanassa panāti pana-saddo visesatthajotano, tena mahāsudassanamahārājā jhānābhiññāsamāpattiyo nibbattesi, tadaggena parisuddhe ca samaṇabhāve patiṭṭhito, yato vidhuya eva kāmavitakkādisamaṇabhāvasaṃkilesaṃ suññāgāraṃ pāvisi, evaṃbhūtassāpi tassa kālaṃ kiriyato sattame divase sabbā cakkavattisampatti antarahitā, na tato paraṃ, aho acchariyamanusso anaññasādhāraṇaguṇavisesoti imaṃ visesaṃ dasseti.

Regarding 'Mahāsudassanassa pana,' the word 'pana' serves to illuminate a special meaning. Thus, King Mahāsudassana developed the jhānas, higher knowledges, and meditative attainments, and at their apex, he was established in a pure state of recluseship. Because, having shaken off the defilements of the recluse's state, such as sensual thoughts, he entered an empty dwelling. Even for such a one, on the seventh day after his death, all the wealth of a universal monarch vanished, not remaining thereafter. This demonstrates this special point: 'Ah, what a wonderful man, with extraordinary and uncommon qualities!'

Anāruḷhanti “rājā kira pubbe gahapatikule nibbattī”tiādinā, (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.260) “puna theraṃ āmantesī”tiādinā (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.272) ca vuttamatthaṃ [V 2.0186] sandhāyāha. So hi imasmiṃ sutte saṅgītiṃ anāruḷho, aññattha pana āgato imissā desanāya piṭṭhivattakabhāvena. Yaṃ panettha atthato na vibhattaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyaṃ evāti.

'Anāruḷhaṃ' (not included): he says this with reference to the meaning stated in "It is said that the king was previously born in a householder’s family," etc., (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.260) and "Then he addressed the elder," etc. (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.272). For that was not included in the recitation of this sutta, but came elsewhere as a backstory for this teaching. Whatever is not analyzed here in terms of meaning should be easily understood.

Mahāsudassanasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

Elucidation of the Obscure Meaning in the Commentary on the Mahāsudassana Sutta.

5. Janavasabhasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Janavasabha Sutta.

Nātikiyādibyākaraṇavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Declaration concerning the People of Nātika and Others.

273-275. “Parito”ti [P 2.0261][V 2.0187][M 2.0204] padaṃ yathā samantatthavācako, evaṃ samīpatthavācakopi hotīti samantā sāmantāti attho vutto. Āmeḍitena pana samantattho jotito. Yassa pana sāmantā janapadesu “nātike viharatī”ti vuttattā nātikassāti viññāto yamattho. Yassa parito janapadesu byākaroti, tattha paricārakārakānaṃ byākaraṇaṃ avuttasiddhaṃ, nidassanavasena vā tassa vakkhamānattā “parito parito janapadesu” icceva vuttaṃ. Paricāraketi upāsake. Tenāha “buddhadhammasaṅghānaṃ paricārake”ti. Upapattīsūti nibbattīsu. Ñāṇagatipuññānaṃ upapattīsūti ettha ñāṇagatūpapatti nāma tassa tassa maggañāṇagamanassa nibbatti. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ parikkhayā”tiādi. Puññūpapatti nāma taṃtaṃdevanikāyūpapatti. Sabbatthāti “vajjimallesū”tiādike sabbattha catūsupi padesu. Purimesūti pāḷiyaṃ vutte sandhāyāha. Dasasuyevāti tesu eva dasasu janapadesu. Paricārake byākaroti byakātabbānaṃ bahūnaṃ tattha labbhanato. Nātike bhavā nātikiyā.

The word 'parito' conveys the meaning 'all around,' just as it denotes 'in the vicinity'; hence the meaning is given as 'samantā' (all around) and 'sāmantā' (in the vicinity). The sense of 'all around' is illuminated through repetition. However, because it is said, 'he dwells in Nātika' in the surrounding regions, its meaning is understood as 'of Nātika.' Wherever he makes a declaration in the surrounding regions, the declaration regarding his attendants is implicitly established, or alternatively, since it will be explained by way of example, the phrase 'all around, all around in the regions' is used. 'Paricārake' refers to lay followers. Hence, it is said, 'attendants of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha.' 'Upapattīsu' means 'in rebirths.' Herein, regarding 'in the rebirths of knowledge-attainment and merit,' 'rebirth of knowledge-attainment' refers to the arising of the path-knowledge for each respective stage, in reference to which it is said: 'with the destruction of the five lower fetters,' etc. 'Rebirth of merit' denotes rebirth in the various divine assemblies. 'Sabbattha' means in all four places, such as 'among the Vajjis and Mallas,' etc. 'Purimesu' refers to what was said previously in the Pāli text. 'Dasasu yeva' means specifically in just those ten regions. 'He makes a declaration concerning the attendants' because many who are to be declared are found there. 'Nātike bhavā nātikiyā' means 'those who are in Nātika are the people of Nātika.'

Niṭṭhaṅgatāti niṭṭhaṃ nicchayaṃ upagatā.

'Niṭṭhaṅgatā' means having reached the end, a definitive conclusion.

Ānandaparikathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse concerning Ānanda.

276. Yasmā saṅghasuppaṭipatti nāma dhammasudhammatāya, dhammasudhammatā ca buddhasubuddhatāya, tasmā “aho dhammo, aho saṅgho”ti dhammasaṅghaguṇakittanāpi atthato buddhaguṇakittanā eva hotīti “bhagavantaṃ [P 2.0262] kittayamānarūpā”ti padassa “aho dhammo”tiādināpi attho vutto.

276. Because the good practice of the Saṅgha is due to the Dhamma being well-taught, and the Dhamma being well-taught is due to the Buddha being well-awakened, therefore the praising of the qualities of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha—such as 'Oh, the Dhamma! Oh, the Saṅgha!'—is in essence the praising of the Buddha's qualities. Thus, the meaning of the phrase 'having the nature of praising the Blessed One' is also explained by 'Oh, the Dhamma!' and so on.

278. Ñāṇagatīti [V 2.0188] “pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā”tiādinā āgataṃ pahātabbapahānavasena pavattaṃ maggañāṇagamanaṃ. Yasmā tassā eva ñāṇagatiyā vasena tassa tassa ariyapuggalassa opapātikatādiviseso, tasmā taṃ tādisaṃ tassa abhisamparāyaṃ sandhāyāha “ñāṇābhisamparāyamevā”ti.

278. 'Course of knowledge' (ñāṇagati) refers to the progression of path-knowledge that proceeds by way of abandoning what is to be abandoned, as comes in the phrase 'through the destruction of the five lower fetters,' and so on. Because it is by means of that very course of knowledge that the particular distinction of spontaneous rebirth and so on comes to be for each noble individual, therefore, referring to such a future state for him, it is said: 'a future state determined by knowledge indeed'.

279. Upasantaṃ [M 2.0205] pati sammati ālokīyatīti upasantapatiso. Upasantadassano upasantaussanno. Bhātirivāti ettha ra-kāro padasandhikaro, iva-saddo bhusatthoti āha “ativiya bhātī”ti.

279. He is calmed towards the peaceful and is seen as such, thus he is 'upasantapatiso'. He is one who sees the peaceful, one who is intent on the peaceful. In 'bhātiriva', the letter 'r' is a euphonic connector of words, and the word 'iva' has the sense of 'very much'; hence it is said, 'shines exceedingly'.

Janavasabhayakkhavaṇṇanā

Explanation concerning the Yakkha Janavasabha.

280. Jeṭṭhakabhāvena jane vasabhasadisoti janavasabhoti assa devaputtassa nāmaṃ ahosi.

280. Because he was like a bull among the people due to his pre-eminence, the name of that devaputta became Janavasabha.

Ito devalokā cavitvā sattakkhattuṃ manussaloke rājabhūtassa. Manussalokā cavitvā sattakkhattuṃ devabhūtassa. Etthevāti etasmiṃyeva cātumahārājikabhave, etthāpi vessavaṇassa sahabyatāvasena.

Having passed away from the deva world, he became a king in the human world seven times. Having passed away from the human world, he became a deva seven times. 'Ettheva' means just in this realm of the Four Great Kings, and even here, by way of companionship with Vessavaṇa.

281. Āsisanaṃ āsā, patthanā. Āsāsīsena cettha kattukamyatākusalacchandaṃ vadati. Tenevāha “sakadāgāmimaggatthāyā”tiādi. Yadaggeti ettha agga-saddo ādipariyāyoti āha “taṃ divasaṃ ādiṃ katvā”ti. “Purimaṃ…pe… avinipāto”ti idaṃ yathā tattakaṃ kālaṃ sugatito sugatūpapattiyeva [P 2.0263] ahosi, tathā katūpacitakusalakammattā. Phussassa sammāsambuddhassa kālato pabhuti hi sambhatavivaṭṭūpanissayakusalasambhāro esa devaputto. Anacchariyanti anu anu acchariyaṃ. Tenāha “punappunaṃ acchariyamevā”ti. Sayaṃparisāyāti sakāya parisāya. Bhagavato diṭṭhasadisamevāti āvajjanasamanantaraṃ yathā te bhagavato catuvīsatisatasahassamattā sattā ñāṇagatito diṭṭhā, evaṃ tumhehi diṭṭhasadisameva. Vessavaṇassa sammukhā sutaṃ mayāti vadati.

281. 'Āsisanaṃ' means hope, aspiration. Here, by 'āsāsīsa', it refers to wholesome desire, the wish to act. Therefore, it is said, 'for the sake of the path of the once-returner,' etc. In 'yadagge', the word 'agga' is a synonym for 'beginning'; hence it says, 'taking that day as the beginning.' 'The former... not a bad destination'—this is because for that long a time there was only rebirth in a good destination from a good destination, due to wholesome kamma having been done and accumulated. Indeed, from the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Phussa, this devaputta had been gathering a store of wholesome qualities that are a support for turning away from saṃsāra. 'Anacchariyaṃ' means marvel after marvel. Hence it is said, 'again and again, it was truly a marvel.' 'Sayaṃparisāya' means 'in his own assembly.' 'Just like what was seen by the Blessed One' means: immediately after adverting his mind, just as those beings, numbering 2,400,000, were seen by the Blessed One through his course of knowledge, so too it is just like what was seen by you. He says, 'I heard this in the presence of Vessavaṇa'.

Devasabhāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Assembly of the Devas.

282. Vassūpanāyikasaṅgahatthanti [V 2.0189] vassūpanāyikāya ārakkhāsaṃvidhānavasena bhikkhūnaṃ saṅgahaṇatthaṃ “vassūpagatā bhikkhū evaṃ sukhena samaṇadhammaṃ karontī”ti, pavāraṇasaṅgaho panassa pavāretvā satthu santikaṃ gacchantānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ antarāmagge parissayapariharaṇatthaṃ. Dhammassavanatthaṃ dūraṭṭhānaṃ [M 2.0206] gacchantesupi eseva nayo. Attanāpi āgantvā dhammassavanatthaṃ sannipatiyeva. Etthetthāti ettha ettha ayyānaṃ vasanaṭṭhāne.

282. 'For the purpose of supporting during the rains-residence' means for the purpose of supporting the monks by way of arranging protection during the rains-residence, so that 'monks who have entered the rains may thus happily practice the ascetic's duties.' The support at the Pavāraṇā, however, is for the purpose of warding off dangers on the way for the monks who, after performing the Pavāraṇā, are traveling to the Teacher’s presence. This same principle applies to those who travel to distant places to hear the Dhamma. They themselves also, having come, indeed assemble for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. 'Etthetthāti' means 'here and there, in the dwelling places of the noble ones'.

Tadāpīti “purimāni bhante divasānī”ti vuttakālepi. Eteneva kāraṇenāti vassūpanāyikanimittameva. Tenāha pāḷiyaṃ “tadahuposathe pannarase vassūpanāyikāyā”tiādi. Āsanepi nisajjāya sudhammāya devasabhāya paṭhamaṃ devesu tāvatiṃsesu nisinnesu tassā catūsu dvāresu cattāro mahārājāno nisīdanti, idaṃ nesaṃ āsane nisajjāya cārittaṃ hoti.

'Tadāpi' means even at the time when it was said, 'Venerable sir, in former days.' 'For this very reason' means precisely on account of the rains-residence. Hence, it is said in the Pāli text, 'on that Uposatha day, the fifteenth, of the rains-residence,' etc. Regarding the seating as well: in the Sudhammā assembly hall of the devas, when the Tāvatiṃsa devas have first sat down, the four great kings sit at its four gates. This is their custom regarding taking their seats.

Yenatthenāti yena kiccena yena payojanena. Ārakkhatthanti ārakkhabhūtamatthaṃ. Vuttaṃ vacanaṃ etesanti vuttavacanā, mahārājāno.

'Yenatthena' means for what duty, for what reason. 'Ārakkhatthaṃ' means for the purpose that is protection. 'Vuttavacanā' means those whose word has been spoken, that is, the great kings.

283. Atikkamitvāti abhibhavitvā.

283. 'Atikkamitvā' means having surpassed.

Sanaṅkumārakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse of Sanaṅkumāra.

284. Abhisambhavituṃ adhigantuṃ asakkuṇeyyo anabhisambhavanīyo. Tenāha “appattabbo”tiādi. Cakkhuyeva patho rūpadassanassa maggo upāyoti cakkhupatho, tasmiṃ cakkhupathasminti āha “cakkhupasāde”ti, cakkhussa gocarayoggo vā cakkhupathoti āha “āpāthe vā”ti. Nābhibhavatīti na abhibhavati, gocarabhāvaṃ [P 2.0264] na gacchatīti attho. Heṭṭhā heṭṭhāti tāvatiṃsato paṭṭhāya heṭṭhā heṭṭhā, na cātumahārājikato paṭṭhāya, nāpi brahmapārisajjato paṭṭhāya. “Cātumahārājikā hi tāvatiṃsānaṃ yathā jātirūpāni passituṃ sakkonti, tathā brahmāno heṭṭhimā uparimāna”nti keci, taṃ na yuttaṃ. Na hi heṭṭhimā brahmāno uparimānaṃ mūlapaṭisandhirūpaṃ passituṃ sakkonti, māpitameva passituṃ sakkontīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

284. 'Anabhisambhavanīyo' means unable to be overcome or attained. Therefore, it is said, 'unobtainable,' and so forth. The eye itself is the path, the way, the means for seeing form—thus, 'eye-path' (cakkhupatho). Regarding this 'eye-path' (cakkhupathasmiṃ), it is said, 'in the eye-sensitivity' (cakkhupasāde). Or, what is suitable as the eye's range is the eye-path; thus, it is said, 'or in the field of perception' (āpāthe vā). 'It does not overwhelm' means it does not overcome; the meaning is that it does not enter the state of being its range. 'Lower and lower' means starting from the Tāvatiṃsa realm downwards, not from the realm of the Four Great Kings, nor from the Brahmā's retinue. Some say, 'The devas of the Four Great Kings can see the native forms of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, and likewise, the lower brahmās can see the higher ones.' This is not correct. For the lower brahmās cannot see the fundamental rebirth-linking form of the higher ones; it should be understood that they can only see a created form.

Suṇantova [V 2.0190] niddaṃ okkamīti gatiyo upadhārento bahi visaṭavitakkavicchedena saṅkocaṃ āpannacittatāya. Mayhaṃ ayyakassāti bhagavantaṃ sandhāya vadati.

He fell into drowsiness even while listening because, while considering the destinations, his mind had contracted due to the interruption of externally scattered thoughts.

Pañca sikhā etassāti pañcasikho, pañcasikho viya pañcasikhoti āha “pañcasikhagandhabbasadiso”ti. Mamāyantīti piyāyanti.

'He has five crests,' thus he is Pañcasikha. Because he is like Pañcasikha, it is said, 'resembling the Gandhabba Pañcasikha.' 'Mamāyanti' means they hold dear.

285. Sumuttoti [M 2.0207] saradosehi suṭṭhu mutto. Yehi pittasemhādīhi palibuddhattā saro avissaṭṭho siyā, tadabhāvato vissaṭṭhoti dassento āha “apalibuddho”ti. Viññāpetīti viññeyyo, antogadhahetuattho kattusādhano esa viññeyyasaddoti āha “atthaviññāpano”ti. Sarassa madhuratā nāma maddavanti āha “madhuro mudū”ti. Savanaṃ arahatīti savanīyo. Savanārahatāya ca āpāthasukhatāyāti āha “kaṇṇasukho”ti. Bindūti piṇḍito. Ākoṭitabhinnakaṃsasaddo viya anekāvayavo ahutvā niravayavo, ekabhāvoti attho. Tenāha “ekagghano”ti, etenevassa avisāritā saṃvaṇṇitā daṭṭhabbā. Gambhīruppattiṭṭhānatāya cassa gambhīratāti āha “nābhimūlato”tiādi. Evaṃ samuṭṭhitoti jīvhādippahāramattasamuṭṭhito. Amadhuro ca hoti uppattiṭṭhānānaṃ parilahubhāvato. Na ca dūraṃ sāveti vīrabhāvābhāvato. Ninnādī suvipulabhāvato savisesaṃ ninnādo, pāsaṃsaninnādo vā. Tenāha “mahāmegha…pe… yutto”ti.

285. Sumutto means thoroughly freed from faults of the voice. A voice might be obstructed by bile, phlegm, etc., making it unclear; showing that due to their absence, it is clear, it is said, 'unobstructed.' It makes known, hence it is knowable. Because this word viññeyyo has the sense of an agent with an implied cause, it is said, 'conveying meaning.' The sweetness of the voice is its gentleness; hence, it is said, 'sweet and gentle.' Savanīyo means worthy of hearing. Because it is worthy of hearing and pleasant to the ear, it is said, 'pleasing to the ear.' Bindu means condensed. Unlike the sound of a struck and broken bronze gong, it is not fragmented into many parts but is undivided, a single unity; this is the meaning. Therefore, it is said, 'a single solid mass.' By this, its non-dispersed quality should be understood. Due to the depth of its place of origin, it is deep; hence, it is said, 'from the root of the navel,' and so forth. A voice that arises thus—arising merely from the striking of the tongue, etc.—is not sweet because its places of origin are very light. Nor does it carry far, due to the absence of vigor. Resounding means that due to its great extent, it is a special resounding, or a praiseworthy resounding. Therefore, it is said, 'like a great cloud... endowed.'

Pacchimaṃ pacchimanti dutiyaṃ, catutthaṃ, chaṭṭhaṃ, aṭṭhamañca padaṃ. Purimassa purimassāti yathākkamaṃ paṭhamassa, tatiyassa, pañcamassa, sattamassa ca. Atthoyevāti atthaniddeso eva. Vissaṭṭhatā hissa viññeyyatāya veditabbā, mañjubhāvo savanīyatāya, bindubhāvo avisāritāya, gambhīrabhāvo ninnāditāyāti. Yathāparisanti ettha yathā-saddo parimāṇavācī, na pakārādivācīti āha “yattakā [P 2.0265] parisā”ti, tena parisappamāṇaṃ evassa saro niccharati, ayamassa dhammatāti dasseti. Tenāha “tattakamevā”tiādi.

The phrase 'the latter, the latter' refers to the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth term. The phrase 'of the former, of the former,' in order, refers to the first, the third, the fifth, and the seventh. 'It is just the meaning' means it is just an explanation of the meaning. For its clarity is to be known by its intelligibility, its sweetness by its pleasantness to hear, its compactness by its non-dispersion, and its depth by its resonance. In 'yathāparisaṃ,' the word 'yathā' denotes measure, not kind or the like. Thus it is said, 'as large as the assembly,' meaning that his voice emerges in proportion to the size of the assembly; this is its nature. Therefore, it is said, 'just so much,' and so forth.

“Ye hi kecī”tiādi “yāvañca so bhagavā”tiādinā vuttassa atthassa hetukittanavasena samatthanaṃ saraṇesu nesaṃ niccasevanena, sīlesu ca patiṭṭhāpanena chakāmasaggasampattianuppādanato. Tenāha “ye hi keci…pe… vadatī”ti. Nibbematikagahitasaraṇeti maggenāgatasaraṇagamane. Te hi sabbaso samugghātitavicikicchatāya ratanattaye aveccappasādena samannāgatāyeva, pothujjanikasaddhāya vasena buddhādīnaṃ guṇe ogāhetvā [V 2.0191] jānanti, aparaneyyabuddhino te pariyāyato nibbematikagahitasaraṇā veditabbā. Gandhabbadevagaṇanti gandhabbadevasamūhaṃ. Tukā [M 2.0208] vuccati khīriṇī yā tukātipi vuccati. Tassā cuṇṇaṃ tukāpiṭṭhaṃ. Taṃ koṭṭetvā pakkhittaṃ ghanaṃ nirantaracitaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati.

The phrase 'Whatever beings,' and so forth, up to 'as far as that Blessed One,' is stated as a reason for supporting the purpose mentioned, by their constant devotion to the refuges, and by establishing themselves in virtue, by bringing about the attainment of the six desire-realm heavens. Therefore, it is said, 'whatever beings... speaks.' 'Those who have taken refuge with certainty' refers to taking refuge by means of the path. For they are entirely free from doubt, endowed with unwavering faith in the Triple Gem, and, being those whose wisdom is not to be led by others, they know the qualities of the Buddha and others by engaging with them, not merely through the faith of ordinary people. These are to be understood as having taken refuge with certainty in a qualified sense. 'The host of celestial musicians' means a multitude of celestial musicians. 'Tukā' is called a milky plant, also known as 'tukātī.' Its powder is called 'tukāpiṭṭha.' When pounded and applied, it becomes dense and stands firm without gaps.

Bhāvitaiddhipādavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Development of the Bases of Psychic Power

287. Supaññattāti suṭṭhu pakārehi ñāpitā bodhitā, asaṅkarato vā ṭhapitā, taṃ pana bodhanaṃ, asaṅkarato ṭhapanañca atthato desanā evāti āha “sukathitā”ti. Ijjhanaṭṭhenāti samijjhanaṭṭhena, nippajjanassa kāraṇabhāvenāti attho. Patiṭṭhānaṭṭhenāti adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena. Iddhiyā pādoti iddhipādo, iddhiyā adhigamupāyoti attho. Tena hi yasmā uparūpari visesasaṅkhātaṃ iddhiṃ pajjanti pāpuṇanti, tasmā “pādo”ti vuccati. Ijjhatīti iddhi, samijjhati nippajjatīti attho. Iddhi eva pādo iddhipādo, iddhikoṭṭhāsoti attho. Evaṃ tāva “cattāro iddhipādā”ti ettha attho veditabbo. Iddhipahonakatāyāti iddhiyā nipphādane samatthabhāvāya. Iddhivisavitāyāti iddhiyā nipphādane yogyabhāvāya. Anekatthattā hi dhātūnaṃ yogyattho vi-pubbo [P 2.0266] su-saddo, visavanaṃ vā pajjanaṃ visavitā, tattha kāmakāritā visavitā. Tenāha “punappuna”ntiādi. Iddhivikubbanatāyāti vikubbaniddhiyā vividharūpakaraṇāya. Tenāha “nānappakārato katvā dassanatthāyā”ti.

287. "Well-expounded" (supaññattā) means well made known and understood in proper ways, or established without confusion. That understanding and establishing without confusion is, in terms of meaning, simply a teaching, thus it is said "well-taught." "In the sense of succeeding" (ijjhanaṭṭhena) means in the sense of accomplishment, that is, being the cause of production. "In the sense of foundation" (patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena) means in the sense of support. The "foot of psychic power" (iddhipāda) is the means of attaining psychic power. For since by means of it they reach and attain psychic power, which is called a higher and higher distinction, therefore it is called a "foot." "Psychic power" (iddhi) means that which succeeds, that is, that which is accomplished or produced. Psychic power itself is the foot, the base of psychic power, meaning a component of psychic power. Thus, first, the meaning of "the four bases of psychic power" should be understood here. "By being capable of psychic power" (iddhipahonakatāya) means by being capable of producing psychic power. "By proficiency in psychic power" (iddhivisavitāya) means by being suitable for the production of psychic power. For because roots have many meanings, the root su preceded by vi has the meaning of suitability. Or visavitā means producing or attaining; here, it means acting at will. Therefore, it is said "again and again," etc. "By the transformative power of psychic power" (iddhivikubbanatāya) means for the purpose of manifesting various forms through transformative psychic power. Therefore, it is said, "for the purpose of displaying after creating diverse forms."

“Chandañca bhikkhu adhipatiṃ karitvā labhati samādhiṃ, labhati cittassekaggataṃ, ayaṃ vuccati chandasamādhī”ti (vibha. 432) imāya pāḷiyā chandādhipati samādhi chandasamādhīti adhipatisaddalopaṃ katvā samāso vuttoti viññāyati, adhipatisaddatthadassanavasena pana “chandahetuko, chandādhiko vā samādhi chandasasamādhī”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃvuttanti veditabbaṃ. “Padhānabhūtāti vīriyabhūtā”ti keci vadanti. Saṅkhatasaṅkhārādinivattanatthañhi padhānaggahaṇanti. Atha vā taṃ taṃ visesaṃ saṅkharotīti saṅkhāro, sabbampi vīriyaṃ. Tattha catukiccasādhakato aññassa nivattanatthaṃ padhānaggahaṇanti padhānabhūtā seṭṭhabhūtāti attho. Catubbidhassa pana vīriyassa adhippetattā bahuvacananiddeso kato. Visuṃ samāsayojanavasena yo pubbe iddhipādattho pādassa upāyatthataṃ, koṭṭhāsatthatañca gahetvā yathāyogavasena idha [M 2.0209] vutto, so vakkhamānānaṃ paṭilābhapubbabhāgānaṃ kattukaraṇiddhibhāvaṃ, uttaracūḷabhājanīye vā vuttehi chandādīhi iddhipādehi sādhetabbāya iddhiyā kattiddhibhāvaṃ, chandādīnañca karaṇiddhibhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttoti veditabbo, tasmā “ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhī”ti ettha kattuattho, karaṇattho ca ekajjhaṃ gahetvā [V 2.0192] vuttoti kattuatthaṃ tāva dassetuṃ “nipphattipariyāyena ijjhanaṭṭhena vā”ti vatvā itaraṃ dassento “ijjhanti [P 2.0267] etāyā”tiādimāha. Vuttanti kattha vuttaṃ? Iddhipādavibhaṅgapāṭhe. (Vibha. 434) tathābhūtassāti tenākārena bhūtassa, te chandādidhamme paṭilabhitvā ṭhitassāti attho. “Vedanākkhandho”tiādīhi chandādayo antokatvā cattāropi khandhā kathitā. Sesesūti sesiddhipādesu.

"A bhikkhu, having made zeal the dominant factor, gains concentration, gains one-pointedness of mind. This is called 'zeal-concentration.'" (Vibh. 432) It is understood that in this Pali passage, the compound "zeal-concentration" (chandasamādhi) is stated by omitting the word "dominant" (adhipati), meaning concentration with zeal as the dominant factor. However, it should be known that in the commentary, to show the meaning of the word "dominant," it is said, "concentration caused by zeal or predominated by zeal is 'zeal-concentration.'" Some say, "'Being exertion' (padhānabhūtā) means being energy." For the term "exertion" is used to denote the cessation of conditioned formations, etc. Alternatively, "formation" (saṅkhāro) means that which arranges this or that distinction, and all energy is such. Here, the term "exertion" is used to signify the cessation of other factors in accomplishing the fourfold task, meaning it is the foremost or primary factor. The plural form is used because it refers to the fourfold energy intended here.
