The meaning of "base of psychic power" (iddhipāda) which was previously stated here, taking the meaning of "foot" (pāda) as means and as a component, as appropriate, should be understood as referring to the state of being the agent's psychic power and the instrumental psychic power for those who will attain the preliminary stages, or as referring to the state of being the agent's psychic power for the psychic power to be achieved by the bases of psychic power like zeal, etc., mentioned in the later detailed explanation, and also implying the instrumental role of zeal, etc. Therefore, in "psychic power in the sense of success" (ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhi), both the agent meaning and the instrumental meaning are taken together. To show the agent meaning first, it is said, "in the sense of accomplishment or success," and then to show the other meaning, it says, "by this, they succeed," etc. "Stated" (vuttaṃ) — where is it stated? In the Vibhaṅga text on the Bases of Psychic Power (Vibh. 434). "Of such a one" (tathābhūtassa) means one who has become of that nature, that is, one who has attained and abides in those qualities of zeal, etc. By "the aggregate of feeling," etc., all four aggregates are spoken of by including zeal, etc. "In the rest" (sesesu) refers to the remaining bases of psychic power.

Vīriyiddhipādaniddese “vīriyasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgata”nti dvikkhattuṃ vīriyaṃ āgataṃ. Tattha purimaṃ samādhivisesanaṃ “vīriyādhipati samādhi vīriyasamādhī”ti, dutiyaṃ samannāgamaṅgadassanaṃ. Dveyeva hi sabbattha samannāgamaṅgāni, samādhi, padhānasaṅkhāro ca. Chandādayo hi samādhivisesanāni, padhānasaṅkhāro pana padhānavacaneneva visesito, na chandādīhīti na idha vīriyādhipatitā padhānasaṅkhārassa vuttā hoti. Vīriyañca samādhiṃ visesetvā ṭhitameva, samannāgamaṅgavasena pana padhānasaṅkhāravacanena vuttanti nāpi dvīhi vīriyehi samannāgamo vutto hoti. Yasmā pana chandādīhi visiṭṭho samādhi, tathāvisiṭṭheneva ca tena sampayutto padhānasaṅkhāro, sesadhammā ca, tasmā samādhivisesanānaṃ vasena cattāro iddhipādā vuttā, visesanabhāvo ca chandādīnaṃ taṃtaṃavassayadassanavasena hotīti “chandasamādhi…pe… iddhipāda”nti ettha nissayatthepi pāda-sadde upāyatthena chandādīnaṃ iddhipādatā vuttā hoti. Teneva hi abhidhamme uttaracūḷabhājanīye (vibha. 456) “cattāro iddhipādā chandiddhipādo”tiādinā chandādīnameva iddhipādatā vuttā. Pañhapucchake (vibha. 457 ādayo) “cattāro iddhipādā idha bhikkhu chandasamādhī”tiādinā [P 2.0268] ca uddesaṃ katvāpi puna chandādīnaṃyeva kusalādibhāvo vibhatto. Upāyiddhipādadassanatthameva hi nissayiddhipādadassanaṃ kataṃ, aññathā catubbidhatā na siyāti. Ayamettha pāḷivasena atthavinicchayo veditabbo. Idāni paṭilābhapubbabhāgānaṃ vasena iddhipāde vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi [M 2.0210] vuttaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyameva. Idha iddhipādakathā saṅkhepeneva vuttāti āha “vitthārena pana…pe… vuttā”ti.

In the exposition of the base of psychic power that is energy, the word 'energy' (vīriya) appears twice in the phrase 'endowed with energy-concentration and the formations of striving' (vīriyasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgata). There, the first is a qualifier of concentration, meaning 'concentration with energy as the dominant factor is energy-concentration'; the second indicates the factor of endowment. Indeed, everywhere there are only two factors of endowment: concentration and the formations of striving. For zeal and the like are qualifiers of concentration, but the formations of striving are qualified by the word 'striving' itself, not by zeal and the like. Therefore, the dominance of energy is not stated here with regard to the formations of striving. And energy, having qualified concentration, remains just that. However, by way of the factor of endowment, it is stated by the term 'formations of striving,' and thus endowment by two energies is not stated. But because concentration is qualified by zeal and the like, and the formations of striving are associated with that very qualified concentration, along with the remaining mental states, therefore, the four bases of psychic power are stated by way of the qualifiers of concentration. And the qualifying nature of zeal and the like comes about by showing their respective roles as a basis, as in 'zeal-concentration... base of psychic power.' Here, even when the word 'pāda' is in the sense of a basis, the status of being a base of psychic power is stated for zeal and the like in the sense of a means. For this reason, in the Abhidhamma, in the Uttaracūḷabhājanīya (Vibh. 456), it is said, 'The four bases of psychic power: the base of psychic power that is zeal,' etc., where only zeal and the like are stated as the bases of psychic power. In the question-and-answer section (Vibh. 457 ff.), after stating the summary, 'The four bases of psychic power: here, a bhikkhu has zeal-concentration,' etc., the wholesome and other qualities are further analyzed only for zeal and the like. The demonstration of the base of psychic power as a basis is made precisely to show the base of psychic power as a means; otherwise, the fourfold nature would not be possible. Here, this determination of the meaning should be understood according to the Pāli text. Now, to explain the bases of psychic power by distinguishing them according to the preliminary stages of attainment, 'furthermore,' etc., is stated—this is easily understood. Here, the discussion of the bases of psychic power is briefly stated. Therefore, it is said, 'But in detail... it is stated.'

Kecīti abhayagirivāsino. Tesu hi ekacce “iddhi nāma anipphannā”ti vadanti, ekacce “iddhipādo pana anipphanno”ti vadanti, anipphannoti ca paramatthato asiddho, natthīti attho. Ābhatoti abhidhammapāṭhato (vibha. 458) dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.287) ānīto purimanayato aññenākārena desanāya pavattattā. Chando eva iddhipādo chandiddhipādo. Eseva nayo sesesupi. Ime panāti imasmiṃ sutte āgatā iddhipādā[V 2.0193]. Raṭṭhapālatthero (ma. ni. 2.293; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.210; apa. aṭṭha. 2.raṭṭhapālattheraapadānavaṇṇanāya vitthāro) “chande sati kathaṃ nānujānissantī”ti sattāhaṃ bhattāni abhuñjitvā mātāpitaro anujānāpetvā pabbajitvā chandameva avassāya lokuttaraṃ dhammaṃ nibbattesīti āha “raṭṭhapālatthero…pe… nibbattesī”ti. Soṇatthero (mahāva. 243; a. ni. 6.55; theragā. aṭṭha. terasanipāta; apa. aṭṭha. 2.soṇakoṭivīsattheraapadānavaṇṇanāya vitthāro) bhāvanamanuyutto āraddhavīriyo paramasukhumālo pādesu phoṭesu jātesupi vīriyaṃ nappaṭipassambhesīti āha “soṇatthero vīriyaṃ dhuraṃ katvā”ti. Sambhūtatthero (theragā. aṭṭha. 2.sammūtattheragāthāvaṇṇanāya vitthāro) “cittavato kiṃ nāma na sijjhatī”ti cittaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā bhāvanaṃ ārādhesīti āha “sambhūtatthero cittaṃ dhuraṃ katvā”ti. Moghatthero vīmaṃsaṃ avassayi, tasmā tassa bhagavā “suññato lokaṃ avekkhassū”ti (su. ni. 1125; bu. vaṃ. 54.353; mahā. ni. 186; cūḷani. mogharājamāṇavapucchā 144; mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddese 88; netti. 5; peṭako. 22, 31) suññatākathaṃ kathesi, paññānissitamānaniggahatthaṃ, paññāya pariggahatthañca dvikkhattuṃ pucchito samāno pañhaṃ [P 2.0269] kathesi. Tenāha “āyasmā mogharājā vīmaṃsaṃ dhuraṃ katvā”ti.

"Some" refers to the residents of Abhayagiri. Among them, some say, "Psychic power is unproduced," while others say, "But the base of psychic power is unproduced." And "unproduced" means ultimately unestablished, that is, it does not exist. "Ābhata" means brought from the Abhidhamma text (Vibh. 458) and the Dīghanikāya commentary (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.287), because the teaching proceeds in a different manner from the previous method. Zeal itself is the base of psychic power, the base of psychic power that is zeal. The same method applies to the rest. "But these" refers to the bases of psychic power that occur in this sutta. The elder Raṭṭhapāla (M. II 293; A. I 1.210; Ap. A. II, detailed in the commentary on Raṭṭhapāla Thera's Apadāna) said, "If there is zeal, how will they not permit it?" Without eating meals for seven days, he persuaded his parents to give permission and went forth. Relying solely on zeal, he developed the supramundane Dhamma. Thus it is said, "The elder Raṭṭhapāla… developed it." The elder Soṇa (Mv. 243; A. III 55; Thag. A. Terasanipāta; Ap. A. II, detailed in the commentary on Soṇakoṭivīsa Thera's Apadāna), devoted to development and with aroused energy, did not relax his energy even when blisters arose on his feet, though he was extremely delicate. Thus it is said, "The elder Soṇa, having made energy foremost." The elder Sambhūta (Thag. A. II, detailed in the commentary on Sambhūta Thera's verses) said, "What is not accomplished for one with mind?" Having made mind foremost, he accomplished the development. Thus it is said, "The elder Sambhūta, having made mind foremost." The elder Mogha relied on investigation. Therefore, the Blessed One told him, "Look upon the world as empty" (Sn. 1125; Bv. 54.353; Mahā. Ni. 186; Cūḷani. Mogharājamāṇavapucchā 144; Mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 88; Netti. 5; Peṭako. 22, 31), teaching him the talk on emptiness—for the purpose of subduing pride based on wisdom, and for the purpose of embracing wisdom. Being asked twice, he asked the question. Therefore, it is said, "The venerable Mogharāja, having made investigation foremost."

Punappunaṃ chanduppādanaṃ pesanaṃ viya hotīti chandassa upaṭṭhānasadisatā vuttā.

The repeated generation of zeal is like a dispatching; thus, the similarity of zeal to attendance is stated.

Parakkamenāti parakkamasīsena sūrabhāvaṃ vadati. Thāmabhāvato ca vīriyassa sūrabhāvasadisatā daṭṭhabbā.

By "striving," he speaks of heroism by way of supreme striving. And the similarity of energy to heroism should be understood from its quality of strength.

Cintanappadhānattā cittassa mantasaṃvidhānasadisatā vuttā.

Due to the predominance of thinking, the similarity of the mind to the arrangement of a plan is stated.

Jātisampatti [M 2.0211] nāma visiṭṭhajātitā. “Sabbadhammesu ca paññā seṭṭhā”ti vīmaṃsāya jātisampattisadisatā vuttā. Sammohavinodaniyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 433) pana cittiddhipādassa jātisampattisadisatā, vīmaṃsiddhipādassa mantabalasadisatā ca yojitā.

Excellence of birth means being of distinguished birth. Because it is said that 'wisdom is the best among all things,' a similarity of investigation to excellence of birth is stated. But in the Sammohavinodanī (Vibhaṅga Aṭṭhakathā 433), the similarity of the base of psychic power of mind to excellence of birth, and the similarity of the base of psychic power of investigation to the strength of counsel are connected.

Anekaṃ vihitaṃ vidhaṃ etassāti anekavihitanti āha “anekavidha”nti. Vidha-saddo koṭṭhāsapariyāyo “ekavidhena ñāṇavatthū”tiādīsu (vibha. 751) viyāti āha “iddhividhanti iddhikoṭṭhāsa”nti.

He says `anekavidhaṃ` ('of many kinds') for `anekavihitaṃ`, which is derived from `anekaṃ vihitaṃ vidhaṃ etassa` ('it has many arranged kinds'). The word `vidha` is a synonym for `koṭṭhāsa` (part), as in `ekavidhena ñāṇavatthū` ('the ground of knowledge in one part'), and so on. Thus he says, `iddhividhaṃ` means `iddhikoṭṭhāsa` ('a part of psychic power').

Tividhaokāsādhigamavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Threefold Attainment of Opportunity

288. “Sukhassā”ti [V 2.0194] idaṃ tiṇṇampi sukhānaṃ sādhāraṇavacananti āha “jhānasukhassa maggasukhassa phalasukhassā”ti. Nānappanāpattatāya pana appadhānattā upacārajjhānasukhassa, vipassanāsukhassa cettha aggahaṇaṃ. Purimesu tāva dvīsu okāsādhigamesu tīṇipi sukhāni labbhanti, tatiye pana kathanti? Tattha kāmaṃ tīṇi na labbhanti, dve pana labbhantiyeva. Yathālābhavasena hetaṃ vuttaṃ. “Sakkharakathalampi macchagumbampi carantampi tiṭṭhantampī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.249; ma. ni. 1.433; 2.259; a. ni. 1.45, 46) viya. Saṃsaṭṭhoti saṃsaggaṃ upagato samaṅgībhūto, so pana tehi samannāgatacittopi hotīti vuttaṃ “sampayuttacitto”ti. Ariyadhammanti ariyabhāvakaraṃ dhammaṃ. Upāyatoti vidhito. Pathatoti maggato. Kāraṇatoti hetuto. Yena hi vidhinā dhammānudhammapaṭipatti hoti, so [P 2.0270] upeti etenāti upāyo, so tadadhigamassa maggabhāvato patho, tassa karaṇato kāraṇanti ca vuccati.

288. The word "sukhassa" ('of happiness') is a general term for three types of happiness; hence it is said, 'the happiness of jhāna, the happiness of the path, and the happiness of the fruit'. However, the happiness of access concentration and the happiness of insight are not included here because of their non-prominence, due to their not being invariably attained. In the first two attainments of opportunity, all three types of happiness can be obtained, but how is it in the third? There, indeed, all three may not be obtained, but two certainly can. This is stated according to what is attainable, as in such phrases as 'a gravel-and-pebble shoal, and a school of fish, whether walking or standing' (Dīgha Nikāya 1.249; Majjhima Nikāya 1.433, 2.259; Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.45, 46). "Saṃsaṭṭho" means having entered into association, united; and since one's mind is endowed with these, it is said to be "sampayuttacitto" ('with associated mind'). "Ariyadhammaṃ" means the Dhamma that makes one noble. "Upāyato" is from 'method' (vidhi). "Pathato" is from 'path' (magga). "Kāraṇato" is from 'cause' (hetu). For by whatever method the practice in accordance with the Dhamma occurs, one approaches (upeti) by means of it (etena), thus it is a means (upāya); because it is the path (patha) to that attainment, it is called a path; and because it is the cause (kāraṇa) of it, it is called a cause.

“Aniccantiādivasena manasi karotī”ti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “yoniso manasikāro nāmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha upāyamanasikāroti kusaladhammappavattiyā kāraṇabhūto manasikāro. Pathamanasikāroti tassa eva maggabhūto manasikāro. Anicceti ādiantavantatāya, anaccantikatāya ca anicce tebhūmake saṅkhāre “anicca”nti manasikāroti yojanā. Eseva nayo sesesupi. Ayaṃ pana viseso tasmiṃyeva udayabbayapaṭipīḷanatāya dukkhanato, dukkhamato ca dukkhe, avasavattanatthena, anattasabhāvatāya ca anattani, asucisabhāvatāya [M 2.0212] asubhe. Sabbampi hi tebhūmakaṃ saṅkhataṃ kilesāsucipaggharaṇato “asubha”ntveva vattuṃ arahati. Saccānulomikena vāti saccābhisamayassa anulomanavasena. “Cittassa āvaṭṭanā”tiādinā āvajjanāya paccayabhūtā tato purimuppannā manodvārikā kusalajavanappavatti phalavohāreneva tathā vuttā. Tassā hi vasena sā kusaluppattiyā upanissayo hotīti. Āvajjanā hi bhavaṅgacittaṃ āvaṭṭetīti cittassa āvaṭṭanā, anu anu āvaṭṭetīti anvāvaṭṭanā. Bhavaṅgārammaṇato aññaṃ ābhujatīti ābhogo. Samannāharatīti samannāhāro. Tadevārammaṇaṃ attānaṃ anubandhitvā anubandhitvā uppajjamāne manasi karoti ṭhapetīti manasikāro. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ upāyamanasikāralakkhaṇo yonisomanasikāro nāma vuccati, yassa vasena puggalo dukkhādīni saccāni āvajjituṃ sakkoti.

To elucidate the meaning briefly stated as 'one attends in terms of impermanence, and so on,' the text beginning 'What is called proper attention' was stated. Therein, skilful attention (upāyamanasikāra) is the attention that is the cause for the arising of wholesome states. Initial attention (pathamanasikāra) is that very attention which is the path. The construction is as follows: attention to formations in the three realms as 'impermanent' because they are impermanent due to having a beginning and an end, and due to not being perpetual. This same method applies to the rest. This, however, is the distinction: in that very case, it is suffering because of the oppression of arising and passing away and because it is suffering by nature; it is not-self due to the characteristic of being uncontrollable and due to the nature of not-self; it is foul due to the nature of impurity. For all conditioned things in the three realms deserve to be called 'foul' because they exude the impurity of defilements. Or, 'in accordance with the truths' means in a way that is conducive to the comprehension of the truths. By 'the turning of the mind,' and so on, the process of wholesome impulsion at the mind-door, which arose previously and is a condition for adverting, is so called by way of speaking of its result. For by means of that, it becomes a decisive support for the arising of the wholesome. Adverting turns the life-continuum consciousness, hence it is 'the turning of the mind'; it turns again and again, hence it is 'repeated turning.' It bends towards an object other than that of the life-continuum, hence it is 'directing.' It brings together, hence it is 'combining.' It places that very object in the mind as it arises, following it again and again; this is 'attention.' This is said: this proper attention, characterized as skilful attention, is so called, by means of which a person is able to advert to the truths such as suffering.

Asaṃsaṭṭhoti [V 2.0195] na saṃsaṭṭho kāmādīhi vivitto vinābhūto. Kāmādivisaṃsaggahetu uppajjanakasukhaṃ nāma vivekajaṃ pītisukhanti [P 2.0271] āha “paṭhamajjhānasukha”nti. Kāmaṃ paṭhamajjhānasukhampi somanassameva, suttesu pana taṃ kāyikasukhassāpi paccayabhāvato visesato “sukha”ntveva vuccatīti idhāpi jhānabhūtaṃ somanassaṃ sukhanti, itaraṃ somanassaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “sukhā”ti. Hetumhi nissakkavacananti āha “jhānasukhapaccayā”ti. Aparāparaṃ somanassanti jhānādhigamahetu paccavekkhaṇādivasena punappunaṃ uppajjanakasomanassaṃ.

'Unassociated' means not associated, secluded from, and devoid of sensual pleasures and the like. The happiness that arises due to disassociation from sensual pleasures and the like is joy and happiness born of seclusion; therefore, it is said, 'the happiness of the first jhāna.' Although the happiness of the first jhāna is itself gladness, in the suttas, because it is also a condition for bodily happiness, it is specifically called just 'happiness.' So here too, the gladness that constitutes jhāna is 'happiness,' while other gladness is 'gladness.' Therefore, it is said, 'from happiness.' It is a statement in the ablative signifying a cause; hence it is said, 'because of the happiness of jhāna.' 'Successive gladness' is the gladness that arises again and again by way of reviewing and so on, which is a cause for the attainment of jhāna.

Pamodanaṃ pamudo, taruṇapīti, tato pamudā. “Pāmojjaṃ pītatthāyā”tiādīsu taruṇapīti “pāmojja”nti vuccati, idha pana pakaṭṭho mudo pamudo pāmojjanti adhippetaṃ, tañca somanassarahitaṃ natthīti avinābhāvitāya “balavataraṃ pītisomanassa”nti vuttaṃ. Jhānassa ujuvipaccanīkataṃ sandhāya “pañca nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhetvā”ti vuttaṃ. Jhānaṃ pana tadekaṭṭhe sabbepi kilese, sabbepi akusale dhamme vikkhambhetiyeva, attano okāsaṃ gahetvā tiṭṭhati paṭipakkhadhammehi anabhibhavanīyato. Tasmāti okāsaggahaṇato, laddhokāsatāyāti attho. Maggaphalasukhādhigamāya okāsabhāvato vā okāso, assa adhigamo okāsādhigamo. Purimapakkhe pana okāsaṃ avasaraṃ adhigacchati etenāti okāsādhigamo.

Rejoicing (pamodanaṃ) is delight (pamudo), which is tender joy; from that comes delight (pamudā). In phrases like 'joy is for the sake of rapture,' tender joy is called 'joy' (pāmojja). Here, however, intense gladness, delight, is intended as joy, and since that does not exist without gladness, due to its inseparability it is said to be 'stronger rapture and gladness.' With reference to the jhāna's direct opposition, it is said, 'having suppressed the five hindrances.' Jhāna, indeed, suppresses all defilements and all unwholesome states in that same place; having seized its opportunity, it stands firm, being unconquerable by opposing states. 'Therefore' means 'from the seizing of the opportunity'; the meaning is 'due to the opportunity having been obtained.' Or, it is an opportunity because it is the opportunity for attaining the happiness of the path and fruition; its attainment is the 'attainment of opportunity.' In the former alternative, however, 'one attains the opportunity, the occasion, by means of this'; hence, 'attainment of opportunity.'

Rūpasabhāvatāya[M 2.0213], ekantarūpādhīnavuttitāya, savipphārikatāya ca ānāpānavitakkavicārānaṃ thūlabhāvaṃ anujānanto “kāyavacīsaṅkhārā tāva oḷārikā hontū”ti āha. Tabbidhuratāya pana ekaccānaṃ vedanāsaññānaṃ thūlataṃ ananujānanto “cittasaṅkhārā kathaṃ oḷārikā”ti āha. Itaro “appahīnattā”ti kāraṇaṃ vatvā “kāyasaṅkhārā hī”tiādinā tamatthaṃ vivarati. Teti cittasaṅkhārā. Appahīnā saṅkhārā labbhamānasaṅkhāranimittatāya “oḷārikā”ti vattuṃ arahanti, pahīnā pana tadabhāvato “sukhumā”ti āha “pahīne upādāya [P 2.0272] appahīnattā oḷārikā nāma jātā”ti. Pāḷiyaṃ “kāyasaṅkhārānaṃ paṭippassaddhiyā”ti vuttattā “sukhanti catutthajjhānikaphalasamāpattisukha”nti vuttaṃ. “Cittasaṅkhārānaṃ paṭippassaddhiyā”ti pana vuttattā “nirodhā vuṭṭhahantassā”ti vuttaṃ. Vacīsaṅkhārapaṭippassaddhi kāyasaṅkhārapaṭippassaddhiyāva siddhāti veditabbā. Tenevāha “dutiya…pe… visuṃ na vuttānī”ti. Pāḷiyaṃ pana atthato siddhāpi supākaṭabhāvena vibhāvetuṃ sarūpato gaṇhāti. Na hi ariyavinaye atthāpattivibhāvanā abhidhammadesanāya pakatīti. Yathā nīvaraṇavikkhambhanañca paṭhamassa jhānassa adhigamāya upāyo, evaṃ sukhadukkhavikkhambhanaṃ catutthassa [V 2.0196] jhānassa adhigamāya upāyoti “catutthajjhānaṃ sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ vikkhambhetvā”ti vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

Acknowledging the grossness of in-and-out breathing, initial thought, and sustained thought due to their nature as form, their occurrence being dependent entirely on form, and their pervasiveness, he said, 'For now, let the bodily and verbal formations be gross.' However, not acknowledging the grossness of certain feelings and perceptions due to their being devoid of that nature, he said, 'How can the mental formations be gross?' The other, stating the reason as 'Because they are not abandoned,' explains that meaning with 'For the bodily formations…' and so on. Those are the mental formations. Unabandoned formations deserve to be called 'gross' because a sign of the formations is obtainable; but abandoned ones, due to the absence of that, are 'subtle.' He said, 'In comparison to the abandoned, because they are unabandoned, they have become what is called gross.' Because it is said in the Pāli text, 'with the calming of the bodily formations,' it is said, '“happiness” is the happiness of the attainment of fruition of the fourth jhāna.' And because it is said, 'with the calming of the mental formations,' it is stated, 'for one emerging from cessation.' The calming of the verbal formations should be understood as accomplished by the very calming of the bodily formations. Therefore he said, 'the second… etc.… are not stated separately.' In the Pāli text, however, although it is established by implication, it is taken up explicitly in order to explain it with great clarity. For in the noble discipline, the explanation of what is arrived at by implication is not the custom of the Abhidhamma teaching. Just as the suppression of the hindrances is the means for attaining the first jhāna, so the suppression of pleasure and pain is the means for attaining the fourth jhāna; thus it is said, 'the fourth jhāna, having suppressed pleasure and pain…' The rest is as stated before.

Avijjārāgādīhi saha vajjehīti sāvajjaṃ, akusalaṃ, tadabhāvato anavajjaṃ kusalaṃ. Attano hitasukhaṃ ākaṅkhantena sevanīyato sevitabbaṃ, kusalaṃ, tabbipariyāyato na sevitabbaṃ, akusalaṃ. Lāmakabhāvena hīnaṃ, akusalaṃ, seṭṭhabhāvena paṇītaṃ, kusalanti sāvajjadukādayo tayopi dukā yathārahaṃ etesaṃ kusalākusalakammapathānaṃ vaseneva veditabbā. Sabbanti yathāvuttaṃ sabbaṃ catūhi dukehi saṅgahitaṃ dhammajātaṃ. Yathārahaṃ kaṇhañca sukkañca paṭidvandibhāvato, sappaṭibhāgañca appaṭibhāgañca advayabhāvato. Vaṭṭapaṭicchādikā avijjā pahīyati catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ sammadeva paṭivijjhanato. Tato eva arahattamaggavijjā uppajjati. Sukhanti evaṃ kammapathamukhena tebhūmakadhamme sammasitvā vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā maggapaṭipāṭiyā arahatte patiṭṭhahantassa yaṃ arahattamaggasukhañceva arahattaphalasukhañca, taṃ idha “sukha”nti adhippetaṃ. Antogadhā eva nānantariyabhāvato.

'With faults' (sāvajjaṃ) means with faults such as ignorance and lust; it is unwholesome. Due to their absence, 'blameless' (anavajjaṃ) is wholesome. 'To be cultivated' (sevitabbaṃ) is wholesome, because it should be cultivated by one desiring one's own welfare and happiness. The opposite of that, 'not to be cultivated,' is unwholesome. 'Inferior' (hīnaṃ) due to its base nature is unwholesome; 'superior' (paṇītaṃ) due to its excellent nature is wholesome. Thus the three pairs beginning with the blameworthy-pair should be understood as appropriate by way of these wholesome and unwholesome courses of action. 'All' means the entire collection of phenomena as described, included in the four pairs. As appropriate, they are 'dark and bright' due to being opposites, and 'with a counterpart and without a counterpart' due to not being a dyad. The ignorance that conceals the round of existence is abandoned because of the right penetration of the Four Noble Truths. From that very penetration, the knowledge of the path to arahantship arises. 'Happiness': here 'happiness' is intended as both the happiness of the path to arahantship and the happiness of the fruition of arahantship for one who, having thus comprehended the phenomena of the three realms by way of the courses of action, and having made an effort in insight, becomes established in arahantship by the sequence of the path. They are indeed included, because there is no interval.

Aṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇavasenāti [M 2.0214][P 2.0273] pāḷiyaṃ āgatānaṃ aṭṭhatiṃsāya kammaṭṭhānānaṃ vasena. Vitthāretvā kathetabbā paṭhamajjhānādivasena āgatattāti adhippāyo. “Katha”ntiādinā tameva vitthāretvā kathanaṃ nayato dasseti. “Catuvīsatiyā ṭhānesū”tiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ mahāparinibbānavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.219) vuttameva. “Nirodhasamāpattiṃ pāpetvā”ti iminā arūpajjhānānipi gahitāni honti tehi vinā nirodhasamāpattisamāpajjanassa asambhavato, catutthajjhānasabhāvattā ca tesaṃ. Dasa upacārajjhānānīti ṭhapetvā kāyagatāsatiṃ ānāpānañca aṭṭha anussatiyo, saññāvavatthānañcāti dasa upacārajjhānāni. Adhisīlaṃ nāma samādhisaṃvattaniyanti tassa heṭṭhimantena paṭhamajjhānaṃ pariyosānanti vuttaṃ “adhisīlasikkhā paṭhamaṃ okāsādhigamaṃ bhajatī”ti. Adhicittaṃ nāma catutthajjhānaniṭṭhaṃ tadantogadhattā arūpajjhānānaṃ, tappariyosānattā phalajjhānānanti vuttaṃ “adhicittasikkhā dutiya”nti. Matthakappattā adhipaññāsikkhā nāma aggamaggavijjāti āha “adhipaññāsikkhā tatiya”nti. Sikkhattayavasena tayo okāsādhigame nīharantena yathārahaṃ taṃtaṃsuttavasenapi nīharitabbanti dassento “sāmaññaphalepī”tiādimāha.

“By means of thirty-eight objects”—this refers to the thirty-eight meditation subjects found in the Pāli texts. The intention is that they should be explained in detail according to the first jhāna and so on, as they are presented. The phrase “How” and so on shows the method of explaining it in detail. Whatever needs to be said about “in twenty-four places” and so on has already been stated in the commentary on the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.219). By “having attained the cessation attainment,” the formless jhānas are also included, because without them, entering the cessation attainment is impossible, and because they share the nature of the fourth jhāna. The ten access jhānas are the eight recollections, the perception of loathsomeness in food, and the analysis of the four elements, excluding mindfulness of the body and mindfulness of breathing. Higher virtue, which is conducive to concentration, is said to have the first jhāna as its culmination, as stated: “The training in higher virtue first serves the attainment of opportunity.” Higher mind culminates in the fourth jhāna, because the formless jhānas are included within it, and the fruition jhānas culminate in it, as stated: “The training in higher mind is second.” The training in higher wisdom, having reached its peak, is the knowledge of the supreme path, as stated: “The training in higher wisdom is third.” To show that just as one extracts the three attainments of opportunity by means of the threefold training, they should also be extracted appropriately according to the respective suttas, it is said, “Even in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta,” and so on.

Yadaggena ca tisso sikkhā yathākkamaṃ tayo okāsādhigame bhajanti, tadaggena tappadhānattā yathākkamaṃ tīṇi piṭakāni te bhajantīti dassetuṃ “tīsu panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tīṇi [V 2.0197] piṭakāni vibhajitvāti tiṇṇaṃ okāsādhigamānaṃ vasena yathānupubbaṃ tīṇi piṭakāni vitthāretvā kathetuṃ labhissāmāti. Samodhānetvāti samāyojetvā tattha vuttamatthaṃ imassa suttassa atthabhāvena samānetvā. Dukkathitanti asambandhakathanena, atipapañcakathanena vā duṭṭhu kathitanti na sakkā vattuṃ tathākathanasseva sukathanabhāvatoti āha “tepiṭakaṃ…pe… sukathitaṃ hotī”ti.

Moreover, to show that just as the three trainings, in their respective order, lead to the three attainments of opportunity, so too, due to their predominance, the three Piṭakas lead to them in order, it is said, “But in the three…” and so on. “Having divided the three Piṭakas” means that by means of the three attainments of opportunity, according to their sequence, we will be able to expound the three Piṭakas in detail. “Connecting” means having combined them, having brought together the meaning stated there with the meaning of this sutta. “Ill-spoken”—it cannot be said that it is poorly spoken due to disconnected speech or overly elaborate speech, since such speech is indeed well-spoken. Hence it is said, “The Tipiṭaka… is well-spoken.”

Catusatipaṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Four Establishments of Mindfulness

289. Na kevalaṃ abhidhammapariyāyeneva kusalaṭṭho gahetabbo, atha kho bāhitikapariyāyena pīti āha “phalakusalassa cā”ti. Khemaṭṭhenāti catūhipi yogehi anupaddavabhāvena[P 2.0274]. Sammā samāhitoti samathavasena [M 2.0215] ceva vipassanāvasena ca suṭṭhu samāhito. Ekaggacittoti vikkhepassa dūrasamussāritattā ekaggataṃ avikkhepaṃ pattacitto. Attano kāyatoti ajjhattaṃ kāye kāyānupassanāvasena sammā samāhitacitto samāno “samāhito yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti passatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.5; 5.1071, 1072; netti. 40; mi. pa. 1.14) vacanato. Tattha ñāṇadassanaṃ nibbattento tato bahiddhā parassa kāyepi ñāṇadassanaṃ nibbatteti. Tenāha “parassa kāyābhimukhaṃ ñāṇaṃ pesetī”ti. Sammā vippasīdatīti sammā samādhānapaccayena abhippasādena ñāṇūpasañhitena ajjhattaṃ kāyaṃ okappeti. Sabbatthāti sabbaṭṭhānesu. Sati kathitāti yojanā. Lokiyalokuttaramissakā kathitā anupassanāñāṇadassanānaṃ tadubhayasādhāraṇabhāvato.

289. The meaning of ‘kusala’ should not be understood only through the Abhidhamma method, but also through the ‘bāhitika’ method, as it is said: “and of one skilled in results.” By the meaning of ‘khema’ (security)—through the state of being free from danger by way of the four yokes. ‘Rightly concentrated’ means well concentrated through both serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). ‘One-pointed mind’ means a mind that has attained one-pointedness and non-distraction, being far removed from distraction. ‘On one’s own body’ means that being rightly concentrated internally on one’s own body through body contemplation, one acts according to the saying, “being concentrated, one understands and sees as it really is” (Saṃ. Ni. 3.5; 5.1071, 1072; Netti. 40; Mi. Pa. 1.14). There, generating knowledge and vision, one also generates knowledge and vision externally toward another’s body. Hence it is said: “directs knowledge toward another’s body.” ‘Becomes rightly serene’ means one settles internally on the body through the serene faith (abhippasāda) conditioned by right concentration, imbued with knowledge. ‘Everywhere’ means in all places. ‘Mindfulness is spoken of’—this is the connection. Mundane and supramundane are spoken of as mixed because contemplation, knowledge, and vision are common to both.

Sattasamādhiparikkhāravaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Seven Requisites for Concentration

290. Etthāti imissā kathāya. Jhānakkhassa vīriyacakkassa ariyamaggarathassa sīlaṃ vibhūsanabhāvena vuttanti āha “alaṅkāro parikkhāro nāmā”ti. Sattahi nagaraparikkhārehīti nagaraṃ parivāretvā rakkhaṇakehi kataparikkhepo, parikhā, uddāpo, pākāro, esikā, palighā, pākārapakkhaṇḍilanti imehi sattahi nagaraparikkhārehi. Sambharīyati phalaṃ etenāti sambhāro, kāraṇaṃ. Bhesajjañhi byādhivūpasamanena jīvitassa kāraṇaṃ. Parivāraparikkhāravasenāti parivārasaṅkhātaparikkhāravasena. Parikkhāro hi sammādiṭṭhiyādayo maggadhammā sammāsamādhissa sahajātādipaccayabhāvena parikaraṇato abhisaṅkharaṇato. Upecca nissīyatīti upanisā, saha upanisāyāti saupanisoti [P 2.0275] āha “saupanissayo”ti, sahakārīkāraṇabhūto dhammasamūho idha “upanissayo”ti [V 2.0198] adhippeto. Sammā pasatthā sundarā diṭṭhi etassāti sammādiṭṭhi, puggalo, tassa sammādiṭṭhissa. So pana yasmā patiṭṭhitasammādiṭṭhiko, tasmā vuttaṃ “sammādiṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhitassā”ti. Sammāsaṅkappo pahotīti maggasammādiṭṭhiyā dukkhādīsu parijānanādikiccaṃ sādhentiyā kāmavitakkādike samugghāṭento sammāsaṅkappo yathā attano kiccasādhane pahoti, tathā pavattiṃ panassa dassento āha “sammāsaṅkappo pavattatī”ti. Esa nayo sabbapadesūti “sammāsaṅkappassa sammāvācā pahotī”tiādīsu sesapadesu yathāvuttamatthaṃ atidisati.

290. Here, in this discussion, it is said that virtue is an adornment for the jhāna-axle, the effort-wheel, and the noble-path chariot; hence, it is called “an ornament and requisite.” “With the seven city requisites” refers to the enclosure made to protect the city by surrounding it with seven protective measures: the moat, the rampart, the wall, the gatehouse, the barricade, the crossbar, and the wall’s battlement. “It produces the fruit” (sambhāro) means it is the cause. For medicine is the cause of life by pacifying disease. “By means of surrounding requisites” refers to the requisites consisting of the retinue. For the requisites—right view and other path factors—serve as accessories and supporting conditions for right concentration through their co-arising and conditioning roles, thus constituting its equipment. “Approaching and relying upon” is dependence (upanisā). “With dependence” is saupaniso; thus he says “with supporting condition” (saupanissayo). Here, “supporting condition” (upanissayo) is intended to mean the aggregate of factors that act as cooperative causes. “Right view is well-praised, beautiful in him” refers to the person who possesses right view. Because he is established in right view, it is said, “for one who is grounded in right view.” “Right intention succeeds” means that while path-right-view is accomplishing its task of fully understanding suffering and so on, right intention, by uprooting sensual thoughts and the like, becomes capable of accomplishing its own task. To show its proceeding thus, it is said, “right intention proceeds.” “This is the method in all instances” means that he applies the meaning as explained to the remaining cases, such as “for one with right intention, right speech succeeds,” and so on.

Ettha [M 2.0216] ca yasmā nibbānādhigamāya paṭipannassa yogino bahūpakārā sammādiṭṭhi. Tathā hi sā “paññāpajjoto, paññāsattha”nti ca vuttā. Tāya hi so avijjandhakāraṃ vidhamitvā kilesacore ghātento khemena nibbānaṃ pāpuṇāti, tasmā ariyamaggakathāyaṃ sammādiṭṭhi ādito gayhati, idha pana puggalādhiṭṭhānadesanāya “sammādiṭṭhissā”ti vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana sammādiṭṭhipuggalo nekkhammasaṅkappādivasena sammadeva saṅkappeti, na micchākāmasaṅkappādivasena, tasmā sammādiṭṭhissa sammāsaṅkappo pahoti. Yasmā ca sammāsaṅkappo sammāvācāya upakārako. Yathāha “pubbe kho gahapati vitakketvā vicāretvā pacchā vācaṃ bhindatī”ti, (saṃ. ni. 2.348) tasmā sammāsaṅkappassa sammāvācā pahoti. Yasmā pana “idañcidañca karissāmā”ti hi paṭhamaṃ vācāya saṃvidahitvā yebhuyyena te te kammantā sammā payojīyanti, tasmā vācā kāyakammassa upakārikāti sammāvācassa sammākammanto pahoti. Yasmā pana catubbidhaṃ vacīduccaritaṃ, tividhañca kāyaduccaritaṃ pahāya ubhayaṃ sucaritaṃ pūrentasseva ājīvaṭṭhamakasīlaṃ pūrati, na itarassa[P 2.0276], tasmā sammāvācassa sammākammantassa ca sammāājīvo pahoti. Visuddhidiṭṭhisamudāgatasammāājīvassa yoniso padhānassa sambhavato sammāājīvassa sammāvāyāmo pahoti. Yoniso padahantassa kāyādīsu catūsu vatthūsu sati sūpaṭṭhitā hotīti sammāvāyāmassa sammāsati pahoti. Yasmā evaṃ sūpaṭṭhitā sati samādhissa upakārānupakārānaṃ dhammānaṃ gatiyo samannesitvā pahoti ekattārammaṇe cittaṃ samādhātuṃ, tasmā sammāsatissa sammāsamādhi pahotīti. Ayañca nayo pubbabhāge nānākkhaṇikānaṃ sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ vasena vutto, maggakkhaṇe pana sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ tassa tassa sahajātādivasena vutto “sammādiṭṭhissa sammāsaṅkappo pahotī”tiādīnaṃ padānamattho yutto, ayameva ca idhādhippeto. Tenāha “ayaṃ panattho”tiādi.

And here, since right view is of great benefit to the yogi who is practicing for the attainment of Nibbāna. For it is said, 'the light of wisdom, the weapon of wisdom.' By it, indeed, one dispels the darkness of ignorance, destroys the thieves that are the defilements, and safely reaches Nibbāna. Therefore, in the discourse on the noble path, right view is taken up first. But here, in the teaching based on the individual, it is said, 'for one with right view.' Since a person with right view conceives rightly through thoughts of renunciation and so on, not through wrong thoughts of sensual desire and the like, therefore, for one with right view, right intention arises. And since right intention is a benefactor to right speech, as it is said: 'First, householder, one reflects and considers, and afterwards one utters speech' (Saṃ. Ni. 2.348), therefore, for one with right intention, right speech arises. Moreover, since one first arranges by speech, thinking, 'I will do this and that,' and then for the most part those tasks are properly undertaken, therefore speech is a benefactor to bodily action. Thus, for one with right speech, right action arises. Since for one who abandons the fourfold verbal misconduct and the threefold bodily misconduct and fulfills both kinds of good conduct, the virtue that is the eighth factor, right livelihood, is fulfilled—but not for another—therefore, for one with right speech and right action, right livelihood arises. For one whose right livelihood arises from purified view, right effort arises from the possibility of wise striving. For one who strives wisely, mindfulness is well-established in the four foundations—body and so on—therefore, for one with right effort, right mindfulness arises. Since when mindfulness is thus well-established, it is able to investigate the courses of mental states that aid or hinder concentration, and is able to concentrate the mind on a single object, therefore, for one with right mindfulness, right concentration arises. And this method is stated in the preliminary stage by way of right view and so on occurring at different moments, but at the moment of the path, the meaning of the phrases 'for one with right view, right intention arises' and so on is appropriate, being stated by way of their co-arising and so on. This is indeed what is intended here. Therefore he said, 'But this is the meaning,' and so on.

Maggañāṇeti maggapariyāpannañāṇe ṭhitassa taṃsamaṅgino. Maggapaññā hi catunnaṃ saccānaṃ sammādassanaṭṭhena “maggasammādiṭṭhī”ti vuttā, sā eva nesaṃ yāthāvato jānanato paṭivijjhanato idha [V 2.0199] “maggañāṇa”ntipi vuttā. Maggavimuttīti maggena kilesānaṃ vimuccanaṃ samucchedappahānameva. Phalasammādiṭṭhi eva [M 2.0217] “phalasammāñāṇa”nti pariyāyena vuttaṃ, pariyāyavacanañca vuttanayānusārena veditabbaṃ. Phalavimutti pana paṭippassaddhippahānaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Knowledge of the path' means the knowledge included in the path, for one who is established in it and endowed with it. For the wisdom of the path, in the sense of rightly seeing the four truths, is called 'right view of the path'; that same wisdom, because of knowing and penetrating them as they actually are, is also called here 'knowledge of the path.' 'Liberation of the path' is the liberation from defilements by the path, that is, their abandonment by way of eradication. Right view of the fruit is called 'right knowledge of the fruit' by way of synonym, and this synonymous expression should be understood in accordance with the method stated. Liberation of the fruit, however, should be regarded as abandonment by way of tranquilization.

Amatassa dvārāti ariyamaggamāha. So pana vinā ca ācariyamuṭṭhinā anantaraṃ abāhiraṃ karitvā yāvadeva manussehi suppakāsitattā vivaṭo. Dhammavinītāti ariyadhamme vinītā. So panettha kilesānaṃ samucchedavinayavasena veditabboti āha “sammāniyyānena niyyātā”ti.

“The door to the Deathless” refers to the Noble Path. That path, without the teacher's closed fist, making no distinction between inner and outer, is wide open, being well proclaimed to human beings. “Trained in the Dhamma” means trained in the Noble Dhamma. Here, this should be understood as training by way of the eradication of defilements; hence he says, “led forth by the right leading forth.”

Atthīti puthutthavisayaṃ nipātapadaṃ “atthi [P 2.0277] imasmiṃ kāye kesā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.377; ma. ni. 1.110; 3.154; saṃ. ni. 4.127; a. ni. 6.29; 10.60; vibha. 356; khu. pā. 2.1.dvattiṃsaākāra; netti. 47) viyāti āha “anāgāmino ca atthī”ti. Tenevāha “atthi cevettha sakadāgāmino”ti. Bahiddhā saṃyojanapaccayo nibbattihetubhūto puññabhāgo etissā atthīti puññabhāgā, atisayavisiṭṭho cettha atthiattho veditabbo. Ottappamānoti uttasanto bhāyanto. Na pana natthi, atthi evāti dīpeti.

The word 'atthi' (there is) is a particle with a wide range of application, as in 'there are hairs on this body,' etc. (Dī. Ni. 2.377; Ma. Ni. 1.110; 3.154; Saṃ. Ni. 4.127; A. Ni. 6.29; 10.60; Vibha. 356; Khu. Pā. 2.1.dvattiṃsaākāra; Netti. 47), as he says, 'and there is the non-returner.' Therefore he also says, 'and here there is the once-returner.' Because a portion of merit, which is an external factor for the fetters and a cause for rebirth, exists for her, she is called 'one who has a portion of merit.' Here, the meaning of 'atthi' should be understood as surpassing excellence. 'Ottappamāno' means trembling, being afraid. It is not that it does not exist; it certainly exists, thus he shows.

291. Assāti vessavaṇassa. Laddhi pana na atthi paṭividdhasaccattā. “Abhisamaye viseso natthī”ti etena sabbepi sabbaññuguṇā sabbabuddhānaṃ sadisā evāti dasseti.

291. “Assā” refers to Vessavaṇa. But there is no attainment, because of having penetrated the truths. By “There is no distinction in realization,” he shows that all the qualities of an omniscient one are similar for all Buddhas.

292. Kāraṇassa ekarūpattā imāni pana padānīti na kevalaṃ “tayidaṃ brahmacariya”ntiādīni padāni, atha kho “imamatthaṃ janavasabho yakkho”tiādīni padāni pīti.

292. Because the reason is uniform, these words—not only phrases such as “this holy life,” etc., but also phrases such as “this matter, the yakkha Janavasabha,” etc.—are also relevant.

Janavasabhasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

In the Commentary on the Janavasabha Sutta, the Clarification of the Hidden Meaning.

6. Mahāgovindasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Mahāgovinda Sutta

293. Pañcakuṇḍalikoti [P 2.0278][V 2.0200][M 2.0218] vissaṭṭhapañcaveṇiko. Catumaggaṭṭhānesūti catunnaṃ maggānaṃ vinivijjhitvā gataṭṭhānesu. Tattha hi katā sālādayo catūhi disāhi āgatamanussānaṃ upabhogakkhamā honti. “Evarūpānī”ti iminā rukkhamūlasodhanādīni ceva yathāsatti annadānādīni ca puññāni saṅgaṇhāti. “Suvaṇṇakkhandhasadiso attabhāvo iṭṭho kanto manāpo ahosī”ti pāṭho. Sakaṭasahassamattanti vāhasahassamattaṃ, vāho pana vīsati khārī, khārī soḷasadoṇamattā, doṇaṃ soḷasa nāḷiyo veditabbā. Kumbhaṃ dasambaṇāni. “Sahassanāḷiyo”ti keci. Rattasuvaṇṇakaṇṇikanti rattasuvaṇṇamayaṃ vaṭaṃsakaṃ.

293. “Pañcakuṇḍalika” means one with five released braids. “At the four crossroads” means at the places reached by piercing through the four paths. There, indeed, halls and the like were built, suitable for use by people arriving from the four directions. By “Such as these,” he includes both meritorious deeds like cleaning the roots of trees and the like, as well as giving food and so forth according to one's ability. The reading is: “A body like a golden mass, desirable, charming, and delightful.” “A thousand carts” means a thousand loads; a load is twenty khārīs, a khārī is sixteen doṇas, and a doṇa should be understood as sixteen nāḷis. A kumbha is ten ambaṇas. Some say, “A thousand nāḷis.” “A red-gold ear-flower” means a red-gold round ornament.

Yasmā majjhimayāme eva devatā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamituṃ avasaraṃ labhanti, tasmā “ekakoṭṭhāsaṃ atītāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Atikkantavaṇṇoti ativiya kamanīyarūpo, kevalakappanti vā manaṃ ūnaṃ avasesaṃ, īsakaṃ asamattanti attho bhagavato hi samīpaṭṭhānaṃ muñcitvā sabbo gijjhakūṭavihāro tena obhāsito. Tenāha “candimā viyā”tiādi.

Since the deities get the opportunity to approach the Teacher only in the middle watch of the night, therefore it is said, “when one portion had passed.” “Of surpassing beauty” means of exceedingly lovely form. Or “the entire” means not in the least deficient, without remainder, that is, not slightly incomplete; for the entire Vulture Peak monastery was illuminated by him, except for the immediate vicinity of the Blessed One. Therefore he said, “like the moon,” and so on.

Devasabhāvaṇṇanā

Description of the Assembly of Devas.

294. Ratanamattakaṇṇikarukkhanissandenāti ratanappamāṇarukkhamayakūṭadānapuññanissandena, tassa vā puññassa nissandaphalabhāvena. Nibbattasabhāyanti samuṭṭhitaupaṭṭhānasālāyaṃ. Maṇimayāti padumarāgādimaṇimayā. Āṇiyoti thambhatulāsaṅghāṭakādīsu vāḷarūpādisaṅghāṭanakaāṇiyo.

294. “By the outflow from the jewel-sized Kaṇikāra tree” means by the outflow of merit from the gift of a pavilion made of jewel-sized trees, or by its state as the outflowing fruit of that merit. “In the arisen assembly hall” means in the attendance hall that has arisen. “Made of jewels” means made of jewels such as rubies and the like. “Pegs” means the joining pegs, such as those with animal figures, on pillars, beams, tie-beams, and so on.

Gandhabbarājāti gandhabbakāyikānaṃ devatānaṃ rājā. Ye [P 2.0279] tāvatiṃsānaṃ āsannavāsino cātumahārājikā devā, te purato karonto “dvīsu devalokesu devatā purato katvā nisinno”ti vutto. Sesesupi tīsu ṭhānesu eseva nayo.

“King of the Gandharvas” means the king of the deities belonging to the Gandharva group. Those Cātumahārājika deities who dwell near the Tāvatiṃsa gods—placing them in front, he is said to be “seated having placed the deities of two divine realms in front.” The same method applies to the remaining three places.

Nāgarājāti [V 2.0201] nāgānaṃ adhipati, na pana sayaṃ nāgajātiko.

“King of Nāgas” means the lord of nāgas, but he is not himself of the nāga race.

Āsati nisīdati etthāti āsanaṃ, nisajjaṭṭhānanti āha “nisīdituṃ okāso”ti. “Etthā”ti padaṃ nipātamattaṃ, etthāti vā etasmiṃ pāṭhe. Atthuddhāranayena [M 2.0219] vattabbaṃ pubbe vuttaṃ catubbidhameva. Tāvatiṃsā, ekacce ca cātumahārājikā yathāladdhāya sampattiyā thāvarabhāvāya, āyatiṃ sodhanāya ca pañca sīlāni rakkhanti, te tassa visodhanatthaṃ pavāraṇāsaṅgahaṃ karonti. Tena vuttaṃ “mahāpavāraṇāyā”tiādi.

“One sits down in this, thus it is a seat (āsana); a place for sitting,” thus he said, “an opportunity to sit.” The word “ettha” is merely a particle; or, in this reading, “ettha” means “in this.” What is to be said according to the method of extracting the meaning is just the fourfold division previously stated. The Tāvatiṃsa devas, and some Cātumahārājika devas, observe the five precepts according to the prosperity they have attained, for the sake of stability and for future purification. They perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony for the purpose of its purification. Therefore, it is said, “for the great Pavāraṇā,” and so on.

Vassasahassanti manussagaṇanāya vassasahassaṃ.

“A thousand years” means a thousand years by human reckoning.

Pannapalāsoti patitapatto. Khārakajātoti jātakhuddakamakuḷo. Ye hi nīlapattakā ativiya khuddakā makuḷā, te “khārakā”ti vuccanti. Jālakajātoti tehiyeva khuddakamakuḷehi jātajālako sabbaso jālo viya jāto. Keci pana “jālakajātoti ekajālo viya jāto”ti atthaṃ vadanti. Pārichattako kira khārakaggahaṇakāle sabbatthakameva pallaviko hoti, te cassa pallavā pabhassarapavāḷavaṇṇasamujjalā honti, tena so sabbaso samujjalanto tiṭṭhati. Kuṭumalakajātoti sañjātamahāmakuḷo. Korakajātoti sañjātasūcibhedo sampati vikasamānāvattho. Sabbapāliphulloti sabbaso phullitavikasito.

“Pannapalāso” means one with fallen leaves. “Khārakajāto” means one with newly-grown tiny buds. Indeed, the very small buds with bluish leaves are called “khārakā.” “Jālakajāto” means that from those very tiny buds a network has formed, becoming entirely like a net. Some, however, explain the meaning as “having become like a single net.” It is said that at the time of the appearance of the khārakā, the Pārichattaka tree is entirely covered with shoots, and those shoots shine with a radiant coral color, so that it stands completely resplendent. “Kuṭumalakajāto” means one with large buds arisen. “Korakajāto” means one with needle-like points arisen, now at the stage of opening. “Sabbapāliphullo” means fully flowered and blossomed.

Kantanakavātoti devānaṃ puññakammapaccayā pupphānaṃ chindanakavāto. Kantatīti chindati. Sampaṭicchanakavātoti chinnānaṃ chinnānaṃ pupphānaṃ sampaṭiggaṇhanakavāto[P 2.0280]. Naccantoti nānāvidhabhattiṃ sannivesavasena naccanaṃ karonto. Aññataradevatānanti nāmagottavasena appaññātadevatānaṃ.

“The cutting wind” means the wind that cuts flowers on account of the meritorious deeds of the devas. To cut (kantati) means to sever (chindati). “The receiving wind” means the wind that receives the flowers as they are severed. “Dancing” means performing a dance by way of arranging various patterns. “Of certain deities” refers to deities not known by name or clan.

Reṇuvaṭṭīti reṇusaṅghāto. Kaṇṇikaṃ āhaccāti sudhammāya kūṭaṃ āhantvā.

“A whirl of pollen” means a mass of pollen. “Having struck the pinnacle” means having struck the peak of the Sudhammā Hall.

Aṭṭha divaseti pañcamiyā saddhiṃ pakkhe cattāro divase sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yathāvuttesu aṭṭhasu divasesu dhammassavanaṃ nibaddhaṃ tadā pavattatīti tato aññadā kāritaṃ sandhāyāha “akāladhammassavanaṃ kārita”nti. Cetiye chattassa heṭṭhā kātabbavedikā chattavedikā. Cetiyaṃ parikkhipitvā padakkhiṇakaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ antokatvā kātabbavedikā puṭavedikā. Cetiyassa kucchiṃ parikkhipitvā [V 2.0202] taṃ sambandhameva katvā kātabbavedikā kucchivedikā. Sīharūpapādakaṃ āsanaṃ sīhāsanaṃ. Ubhosu passesu sīharūpayuttaṃ sopānaṃ sīhasopānaṃ.

“Eight days” is said with reference to four days in a fortnight, together with the fifth day. Listening to the Dhamma regularly occurs on the eight aforesaid days; therefore, with reference to it being arranged at another time, it is said, “untimely Dhamma listening was arranged.” The platform to be made beneath the umbrella of a cetiya is the “umbrella platform.” The platform to be made encircling the cetiya, enclosing the space for circumambulation, is the “container platform.” The platform to be made encircling the interior of the cetiya, and made connected to it, is the “interior platform.” A seat with lion-shaped legs is a “lion seat.” A staircase with lion figures on both sides is a “lion staircase.”

Attamanā [M 2.0220] honti aniyāmanakabhāvato. Tenevāha “mahāpuññe purakkhatvā”tiādi. Pavāraṇāsaṅgahatthāya sannipatitāti veditabbā “tadahuposathe pannarase pavāraṇāya puṇṇāya puṇṇamāya rattiyā”ti (dī. ni. 2.294) vacanato.

They are delighted because of their unconstrained state. Hence it is said, “Having given precedence to great merit,” and so on. They should be understood as having assembled for the purpose of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, according to the text, “On that Uposatha day, the fifteenth, the full moon night of the full Pavāraṇā” (Dī. Ni. 2.294).

295. Navahi kāraṇehīti “itipi so bhagavā araha”ntiādinā (dī. ni. 1.157, 255) vuttehi arahattādīhi navahi buddhānubhāvadīpanehi kāraṇehi. Dhammassa cāti ettha ca-saddo avuttasamuccayatthoti tena sampiṇḍitamatthaṃ dassento “ujuppaṭipannatādibhedaṃ saṅghassa ca suppaṭipatti”nti āha.

295. “By nine reasons” means by the nine reasons that illuminate the Buddha's power, namely Arahantship and so on, which are stated in the passage (at Dī. Ni. 1.157, 255) beginning, “Thus indeed, the Blessed One is an Arahant.” In “And of the Dhamma,” here the particle “ca” (and) has the meaning of including what is unstated. Therefore, showing the meaning thus combined, he says this refers to “and the good practice of the Sangha, with its divisions such as upright practice.”

Aṭṭhayathābhuccavaṇṇanā

The Eighth: The Explanation of the True Nature

296. Yathā anantameva ānañcaṃ, bhisakkameva bhesajjaṃ[P 2.0281], evaṃ yathābhūtā eva yathābhuccāti pāḷiyaṃ vuttanti āha “yathābhucceti yathābhūte”ti. Vaṇṇetabbato kittetabbato vaṇṇā, guṇā. Kathaṃ paṭipannoti hetuavatthāyaṃ, phalaavatthāyaṃ, sattānaṃ upakārā vatthāyanti tīsupi avatthāsu lokanāthassa bahujanahitāya paṭipattiyā kathetukamyatāpucchā. Tathā hi naṃ ādito paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānā saṅkhepeneva dassento “dīpaṅkarapādamūle”tiādimāha. Tattha abhinīharamānoti abhinīhāraṃ karonto. Yaṃ panettha mahābhinīhāre, pāramīsu ca vattabbaṃ, taṃ brahmajālaṭīkāyaṃ (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.7) vuttaṃ evāti tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

296. Just as “ananta” is “ānañca,” and “bhisakka” is “bhesajja,” so “yathābhūta” is “yathābhucca,” as it is said in the Pāḷi. Thus he says, “‘yathābhucce’ means ‘yathābhūte’ (as it truly is).” Praises (vaṇṇā) are virtues (guṇā), because they are to be described (vaṇṇetabbato) and praised (kittetabbato). “How did he practice?” This is a question expressing the desire to speak about the practice of the Lord of the World for the welfare of many people, in three states: the state of the cause, the state of the fruit, and the state of benefiting beings. Thus, showing it briefly from the beginning to the end, he says, beginning with, “At the feet of Dīpaṅkara.” Here, “abhinīharamāno” means “making an aspiration.” And what should be said here regarding the great aspiration and the perfections has been stated in the Brahmajāla Subcommentary (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.7); thus, it should be understood according to the method stated there.

“Khantivāditāpasakāle”tiādi (jā. 1.khantīvādījātaka) hetuavatthāyameva anaññasādhāraṇāya sudukkarāya bahujanahitāya paṭipattiyā vibhāvanaṃ. Yathādhippetaṃ hitasukhaṃ yāya kiriyāya vinā na ijjhati, sāpi tadatthā evāti dassetuṃ “tusitapure yāvatāyukaṃ tiṭṭhantopī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

“At the time of the ascetic Khantivādi,” etc. (Jā. 1.khantīvādījātaka) is an elucidation of the practice for the welfare of many—a practice extremely difficult and not shared with others—solely in terms of the state of the cause. To show that the desired benefit and happiness cannot be achieved without that action, and that this action is indeed for that purpose, it is said, beginning with, “Even while dwelling in the Tusita heaven for a full lifespan.”

Dhammacakkappavattanādi (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 13; paṭi. ma. 3.30) pana nibbattitā bahujanahitāya paṭipatti. Āyusaṅkhārossajjanampi “ettakaṃ kālaṃ tiṭṭhāmī”ti pavattiyā bahujanahitāya paṭipatti. Anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbānavasena bahujanahitāya [V 2.0203] paṭipatti. Tenāha “yāvassā”tiādi. Sesapadānīti “bahujanasukhāyā”tiādīni padāni. Pacchimanti “atthāya hitāya sukhāyā”ti [M 2.0221] padattayaṃ. Purimassāti tato purimassa padattayassa. Atthoti atthaniddeso.

Now, the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma and so on (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1081; Mahāva. 13; Paṭi. Ma. 3.30) is a practice accomplished for the welfare of many. The relinquishing of the life-formation, with the resolve, “I shall remain for this much time,” is also a practice for the welfare of many. The final Nibbāna by way of the Nibbāna element without residue is also a practice for the welfare of many. Therefore, he said, beginning with, “as long as his…” ‘The remaining terms’ refers to the terms beginning with ‘for the happiness of many.’ ‘The latter’ refers to the three terms: ‘for the benefit, for the welfare, for the happiness.’ ‘Of the former’ refers to the three terms preceding that. ‘Meaning’ is an explanation of the meaning.

Yadipi atītenaṅgena samannāgatā satthāro ahesuṃ, tepi pana buddhā evāti atthato amhākaṃ satthā anaññoti āha “atītepi buddhato aññaṃ na samanupassāmā”ti. Yathā ca atīte, evaṃ anāgate cāti ayamattho nayato labbhatīti katvā vuttaṃ “anāgatepi na samanupassāmā”ti. Sakko pana devarājā tamatthaṃ atthāpannameva katvā “na panetarahi” iccevāha. Kiṃ sakko kathetīti vicāretvāti “neva atītaṃse samanupassamā’ti [P 2.0282] vadanto sakko kiṃ kathetī”ti vicāraṇaṃ samuṭṭhapetvā. Yasmā atīte buddhā ahesuṃ, anāgate bhavissantīti nāyamattho sakkena devarājena pariññāto, te pana buddhasāmaññena amhākaṃ bhagavatā saddhiṃ gahetvā etarahi aññassa sabbena sabbaṃ abhāvato tathā vuttanti dassetuṃ “etarahī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Svākkhātādīnīti svākkhātapadādīni. Kusalādīnīti “idaṃ kusala”ntiādīni padāni.

Although there were teachers in the past endowed with the same qualities, they too were Buddhas; thus, in essence, our Teacher is not other than them. Therefore, he said, “In the past, too, I do not perceive anyone other than the Buddha.” And “as in the past, so too in the future”—because this meaning is obtained by inference, it was said, “In the future, too, I do not perceive anyone.” But Sakka, the king of devas, having made that meaning his own, said only, “But not at present.” Having considered, “What is Sakka saying?”—that is, having raised the investigation, “What is Sakka saying when he says, ‘I do not perceive anyone in the past’?”—it is to show the following that the passage beginning “at present” was said: because this meaning—that Buddhas existed in the past and will exist in the future—was not fully comprehended by Sakka, the king of devas, but rather he spoke as he did because, having taken them together with our Blessed One by virtue of their common Buddhahood, there is now absolutely no other at all. “Svākkhātādīni” (well-proclaimed, etc.) refers to terms beginning with “svākkhāta” (well-proclaimed). “Kusalādīni” (skillful, etc.) refers to terms beginning with “idaṃ kusalaṃ” (this is skillful).

Gaṅgāyamunānaṃ asamāgamaṭṭhāne udakaṃ bhinnavaṇṇaṃ hontampi samāgamaṭṭhāne abhinnavaṇṇaṃ evāti āha “vaṇṇenapi saṃsandati sametī”ti. Tattha kira gaṅgodakasadisameva yamunodakaṃ. Yathā nibbānaṃ kenaci kilesena anupakkiliṭṭhatāya parisuddhaṃ, evaṃ nibbānagāminipaṭipadāpi kenaci kilesena anupakkiliṭṭhatāya parisuddhāva icchitabbā. Tenāha “na hī”tiādi. Yena parisuddhatthena nibbānassa, nibbānagāminiyā paṭipadāya ca ākāsūpamatā, so kenaci anupalepo, anupakkileso cāti āha “ākāsampi alaggaṃ parisuddha”nti. Idāni tamatthaṃ nidassanena vibhūtaṃ katvā dassetuṃ “candimasūriyāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Saṃsandati yujjati paṭipajjitabbatāpaṭipajjanehi aññamaññānucchavikatāya.

Even though the waters of the Ganges and Yamuna are of a different color at the place where they do not meet, at their meeting point they are indeed of an undifferentiated color. Therefore, it is said, 'They merge and unite even in color.' There, it is said, the water of the Yamuna is indeed similar to the water of the Ganges. Just as Nibbāna is pure through being undefiled by any defilement, so too the path leading to Nibbāna should be desired as pure, through being undefiled by any defilement. Therefore, he said, beginning with 'For indeed...'. The purity by which Nibbāna and the path leading to Nibbāna are likened to space is that they are unsullied and undefiled by anything. Therefore, it is said, 'Space too is unattached, pure.' Now, to make that meaning clear by means of an illustration, it is said, beginning with 'The moon and the sun...'. They merge and are fitting due to the mutual suitability of what is to be practiced and the practice itself.

Paṭipadāya ṭhitānanti paṭipadaṃ maggapaṭipattiṃ paṭipajjamānānaṃ. Vusitavatanti brahmacariyavāsaṃ vusitavantānaṃ etesaṃ. Laddhasahāyoti etāsaṃ paṭipadānaṃ vasena laddhasahāyo. Tattha tattha sāvakehi satthu kātabbakicce. Idaṃ pana “adutiyo”tiādi suttantare āgatavacanaṃ aññehi asadisaṭṭhena vuttaṃ, na yathāvuttasahāyābhāvato. Apanujjāti apanīya vivajjetvā. “Apanujjā”ti ca antogadhāvadhāraṇaṃ [P 2.0283] idaṃ vacanaṃ ekantikattā tassa apanodassāti vuttaṃ “apanujjevā”ti.

'Of those established in the practice' means of those who are undertaking the path, the practice of the path. 'Of those who have lived the holy life' means of these who have lived the holy life. 'Having gained a companion' means one who has gained a companion by means of these practices. Here and there, regarding the duties to be performed by the disciples for the Teacher. This statement, however, beginning with 'without a second,' which appears in another discourse, is spoken in the sense of being incomparable to others, not due to the absence of a companion as mentioned above. 'Having driven away' means having removed and avoided. And this word 'having driven away' contains an implicit emphasis; because that removal is absolute, it is said 'having driven away indeed'.

Labbhatīti [V 2.0204][M 2.0222] lābho, so pana ukkaṃsagativijānanena sātisayo, vipulo eva ca idhādhippetoti āha “mahālābho uppanno”ti. Ussannapuññanissandasamuppannoti yathāvuttakālaṃ sambhatasuvipulauḷāratarapuññābhisandato nibbatto.“Ime nibbattā, ito paraṃ mayhaṃ okāso natthī”ti ussāhajāto viya uparūpari vaḍḍhamāno udapādi. Sabbadisāsu hi yamakamahāmegho uṭṭhahitvā mahāmeghaṃ viya sabbapāramiyo “ekasmiṃ attabhāve vipākaṃ dassāmā”ti sampiṇḍitā viya bhagavato idaṃ lābhasakkārasilokaṃ nibbattayiṃsu, tato annapānavatthayānamālāgandhavilepanādihatthā khattiyabrāhmaṇādayo upagantvā “kahaṃ buddho, kahaṃ bhagavā, kahaṃ devadevo, kahaṃ narāsabho, kahaṃ purisasīho”ti bhagavantaṃ pariyesanti, sakaṭasatehipi paccaye āharitvā okāsaṃ alabhamānā samantā gāvutappamāṇampi sakaṭadhurena sakaṭadhuraṃ āhacca tiṭṭhanti ceva anubandhanti ca andhakavindabrāhmaṇādayo viya. Sabbaṃ khandhake, tesu tesu ca suttesu āgatanayena veditabbaṃ. Tenāha “lābhasakkāro mahogho viyā”tiādi.

'It is obtained,' thus it is 'gain'; but here, it is intended that this gain is extraordinary and vast, being known as a superior attainment. Therefore, it is said, 'A great gain has arisen.' 'Arisen from an overflowing stream of merit' means that it was produced from the outflow of a very vast and magnificent accumulation of merit gathered during the aforementioned period. As if with enthusiasm born from the thought, 'These have been produced, and beyond this, there is no further opportunity for me,' it arose, increasing more and more. For just as a great twin cloud rises in all directions and gathers like a massive cloud, so too did all the perfections, as if declaring, 'We will give our fruit in this single existence,' converge and thus generate this gain, honor, and fame for the Blessed One. Then, warrior-nobles, brahmins, and others, with food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, and so forth in their hands, approached searching for the Blessed One, asking, 'Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the god of gods? Where is the bull among men? Where is the lion among men?' Even when bringing hundreds of cartloads of requisites, they were unable to find an opportunity, and stood cart-yoke to cart-yoke for even a gāvuta all around, and they followed him persistently, like the brahmin Andhakavinda and others. All this should be understood according to the method that appears in the Khandhaka and in those various suttas. Therefore, it is said, beginning with 'Gain and honor are like a great flood...'

Paṭipāṭibhattanti bahūsu “dānaṃ dassāmā”ti āhaṭapaṭipāṭikāya uṭṭhitesu anupaṭipāṭiyā dātabba bhattaṃ.

'Food given in order' means food to be given in sequence when many have come forward in an established order, saying, 'We will give a gift.'

Matthakaṃ patto anaññasādhāraṇattā tassa dānassa. Upāyaṃ ācikkhi nāgarānaṃ asakkuṇeyyarūpena dānaṃ dāpetuṃ. Sālakalyāṇirukkhā rājapariggahā aññehi asādhāraṇā, tasmā tesaṃ padarehi maṇḍapo kārito, hatthino ca rājabhaṇḍabhūtā nāgarehi na sakkā laddhunti tehi chattaṃ dhārāpitaṃ, tathā khattiyadhītāhi veyyāvaccaṃ kāritaṃ. “Pañca āsanasatānī”ti idaṃ sālakalyāṇimaṇḍape paññatte sandhāya vuttaṃ, tato bahi pana bahūni paññattāni ahesuṃ[P 2.0284]. Catujjātiyagandhaṃ pisati buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa pūjanatthañceva pattassa ubbaṭanatthañca. Udakanti pattadhovanaudakaṃ. Anagghāni ahesuṃ anaggharatanābhisaṅkhatattā.

It reached its peak because that gift was not common to others. He pointed out a means for the citizens to have a gift given in a way that would have been impossible for them. The Sālakalyāṇi trees were royal property, not common to others; therefore, a pavilion was made from their planks. And the elephants, being royal property, could not be obtained by the citizens, so parasols were held by them. Similarly, services were performed by the daughters of warrior-nobles. 'Five hundred seats'—this was said with reference to those arranged in the Sālakalyāṇi pavilion, but outside of it many more were arranged. He ground the four kinds of perfume for the worship of the Sangha headed by the Buddha and also for anointing the bowl. 'Water' refers to the water for washing the bowl. They were priceless because they were composed of invaluable gems.

Sattadhā muddhā phalissati anādarakāraṇādinā. Kāḷaṃ olokessāmīti kāḷaṃ evaṃ anupekkhissāmi, tassa uppajjanakaṃ anatthaṃ pariharissāmīti attho.

One's head will split into seven pieces due to the cause of disrespect, and so forth. 'I will watch for the right time' means: 'For a time I will thus be indifferent, and I will avert the harm that would arise from it'—this is the meaning.

Kadariyāti [M 2.0223] thaddhamaccharino puññakammavimukhā. Devalokaṃ na vajanti puññassa akatattā, maccharibhāvena ca pāpassa pasutattā. Bālāti duccintitacintanādinā bālalakkhaṇayuttā. Nappasaṃsanti dānaṃ pasaṃsitumpi na visahanti. Dhīroti dhītisampanno uḷārapañño parehi kataṃ dānaṃ [V 2.0205] anumodamānopi, teneva dānānumodaneneva. Sukhī paratthāti paraloke kāyikacetasikasukhasamaṅgī hoti.

'The miserly' are stubborn, stingy, and averse to meritorious deeds. They do not go to the heavenly world because merit has not been done and because they are devoted to evil due to stinginess. 'Fools' are characterized by the marks of a fool, such as thinking ill-conceived thoughts, and so forth. They do not praise giving, nor are they able to praise it. 'The wise' is one endowed with fortitude and great wisdom; even while rejoicing in the giving done by others, through that very rejoicing in giving, he is endowed with bodily and mental happiness in the next world.

Vararojo nāma tasmiṃ kāle eko khattiyo, tassa vararojassa. Anavajja…pe… phaleyya abhūtavādibhāvatoti adhippāyo. Atirekapadasahassena tiṃsādhikena aḍḍhateyyagāthāsatena vaṇṇameva kathesi rūpappasannatāya ca.

At that time, there was a warrior-noble named Vararoja. Of that Vararoja. The words 'faultless... may it bear fruit' mean the intention is that he would not be a speaker of falsehood. With more than a thousand words and two hundred and eighty verses, he spoke only praise of his excellence and radiant beauty.

Yāva maññe khattiyāti ettha yāvāti avadhiparicchedavacanaṃ, aññeti nipātamattaṃ, yāva khattiyā khattiye avadhiṃ katvā sabbe devamanussāti adhippāyo. Tenāha “khattiyā brāhmaṇā”tiādi. Madapamattoti lābhasakkārasilokamadena pamatto ceva tadanvayena pamādena pamatto ca hutvā.

In 'as far as warrior-nobles, I suppose,' here 'yāva' is a term denoting a limit, and 'maññe' is merely a particle. The meaning is 'all devas and humans,' with warrior-nobles as the limit. Therefore, it is said, beginning with 'warrior-nobles, brahmins...'. 'Intoxicated and heedless' means being intoxicated with the pride of gain, honor, and renown, and also being heedless due to the heedlessness that follows from it.

Tadanvayamevāti tadanugatameva. Vācā…pe… sametīti vacīkammakāyakammāni aññamaññaṃ aviruddhāni, aññadatthu saṃsandanti. Ajā eva migāti ajāmigā, te ajāmige.

'Following that very course' means 'adhering to it.' 'Speech... unites' means that verbal and bodily actions are not in conflict with each other, but rather they harmonize. `Ajāmigā` means 'goats and deer'; the text refers to those goats and deer.

Tiṇṇavicikiccho sabbaso atikkantavicikicchākantāro[P 2.0285]. Nanu ca sabbepi sotāpannā tiṇṇavicikicchā, vigatakathaṃkathā ca? Saccametaṃ, idaṃ pana na tādisaṃ tiṇṇavicikicchataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, atha kho sabbasmiṃ ñeyyadhamme sabbākārāvabodhasaṅkhātasanniṭṭhānavasena sabbaso nirākataṃ sandhāyāti dassento “yathā hī”ti ādimāha. Ussannussannattāti paroparabhāvato, ayañca attho bhagavato anekadhātunānādhātuñāṇabalenapi ijjhati. Sabbattha vigatakathaṃkatho sabbadassāvibhāvato. Sabbesaṃ paramatthadhammānaṃ saccābhisamayavasena paṭividdhattā vuttaṃ “vohāravasenā”ti vā nāmagottādivasenāti attho.

'One who has crossed beyond doubt' means one who has completely traversed the wilderness of doubt. But are not all stream-enterers those who have crossed beyond doubt and are free from uncertainty? This is true, but this is not said with reference to that kind of crossing beyond doubt. Rather, it is said with reference to the complete removal of doubt in all knowable phenomena by way of the firm conclusion known as thorough comprehension in all aspects, as indicated by the phrase beginning with 'just as…'. 'By way of being successively prominent' means by way of being higher and higher, and this meaning is also achieved through the Blessed One's power of knowledge of the many and various elements. 'Free from uncertainty in all things' is due to being of unimpaired vision in everything. It is said 'by way of convention' because all ultimate realities have been penetrated through the realization of the truths; or the meaning is 'by way of names, clans, and the like.'

Pariyositasaṅkappoti sabbaso niṭṭhitamanoratho. Nanu ca ariyamaggena pariyositasaṅkappatā nāma soḷasakiccasiddhiyā katakaraṇīyabhāvena, na sabbañeyyadhammāvabodhenāti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “pubbe [M 2.0224] ananussutesū”tiādi. Sāvakānaṃ sāvakapāramiñāṇaṃ viya, hi paccekabuddhānaṃ paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ viya ca sammāsambuddhānaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ catusaccābhisambodhapubbakamevāti. Ananussutesūti na anussutesu. Sāmanti sayameva. Padadvayenāpi parato ghosena vināti dasseti. Tatthāti nimittatthe bhummaṃ, saccābhisambodhanimittanti attho. Saccābhisambodho ca aggamaggavasenāti [V 2.0206] daṭṭhabbaṃ. Balesu ca vasībhāvanti dasannaṃ balañāṇānaṃ yathāruci pavatti. Jātattā jātāti sammāsambuddhe vadati.

"Pariyositasaṅkappo" (one whose intentions are fulfilled) means one whose aspirations are completely accomplished. Is it not, however, the case that the fulfillment of intentions through the noble path refers to the accomplishment of the sixteen tasks, as having done what should be done, and not to the full understanding of all knowable phenomena? This objection is addressed by the words, "previously unheard of," and so on. For just as there is the knowledge of a disciple's perfections for disciples, and the knowledge of independent enlightenment for Paccekabuddhas, so too for the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, the knowledge of omniscience is preceded by the realization of the four truths. "Ananussutesu" means not heard before. "Sāmaṃ" means by oneself. The pair of words also indicates the absence of reliance on the voice of another. "Tattha" is a locative in the sense of a reason; the meaning is the reason for the realization of the truths. And the realization of the truths should be understood as occurring by way of the supreme path. "Balesu ca vasībhāvaṃ" (mastery over the powers) means the unimpeded exercise of the ten powers of knowledge as desired. "Jātattā jāta" (because of being born, he is born) refers to the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

297. Tattha tattha rājadhāniādike nibaddhavāsaṃ vasanto. Tīsu maṇḍalesu yathākālaṃ cārikaṃ caranto.

297. Dwelling in various royal cities and the like, living in a fixed residence. Wandering on tour at the proper time in the three districts.

298. Assāti phalassa. Tanti kāraṇaṃ. Dvinnampi ekato uppattiyā kāraṇaṃ natthi, pageva tiṇṇaṃ, catunnaṃ vāti. “Ettha cā”tiādi “ekissā lokadhātuyā”ti vuttalokadhātuyā [P 2.0286] pamāṇaparicchedadassanatthaṃ āraddhaṃ.

298. "Assa" means of the fruit. "Taṃ" means the cause. For two things, there is no cause for their arising together, let alone for three or four. "Ettha ca" and so on, is begun in order to show the delimitation of the measure of the world-system that was spoken of as "one world-system."

Yāvatāti yattakena ṭhānena. Pariharantīti sineruṃ parikkhipantā parivattanti. Disāti disāsu, bhummatthe etaṃ paccattavacanaṃ. Bhanti dibbanti. Virocanāti obhāsantā, virocanā vā sobhamānā candimasūriyā bhanti, tato eva disā ca bhanti. Tāva sahassadhāti tattako sahassaloko.

"Yāvatā" means to that extent of place. "Pariharanti" means surrounding Mount Sineru, they revolve. "Disā" refers to the directions; this is a singular form in the sense of the locative. "Bhanti" means they shine. "Virocanā" means shining, or the radiant sun and moon shine; and from that, the directions also shine. "Tāva sahassadhā" means that much of a thousandfold world.

Ettakanti imaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ majjhe katvā imināva saddhiṃ cakkavāḷaṃ dasasahassaṃ. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ mahāpadānavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttameva. Na paññāyatīti tīsu piṭakesu anāgatattā.

"Ettakaṃ" means this world-system, placing it in the middle, along with this one, ten thousand world-systems. What should be said on this matter has already been stated in the Commentary on the Mahāpadāna Sutta. "Na paññāyati" (it is not found) because it does not occur in the three Piṭakas.

Sanaṅkumārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Sanaṅkumāra

300. Vaṇṇenāti rūpasampattiyā. Suviññeyyattā taṃ anāmasitvā yasasaddasseva atthamāha. Alaṅkāraparivārenāti alaṅkārena ca parivārena ca. Puññasiriyāti puññiddhiyā.

300. "Vaṇṇena" means by excellence of form. Due to its being easily understood, without touching upon that, it states the meaning of the word 'fame' only. "Alaṅkāraparivārena" means with adornments and with a retinue. "Puññasiriyā" means by the spiritual power of merit.

301. Sampasādaneti sampasādajanane. Saṃpubbo khā-saddo jānanattho “saṅkhāyetaṃ paṭisevatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.168) viyāti āha “jānitvā modāmā”ti.

301. "Sampasādane" means in producing confidence. The word "khā" with the prefix "saṃ" has the meaning of knowing, as in passages such as "saṅkhāyetaṃ paṭisevatī" (Majjhima Nikāya 2.168); therefore it is said, "knowing, we rejoice."

Govindabrāhmaṇavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of the Brahmin Govinda

304. Yāva [M 2.0225] dīgharattanti yāva parimāṇato, aparimitakālaparidīpanametanti āha “ettakanti…pe… aticiraratta”nti. Mahāpaññova so bhagavāti tena brahmunā anumatipucchāvasena [V 2.0207] devānaṃ vuttanti dassento “mahāpaññova so bhagavā. Noti kathaṃ tumhe maññathā”ti āha. Sayamevetaṃ pañhaṃ byākātukāmo “bhūtapubbaṃ bho”ti ādiṃ āhāti sambandho. Evaṃ pana byākarontena atthato ayampi attho vutto nāma hotīti dassento “anacchariyameta”nti ādimāha. Tiṇṇaṃ mārānanti [P 2.0287] kilesābhisaṅkhāradevaputtamārānaṃ. “Anacchariyameta”nti vuttamevatthaṃ nigamanavasena “kimettha acchariya”nti punapi vuttaṃ.

304. "Yāva dīgharattaṃ" (for a long time) means as to its measure; this is an indication of an immeasurable period of time, as he says, "so much... for a very long time." "Mahāpaññova so bhagavā" (that Blessed One is indeed of great wisdom)—showing that this was spoken by that Brahmā to the devas by way of a question seeking their approval, he says, "That Blessed One is indeed of great wisdom. Is it not so? What do you think?" Wishing to explain this question himself, the connection is that he begins with "Formerly, sirs," and so on. Yet, in explaining thus, to show that this meaning too is stated in essence, he begins with, "This is not astonishing." "Tiṇṇaṃ mārānaṃ" (of the three Māras) means of the Māras of defilements, volitional formations, and the son of a deva. The very meaning stated as "Anacchariyametaṃ" (this is not astonishing) is stated again by way of conclusion as "What is astonishing here?"

Rañño diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaatthānaṃ puro dhānato pure pure saṃvidhānato purohitoti āha “sabbakiccāni anusāsanapurohito”ti. Govindiyābhisekenāti govindassa ṭhāne ṭhapanābhisekena. Taṃ kira tassa brāhmaṇassa kulaparamparāgataṃ ṭhānantaraṃ. Jotitattāti āvudhānaṃ jotitattā. Pālanasamatthatāyāti rañño, aparimitassa ca sattakāyassa anatthato paripālanasamatthatāya.

"Purohita" (chaplain) is so called because he is foremost (`puro`) in undertaking (`dhānato`) the king's worldly and otherworldly benefits, and foremost in planning in the city (`pure`); hence it is said, "The chaplain who instructs in all duties." "Govindiyābhisekena" (by the consecration to the Govindaship) means by the consecration that establishes him in Govinda's position. Indeed, that office was a hereditary position in that brahmin's family. "Jotitattā" (because of his brilliance) means due to the brilliance of his weapons. "Pālanasamatthatāya" (because of his ability to protect) means his ability to protect the king and the immeasurable multitude of beings from harm.

Sammā vossajjitvāti suṭṭhu tassevāgāravabhāvena vissajjitvā niyyātetvā. Taṃ tamatthaṃ kiccaṃ passatīti atthadaso.

"Sammā vossajjitvā" means having thoroughly relinquished and handed over, with a lack of regard for it. "Atthadaso" means he sees that purpose and duty; thus, he is one who sees the meaning.

305. Bhavanaṃ vaḍḍhanaṃ bhavo, bhavati etenāti vā bhavo, vaḍḍhikāraṇaṃ sandhivasena ma-kārāgamo, o-kārassa ca a-kārādesaṃ katvā “bhavamatthū”ti vuttaṃ. Bhavantaṃ jotipālanti pana sāmiatthe upayogavacananti āha “bhoto”ti. Mā paccabyāhāsīti mā paṭikkhipīti attho. So pana paṭikkhepo paṭivacanaṃ hotīti āha “mā paṭibyāhāsī”ti. Abhisambhosīti kammantānaṃ saṃvidhāne samattho hotīti āha “saṃvidahitvā”ti. Bhavābhavaṃ, paññañca vindi paṭilabhīti govindo, mahanto govindo mahāgovindo. “Go”ti hi paññāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ gacchati atthe bujjhatīti.

305. Growth (`bhavanaṃ`) or increase (`vaḍḍhanaṃ`) is `bhavo`; or, because one becomes (`bhavati`) through it, it is `bhavo`, a cause of increase. The insertion of the letter 'm' is due to euphonic combination, and by substituting 'a' for 'o', it is said as "bhavamatthu." Regarding "Bhavantaṃ Jotipāla," it is a term of address used in the sense of lordship, hence it is said as "bhoto." "Mā paccabyāhāsi" means "do not reject." That rejection is a reply, hence it is said, "mā paṭibyāhāsi" (do not reply). "Abhisambhosīti" means one is capable of managing tasks; hence, it is said, "saṃvidahitvā" (having arranged). He found (`vindi`) and obtained (`paṭilabhi`) becoming and non-becoming (`bhavābhavaṃ`) and wisdom (`paññañca`), thus he is Govinda. The great Govinda is Mahāgovinda. For "go" is a term for wisdom; it means one who goes to the meaning, one who understands.

Rajjasaṃvibhajanavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Division of the Kingdom

306. Ekapitikā [M 2.0226] vemātukā kaniṭṭhabhātaro. Ayaṃ abhisittoti ayaṃ reṇu rājakumāro pitu accayena rajje abhisitto. Rājakārakāti rājaputtaṃ rajje patiṭṭhāpetāro.

306. Younger brothers from the same father but different mothers. "Ayaṃ abhisitto" (this one is anointed) means this Prince Reṇu was anointed to the kingship after his father's passing. "Rājakārakā" (king-makers) means those who establish a prince in the kingship.

307. Madentīti [P 2.0288] madanīyāti kattusādhanataṃ dassento “madakarā”ti āha. Madakaraṇaṃ pana pamādassa visesakāraṇanti vuttaṃ “pamādakarā”ti.

307. "Madentī" means they intoxicate; showing this to be an agent-noun derivation, it is said "madakarā" (intoxicating). The act of intoxicating, however, is a specific cause of heedlessness; thus it is stated "pamādakarā" (causing heedlessness).

308. Reṇussa [V 2.0208] rajjasamīpe dasagāvutamattavitthatāni hutvā aparabhāge tiyojanasataṃ vitthatattā sabbāni cha rajjāni sakaṭamukhāni paṭṭhapesi. Vitānasadisaṃ caturassabhāvato.

308. Having been ten gāvutas in extent in the vicinity of Reṇu's kingdom, and later three hundred yojanas in extent in the further part, he established all six kingdoms shaped like the front of a cart. It was like a canopy, due to its square shape.
