310. Sahāti gāthāya padaparipūraṇatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tassa atthaṃ dassento “teneva sahā”ti āha. Sahāti vā avinābhāvatthe nipāto, so saha āsuṃ satta bhāradhāti yojetabbo, tena te desantare vasantā vicittena sahabhāvino avinābhāvinoti dīpeti. Rajjabhāraṃ dhārenti attani āropenti vahantīti bhāradhā.

310. The word "sahā" is used in the verse to complete the line. Explaining its meaning, it is said, "together with that very one." Alternatively, "sahā" is a particle in the sense of inseparability; it should be construed as "so saha āsuṃ satta bhāradhā." By this, it indicates that they, dwelling in other lands, were in various ways mutually associated and inseparable. "Bhāradhā" means those who bear the burden, taking upon themselves and carrying the weight of the kingdom.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the First Recitation Section is concluded.

Kittisaddaabbhuggamanavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Rise of the Sound of Fame

311. Anupurohite ṭhapesīti anupurohite katvā ṭhapesi, anupurohite vā ṭhāne ṭhapesi. Tisavanaṃ karonte sandhāya “divasassa tikkhattu”nti vuttaṃ. Dvīsu sandhīsu savanaṃ karonte sandhāya “sāyaṃ, pāto vā”ti vuttaṃ. Tato paṭṭhāyāti vatacariyaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā nhātakālato pabhuti.

311. "Anupurohite ṭhapesi" means he established him having made him a subordinate chaplain, or he placed him in the position of a subordinate chaplain. With reference to those who perform the three recitations, it is said, "three times a day." With reference to those who perform the recitation at the two junctures, it is said, "in the evening or morning." "Tato paṭṭhāya" (from then onward) means from the time of bathing, after having brought the observance of the vow to its culmination.

312. Abhiuggacchīti uṭṭhahi udapādi. Acintetvāti “kathaṃ kho ahaṃ brahmunā saddhiṃ manteyya”nti acintetvā evaṃ cittampi anuppādetvā. Tena samāgamanasseva abhāvato amantetvā. Taṃ disvāti taṃ karuṇābrahmavihārabhāvanaṃ brahmadassanūpāyaṃ disvā ñāṇacakkhunā.

312. "Abhiuggacchi" means he arose or appeared. "Acintetvā" means without thinking, "How shall I converse with Brahmā?"—without even giving rise to such a thought. Thus, because there was no meeting, he did not converse. "Taṃ disvā" means seeing with the eye of wisdom that means to behold Brahmā, that is, the meditation on the divine abiding of compassion.

313. Evanti [M 2.0227] evaṃ rañño ārocetvā paṭisallānaṃ upagate. Sabbatthāti sabbesu channaṃ khattiyānaṃ, sattannaṃ brāhmaṇamahāsālānaṃ[P 2.0289], sattannaṃ nāṭakasatānaṃ, cattārīsāya ca bhariyānaṃ āpucchanavāresu.

313. "Evaṃ" means thus, having informed the king, when he had entered seclusion. "Sabbattha" means in all instances of leave-taking from the six khattiyas, the seven great sāl brahmins, the seven hundred actors, and the forty wives.

316. Sādisiyoti jātiyā sādisiyoti āha “samavaṇṇā samajātikā”ti.

316. "Sādisiyo" means similar by birth; hence it is said, "of equal complexion and equal birth."

317. Santhāgāranti jhānamanasikārena bahi visaṭavitakkavūpasamanena cittassa santhambhanaṃ [V 2.0209] agāraṃ, jhānasālanti attho. Gahitāvāti bhāvanānuyogena mahāsattena attano cittasantāne uppādanavasena gahitā eva. Natthi jhāneneva vikkhambhitattā. Visesato hissa karuṇāya bhāvitattā anabhirati ukkaṇṭhanā natthi, mettāya bhāvitattā bhayaparitassanā natthi. Ukkaṇṭhanāti pana brahmadassane ussukkaṃ, paritassanāti tadabhipatthanāti āha “brahmuno panā”tiādi.

317. "Santhāgāra" means a house which is the stabilization of the mind through meditative attention and the calming of externally scattered thoughts; the meaning is a meditation hall. "Gahitāvā" means that they were indeed grasped by the great being in his own mental continuum by way of production through the practice of meditative cultivation. There is none of this, because it is suppressed by jhāna. Specifically, for him, because compassion had been developed, there was no discontent or agitation; because loving-kindness had been developed, there was no fear or anxiety. "Ukkaṇṭhanā" here means eagerness for a vision of Brahmā, and "paritassanā" means longing for that, as stated, "but Brahmā," etc.

Brahmunāsākacchāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Conversation with Brahmā

318. Cittutrāsoti cittassa utrāsanamattaṃ. Kathanti sattanikāyanivāsaṭṭhānanāmagottādīnaṃ vasena kena pakārena. Tenāha “ki”ntiādi.

318. "Cittutrāso" means mere agitation of the mind. "Katham" means: in what manner, by way of the dwelling places, names, clans, and so on, of the seven groups of beings. Hence, it is said, "what," etc.

Soti ye te panakanasanantabandhasatanasanaṅkumārakālanāmakā loke pākaṭā paññātā brahmāno, tesu sanaṅkumāro nāmāhanti dasseti.

"He is": He indicates, "Among those Brahmās who are well-known and renowned in the world by the names of Panaka, Nasananta, Bandha, Satana, Sanaṅkumāra, and Kāla, I am the one named Sanaṅkumāra."

Agghanti garuṭṭhāniyānaṃ dātabbaṃāhāraṃ. Madhusākanti madhurāhāraṃ, yaṃ kiñci atithino dātabbaṃ āhāraṃ upacāravasena evaṃ vadati. Tenāha “madhusākaṃ panā”tiādi. Pucchāmāti nimantanavasena pucchāma.

"Aggham" means food that should be given to those in a venerable position. "Madhusāka" means sweet food; it speaks thus figuratively of whatever food should be given to a guest. Hence it is said, "but madhusāka," and so on. "We ask" means we ask by way of invitation.

319. Mahāsatto cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā ṭhitopi tesu “brahmasahabyatāya maggo”ti anibbematikatāya “kaṅkhī”ti avoca. Keci pana “tapokammena parikkhīṇasarīratāya, brahmasamāgamena bhayādisamuppattiyā ca paṭiladdhamattehi brahmavihārehi parihīno ahosi, tasmā avikkhambhitavicikicchatāya ‘kaṅkhī’ti avocā”ti vadanti. Parassa vediyā viditā paravediyā, te pana tassa pākaṭā vibhūtāti āha “parassa [M 2.0228] pākaṭesu paravediyesū”ti. Tattha kāraṇamāha “parena sayaṃ abhisaṅkhatattā”ti. Mamāti [P 2.0290] kammaṃ mamaṃkāro, mamattanti āha “idaṃ mama…pe… taṇha”nti. “Mama”nti karoti etenāti hi mamaṃkāro, tathāpavattā taṇhā. Manujesūti niddhāraṇe bhummaṃ, na visayeti āha “manujesu yo kocī”ti. “Ekodibhūto”ti padassa bhāvatthaṃ tāva dassento “ekībhūto”ti vatvā puna taṃ vivaranto “eko tiṭṭhanto eko nisīdanto”ti āha. Tādisoti eko hutvā pavattanako. Bhūtoti jāto. Jhāne adhimutti nāma tasmiṃ nibbattite, anibbattite kuto adhimuttīti āha “jhānaṃ nibbattetvāti attho”ti. Vissagandho nāma kodhādikilesaparibhāvanāti tesaṃ vikkhambhanena [V 2.0210] vissagandhavirahito. Etesu dhammesūti pabbajjānaṃ vivekavāsakaruṇābrahmavihārādidhammesu.

319. The Great Being, although established having developed the four divine abodes, spoke of being a doubter due to his lack of certainty about them, wondering, "Is this the path to companionship with Brahmā?" Some, however, say that due to the exhaustion of his body through ascetic practices and the arising of fear and so on upon meeting Brahmā, he had fallen away from the divine abodes which he had only just attained. Therefore, because his doubt was unsuppressed, he spoke of being a doubter. "Paravediyā" means the feelings of another are known; but for him they are manifest and clear, thus it is said, "in the manifest feelings of another." Therein the reason is stated: "because they are constructed by another himself." The action regarding "mama" (mine) is "mamaṅkāro" (mine-making); "mamattaṃ" (my-ness), it is said, is "this is mine... craving." For, because one makes "mine" with this, it is "mine-making"; craving is that which proceeds in such a way. "Among humans": the locative is for specification, not domain; thus it is said, "whoever among humans." First, showing the meaning of the word "ekodibhūto," it is said, "ekībhūto" (become one), then, elaborating on it again, "standing alone, sitting alone." "Tādiso" means one who proceeds having become one. "Bhūto" means produced. Zeal for jhāna arises when it is produced; when it is not produced, whence zeal? Hence, it is said, "the meaning is 'having produced jhāna.'" The "foul odor" is the pervasion by defilements such as anger; by their suppression, one is free from the foul odor. "In these dhammas" refers to the dhammas of renunciation, secluded living, compassion, the divine abodes, and so forth.

320. Avidvāti na viditavā. Āvaritāti kusalānaṃ uttarimanussadhammānaṃ uppattinivāraṇena āvaritā. Pūtikāti byāpannacittatādinā pūtibhūtā. Kilesavasena duggandhaṃ vissagandhaṃ vāyati. Nirayādiapāyesu nibbattanasīlatāya āpāyikāti āha “apāyūpagā”ti. Corādīhi upaddutassa pavisitukāmassa pākārakavāṭaparikhādīhi viya nagaraṃ kodhādīhi nivuto pihito brahmaloko assāti nivutabrahmaloko. Pucchati “kenāvaṭā”ti vadanto.

320. "Avidvā" means not having known. "Āvaritā" means obstructed by hindering the arising of wholesome qualities and superior human states. "Pūtikā" means rotten, having become putrid due to a mind of ill-will and the like. It emits a bad smell, a foul odor, on account of defilements. Because of its nature of leading to rebirth in hell and other woeful states, it is called āpāyikā; he says "apāyūpagā." Just as a city is shut off by ramparts, gates, moats, and the like for one who is afflicted by thieves and others and wishes to enter, so the Brahma-world is veiled and obstructed by anger and other defilements; hence "nivutabrahmaloko." He asks, saying, "By what is it veiled?"

Musāvādova mosavajjaṃ yathā bhisakkameva bhesajjaṃ. Kujjhanaṃ dussanaṃ. Diṭṭhādīsu adiṭṭhādivāditāvasena paresaṃ visaṃvādanaṃ paravisaṃvādanaṃ. Sadisaṃ patirūpaṃ dassetvā palobhanaṃ sadisaṃ dassetvā vañcanaṃ. Mittānaṃ vihiṃsanaṃ mettibhedo mittadubbhanaṃ. Daḷhamaccharitā thaddhamacchariyaṃ. Attani vijjamānaṃ nihīnataṃ, sadisataṃ vā atikkamitvā maññanaṃ. Paresaṃ sampattiyā asahanaṃ khīyanaṃ. Attasampattiyā nigūhanavasena, parehi sādhāraṇabhāvāsahanavasena ca vividhā icchā ruci etassāti vivicchā. Kadariyatāya [P 2.0291] mudukaṃ macchariyaṃ. Yattha katthacīti sakasantake, parasantake, hīnātike cāti yattha katthaci ārammaṇe. Lubbhanaṃ ārammaṇassa gahaṇaṃ abhigijjhanaṃ. Majjanaṃ seyyādivasena madanaṃ sampaggaho. Muyhanaṃ ārammaṇassa anavabodho. Etesūti etesu yathāvuttesu kodhādīsu sattasantānassa kilissanato vibādhanato, upatāpanato ca kilesasaññitesu pāpadhammesu. Yuttā payuttā sampayuttā avirahitā.

"Musāvāda" itself is a fault of deceit, just as "bhisakka" (physician) is a remedy. Anger is corruption. Deceiving others is the misleading of others by way of speaking of the unseen, etc., as seen, etc., in matters of the seen, etc. Deception is enticing by showing something similar or suitable, deluding by showing a resemblance. Harming friends is the breaking of friendship, treachery to friends. Strong stinginess is rigid stinginess. Conceit is thinking of oneself as having surpassed one's actual state of inferiority or equality. Envy is the inability to endure the success of others. "Vivicchā" is one who has varied desire and inclination by way of concealing one's own success and by way of being unable to endure sharing with others. Pettiness is soft stinginess. "Wherever" means in one's own possession, in another's possession, or in what is inferior, etc.; that is, in any object whatsoever. Greed is the grasping of and craving for an object. Intoxication is being intoxicated, a strong grasping, by way of superiority and so forth. Confusion is the non-understanding of an object. "Among these" means among these evil qualities as stated, such as anger, which are designated as defilements because they stain, afflict, and torment the continuum of a being. They are connected, applied, conjoined, and inseparable.

Ettha [M 2.0229] cāyaṃ brahmā mahāsattena āmagandhe supuṭṭho attano yathāupaṭṭhite pāpadhamme cuddasahi padehi vibhajitvā kathesi, te pana tādisaṃ pavattivisesaṃ upādāya vuttāpi keci puna vuttā, āmagandhasutte (su. ni. 242) pana vuttāpi keci idha sabbaso na vuttā, evaṃ santepi lakkhaṇahāranayena, tadekaṭṭhatāya vā tesaṃ pettha saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tenāha “idaṃ pana sutta”ntiādi. Tattha āmagandhasuttena dīpetvāti idha sarūpato avutte āmagandhepi vuttehi ekalakkhaṇatādinā āmagandhasuttena pakāsetvā kathetabbaṃ tattha nesaṃ sarūpato kathitattā. Āmagandhasuttampi iminā dīpetabbaṃ idha vuttānampi kesañci āmagandhānaṃ tattha avuttabhāvato. Yasmā āmagandhasutte vuttāpi āmagandhā atthato idha saṅgahaṃ samosaraṇaṃ gacchanti, tasmā idha vutte pariharaṇavasena dassentena yasmā cettha keci abhidhammanayena akilesasabhāvāpi sattasantānassa [V 2.0211] vibādhanaṭṭhena “kilesā”ti vattabbataṃ arahanti, tasmā “cuddasasu kilesesū”ti vuttaṃ.

Here, this Brahmā, being well questioned by the Great Being about the "foul odor," spoke, analyzing the evil qualities that occurred to him into fourteen points. However, some of these, though stated with reference to such a particular occurrence, were repeated; and some, though stated in the Āmagandha Sutta (Snp 2.2), were not stated here at all. Even so, their inclusion here should be understood by the method of extracting characteristics or because of their single meaning. Hence it is said, "But this sutta," and so on. Therein, "to be illuminated by the Āmagandha Sutta" means that even the foul odors not mentioned here in their own form should be explained and clarified by the Āmagandha Sutta through their having a single characteristic with those that are mentioned, because their own form is stated there. The Āmagandha Sutta should also be illuminated by this, because some of the foul odors mentioned here are not mentioned there. Because even the foul odors mentioned in the Āmagandha Sutta are included and converge here in terms of meaning, and because here some things, although by the Abhidhamma method they are not of the nature of defilements, are fit to be called "defilements" on account of afflicting the continuum of a being, therefore, by showing them by way of avoiding what is stated here, it is said, "among the fourteen defilements."

Nimmādaṃ milāpanaṃ khepananti āha “nimmādetabbā pahātabbā”ti. Buddhatantīti buddhabhāvīnaṃ paveṇī, buddhabhāvinopi “buddhā”ti vuccanti yathā “agamā rājagahaṃ buddho”ti. Mahāpurisassa daḷhīkammaṃ katvāti mahāpurisassa “pabbajissāmaha”nti [P 2.0292] pavattacittuppādassa daḷhīkammaṃ katvā.

"Nimmādaṃ" means causing to wither, discarding; thus he said, "they should be made prideless, they should be abandoned." "Buddha-tradition" means the lineage of future Buddhas; even future Buddhas are called "Buddhas," as in "The Buddha went to Rājagaha." "Having made it firm for the Great Being" means having made firm the arising of the thought of the Great Being, "I will go forth."

Reṇurājaāmantanāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of King Reṇu's Address

321. Mama manaṃ haritvāti mama cittaṃ apanetvā tassa vasena avattitvā.

321. "Having taken my mind" means having removed my mind, not proceeding according to his will.

Ekībhāvaṃ upagantvā vutthassāti kāyavivekaparibrūhanena ekībhāvaṃ upagantvā tapokammavasena vutthassa. Kusapattehi paritthatoti barihisehi vediyā samantato santharito. Akācoti vaṇo vaṇasadisakhaṇḍiccavirahito. Tenāha “akakkaso”ti.

"Of him who dwelt having attained a state of oneness" means of him who dwelt by way of ascetic practice, having attained a state of oneness by the cultivation of bodily seclusion. "Spread around with kusa leaves" means spread all around the altar with kusa grass. "Akāco" means a wound free from breakage similar to a wound. Therefore it is said, "not rough."

Chakhattiyaāmantanāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Six Khattiyas' Address

322. Sikkheyyāmāti sikkhāpeyyāma, sikkhāpanañcettha atthibhāvāpādananti āha “upalāpeyyāmā”ti.

322. "Sikkheyyāma" means "we should instruct"; and here, instructing means bringing into being, thus he said, "we should persuade."

323. Yassa [M 2.0230] vīriyārambhassa, khantibalassa ca abhāvena pabbajitānaṃ samaṇadhammo paripuṇṇo, parisuddho ca na hoti, tesu vīriyārambhakhantibalesu te te niyojetuṃ “ārambhavho”tiādi vuttaṃ.

323. For those who have gone forth, whose ascetic practice is not complete and pure due to the lack of energetic exertion and the power of patience, to engage them in those very qualities of energetic exertion and the power of patience, it is said, 'Exert yourselves!' and so on.

Karuṇājhānamaggoti karuṇājhānasaṅkhāto maggo. Ujumaggoti brahmalokagamane ujubhūto maggo. Anuttaroti seṭṭho brahmavihārasabhāvato. Tenāha “uttamamaggo nāmā”ti. Sabbhi rakkhito sādhūhi yathā parihāni na hoti, evaṃ paṭipakkhadūrīkaraṇena rakkhito gopito. “Saddhammo sabbhi vakkhito”ti keci paṭhanti, tesaṃ saparahitasādhanena sādhūhi buddhādīhi kathito paveditoti attho.

'The path of compassion meditation' means the path known as compassion meditation. 'The straight path' means the path that is straight for going to the Brahma world. 'The unsurpassed' means the best because of its nature as a divine abiding. Therefore it is said, 'It is called the supreme path.' 'Protected by the virtuous' means protected and guarded by the good ones in such a way that there is no decline, by keeping away opposing factors. Some recite, 'The True Dhamma is proclaimed by the virtuous'; for them, the meaning is that it is spoken and made known by the virtuous, such as the Buddhas, for accomplishing one's own and others' welfare.

Taṅkhaṇaviddhaṃsanadhammanti [V 2.0212] yasmiṃ khaṇe virodhidhammasamāyogo, tasmiṃyeva khaṇe vinassanasabhāvaṃ, yo vā so gamanassādānaṃ devaputtānaṃ heṭṭhupariyena paṭimukhaṃ dhāvantānaṃ sirasi, pāde ca baddhakhuradhārāsamāgamanatopi sīghataratāya atiittaro pavattikkhaṇo, teneva vinassanasabhāvaṃ. Tassa jīvitassa. Gatinti niṭṭhaṃ. Mantāyanti manteyyanti [P 2.0293] vuttaṃ hotīti āha “mantetabba”nti. Karaṇatthe vā bhummanti “mantāya”nti idaṃ bhummaṃ karaṇatthe daṭṭhabbaṃ yathā “ñātāya”nti. Sabbapalibodheti sabbepi kusalakiriyāya vibandhe uparodhe.

'Of the nature to vanish in an instant' means of the nature to vanish at the very moment when the conjunction of opposing factors occurs. Or, that moment of arising is more extremely swift than the meeting of the sharp edges of hooves fastened on the heads and feet of devaputtas running face to face, up and down, and therefore it is of the nature to vanish. 'Of his life. Gone' means conclusion. 'Mantāya' means 'it should be deliberated,' thus he said, 'it should be deliberated.' Or, 'mantāya' is to be seen as a locative case in the sense of instrumentality, like 'ñātāya' (by knowing). 'All impediments' means all hindrances and obstructions to skillful actions.

Brāhmaṇamahāsālādīnaṃ āmantanāvaṇṇanā

The Account of the Invitation of the Great Wealthy Brahmins and So On

324. Appesakkhāti appānubhāvāti āha “pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāyā”tiādi.

324. 'Of little influence' means 'of little power,' thus he said, 'from the time of going forth,' and so on.

Cakkavatti rājā viya sambhāvito.

Like a wheel-turning monarch, he was esteemed.

Mahāgovindapabbajjāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Great Govinda's Going Forth

328. Samāpattīnaṃ ājānanaṃ nāma attapaccakkhatā, sacchikiriyāti āha “na sakkhiṃsu nibbattetu”nti.

328. 'Knowing the attainments' means direct personal experience, realization—thus he said, 'they could not realize.'

329. Imināti “sarāmaha”nti iminā padena. “Sarāmaha”nti hi vadantena bhagavato mahābrahmunā kathitaṃ “tatheva ta”nti bhagavatā paṭiññātameva jātanti. Na vaṭṭe nibbindanatthāya catusaccakammaṭṭhānakathāya abhāvato. Asati pana vaṭṭe nibbidāya virāgānaṃ asambhavo evāti āha [M 2.0231] “na virāgāyā”tiādi. Ekantameva vaṭṭe nibbindanatthāya anekākāravokāravaṭṭe ādīnavavibhāvanato.

329. 'By this' means by the word 'sarāmaha' (I remember). For when one says 'sarāmaha' (I remember), it means that what was spoken by the Great Brahmā to the Blessed One, 'Thus it is,' was acknowledged by the Blessed One. It was not for the purpose of disenchantment with the round of existence, because of the absence of a discourse on the four truths as a meditation subject. But in the absence of disenchantment with the round of existence, there is indeed no possibility of dispassion—thus he said, 'not for dispassion,' and so on. It is solely for the purpose of disenchantment with the round of existence, through the declaration of the dangers in the round of existence in its diverse forms and spheres.

“Nibbidāyā”ti iminā padena vipassanā vuttā. Esa nayo sesesupi. Vavatthānakathāti vipassanāmagganibbānānaṃ taṃtaṃpadehi vavatthapetvā kathā. Ayamettha nippariyāyakathāti āha “pariyāyena panā”tiādi.

'Nibbidāya' (for disenchantment)—by this word, insight is stated. The same method applies to the rest. 'The discourse on definition' means the discourse distinguishing insight, the path, and Nibbāna by their respective terms. Here, this is the direct explanation—thus he said, 'but by way of indirect explanation,' and so on.

330. Paripūretunti bhāvanāpāripūrivasena paripuṇṇe kātuṃ, nibbattetunti attho. Brahmacariyaciṇṇakulaputtānanti [V 2.0213] ciṇṇamaggabrahmacariyānaṃ kulaputtānanti ukkaṭṭhaniddesena arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhapesi.

330. 'To fulfill' means to make complete in the sense of perfecting development, that is, to bring about. 'Sons of good families who have practiced the holy life' refers to sons of good families who have practiced the holy life of the path; he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of arahantship by means of an emphatic designation.

Abhinandanaṃ nāma sampaṭicchanaṃ “abhinandanti āgata”ntiādīsu [P 2.0294] viya, tañcettha atthato cittassa attamanatāti āha “cittena sampaṭicchanto abhinanditvā”ti. “Sādhu sādhū”ti vācāya sampahaṃsanā anumodanāti āha “vācāya sampahaṃsamāno anumoditvā”ti.

'Abhinandana' (delight) means acceptance, as in phrases like 'they delight in what has come,' and so on; and here, in meaning, it is the mind's satisfaction—thus he said, 'accepting with the mind, having delighted.' 'Sādhu, sādhu!' (Excellent, excellent!) is verbal rejoicing and approval—thus he said, 'rejoicing verbally, having approved.'

Mahāgovindasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

The Clarification of the Hidden Meaning in the Exposition of the Mahāgovinda Sutta

7. Mahāsamayasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Mahāsamaya Sutta

Nidānavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Introduction

331. Udānanti [P 2.0295][V 2.0214][M 2.0232] raññā okkākena jātisambhedaparihāranimittaṃ pavattitaṃ udānaṃ paṭicca. Ekopi janapado ruḷhisaddena “sakkā”ti vuccatīti ettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ mahānidānavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Aropiteti kenaci aropite.

331. 'Udāna' means referring to the utterance begun by King Okkāka on account of the indication for avoiding the mixing of castes. Even a single district is called 'Sakya' by convention; regarding what should be said here, that should be understood in the manner explained in the commentary to the Mahānidāna Sutta. 'Imposed' means imposed by someone.

Āvaraṇenāti setunā. Bandhāpetvāti paṃsupalāsapāsāṇamattikākhaṇḍādīhi āḷiṃ thiraṃ kārāpetvā.

'By a barrier' means by a dam. 'Having caused to be built' means having caused a firm embankment to be constructed with lumps of earth, straw, stones, clay fragments, and so on.

“Jātiṃ ghaṭṭetvā kalahaṃ vaḍḍhayiṃsū”ti saṅkhepena vuttamatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “koliyakammakarā vadantī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'Having clashed over their origins, they increased the quarrel'—to make the meaning stated briefly clearer, it is said, 'the Koliyan laborers said,' and so forth.

Tīṇi jātakānīti phandanajātakapathavīundriyajātakalaṭukikajātakāni dve jātakānīti rukkhadhamma vaṭṭakajātakāni.

'Three Jātakas' means the Phandana Jātaka, the Pathavīundriya Jātaka, and the Laṭukika Jātaka. 'Two Jātakas' means the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka and the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka.

Tenāti bhagavatā. Kalahakāraṇabhāvoti kalahakāraṇassa atthibhāvo.

'By that' means by the Blessed One. 'The condition of being a cause of quarrel' means the existence of a cause of quarrel.

Aṭṭhāneti akāraṇe. Veraṃ katvāti virodhaṃ uppādetvā. “Kuṭhārihattho puriso”tiādinā phandanajātakaṃ kathesi. “Duddubhāyati bhaddante”tiādinā pathavīundriyajātakaṃ kathesi. “Vandāmi taṃ kuñjarā”tiādinā laṭukikajātakaṃ kathesi.

'Without reason' means without cause. 'Having made enmity' means having created opposition. 'A man with an axe in hand,' and so forth, he related the Phandana Jātaka. 'It thunders, venerable sir,' and so forth, he related the Pathavīundriya Jātaka. 'I bow to you, O elephant,' and so forth, he related the Laṭukika Jātaka.

“Sādhū [V 2.0215] sambahulā ñātī; api rukkhā araññajā;

Vāto vahati ekaṭṭhaṃ, brahantampi vanappati”nti. –

'Good are many relatives, even as trees born in the forest. The wind overthrows a tree that stands alone, even a mighty one.'

Ādinā rukkhadhammajātakaṃ kathesi.

Beginning with this, he related the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka.

“Sammodamānā [P 2.0296] gacchanti, jālaṃ ādāya pakkhino;

Yadā te vivadissanti, tadā ehinti me vasa”nti. –

'Birds go along harmoniously, carrying the net; When they quarrel, then they will come into my power.'

Ādinā vaṭṭakajātakaṃ kathesi.

Beginning with this, he related the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka.

“Attadaṇḍā [M 2.0233] bhayaṃ jātaṃ, janaṃ passatha medhagaṃ;

Saṃvegaṃ kittayissāmi, yathā saṃvijitaṃ mayā”ti. (su. ni. 1.941);

'Fear is born from taking up the rod; look at people in conflict. I will declare my agitation, as I have experienced it.'

Ādinā attadaṇḍasuttaṃ kathesi.

Beginning with this, he related the Attadaṇḍa Sutta.

Taṃtaṃpalobhanakiriyā kāyavācāhi parakkamantiyo “ukkaṇṭhantū”ti sāsanaṃ pesenti.

Striving with body and speech through various enticing actions, they send forth the message, saying, 'Let them be discontented.'

Kuṇāladaheti kuṇāladahatīre patiṭṭhāya. Pucchitapucchitaṃ kathesi (jā. 2.kuṇālajātaka) “anukkamena kuṇālasakuṇarājassa pucchanappasaṅgena kuṇālajātakaṃ kathessāmī”ti. Anabhiratiṃ vinodesi itthīnaṃ dosadassanamukhena kāmānaṃ ādīnavokārasaṃkilesavibhāvanena.

'At the Kuṇāla lake' means standing on the bank of the Kuṇālada lake. Having been asked repeatedly, he related the Kuṇāla Jātaka: 'Gradually, on the occasion of the questioning of the king of the Kuṇāla birds, I will narrate the Kuṇāla Jātaka.' He dispelled discontent by showing the faults of women, and through revealing the dangers, the degradation, and the defilements of sensual pleasures.

Kosajjaṃ vidhamitvā purisathāmaparibrūhanena “uttamapurisasadisehi no bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti uppannacittā.

Having overcome laziness, with the development of manly strength, the thought arose in them: 'It is fitting for us to become like the best of men.'

Avissaṭṭhakammantāti arativinodanato paṭṭhāya avissaṭṭhasamaṇakammantā, aparicattakammaṭṭhānāti attho. Nisīdituṃ vaṭṭatīti bhagavā cintesīti yojanā.

"Avissaṭṭhakammantā" means that from the dispelling of discontent onwards, their monastic duties were not relinquished; the meaning is that they had not abandoned their meditation subject. The connection is that the Blessed One thought, "It is fitting to sit" (Nisīdituṃ vaṭṭatīti bhagavā cintesi).

Paduminiyanti padumassare. Vikasiṃsu guṇagaṇavibodhena. “Ayaṃ imassa…pe… na kathesī”ti iminā sabbepi te bhikkhū tāvadeva paṭipāṭiyā āgatattā aññamaññassa lajjamānā [V 2.0216] attanā paṭividdhavisesaṃ bhagavato nārocesunti dasseti. “Khīṇāsavāna”ntiādinā tattha kāraṇamāha.

"In a lotus pond" (paduminiyaṃ) means in a lotus lake. They blossomed with the awakening of their multitude of virtues. By this, "This one of his... he did not speak," it is shown that all those monks, having arrived in succession just then, feeling ashamed before one another, did not report to the Blessed One the special distinction they had themselves attained. With "of those whose taints are destroyed," and so forth, he states the reason for this.

Osīdamatteti bhagavato santikaṃ upagatamatte. Ariyamaṇḍaleti ariyasamūhe. Pācīnayugandharaparikkhepatoti yugandharapabbatassa pācīnaparikkhepato, na bāhirakehi uccamānaudayapabbatato. Rāmaṇeyyakadassanatthanti buddhuppādapaṭimaṇḍitattā visesato ramaṇīyassa lokassa ramaṇīyabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Ullaṅghitvāti [P 2.0297] uṭṭhahitvā. Evarūpe khaṇe laye muhutteti yathāvutte candamaṇḍalassa uṭṭhitakkhaṇe uṭṭhitavelāyaṃ uṭṭhitamuhutteti uparūpari kālassa vaḍḍhitabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

"Just upon approaching" (osīdamatte) means just upon approaching the Blessed One's presence. "In the noble assembly" (ariyamaṇḍale) means in the assembly of noble ones. "From the eastern boundary of Yugandhara" (pācīnayugandharaparikkhepato) means from the eastern boundary of the Yugandhara mountain, not from the outer Uccamāna and Udaya mountains. "For the purpose of seeing the beauty" (rāmaṇeyyakadassanatthaṃ) means for the purpose of seeing the beautiful state of the world, which is especially beautiful because it is adorned by the arising of a Buddha. "Having risen" (ullaṅghitvā) means having risen. "At such a moment, at such a lapse, at such an instant" (evarūpe khaṇe laye muhutte) refers to the moment of the moon's disk rising, the time of rising, the instant of rising; this is said to show the progressive increase of time, moment by moment.

Tathā [M 2.0234] tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ jātiādivasena bhagavato anurūpaparivāritaṃ dassento “tatthā”ti ādimāha.

Thus, showing that the monks surrounding the Blessed One were a befitting retinue in terms of their birth and so forth, he begins with "there."

Samāpannadevatāti āsannaṭṭhāne jhānasamāpatti samāpannadevatā. Caliṃsūti uṭṭhahiṃsu. Kosamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ saddantaraṃ. Jambudīpe kira ādito tesaṭṭhimattāni nagarasahassāni uppannāni, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, taṃ sandhāyāha “tikkhattuṃ tesaṭṭhiyā nagarasahassesū”ti. Te pana sampiṇḍetvā satasahassato paraṃ asītisahassāni, navasahassāni ca honti. Navanavutiyā doṇamukhasatasahassesūti navasatasahassādhikesu navutisatasahassesu doṇamukhesu. Doṇamukhanti ca mahānagarassa āyuppattiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ pādanagaraṃ vuccati. Channavutiyā paṭṭanakoṭisatasahassesūti chakoṭiadhikanavutikoṭisatasahassapaṭṭanesu. Tambapaṇṇidīpādīsu chapaṇṇāsāya ratanākaresu. Evaṃ pana nagaradoṇimukhapaṭṭanaratanākarādivibhāgena kathanaṃ taṃtaṃadhivatthāya vasantīnaṃ devatānaṃ bahubhāvadassanatthaṃ. Yadi dasasahassacakkavāḷesu devatā sannipatitā, atha kasmā pāḷiyaṃ “dasahi ca lokadhātūhī”ti vuttanti āha “dasasahassa…pe… adhippetā”ti, tena sahassilokadhātu idha “ekā lokadhātū”ti vuttāti veditabbaṃ.

"Deities who had attained absorption" (samāpannadevatā) refers to deities who had attained jhāna absorption in a nearby place. "They moved" (caliṃsu) means they arose. The space between sounds was a distance of one kosa. In Jambudīpa, it is said that initially sixty-three thousand cities arose, then a second time, and a third time similarly. Referring to this, it is said, "three times in sixty-three thousand cities." But when combined, they amount to one hundred and eighty-nine thousand. "In ninety-nine hundred-thousand doṇamukhas" (navanavutiyā doṇamukhasatasahassesu) means in ninety hundred-thousand doṇamukhas plus nine hundred-thousand. A "doṇamukha" is a dependent town that serves as the life-supporting base of a great city. "In ninety-six koṭi-hundred-thousands of port cities" (channavutiyā paṭṭanakoṭisatasahassesu) means in ninety koṭi-hundred-thousand port cities with an addition of six koṭi. In Tambapaṇṇi Island and others, there were fifty-six jewel mines. This detailed description of cities, doṇamukhas, ports, and jewel mines is meant to show the great number of deities dwelling in those respective places. If deities assembled from ten thousand world-systems, why does the Pāli say "from ten world-systems"? To this, it is said, "ten thousand... is intended," by which it should be understood that here a thousandfold world-system is referred to as "one world-system."

Lohapāsādeti ādito kate lohapāsāde. Brahmaloketi heṭṭhime brahmaloke. Yadi tā devatā evaṃ nirantarā, pacchā āgatānaṃ okāso eva na bhaveyyāti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “yathā kho panā”tiādi. Suddhāvāsakāyaṃ upapannā suddhāvāsakāyikā, tāsaṃ pana yasmā suddhāvāsabhūmi nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “suddhāvāsavāsīna”nti. Āvāsāti āvāsanaṭṭhānabhūtā[P 2.0298][V 2.0217], devatā pana orambhāgiyānaṃ, itaresañca saṃyojanānaṃ samucchindanena suddho āvāso etesanti suddhāvāsā.

"In the Lohapāsāda" (lohapāsāde) means in the Lohapāsāda that was initially constructed. "In the Brahmā world" (brahmaloke) means in a lower Brahmā world. In reference to the objection, "If those deities were so continuous, there would be no space for those arriving later," he says, "But just as..." and so forth. Those reborn in the Pure Abode realm (suddhāvāsakāyaṃ upapannā) are the suddhāvāsakāyikā. Since the Pure Abode plane is their dwelling place, it is said, "of the dwellers in the Pure Abodes." "Abodes" (āvāsā) means places of dwelling. But for these deities, because their abode is pure through the eradication of the lower fetters and the other fetters, they are called "Pure Abodes" (suddhāvāsā).

332. Puratthimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ otari aññattha okāsaṃ alabhamāno. Evaṃ sesāpi. Buddhānaṃ abhimukhamaggo buddhavīthi. Yāva cakkavāḷā ottharituṃ ovarituṃ na sakkā. Pahaṭabuddhavīthiyāvāti buddhānaṃ santikaṃ upasaṅkamantehi tehi devabrahmehi vaḷañjitavīthiyāva. Samiti saṅgati sannipāto samayo, mahanto samayo mahāsamayoti āha “mahāsamūho”ti[M 2.0235]. Pavaddhaṃ vanaṃ pavananti āha “vanasaṇḍo”ti. Devaghaṭāti devasamūhā.

332. Finding no space elsewhere, he descended onto the rim of the eastern world-system. The same applies to the rest. The path facing the Buddhas is the Buddha-path. It is not possible to spread out and cover the entire world-system. "By the trodden Buddha-path" (pahaṭabuddhavīthiyāva) means by the very path used by those deities and Brahmās approaching the presence of the Buddhas. An assembly (samiti), a gathering (saṅgati), a meeting (sannipāto), an occasion (samayo); a great occasion (mahanto samayo) is a mahāsamayo. Thus he says, "a great multitude" (mahāsamūho). A thriving forest (pavaddhaṃ vanaṃ) is a pavanaṃ. Thus he says, "a grove of trees" (vanasaṇḍo). "A host of deities" (devaghaṭā) means a multitude of deities.

Samādahaṃsūti samādahitaṃ lokuttarasamādhinā suṭṭhu appitaṃ akaṃsu, yathāsamāhitaṃ pana samādhinā yojitaṃ nāma hotīti vuttaṃ “samādhinā yojesu”nti. Sabbesaṃ gomuttavaṅkādīnaṃ dūrasamūhanitattā sabbe…pe… akariṃsu. Nayati asse etehīti nettāni, yottāni. Avīthipaṭipannānaṃ assānaṃ vīthipaṭipādanaṃ rasmiggahaṇena pahotīti “sabbayottāni gahetvā acodento”ti vatvā taṃ pana acodanaṃ avāraṇaṃ evāti āha “acodento avārento”ti.

"They concentrated" (samādahaṃsu) means they made their minds well-applied with supramundane concentration. But because that which is well-concentrated is indeed conjoined by concentration, it is said, "they yoked by concentration" (samādhinā yojesuṃ). Because all crooked things like the path of cow's urine were removed far away, they made all... "Those by which one leads horses" (nayati asse etehi) are reins (nettāni), or tethers (yottāni). Since guiding horses that are not following the course onto the course is possible by grasping the reins, having said, "taking all the tethers without urging," he then says that this non-urging is simply non-hindrance, hence "without urging, without hindering."

Yathā khīlaṃ bhittiyaṃ vā bhūmiyaṃ vā ākoṭitaṃ dunnīharaṇaṃ, yathā ca palighaṃ nagarappavesanivāraṇaṃ, yathā ca indakhīlaṃ gambhīranemi sunikhātaṃ dunnīharaṇaṃ, evaṃ rāgādayo sattasantānato dunnīharaṇā, nibbānanagarappavesanivāraṇā cāti te “khīlaṃ, palighaṃ, indakhīla”nti ca vuttā. Taṇhāejāya abhāvena anejā paramasantuṭṭhabhāvena cātuddisattā appaṭihatacārikaṃ caranti.

Just as a stake hammered into a wall or the ground is difficult to remove, just as a crossbar prevents entry into a city, and just as a city pillar is deeply and firmly embedded and difficult to dislodge, so too are lust and other defilements difficult to remove from the continuum of a being, and they prevent entry into the city of Nibbāna. Thus, they are called "stake," "crossbar," and "city pillar." Because of the absence of craving's agitation, they are unagitated; being utterly content, they wander with unimpeded travel in the four directions.

Gatāseti gatā eva, na pana gamissanti pariniṭṭhitasaraṇagamanattāti[P 2.0299]. Lokuttarasaraṇagamanaṃ adhippetanti āha “nibbematikasaraṇagamanena gatā”ti. Te hi niyamena apāyabhūmiṃ na gamissanti, devakāyañca paripūressanti. Ye pana lokiyena saraṇagamanena buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gatāse, na te gamissanti apāyabhūmiṃ, sati ca paccayantarasamavāye pahāya mānusaṃ dehaṃ, devakāyaṃ paripūressantīti ayamettha attho.

"They have gone" (gatāse) means they have indeed gone; they will not go again, because their going for refuge is completed. The supramundane going for refuge is intended; hence it is said, "they have gone with an unwavering going for refuge." For they will certainly not go to a plane of misery, and they will fulfill a divine existence. But as for those who have gone to the Buddha for refuge with a mundane going for refuge, they will not go to a plane of misery, and if there is a convergence of other conditions, having abandoned the human body, they will fulfill a divine existence. This is the meaning here.

Devatāsannipātavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Assembly of Deities

333. Etesanti [V 2.0218] devatāsannipātānaṃ. Idānīti imasmiṃ kāle. Buddhānanti aññesaṃ buddhānaṃ abhāvā. Cittakallatā cittamaddavaṃ.

333. "Etesaṃ" means of the assemblies of deities. "Idāni" means at this time. "Buddhānaṃ" means because of the absence of other Buddhas. "Cittakallatā" is tenderness of mind (cittamaddavaṃ).

Kiṃ pana bhagavatāva mahante devatāsamāgame tesaṃ nāmagottaṃ kathetuṃ sakkāti? Āma sakkāti dassetuṃ “buddhā nāma mahantā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha diṭṭhanti rūpāyatanamāha, sutanti saddāyatanaṃ, mutanti sampattaggāhiindriyavisayaṃ gandharasaphoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ, viññātanti vuttāvasesaṃ sabbaṃ [M 2.0236] ñeyyaṃ, pattanti pariyesitvā, apariyesitvā vā sampattaṃ, pariyesitanti pattaṃ, appattaṃ vā pariyiṭṭhaṃ. Anuvicaritaṃ manasāti kevalaṃ manasā ālocitaṃ. Katthaci nīlādivasena vibhattarūpārammaṇeti abhidhamme (dha. sa. 615) “nīlaṃ pītaka”ntiādinā vibhatte yattha katthaci rūpārammaṇe kiñci rūpārammaṇaṃ vā na atthīti yojanā. Bherisaddādivasenāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Yanti yaṃ ārammaṇaṃ. Etesanti buddhānaṃ.

But was it possible for the Blessed One to declare their names and clans in such a great assembly of deities? Yes, it was possible. To demonstrate this, it was said, "The Buddhas are indeed great," and so on. Here, "seen" refers to the visible-form base; "heard" refers to the sound base; "sensed" refers to the sense objects grasped by contact—the bases of smell, taste, and touch; "cognized" refers to all remaining knowables. "Attained" means reached, whether sought or unsought. "Sought" means sought, whether attained or not yet attained. "Examined with the mind" means considered solely by the mind. Regarding "in some differentiated form-object according to blue, etc.": in the Abhidhamma (Dhs 615), where it is differentiated by such as "blue, yellow," the connection is: "wherever in any form-object there is some form-object, or none at all." "By means of sounds like a drum, etc.": here too, the same principle applies. "Yaṃ" means that which is the object. "Etesaṃ" means of the Buddhas.

Idāni yathāvuttamatthaṃ pāḷiyā samatthetuṃ “yathāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tadā jānanakiriyāya apariyositabhāvadassanatthaṃ “jānāmī”ti vatvā yasmā yaṃ kiñci neyyaṃ nāma, sabbaṃ taṃ bhagavatā aññātaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā vuttaṃ “tamahaṃ abbhaññāsi”nti.

Now, to support the meaning stated as before with the Pāli text, ‘as he said,’ and so on, was stated. Then, to show the uncompleted nature of the act of knowing, having said, ‘I know,’ because whatever is knowable, none of that is unknown to the Blessed One—therefore it is said, ‘that I have fully understood.’

Na olokenti payojanābhāvato. Viparītā “na kammāvaraṇena samannāgatā”tiādinā nayena vuttā. “Yassa maṅgalā samūhatā”ti (su. ni. 362) ārabhitvā “rāgaṃ [P 2.0300] vinayetha mānusesu dibbesu kāmesu cā”tiādinā (su. ni. 363) ca rāganiggahakathābāhullato sammāparibbājanīyasuttaṃ rāgacaritānaṃ sappāyaṃ, “piyamappiyabhūtā kalaha vivādā paridevasokā sahamaccharā cā”tiādinā (su. ni. 869; mahāni. 98) kalahādayo yato dosato samuṭṭhahanti, so ca doso yato piyabhāvato, so ca piyabhāvo yato chandato samuṭṭhahanti, iti phalato, kāraṇaparamparato ca dose ādīnavavibhāvanabāhullato kalahavivādasuttaṃ (su. ni. 869; mahāni. 98) dosacaritānaṃ sappāyaṃ –

They do not look because there is no purpose. The opposite is stated by the method beginning with ‘not endowed with the obstacle of kamma,’ and so on. Starting with ‘For whom auspicious signs are eradicated’ (Snp 362) and continuing with ‘One should remove lust among humans and for divine sensual pleasures’ (Snp 363) and so on, due to the abundance of discussion on restraining lust, the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta is suitable for those of lustful temperament. ‘Beloved and unbeloved beings, quarrels, disputes, lamentation, sorrow, and envy’ (Snp 869; Mahāni. 98)—since quarrels and so on arise from hatred, and that hatred arises from the state of being dear, and that state of being dear arises from desire—thus, by result and by the sequence of causes, due to the abundance of exposition of the dangers of hatred, the Kalahavivāda Sutta (Snp 869; Mahāni. 98) is suitable for those of hateful temperament.

“Appañhi etaṃ na alaṃ samāya,

Duve vivādassa phalāni brūmi;

Etampi [V 2.0219] disvā na vivādayetha,

Khemābhipassaṃ avivādabhūmi”nti. (su. ni. 902; mahāni. 131) –

“For this is little, not enough for peace,

I declare two fruits of dispute;

Seeing this as well, one should not engage in dispute,

Perceiving the secure ground of non-dispute.” (Snp 902; Mahāni. 131)

Ādinā nayena sammohavidhamanato, paññāparibrūhanato ca mahābyūhasuttaṃ mohacaritānaṃ sappāyaṃ –

In this way, because it dispels delusion and expands wisdom, the Mahābyūha Sutta is suitable for those of a deluded temperament.

“Parassa [M 2.0237] ce dhammaṃ anānujānaṃ,

Bālo, mago hoti nihīnapañño;

Sabbeva bālā sunihīnapaññā,

Sabbevime diṭṭhiparibbasānā”ti. (su. ni. 886; mahāni. 115) –

“If, not approving another’s teaching,

A fool, like a beast he is, of deficient wisdom.

All fools indeed are of very deficient wisdom,

All these are clinging to their own views.” (Snp 886; Mahāni. 115)

Ādinā nayena sandiṭṭhiparāmāsitāpanayanamukhena savisayesu diṭṭhiggahaṇesu visaṭavitakkavicchindanavasena pavattattā cūḷabyūhasuttaṃ vitakkacaritānaṃ sappāyaṃ –

In this way, because it proceeds by removing the clinging to one’s own views and by cutting off discursive thoughts that have spread into the grasping of views in their respective objects, the Cūḷabyūha Sutta is suitable for those of a speculative temperament.

“Mūlaṃ [P 2.0301] papañcasaṅkhāya (iti bhagavā),

Mantā asmīti sabbaṃ uparundhe;

Yā kāci taṇhā ajjhattaṃ,

Tāsaṃ vinayā sadā sato sikkhe”ti. (su. ni. 922; mahāni. 151) –

“Having understood the root of proliferation (thus said the Blessed One),

By wisdom, he should restrain all thoughts of ‘I am’;

Whatever craving exists within,

Always mindfully he should train himself for their abandonment.” (Snp 922; Mahāni. 151)

Papañcasaṅkhāya mūlaṃ avijjādikilesajātaṃ asmīti pavattamānañcāti sabbaṃ mantā paññāya uparundheyya. Yā kāci ajjhattaṃ rūpataṇhādibhedā taṇhā uppajjeyya, tāsaṃ vinayā vūpasamāya sadā sato upaṭṭhitassati hutvā sikkheyyāti evamādi upadesassa saddhova bhājanaṃ. Tassa hi so atthāvahoti tuvaṭṭakasuttaṃ saddhācaritānaṃ sappāyaṃ –

The root of proliferation, the aggregate of defilements beginning with ignorance, and all that arises as ‘I am’—all this one should obstruct with wisdom. Whatever craving arises internally, such as craving for form and so on, for their abandonment and stilling, one should always train, having established mindfulness. For such instruction, faith alone is a vessel, for it brings benefit to him. The Tuvaṭṭaka Sutta is suitable for those of faithful temperament.

“Vītataṇho purā bhedā (iti bhagavā),

Pubbamantamanissito;

Vemajjhe [V 2.0220] nupasaṅkheyyo,

Tassa natthi purakkhata”nti. (su. ni. 855; mahāni. 84) –

“Free from craving before the break-up (thus said the Blessed One),

Not relying on the past or the future;

Not reckoned in the middle,

For him there is no preference.” (Snp 855; Mahāni. 84)

Yo sarīrabhedato pubbeva pahīnataṇho, tato eva atītaddhasaññitaṃ purimakoṭṭhāsaṃ taṇhānissayena anissito, vemajjhe paccuppannepi addhani “ratto”tiādinā upasaṅkhātabbo, tassa arahato taṇhādiṭṭhipurakkhārānaṃ abhāvā anāgate addhani kiñci purakkhataṃ natthīti ādinā evaṃ gambhīrakathābāhullato pūrābhedasuttaṃ (su. ni. 855; mahāni. 84) buddhicaritānaṃ sappāyanti katvā vuttaṃ “atha nesaṃ sappāyaṃ …pe… vavatthapetvā”ti. Manasākāsīti evaṃ cariyāya vasena manasi katvā puna taṃ sadisaṃ attano [M 2.0238] desanānikkhepayogyatāvasena manasi akāsi. Attajjhāsayena nu kho jāneyyāti parajjhāsayādiṃ anapekkhitvā mayhaṃyeva ajjhāsayena āraddha desanaṃ [P 2.0302] jāneyya nu kho. Parajjhāsayenāti sannipatitāya parisāya kassaci ajjhāsayena. Aṭṭhuppattikenāti idha samuṭṭhitaaṭṭhuppattiyā. Pucchāvasenāti kassaci pucchantassa pucchāvasena. Āraddhadesanaṃ jāneyyāti. “Sace paccekabuddho bhaveyyā”ti idaṃ imesaṃ suttānaṃ desanāya pucchā paccekabuddhānaṃ bhāriyā, avisayā cāti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tenāha “sopi na sakkuṇeyyā”ti.

One who has abandoned craving even before the breaking of the body, and is therefore not dependent, through craving, on the former portion designated as the past; and who, in the middle, in the present time, is not to be reckoned as 'attached' and so on; for that Arahant, due to the absence of placing craving and views foremost, in the future time there is nothing placed foremost—due to the abundance of such profound discourse, the Pūrābheda Sutta (Snp 855; Mahāni. 84) is said to be suitable for those of intellectual temperament, and so it was said, ‘Then what is suitable for them... having determined...’ ‘He considered in his mind’ means: having thus considered by way of temperament, he again considered it in his mind as being similar and suitable for the exposition of his own teaching. ‘Would one know by one’s own inclination?’ means: without regard for the inclinations of others, etc., would one know the teaching undertaken solely by my own inclination? ‘By another’s inclination’ means: by the inclination of someone in the assembled gathering. ‘By an arisen occurrence’ means: by an occurrence that has arisen here. ‘By the occasion of a question’ means: by the occasion of someone asking a question. ‘Would one know the teaching undertaken?’ ‘If there were a Paccekabuddha...’: this is said to show that the question for the teaching of these discourses is burdensome for Paccekabuddhas, and not their domain. Therefore, he said: ‘Even he would not be able.’

Ettha ca yasmā na anumatipucchā, kathetukamyatāpucchā vā yuttā, atha kho diṭṭhasaṃsandanapucchāsadisī vā vimaticchedanapucchāsadisī vā pucchā yuttā, tāva puggalajjhāsayavasena pavattitā nāma honti, na yathādhammavasena, tattha yadi bhagavā tathā sayameva pucchitvā sayameva vissajjeyya, suṇantīnaṃ devatānaṃ sammoho bhaveyya “kiṃ nāmetaṃ bhagavā paṭhamaṃ evamāha, punapi evamāhā”ti, andhakāraṃ paviṭṭhā viya honti, tasmā vuttaṃ “evaṃ petā devatā na sakkhissanti paṭivijjhitu”nti. Yathādhammadesanāyaṃ pana kathetukamyatāvasena pucchanena sammoho hotīti. Sūriyo uggatoti āha devasaṅgho āsannatarabhāvena obhāsassa vipulauḷārabhāvato. Ekissā lokadhātuyāti sutte (dī. ni. 3.161; ma. ni. 3.129; a. ni. 1.277; vibha. 809; netti. 57; mi. pa. 5.1.1) āgatanayena sabbattheva pana apubbaṃ acarimaṃ dve buddhā na honteva. Tenevāha – “anantāsu…pe… addasā”ti.

Here, since neither a request for approval nor a question about the desire to speak is suitable, but rather a question similar to one for clarifying views or one for resolving doubts is suitable, such questions arise based on the inclinations of individuals, not according to the Dhamma. If the Blessed One were Himself to ask and Himself to answer, the listening deities would be confused, thinking, ‘Why does the Blessed One first say this and then say that?’ They would be as if plunged into darkness. Therefore, it is said, ‘Thus these deities will not be able to penetrate it.’ However, in the teaching of the Dhamma, confusion arises from questioning out of a desire to speak. ‘The sun has risen,’ said the assembly of devas, due to their very close proximity and the immense and magnificent radiance of its brilliance. ‘Within one world-system’: according to the method found in the suttas (Dī. Ni. 3.161; Ma. Ni. 3.129; A. Ni. 1.277; Vibha. 809; Netti. 57; Mi. Pa. 5.1.1)—it is the case everywhere that two Buddhas never arise simultaneously, either in the past or in the future. Therefore, he said: ‘In infinite... he saw.’

Gāthāyaṃ pucchāmīti nimmitabuddho bhagavantaṃ pucchituṃ okāsaṃ kārāpesi. Muninti buddhamuniṃ[V 2.0221]. Pahūtapaññanti mahāpaññaṃ. Tiṇṇanti caturoghatiṇṇaṃ. Pāraṅgatanti nibbānappattaṃ, sabbassa vā ñeyyassa pāraṃ pariyantaṃ gataṃ. Parinibbutaṃ saupādisesanibbānavasena. Ṭhitattanti avaṭṭhitacittaṃ lokadhammehi akampaneyyatāya. Nikkhamma gharā panujja kāmeti vatthukāme panūditvā gharāvāsā nikkhamma. Kathaṃ bhikkhu sammā so loke paribbajeyyāti so bhikkhu kathaṃ sammā paribbajeyya gaccheyya vihareyya, anupalitto hutvā lokaṃ atikkameyyāti attho.

‘I ask in verse’: the created Buddha sought permission to question the Blessed One. ‘The Sage’: the Buddha-sage. ‘Abundant in wisdom’: greatly wise. ‘Crossed over’: having crossed the four floods. ‘Gone beyond’: attained to Nibbāna, or gone to the far shore, the limit of all that is to be known. ‘Fully extinguished’: by way of the Nibbāna with residue remaining. ‘Steadfast’: with a mind established, unshaken by worldly conditions. ‘Having left home, rejecting sensual pleasures’: having abandoned material sensual pleasures and gone forth from the household life. ‘How, monk, should one rightly wander in the world?’: how should that monk rightly wander, go, or dwell, being unstained, transcending the world—this is the meaning.

334. Silokaṃ [P 2.0303] anukassāmīti [M 2.0239] ettha siloko nāma pādasamudayo, isīhi vuccamānā gāthātipi vuccati. Pādova niyatavaṇṇānupubbikānaṃ padānaṃ samūho, taṃ silokaṃ anukassāmi pavattayissāmīti atthoti āha “akkhara…pe… pavattayissāmī”ti. Yatthāti adhikaraṇe bhummaṃ. Āmeḍitalopenāyaṃ niddesoti āha “yesu yesu ṭhānesū”ti. Bhummāti bhūmipaṭibaddhanivāsā. Taṃ taṃ nissitā taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ nissitavanto nissāya vasamānā, tehi saddhiṃ silokaṃ anukassāmīti adhippāyo. “Ye sitā girigabbhara”nti iminā tesaṃ vivekavāsaṃ dasseti, “pahitattā samāhitā”ti iminā bhāvanābhiyogaṃ.

334. ‘I will recite a verse’: here, ‘verse’ refers to a collection of lines, also called a ‘stanza’ as spoken by the sages. A line is a group of words in a fixed sequence of syllables, and that verse I will recite and proclaim—this is the meaning, as he said: ‘I will proclaim... the syllables.’ ‘Where’: is in the locative case, indicating a basis. This is an explanation by means of elided reduplication: ‘in whatever places.’ ‘On the ground’: means dwellings connected to the earth. Dependent on that, relying on that place, living in dependence—this is the intent of ‘together with them, I will recite a verse.’ ‘Those who dwell in mountain caves’: this shows their solitary dwelling. ‘With resolute minds, composed’: this indicates their application to meditation.

Bahujanā pañcasatasaṅkhyattā. Paṭipakkhābhibhavanato, tejussadatāya ca sīhā viya pavivittatāya nilīnā. Ekattanti ekībhāvaṃ. Odātacittā hutvā suddhāti arahattamaggādhigamena pariyodātacittā hutvā suddhā, na kevalaṃ sarīrasuddhiyāva. Vippasannāti ariyamaggappasādena visesato pasannā. Cittassa āvilabhāvakarānaṃ kilesānaṃ abhāvena anāvilā.

The multitude numbered five hundred. Due to overcoming adversaries and their majesty, they were hidden like lions in seclusion. 'Unity' means oneness. Having pure minds, they became stainless—purified through the attainment of the path to Arahantship, not merely through bodily purity. 'Serene' means especially clear through the clarity of the noble path. Their minds were unclouded, without the defilements that cause turbidity of mind.

Bhikkhū jānitvāti bhinnakilese bhikkhū “ime dibbacakkhunā ete devakāye passantīti jānitvā. Savanante jātattāti dhammassavanapariyosāne ariyajātiyā jātattā. Idaṃ sabbanti idaṃ “bhiyyo pañcasate”tiādikaṃ sabbaṃ.

The monks, knowing—having broken their defilements—understood, 'These see these divine beings with the divine eye.' 'Born at the end of hearing' means born into the noble lineage at the conclusion of the Dhamma hearing. 'All this' refers to everything, such as 'more than five hundred,' etc.

Tadatthāya vīriyaṃ kariṃsūti dibbacakkhuñāṇābhinīhāravasena vīriyaṃ ussāhaṃ akaṃsu. Tenāha “na taṃ tehī”tiādi. Sattarinti ta-kārassa ra-kārādesaṃ katvā vuttaṃ, sattatinti attho. “Sahassa”nti pana anuvattati, sattatiyogena bahuvacanaṃ. Tenāha “eke sahassaṃ. Eke sattatisahassānī”ti.

'For that purpose, they exerted energy' means they made an effort, an exertion, by way of aspiration for the knowledge of the divine eye. Therefore, it is said, 'Not by them,' etc. 'Seventy' is said by substituting the letter 'ra' for the letter 'ta,' the meaning being seventy. 'Thousand,' however, is carried over; the plural is used in conjunction with seventy. Hence, it is said, 'Some, a thousand; some, seventy thousand.'

Anantanti antarahitaṃ, taṃ pana ativiya mahantaṃ nāma hotīti āha “vipula”nti.

'Boundless' means without interval; and because it is indeed exceedingly vast, it is called 'extensive.'

Avekkhitvāti [P 2.0304][V 2.0222] ñāṇacakkhunā visuṃ visuṃ avekkhitvā “vavatthitvānā”tipi paṭhanti, so evattho. Taṃ avekkhanaṃ nicchayakaraṇaṃ hotīti āha “vavatthapetvā”ti. Pubbe vuttagāthāsu tatiyagāthāya pacchimaddhaṃ, catutthagāthāya purimaddhañca sandhāyāha “pubbe vuttagāthamevā”ti.

'Having discerned' means having examined individually with the eye of knowledge. Some also read 'vavatthitvānā,' which has the same meaning. Because that discernment is a determination, it is said, 'having determined.' Referring to the latter half of the third verse and the first half of the fourth verse among the previously stated verses, it is said, 'the previously stated verse only.'

Vijānanampi [M 2.0240] dassanaṃ evāti āha “passatha olokethā”ti. Vācāyatapavattitabhāvato “anupaṭipāṭiyāva kittayissāmī”ti vadati.

'Knowing is also seeing'—hence it is said, 'see, look.' Because of the nature of speech proceeding sequentially, he says, 'I will proclaim it in due order.'

335. Satta sahassāni saṅkhāyāti satta sahassā. Yakkhāyevāti yakkhajātikā eva. Ānubhāvasampannāti mahesakkhā. Iddhimantoti vā mahānubhāvā. Jutimantoti mahappabhā. Vaṇṇavantoti atikkantavaṇṇā. Yasassinoti mahāparivārā ceva patthaṭakittisaddā ca. Samiti-saddo samīpatthoti adhippāyenāha “bhikkhūnaṃ santika”nti.

335. 'Numbering seven thousand' means seven thousand. 'Indeed yakkhas' means only of the yaksha kind. 'Endowed with power' means greatly mighty. 'Possessing psychic power' means or of great power. 'Radiant' means of great splendor. 'Beautiful' means of surpassing beauty. 'Famous' means with great retinues and widespread fame. The word 'assembly' has the meaning of nearness—hence it is said, 'near the monks.'

Hemavatapabbateti himavato samīpe ṭhitapabbate.

'On Hemavata Mountain' means on a mountain standing near the Himavata.

Ete sabbepīti ete sattasahassā kāpilavatthavā, chasahassā hemavatā, tisahassā sātāgirāti yathāvuttā sabbepi soḷasasahassā.

'All these' means these seven thousand from Kapilavatthu, six thousand from Hemavata, and three thousand from Sātāgira—as stated, all sixteen thousand.

Rājagahanagareti rājagahanagarassa samīpe. Tanti kumbhīraṃ.

'In the city of Rājagaha' means near the city of Rājagaha. That one is Kumbhīra.

336. Kāmaṃ pācīnadisaṃ pasāsati, tathāpi catūsupi disāsu saparivāradīpesu catūsupi mahādīpesu gandhabbānaṃ jeṭṭhako, kathaṃ? Sabbe te tassa vase vattanti. Kumbhaṇḍānaṃ adhipatītiādīsupi eseva nayo.

336. Though he rules over the eastern direction, he is nevertheless the chief of the Gandhabbas in all four directions, in the surrounding islands, and in the four great continents. How so? All of them are under his control. The same principle applies to being the lord of the Kumbhaṇḍas, and so on.

Tassāpi viruḷhassa. Tādisāyevāti dhataraṭṭhassa puttasadisā eva puthutthato, nāmato, balato, iddhiādivisesato ca.

Of that Virūḷha also. 'Just like that' means they are just like the sons of Dhataraṭṭha in terms of abundance, name, strength, and special qualities such as psychic power.

Sabbasaṅgāhikavasenāti dasasahassilokadhātuyā paccekaṃ cattāro [P 2.0305] cattāro mahārājānoti tesaṃ sabbesaṃ saṅgaṇhanavasena. Tenāha “ayañcetthā”tiādi.

'By way of all-inclusiveness' means by way of including all of them, that is, the four Great Kings in each of the ten-thousandfold world-systems. Therefore, it was said, 'And this one here...' and so on.

Caturo disāti catūsu disāsu. Caturo disā jalamānā samujjalantā obhāsentā. Yadi [V 2.0223] evaṃ mahatiyā parisāya āgatānaṃ kathaṃ kāpilavatthave vane ṭhitāti āha “te panā”tiādi.

'The four directions' means in the four directions. [They were] blazing, shining brightly, and illuminating the four directions. If such a great assembly has arrived, how could they stand in the Kāpilavatthu grove? He explains this by saying, 'But they…' and so on.

337. Tesaṃ mahārājānaṃ dāsāti yojanā. Māyāya yuttā, tasmā māyāvino. Vañcanaṃ etesu atthi, vañcane vā niyuttāti vañcanikā. Kerāṭiyasāṭheyyenāti nihīnasaṭhena kammena. Māyā etesaṃ atthīti [M 2.0241] māyā, te ca paresaṃ vañcanatthaṃ yena māyākaraṇena “māyā”ti vuttā, taṃ dassento “māyākārakā”ti āha.

337. The meaning is: they are the attendants of the Great Kings. They are endowed with deceit, therefore they are Māyāvins. Deception exists in them, or they are engaged in deception, therefore they are deceivers. 'With Kerāṭiya craftiness' means through base and crafty actions. They possess deceit (māyā), thus they are called Māyā. And showing that it is by the practice of deceit for the purpose of deceiving others that they are called Māyā, he said 'illusion-makers.'

Ettakā dāsāti ettakā kuṭeṇḍuādikā nighaṇḍupariyosānā aṭṭhamahārājānaṃ dāsā.

'So many attendants' means these, beginning with Kuṭeṇḍu and ending with Nighaṇḍu, were attendants of the eight Great Kings.

Devarājānoti devā hutvā taṃtaṃdevakāyassa rājāno. Citto ca seno ca cittaseno cāti tayo ete devaputtā pāḷiyaṃ ekasesanayena vuttāti āha “citto cā”tiādi.

'Deva kings' means having become devas, they are kings of their respective deva groups. Citta, Sena, and Cittasena—these three devaputtas are mentioned in the Pāli by the method of ekasesa. Hence it is said, 'Citta and…' and so on.

Bhikkhusaṅgho samito sannipatito etthāti bhikkhusaṅghasamiti, imaṃ vanaṃ.

Because the Bhikkhu Saṅgha is assembled and gathered together here, this forest is a 'Bhikkhu Saṅgha assembly.'

338. Nāgasadahavāsikāti nāgasadahanivāsino. Tattheko kira nāgarājā, cirakālaṃ vasato tassa parisā mahatī paramparāgatā atthi, taṃ sandhāyāha “tacchakanāgaparisāyā”ti.

338. 'The Nāgas dwelling in Nāgasadaha' means those residing in Nāgasadaha. There, it is said, was a Nāga king. Because he had lived for a long time, his retinue was vast and inherited through generations. Referring to that, he said, 'Of the Tacchaka Nāga's retinue…'

Yamunavāsinoti yamunāyaṃ vasanakanāgā. Nāgavohārenāti hatthināgavohārena.

'The Yamuna-dwellers' means Nāgas dwelling in the Yamuna. 'By Nāga designation' means by the designation of elephant-Nāgas.

Vuttappakāreti kambalassatare ṭhapetvā itare vuttappakāranāgā. Lobhābhibhūtāti āhāralobhena abhibhūtā. Dibbānubhāvatāti dibbānubhāvato, dibbānubhāvahetu vā dibbā. “Citrasupaṇṇā”ti nāmaṃ vicitrasundarapattavantatāya.

'Of the type described' means, having set aside Kambala and Assatara, the other Nāgas are of the type described. 'Overcome by greed' means overcome by greed for food. 'By divine power' means from divine power, or divine by reason of divine power. The name 'Citrasupaṇṇā' is due to having beautifully variegated wings.

Upavhayantāti [P 2.0306] upecca kathentā. Kākolūkaahinakulādayo viya aññamaññaṃ jātisamudāgataverāpi samānā mittā viya…pe… haṭṭhatuṭṭhacittā aññamaññasminti adhippāyo. Buddhaṃyeva te saraṇaṃ gatā “buddhānubhāveneva mayaṃ aññamaññasmiṃ mettiṃ paṭilabhimhā”ti.

'Approaching and conversing' means approaching and speaking. Like crows and owls, snakes and mongooses, and others, although naturally hostile to one another, they are like friends… with joyful and uplifted minds towards one another—this is the meaning. They have gone to the Buddha alone for refuge, thinking, 'It is only by the Buddha's power that we have obtained mutual goodwill.'

339. Bhātaroti methunabhātaro. Tenāha “sujāya asurakaññāya kāraṇā”ti.

339. 'Brothers' means brothers-in-law. Therefore, it is said, 'because of Sujā, the Asura maiden.'

Tesūti [V 2.0224] asuresu. Kālakañcāti evaṃ nāmā. Mahābhismāti bhiṃsanakamahāsarīrā. Abhabbāti sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamituṃ na bhabbā acchandikattā tādisassa chandasseva abhāvato.

'Among them' means among the Asuras. 'Kālakañcā' means so-named. 'Greatly terrible' means having terrifying and massive bodies. 'Incapable' means incapable of entering the fixed course of rightness, due to a lack of desire, because of the very absence of such a desire.

Balino [M 2.0242] mahāasurassa abbhatītattā tassa putte eva kittento bhagavā “satañca baliputtāna”nti ādimāha. So kira sukhumaṃ attabhāvaṃ māpetvā upagacchi.

Since the great Asura Bali had passed away, the Blessed One, praising only his sons, began with 'and the hundred sons of Bali.' It is said that he approached after creating a subtle body.

340. Kammaṃ katvāti parikammaṃ katvā. Nibbattāti upacārajjhānena nibbattā. Appanājhānena pana nibbattā brahmāno honti, te parato vakkhati “subrahmā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.341), ayañca kāmāvacaradevatā vuccati. Tenevāha – “mettākaruṇākāyikāti mettājhāne ca karuṇājhāne ca parikammaṃ katvā nibbattadevā”ti. Mettājhāne karuṇājhāneti mettājhānanimittaṃ karuṇājhānanimittaṃ, tadatthanti attho.

340. 'Having done an action' means having done the preliminary work. 'Arisen' means arisen through access concentration. But those who have arisen through absorption concentration become Brahmās; they will be spoken of later with 'Subrahmā,' etc. (Dī. Ni. 2.341), and this one is called a sense-sphere deity. Therefore, he said: 'Those of the loving-kindness and compassion group' means deities who have arisen after doing the preliminary work on loving-kindness meditation and compassion meditation. 'In loving-kindness meditation and in compassion meditation' means for the sake of the object of loving-kindness meditation and the object of compassion meditation; this is the meaning.

Te āpodevādayo yathāsakaṃ vaggavasena ṭhitattā dasadhā ṭhitā. Yāva karuṇākāyikā dasa devakāyā. Nānattavaṇṇāti nānāsabhāvavaṇṇavanto.

These deities, beginning with the water deities, being established according to their respective groups, are established in ten ways. Up to the compassion group, there are ten deva groups. 'Of diverse appearances' means possessing complexions of diverse natures.

Veṇḍudevatāti veṇḍu nāma devatā, evaṃ sahali devatā. Asamadevatā, yamakadevatāti “dve ayaniyo”ti vadanti, tappamukhā dve devanikāyāti. Candassūpanisā devā candassa upanissayato vattamānā tassa purato ca pacchato ca passato ca dhāvanakadevā. Tenāha “candanissitakā devā”ti. Sūriyassūpanisā, nakkhattanissitāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Kevalaṃ vātavāyanahetavo devatā vātavalāhakā. Tathā kevalaṃ abbhapaṭalasañcaraṇahetavo abbhavalāhakā. Uṇhappavattihetavo [P 2.0307] uṇhavalāhakā. Vassavalāhakā pana pajjunnasadisāti. Te idha na vuttā. Vasudevatā nāma eko devanikāyo, tesaṃ pubbaṅgamattā vāsavo, sakko.

'Veṇḍu deities' means deities named Veṇḍu; likewise, the Sahali deities. The Asama deities and the Yamaka deities are called 'those with two paths,' referring to two classes of deities headed by them. 'Deities attendant on the moon' are those who exist in dependence on the moon, running before, behind, and beside it. Therefore, it is said, 'Deities supported by the moon.' The same method applies to 'deities attendant on the sun' and 'deities supported by the stars.' Deities who are solely the cause for the blowing of wind are the wind-cloud deities. Likewise, those who are solely the cause for the movement of cloud-masses are the cloud-mass deities. Those who are the cause for the arising of heat are the heat-cloud deities. The rain-cloud deities, however, are like Pajjunna; they are not mentioned here. 'Vasudevatā' is a class of deities, of whom Vāsava, that is, Sakka, is the foremost.

Daseteti ete veṇḍudevatādayo vāsavapariyosānā dasa devakāyā.

'These ten' refers to these ten classes of deities, beginning with the Veṇḍu deities and ending with Vāsava.

Imānīti “jalamaggī”ti ca “sikhārivā”ti ca imāni tesaṃ nāmāni. Keci pana ma-kāro padasandhikaro “jalā”ti ca “aggī”ti ca “sikhārivā”ti ca imāni tesaṃ nāmānīti vadanti. Eteti tesu eva “ariṭṭhakā, rojā”ti ca vuttadevesu ekacce,umāpupphanibhāsino [V 2.0225] vaṇṇato umāpupphasadisāti evamattho gahetabbo, aññathā ekādasa devakāyā siyuṃ.

'These' means 'Jalamaggī' and 'Sikhārivā'; these are their names. Some, however, say that the letter 'm' is a euphonic connective, making 'Jalā,' 'Aggī,' and 'Sikhārivā' their names. 'These' refers to some among those deities already mentioned, namely 'Ariṭṭhakā' and 'Rojā.' 'Those whose complexion is like an umā flower' means they are similar in color to an umā flower; this is how the meaning should be understood, for otherwise there would be eleven classes of deities.

Daseteti [M 2.0243] ete dasa sahabhūdevādayo vāsavanesipariyosānā dasa devakāyā. Teneva nikāyabhedavasena dasadhāva āgatā.

'These ten' refers to these ten classes of deities, beginning with the Sahabhū deities and ending with the Vāsavanesī deities. Thus, according to the division of their classes, they are presented as tenfold.

“Samānā”tiādi tesaṃ devānaṃ nikāyasamudāyagataṃ nāmaṃ. Evaṃ sesānampi.

'Samānā,' etc., is the collective name for that group of deities. The same applies to the others.

Daseteti ete samānādikā mahāpāragapariyosānā dasa devakāyā. Teneva nikāyabhedena dasadhā āgatā.

'These ten' refers to these ten classes of deities, beginning with the Samāna and ending with the Mahāpāraga. Thus, according to that division of classes, they are presented as tenfold.

Sukkādayo tayo devakāyā. Pāmokkhadevāti pamukhā padhānabhūtā devā.

The three classes of deities beginning with the Sukkā. 'Pāmokkha deities' means foremost, principal deities.

Disāti disāsu. Devoti megho. Daseteti ete sukkādayo pajjunnapariyosānā dasa devakāyā, te devanikāyabhedena dasadhā āgatā.

'Disā' means 'in the directions.' 'Devo' means 'a cloud.' 'These ten' refers to these ten classes of deities, beginning with the Sukkā and ending with Pajjunna; they are presented as tenfold according to the division of their deva classes.

Daseteti ete khemiyādayo paranimmitapariyosānā dasa devakāyā, te devanikāyabhedena dasadhāva āgatā. Tattha “khemiyā, kaṭṭhakādayo ca pañcāpi sadevakāyā tāvatiṃsakāyikā”ti vadanti. Nāmanvayenāti [P 2.0308] nāmānugamena “āpodevatā”tiādināmasabhāgena. Tenevāha “nāmabhāgena nāmakoṭṭhāsenā”ti. Sabbā devatāti dasasahassilokadhātūsu sabbāpi devatā. Niddisati taṃtaṃnāmasabhāgena ekajjhaṃ katvā.

'These ten' refers to these ten classes of deities, beginning with the Khemiyā and ending with the Parinimmita; they are presented as tenfold according to the division of their deva classes. Therein, they say: 'The Khemiyā, the Kaṭṭhaka and others—these five classes of deities belong to the retinue of the Tāvatiṃsa.' 'By name' means by following the name, by the category of name such as 'water deities.' Therefore it is said, 'by the category of name, by the division of name.' 'All deities' means all the deities in the ten-thousand-world system. He indicates them, having grouped them together according to their respective name-categories.

Pavutthāti pavāsaṃ gatā viya apetāti āha “vigatā”ti. Pavutthā vā pakārato vutthā vusitā, tena jāti vusitabbā assāti pavuṭṭhajāti. Kāḷakabhāvā saṃkilesadhammā, sabbaso tadabhāvato kāḷakabhāvātītaṃ dasabalaṃ. Lañcanābhāvena vā asitātigo kāḷakabhāvātītāya siriyā cando, tādisaṃ candaṃ viya siriyā virocamānaṃ.

'Pavutthā' means gone away, as if gone abroad; hence it is said 'vigatā' (departed). Or, 'pavutthā' means having lived out in a special way; hence 'pavuṭṭhajāti' means one for whom the round of birth has been lived out. 'The state of darkness' refers to defiling states. Because he is entirely without them, the Ten-Powered One has transcended the state of darkness. Or, like the moon which, through its freedom from spots and having gone beyond darkness, transcends the state of darkness with its splendor, so too he shines with splendor.

341. Eko brahmāti sagāthakavagge (saṃ. ni. 1.98) āgato subrahmadevaputto. Brahmaloke nibbattitvā heṭṭhimesu patiṭṭhitā ariyabrahmāno, na [M 2.0244] suddhāvāsabrahmāno. Tissamahābrahmā puthujjano, yo aparabhāge manussesu nibbattitvā moggaliputtatissatthero jāto.

341. 'One Brahmā' refers to the devaputta Subrahmā who appears in the Sagāthakavagga (SN 1.98). The noble Brahmās are those who, having been reborn in the Brahmā world, are established in the lower Brahmā worlds; they are not the Suddhāvāsa Brahmās. Tissa Mahābrahmā was a worldling, who was later reborn among humans and became the elder Moggaliputtatissa.

Sahassaṃ [V 2.0226] brahmalokānanti brahmaloko etesanti brahmalokā, brahmāno, tesaṃ brahmalokānaṃ sahassaṃ sattalokapariyāyo cāyaṃ lokasaddoti āha “mahābrahmānaṃ sahassaṃ āgata”nti. Anantaragāthāyaṃ “āgatā”ti vuttapadameva atthavasena vadati. Yatthāti yasmiṃ brahmasahasse. Aññe brahmeti tadaññe brahmāno. Abhibhavitvā tiṭṭhati vaṇṇena, yasasā āyunā ca.

'A thousand of Brahmā worlds': those who have a Brahmā world are 'Brahmā-worlds,' that is, Brahmās. A thousand of these 'Brahmā-worlds.' And this word 'loka' is a term for the world of beings. Therefore, it is said, 'a thousand Great Brahmās have come.' In the following verse, he states the word 'āgatā' (have come) according to its meaning. 'Where' means 'in which thousand of Brahmās.' 'Other Brahmās' means Brahmās other than him. He stands surpassing them in complexion, glory, and lifespan.

Issarāti teneva vasapavattanena sesabrahmānaṃ adhipatino.

'Issarā' means lords, masters of the remaining Brahmās, by that very wielding of power.

342. Kāḷakadhammasamannāgato kāḷakassa pāpimassa mārassa bālabhāvaṃ passatha, yo attano avisaye niratthakaṃ parakkamituṃ vāyamati.

342. Behold the foolishness of the dark one, the evil Māra, who strives uselessly to exert himself in a domain that is not his.

Vītarāgabhāvāvahassa dhammassavanassa antarāyakaraṇena [P 2.0309] avītarāgā rāgena baddhā eva nāma hontīti vuttaṃ “rāgena baddhaṃ hotū”ti.

By creating an obstacle to the hearing of the Dhamma, which brings about the state of freedom from passion, those who are not free from passion are indeed bound by passion. Thus it is said, 'May they be bound by passion.'

Bhayānakaṃ sarañca katvāti bheravaṃ mahantaṃ saddaṃ samuṭṭhapetvā.

'And having made a terrifying sound' means having produced a dreadful, loud noise.

Idāni taṃ saddaṃ upamāya dassento “yathā”ti ādimāha. Kañcīti tasmiṃ samāgame kañci devataṃ, mānusakaṃ vā attano vase vattetuṃ asakkonto asayaṃvase sayañca na attano vase ṭhito. Tenāha “asayaṃvasī”tiādi.

Now, illustrating that sound with a simile, he begins with 'yathā' (just as). 'Any' means any deity or human in that assembly. Being unable to bring another under his control, he himself was not self-controlled and not established in his own power. Hence it is said, 'asayaṃvasī' (not self-controlled), etc.

343. “Vītarāgehī”ti desanāsīsametaṃ. Sabbāyapi hi tattha samāgataparisāya mārasenā apakkantāva. Nesaṃ lomampi iñjayuṃ tesaṃ lomamattampi na cālesuṃ, kuto antarāyakaraṇaṃ. Iti yattakā tattha visesaṃ adhigacchiṃsu, tesaṃ sabbesampi antarāyākaraṇavasena attho vibhāvetabbo, vītarāgaggahaṇena vā sarāgavītarāgavibhāvino ca tattha saṅgahitāti veditabbaṃ. Māro imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi acchariyabbhutacittajāto. Kathañhi nāma tāva ghorataraṃ mahatiṃ vibhiṃsakaṃ mayi karontepi sabbe pime nibbikārā samāhitā eva. Kasmā? Vijitāvino ime uttamapurisāti. Tenāha “sabbe”tiādi. Yādiso ariyānaṃ dhammanissito [M 2.0245] pamodo, na kadāci tādiso anariyānaṃ hotīti “sāsane bhūtehi ariyehi” iccetaṃ vuttaṃ. Vi-saddena vinā kevalopi suta-saddo vikhyātatthavacano hoti “sutadhammassā”tiādīsu (mahāva. 5; udā. 11) viyāti āha “jane vissutā”ti.

343. 'By those free from passion' is the heading of the teaching. Indeed, Māra's army had already departed from the entire assembled gathering there. They did not stir even a hair of theirs; they did not move so much as a hair of theirs—how much less could they cause any hindrance? Thus, the meaning should be interpreted for all of them, in terms of not causing a hindrance to however many attained a special distinction there. Or, by the inclusion of 'free from passion,' it should be understood that both those with passion and those free from passion are included there. Māra spoke this verse with a mind filled with wonder and astonishment: 'How is it that even while I create such a terrifying and dreadful display, all these remain undisturbed and composed? Why? Because these supreme men are victors.' Hence it is said, 'all,' etc. The joy dependent on the Dhamma of the noble ones is never found in the ignoble. Thus it is said, 'by the noble ones who have come to be in the Dispensation.' The word 'suta-' itself, even without the prefix 'vi-,' can signify 'renowned,' as in 'sutadhammassā,' etc. Therefore it is said, 'renowned among people'.

Dūreti [V 2.0227] dūre padese. Daharassa antarāyaṃ pariharantī “na sakkā bhante sakalaṃ kāyaṃ dassetu”nti avocāti.

'Dūre' means 'in a distant place.' Protecting the young one from danger, she said, "Venerable sir, it is not possible to show the entire body."

Mahāsamayasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Mahāsamaya Sutta.

8. Sakkapañhasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Sakkapañha Sutta

Nidānavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Introduction

344. Ambasaṇḍānaṃ [P 2.0310][V 2.0228][M 2.0246] adūrabhavattā ekopi so brāhmaṇagāmo “ambasaṇḍā”tveva bahuvacanavasena vuccati, yathā “varaṇā nagara”nti. Vedi eva vediko, vediko eva vediyo ka-kārassa ya-kāraṃ katvā, tasmiṃ vediyake. Tenāha “maṇivedikāsadisenā”tiādi, indanīlādimaṇimayavedikāsadisenāti attho. Pubbepīti leṇakaraṇato pubbe, guhārūpena ṭhitā, dvāre indasālarukkhavatī ca, tasmā “indasālaguhā”ti vuttā purimavohārena.

344. Due to its proximity to Ambasaṇḍa, that single brahmin village is referred to in the plural as 'Ambasaṇḍā,' just as 'Varaṇā nagara' is. 'Vedi' is the same as 'vedika,' and 'vedika' is the same as 'vediya,' by changing the letter 'ka' to 'ya'; thus 'on the vediyaka.' Therefore it is said, 'like a jeweled railing,' etc., the meaning being, 'resembling a railing made of gems such as sapphire.' 'Formerly' means before it was made into a dwelling-cave; it existed in the form of a grotto and had an Indasāla tree at its entrance. Therefore, by former convention, it was called 'Indasāla Cave'.

Ussukkaṃ vuccati abhiruci, taṃ pana buddhadassanakāmatāvasena, tathā ussāhanavasena ca pavattiyā “dhammiko ussāho”ti vuttaṃ. Sakkena sadiso…pe… natthīti. Yathāha “appamādena maghavā, devānaṃ seṭṭhataṃ gato”ti (dha. pa. 30). Parittakenāti aparāparaṃ bahuṃ puññakammaṃ akatvā appamattakeneva puññakammena.

"Ussukkaṃ" is called 'delight' or 'eagerness'. That, however, is said to be "dhammiko ussāho" (righteous eagerness) because it arises from the desire to see the Buddha and from exertion of effort. "Sakkena sadiso…pe… natthi" (there is none like Sakka). As it is said: "Through heedfulness, Maghavā attained the chief state among the devas" (Dhp. 30). "Parittakena" means 'by only a trifling act of merit', without having repeatedly done much meritorious action.

Sakkopi kāmaṃ mahāpuññakatabhīruttāno hoti, sātisayāya pana dibbasampattiyā viyogahetukena sokena diguṇitena maraṇabhayena [P 2.0311] saṃtajjito jāto. Tenāha “sakko pana maraṇabhayābhibhūto ahosī”ti.

Even Sakka, though greatly meritorious and uplifted, was terrified by the fear of death, intensified by sorrow due to separation from his exceeding divine prosperity. Therefore it was said, "But Sakka was overcome by the fear of death."

Dibbacakkhunā devatānaṃ dassanaṃ nāma paṭivijjhanasadisanti āha “paṭivijjhī”ti. Pāṭiyekko vohāroti āveṇiko piyasamudāhāro. Marisaniyasampattikāti mārisā. Tesañhi sampattiyo mahānubhāvatāya sahanti upaṭṭhahanti, aññe ayonisomanasikāratāya ceva appahukāya ca na sahantiyeva, sā pana nesaṃ marisaniyasampattikatā dukkhavirahitāyāti vuttaṃ “niddukkhātipi vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Ekako vāti devaparisāya vinā āgatattā vuttaṃ, mātaliādayo [V 2.0229] pana tādisā sahāyā tadāpi ahesuṃyeva. Tathā hi vakkhati “api cāyaṃ āyasmato cakkanemisaddena tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhito”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.352). Okāsaṃ nākāsi [M 2.0247] sakkassa ñāṇaparipākaṃ āgamento, aññesañca bahūnaṃ devānaṃ dhammābhisamayaṃ upaparikkhamāno. Soti sakko.

"Dibbacakkhunā devatānaṃ dassanaṃ nāma paṭivijjhanasadisanti" (seeing devas with the divine eye is like penetrating insight)—hence it is said, "paṭivijjhī" (he penetrated). "Pāṭiyekko vohāro" means a unique expression, a special and beloved phrase. "Marisaniyasampattikā" means 'O venerable one' (mārisā). Their attainments, due to great power, endure and are present; while others, due to unwise attention and being incapable, cannot endure them at all. But their state of having venerable attainments is free from suffering—hence, it is also said, "it is also spoken of as free from suffering." "Ekako vā" means he came without a retinue of devas, though at that time, companions like Mātali and others were indeed present. As it will be said: "Moreover, this venerable one arose from that concentration at the sound of Cakkanemi" (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.352). He did not make an opportunity, awaiting the maturation of Sakka’s knowledge and examining the realization of the Dhamma by many other devas. "So" refers to Sakka.

Evanti vacanasampaṭicchane nipātoti āha “evaṃ hotū”tiādi. Bhaddaṃtavāti pana sakkaṃ uddissa nesaṃ āsi vādo.

"Evanti" is a particle indicating acceptance of speech; hence, "evaṃ hotu" (so be it), etc. "Bhaddaṃtavāti," however, was their address to Sakka.

345. Vallabho…pe… dhammaṃ suṇātīti ayamattho govindasuttādīhi (dī. ni. 2.294) dīpetabbo. Iminā katokāseti iminā pañcasikhena katokāse bhagavati.

345. "Vallabho…pe… dhammaṃ suṇāti" (beloved... listens to the Dhamma)—this meaning should be explained by the Govinda Sutta and others (Dī. Ni. 2.294). "Iminā katokāse" means 'when an opportunity was made for the Blessed One by this Pañcasikha'.

Anucariyanti anucaraṇabhāvaṃ, taṃ panassa anucaraṇaṃ nāma saddhiṃ gamanamevāti āha “sahacaraṇaṃ ekato gamana”nti.

"Anucariyam" means 'the state of following'. That following, however, is simply accompanying. Therefore it is said, "sahacaraṇaṃ ekato gamana" (accompanying, going together).

Sovaṇṇamayanti [P 2.0312] suvaṇṇamayaṃ. Pokkharanti vīṇāya doṇimāha. Daṇḍoti vīṇadaṇḍo. Veṭhakāti tantīnaṃ bandhanāya ceva uppīḷanāya ca dhametabbā veṭhakā. Pattakanti pokkharaṃ. Samapaññāsamucchanā mucchetvāti yathā samapaññāsamucchanā kamato tattha saṃmucchanaṃ kātuṃ sakkā, evaṃ taṃ sajjetvāti attho. “Samapaññāsamucchanā saṃmucchetvā”ti ca idaṃ devaloke niyataṃ vīṇāvādanavidhiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Manussaloke pana ekavīsati mucchanā. Tenevāha vīṇopamasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ –

"Sovaṇṇamayaṃ" means 'golden', made of gold. "Pokkhara" means the resonator of the lute. "Daṇḍo" means the neck of the lute. "Veṭhakā" are the tuning pegs that are to be turned for securing and tightening the strings. "Pattaka" is the resonator. "Samapaññāsamucchanā mucchetvā" means 'having tuned the fifty modes'—meaning that just as it is possible to arrange the fifty modes there in sequence, so it should be tuned. And this "Samapaññāsamucchanā saṃmucchetvā" (having tuned the fifty modes) is said with reference to the fixed method of lute-playing in the deva-world.
