In the human world, however, there are twenty-one modes. Therefore, it is said in the commentary on the Lute Simile Sutta:

“Satta sarā tayo gāmā, mucchanā ekavīsati;

Tānā cekūnapaññāsa, iccete saramaṇḍalā”ti. (a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.55; sārattha. ṭī. 3.243);

"Seven notes, three scales, twenty-one modulations; And forty-nine tones: these are the circle of notes."

Tattha chajjo, usabho, gandhāro, majjhimo, pañcamo, dhevato, nisādoti ete satta sarā. Chajjagāmo, majjhimagāmo, sādhāraṇagāmoti tayo gāmā, sarasamūhāti attho. Manussaloke vādanavidhinā ekekasseva ca sarassa vasena tayo tayo mucchanā katvā ekavīsati mucchanā. Ekekasseva ca sarassa satta satta tānabhedā, yato sarassa mandataravavatthānaṃ hoti, te ekūnapaññāsa tānavisesāti, tisso duve catasso, catasso tisso duve catassoti dvāvīsati sutibhedā [V 2.0230] icchitā, ayaṃ pana ekekassa sarassa vasena satta satta mucchanā, antarasarassa ca ekāti samapaññāsāya mucchanānaṃ yogyabhāvena vīṇaṃ vajjesi. Tena vuttaṃ “samapaññāsa [M 2.0248] mucchanā saṃmucchetvā”ti. Sesadeve jānāpento sakkassa gamanakālanti yojanā.

There are these seven notes: Chajja, Usabha, Gandhāra, Majjhima, Pañcama, Dhevata, and Nisāda. There are three scales: the Chajja scale, the Majjhima scale, and the Sādhāraṇa scale—meaning a group of notes. In the human world, according to the method of playing, for each note, three modulations are made, totaling twenty-one modulations. And for each note, there are seven kinds of tonal variations, since a note has softer and more intense positions; these are the forty-nine tonal differences. Three, two, four; four, three, two, four—these are the twenty-two microtonal differences desired. However, this one played the vīṇā with the suitability of fifty modulations: seven modulations for each note, and one intermediate note. Therefore, it is said: "Having combined fifty modulations." The construction is: 'informing the other devas about the time of Sakka's departure'.

346. Atirivāti ra-kāro padasandhikaro, atīva ativiyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Pakati [P 2.0313] …pe… agamāsi maraṇabhayasaṃtajjitattā taramānarūpo. Tenevāha “nanu cā”tiādi.

346. The letter 'ra' in 'atiriva' is a euphonic conjunction, meaning 'exceedingly' or 'very much,' that is, 'ativiya.' The usual... and so on... He departed, terrified by the fear of death, in a state of haste. Therefore, he said, "Indeed, and so on."

347. Buddhā nāma mahākāruṇikā, sadevakassa lokassa hitasukhatthāya eva uppannā, te kathaṃ atthikehi durupasaṅkamāti āha “ahaṃ sarāgo”tiādi. Tadantaraṃ paṭisallīnāti yena antarena yena khaṇena upasaṅkameyya, tadantaraṃ paṭisallīnā jhānaṃ samāpannā. Tadantara-saddo vā “etarahī”ti iminā samānatthoti āha “sampati paṭisallīnā vā”ti.

347. The Buddhas are indeed greatly compassionate, arisen solely for the welfare and happiness of the world with its deities. How then are they difficult for those in need to approach? It is said, "I am passionate," and so on. The phrase 'tadantaraṃ paṭisallīnā' means: during that interval, during that moment when one might approach, they are in seclusion, absorbed in jhāna. Or the word 'tadantara' has the same meaning as 'etarahi,' which is 'now.' Hence it is said, 'or if they are presently in seclusion.'

Pañcasikhagītagāthāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Verses of Pañcasikha's Song

348. Sāvesīti yathādhippetamucchanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā vīṇaṃ vādento taṃtaṃṭhānuppattiyā pākaṭībhūtamandatāvavatthaṃ dassento sumadhurakomalamadhupānamattamadhukāravirutāpahāsinilakkhaṇo pasannabhānī samaravaṃ tantissaraṃ sāvesi.

348. The word 'sāvesi' means that, playing the vīṇā, having set it up with the desired modulation and displaying the states of softness and intensity that became manifest through the arising of various notes, he, speaking pleasantly, made audible the harmonious sound of the strings, which had the characteristic of being very sweet and soft, surpassing the humming of bees intoxicated from drinking honey.

“Sakyaputtova jhānena, ekodi nipako sato;

Amataṃ muni jigīsāno….

"Like a son of the Sakyans, with meditation, unified, skilled, mindful; the sage, wishing to conquer the deathless..."

Yathāpi muni nandeyya, patvā sambodhiṃ uttama”nti. (dī. ni. 2.348);

Just as the sage would rejoice, having attained the supreme enlightenment.

Ca evaṃ buddhūpasañhitā. Buddhūpasañhitā pana buddhānaṃ dhammasarīraṃ ārabbha nissayaṃ katvā pavattitāti āha “dhammo arahatāṃ ivā”ti. Dhammūpasañhitā, arahattūpasañhitā ca veditabbā.

And thus, it is connected with the Buddha. However, being connected with the Buddha, it proceeds by relying on and referring to the Dhamma-body of the Buddhas; therefore, it is said, "The Dhamma is like that of the Arahants." It should be understood as connected with the Dhamma and connected with Arahantship.

Sūriyasamānasarīrāti sūriyasamānappabhāsarīrā. Tenāha “tassā kirā”tiādi. Yasmā timbaruno gandhabbadevarājassa sūriyavaccha sā [P 2.0314] aṅke jātā, tasmā āha “yaṃ timbaruṃ devarājānaṃ [V 2.0231] nissāya tvaṃ jātā”ti. Kalyāṇaṅgatāya “kalyāṇī”ti vuttāti āha “sabbaṅgasobhanā”ti.

The phrase 'sūriyasamānasarīrā' means 'possessing a body with a radiance like the sun.' Therefore, it is said: "For she, indeed..." Since she, Suriyavacchasā, was born on the lap of Timbaru, the gandhabba divine king, therefore it is said: "You were born relying on Timbaru, the divine king." Because of her possessing beautiful limbs, she is called 'kalyāṇī' (beautiful); hence it is said: 'Beautiful in all her limbs.'

Rāgāvesavasena [M 2.0249] pubbe vuttā gāthā idānipi tameva ārabbha purato ṭhitaṃ viya ālapanto vadati.

The verse previously spoken under the influence of lust now addresses the same subject, as if conversing with one standing before him.

Thanudaranti payodharañca udarañca adhippetanti āha “thanavemajjhaṃ udarañcā”ti.

The word 'thanudara' means 'breasts and belly,' referring to the breasts and the belly; hence it is said: 'The space between the breasts and the belly.'

Kiñci kāraṇanti kiñci pīḷaṃ.

The phrase 'kiñci kāraṇaṃ' means 'some affliction.'

Pakatiṃ jahitvā ṭhitaṃ abhirattabhāvena.

Standing, having abandoned her natural state, due to infatuation.

Vāmūrūti ruciraūrū. Tenāha “vāmākārenā”tiādi. Vāmavikasitarucirasundarābhirūpacārusaddā hi ekatthā daṭṭhabbā. Na tikhiṇanti na tikkhaṃ na lūkhaṃ na kakkhaḷaṃ. Mandanti mudu siniddhaṃ.

The word 'vāmūrū' means 'beautiful thighs.' Therefore, it is said, "In a charming way..." Indeed, the words 'vāma,' 'vikasita,' 'rucira,' 'sundara,' 'abhirūpa,' and 'cāru' should be understood as having the same meaning. The phrase 'na tikhiṇaṃ' means 'not sharp,' that is, 'not rough' or 'not harsh.' The word 'mandaṃ' means 'soft' and 'smooth.'

Anekabhāvoti anekasabhāvo, so pana bahuvidho nāma hotīti āha “anekavidho jāto”ti. Anekabhāgoti anekakoṭṭhāso.

The word 'anekabhāvo' means 'having many natures'; however, since that is of various kinds, hence it is said: 'born of many kinds.' The word 'anekabhāgo' means 'having many sections.'

Tayā saddhiṃ vipaccatanti tayā sahitaṃyeva me taṃ kammaṃ vipaccatu, tayā saheva tassa kammassa phalaṃ anubhaveyyanti adhippāyo. Tayā saddhimevāti yathā cakkavattisaṃvattaniyakammaṃ tassa nissandaphalabhūtena itthiratanena saddhiṃyeva vipākaṃ deti, evaṃ taṃ me kammaṃ tayā saddhiṃyeva mayhaṃ vipākaṃ detu.

The phrase 'tayā saddhiṃ vipaccatu' means: 'May that kamma ripen together with you; may I experience the fruit of that kamma together with you'—this is the meaning. The phrase 'tayā saddhimeva' means: just as the kamma leading to a wheel-turning monarch yields its resultant fruit together with the treasure of a woman, so too may that kamma of mine yield its result for me together with you.

Ekodīti ekodibhāvaṃ gato, samāhitoti attho. Jigīsānoti jigīsamāno hoti. Tathābhūtova jigīsati nāmāti tathā paṭhamavikappo vutto. Dutiyavikappe pana “vicaratī”ti kiriyāpadaṃ āharitvā attho vutto.

The word 'ekodī' means 'having attained a state of one-pointedness,' that is, 'concentrated.' The word 'jigīsāno' means 'desiring victory.' Being in such a state, he desires victory—thus is the first interpretation stated. In the second interpretation, however, the meaning is explained by supplying the verb 'vicarati' ('wanders').

Nandeyyanti samāgamaṃ patthento vadati atisassirikarūpasobhāya.

The word 'nandeyya' means 'would rejoice,' spoken by one longing for union because of the surpassing loveliness of her form.

349. Saṃsandatīti [P 2.0315][V 2.0232] sameti, yāya mucchanāya, yena ca ākārena tantissaro pavatto, taṃ mucchanaṃ anativattento, teneva ca ākārena gītassaropi pavattoti attho. Yena ajjhāsayena bhagavā pañcasikhassa gandhabbe vaṇṇaṃ kathesi, yadatthañca kathesi, taṃ sabbaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “kasmā”tiādimāha. Natthi bodhimūle eva samucchinnattā. Upekkhako bhagavā anupalittabhāvato. Suvimuttacitto bhagavā chandarāgato, sabbasmā [M 2.0250] ca kilesā. Yadi evaṃ kasmā pañcasikhassa gandhabbe vaṇṇaṃ kathesīti āha “sace panā”tiādi.

349. The word 'saṃsandati' means 'it harmonizes,' meaning that the sound of the song also proceeds in the same manner, not exceeding the modulation by which and in the manner in which the sound of the lute proceeds—this is the meaning. To explain fully by what intention the Blessed One spoke in praise of Pañcasikha's music, and for what purpose he spoke, the text introduces the question, 'Why?' and so on. There is none, because it was completely cut off at the very root of awakening. The Blessed One is equanimous due to his unsullied state. The Blessed One is fully liberated in mind from sensual desire, and from all defilements. If so, why did he speak in praise of Pañcasikha's music? To this, it is said, 'But if...' and so on.

Ganthitāti sandahitā, tā pana nirantaraṃ kathiyamānā rāsikatā viya hontīti āha “piṇḍitā”ti. Vohāravacananti bhagavato, bhikkhūnañca purato vattabbaṃ upacāravacanaṃ.

The word 'ganthitā' means 'connected'; however, since those continuously spoken become like a heap, it is said 'compacted.' The phrase 'vohāravacanaṃ' refers to conventional speech, that is, the polite speech that should be addressed in the presence of the Blessed One and the bhikkhus.

Upanaccantiyāti upagantvā naccantiyā.

The word 'upanaccantiyā' means 'of one approaching and dancing.'

Sakkūpasaṅkamanavaṇṇanā

The Description of Sakka's Approach

350. “Kadā saṃyūḷhā”tiādīni vadanto paṭisammodati. Vippakārampi dasseyyāti aḍḍhakatābhinayavasena naccampi dasseyya.

350. Saying, 'When were they arrayed?' and so on, he exchanges greetings. 'He might even show discord' means he might even display dancing by means of acting like a half-courtesan.

351. “Abhivadito sakko devānamindo”tiādīnaṃ “tena kho pana samayenā”tiādīnaṃ (pārā. 16, 24) viya saṅgītikāravacanabhāve saṃsayo natthi, “evañca pana tathāgatā”ti idha pana siyā saṃsayoti “dhammasaṅgāhakattherehi ṭhapitavacana”nti vatvā itarassāpi tathābhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “sabbameta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Vuḍḍhivacanena vuttoti “sukhī hotu pañcasikha sakko devānaṃ indo”ti āsīsavādaṃ vutto. “Bhagavato pāde sirasā vandatī”ti vadanto abhivādeti nāma “sukhī hotū”ti āsīsavādassa vadāpanato. Tathā pana āsīsavādaṃ vadanto abhivadati nāma sabbakālaṃ tatheva tiṭṭhanato.

351. Regarding 'Sakka, the lord of the devas, paid homage,' and so on, there is no doubt that these are the words of the compilers, just like 'At that time,' and so on (Pārā. 16, 24). Here, however, there might be doubt about 'And thus the Tathāgatas...' Therefore, having said, 'This is a statement established by the elders who compiled the Dhamma,' then to show that the other is also of the same nature, 'all this,' and so on, is said. It is spoken as a word of blessing, namely, the benediction, 'May Pañcasikha be happy, may Sakka, the lord of the devas, be happy,' is spoken. Saying, 'He bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet,' is called 'paying homage' because it causes the utterance of the benediction 'May he be happy.' Similarly, one who utters a benediction is called 'one who pays homage' because he always remains in that state.

Uruṃ [P 2.0316] vepullaṃ dassati dakkhatīti urundā vibhattialopena. Vivaṭā aṅgaṇaṭṭhānaṃ. Yo pakatiyā guhāyaṃ andhakāro, so antarahitoti yo tassaṃ guhāyaṃ satthu samantato asītihatthato ayaṃ pākatiko andhakāro, so devānaṃ vatthābharaṇasarīrobhāsehi antarahito, āloko sampajji. Asītihatthe pana buddhālokeneva andhakāro antarahito, na ca samattho devānaṃ obhāso buddhānaṃ abhibhavituṃ.

The word 'urundā' means 'one will see a great expanse,' with the elision of a case ending. The open space is like a courtyard. The darkness which is naturally in the cave—that is, the natural darkness in that cave for eighty cubits around the Teacher—was dispelled by the radiance of the devas' garments, ornaments, and bodies, and light arose. But within those eighty cubits, the darkness was dispelled by the Buddha's light alone, and the radiance of the devas is not capable of overpowering the Buddha's light.

352. Cirappaṭikāhanti [V 2.0233] cirappabhutiko ahaṃ. Aḍḍakaraṇaṃ nāma natthi avivādādhikaraṇaṭṭhāne nibbattattā. Kīḷādīnipīti ādi-saddena dhammassavanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

352. 'Cirappaṭikāhaṃ' means 'I am from a long time ago.' There is no such thing as partiality, because I was born in a place free from disputes. In 'Play, etc.,' the word 'etc.' includes listening to the Dhamma, and so on.

Salaḷamayagandhakuṭiyanti [M 2.0251] salaḷarukkhehi raññā pasenadinā kāritagandhakuṭiyaṃ. Tenassāti tena phaladvayādhigamena pahīnaoḷārikakāmarāgatāya assā bhūjatiyā devaloke abhiratiyeva natthi. Cakkanemisaddena tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhitoti ettha adhippāyaṃ ajānantā “ārammaṇassa adhimattatāya samāpattito vuṭṭhānaṃ jāta”nti maññeyyunti taṃ paṭikkhipanto “samāpanno saddaṃ suṇātīti no vata re vattabbe”ti āha. Sati ca ārammaṇasaṅghaṭṭanāyaṃ gahaṇenapi bhavitabbanti adhippāyena “suṇātī”ti vuttaṃ, itaro “paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa saddo kaṇṭako”ti vacanamattaṃ nissāya sabbassāpi jhānassa saddo kaṇṭakoti adhippāyena paṭikkhepaṃ asahanto “nanu bhagavā…pe… [P 2.0317] bhaṇatī”ti imameva suttapadaṃ uddhari. Tattha yathā dosadassanapaṭipakkhabhāvanāvasena paṭighasaññānaṃ suppahīnattā mahatāpi saddena arūpasamāpattito na vuṭṭhānaṃ, evaṃ “uppādo bhayaṃ, anuppādo khema”ntiādinā sammadeva dosadassanapaṭipakkhabhāvanāvasena sabbāsampi lokiyasaññānaṃ aggamaggena samatikkantattā ārammaṇādhigamatāya na kadāci phalasamāpattito vuṭṭhānaṃ hotīti. Tathā pana na suppahīnattā paṭighasaññānaṃ sabbarūpasamāpattito vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, paṭhamajjhānaṃ pana appakampi saddaṃ na sahatīti taṃsamāpannassa “saddo kaṇṭako”ti vuttaṃ. Yadi pana paṭighasaññānaṃ vikkhambhitattā mahatāpi saddena arūpasamāpattito na vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, pageva maggaphalasamāpattito. Tenāha “cakkanemisaddenā”tiādi. Cakkanemisaddenāti ca nayidaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ hetumhi, karaṇe vā atha kho sahayoge. Imameva hi atthaṃ dassetuṃ “bhagavā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'In the fragrant hut made of salaḷa wood' means in the fragrant hut built by King Pasenadi with salaḷa trees. 'For her'—due to that attainment of the twofold fruit and the abandonment of gross sensual desire, there was no delight at all in the deva world for that noble lady. 'With the sound of a chariot wheel, he emerged from that concentration.' Here, not understanding the intended meaning, some might think, 'Emergence from the attainment occurred due to the excessive intensity of the object.' Refuting this, it is said, 'It should not be said, “One in attainment hears a sound.”' And with the intention that when there is an impact with an object, grasping can also occur, it is said, 'He hears.' The other, relying solely on the statement, 'For one who has attained the first jhāna, sound is a thorn,' and with the idea that sound is a thorn for every jhāna, being unable to bear the refutation, quoted this very sutta passage, 'But did not the Blessed One... etc.' Therein, just as, due to the thorough abandonment of perceptions of hostility through the development of the counterpart to seeing aversion, there is no emergence from a formless attainment even with a great sound, so too, due to having transcended all worldly perceptions by the supreme path through the correct development of the counterpart to seeing danger—as in 'arising is fear, non-arising is security'—there is never any emergence from the attainment of fruition, because its object has been attained. However, because perceptions of hostility are not thoroughly abandoned, there is emergence from all form attainments. But the first jhāna does not tolerate even a slight sound; hence for one who has attained it, it is said, 'sound is a thorn.' If, due to the suppression of perceptions of hostility, there is no emergence from a formless attainment even with a great sound, how much less so from the attainment of path and fruition. Therefore, it is said, 'with the sound of a chariot wheel,' etc. And 'with the sound of a chariot wheel' is not an instrumental case indicating cause or means, but rather indicates accompaniment. To clarify this very point, it is said, 'But the Blessed One,' etc.

Gopakavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Description of the Story of Gopaka

353. Paripūrakārinīti paripuṇṇāni, parisuddhāni ca katvā rakkhitavatī. “Itthitta”ntiādi tattha virajjanākāradassanaṃ. Dhitthibhāvaṃitthibhāvassa dhikkāro hetūti attho. Alanti paṭikkhepavacanaṃ, payojanaṃ natthīti attho. Virājetīti jigucchati. Etā sampattiyoti cakkavattisiriādikā etā yathāvuttasampattiyo. Tasmā pubbaparicayena upaṭṭhitanikantivasena. Upaṭṭhānasālanti sudhammadevasabhaṃ.

353. 'She who fulfills her duties' means having made them complete and pure, she protected them. 'Womanhood' and so on—therein is the showing of the mode of dispassion. The meaning is that the contemptible state is due to the scorn for womanhood. 'Alaṃ' is a word of rejection, meaning 'there is no purpose.' 'She detests' means she feels disgust. 'These attainments'—these are the attainments, such as the glory of a wheel-turning monarch, as described. Therefore, by way of the arising of longing due to previous familiarity. 'The assembly hall' is the Sudhammā divine assembly hall.

Soti [P 2.0318][M 2.0252][V 2.0234] gopakadevaputto. Vaṭṭetvā vaṭṭetvāti tomarādiṃ vattentena viya codanavacanaṃ parivaṭṭetvā parivaṭṭetvā. Gāḷhaṃ vijjhitabbāti gāḷhataraṃ ghaṭṭetabbā.

'He' means the devaputta Gopaka. 'Turning and turning' is like one wielding a spear or the like, repeatedly turning over the words of urging. 'Must be deeply pierced' means it must be struck even more strongly.

Kuto mukhāti kuto pavattañāṇamukhā. Tenāha “aññavihitakā”ti. Katapuññeti sammā katapuññe dhamme.

'From where the mouth?' means from where is the opening of arisen knowledge. Hence it is said, 'distracted.' 'Where merit has been done' refers to the Dhamma, where meritorious deeds have been rightly performed.

Dāyoti lābho. So hi dīyati tehi dātabbattā dāyo, yesaṃ dīyati, tehi laddhattā lābhoti ca vuccati. Saṅkhāre…pe… patiṭṭhahiṃsu katādhikārattā. Tattha tāvatiṃsabhavane ṭhitānaṃyeva nibbatto yathā sakkassa indasālaguhāyaṃ ṭhitasseva sakkattabhāvo.

'Gift' means gain. It is called 'gift' because it is to be given by those who should give it. And it is called 'gain' because it is obtained by those to whom it is given. The formations...they became established due to their having made an aspiration. There, rebirth occurs for those dwelling in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven just as the state of Sakka arises for one abiding in Sakka's Indasāla Cave.

Nikantiṃ tasmiṃ gandhabbakāye ālayaṃ samucchindituṃ na sakkonto.

Being unable to completely uproot the longing and attachment to that Gandhabba-body.

354. Attanāva veditabboti attanāva adhigantvā veditabbo, na parappaccayikena. Tumhehi vuccamānānīti kevalaṃ tumhehi vuccamānāni.

354. 'To be known by oneself' means it must be understood by oneself, having realized it oneself, not through reliance on others.

Viyāyāmāti vissaṭṭhaṃ vīriyaṃ santāne pavattema. Pakatiyāti rūpāvacarabhāvena, “anussara”nti vā pāṭho.

'We exert' means we apply released effort in the continuum. 'By nature' means by way of the form realm; alternatively, the reading is 'anussara' (recollect).

Kāmarāgo eva “chando rāgo chandarāgo”tiādi pavattibhedena saṃyojanaṭṭhena “kāmarāgasaṃyojanānī”ti, yogaganthādipavattiākārabhedena “kāmabandhanānī”ti ca vutto. Pāpimayogānīti ettha pana sesayogaganthānampi vasena attho veditabbo.

Sensual desire itself, according to its various modes of occurrence, is called 'desire, passion, desire-passion,' and so on. In the sense of a fetter, it is called 'the fetters of sensual desire'; and according to the various modes of its occurrence as yokes, knots, and so on, it is called 'the bonds of sensuality.' Here, however, in the phrase 'the yokes of the Evil One,' the meaning should be understood in terms of the remaining yokes and knots as well.

Duvidhānanti [P 2.0319] vatthukāmakilesakāmavasena duvidhānaṃ.

'Twofold' refers to the twofold division into object-sensuality and defilement-sensuality.

“Ettha kiṃ, tattha ki”nti ca padadvaye kinti nipātamattaṃ. Cātuddisabhāveti tesaṃ buddhādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ catuddisayogyabhāve appaṭihaṭabhāve. Buddharatanañhi mahākāruṇikatāya, anāvaraṇañāṇatāya, paramasantuṭṭhatāya ca cātuddisaṃ, dhammaratanaṃ svākkhātatāya, saṅgharatanaṃ suppaṭipannatāya. Tenāha “sabbadisāsu asajjamāno”ti.

In the two phrases 'What here, what there,' the word 'kiṃ' is merely a particle. 'Universal in the four directions' refers to the unimpeded nature of the three jewels—the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha—in being suitable for the four directions. For the Buddha-jewel is universal due to great compassion, unobstructed knowledge, and supreme contentment; the Dhamma-jewel, due to being well-proclaimed; and the Saṅgha-jewel, due to good practice. Hence it is said, 'unobstructed in all directions.'

Majjhimassa paṭhamajjhānassa adhigatattā tāvadeva kāyaṃ brahmapurohitaṃ adhigantvā tāvadeva purimaṃ [V 2.0235] jhānasatiṃ paṭilabhitvā taṃ jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā orambhāgiyasaṃyojanasamucchindanena maggaphalavisesaṃ anāgāmiphalasaṅkhātaṃ visesaṃ ajjhagaṃsu adhigacchiṃsu. Keci pana “kāmāvacarattabhāvena [M 2.0253] maggaphalāni adhigacchiṃsūti adhippāyena pañcamassa jhānassa anadhigatattā suddhāvāsesu na uppajjiṃsu, paṭhamajjhānalābhitāya pana brahmapurohitesu nibbattiṃsū”ti vadanti.

Due to having attained the first jhāna of the intermediate level, they immediately attained the realm of Brahmā's ministers and regained their previous jhāna-mindfulness. Making that jhāna a foundation, they developed insight and, by cutting off the lower fetters, attained the distinction of path and fruit, the distinction known as the fruit of non-returning. Some, however, say that because they attained the path and fruits with a sense-sphere existence, they were not reborn in the Pure Abodes due to not having attained the fifth jhāna; but because they were attainers of the first jhāna, they were reborn among Brahmā's ministers.

Maghamāṇavavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of the Youth Magha

355. Visuddhoti visuddhaajjhāsayo, upanissayasampannoti adhippāyo. Gāmakammakaraṇaṭṭhānanti gāmikānaṃ upaṭṭhānaṭṭhānaṃ vadati. Tāvatakenevāti attanā sodhitaṭṭhāneva aññassa āgantvā avaṭṭhāneneva. Satiṃ paṭilabhitvāti “aho mayā katakammaṃ saphalaṃ jāta”nti yoniso cittaṃ uppādetvā.

355. 'Visuddha' means one of pure intention; the meaning is 'endowed with a supporting condition.' 'Gāmakammakaraṇaṭṭhāna' refers to a place of attendance for the villagers. 'Tāvatakeneva' means merely by another coming and standing in the very place purified by oneself. 'Satiṃ paṭilabhitvā' means having wisely generated the thought, 'Oh, the deed I have done has borne fruit.'

Pāsāṇeti maggamajjhe uccatarabhāvena ṭhitapāsāṇe. Uccāletvāti uddharitvā. Etassa saggassa gamanamagganti etassa candādīnaṃ uppattiṭṭhānabhūtassa saggassa gamanamaggaṃ puññakammaṃ.

'Pāsāṇe' refers to a stone standing in the middle of the road due to its being higher. 'Uccāletvā' means having lifted it up. 'Etassa saggassa gamanamagga' refers to the path to this heaven, which is the place of origin for the moon and so on, meaning the meritorious deed.

Sugativasena laddhabbaṃ, kahāpaṇañcāti kahāpaṇaṃ, daṇḍavasena laddhabbaṃ bali daṇḍabali. Gahapatikā [P 2.0320] kiṃ karissantīti gahapatikā nāma aṭavikā viya visamanissitā, te na kañci anatthaṃ karissanti, evaṃ tayā jānamānena kasmā mayhaṃ na kathitanti yadipi pubbe na kathitaṃ, etarahi pana bhayena kathitaṃ, mā mayhaṃ dosaṃ kareyyātha, ārocitakālato paṭṭhāya na mayhaṃ dosoti vadati.

What is to be obtained by way of a happy destination. 'And a kahāpaṇa' means a kahāpaṇa. Tribute to be obtained by way of punishment is `daṇḍabali`. 'What will the householders do?' The householders are like forest-dwellers, relying on difficult terrain; they will not cause any harm. 'Knowing this, why did you not tell me?' Although it was not told before, now it is told out of fear. 'Do not find fault with me.' He says, 'From the time it was reported, there is no fault on my part.'

Nibaddhanti ekantikaṃ.

'Nibaddhaṃ' means certain, absolute.

Pisuṇesīti pisuṇakammamakāsi, tumhākaṃ antare mayhaṃ pesuññaṃ upasaṃharatīti attho. Puna aharaṇīyaṃ brahmadeyyaṃ katvā. Mayhampīti mayhampi atthāya maṃ uddissa puññakammaṃ karotha. Nīluppalaṃ nāma vikasamānaṃ udakato uggantvāva vikasati, evaṃ ahutvā antoudake pupphitaṃ nīluppalaṃ viya. Amhākaṃ panidaṃ puññakammaṃ bhavantarūpapattiyā vinā imasmiṃyeva attabhāve vipākaṃ detīti yojanā. Cintāmattakampīti domanassavasena cintāmattakampi.

'Pisuṇesi' means he performed the act of slander; the meaning is 'he brings slander about me between you.' Again, having made it a `brahmadeyya`, a gift not to be taken back. 'Mayhampi' means, 'For my sake too, perform a meritorious deed, dedicating it to me.' A blue lotus, when blooming, rises out of the water and then blooms; not being like that, this is like a blue lotus that has blossomed within the water. The construction is: 'This meritorious deed of ours yields its result in this very existence, without rebirth into another state of being.' 'Cintāmattakampi' means 'even a mere thought' due to sadness.

Pagevāti [V 2.0236] kālasseva, ativiya pātoti attho. Kaṇṇikūpaganti kaṇṇikayogyaṃ. Tacchetvā maṭṭhaṃ katvā kaṇṇikāya kattabbaṃ sabbaṃ niṭṭhapetvā. Tathā hi sā vatthena veṭhetvā ṭhapitā.

'Pageva' means at the proper time; the meaning is 'very early.' 'Kaṇṇikūpagaṃ' means suitable for the hub. Having carved and polished it, and having completed everything that needed to be done for the hub. For it was wrapped in cloth and set aside.

Cayabandhanaṃ [M 2.0254] sālāya adhiṭṭhānasajjanaṃ. Kaṇṇikamañcabandhanaṃ kaṇṇikārohanakāle āruhitvā avaṭṭhānaaṭṭakaraṇaṃ.

'Cayabandhanaṃ' is the preparation of the foundation for the hall. 'Kaṇṇikamañcabandhanaṃ' is the making of a scaffold to stand upon after climbing up at the time of raising the hub.

Yassa atthate phalake yassa phalake atthateti yojanā.

The construction of 'yassa atthate phalake' (on the plank laid for whom) is 'yassa phalake atthata' (for whom the plank is laid).

Avidūreti sālāya, koviḷārarukkhassa ca avidūre. Sabbajeṭṭhikāti sabbāsaṃ tassa bhariyānaṃ jeṭṭhikā sujātā.

'Avidūre' means not far from the hall and not far from the koviḷāra tree. 'Sabbajeṭṭhikā' means Sujātā, the eldest of all his wives.

Tassevāti sakkasseva. Santiketi samīpe santikāvacarā hutvā nibbattā. Dhajena saddhiṃ sahassayojaniko pāsādo.

'Tasseva' means of Sakka himself. 'Santike' means reborn in his vicinity, having become his close attendants. The palace, together with its banner, is a thousand yojanas in extent.

Kakkaṭakavijjhanasūlasadisanti [P 2.0321] kakkaṭake gaṇhituṃ tassa bilapariyantassa vijjhanasūcisadisaṃ.

'Kakkaṭakavijjhanasūlasadisaṃ' means resembling a spike for piercing crabs; that is, like a needle for piercing at the edge of its hole in order to catch them.

Maccharūpenāti matamaccharūpena. Osaratīti pilavanto gacchati. Tassāpi bakasakuṇikāya pañca vassasatāni āyu ahosi devanerayikānaṃ viya manussapetatiracchānānaṃ āyuno aparicchinnattā.

'Maccharūpena' means in the form of a dead fish. 'Osarati' means it goes along while floating. For that crane too, the lifespan was five hundred years, because the lifespans of humans, hungry ghosts, and animals are not fixed, unlike those of gods and hell-beings.

Ukkuṭṭhimakāsīti uccāsaddamakāsi.

'Ukkuṭṭhimakāsi' means he made a loud sound.

Pubbasannivāsenāti purimajātīsu cirasannivāsena. Evañhi ekaccānaṃ diṭṭhamattenapi sineho uppajjati. Tenāha bhagavā –

'Pubbasannivāsena' means due to long association in previous lives. For thus, affection arises in some even at the mere sight. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Pubbeva sannivāsena, paccuppannahitena vā;

Evaṃ taṃ jāyate pemaṃ, uppalaṃva yathodake”ti. (jā. 1.2.174);

‘Through past association, or through present benefit, thus is that love born, like a lotus in the water.’ (Jā. 1.2.174)

Avasesesūti [V 2.0237] asure, sakkaṃ ṭhapetvā dvīsu devalokesu deveva sandhāya vadati.

'Avasesesu' refers to the asuras and the gods in the two deva worlds, excluding Sakka.

Atthanissitanti attano, paresañca atthameva hitameva nissitaṃ, taṃ pana hitaṃ sukhassa nidānanti āha “kāraṇanissita”nti.

'Atthanissitaṃ' means dependent on the welfare and benefit of oneself and others. And since that benefit is the cause of happiness, it is said to be 'kāraṇanissitaṃ,' dependent on a cause.

Pañhaveyyākaraṇavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Analysis of Questions

357. Kiṃsaṃyojanāti kīdisasaṃyojanā. Satte anatthe saṃyojenti bandhantīti saṃyojanānīti āha “kiṃbandhanā, kena bandhanena baddhā”ti. Puthukāyāti bahū sattakāyāti āha “bahū janā”ti. Veraṃ vuccati dosoti āha “averāti appaṭighā”ti. Āvudhena [M 2.0255] sarīre daṇḍo āvudhadaṇḍo, dhanassa dāpanatthena daṇḍo dhanadaṇḍo, tadubhayākaraṇena tato vinimutto adaṇḍo, sampattiharaṇato, saha anatthuppattito ca sapatto, paṭisattūti āha “asapattāti apaccatthikā”ti. Byāpajjhaṃ [P 2.0322] vuccati cittadukkhaṃ, tabbirahitā abyāpajjhāti āha “vigatadomanassā”ti. Pubbe “averā”ti padena sambaddhāghātakābhāvo vutto. Tenāha “appaṭighā”ti. “Averino”ti pana imināpi kopamattassapi anuppādanaṃ. Tenāha “katthaci kopaṃ na uppādetvā”ti. “Viharemū”ti ca padaṃ purimapadehipi yojetabbaṃ “averā viharemū”tiādinā. Ayañca averādibhāvo saṃvibhāgena pākaṭo hotīti dassetuṃ “accharāyā”ti ādiṃ vatvā “iti ce nesaṃ hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Cittuppatti daḷhatarāpi hutvā pavattatīti dassetuṃ “dānaṃ datvā, pūjaṃ katvā ca patthayantī”ti vuttaṃ. Iti ceti ce-saddo anvayasaṃsaggena parikappetīti āha “evañca nesa”nti.

357. 'Kiṃsaṃyojanā' means 'what kind of fetters?' Because they bind beings to what is not beneficial, they are called 'fetters'; thus it is said, 'What are the bonds? By what bond are they bound?' 'Puthukāyā' means 'many groups of beings'; thus it is said, 'many people.' 'Vera' is called hatred; thus it is said, 'averā' means 'without opposition.' A rod for the body by means of a weapon is an 'āvudhadaṇḍa'; a rod for the purpose of exacting wealth is a 'dhanadaṇḍa'; by not doing either of these two, one is freed from them and is 'adaṇḍa.' Because of seizing possessions and the co-arising of harm, one with enemies is a 'sapatta,' an adversary; thus it is said, 'asapattā' means 'without adversaries.' 'Byāpajjha' is called mental suffering; being without it is 'abyāpajjhā'; thus it is said, 'free from sorrow.' Previously, by the word 'averā,' the absence of associated harm was stated; therefore, it is said, 'without opposition.' But by this word 'averino,' the non-arising of even a mere trace of anger is meant; therefore, it is said, 'not arousing anger anywhere.' The word 'viharemu' should be connected with the preceding words, as in 'averā viharemu.' To show that this state of being without enmity, etc., becomes manifest through sharing, after saying 'like an Apsara,' etc., it is said, 'if this is their wish.' To show that the arising of thought proceeds even more strongly, it is said, 'having given a gift and made an offering, they aspire.' In 'iti ce,' the word 'ce' implies by connection with the sequence; thus it is said, 'and if this is their wish.'

Yāya kāyaci paresaṃ sampattiyā khīyanaṃ usūyanaṃ asahanaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etissāti parasampattikhīyanalakkhaṇā, yadaggena attasampattiyā parehi sādhāraṇabhāvaṃ asahanalakkhaṇaṃ, tadaggenassa “nigūhanalakkhaṇa”ntipi vattabbaṃ. Tathā hissa porāṇā “mā idaṃ acchariyaṃ aññesaṃ hotu, mayhameva hotūti macchariya”nti nibbacanaṃ vadanti. Abhidhamme “yā paralābhasakkāragarukāramānanavandanapūjanāsu issā issāyanā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1126) nikkhepakaṇḍe, “yā etesu paresaṃ lābhādīsu kiṃ iminā imesa”ntiādinā taṃsaṃvaṇṇanāyañca vuttāneva, tasmā tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbānīti adhippāyo.

Its characteristic is being vexed, envious, and intolerant of any success of others; thus, it has the characteristic of being vexed by others' success. Insofar as it has the characteristic of being intolerant of one's own success being shared with others, to that extent it should also be called 'having the characteristic of concealing.' For thus the ancients state its etymology: 'Stinginess is the thought, "May this wonder not belong to others, may it be mine alone."' In the Abhidhamma, in the section on exposition, it is stated with the words, 'Whatever envy, envying, is with regard to others' gain, honor, respect, esteem, reverence, and worship...' (Dhs. 1126), and in its commentary with, 'Whatever, with regard to these gains, etc., of others, is the thought, "What is this to them?"...' and so on. Therefore, the meaning is that they are to be understood in the manner stated there.

Yasmā pana issāmacchariyāni bahvādīnavāni, tesaṃ vibhāvanā lokassa bahukārā[P 2.0323], tasmā abhidhammaṭṭhakathāyaṃ [V 2.0238] (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1125) vibhāvitānampi tesaṃ diṭṭhadhammikepi samparāyike piādīnave dassento “āvāsamacchariyena panā”tiādimāha. Etthāti etesu issāmacchariyesu, etesu vā āvāsamacchariyādīsu pañcasu macchariyesu. Saṅkāraṃ sīsena ukkhipitvāva vicarati [M 2.0256] tattha laggacittatāya, nihīnajjhāsayatāya ca. Mamāti mayā, ayameva vā pāṭho. Lohitampi mukhato uggacchati cittavighātena saṃtattahadayatāya. Kucchivirecanampi hoti atijalaggino. Añño vibhavapaṭivedhadhammo ariyānaṃyeva hoti, te ca taṃ na maccharāyanti macchariyassa sabbaso pahīnattā. Paṭivedhadhamme macchariyassa asambhavo evāti āha “pariyattidhammamacchariyena cā”ti. Vaṇṇamacchariyena dubbaṇṇo, dhammamacchariyena eḷamūgo duppañño hoti.

However, since envy and stinginess have many drawbacks, and their elucidation is of great benefit to the world, therefore, even though they have been elucidated in the Abhidhamma Commentary (Dhs. A. 1125), it further states, 'And with dwelling-stinginess,' etc., showing their drawbacks in this very life and in future lives. Herein, 'here' refers to this envy and stinginess, or to these five kinds of stinginess such as dwelling-stinginess. He wanders about as if carrying filth on his head, due to his mind clinging to it and his base intention. 'Mama' means 'by me,' or this is the alternative reading. Blood even gushes from his mouth because his heart is inflamed by mental distress. He also suffers from severe diarrhea due to excessive greed. The Dhamma of penetration is another matter; it belongs only to the noble ones, and they are not stingy with it, as stinginess has been completely abandoned by them. Since stinginess regarding the Dhamma of penetration is impossible, it is said, 'And with stinginess regarding the Dhamma of learning.' Through stinginess regarding beauty, one becomes ugly; through stinginess regarding the Dhamma, one becomes mute and dull-witted.

“Apicā”tiādi pañcannaṃ macchariyānaṃ vasena kammasarikkhakavipākadassanaṃ. Āvāsamacchariyena lohagehe paccati paresaṃ āvāsapaccayahitasukhanisedhanato. Kulamacchariyena appalābho hoti parehi kulesu laddhabbalābhanisedhanato, appalābhoti ca alābhoti attho. Lābhamacchariyena gūthaniraye nibbattati lābhahetu parehi laddhabbassa assādanisedhanato. Sabbathāpi nirassādo hi gūthanirayo. Vaṇṇo nāma na hotīti sarīravaṇṇo, guṇavaṇṇoti duvidhopi vaṇṇo nāmamattenapi na hoti, tattha tattha nibbattamāno virūpo eva hoti. Sampattinigūhanasabhāvena macchariyena virūpite santāne yebhuyyena guṇā patiṭṭhameva na labhanti, ye ca patiṭṭhaheyyuṃ, tesampi vasenassa vaṇṇo na bhaveyya. Te hi tassa loke rattiṃ khittā sarā viya na paññāyanti. Dhammamacchariyena kukkuḷaniraye. Sotāpattimaggena [P 2.0324] pahīyati apāyagamanīyabhāvato. Verādīhi na parimuccantiyeva tapparimuccanāya icchāya appattabbattā jātiādidhammānaṃ sattānaṃ jātiādīhi viya.

The passage beginning 'Furthermore...' shows the karmic result resembling the action, according to the five kinds of stinginess. Through dwelling-stinginess, one is cooked in a copper house, because of preventing others from the happiness and benefit of dwelling-requisites. Through family-stinginess, one gains little, because of preventing others from obtaining gains in families; and 'gaining little' means 'no gain.' Through gain-stinginess, one is reborn in the excrement hell, because of preventing others from enjoying what they should have obtained as gains. Indeed, the excrement hell is utterly devoid of delight. 'Beauty' does not exist even in name, meaning neither physical beauty nor the beauty of virtues; both kinds of beauty do not exist even in name, and one is reborn in various places as deformed. In a mental continuum disfigured by stinginess, which has the nature of concealing prosperity, virtues mostly do not find a footing; and even if they were to find a footing, no beauty would arise on account of them. For in that world, they are not perceived, like arrows shot at night. Through Dhamma-stinginess, one is reborn in the hell of hot ashes. It is abandoned by the path of stream-entry because it leads to states of woe. One is not freed from enmity and so on, just as beings subject to birth and so on are not freed from birth and so on, because the wish for freedom from them is unattainable.

Tiṇṇā mettha kaṅkhāti ma-kāro padasandhikaro. Etasmiṃ pañheti etasmiṃ “kiṃsaṃyojanā nu kho”ti evaṃ ñātuṃ icchite atthe. Tumhākaṃ vacanaṃ sutvāti “issāmacchariyasaṃyojanā”ti evaṃ pavattaṃ tumhākaṃ vissajjanavacanaṃ sutvā. Kaṅkhā tiṇṇāti yathāpucchite atthe saṃsayo tarito vigato desanānussaraṇamattena, na samucchedavasenāti āha “na maggavasenā”tiādi. Ayampi kathaṃkathā vigatāti kaṅkhāya vigatattā eva tassā pavattiākāravisesabhūtā “idaṃ katha idaṃ katha”nti ayampi kathaṃkathā vigatā apagatā.

In 'tiṇṇā mettha kaṅkhā' (my doubt here is crossed over), the letter 'm' is a euphonic conjunction. 'In this question' means in this matter desired to be known, namely, 'What, indeed, are the fetters?' 'Having heard your words' means having heard your reply, which was given thus: 'the fetters of envy and stinginess.' 'Doubt is crossed over' means that the uncertainty regarding the question as asked has been overcome and removed merely by recollecting the teaching, not by way of eradication. Hence it is said, 'not by way of the path,' and so forth. 'This questioning too is gone' means that because doubt has vanished, this questioning, which is a particular mode of its occurrence, namely, 'How is this? How is this?'—this questioning too is gone, departed.

358. Nidānādīni [M 2.0257] mahānidānasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.95) vuttatthāneva. Piyānaṃ [V 2.0239] attano pariggahabhūtānaṃ sattasaṅkhārānaṃ parehi sādhāraṇabhāvāsahanavasena, nigūhanavasena ca pavattanato piyasattasaṅkhāranidānaṃ macchariyaṃ, appiyānaṃ pariggahabhūtānaṃ sattānaṃ, saṅkhārānañca asahanavasena pavattiyā appiyasattasaṅkhāranidānā issā. Yañhi kiñci appiyasambandhaṃ bhaddakampi taṃ kodhanassa appiyamevāti. Ubhayanti macchariyaṃ, issā cāti ubhayaṃ. Ubhayanidānanti piyanidānañceva appiyanidānañca. Piyāti iṭṭhā. Keḷāyitāti dhanāyitā. Mamāyitāti mamattaṃ katvā pariggahitā. Issaṃ karotīti “kiṃ imassa iminā”ti tassa piyasattalābhāsahanavasena ussūyati, tameva piyasattaṃ yācito. Aho vatassāti sādhu vata assa. “Imassa puggalassa evarūpaṃ piyavatthu na bhaveyyā”ti issaṃ karoti usūyaṃ uppādeti. Mamāyantāti keḷāyantā. Appiyeti appiye satte tesaṃ satāpato. Assāti puggalassa, yena te laddhā. Teti [P 2.0325] sattasaṅkhārā, sacepi amanāpā honti appiyehi samudāgatattā. Viparītavuttitāyāti ayāthāvagāhitāya. Ko añño evarūpassa lābhīti tena attānaṃ sambhāvento issaṃ vā karoti. Aññassa tādisaṃ uppajjamānampi “aho vatassa evarūpaṃ na bhaveyyā”ti issaṃ vā karoti, ayañca nayo heṭṭhā vuttanayattā na gahito.

358. The terms 'origin' and so forth are to be understood in the same sense as explained in the commentary to the Mahānidāna Sutta. Stinginess has as its origin beloved beings and formations because it arises from the inability to bear the sharing of beings and formations that one considers one's own with others, and from concealing them. Envy has as its origin disliked beings and formations because it arises from the inability to bear disliked beings and formations. For whatever is connected with what is disliked, even if it is good, is disliked by an angry person. 'Both' means both stinginess and envy. 'Having both as origin' means having both the beloved and the disliked as origin. 'Beloved' means agreeable. 'Cherished' means treated as a treasure. 'Claimed as one’s own' means grasped with a sense of 'mine.' 'One envies' means one is resentful through inability to bear another's gain of a beloved thing, thinking, 'What is this to this person?' or when asked for that very beloved thing. 'Oh, if only they did not have it!' means 'It would be good if they did not have it.' One generates envy, thinking, 'May this person not possess such a beloved thing.' 'Claiming as one’s own' means cherishing. 'Regarding the disliked' means regarding disliked beings, because of the affliction from them. 'Of that person' means of the person by whom they are obtained. 'They' refers to beings and formations, even if they are disagreeable, because they have arisen from the disliked. 'Due to perverse conduct' means due to incorrect understanding. Thinking, 'Who else is a gainer like this?' and thus esteeming oneself, one envies. Or when something similar arises for another, one envies, thinking, 'Oh, if only they did not have such a thing.' This method, however, is not taken up here because it has been explained below.

Vatthukāmānaṃ pariyesanavasena pavatto chando pariyesanachando. Paṭilābhapaccayo chando paṭilābhachando. Paribhuñjanavasena pavatto chando paribhogachando. Paṭiladdhānaṃ sannidhāpanavasena, saṅgopanavasena ca pavatto chando sannidhichando. Diṭṭhadhammikameva payojanaṃ cintetvā vissajjanavasena pavatto chando vissajjanachando. Tenāha “katamo”tiādi.

The desire that arises by way of seeking objects of sensual pleasure is the desire for seeking. The desire that is conditioned by acquisition is the desire for acquisition. The desire that arises by way of enjoyment is the desire for enjoyment. The desire that arises by way of accumulating and hoarding what has been acquired is the desire for accumulation. The desire that arises by way of giving away, having considered only a purpose in this life, is the desire for giving away. Therefore, it is said, 'What...' and so forth.

Ayaṃ pañcavidhopi atthato taṇhāyanamevāti āha “taṇhāmattamevā”ti.

This fivefold desire, in terms of its meaning, is simply craving. Hence it is said, 'merely craving.'

Evaṃ vutto “lābhaṃ paṭicca vinicchayo”ti evaṃ mahānidānasutte (dī. ni. 2.103) vutto vinicchayavitakko vitakko nāma, na yo koci vitakko. Idāni yathāvuttaṃ [M 2.0258] vinicchayavitakkaṃ atthuddhāranayena nīharitvā dassetuṃ “vinicchayo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhasatanti aṭṭhādhikaṃ sataṃ, tañca kho taṇhāvicaritānaṃ sataṃ, na yassa kassacīti dassetuṃ “taṇhāvicarita”nti vuttaṃ. Taṇhāvinicchayo nāma taṇhāya vasena vakkhamānanayena ārammaṇassa vinicchinanato. Diṭṭhidassanavasena “idameva saccaṃ, moghaṃ añña”nti vinicchinanato diṭṭhivinicchayo nāma. Iṭṭhaṃ paṇītaṃ, aniṭṭhaṃ appaṇītaṃ, piyāyitabbaṃ piyaṃ, appiyāyitabbaṃ appiyaṃ, tesaṃ vavatthānaṃ taṇhāvasena na hoti. Taṇhāvasena hi ekacco kiñci vatthuṃ paṇītaṃ maññati, ekacco [P 2.0326] hīnaṃ, ekacco piyāyati, ekacco nappiyāyati. Tenāha “tadeva hī”tiādi[V 2.0240]. “Dassāmī”ti idaṃ vissajjanachande vuttanayena ceva vaṭṭūpanissayadānavasena ca veditabbaṃ. Tampi hi taṇhāchandahetukanti.

When it is said, 'judgment conditioned by gain,' this refers to the thought of judgment (vinicchayavitakko) as stated in the Mahānidāna Sutta (Dī. Ni. 2.103), not just any thought. Now, to extract and show the aforementioned thought of judgment by way of its meaning, the phrase 'judgment' and so forth is stated. 'One hundred and eight' (aṭṭhasataṃ) means one hundred plus eight, and that refers to the hundred types of craving-driven conduct, not just anyone's, which is why the term 'craving-driven conduct' (taṇhāvicaritaṃ) is used. 'Judgment based on craving' (taṇhāvinicchayo) is so called from the determination of an object by way of craving, in the manner that will be explained. 'Judgment based on views' (diṭṭhivinicchayo) is so called from the determination, by way of adopting a view, that 'this alone is true, all else is false.' What is agreeable and refined, what is disagreeable and unrefined, what is to be cherished as dear, what is not to be cherished as not dear—their determination is not made by way of craving. For by way of craving, one person considers a certain thing refined, another considers it inferior; one cherishes it, another does not. Therefore, it is said, 'that very thing...' and so on. 'I will give'—this should be understood both in the manner explained in the section on the desire for giving, and as giving that is a supporting condition for the round of existence. For that too is caused by the desire and wish of craving.

Yattha sayaṃ uppajjanti, taṃ santānaṃ saṃsāre papañcenti vitthārayantīti papañcā. Yassa ca uppannā, taṃ “ratto”ti vā “satto”ti vā “micchābhiniviṭṭho”ti vā papañcenti byañjentīti papañcā. Yasmā taṇhādiṭṭhiyo adhimattā hutvā pavattamānā taṃsamaṅgīpuggalaṃ pamattākāraṃ pāpenti, māno pana jātimadādi vasena mattākārampi, tasmā “mattapamattākārapāpanaṭṭhenā”ti vuttaṃ. Saṅkhā vuccati koṭṭhāso bhāgaso saṅkhāyati upaṭṭhātīti. Yasmā papañcasaññā taṃtaṃdvāravasena, ārammaṇavasena ca bhāgaso vitakkassa paccayā honti, na kevalā, tasmā papañcasaññāsaṅkhānidāno vitakko vutto, papañcasaññānaṃ vā anekabhedabhinnattā taṃsamudāyo “papañcasaññāsaṅkhā”ti vutto. Papañcasaññāsaṅkhāggahaṇena ca anavaseso dukkhasamudayo vutto taṃtaṃ nimittattā vaṭṭadukkhassāti.

Where they arise, they proliferate, that is, they expand the continuity in the cycle of existence; hence they are called 'proliferations' (papañcā). And in whom they have arisen, they proliferate, that is, they make that person manifest as 'lustful,' 'attached,' or 'wrongly insistent'; hence they are called 'proliferations.' Because craving and views, when they occur excessively, lead the person endowed with them to a state of negligence, while conceit, by way of pride of birth and so on, leads even to a state of intoxication, it is therefore said to be 'for the purpose of leading to a state of intoxication and negligence.' 'Category' (saṅkhā) is so called because it is a portion; it is reckoned, it appears, part by part. Since perceptions of proliferation, by way of the various sense doors and objects, are conditions for thought part by part—not solely—thought is said to have its source in the category of perceptions of proliferation. Or, because perceptions of proliferation are divided into many different kinds, their collection is called 'the category of perceptions of proliferation' (papañcasaññāsaṅkhā). And by the term 'the category of perceptions of proliferation,' the origin of suffering is stated without remainder, because it is the sign for the suffering of the round of existence.

Yo nirodho vūpasamoti nirodhasaccamāha. Tassa sāruppanti tassa papañcasaññāsaṅkhāya nirodhassa vūpasamassa adhigamupāyatāya sāruppaṃ anucchavikaṃ, etena vipassanaṃ vadati. Tattha yathāvuttanirodhe ārammaṇakaraṇavasena gacchati pavattatīti tatthagāminī, etena maggaṃ. Tenāha “saha vipassanāya maggaṃ pucchatī”ti.

That which is cessation is peace; thus, he speaks of the Truth of Cessation. 'What is suitable for that' (tassa sāruppaṃ) means what is suitable and appropriate (anucchavikaṃ) as a means to attain the cessation, the calming, of that category of perceptions of proliferation. By this, he refers to insight (vipassanā). Therein, 'leading there' (tatthagāminī) means it goes, it proceeds, by way of making the aforementioned cessation its object. By this, he refers to the path. Therefore, he says: 'He asks about the path together with insight.'

Vedanākammaṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Meditation Subject of Feeling

359. Pucchitameva kathitaṃ. Yasmā sakkena devānaṃ indena papañcasaññāsaṅkhānirodhagāminipaṭipadā pucchitāva, bhagavā ca tadadhigamupāyaṃ arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ tassa [M 2.0259] ajjhāsayavasena vedanāmukhena kathento tisso vedanā ārabhi, iti pucchitameva kathentena pucchānusandhivasena [P 2.0327] sānusandhimeva ca kathitaṃ. Na hi buddhānaṃ ananusandhikā kathā nāma atthi. Idānissa vedanāmukhena arūpakammaṭṭhānasseva kathane kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “devatānañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Karajakāyassa sukhumatāvacaneneva accantamudusukhumālabhāvāpi vuttā evāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kammajanti kammajatejaṃ. Tassa balavabhāvo uḷārapuññakammanibbattattā, ativiya garumadhurasiniddhasuddhāhārajīraṇato ca. Ekāhārampīti ekāhāravārampi. “Vilīyantī”ti etena karajakāyassa mandatāya kammajatejassa balavabhāvena āhāravelātikkamena nesaṃ balavatī dukkhavedanā uppajjamānā supākaṭā hotīti dasseti. Nidassanamattañcetaṃ[V 2.0241], sukhavedanāpi pana nesaṃ uḷārapaṇītesu ārammaṇesu uparūpari aniggahaṇavasena pavattamānā supākaṭā hutvā upaṭṭhātiyeva. Upekkhāpi tesaṃ kadāci uppajjamānā santapaṇītarūpā eva iṭṭhamajjhatte eva ārammaṇe pavattanato. Tenevāha “tasmā”tiādi.

359. What was asked has been spoken of. Since Sakka, the lord of the devas, asked about the path leading to the cessation of the category of perceptions of proliferation, the Blessed One, in accordance with Sakka's disposition, while teaching the means for its attainment—the formless meditation subject—by way of feeling as the entry point, began with the three feelings. Thus, in speaking of what was asked, it was spoken with connection, following the sequence of the question. For there is no such thing as a disconnected discourse of the Buddhas. Now, to show the reason for teaching the formless meditation subject by way of feeling, the passage beginning 'For the devas...' was stated. By the very mention of the subtlety of the body born of action, its exceedingly soft, subtle, and delicate nature should be understood as having been stated. 'Born of kamma' means the fire-element born of kamma. Its strength is due to its having been produced by great meritorious kamma, and from the digestion of extremely heavy, sweet, rich, and pure food. 'Even a single meal' means even a single mealtime. By the phrase 'they dissolve,' it is shown that due to the weakness of the body born of action and the strength of the fire-element born of kamma, when they go past a mealtime, a strong painful feeling arises in them and becomes very evident. And this is just an illustration. For pleasant feeling also arises and becomes very evident for them when it occurs repeatedly without restraint in regard to sublime and refined objects. Equanimity, too, when it sometimes arises for them, is of a peaceful and refined nature, as it occurs only in regard to an agreeable or neutral object. For that reason, he said, 'Therefore...' and so on.

Rūpakammaṭṭhānanti rūpapariggahaṃ, rūpamukhena vipassanābhinivesanti attho. Arūpakammaṭṭhānanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tattha rūpakammaṭṭhānena samathābhinivesopi saṅgayhati, vipassanābhiniveso pana idhādhippetoti dassento “rūpapariggaho arūpapariggahotipi etadeva vuccatī”ti āha. Catudhātuvavatthānanti ettha yebhuyyena catudhātuvavatthānaṃ vitthārento rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetīti adhippāyo. Rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ dassetvāva katheti “evaṃ rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ vuccamānaṃ suṭṭhu vibhūtaṃ pākaṭaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhātī”ti. “Etena idhāpi rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ ekadesena vibhāvitamevā”ti vadanti.

'Meditation subject of form' means the comprehension of form; the meaning is the application of insight by way of form as the entry point. 'Meditation subject of the formless'—here too, the same method applies. Therein, by 'meditation subject of form,' the application of serenity is also included, but to show that here the application of insight is intended, he said: 'The comprehension of form and the comprehension of the formless—this too is called just that.' In the phrase 'the defining of the four elements,' the intention is that he teaches the meditation subject of form by generally elaborating on the defining of the four elements. Having shown the meditation subject of form, he says, 'Thus, the meditation subject of form, being spoken of, becomes well-manifest and clear, and it appears.' Some say, 'By this, even here, the meditation subject of form is indeed partly clarified.'

Kāmañcettha vedanāvasena arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ āgataṃ, tadaññadhammavasenapi arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ labbhatīti taṃ vibhāgena dassetuṃ “tividho hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha abhinivesoti anuppaveso, ārambhoti attho. Ārambhe eva hi ayaṃ vibhāgo, sammasanaṃ pana anavasesatova dhamme pariggahetvā pavattatīti. “Pariggahite rūpakammaṭṭhāne”ti [P 2.0328] idaṃ rūpamukhena vipassanābhinivesaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, arūpamukhena pana vipassanābhiniveso yebhuyyena samathayānikassa icchitabbo, so ca [M 2.0260] paṭhamaṃ jhānaṅgāni pariggahetvā tato paraṃ sesadhamme pariggaṇhāti. Paṭhamābhinipātoti sabbe cetasikā cittāyattā cittakiriyābhāvena vuccantīti phasso cittassa paṭhamābhinipāto vutto. Taṃ ārammaṇanti yathāpariggahitaṃ rūpakammaṭṭhānasaññitaṃ ārammaṇaṃ. Uppannaphasso puggalo, cittacetasikarāsi vā ārammaṇena phuṭṭho phassasahajātāya vedanāya taṃsamakālameva vedeti, phasso pana obhāsassa viya padīpo vedanādīnaṃ paccayaviseso hotīti purimakālo viya vuccati, yā tassa ārammaṇābhiniropanalakkhaṇatā vuccati. Phusantoti ārammaṇassa phusanākārena. Ayañhi arūpadhammattā ekadesena anallīyamānopi rūpaṃ viya cakkhuṃ, saddo viya ca sotaṃ, cittaṃ, ārammaṇañca phusanto viya, saṅghaṭṭento viya ca pavattatīti. Tathā hesa “saṅghaṭṭanaraso”ti vuccati.

And although here the formless meditation subject has been introduced by way of feeling, it can also be obtained by way of other phenomena. To show this with a classification, the passage beginning 'For it is threefold...' was stated. Therein, 'application' (abhinivesa) means entering into; the meaning is 'commencement' (ārambha). For this classification applies only at the commencement; comprehension (sammasana), however, proceeds by grasping all phenomena without remainder. 'When the meditation subject of form has been comprehended'—this is said with reference to the application of insight by way of form. The application of insight by way of the formless, however, is generally to be desired by one who follows the serenity vehicle, and such a person first comprehends the jhāna factors and thereafter comprehends the remaining phenomena. 'First impingement': since all mental factors are dependent on the mind, they are spoken of in terms of the mind's activity; thus, contact is called the mind's first impingement. 'That object' means the object designated as the comprehended meditation subject of form. The person in whom contact has arisen, or the aggregate of mind and mental factors, being touched by the object, feels at that very same moment with the feeling that is co-arisen with contact. But contact, like a lamp for light, is a specific condition for feeling and the others, so it is spoken of as if it were a prior moment; this is what is called its characteristic of directing towards the object. 'Touching' means in the manner of touching the object. For this contact, being a formless phenomenon, although it does not adhere in one part—as the eye does to form or the ear to sound—proceeds as if touching, as if colliding with, the mind and the object. Thus it is said that 'its characteristic is collision.'

Ārammaṇaṃ anubhavantīti issaravatāya visavitāya sāmibhāvena ārammaṇarasaṃ saṃvedentī. Phassādīnañhi sampayuttadhammānaṃ ārammaṇe ekadeseneva pavatti phusanādimattabhāvato, vedanāya pana [V 2.0242] iṭṭhākārasambhogādivasena pavattanato ārammaṇe nippadesato pavatti. Phusanādibhāvena hi ārammaṇaggahaṇaṃ ekadesānubhavanaṃ, vedayitabhāvena gahaṇaṃ yathākāmaṃ sabbānubhavanaṃ, evaṃsabhāvāneva tāni gahaṇānīti na vedanāya viya phassādīnampi yathā sakakiccakaraṇena sāmibhāvānubhavanaṃ codetabbaṃ. Vijānantanti paricchindanavasena visesato jānantaṃ. Viññāṇañhi minitabbavatthuṃ nāḷiyā minanto puriso viya ārammaṇaṃ paricchijja vibhāventaṃ pavattati, na saññā viya sañjānanamattaṃ [P 2.0329] hutvā. Tathā hi anena kadāci lakkhaṇattayavibhāvanāpi hoti, imesaṃ pana phassādīnaṃ tassa tassa pākaṭabhāvo paccayavisesasiddhassa pubbabhāgassa vasena veditabbo.

Experiencing the object—thus, by way of mastery, sovereignty, and ownership, it thoroughly savors the flavor of the object. For while the associated states such as contact occur in the object only partially, merely by the act of touching and so on, feeling occurs in the object completely, as it arises through the enjoyment of agreeable aspects and the like. For grasping the object by way of contact and so on is experiencing it partially, whereas grasping it by way of feeling is experiencing it entirely, as desired. Such is the nature of these acts of grasping; thus, one should not demand that contact and the others, like feeling, experience ownership by performing their respective functions. Knowing distinctly—it knows by way of delimiting in a particular way. For consciousness arises by delimiting and distinguishing the object, like a man measuring a measurable object with a measuring tube, not by merely being aware of it as perception is. Indeed, sometimes this also involves the clarification of the three characteristics. However, the prominence of each of these—contact and the rest—should be understood by way of the preceding stage established through specific conditions.

Evaṃ tassa tasseva pākaṭabhāvepi “sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, abhiññeyya”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.46; paṭi. ma. 1.3), “sabbañca kho, bhikkhave, abhijāna”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.27) ca evamādi vacanato sabbe sammasanupagā dhammā pariggahetabbāti dassento “tattha yassā”tiādimāha. Tattha phassapañcamakeyevāti avadhāraṇaṃ tadantogadhattā taggahaṇeneva gahitattā catunnaṃ arūpakkhandhānaṃ. Phassapañcamakaggahaṇañhi tassa sabbassa sabbacittuppādasādhāraṇabhāvato[M 2.0261]. Tattha ca phassacetanāggahaṇena sabbasaṅkhārakkhandhadhammasaṅgaho cetanappadhānattā tesaṃ. Tathā hi suttantabhājanīye saṅkhārakkhandhavibhaṅge “cakkhusamphassajā cetanā”tiādinā (vibha. 21) cetanāva vibhattā, itare pana khandhā sarūpeneva gahitā.

Thus, even when this or that particular state is prominent, in accordance with such sayings as, 'All, monks, is to be fully known' (Saṃ. Ni. 4.46; Paṭi. Ma. 1.3), and 'And all, monks, I directly know' (Saṃ. Ni. 4.27), he shows that all phenomena subject to comprehension are to be grasped, saying, 'Therein, of which...' and so on. Here, the specification 'the group of five with contact' is made because the four formless aggregates are included within it, being grasped by its very grasping. For the grasping of the group of five with contact is due to its being common to every arising of consciousness. And therein, by the grasping of contact and volition, all phenomena of the formations aggregate are included, because volition is predominant among them. Indeed, in the analysis of the formations aggregate in the Suttanta exposition, only volition is analyzed, with the words, 'volition born of eye-contact,' and so on (Vibh. 21), while the other aggregates are grasped by their own nature.

Vatthunissitāti ettha vatthu-saddo karajakāyavisayo, na chabbatthuvisayoti. Kathamidaṃ viññāyatīti āha “yaṃ sandhāya vutta”nti. Kattha pana vuttaṃ? Sāmaññaphalasutte. Soti karajakāyo. “Pañcakkhandhavinimuttaṃ nāmarūpaṃ natthī”ti idaṃ adhikāravasena vuttaṃ. Aññathā hi khandhavinimuttampi nāmaṃ atthevāti. Avijjādihetukāti avijjātaṇhupādānādihetukā. “Vipassanāpaṭipāṭiyā aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattāti sammasanto vicaratī”ti iminā balavavipassanaṃ vatvā puna tassa ussukkāpanaṃ, visesādhigamañca dassento “so”tiādimāha.

Herein, regarding 'dependent on a physical basis,' the word 'basis' refers to the physical body, not to the six bases. How is this known? He says, 'in reference to which it was said.' And where was it said? In the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. That is, the physical body. The statement, 'There is no name-and-form apart from the five aggregates,' is said in this specific context. For otherwise, there does exist 'name' that is apart from the aggregates. 'Caused by ignorance, etc.' means caused by ignorance, craving, clinging, and so on. Having spoken of powerful insight with the words, 'He dwells contemplating as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, in accordance with the order of insight,' then to encourage him and to show the attainment of a special state, he says, 'He...' and so on.

Idhāti imasmiṃ sakkapañhasutte. Vedanāvasena cettha arūpakammaṭṭhānakathane kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva[P 2.0330]. Yathāvuttesu ca tīsu kammaṭṭhānābhinivesesu vedanāvasena kammaṭṭhānābhiniveso sukaro vedanānaṃ vibhūtabhāvatoti dassetuṃ “phassavasena hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Na pākaṭaṃ hotī”ti idaṃ sakkapamukhānaṃ tesaṃ devānaṃ yathā vedanā vibhūtā hutvā upaṭṭhāti, na evaṃ itaradvayanti [V 2.0243] katvā vuttaṃ. Vedanāya eva ca nesaṃ vibhūtabhāvo vedanāmukhenevettha bhagavatā desanāya āraddhattā. “Vedanānaṃ uppattiyā pākaṭatāyā”ti idaṃ sukhadukkhavedanānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Tāsañhi pavatti oḷārikā, na itarāya. Tadubhayaggahaṇamukhena vā gahetabbattā itarāyapi pavatti viññūnaṃ pākaṭā evāti sukhadukkhavedanānañhī”ti visesaggahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Yadā sukhaṃ uppajjatī”tiādi sukhavedanāya pākaṭabhāvavibhāvanaṃ, tayidaṃ asamāhitabhūmivasena veditabbaṃ. Tattha “sakalaṃ sarīraṃ kho bhante”ntiādinā kāmaṃ pavattioḷārikatāya avūpasantasabhāvametaṃ sukhaṃ, sātalakkhaṇatāya pana sampayuttadhamme, nissayañca anuggaṇhantameva pavattatīti dasseti. “Yadā dukkhaṃ uppajjatī”tiādīsu vuttavipariyāyena attho veditabbo.

Here means in this Sutta on Sakka's Questions. The reason for discussing the formless meditation subjects here by way of feeling is the same as the method stated previously. And to show that among the three aforementioned types of adherence to meditation subjects, adherence by way of feeling is easy because feelings are manifest, it is said, 'For by way of contact...' and so on. The statement, 'It is not manifest,' is made because for those devas headed by Sakka, feeling arises manifestly, but this is not so for the other two. And for them, it is only feeling that is manifest, because the Blessed One began the teaching here with feeling as the entry point. The phrase, 'because of the manifest nature of the arising of feelings,' is said with reference to pleasant and painful feelings. For their occurrence is gross, not so that of the other. Or, since the occurrence of the other is also manifest to the wise, as it is to be grasped by way of grasping both of those, the specific mention 'for pleasant and painful feelings' should be seen in this way. The passage beginning, 'When pleasure arises,' is an explanation of the manifest nature of pleasant feeling; this should be understood with reference to the unconcentrated plane. Therein, the passage beginning, 'The entire body, venerable sir,' shows that although this pleasure is of an unpacified nature due to the grossness of its occurrence, it nevertheless arises supporting its associated states and its physical basis by its characteristic of satisfaction. The meaning of the passage beginning, 'When pain arises,' should be understood in the opposite way to what has been stated.

Duddīpanāti ñāṇena dīpetuṃ asakkuṇeyyā, dubbiññeyyāti attho. Tenāha “andhakārā abhibhūtā”ti. Andhakārāti andhakāragatasadisī, jānitukāme [M 2.0262] ca andhakārinī. Pubbāparaṃ samaṃ sukare supalakkhitamaggavasena pāsāṇatale migagatamaggo viya iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇesu sukhadukkhānubhavanehi majjhattārammaṇesu anuminitabbatāya vuttaṃ “sā sukhadukkhānaṃ…pe… pākaṭā hotī”ti. Tenāha “yathā”tiādi. Nayato gaṇhantassāti etthāyaṃ nayo – yasmā iṭṭhāniṭṭhavisayāya ārammaṇūpaladdhiyā anubhavanato niṭṭhāmajjhattavisayā ca upaladdhi, tasmā na tāya niranubhavanāya [P 2.0331] bhavitabbaṃ, yaṃ tatthānubhavanaṃ, sā adukkhamasukhā. Tathā anupalabbhamānaṃ rūpādianubhuyyamānaṃ diṭṭhaṃ upalabbhati, yo pana majjhattārammaṇaṃ tabbisayassa viññāṇappavattiyaṃ, tasmā ananubhuyyamānena tena na bhavitabbaṃ. Sakkā hi vattuṃ anubhavamānā majjhattavisayupaladdhi upaladdhibhāvato. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhavisayupaladdhivisayaṃ pana niranubhavanaṃ taṃ anupaladdhisabhāvameva diṭṭhaṃ, taṃ yathārūpanti. Nivattetvāti nīharitvā, “somanassaṃpāha”ntiādinā samānajātiyampi bhindanto aññehi arūpadhammehi vivecetvā asaṃsaṭṭhaṃ katvāti attho.

'Difficult to illuminate' means it cannot be illuminated by knowledge; the meaning is that it is difficult to understand. Therefore it is said, 'overcome by darkness.' 'Darkness' means it is like being in darkness, and it brings darkness to those who wish to know. Just as the path taken by a deer on a stone slab is difficult to discern before and after, so too, because it has to be inferred in the case of neutral objects from the experience of pleasure and pain in desirable and undesirable objects, it is said, 'it becomes manifest in relation to pleasure and pain.' Therefore, he says, 'Just as...' and so on. For one who grasps it by way of this method, the method is as follows: since the apprehension of desirable and undesirable objects is established from experience, and there is also apprehension of neutral objects, that apprehension should not be without experience. Whatever experience is there, that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Similarly, form and so on, while being experienced, are seen and apprehended, yet are as if not apprehended. But when consciousness occurs with a neutral object as its resort, it should not be unexperienced. For it can be said that the apprehension of a neutral object is an apprehension because it is experienced. But non-experience with regard to the apprehension of desirable and undesirable objects is seen to be of the nature of non-apprehension itself. Such is its nature. 'Having removed' means having extracted; the meaning is: by distinguishing even what is of the same kind, as in the phrase 'joy, I say,' and separating it from other formless states, having made it unmixed.

Ayañca rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ vedanāvasena nivattetvā desanā tathāvinetabbapuggalāpekkhāya suttantaresupi (dī. ni. 2.373; ma. ni. 1.106, 390, 413, 450, 465, 467; ma. ni. 2.306, 209; 3.67, 342; saṃ. ni. 4.248) āgatā evāti dassento “na kevala”ntiādimāha. Tattha mahāsatipaṭṭhāne (dī. ni. 2.273) tathā desanāya āgatabhāvo anantarameva āvi bhavissati, majjhimanikāye satipaṭṭhānadesanāpi (ma. ni. 1.106) tādisī eva. Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaye “evaṃ cetaṃ, devānaṃ inda, bhikkhuno sutaṃ hoti ‘sabbe dhammā nālaṃ abhinivesāyā’ti, so sabbaṃ dhammaṃ abhijānāti[V 2.0244], sabbaṃ dhammaṃ abhiññāya sabbaṃ dhammaṃ parijānāti, sabbaṃ dhammaṃ pariññāya yaṃ kiñci vedanaṃ vedeti sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā, so tāsu vedanāsu aniccānupassī viharati, virāgānupassī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.390) āgataṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ vedanāvasena nivattetvā dassesī”ti. Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaye pana “so [P 2.0332] evaṃ anurodhavirodhavippahīno yaṃ kiñci vedanaṃ vedeti sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā, so taṃ vedanaṃ nābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa taṃ vedanaṃ anabhinandato anabhivadato anajjhosāya tiṭṭhato yā vedanāsu nandī [M 2.0263] sā nirujjhatī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.414) āgataṃ. Cūḷavedalle “kati panāyyevedanā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.465) āgataṃ. Mahāvedalle “vedanāti, āvuso, vuccati, kittāvatā nu kho, āvuso, ‘vedanā’ti vuccatī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.450) āgataṃ. Evaṃ raṭṭhapālasuttādīsupi (ma. ni. 2.305) vedanākammaṭṭhānassa āgataṭṭhānaṃ uddharitvā vattabbaṃ.

Having explained this meditation subject on form, and then reverting to the formless meditation subject by way of feeling, he says 'Not only...' and so forth, to show that such a teaching also occurs in other suttas, with reference to individuals to be trained in that way (Dī. Ni. 2.373; Ma. Ni. 1.106, 390, 413, 450, 465, 467; Ma. Ni. 2.306, 209; 3.67, 342; Saṃ. Ni. 4.248). Here, in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta (Dī. Ni. 2.273), the occurrence of such a teaching will become evident immediately. Similarly, the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness in the Majjhima Nikāya (Ma. Ni. 1.106) is also of that kind. In the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta (Ma. Ni. 1.390), it occurs thus: 'Thus, O Sakka, lord of the devas, a bhikkhu hears: "All phenomena are not to be clung to." He directly knows all phenomena; having directly known all phenomena, he fully comprehends all phenomena; having fully comprehended all phenomena, whatever feeling he experiences—pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he dwells contemplating impermanence in those feelings, contemplating dispassion,' and so forth. Therefore it is said, 'He showed the formless meditation subject by reverting to the aspect of feeling.' In the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta (Ma. Ni. 1.414), it occurs thus: 'Thus, devoid of attraction and aversion, whatever feeling he experiences—pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he does not delight in that feeling, welcome it, or remain holding to it. When he does not delight in that feeling, welcome it, or remain holding to it, the delight in feelings ceases,' and so forth. In the Cūḷavedalla Sutta (Ma. Ni. 1.465), it occurs thus: 'How many feelings are there, venerable sir?' and so forth. In the Mahāvedalla Sutta (Ma. Ni. 1.450), it occurs thus: 'Friend, it is called "feeling." But to what extent, friend, is it called "feeling"?' and so forth. Similarly, in the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta and others (Ma. Ni. 2.305), the passages where the meditation subject of feeling occurs should be extracted and stated.

“Paṭhamaṃ rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā”ti vuttaṃ, kathaṃ tamettha kathitanti āha “rūpakammaṭṭhāna”ntiādi. Saṅkhittaṃ, kathaṃ saṅkhittaṃ? Vedanāya ārammaṇamattakaṃyeva, yebhuyyena vedanā rūpadhammārammaṇā pañcadvāravasena pavattanato. Tena cassā purimasiddhā eva ārammaṇanti vedanaṃ vadantena tassārammaṇadhammā atthato paṭhamataraṃ gahitā eva nāma hontīti imāya atthāpattiyā rūpakammaṭṭhānassevettha paṭhamaṃ gahitatā jotitā, na sarūpeneva gahitattā. Tenāha “tasmā pāḷiyaṃ nāruḷhaṃ bhavissatī”ti.

'Having first spoken of the meditation subject on form,' it is said. How is it stated here? He says, 'the meditation subject on form,' and so forth. It is brief. How is it brief? It is merely the object of feeling, for feelings mostly arise with form phenomena as their object through the five sense doors. Therefore, since its object is already established beforehand, by speaking of feeling, its object-phenomena are implicitly grasped earlier in meaning. Thus, by this implication, the priority of taking the meditation subject on form here is illuminated—not because it was taken in its own form. Therefore he says, 'Therefore, it will not be found in the Pāli text.'

360. Dvīhi koṭṭhāsehīti sevitabbāsevitabbabhāgehi. Evarūpanti yaṃ akusalānaṃ abhibuddhiyā, kusalānañca parihānāya saṃvattati, evarūpaṃ, taṃ pana kāmūpasañhitatāya “gehanissita”nti vuccatīti āha “gehasitasomanassa”nti. Iṭṭhānanti piyānaṃ. Kantānanti kamanīyānaṃ. Manāpānanti manavaḍḍhanakānaṃ. Tato eva mano ramentīti manoramānaṃ. Lokāmisapaṭisaṃyuttānanti [P 2.0333] taṇhāsannissitānaṃ kāmūpasañhitānaṃ. Paṭilābhato samanupassatoti “aho mayā imāni laddhānī”ti yathāladdhāni rūpārammaṇādīni assādayato. Atītanti atikkantaṃ. Niruddhanti nirodhappattaṃ. Vipariṇatanti sabhāvavigamena vigataṃ. Samanussaratoti assādanavasena anucintayato. Gehasitanti kāmaguṇanissitaṃ. Kāmaguṇā hi kāmarāgassa gehasadisattā idha “geha”nti adhippetā.

360. By two categories: namely, the aspects of what should be cultivated and what should not be cultivated. 'Such' refers to that which conduces to the increase of unwholesome states and the decline of wholesome states. Such a thing is called 'house-based' because it is connected with sensual pleasures. Therefore, he says, 'house-based joy.' 'Pleasing' means dear. 'Desirable' means charming. 'Agreeable' means increasing delight. Because of this, the mind delights—thus, 'mind-pleasing.' 'Connected with worldly gains' means rooted in craving and connected with sensual pleasures. 'One reflects on acquisition' means one delights in the forms and other objects obtained, thinking: 'Oh, these have been obtained by me!' 'Past' means gone beyond. 'Ceased' means reached cessation. 'Changed' means vanished due to the loss of its own nature. 'One recollects' means one contemplates by way of delight. 'House-based' means based on sensual qualities. For sensual qualities are here intended by 'house,' being like a house for sensual desire.

Evarūpanti yaṃ akusalānaṃ parihānāya, kusalānañca abhibuddhiyā saṃvattati, evarūpaṃ, taṃ [V 2.0245] pana pabbajjādivasena pavattiyā nekkhammūpasañhitanti āha “nekkhammasitaṃ somanassa”nti. Idāni taṃ pāḷivaseneva dassetuṃ “tattha katamānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha vipassanālakkhaṇe nekkhamme [M 2.0264] dassite itarāni tassa kāraṇato, phalato, atthato ca dassitāneva hontīti vipassanālakkhaṇameva taṃ dassento “rūpānantvevā”tiādimāha. Vipariṇāmavirāganirodhanti jarāya vipariṇāmetabbatañceva jarāmaraṇehi palujjanaṃ nirujjhanañca viditvāti yojanā. Uppajjati somanassanti vipassanāya vīthipaṭipattiyā kamena uppannānaṃ pāmojjapītipassaddhīnaṃ upari anappakaṃ somanassaṃ uppajjati. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

'Such' refers to that which conduces to the decline of unwholesome states and the increase of wholesome states. Such a thing is connected with renunciation by way of its occurrence through going forth and so on. Therefore, he says, 'joy based on renunciation.' Now, in order to show this according to the Pāli text itself, 'therein, what are...' and so forth, was said. Therein, when renunciation is shown as having the characteristic of insight, the others are implicitly shown as its cause, fruit, and meaning. Therefore, showing only that characteristic of insight, he says, 'Form, indeed...' and so forth. 'Change, dispassion, cessation' is to be construed as understanding both its susceptibility to change through aging, and its breaking up and ceasing through aging and death. 'Joy arises' means that through the gradual path of insight practice, after gladness, rapture, and tranquility have arisen, a not insignificant joy arises above them. With reference to which it is said:

“Suññāgāraṃ paviṭṭhassa, santacittassa bhikkhuno;

Amānusī rati hoti, sammā dhammaṃ vipassato.

For a bhikkhu who has entered an empty dwelling, whose mind is peaceful, there is a joy transcending the human, as he rightly contemplates the Dhamma.

Yato yato sammasati, khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ;

Labhatī pītipāmojjaṃ, amataṃ taṃ vijānata”nti. (dha. pa. 374) ca –

Whenever one discerns the rise and fall of the aggregates, one gains rapture and gladness — that, for the discerning, is the deathless. (Dhp. 374)

Nekkhammavasenāti pabbajjādivasena. “Vaṭṭadukkhato nittharissāmī”ti pabbajituṃ bhikkhūnaṃ santikaṃ gacchantassa, pabbajantassa, catupārisuddhisīlaṃ anutiṭṭhantassa, taṃ sodhentassa, dhutaguṇe samādāya vattantassa, kasiṇaparikammādīni karontassa ca yā paṭipatti, sabbā sā idha “nekkhamma”nti adhippetā. Yebhuyyena anussatiyā [P 2.0334] upacārajjhānaṃ niṭṭhātīti katvā “anussativasenā”ti vatvā “paṭhamajjhānādivasenā”ti vuttaṃ. Ettha ca yathā pabbajjā gharabandhanato nikkhamanaṭṭhena nekkhammaṃ, evaṃ vipassanādayopi taṃpaṭipakkhato. Tenāha –

'By means of renunciation' means by way of going forth, etc. Thinking, 'I will escape from the suffering of the round of existence,' one approaches the bhikkhus in order to go forth, goes forth, observes the fourfold purified morality, purifies it, undertakes the ascetic practices and lives accordingly, performs the preliminary work on the kasiṇas, etc.—all such practice is here intended by 'renunciation.' For the most part, since access concentration is accomplished through recollection, it is said 'by way of recollection,' and then it is said 'by way of the first jhāna, etc.' Here, just as going forth is renunciation in the sense of departing from the bondage of household life, so too are insight and the like, due to their being the opposite of that. Therefore, he says—

“Pabbajjā paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ, nibbānañca vipassanā;

Sabbepi kusalā dhammā, nekkhammanti pavuccare”ti. (itivu. aṭṭha. 109);

"Going forth, the first jhāna, Nibbāna, and insight; all wholesome states are called renunciation." (Iti-a. 109)

Yaṃ ceti ettha ceti nipātamattaṃ somanassassa adhippetattā. Catukkanayavaseneva ca suttantesu jhānakathāti vuttaṃ “dutiyatatiyajjhānavasenā”ti. Dvīsūti “savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ avitakkaṃ avicāra”nti vuttesu dvīsu somanassesu.

Here, 'ce' is merely a particle, because joy is intended. And since in the suttas the discourse on jhāna is by way of the fourfold method, it is said, 'by way of the second and third jhāna.' 'In the two' refers to the two kinds of joy mentioned as 'with applied thought and sustained thought' and 'without applied thought and sustained thought'.

Savitakkasavicāre somanasseti parittabhūmike, paṭhamajjhāne vā somanasse. Abhiniviṭṭhasomanassesūti vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapitasomanassesu. Pi-saddena sammaṭṭhasomanassesu pīti imamatthaṃ [V 2.0246] dasseti. Somanassavipassanātopīti [M 2.0265] savitakkasavicārasomanassapavattivipassanātopi. Avitakkaavicāra vipassanā paṇītatarā sammasitadhammavasenapi vipassanāya visesasiddhito, yato maggepi tathārūpā visesā ijjhanti. Ayaṃ panattho “ariyamagga bojjhaṅgādivisesaṃ vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtā khandhā niyamentī”ti evaṃ pavattena moravāpīvāsimahādattattheravādena dīpetabbo.

'In the joy with applied thought and sustained thought' refers to joy in the limited sphere, or joy in the first jhāna. 'In the joy that is firmly established' refers to the joy that has established insight. By the particle 'pi', it shows that rapture is also meant in the well-contemplated joys. 'From insight into joy also' refers to insight into the process of joy accompanied by applied and sustained thought. Insight without applied thought and sustained thought is more refined, because distinctions are achieved through insight even by way of the contemplated phenomena, since on the path, too, such distinctions are accomplished. This meaning should be illuminated by the statement of the Elder Mahādatta, resident of Moravāpi, who said: 'The aggregates, which are the object of insight, determine the distinctions of the noble path, the factors of enlightenment, and so on.'

361. Gehasitadomanassaṃ nāma kāmaguṇānaṃ appaṭilābhanimittaṃ, vigatanimittañca uppajjanakadomanassaṃ. Appaṭilābhato samanupassatoti appaṭilābhena “ahameva na labhāmī”ti paritassanato. Samanussaratoti “ahu vata [P 2.0335] me taṃ vata natthī”tiādinā anussaraṇavasena cintayato. Tenāha “evaṃ chasu dvāresū”tiādi.

361. The displeasure rooted in household life is called the displeasure that arises on account of the non-acquisition of sense-pleasures and on account of a vanished sign. The phrase 'one perceives from non-acquisition' means one laments due to non-acquisition, thinking, 'Only I do not obtain.' The phrase 'one recollects' means one thinks by way of recollection, 'Alas, I once had it, but now I do not,' and so on. Therefore, it is said: 'Thus, in these six doors,' etc.

Anuttaresu vimokkhesūti suññataphalādiariyaphalavimokkhesu. Pihanti apekkhaṃ, āsanti attho. Kathaṃ pana lokuttaradhamme ārabbha āsā uppajjatīti? Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ “yaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇavasena tattha pihā pavattatī”ti avisayattā, puggalassa ca anadhigatabhāvato. Anussavūpaladdhe pana anuttaravimokkhe uddissa pihaṃ upaṭṭhapento “tattha pihaṃ upaṭṭhapetī”ti vutto. Tenāha “kudāssu nāmāha”ntiādi.
