Chasu dvāresu iṭṭhārammaṇe āpāthagate aniccādivasena vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvāti yojanā. “Iṭṭhārammaṇe”ti ca iminā nayidaṃ domanassaṃ sabhāvato aniṭṭhadhammeyeva ārabbha uppajjanakaṃ, atha kho icchitālābhahetukaṃ icchābhighātavasena yattha katthaci ārammaṇe uppajjanakanti dasseti. Evaṃ “kudāssu nāmāha”nti vuttākārena pihaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā evaṃ imampi pakkhaṃ…pe… nāsakkhinti anusocatoti yojanā. “Imasmiṃ pakkhe, imasmiṃ māse, imasmiṃ saṃvacchare pabbajituṃ nāladdhaṃ, kasiṇaparikammaṃ kātuṃ nāladdha”ntiādivasena pavattiṃ sandhāya “nekkhammavasenā”ti vuttaṃ. “Vipassanāvasenā”tiādīsupi iminā nayena yojanā veditabbā.

The phrase 'in the unsurpassed liberations' refers to the noble fruit liberations such as the fruit of emptiness. The word 'pihanti' means expectation; its meaning is yearning. But how does hope arise concerning supramundane states? However, this should not be seen as 'longing arises there by way of making it an object,' due to its not being an object of direct experience, and due to the individual's not having attained it. But when one establishes longing, directing it to the unsurpassed liberation which is grasped through tradition, it is said, 'one establishes longing there.' Therefore, it is said, 'When indeed will I...' and so on. The construction is: 'When a pleasing object has come into range at the six sense doors, one establishes insight by way of impermanence, etc.' By the phrase 'pleasing object,' it shows that this displeasure does not arise only concerning naturally unpleasant phenomena, but rather it arises concerning any object due to the non-acquisition of what is desired, by way of the frustration of desire. The construction is: 'Thus, having established longing in the manner stated, "When indeed will I...", one laments, "I was unable in this aspect..."' The phrase 'by way of renunciation' is said with reference to occurrences such as, 'I did not get to go forth in this fortnight, in this month, in this year,' or 'I did not get to do the preliminary work for the kasiṇas,' and so on. The phrases 'by way of insight' and so on should be understood in the same way.

Yato eva-kāro, tato aññattha niyamoti katvā “tasmimpi…pe… gehasitadomanassamevā”ti vuttaṃ. Na hettha gehasitadomanassatā savitakkasavicāre niyatā, atha kho gehasitadomanasse savitakkasavicāratā [M 2.0266] niyatā paṭiyoginivattanatthattā eva-kārassa. “Gehasitadomanassaṃ savitakkasavicārameva, na avitakkaavicāra”nti. Nekkhammasitadomanassaṃ pana siyā savitakkasavicāraṃ, siyā avitakkaavicāraṃ. Savitakkasavicārasseva [P 2.0336] kāraṇabhūtaṃ domanassaṃ savitakkasavicāradomanassaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Gehasitadomanassaṃ[V 2.0247], yaṃ pana nekkhammādivasena uppannaṃ, taṃ avitakkaavicārassa kāraṇabhūtaṃ avitakkaavicāradomanassanti. Ayañca nayo pariyāyavasena vuttoti āha “nippariyāyena panā”tiādi. Yadi evaṃ kasmā “yaṃ ce avitakkaṃ avicāra”nti pāḷiyaṃ vuttanti āha “etassa panā”tiādi. Maññanavasenāti parikappanavasena. Vuttaṃ pāḷiyaṃ.

Since the word 'eva' (only) is used, a restriction is thereby made on the other term; thus it is said: 'in that also... only household-based displeasure.' Here, household-based displeasure is not restricted to being with applied thought and sustained thought; rather, being with applied thought and sustained thought is restricted to household-based displeasure, because the word 'eva' serves the purpose of excluding the opposite. 'Household-based displeasure is only with applied thought and sustained thought, not without applied thought and sustained thought.' However, displeasure based on renunciation may be with applied thought and sustained thought, or it may be without applied thought and sustained thought. Displeasure that is the cause of that which is with applied thought and sustained thought is called 'displeasure with applied thought and sustained thought.' What is that? It is household-based displeasure. But that which arises by way of renunciation and the like is the cause of that which is without applied thought and sustained thought, hence it is called 'displeasure without applied thought and sustained thought.' And this method is stated indirectly; hence it is said: 'But in the direct sense...' If so, why is it said in the Pāli text: 'Whatever is without applied thought and sustained thought...'? It is explained: 'But of this...' The phrase 'by way of conceiving' means by way of conceptualization. This is stated in the Pāli.

Tatrāti tasmiṃ maññane. Ayaṃ idāni vuccamāno nayo. Domanassapaccayabhūteti domanassassa paccayabhūte. Upacārajjhānañhi paṭhamajjhānādīni vā pādakāni katvā maggaphalāni nibbattetukāmassa tesaṃ alābhe domanassassa uppajjane tāni tassa paccayā nāma honti iti te dhammā phalūpacārena “domanassa”nti vuttā. Yo pana tathā uppannadomanasso dhuranikkhepaṃ akatvā anukkamena vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā maggaphaladhamme nibbatteti, te kāraṇūpacārena “domanassa”nti vuttāti imamatthaṃ dassento “idha bhikkhū”tiādimāha. Nanu etassa tadā domanassameva uppannaṃ, na domanassahetukā vipassanāmaggaphaladhammā uppannā, tattha kathaṃ domanassasamaññaṃ āropetvā voharatīti āha “aññesaṃ paṭipattidassanavasena domanassanti gahetvā”tiādi. Savitakkasavicāradomanasseti savitakkasavicāranimitte domanasse. Tīhi māsehi nibbattetabbā temāsikā, taṃ temāsikaṃ. Imā ca temāsikādayo paṭipadā tathāpavattaukkaṭṭhamajjhimamudindriyavasena veditabbā, adhikamajjhimamudussāhavasena vā. Jaggatīti jāgarikaṃ anuyuñjati.

The phrase 'in that' refers to that conceiving. This is the method now being described. The phrase 'being a condition for displeasure' means 'in that which is a condition for displeasure.' Indeed, for one who desires to generate the path and fruition by making access concentration or the first jhāna, etc., a basis, when displeasure arises due to their non-acquisition, those states are indeed conditions for it. Thus, those phenomena are called 'displeasure' by figurative usage based on the result. But when one with such arisen displeasure does not abandon the effort but gradually arouses insight, generating the path and fruition states, then by figurative usage based on the cause, they are called 'displeasure.' Showing this meaning, it is said, 'Here, a bhikkhu...' and so on. But at that time, only displeasure arose for him, not insight, path, or fruition states caused by displeasure. So how then can the designation 'displeasure' be applied and used there? It is said, 'by taking it as 'displeasure' by way of showing the practice of others,' and so on. The phrase 'displeasure with applied thought and sustained thought' refers to displeasure that has applied thought and sustained thought as its sign. That which is to be produced in three months is 'temāsikā'; that is the three-month practice. And these three-month practices, etc., should be understood by way of the faculties that have thus arisen, whether keen, moderate, or dull, or by way of superior, moderate, or slack effort. The word 'jaggati' (is vigilant) means one practices wakefulness.

Mahāsivattheravatthuvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Story of the Elder Mahāsiva

Sahassadvisahassasaṅkhyattā mahāgaṇe.

In the great assembly numbering one or two thousand.

Aṭṭhakathātherāti aṭṭhakathāya atthapaṭipucchanakatherā. Antarāmaggeti bhikkhaṃ gahetvā gāmato vihāraṃ paṭigamanamagge[P 2.0337]. Tayo…pe… gāhāpetvāti tīṇi cattāri uṇhāpanāni.

The 'commentary elders' are those elders who ask about the meaning of the commentary. “On the way between” means on the path of returning from the village to the monastery after collecting alms. “Three… having made him take” means three or four warmings.

Kenaci [M 2.0267] papañcenāti kenaci sarīrakiccabhūtena papañcena. Saññaṃ akāsi rattiyaṃ pacchato gacchantaṃ asallakkhento.

“By some proliferation” means by some proliferation that is a bodily function. He made a sign at night, not noticing the one going behind.

Kasmā pana thero antevāsikānaṃ anārocetvāva gatoti āha “thero kirā”tiādi. Arahattaṃ nāma kinti tadadhigamassa adukkarabhāvaṃ sandhāya vadati. Catūhi iriyāpathehīti catūhipi [V 2.0248] iriyāpathehi pavattamānassa, tasmā yāva arahattādhigamā sayanaṃ paṭikkhipāmīti adhippāyo.

But why did the elder go without informing his pupils? It is said, “The elder, it is said,” and so on. “What is arahantship?” He speaks referring to the not-difficult nature of its attainment. “With the four postures” means for one conducting himself in all four postures. Therefore, the intention is, “Until the attainment of arahantship, I will reject lying down.”

“Anucchavikaṃ nu kho te eta”nti saṃvegajāto vīriyaṃ samuttejento arahattaṃ aggahesi ettakaṃ kālaṃ vipassanāya suciṇṇabhāvato ñāṇassa paripākaṃ gatattā.

“Is this suitable for you?” Stirred by a sense of urgency, he roused his energy and attained arahantship, due to insight having been well-practiced for such a long time and his knowledge having reached maturity.

Parimajjīti parimasi. Keci pana “parimajjīti parivattetvā therena dhoviyamānaṃ pariggahetvā dhovī”ti atthaṃ vadanti.

“Parimajjī” means “parimasi” (he handled it). Some, however, say that the meaning of “parimajjī” is “having turned it over, he took hold of what was being washed by the elder and washed it.”

Vipassanāya ārammaṇaṃ nāma upacārajjhānapaṭhamajjhānādi.

The object of insight is, namely, access concentration, the first jhāna, and so forth.

“Savitakkasavicāradomanasse”tiādīsu vattabbaṃ somanassesu vuttanayānusārena veditabbaṃ.

What is to be said regarding “displeasure with applied and sustained thought,” etc., should be understood according to the method stated for cases of joy.

362. Evarūpāti yā akusalānaṃ abhibuddhiyā, kusalānaṃ parihānāya ca saṃvattati, evarūpā, sā pana kāmūpasañhitatāya “gehasitā”ti vuccatīti āha “gehasitaupekkhā”ti. “Bālassā”tiādīsu bālakaradhammayogato bālassa attahitaparahitabyāmūḷhatāya mūḷhassa puthūnaṃ kilesādīnaṃ jananādīhi kāraṇehi puthujjanassa kilesodhīnaṃ maggodhīhi ajitattā anodhijinassa, odhijino vāyapekkhā, odhiso ca kilesānaṃ jitattā, tenassa sekkhabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati. Sattamabhavādito uddhaṃ pavattanavipākassa ajitattā avipākajinassa, vipākajinā vā arahanto appaṭisandhikattā, tenassa asekkhattaṃ paṭikkhipati. Anekādīnave sabbesampi pāpadhammānaṃ [P 2.0338] mūlabhūte sammohe ādīnavānaṃ adassanasīlatāya anādīnavadassāvino. Āgamādhigamābhāvā assutavato. Ediso ekaṃsena andhaputhujjano nāma hotīti tassa andhaputhujjanabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ punapi “puthujjanassā”ti vuttaṃ. Evarūpāti vuttappakārā [M 2.0268] sammohapubbikā. Rūpaṃ sā nātivattatīti rūpānaṃ samatikkamanāya kāraṇaṃ na hoti, rūpārammaṇe kilese nātikkamatīti adhippāyo. Aññāṇāvibhūtatāya ārammaṇe ajjhupekkhanavasena pavattamānā lobhasampayuttaupekkhā idhādhippetāti tassa lobhassa anucchavikameva ārammaṇaṃ dassento “iṭṭhārammaṇe”ti āha. Anativattamānā anādīnavadassitāya. Tato eva assādānupassanato tattheva laggā. Abhisaṅgassa lobhassa vasena, dummocanīyatāya ca tena laggitā viya hutvā uppannā.

362. ‘Such’ refers to that which leads to the increase of unwholesome states and the decline of wholesome ones. That equanimity, being connected with sensual pleasure, is called ‘household-based’; thus it is said, ‘household-based equanimity.’ In the phrases beginning with ‘of a fool,’ it is said ‘of a fool’ because of his association with foolish qualities; ‘of one deluded’ because of his confusion regarding his own welfare and that of others; ‘of an ordinary person’ because of reasons such as generating various defilements; ‘of one who has not conquered the floods’ because he has not conquered the floods of defilements by the floods of the path. Or, a flood-conqueror is one who has conquered the defilements by the flood of the path; this denies his state as a learner. ‘Of one unconquered by the result’ is said because of not having conquered the result that arises from the seventh existence onwards. Or, arahants are ‘conquerors of the result’ due to having no further rebirth; this denies his state as a non-learner. ‘Of one who does not see danger’ is said due to his nature of not seeing the dangers in delusion, which is the root of all evil states and has many dangers. ‘Of one unlearned’ is said due to the absence of scriptural learning and realization. Such a person is indeed a blind ordinary worldling; to show his state as a blind ordinary worldling, it is again stated ‘of an ordinary person.’ ‘Such’ refers to the aforementioned equanimity preceded by delusion. ‘It does not transcend form’ means it is not a cause for surpassing forms; the meaning is that it does not overcome defilements regarding form as an object. Here, the intended equanimity is that associated with greed, which proceeds by way of indifference towards the object due to being overcome by ignorance. To indicate that its object is exactly suitable for that greed, it is said, ‘with a desirable object.’ Not transcending, due to not seeing the danger. Because of that, from seeing only the gratification, it clings right there. By the power of clinging greed, and due to its difficult-to-release nature, it arises as if stuck by it.

Evarūpāti [V 2.0249] yā akusalānaṃ pahānāya, kusalānañca abhibuddhiyā saṃvattati, evarūpā, sā pana pabbajjādivasena pavattiyā nekkhammūpasañhitāti āha “nekkhammasitā”ti. Idāni taṃ pāḷivasena dassetuṃ “tattha katamā”tiādi vuttaṃ, tassattho heṭṭhā vuttanayānusārena veditabbo. Rūpaṃ sā ativattatīti rūpasmiṃ sammadeva ādīnavadassanato. Rūpaniyātāti kilesehi anabhibhavanīyato. Iṭṭheti sabhāvato, saṅkappato ca iṭṭhe ārammaṇe. Arajjantassāti na rajjantassa rāgaṃ anuppādentassa. Aniṭṭhe adussantassāti ettha vuttanayena attho veditabbo. Samaṃ sammā yoniso na pekkhanaṃ asamapekkhanaṃ, taṃ pana iṭṭhāniṭṭhamajjhatte viya iṭṭhāniṭṭhesupi bālassa hotīti “iṭṭhāniṭṭhamajjhatte”ti avatvā “asamapekkhanena asammuyhantassā”ti vuttaṃ, tividhepi ārammaṇe asamapekkhanavasena muyhantassāti attho. Vipassanāñāṇasampayuttā upekkhā. Nekkhammasitā upekkhā vedanāsabhāgāti udāsinākārena pavattiyā, upekkhā [P 2.0339] vedanāya ca sabhāgā. Ettha upekkhā vāti ettha etasmiṃ upekkhāniddese “upekkhā”ti gahitā eva. Tasmāti tatramajjhattupekkhāyapi idha upekkhāggahaṇena gahitattā. Tañhi sandhāya “paṭhamadutiyatatiyacatutthajjhānavasena uppajjanakaupekkhā”ti vuttaṃ.

‘Of such a kind’ refers to that which leads to the abandoning of unwholesome qualities and the increase of wholesome qualities. That equanimity, by its occurrence by way of going forth and so on, is connected with renunciation; thus it is called ‘based on renunciation.’ Now, to explain it according to the Pāli text, ‘Herein, what is…’ and so on is stated. Its meaning should be understood according to the method explained previously. ‘It transcends form’ means because of rightly seeing the danger in form. ‘It is unconquered by form’ means because it cannot be overpowered by defilements. ‘Desirable’ means in a desirable object, both by nature and by thought. ‘Not lusting’ means for one not lusting, not producing lust. ‘Undisturbed by the undesirable’—here, the meaning should be understood in the way explained. Not looking equally, rightly, and wisely is ‘unequal looking.’ But since this occurs in a fool regarding desirable and undesirable objects as well as desirable, undesirable, and neutral ones, instead of saying ‘in the desirable, undesirable, and neutral,’ it is said ‘not being deluded by unequal looking’—the meaning is that one is deluded in all three types of objects due to unequal looking. It is equanimity associated with insight-knowledge. Equanimity based on renunciation shares the nature of feeling because it proceeds in a detached manner, and it shares the nature of equanimous feeling. Here, in this exposition of equanimity, the word ‘equanimity’ is simply taken as such. Therefore, because even the equanimity of neutrality is included here by the term ‘equanimity,’ with reference to that it is said: ‘The equanimity that arises by way of the first, second, third, and fourth jhānas.’

Tāyapi nekkhammasitaupekkhāyāti niddhāraṇe bhummaṃ. “Yaṃ nekkhammavasenā”tiādi heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttā natthameva.

‘Even by that equanimity based on renunciation’ is the locative case in the sense of specification. As for ‘That which is by way of renunciation,’ and so on, because the method is stated below, the meaning is plain.

363. Yadi sakkassa tadā sotāpattiphalapattiyāva upanissayo, atha kasmā bhagavā yāva arahattaṃ desanaṃ vaḍḍhesīti āha “buddhānañhī”tiādi. Taruṇasakkoti abhinavo adhunā pātubhūto sakko. Sampati [M 2.0269] pātubhāvañhi sandhāya “taruṇasakko”ti vuttaṃ, na tassa kumāratā, vuddhatā vā atthi. Gatāgataṭṭhānanti gamanāgamanakāraṇaṃ. Na paññāyati na upalabbhati. Gabbhaseyyakānañhi cavantānaṃ kammajarūpaṃ vigacchati anudeva cittajaṃ, āhārajañca paccayābhāvato, utujaṃ pana sucirampi kālaṃ paveṇiṃ ghaṭṭentaṃ bhassantaṃ vā sosantaṃ vā kilesantaṃ vā viṭṭhataṃ vā hoti, na evaṃ devānaṃ. Tesañhi opapātikattā kammajarūpe antaradhāyante sesatisantatirūpampi tena saddhiṃ antaradhāyati. Tenāha “dīpasikhāgamanaṃ viya hotī”ti. Sesadevatā na jāniṃsu punapi sakkattabhāvena tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne nibbattattā. Tīsu ṭhānesūti somanassadomanassaupekkhāvissajjanāvasānaṭṭhānesu. Nibbattitaphalamevāti sappimhā sappimaṇḍo viya āgamanīyapaṭipadāya nibbattitaphalabhūtaṃ lokuttaramaggaphalameva kathitaṃ. Sakuṇikāya viya kiñci gayhūpagaṃ [P 2.0340] uppatitvā uḍḍetvā ullaṅghitvā. Assāti maggaphalasaññitassa ariyassa dhammassa.

363. If at that time Sakka had the supporting condition only for attaining the fruit of stream-entry, then why did the Blessed One extend the teaching up to arahantship? To this it is said, ‘For Buddhas…,’ and so on. ‘Young Sakka’ means the newly appeared Sakka, who has now manifested. It is called ‘young Sakka’ with reference to his recent manifestation; it is not that he is a youth or an elder. ‘The place of coming and going’ means the reason for coming and going. It is not perceived or found. For beings lying in the womb, when they pass away, the kamma-born form ceases, and immediately the mind-born and nutriment-born forms also cease due to the absence of their conditions. But the temperature-born form persists for a long time, continuing in its series, or falling apart, or drying up, or decaying, or becoming scattered—it is not so for devas. For them, being of spontaneous rebirth, when the kamma-born form disappears, the remaining continuity of form also disappears along with it. Hence it is said, ‘It is like the going of a lamp’s flame.’ The other deities did not know because he was reborn in that very same place with the state of being Sakka. ‘In three places’ refers to the places which are the conclusion of the abandoning of joy, displeasure, and equanimity. ‘Only the produced fruit’ means: just as the cream of ghee is produced from ghee, so the supramundane path and fruit, which have become the fruit produced by the practice that is to be undertaken, are spoken of. ‘Like a bird’ means having taken hold of something graspable, having flown up, having soared, and having leaped over. ‘Of this’ refers to the noble Dhamma, designated as the path and fruit.

Pātimokkhasaṃvaravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Pātimokkha Restraint

364. Pātimokkhasaṃvarāyāti [V 2.0250] pātimokkhabhūtasīlasaṃvarāyāti ayamettha atthoti āha “uttamajeṭṭhakasīlasaṃvarāyā”ti. “Pātimokkhasīlañhi sabbasīlato jeṭṭhakasīla”nti dīghavāpīvihāravāsi sumatthero vadati, antevāsiko panassa tepiṭakacūḷanāgatthero “pātimokkhasaṃvaro eva sīlaṃ, itarāni pana ‘sīlanti vuttaṭṭhānaṃ nāma atthī’ti ananujānanto indriyasaṃvaro nāma chadvārarakkhāmattakaṃ, ājīvapārisuddhi dhammena samena paccayuppādanamattakaṃ, paccayasannissitaṃ paṭiladdhapaccaye ‘ida mattha’nti paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjanamattakaṃ, nippariyāyena pātimokkhasaṃvarova sīlaṃ. Tathā hi yassa so bhinno, so itarāni rakkhituṃ abhabbattā asīlo hoti. Yassa pana sabbaso arogo sesānaṃ rakkhituṃ bhabbattā sampannasīlo”ti vadati, tasmā itaresaṃ tassa parivārabhāvato, sabbaso ekadesena ca tadantogadhabhāvato tadeva padhānasīlaṃ nāmāti āha “uttamajeṭṭhakasīlasaṃvarāyā”ti. Tattha yathā heṭṭhā papañcasaññāsaṅkhānirodhasāruppagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pucchitena bhagavatā papañcasaññānaṃ, paṭipadāya ca mūlabhūtaṃ vedanaṃ vibhajitvā paṭipadā desitā sakkassa ajjhāsayavasena saṃkilesadhammappahānamukhena vodānadhammapāripūrīti, evaṃ tassā eva paṭipadāya mūlabhūtampi sīlasaṃvaraṃ pucchitena bhagavatā [M 2.0270] yato so visujjhati, yathā ca visujjhati, tadubhayaṃ sakkassa ajjhāsayavasena vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “kāyasamācārampī”tiādi vuttaṃ saṃkilesadhammappahānamukhena vodānadhammapāripūrīti katvā. Sīlakathāyaṃ asevitabbakāyasamācārādikathane kāraṇaṃ vuttameva, tasmā kammapathavasenāti kusalākusalakammapathavasena.

364. 'For the restraint of the Pātimokkha' means for the restraint of virtue that is the Pātimokkha. This is its meaning here, as stated: 'for the restraint of the supreme and foremost virtue.' 'For the Pātimokkha virtue is the foremost virtue among all virtues,' says the Elder Sumana, resident of Dīghavāpi Monastery. His pupil, however, the Elder Cūḷanāga, a master of the three Piṭakas, not conceding that the term 'virtue' applies elsewhere, says: 'Only the Pātimokkha restraint is virtue. As for the others: restraint of the senses is merely guarding the six sense doors; purity of livelihood is merely producing requisites righteously and equitably; virtue dependent on requisites is merely using them after reflecting, "This is for this purpose," upon receiving them. Unconditionally, only the Pātimokkha restraint is virtue. For one whose restraint is broken becomes unvirtuous, being incapable of guarding the others. But one who is entirely faultless in this respect is of accomplished virtue, being capable of guarding the rest.' Therefore, because the other forms of virtue are its retinue and because they are included within it, either wholly or in part, it is called the 'supreme and foremost virtue.' Here, just as the Blessed One, when asked by Sakka about the path leading to the cessation of proliferating perceptions and thoughts, analyzed feeling—the root cause of both proliferating perceptions and thoughts and of the path—and taught the path accordingly, in line with Sakka’s inclination, through the abandonment of defiling states and the fulfillment of purifying states, so too, when asked about the root of that very path—the restraint of virtue—the Blessed One said, 'bodily conduct etc.,' in order to explain whereby it is purified and how it is purified, in accordance with Sakka’s inclination, through the abandonment of defiling states and the fulfillment of purifying states. In the discourse on virtue, the reason for explaining bodily conduct, etc., that should not be cultivated has already been stated. Therefore, 'by way of the courses of action' means by way of wholesome and unwholesome courses of action.

Kammapathavasenāti ca kammapathavicāravasena[P 2.0341]. Kammapathabhāvaṃ apattānampi hi kāyaduccaritādīnaṃ asevitabbakādīnaṃ asevitabbakāyasamācārādibhāvo idha vuccatīti. Paṇṇattivasenāti sikkhāpadapaṇṇattivasena. Yato yato hi yā yā veramaṇī, tadubhayepi vibhāvento paṇṇattivasena katheti nāma. Tenāha “kāyadvāre”tiādi. Sikkhāpadaṃ vītikkamati etenāti sikkhāpadavītikkamo, sikkhāpadassa vītikkamanākārena pavatto akusaladhammo yaṃ, tassa asevitabbakāyasamācārāditā. Vītikkamapaṭipakkho avītikkamo, na vītikkamati etenāti avītikkamo, sīlaṃ.

'By way of the courses of action' means by way of considering the courses of action. For here it is said that even for things that have not reached the status of a course of action, such as bodily misconduct, etc., there is the state of bodily conduct, etc., that should not be cultivated. 'By way of proclamation' means by way of the proclamation of the training rules. For when one analyzes both—from whatever source, whatever abstinence there is—one speaks by way of proclamation. Therefore, it is said, 'through the bodily door,' etc. 'Transgression of a training rule' means that by which one transgresses a training rule. The unwholesome state that proceeds in the manner of transgressing a training rule: that is the nature of bodily conduct, etc., that should not be cultivated. The opposite of transgression is non-transgression. 'Non-transgression' means that by which one does not transgress; this is virtue.

Micchā sammā ca pariyesati etāyāti pariyesanā, ājīvo, atthato paccayagavesanabyāpāro kāyavacīdvāriko. Yadi evaṃ kasmā visuṃ gahaṇanti āha “yasmā”tiādi[V 2.0251]. Ariyā niddosā pariyesanā gavesanāti ariyapariyesanā, ariyehi sādhūhi pariyesitabbātipi ariyapariyesanāti. Vuttavipariyāyato anariyapariyesanā veditabbā.

'Seeking' (pariyesanā) is that by which one seeks, both wrongly and rightly; it is livelihood. In meaning, it is the activity of searching for requisites through the doors of body and speech. If so, why is it taken up separately? It is said, 'Because...' etc. Noble seeking is faultless seeking. Or, because it is to be sought by the noble and good, it is noble seeking. Ignoble seeking is to be understood as the opposite of what has been said.

Jātidhammoti jāyanasabhāvo jāyanapakatiko. Jarādhammoti jīraṇasabhāvo. Byādhidhammoti byādhisabhāvo. Maraṇadhammoti mīyanasabhāvo. Sokadhammoti socanakasabhāvo. Saṃkilesadhammoti saṃkilissanasabhāvo.

'Subject to birth' means having the nature of arising, having the characteristic of arising. 'Subject to aging' means having the nature of decaying. 'Subject to illness' means having the nature of sickness. 'Subject to death' means having the nature of dying. 'Subject to sorrow' means having the nature of sorrowing. 'Subject to defilement' means having the nature of becoming defiled.

Puttabhariyanti puttā ca bhariyā ca. Esa nayo sabbattha. Dvandekattavasena tesaṃ niddeso. Jātarūparajatanti ettha pana yato vikāraṃ anāpajjitvā sabbaṃ jātarūpameva hotīti jātarūpaṃ nāma suvaṇṇaṃ. Dhavalasabhāvatāya rajatīti rajataṃ, rūpiyaṃ. Idha pana suvaṇṇaṃ ṭhapetvā yaṃ kiñci upabhogaparibhogārahaṃ “rajata”ntveva gahitaṃ vohārūpagamāsakādi. Jātidhammā hete, bhikkhave, upadhayoti [P 2.0342] ete kāmaguṇūpadhayo nāma honti, te sabbepi jātidhammāti dasseti.

'Children and wives' (puttabhariyā) means children and wives. This principle applies everywhere. Their designation is by way of a dvandva compound used as a collective singular. As for 'gold and silver' (jātarūparajata), here, because without undergoing any transformation it is all simply 'in its born form,' 'jātarūpa' means gold. Due to its bright nature, it 'shines' (rajati), thus it is 'rajata,' silver. Here, however, apart from gold, whatever is suitable for use and enjoyment is taken simply as 'rajata'—such as currency for exchange and the like. 'These, bhikkhus, are acquisitions subject to birth'—this shows that these are called the acquisitions of sensual pleasures, and that all of them are subject to birth.

Byādhidhammavārādīsu [M 2.0271] jātarūparajataṃ na gahitaṃ. Na hetassa sīsarogādayo byādhayo nāma santi, na sattānaṃ viya cutisaṅkhātaṃ maraṇaṃ, na soke uppajjati, cutisaṅkhātaṃ maraṇanti ca ekabhavapariyāpannakhandhanirodho, so tassa natthi, khaṇikanirodho pana khaṇe khaṇe labbhateva. Rāgādīhi pana saṃkilesehi saṃkilissatīti saṃkilesadhammavāre gahitaṃ jātarūpaṃ, tathā utusamuṭṭhānattā jātidhammavāre, malaṃ gahetvā jīraṇato jarādhammavāre ca. Ariyehi na araṇīyā, pariyesanātipi anariyapariyesanā.

In the sections on being subject to disease and so on, gold and silver are not included. For they have no diseases such as headaches, nor death in the sense of the passing away of beings, nor does sorrow arise for them. Death in the sense of passing away is the cessation of the aggregates pertaining to a single existence; that does not exist for them, but momentary cessation is indeed found moment by moment. But because gold is defiled by defilements such as lust, it is included in the section on being subject to defilement; likewise, because it arises from physical conditions, it is in the section on being subject to birth; and because it becomes tarnished and decays, it is in the section on being subject to aging. Also, ignoble seeking (anariyapariyesanā) is seeking that is not to be undertaken (na araṇīyā) by the noble ones (ariyan).

Idāni anesanāvasenāpi taṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Iminā nayena sukkapakkhepi attho veditabbo.

Now, to show this also by way of wrong seeking, the phrase 'furthermore,' etc., is stated. By this method, the meaning should be understood in the bright section as well.

Sambhārapariyesanaṃ paharaṇavisādigavesanaṃ, payogavasena payogakaraṇaṃ tajjāvāyāmajananaṃ tādisaṃ upakkamanibbattanaṃ, pāṇātipātādiatthaṃ gamanaṃ, paccekaṃ kāla-saddo yojetabbo “sambhārapariyesanakālato paṭṭhāya, payogakaraṇakālato paṭṭhāya, gamanakālato paṭṭhāyā”ti. Itaroti “sevitabbo”ti vuttakāyasamācārādiko. Cittampi uppādetabbaṃ. Tathā uppāditacitto hi sati paccayasamavāye tādisaṃ payogaṃ parakkamaṃ karonto paṭipattiyā matthakaṃ gaṇhāti. Tenāha “cittuppādampi kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, kusalesu dhammesu bahupakāraṃ vadāmī”ti (ma. ni. 1.84).

The search for materials is the seeking of weapons, poisons, etc.; making the preparation is generating the appropriate effort, producing such an endeavor; going for the purpose of killing living beings, etc. The word 'time' should be connected with each term: 'starting from the time of searching for materials, starting from the time of making the preparation, starting from the time of going.' The other refers to bodily conduct, etc., spoken of as 'should be cultivated.' The mind, too, should be aroused. For one whose mind is thus aroused, when there is a convergence of conditions, by making such an application and exertion, reaches the culmination of the practice. Therefore, it is said: 'I declare, bhikkhus, that the arising of mind is of great benefit in wholesome qualities' (MN 1.84).

Idāni [V 2.0252] taṃ matthakappattaṃ asevitabbaṃ, sevitabbañca dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Saṅghabhedādīnanti ādi-saddena lohituppādanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Buddharatanasaṅgharatanupaṭṭhāneheva dhammaratanupaṭṭhānasiddhīti āha “divasassa dvattikkhattuṃ tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ upaṭṭhānagamanādivasenā”ti[P 2.0343]. Dhanuggahapesanaṃ dhanuggahapurisānaṃ uyyojanaṃ. Ādi-saddena pañcavarayācanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. “Ajātasattuṃ pasādetvā lābhuppādavasena parihīnalābhasakkārassa kulesu viññāpana”nti evamādiṃ anariyapariyesanaṃ pariyesantānaṃ.

Now, to show that which should not be cultivated and that which should be cultivated, having reached their culmination, the phrase 'furthermore,' etc., is stated. By 'schism in the Sangha, etc.,' the word 'etc.' includes shedding the blood of a Buddha and so on. The accomplishment of attending to the Dhamma jewel is through attending to the Buddha jewel and the Sangha jewel. Hence, it is said: 'by way of going to attend to the three jewels two or three times a day, and so on.' 'Sending of archers' is the dispatching of men with bows. By 'etc.' is included asking for the five boons and so on. For those who engage in ignoble seeking such as: 'making it known among families that one's gain and honor have declined, as a way of producing gain by having won the favor of Ajātasattu.'

Pāripūriyāti pāripūriatthaṃ. Aggamaggaphalavaseneva hi sevitabbānaṃ pāripūrīti tadatthaṃ sabbā pubbabhāgapaṭipadā, pātimokkhasaṃvaropi aggamaggeneva paripuṇṇo [M 2.0272] hotīti tadatthaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ vatvā nigamento “pātimokkho…pe… hotī”ti āha.

'For fulfillment' means for the purpose of fulfillment. For the fulfillment of things that should be cultivated is indeed by means of the supreme path and fruit; for that purpose is the entire preliminary practice. The Pātimokkha restraint, too, is perfected only by the supreme path. Therefore, having stated the preliminary practice for that purpose, he concludes by saying, 'the Pātimokkha... is...'

Indriyasaṃvaravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Restraint of the Senses

365. Indriyānaṃ pidhānāyāti indriyānaṃ pidahanatthāya. Indriyāni ca cakkhādīni dvārāni, tesaṃ pidhānaṃ saṃvaraṇaṃ akusaluppattito gopanāti āha “guttadvāratāyā”ti. Asevitabbarūpādivasena indriyesu aguttadvāratā asaṃvaro, saṃkilesadhammavippahānavasena vodānadhammapārisuddhīti. Kāmaṃ pāḷiyaṃ asevitabbampi rūpādi dassitaṃ, sakkena pana indriyasaṃvarāya paṭipatti pucchitāti tameva nivattetvā dassetuṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃvuttaṃ “cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpampītiādi sevitabbarūpādivasena indriyasaṃvaradassanatthaṃ vutta”nti. “Tuṇhī ahosī”ti vatvā tuṇhībhāvassa kāraṇaṃ byatirekamukhena vibhāvetuṃ “kathetukāmopī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ayanti sakko devānaṃ indo.

365. "For the restraint of the senses" means for the purpose of restraining the senses. The senses, such as the eye, are doors; their restraint is guarding, protecting them from the arising of unwholesome states—thus it is said, "by guardedness of the doors." Unguardedness of the doors regarding the senses, by way of forms and so on that should not be cultivated, is lack of restraint. Through the abandoning of defiling states, there is purity of cleansing states. Although in the Pāḷi text, forms and so on that should not be cultivated are also shown, since Sakka asked about the practice for sense-restraint, in order to turn back and show just that, it is said in the commentary: "‘Forms cognizable by the eye,’ and so on, is said for the purpose of showing sense-restraint by way of forms and so on that should be cultivated." Having said, "He remained silent," in order to explain the reason for his silence by way of contrast, "Though desiring to speak," and so on, was said. This is Sakka, the lord of the devas.

Rūpanti rūpāyatanaṃ, tassa asevanaṃ nāma adassanaṃ evāti āha “na sevitabbaṃ na daṭṭhabba”nti. Yaṃ pana sattasantānagataṃ rūpaṃ passato paṭikūlamanasikāravasena, asubhasaññā vā saṇṭhāti dassanānuttariyavasena. Atha vā kammaphalasaddahanavasena pasādo vā uppajjati. Hutvā abhāvākārasallakkhaṇena aniccasaññāpaṭilābho vā hoti.

"Form" refers to the form-base. Not cultivating it means not seeing it; thus it is said, "It should not be cultivated; it should not be seen." However, for one who sees a form belonging to the continuity of a being, either the perception of foulness is established by means of attention to the repulsive, or confidence arises by means of the unsurpassed nature of seeing or by means of faith in the fruit of kamma, or the acquisition of the perception of impermanence occurs by noting the characteristic of having-been-and-then-not-being.

Pariyāyakkharaṇato [P 2.0344] akkharaṃ, vaṇṇo, so eva nirantaruppattiyā samuddito padavākyasaññito, adhippetamatthaṃ byañjetīti byañjanaṃ, tayidaṃ kābyanāṭakādigatavevacanavasena, uccāraṇavasena ca vicittasannivesatāya tathāpavattavikappanavasena cittavicittabhāvena upatiṭṭhanakaṃ [V 2.0253] sandhāyāha “yaṃ cittakkharaṃ cittabyañjanampi saddaṃ suṇato rāgādayo uppajjantī”ti. Atthanissitanti samparāyikatthanissitaṃ. Dhammanissitanti vivaṭṭadhammanissitaṃ, lokuttararatanattayadhammanissitaṃ vā. Pasādoti ratanattayasaddhā, kammaphalasaddhāpi. Nibbidā vāti aniccasaññādivasena vaṭṭato ukkaṇṭhā vā.

A letter (`vaṇṇo`) is called a syllable (`akkharaṃ`) from its function in speech (`pariyāyakkharaṇato`). That very thing, arising uninterruptedly and being proclaimed, is designated as "word" and "sentence." Because it makes manifest (`byañjeti`) the intended meaning, it is an "expression" (`byañjanaṃ`). Referring to this—which, by way of synonyms found in poetry, drama, and so on, and by way of utterance, due to its variegated arrangement and by way of the various alternatives of its occurrence, presents itself with variety and diversity—it is said: "When one hears a sound that is of variegated syllables and variegated expressions, lust and so on arise." "Based on the meaning" means based on the meaning pertaining to the future life. "Based on the Dhamma" means based on the Dhamma that leads away from the round of existence, or based on the Dhamma of the supramundane Triple Gem. "Confidence" is faith in the Triple Gem, and also faith in the fruit of kamma. "Disenchantment" is dissatisfaction with the round of existence by way of the perception of impermanence and so on.

Gandharasāviparodhādivasena seviyamānaṃ ayoniso paṭipannattā asevitabbaṃ nāma. Yoniso paccavekkhitvā seviyamānaṃ sampajaññavasena gahaṇato sevitabbaṃ nāma. Tena vuttaṃ “yaṃ gandhaṃ ghāyato”tiādi.

That which, being cultivated by way of opposition from scents, tastes, and so on, is called 'not to be cultivated' because it is practiced unwisely. That which, being cultivated after wise reflection, is called 'to be cultivated' because it is taken up by way of clear comprehension. Therefore it was said: "When smelling a scent," and so on.

Yaṃ [M 2.0273] pana phusatoti yaṃ pana sevitabbaṃ phoṭṭhabbaṃ anipphannasseva phusato. Āsavakkhayo ceva hoti jāgariyānuyogassa matthakappattito. Vīriyañca supaggahitaṃ hoti catutthassa ariyavaṃsassa ukkaṃsanato. Pacchimā ca…pe… anuggahitā hoti sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ niyojanato.

But as for "that which one touches," it refers to a tangible object that is to be cultivated, which one touches even when one has not yet attained perfection. And there is the destruction of the taints from having reached the culmination of the dedication to wakefulness. And energy is well undertaken from extolling the fourth noble tradition. And the future generation... is favored by being applied to the right practice.

Ye manoviññeyye dhamme iṭṭhādibhede samannāharantassa āvajjantassa āpāthaṃ āgacchanti. “Manoviññeyyā dhammā”ti vibhatti vipariṇāmetabbā, mettādivasena samannāharantassa ye manoviññeyyā dhammā āpāthaṃ āgacchanti, evarūpā sevitabbāti yojanā. Ādi-saddena karuṇādīnañceva aniccādīnañca saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tiṇṇaṃ therānaṃ dhammāti idāni vuccamānapaṭipattīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ therānaṃ manoviññeyyā dhammā. Bahi dhāvituṃ na adāsinti antopariveṇaṃ āgatameva rūpādiṃ ārabbha imasmiṃ temāse kammaṭṭhānavinimuttaṃ [P 2.0345] cittaṃ kadāci uppannapubbaṃ, antopariveṇe ca visabhāgarūpādīnaṃ asambhavo eva, tasmā visaṭavitakkavasena cittaṃ bahi dhāvituṃ na adāsinti dasseti. Nivāsagehato nivāsanagabbhato. Niyakajjhattakhandhapañcakato vipassanāgocarato. Thero kira sabbampi attanā kātabbakiriyaṃ kammaṭṭhānasīseneva paṭipajjati.

Those mind-cognizable phenomena of the pleasant and other kinds that come into range for one who is bringing them to mind and adverting to them. The case ending of "mind-cognizable phenomena" should be changed; the construction is: "those mind-cognizable phenomena that come into range for one who brings them to mind by way of loving-kindness and so on—such phenomena should be cultivated." By the word "and so on," the inclusion of compassion and the like, and impermanence and the like, should be understood. "The phenomena of the three elders" means the mind-cognizable phenomena for the three elders whose practice is now being spoken of. "He did not allow it to run outside" shows that, with respect to forms and so on that had come within the inner monastery compound, a mind divested of the meditation subject had never once arisen during this three-month period. And within the inner monastery compound, the existence of unsuitable forms and so on was impossible; therefore, he did not allow the mind to run outside by way of scattered thoughts. "From the dwelling house" means from the inner chamber of the dwelling. "From one's own internal five aggregates" means from the domain of insight. It is said that the elder undertook every single duty to be performed by him with the meditation subject as his head.

366. Asammohasampajaññavasena advejjhābhāvato eko anto etassāti ekanto, ekanto vādo etesanti ekantavādā. Tenāha “ekaṃyeva vadantī”ti, abhinnavādāti attho. Ekācārāti samānācārā. Ekaladdhikāti samānaladdhikā. Ekapariyosānāti samānaniṭṭhānā.

366. By means of non-delusion and clear comprehension, being free from doubt, this has one end, thus it is called "one-ended." They have a one-ended doctrine, thus they are "one-ended theorists." Therefore, it is said, "they speak only one thing," meaning they are of undivided doctrine. "Of one practice" means of the same practice. "Of one view" means of the same view. "Of one final goal" means of the same final goal.

Iti sakko pubbe attanā sutaṃ puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ nānāvādā cāraladdhiniṭṭhānaṃ idāni saccapaṭivedhena [V 2.0254] asārato ñatvā ṭhito, tassa kāraṇaṃ ñātukāmo tameva tāva byatirekamukhena pucchati “sabbeva dhammā nu kho”tiādinā.

Thus Sakka, who had previously heard the diverse doctrines, practices, views, and conclusions of various ascetics and brahmins, now stood firm, having known their essencelessness through the penetration of the truth. Wishing to know the reason for this, he first asks by way of contrast, with the words: "Are all phenomena indeed..." and so on.

Dhātūti ajjhāsayadhātu uttarapadalopena vuttā, ajjhāsayadhātūti ca atthato ajjhāsayo evāti āha “anekajjhāsayo nānajjhāsayo”ti. “Ekasmiṃ gantukāme eko ṭhātukāmo hotī”ti idaṃ nidassanavasena vuttaṃ iriyāpathepi nāma sattā ekajjhāsayā dullabhā, pageva [M 2.0274] laddhīsūti dassanatthaṃ. Yaṃ yadeva ajjhāsayanti yaṃ yameva sassatādiajjhāsayaṃ. Abhinivisantīti taṃ taṃ laddhiṃ diṭṭhābhinivesavasena abhimukhā hutvā duppaṭinissaggibhāvena nivisanti, ādānaggāhaṃ gaṇhanti. Thāmena ca parāmāsena cāti diṭṭhithāmena ca diṭṭhiparāmāsena ca. Suṭṭhu gaṇhitvāti ativiya daḷhaggāhaṃ gaṇhitvā. Voharantīti yathābhiniviṭṭhaṃ diṭṭhivādaṃ paññāpenti [P 2.0346] pare hi gāhenti patiṭṭhapenti. Tenāha “kathenti dīpenti kittentī”ti, ugghosentīti attho.

"Element" (`dhātu`) is stated for "element of inclination" (`ajjhāsayadhātu`), by way of elision. And "element of inclination" in meaning is just inclination; thus it is said: "of many inclinations, of various inclinations." The statement "When one wishes to go, another wishes to stay" is given as an example to show that beings of a single inclination are rare even regarding physical postures, let alone regarding views. "Whatever they are inclined towards" means whatever inclination towards eternalism and so on. "They adhere to it" means they face and settle upon that particular view by way of adherence to that view, becoming difficult to relinquish; they take it up with grasping. "With strength and with adherence" means with the strength of a view and with the misapprehension of a view. "Having grasped it well" means having grasped it with an exceedingly firm grasp. "They declare it" means they make known the view to which they have adhered, they make others grasp it, and they establish it. Therefore it is said: "They tell, they show, they glorify," which means they proclaim it.

Antaṃ atītā accantā, accantā niṭṭhā etesanti accantaniṭṭhā. Sabbesanti sabbesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ. Yogakkhemotipi nibbānaṃ catūhipi yogehi anuppaduṭṭhattā. “Accantayogakkhemā”ti vattabbe i-kārena niddesena “accantayogakkhemī”ti vuttaṃ, accantayogakkhemo vā etesaṃ atthīti accantayogakkhemīti. Caranti upagacchanti, adhigacchantīti attho. Pariyassati parikkhissati vaṭṭadukkhantaṃ āgammāti pariyosānantipi nibbānassa nāmaṃ.

Having gone beyond the end (`antaṃ`), they are ultimate (`accantā`). They have an ultimate conclusion (`accantā niṭṭhā`), thus they are of an "ultimate conclusion" (`accantaniṭṭhā`). "For all" means for all ascetics and brahmins. "Security from yokes" (`yogakkhema`) is a name for Nibbāna, because it is unafflicted by the four yokes. When "ultimate security from yokes" (`accantayogakkhemaṃ`) should be said, it is stated as `accantayogakkhemī` with an -ī suffix, indicating possession; or, "they have ultimate security from yokes," thus they are `accantayogakkhemī`. "They fare" (`caranti`) means they approach, they attain. "Final end" (`pariyosānaṃ`) is also a name for Nibbāna, because having come to the end of the suffering of the round, it will be ended (`pariyassati`), it will be exhausted (`parikkhissati`).

Saṅkhiṇātīti samucchindanena khepeti. Vināsetīti tato eva sabbaso adassanaṃ pāpeti. Vimuttāti vaṭṭadukkhato accantaniggamena visesena muttā.

"He has destroyed" (`saṅkhiṇāti`) means he makes an end of it by cutting it off. "He has annihilated" (`vināseti`) means he thereby causes it to completely disappear. "They are liberated" (`vimuttā`) means they are specially freed through the ultimate departure from the suffering of the round.

“Issāmacchariyaṃ eko pañho”ti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu issāmacchariyaṃ vissajjananti? Saccametaṃ, yo pana ñātuṃ icchito attho, so pañho. So eva ca vissajjīyatīti nāyaṃ doso, aññathā ambaṃ puṭṭhassa labujaṃ byākaraṇaṃ viya siyā, evaṃ pañhasīsena pañhabyākaraṇaṃ vadati. Tathā hi “piyāppiya”ntiādinā vissajjanapadāneva gahitāni, “piyāppiyaṃ eko”tiādīsupi eseva nayo. Papañcasaññāti saññāsīsena papañcā eva vuttāti āha “papañco eko”ti. Ettha ca yathā pātimokkhasaṃvarapucchā kāyasamācārādivibhāgena vissajjitattā tayo pañhā jātā, evaṃ indriyasaṃvarapucchā rūpādivibhāgena vissajjitattā cha pañhā [V 2.0255] siyuṃ. Tathā sati ekūnavīsati pucchā siyuṃ, atha indriyasaṃvaratāsāmaññena ekova pañho kato, evaṃ sati pātimokkhasaṃvarapucchābhāvasāmaññena tepi tayo ekova pañhoti sabbeva dvādaseva pañhā bhaveyyunti? Nayidamevaṃ. Yasmā kāyasamācārādīsu vibhajja [P 2.0347] vuccamānesu mahāvisayatāya aparimāṇo vibhāgo sambhavati [M 2.0275] vissajjetuṃ. Sakalampi vinayapiṭakaṃ tassa niddeso. Rūpādīsu pana vibhajja vuccamānesu appavisayatāya na tādiso vibhāgo sambhavati vissajjetuṃ. Iti mahāvisayatāya pātimokkhasaṃvarapucchā tayo pañhā katā, indriyasaṃvarapucchā pana appavisayatāya ekova pañho kato. Tena vuttaṃ “cuddasa mahāpañhā”ti.

Why is it said, 'Envy and stinginess are one question,' when are not envy and stinginess the answer? This is true, but the meaning desired to be known is the question. And that very thing is answered, so this is not a fault. Otherwise, it would be like answering a question about a mango with a breadfruit. Thus, the explanation of the question is stated with the heading of the question. For instance, with 'likes and dislikes,' etc., the very terms of the answer are taken, and in 'likes and dislikes are one,' etc., this is also the method. As for 'proliferating perceptions,' under the heading of 'perceptions,' it is proliferations themselves that are spoken of; hence it is said, 'proliferation is one.' Here, just as the question on restraint by the Pātimokkha, being answered by distinguishing bodily conduct and so on, became three questions, similarly, the question on restraint of the senses, being answered by distinguishing forms and so on, could become six questions. In that case, there would be nineteen questions. But due to the generality of sense-restraint, it is made into one question. If that were so, due to the generality of the nature of the question on Pātimokkha restraint, would those three also be one question, and would all be just twelve questions? This is not so. Because when bodily conduct and so on are explained by way of division, due to the vastness of the subject matter, an immeasurable division is possible to explain. The entire Vinaya Piṭaka is its exposition. But when forms and so on are explained by way of division, due to the limited subject matter, such a division is not possible to explain. Thus, due to its vast subject matter, the question on Pātimokkha restraint was made into three questions, while the question on sense-restraint, due to its limited subject matter, was made into one question. Therefore, it was said, 'fourteen great questions.'

367. Calanaṭṭhenāti kampanaṭṭhena. Taṇhā hi kāmarāgarūparāgaarūparāgādivasena pavattiyā anavaṭṭhitatāya sayampi calati, yattha uppannā, tampi santānaṃ bhavādīsu parikaḍḍhanena cāleti, tasmā calanaṭṭhena taṇhā ejā nāma. Pīḷanaṭṭhenāti vibādhanaṭṭhena tassa tassa dukkhassa hetubhāvena. Padussanaṭṭhenāti adhammarāgādibhāvena, sammukhaparaṃmukhena, kilesāsucipaggharaṇena ca pakārato dussanaṭṭhena gaṇḍo. Anuppaviṭṭhaṭṭhenāti āsayassa dunnīharaṇīyabhāvena anuppavisanaṭṭhena. Kaḍḍhati attano ca ruciyā upaneti. Uccāvacanti paṇītabhāvaṃ, nihīnabhāvañca. Yesu samaṇabrāhmaṇesu. “Yesāha”ntipi pāḷi, tassā keci “yesaṃ aha”nti atthaṃ vadanti. Evanti sutānurūpaṃ, uggahānurūpañca. “Ahaṃ kho pana bhante aññesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ dhammācariyo hontopi bhagavato sāvako…pe… sambodhiparāyaṇo”ti evaṃ attano sotāpannabhāvaṃ jānāpeti.

367. ‘By the meaning of shaking’ means by the meaning of trembling. For craving, due to its instability in proceeding by way of sensual lust, lust for form, lust for the formless, and so on, trembles itself; and wherever it arises, it also causes that continuity to tremble by dragging it into states of becoming and so on. Therefore, by the meaning of shaking, craving is called ‘trembling.’ ‘By the meaning of oppressing’ means by the meaning of tormenting, by being the cause of this and that suffering. ‘By the meaning of corrupting,’ it is a ‘sore’ by the meaning of corrupting in various ways: due to the nature of unrighteous lust and so on, whether manifest or latent, and by the outflow of defilements and impurities. ‘By the meaning of having entered’ means by the meaning of having penetrated, due to the difficulty of removing its underlying tendency. It drags and brings one along according to its own liking. ‘High and low’ means both the refined and the base states. ‘Among those ascetics and brahmins.’ The Pāli also has ‘yesāhaṃ,’ and some explain its meaning as ‘yesaṃ ahaṃ’ (of whom I am). ‘Thus’ means in accordance with what has been heard and what has been grasped. ‘But, venerable sir, even though I am a teacher of the Dhamma to other ascetics and brahmins, I am a disciple of the Blessed One… with enlightenment as my destination’—thus he makes known his state of being a stream-enterer.

Somanassapaṭilābhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Account of the Acquisition of Joy

368. Samāpannoti samogāḷho pavattasampahāro viyātibyūḷho. Jiniṃsūti yathā asurā puna sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, evaṃ devā vijiniṃsuyevāti dassento āha “devā puna apaccāgamanāya asure jiniṃsū”ti. Tādiso hissa jayo sātisayaṃ vedapaṭilābhāya ahosi. Duvidhampi [P 2.0348] ojanti dibbaṃ, asuraṃ cāti dvippakārampi ojaṃ. Devāyeva paribhuñjissanti asurānaṃ pavesābhāvato. Daṇḍassa avacaraṇaṃ āvaraṇaṃ daṇḍāvacaro, saha daṇḍāvacarenāti sadaṇḍāvacaro, daṇḍena paharitvā vā āvaritvā vā sādhetabbanti attho.

368. 'Samāpanno' means deeply immersed, like an attack that has been launched, thoroughly permeated. 'Jiniṃsu' means: showing that just as the asuras were unable to lift their heads again, so the devas were indeed victorious, he says, 'the devas defeated the asuras so they would not return.' For such a victory was especially for the acquisition of joy. 'Both kinds of oja' means the two kinds of nutritive essence: divine and asuran. Only the devas will enjoy it, since the asuras have no access. 'Daṇḍāvacaro' means the warding off or protection by a rod. 'Sadaṇḍāvacaro' means together with the warding off by a rod; the meaning is that it is to be accomplished by striking with a rod or by warding off.

369. Imasmiṃyeva [V 2.0256] okāseti imissameva indasālaguhāyaṃ. Devabhūtassa meti pubbepi devabhūtassa sakkasseva me bhūtassa. Satoti idānipi sakkasseva sato punarāyu ca me laddho.

369. 'Imasmiṃyeva okāse' means in this very Indasāla Cave. 'Devabhūtassa me' means for me, Sakka, who was a deva before. 'Sato' means even now, being Sakka, my life has been regained.

Diviyā [M 2.0276] kāyāti dibbā, khandhapañcakasaṅkhātā kāyāti āha “dibbā attabhāvā”ti. “Amūḷho gabbhaṃ essāmī”ti iminā ariyasāvakānaṃ andhaputhujjanānaṃ viya sammohamaraṇaṃ, asampajānagabbhokkamanañca natthi, atha kho asammohamaraṇañceva sampajānagabbhokkamanañca hotīti dasseti. Ariyasāvakā niyatagatikattā sugatīsu eva uppajjanti, tatthāpi manussesu uppajjantā uḷāresu eva kulesu paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhissanti, sakkassāpi tādiso ajjhāsayo. Tena vuttaṃ pāḷiyaṃ “yattha me ramatī mano”ti, taṃ sandhāyāha “yattha me”tiādi. Sakko pana attano dibbānubhāvenāpi tādisaṃ jānituṃ sakkotiyeva.

'Diviyā kāyā' means divine; the bodies reckoned as the five aggregates, hence it is said, 'divine existences.' By 'I will enter a womb undeluded,' it is shown that for noble disciples, unlike for blind worldlings, there is no deluded death and no entry into a womb without clear comprehension; rather, there is death without delusion and entry into a womb with clear comprehension. Noble disciples, because their destiny is fixed, are reborn only in happy destinations, and even when reborn among humans, they take rebirth only in eminent families. Sakka, too, has such an inclination. Therefore, it is said in the Pāli, 'where my mind delights'; referring to that, it says, 'where my,' etc. Moreover, Sakka is indeed able to know such a thing through his divine power.

Kāraṇenāti yuttena ariyasāvakabhāvassa anucchavikena. Tenāha “samenā”ti.

'Kāraṇena' means by what is fitting and appropriate for the state of a noble disciple. Therefore, he says 'samenā' (rightly).

Sakadāgāmimaggaṃ sandhāya vadati chaṭṭhe atthavase anāgāmimaggassa vakkhamānattā. Ājānitukāmoti appattaṃ visesaṃ paṭivijjhitukāmo. Manussaloke anto bhavissati puna mānussūpapattiyā abhāvato.

He speaks with reference to the path of the once-returner, since in the sixth point of meaning the path of the non-returner is about to be explained. 'Ājānitukāmo' means wishing to penetrate a special attainment not yet reached. 'There will be an end in the human world' because there will be no further rebirth in a human existence.

Punadevāti manussesu uppanno tato cavitvā punadeva[P 2.0349]. Imasmiṃ tāvatiṃsadevalokasmiṃ. Uttamo, kīdisoti āha “sakko”tiādi.

'Again as a deva' means: having been born among humans and having passed away from there, again as a deva. In this Tāvatiṃsa deva world. 'Supreme'—of what sort? He says, 'Sakka,' etc.

Antime bhaveti mama sabbabhavesu antime sabbapariyosāne bhave. “Āyunā”ti iminā ca taṃsahabhāvino sabbepi vaṇṇādike saṅgaṇhāti. “Paññāyā”ti ca iminā sabbepi saddhāsativīriyādike. Tasmiṃ attabhāveti tasmiṃ sabbantime sakkattabhāve. Akaniṭṭhagāmī hutvāti antarāyaparinibbāyiādibhāvaṃ anupagantvā ekaṃsato uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī eva hutvā. Tato eva anukkamena avihādīsu nibbattanto. Evamāhāti “so nivāso bhavissatī”ti evamāha. “Avihādīsu…pe… nibbattissatī”ti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “esa kirā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ayañca nayo na kevalaṃ sakkasseva, atha kho mahāseṭṭhimahāupāsikānampi hotiyevāti dassento “sakko devarājā”tiādimāha.

'Antime bhave' means in my last existence, in the final, ultimate existence of all my existences. By 'āyunā' (by lifespan), he includes all accompanying qualities such as complexion and so on. And by 'paññāya' (by wisdom), all qualities such as faith, mindfulness, energy, and so on. 'Tasmiṃ attabhāve' means in that final existence as Sakka. 'Akaniṭṭhagāmī hutvā' means without becoming one who attains parinibbāna in the interval or the like, but certainly becoming one who flows upwards, one who goes to the Akaniṭṭha realm. From there, being successively reborn in the Avihā realms and so on. 'Evamāha' means he says thus: 'that will be his abode.' To elaborate on the meaning briefly stated as 'in the Avihā realms... will be reborn,' it is said, 'this indeed,' etc. And to show that this principle applies not only to Sakka but also to great merchants and great female lay followers, he says, 'Sakka, the king of devas,' etc.

370. Bhavasampattinibbānasampattīnaṃ vasena aparipuṇṇajjhāsayatāya aniṭṭhitamanoratho taṃ taṃ [V 2.0257] pattukāmoyeva hutvā ṭhito. Ye ca samaṇeti [M 2.0277] ye ca pabbajite. Pavivittavihārinoti “anekavivekattayaṃ paribrūhetvā viharantī”ti maññāmi.

370. Due to an unfulfilled inclination with respect to the attainment of becoming and the attainment of Nibbāna, his aspiration is unaccomplished, and he remains desiring to attain this and that. 'Ye ca samaṇā' (and those ascetics) means and those who have gone forth. 'Pavivittavihārino' (dwelling in seclusion)—I think, 'they dwell having developed the threefold seclusion in many ways.'

Sampādanāti maggassa upasampādanaṃ tassa sampāpanaṃ sammadeva pāpanaṃ. Virādhanāti anārādhanā anupāyapaṭipatti. Na sambhontīti anabhisambhuṇanti. Yathāpucchite atthe anabhisambhuṇanaṃ nāma sammā kathetuṃ asamatthatā evāti āha “sampādetvā kathetuṃ na sakkontī”ti.

'Sampādana' means the undertaking of the path, its attainment, its proper attainment. 'Virādhanā' means failure to attain, the practice of a wrong method. 'Na sambhonti' means they do not comprehend. Not comprehending the meaning as asked is precisely the inability to speak correctly; thus it is said, 'They are unable to speak having accomplished it.'

Tasmāti yasmā ādiccena samānagottatāya. Tenevāha “ādicca nāma gottenā”ti, tasmā[P 2.0350]. Ādicco bandhu etassāti ādiccabandhu, atha vā ādiccassa bandhūti ādiccabandhu, bhagavā, taṃ ādiccabandhunaṃ. Ādicco hi sotāpannatāya bhagavato orasaputto. Tenevāha –

'Tasmā' means because of having the same lineage as the Sun. Hence it is said, 'Ādicca by name, by lineage.' 'Ādiccabandhu' means 'Ādicca is his kinsman,' or alternatively, 'a kinsman of Ādicca,' that is, the Blessed One; to that kinsman of Ādicca. For Ādicca, by being a stream-enterer, is a legitimate son of the Blessed One. Hence it is said –

“Yo andhakāre tamasi pabhaṅkaro,

Verocano maṇḍalī uggatejo;

Mā rāhu gilī caraṃ antalikkhe,

Pajaṃ mamaṃ rāhu pamuñca sūriya”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.91);

'He who in the darkness is a dispeller of gloom, resplendent, the orb-bearer, of blazing splendor; Do not, Rāhu, swallow him who moves in space. Rāhu, release my progeny, the sun.' (saṃ. ni. 1.91);

Sāmanti sāmaṃpayogaṃ, satthu pana sāvakassa sāmaṃpayogo nāma sanipāto evāti āha “namakkāraṃ karomā”ti.

'Sāmaṃ' means personal application. But for a disciple, personal application to the Teacher is indeed association; thus, he says, 'we pay homage.'

371. Parāmasitvāti “imāya nāma pathaviyaṃ nisinnena mayā ayaṃ acchariyadhammo adhigato”ti somanassajāto, “imāya nāma pathaviyaṃ evaṃ acchariyabbhutaṃ buddharatanaṃ uppanna”nti acchariyabbhutacittajāto ca pathaviṃ parāmasitvā. Patthitapañhāti dīgharattānusayitasaṃsayasamugghātatthaṃ “kadā nu kho bhagavantaṃ pucchituṃ labhāmī”ti evaṃ abhipatthitapañhā. Yaṃ panettha atthato na vibhattaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

371. 'Parāmasitvā' means having touched the earth, thinking, 'By sitting on this very earth, I have attained this marvelous quality,' thereby giving rise to joy, and 'On this very earth, such a marvelous and wonderful Buddha-jewel has arisen,' thereby giving rise to a mind of wonder. 'Patthitapañhā' means questions eagerly desired, intended to dispel doubts harbored for a long time, thinking, 'When will I get the chance to ask the Blessed One?' Whatever here is not explicitly explained in meaning, that is indeed easily understood.

Sakkapañhasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meanings in the Commentary on the Sutta of Sakka's Questions.

9. Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness

Uddesavārakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Section concerning the Summary

373. “Kasmā [P 2.0351][V 2.0258][M 2.0278] bhagavā idaṃ suttamabhāsī”ti asādhāraṇaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ pucchati, sādhāraṇaṃ pana “pākaṭa”nti anāmasitvā “kururaṭṭhavāsīna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Samuṭṭhānanti hi desanānidānaṃ, taṃ sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇabhedato duvidhaṃ, sādhāraṇampi ajjhattikabāhirabhedato duvidhaṃ. Tattha sādhāraṇaṃ ajjhattikaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ nāma bhagavato mahākaruṇā. Tāya hi samussāhitassa bhagavato veneyyānaṃ dhammadesanāya cittaṃ udapādi. Yathāha “sattesu ca kāruññataṃ paṭicca buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokesī”tiādi. (Dī. ni. 2.69; ma. ni. 1.283; 2.339; saṃ. ni. 1.172; mahāva. 9) bāhiraṃ pana sādhāraṇaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ nāma dasasahassamahābrahmaparivārassa sahampatimahābrahmuno ajjhesanaṃ. Tathā cāha “brahmuno ca ajjhesanaṃ viditvā”ti. (Dī. ni. 2.69; ma. ni. 1.283; 2.339; saṃ. ni. 1.179; mahāva. 9) tadajjhesanuttarakālañhi dhammapaccavekkhaṇājanitaṃ appossukkataṃ paṭipassambhetvā bhagavā dhammaṃ desetuṃ ussāhajāto ahosi. Yathā ca mahākaruṇā, evaṃ dasabalañāṇādayo ca desanāya ajjhattasamuṭṭhānabhāve vattabbā. Sabbañhi ñeyyadhammaṃ, tesaṃ desetabbappakāraṃ, sattānañca āsayānusayādiṃ yāthāvato jānitvā bhagavā ṭhānāṭṭhānādīsu kosallena veneyyajjhāsayānurūpaṃ vicittanayadesanaṃ pavattesīti. Asādhāraṇampi ajjhattikabāhirabhedato duvidhameva. Tattha ajjhattikaṃ yāya mahākaruṇāya, yena ca desanāñāṇena [P 2.0352] idaṃ suttaṃ pavattitaṃ, tadubhayaṃ veditabbaṃ, bāhiraṃ pana dassetuṃ “kururaṭṭhavāsīna”ntiādimāha. Tena vuttaṃ “asādhāraṇaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ pucchatī”ti, tena “attajjhāsayādīsu catūsu suttanikkhepesu kataroya”nti suttanikkhepo pucchito hotīti itaro “kururaṭṭhavāsīna”ntiādinā “parajjhāsayoyaṃ suttanikkhepo”ti dasseti.

373. "Why did the Blessed One speak this discourse?" This question asks about the particular occasion; the common occasion, however, is not touched upon as it is 'evident,' and what is stated is 'the residents of the Kuru country,' and so on. For 'occasion' means the origin of the teaching, and it is twofold: common and particular. The common occasion is also twofold: internal and external. Therein, the internal common occasion is the Blessed One's great compassion. For, spurred on by this, the Blessed One's mind arose to teach the Dhamma to those who could be trained. As it is said: 'Out of compassion for beings, he surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye,' and so on. The external common occasion is the request of the great Brahmā Sahampati, accompanied by his retinue of ten thousand great Brahmās. And so it is said: 'And having understood Brahmā’s request.' For in the time after that request, having calmed the disinclination born from reflecting on the Dhamma, the Blessed One became zealous to teach the Dhamma. And just as great compassion, so too the ten powers of knowledge and so on should be spoken of as being an internal occasion for the teaching. For the Blessed One, having known as they really are all knowable phenomena, the manner in which they should be taught, and the dispositions, latent tendencies, and so on of beings, with skill in what is appropriate and inappropriate, set in motion a teaching of diverse methods suited to the inclinations of those who could be trained. The particular occasion is also twofold: internal and external. Therein, the internal should be understood as both the great compassion and the knowledge of teaching by which this discourse was set in motion. But to show the external, he said 'the residents of the Kuru country,' and so on. Thus it is said: 'He asks about the particular occasion.' By this, the placement of the discourse is asked: 'Among the four placements of a discourse—personal inclination, etc.—which is this?' The other shows, by 'the residents of the Kuru country,' and so on, that 'This is a discourse placed according to the inclination of others.'

Kururaṭṭhaṃ [V 2.0259] kira tadā taṃnivāsisattānaṃ yonisomanasikāravantatādinā yebhuyyena suppaṭipannatāya, pubbe ca katapuññatābalena tadā utuādisampattiyuttameva ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ “utupaccayādisampannattā”ti. Ādi-saddena bhojanādisampattiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Keci pana “pubbe [M 2.0279] pavattakuruvattadhammānuṭṭhānavāsanāya uttarakuru viya yebhuyyena utuādisampannameva hontaṃ bhagavato kāle sātisayaṃ utusappāyādiyuttaṃ taṃ raṭṭhaṃ ahosī”ti vadanti. Cittasarīrakallatāyāti cittassa, sarīrassa ca arogatāya. Anuggahitapaññābalāti laddhūpakārañāṇānubhāvā, anu anu vā āciṇṇapaññātejā. Ekavīsatiyā ṭhānesuti kāyānupassanāvasena cuddasasu ṭhānesu, vedanānupassanāvasena ekasmiṃ ṭhāne, tathā cittānupassanāvasena, dhammānupassanāvasena pañcasu ṭhānesūti evaṃ ekavīsatiyā ṭhānesu. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ arahatte pakkhipitvāti catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ yathā arahattaṃ pāpeti, evaṃ desanāvasena arahatte pakkhipitvā. Suvaṇṇacaṅkoṭakasuvaṇṇamañjūsāsu pakkhittāni sumanacampakādinānāpupphāni, maṇimuttādisattaratanāni ca yathā bhājanasampattiyā savisesaṃ sobhanti, kiccakarāni ca honti manuññabhāvato, evaṃ sīladassanādisampattiyā bhājanavisesabhūtāya kururaṭṭhavāsiparisāya desitā bhagavato ayaṃ desanā bhiyyoso mattāya sobhati, kiccakārī ca hotīti imamatthaṃ dasseti “yathā hi puriso”tiādinā. Etthāti kururaṭṭhe.

Indeed, at that time, the Kuru country was endowed with excellence of climate and other conditions because its inhabitants were for the most part well-practiced due to possessing wise attention and so on, and by the power of merit made in the past. Therefore, it is said, 'due to the excellence of climate and other conditions.' By the word 'and so on,' he includes the excellence of food and other necessities. Some, however, say: 'Due to the influence of the practice of the ancient Kuru observances, that country, being for the most part endowed with excellence of climate and so on like Uttarakuru, was, in the time of the Blessed One, exceptionally endowed with a suitable climate and other advantages.' 'Due to the fitness of mind and body' means due to the healthiness of mind and body. 'Supported by the power of wisdom' means having the power of knowledge that has received assistance, or the splendor of wisdom that has been repeatedly practiced. 'In twenty-one places' refers to fourteen places by way of the contemplation of the body, one place by way of the contemplation of feeling, likewise one place by way of the contemplation of mind, and five places by way of the contemplation of mental objects—thus, in twenty-one places. 'Having placed the meditation subject in arahantship' means having placed the meditation subject on the four truths in arahantship by way of teaching, in such a way that it leads to arahantship. Just as various flowers like jasmine and champak, placed in golden caskets and golden chests, and the seven kinds of jewels such as pearls and gems, shine with special brilliance due to the excellence of their containers and, being delightful, are effective, so too this teaching of the Blessed One, delivered to the assembly of the residents of the Kuru country—who were a special vessel due to their excellence in virtue, insight, and so on—shines all the more and is effective. This meaning is shown by the passage beginning, 'For just as a person...' 'Here' means in the Kuru country.

Pakatiyāti sarasatopi, imissā satipaṭṭhānasuttadesanāya pubbepīti adhippāyo. Anuyuttā viharanti satthu desanānusārato bhāvanānuyogaṃ.

'By nature' means by its own essence; the intention is that this was so even before this teaching of the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta. They dwell engaged, applying themselves to the practice of meditation in accordance with the Teacher's teaching.

Vissaṭṭhaattabhāvenāti [P 2.0353] aniccādivasena kismiñci yonisomanasikāre cittaṃ aniyojetvā rūpādiārammaṇe abhirativasena vissaṭṭhacittena bhavituṃ na vaṭṭati, pamādavihāraṃ pahāya appamattena bhavitabbanti adhippāyo.

'With a scattered self' means: it is not proper to be of scattered mind—delighting in objects such as forms without applying the mind to any wise attention by way of impermanence and so on. The intention is that, having abandoned dwelling in negligence, one should be diligent.

Ekāyanoti ettha ayana-saddo maggapariyāyo. Na kevalaṃ ayanameva, atha kho aññepi bahū maggapariyāyāti paduddhāraṃ karonto “maggassa hī”ti ādiṃ vatvā yadi maggapariyāyo ayana-saddo, kasmā puna “maggo”ti vuttanti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “tasmā”tiādi. Tattha ekamaggoti eko eva maggo. Na hi nibbānagāmimaggo añño atthīti. Nanu satipaṭṭhānaṃ idha maggoti adhippetaṃ, tadaññe ca bahū maggadhammā atthīti? Saccaṃ atthi, te pana satipaṭṭhānaggahaṇeneva gahitā tadavinābhāvato. Tathā [M 2.0280] hi ñāṇavīriyādayo niddese gahitā, uddese pana satiyā eva gahaṇaṃ veneyyajjhāsayavasenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Na dvidhāpathabhūto”ti iminā [V 2.0260] imassa maggassa anekamaggabhāvābhāvaṃ viya anibbānagāmibhāvābhāvañca dasseti. Ekenāti asahāyena. Asahāyatā ca duvidhā attadutiyatābhāvena vā, yā “vūpakaṭṭhakāyatā”ti vuccati, taṇhādutiyatābhāvena vā, yā “pavivittacittatā”ti vuccati. Tenāha “vūpakaṭṭhena pavivittacittenā”ti. Seṭṭhopi loke “eko”ti vuccati “yāva pare ekāhaṃ vo karomī”tiādīsūti āha “ekassāti seṭṭhassā”ti. Yadi saṃsārato nissaraṇaṭṭho ayanaṭṭho, aññesampi upanissayasampannānaṃ sādhāraṇato, kathaṃ bhagavatoti āha “kiñcāpī”tiādi. Imasmiṃ khoti ettha kho-saddo avadhāraṇe, tasmā imasmiṃ yevāti attho. Desanābhedoyeva heso, yadidaṃ “maggo”ti vā “ayano”ti vā. Ayana-saddo vā kammakaraṇādivibhāgo. Tenāha “atthato pana eko vā”ti.

Herein, in 'ekāyano,' the word 'ayana' is a synonym for path. When analyzing the word, the commentator states that not only is 'ayana' a synonym for path, but there are also many other synonyms for path, beginning with 'For the path…' etc. Addressing the objection, 'If the word 'ayana' is a synonym for path, why then is it also called 'magga'?', he says, 'Therefore…' etc. Here, 'ekamagga' means the one and only path. Indeed, there is no other path leading to Nibbāna. But is not the Foundations of Mindfulness intended here as the path, and are there not many other path-factors? It is true they exist, but they are included by the mention of the Foundations of Mindfulness itself due to their inseparability. For instance, wisdom, energy, and so on, are included in the detailed explanation, but in the summary, only mindfulness is mentioned, in accordance with the inclinations of those to be taught. The phrase 'not becoming a path with two ways' indicates that this path is not multiple paths, and also that it does not fail to lead to Nibbāna. 'Ekena' means 'without a companion.' This absence of companionship is twofold: either through the absence of oneself as a second, which is called 'secluded body,' or through the absence of craving as a companion, which is called 'secluded mind.' Hence, it is said, 'with a secluded body and a secluded mind.' Even the best in the world is called 'one,' as in such sayings as, 'I alone will do this for you.' Therefore, it is said, 'of the one, that is, of the foremost.' If the meaning of 'ayana' is the state of departing from saṃsāra, and this is common to others who are endowed with supporting conditions, how is it of the Blessed One? He says, 'Although…' etc. Herein, in 'imasmiṃ kho,' the word 'kho' is used for emphasis; therefore, the meaning is 'in this very one.' This is merely a distinction in the teaching, whether it is called 'magga' or 'ayana.' Or, the word 'ayana' can be analyzed according to grammatical categories such as agent, instrument, and so on. Hence, it is said, 'but in meaning, it is one indeed.'

Nānāmukhabhāvanānayappavattoti kāyānupassanādimukhena [P 2.0354] tatthāpi ānāpānādimukhena bhāvanānayena pavatto. Ekāyananti ekagāminaṃ, nibbānagāminanti attho. Nibbānañhi adutiyabhāvato, seṭṭhabhāvato ca “eka”nti vuccati. Yathāha “ekañhi saccaṃ na dutīyamatthī”ti (su. ni. 890). “Yāvatā bhikkhave dhammā saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā virāgo tesaṃ aggaṃ akkhāyatī”ti. (A. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90) khayo eva antoti khayanto, jātiyā khayantaṃ diṭṭhavāti jātikhayantadassī. Avibhāgena sabbepi satte hitena anukampatīti hitānukampī. Atariṃsūti tariṃsu. Pubbeti purimakā buddhā, pubbe vā atītakāle.

'Proceeding by way of development with various approaches' means it proceeds by the method of development through the approach of contemplation of the body and so on, and even there, through the approach of mindfulness of breathing and so on. 'The one way' means going to the one, that is, going to Nibbāna. For Nibbāna is called 'one' because it is without a second and because it is the best. As it is said: 'For truth is one, there is no second.' And: 'Bhikkhus, whatsoever things there are, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared the chief among them.' 'Destruction itself is the end, hence 'khayanto'; one who has seen the end of birth is a 'jātikhayantadassī' (seer of the end of birth).' 'He is compassionate for the welfare of all beings without distinction, hence he is 'hitānukampī' (compassionate for their welfare).' 'Atariṃsu' means they crossed over. 'Pubbe' means the former Buddhas, or in a former time.

Tanti tesaṃ vacanaṃ, taṃ vā kiriyāvuttivācakattaṃ na yujjati. Na hi saṅkheyyappadhānatāya sattavācino ekasaddassa kiriyāvuttivācakatā atthi. “Sakimpi uddhaṃ gaccheyyā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 7.72) viya sakiṃ ayanoti iminā byañjanena bhavitabbaṃ. Evamatthaṃ yojetvāti “ekaṃ ayanaṃ assā”ti evaṃ samāsapadatthaṃ yojetvā. Ubhayathāpīti purimanayena, pacchimanayena ca. Na yujjati idhādhippetamaggassa anekavāraṃ pavattisabbhāvato. Tenāha “kasmā”tiādi. “Anekavārampi ayatī”ti purimanayassa ayuttatādassanaṃ, “anekañcassa ayanaṃ hotī”ti pacchimanayassa.

That is their statement. Or, that it signifies an action or occurrence is not valid. For a single word that denotes a being, in which number is predominant, cannot also denote an action or occurrence. As in such phrases as 'Even once he might go upwards,' it should be expressed as 'sakiṃ ayanaṃ' (a single going). Thus, having construed the meaning of the compound word in this way: 'it has one going' (ekaṃ ayanaṃ assa), the commentator explains. In both ways—that is, by the former method and by the latter—it is not suitable, because the path intended here is of a nature to occur many times. Hence, he says, 'Why?' and so on. 'He goes repeatedly' shows the unsuitability of the former method, while 'and his going is manifold' shows that of the latter.

Imasmiṃ [M 2.0281] padeti “ekāyano ayaṃ bhikkhave maggo”ti imasmiṃ vākye, imasmiṃ vā “pubbabhāgamaggo, lokuttaramaggo”ti vidhānapade. Missakamaggoti lokiyena missako lokuttaramaggo[V 2.0261]. Visuddhiādīnaṃ nippariyāyahetukaṃ [P 2.0355] saṅgaṇhanto ācariyatthero “missakamaggo”ti āha. Itaro pariyāyahetu idhādhippetoti “pubbabhāgamaggo”ti avoca.

In this term: in this sentence, 'This, bhikkhus, is the one-way path,' or in this descriptive term, 'the preliminary path, the supramundane path.' 'Mixed path' means the supramundane path mixed with the mundane. The elder teacher, including the direct cause of purification and so on, called it the 'mixed path.' The other, the indirect cause, is intended here, and therefore he said 'preliminary path.'

Saddaṃ sutvāti “kālo bhante dhammasavanāyā”ti kālārocanasaddaṃ paccakkhato, paramparāya ca sutvā. Evaṃ ukkhipitvāti evaṃ “sundaraṃ manoharaṃ imaṃ kathaṃ chaḍḍemā”ti achaḍḍentā ucchubhāraṃ viya paggahetvā na vicaranti. Āluḷetīti viluḷito ākulo hotīti attho. Ekāyanamaggo vuccati pubbabhāgasatipaṭṭhānamaggoti ettāvatā idhādhippetatthe siddhe tasseva alaṅkāratthaṃ so pana yassa pubbabhāgamaggo, taṃ dassetuṃ “maggānaṭṭhaṅgiko”tiādikā gāthāpi paṭisambhidāmaggatova ānetvā ṭhapitā.

Having heard the sound: having heard the announcement of the time, 'Venerable sir, it is time for hearing the Dhamma,' either directly or through tradition. Thus lifting it up: thus, not discarding this beautiful and delightful talk, they do not wander about, having taken it up like a burden of sugarcane. 'Disturbed' means agitated and confused. 'The one-way path is called the preliminary path of the foundations of mindfulness'—with the intended meaning here established by this much, for the sake of embellishing that very meaning, and to show that of which this is the preliminary path, the verse beginning 'The eightfold path…' and so on has also been brought from the Paṭisambhidāmagga and placed here.

Nibbānagamanaṭṭhenāti nibbānaṃ gacchati adhigacchati etenāti nibbānagamanaṃ,soyeva aviparītasabhāvatāya attho, tena nibbānagamanaṭṭhena, nibbānādhigamūpāyatāyāti attho. Magganīyaṭṭhenāti gavesitabbatāya. “Gamanīyaṭṭhenā”ti vā pāṭho, upagantabbatāyāti attho. “Rāgādīhī”ti iminā rāgadosamohānaṃyeva gahaṇaṃ “rāgo malaṃ, doso malaṃ, moho mala”nti (vibha. 924) vacanato. “Abhijjhāvisamalobhādīhī”ti pana iminā sabbesampi upakkilesānaṃ saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ te visuṃ uddhaṭā. “Sattānaṃ visuddhiyā”ti vuttassa atthassa ekantikataṃ dassento “tathā hī”tiādimāha. Kāmaṃ “visuddhiyā”ti sāmaññajotanā, cittasseva pana visuddhi idhādhippetāti dassetuṃ “rūpamalavasena panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Na [P 2.0356] kevalaṃ aṭṭhakathāvacanameva, atha kho idaṃ ettha āhacca bhāsitanti dassento “tathā hī”tiādimāha.

By the meaning of going to Nibbāna: one goes to Nibbāna, one attains it, by means of this, hence it is a 'going to Nibbāna'; that itself is the meaning, due to its unerring nature. By this 'meaning of going to Nibbāna,' the meaning is 'by being the means for the attainment of Nibbāna.' By the meaning of being sought: because it is to be sought. Or the reading is 'by the meaning of being gone to,' which means because it is to be approached. By 'lust, etc.,' only lust, hatred, and delusion are included, in accordance with the statement: 'Lust is a stain, hatred is a stain, delusion is a stain.' But by 'covetousness, unrighteous greed, etc.,' these are specified separately in order to include all the defilements. To show the certainty of the meaning of what was said, 'for the purification of beings,' he stated, 'For thus…' and so on. Although 'for purification' is a general indication, to show that the purification of the mind is intended here, it is said, 'by way of the stain of form…' and so on. To show that this is not merely a statement from the commentary, but that it was spoken specifically in this context, he stated, 'For thus…' and so on.

Sā panāyaṃ cittavisuddhi sijjhamānā yasmā sokādīnaṃ anuppādāya saṃvattati, tasmā vuttaṃ “sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāyā”tiādi. Tattha socanaṃ ñātibyasanādinimittaṃ cetaso santāpo antonijjhānaṃ soko. Ñātibyasanādinimittameva sokāvatiṇṇato “kahaṃ ekaputtaka kahaṃ ekaputtakā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 2.353, 354; saṃ. ni. 2.63) paridevanavasena vācāvippalāpo paridavanaṃ [M 2.0282] paridevo. Āyatiṃ anuppajjanaṃ idha samatikkamoti āha “pahānāyā”ti. Taṃ panassa samatikkamāvahataṃ nidassanavasena dassento “ayañhī”tiādimāha.

And since this purification of the mind, when being accomplished, leads to the non-arising of sorrow and so on, it is therefore said, 'for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation,' and so forth. Herein, sorrow is grieving, a burning of the mind, an inner scorching, on account of the loss of relatives and so on. Lamentation is wailing, a verbal outpouring by way of lament, on account of being overcome by sorrow due to the loss of relatives and so on, as in 'Where is my only son, where is my only son?' and so forth. Here, 'overcoming' means future non-arising, so he says, 'for abandoning.' To show by way of example how this brings about overcoming, he stated, 'For this…' and so on.

Tattha yaṃ pubbe, taṃ visodhehīti atītesu khandhesu taṇhāsaṃkilesavisodhanaṃ vuttaṃ. Pacchāti parato[V 2.0262]. Teti tuyhaṃ. Māhūti mā ahu. Kiñcananti rāgādikiñcanaṃ, etena anāgatesu khandhesu saṃkilesavisodhanaṃ vuttaṃ. Majjheti tadubhayavemajjhe. No ce gahessasīti na upādiyissasi ce, etena paccuppanne khandhappabandhe upādānappavatti vuttā. Upasanto carissasīti evaṃ addhattayagatasaṃkilesavisodhane sati nibbutasabbapariḷāhatāya upasanto hutvā viharissasīti arahattanikūṭena gāthaṃ niṭṭhapesi. Tenāha “imaṃ gātha”ntiādi.

Herein, 'what was before, purify that' means the purification of the defilement of craving in past aggregates is stated. 'After' means later. 'For you' means for you. 'May there not be' means may there not be. 'Anything' means the impediment of lust and so forth; by this, the purification of defilements in future aggregates is stated. 'In between' means in the middle of both. 'If you do not grasp' means if you do not take hold; by this, the non-occurrence of clinging in the present continuum of aggregates is stated. 'Peaceful, you will fare' means thus, when the defilements connected with the three periods of time are purified, you will dwell peacefully, having become calm as all distress is extinguished—thus, he concluded the verse with the pinnacle of arahantship. Hence he said 'this verse,' and so forth.

Puttāti orasā, aññepi vā dinnakakittimādayo ye keci. Pitāti janako, aññepi vā pituṭṭhāniyā. Bandhavāti ñātakā. Ayañhettha attho – puttā vā pitā vā bandhavā vā antakena maccunā adhipannassa abhibhūtassa maraṇato tāṇāya na honti. Kasmā? Natthi ñātīsu tāṇatāti. Na hi ñātīnaṃ vasena maraṇato ārakkhā atthi, tasmā paṭācāre [P 2.0357] “ubho puttā kālaṅkatā”tiādinā (apa. therī 1.498) mā niratthakaṃ paridevi, dhammaṃyeva pana yāthāvato passāti adhippāyo.
