Sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhitāti yathānulomaṃ pavattitāya sāmukkaṃsikāya dhammadesanāya pariyosāne sahassanayapaṭimaṇḍite sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Kathaṃ panāyaṃ satipaṭṭhānamaggavasena sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsīti āha “yasmā panā”tiādi. Na hi catusaccakammaṭṭhānakathāya vinā sāvakānaṃ ariyamaggādhigamo atthi. “Imaṃ gāthaṃ sutvā”ti panidaṃ sokavinodanavasena pavattitāya gāthāya paṭhamaṃ sutattā vuttaṃ, sāpi hi saccadesanāya parivārabandhā eva aniccatākathāti katvā. Itaragāthāyaṃ pana vattabbameva natthi. Bhāvanāti paññābhāvanā. Sā hi idha adhippetā. Tasmāti yasmā rūpādīnaṃ aniccādito anupassanāpi satipaṭṭhānabhāvanāva, tasmā. Tepīti santatimahāmattapaṭācārāpi.

'Sons' means those born from one's own breast, or any others such as adopted or artificial sons. 'Father' means the begetter, or any others who occupy the position of a father. 'Relatives' means kinsmen. The meaning here is this: sons, fathers, or relatives cannot provide refuge from death for one who is seized and overcome by Antaka, the Death-maker. Why? Because there is no refuge among relatives. Indeed, there is no protection from death by means of relatives. Therefore, the intention is: as in the case of Paṭācārā, 'Both my sons have met their end,' and so forth (Apa. Therī 1.498), do not lament uselessly; instead, see the Dhamma as it truly is. 'Established in the fruit of stream-entry': at the conclusion of the progressive, uplifting Dhamma teaching, adorned with a thousand methods, she became established in the fruit of stream-entry. But how did she become established in the fruit of stream-entry through the path of the foundations of mindfulness? He says, 'Because...' and so forth. Indeed, without a discourse on the four noble truths as a subject of meditation, there is no attainment of the noble path for disciples. 'Having heard this verse': this is said because the verse, which was uttered for the dispelling of sorrow, was heard first. For that too, being a discourse on impermanence, is indeed connected to the teaching of the truths. As for the other verse, there is nothing further to be said. 'Development' means the development of wisdom. That is what is intended here. 'Therefore': because the contemplation of impermanence and so on with regard to form and other phenomena is indeed the development of the foundations of mindfulness, therefore. 'They too' means Santati the great minister and Paṭācārā.

Pañcasate [M 2.0283] coreti satasatacoraparivāre pañcacore paṭipāṭiyā pesesi, te araññaṃ pavisitvā theraṃ pariyesantā anukkamena therassa samīpe samāgacchiṃsu. Tenāha “te gantvā theraṃ parivāretvā nisīdiṃsū”ti. Vedanaṃ vikkhambhetvāti ūruṭṭhibhedapaccayaṃ dukkhavedanaṃ amanasikārena vinodetvā. Pītipāmojjaṃ uppajji vippaṭisāralesassapi asambhavato. Tenāha “parisuddhaṃ sīlaṃ nissāyā”ti. Therassa hi sīlaṃ paccavekkhato parisuddhaṃ sīlaṃ nissāya uḷāraṃ pītipāmojjaṃ uppajjamānaṃ ūruṭṭhibhedajanitaṃ dukkhavedanaṃ vikkhambhesi. Tiyāmarattinti accantasaṃyoge upayogavacanaṃ, tenassa vipassanāyaṃ appamādaṃ, paṭipattiussukkāpanañca dasseti. Pādānīti pāde. Saṃyamessāmīti saññapessāmi, saññattiṃ karissāmīti attho. Aṭṭiyāmīti jigucchāmi. Harāyāmīti lajjāmi. Vipassisanti sampassiṃ.

'Five hundred thieves': he sent five chief thieves in succession, each with a retinue of a hundred thieves. They entered the forest searching for the elder and gradually arrived near him. Hence he said, 'They went, surrounded the elder, and sat down.' 'Having suppressed the pain': dispelling the painful feeling caused by the breaking of his thigh-bone by not attending to it. Joy and gladness arose, since even regret was impossible. Therefore he said, 'Relying on purified virtue.' For the elder, reflecting on his virtue, relying on his purified virtue, great joy and gladness arose, suppressing the painful feeling caused by the breaking of his thigh-bone. 'For the three watches of the night': this is an expression denoting continuous connection, thereby showing his diligence in insight and arousing his zeal for practice. 'Feet': this means at his feet. 'I will restrain' means I will inform, that is, I will make a communication. 'I am disgusted' means I feel repugnance. 'I am ashamed' means I feel shame. 'I saw clearly' means I saw thoroughly.

Pacalāyantānanti [P 2.0358][V 2.0263] pacalāyikānaṃ niddaṃ upagatānaṃ. Agatinti agocaraṃ. Vatasampannoti dhutaguṇasampanno. Pamādanti pacalāyanaṃ sandhāyāha. Oruddhamānasoti uparuddhaadhicitto. Pañjarasminti sarīre. Sarīrañhi nhārusambandhaaṭṭhisaṅghāṭatāya idha “pañjara”nti vuttaṃ.

'Those who are drowsy' means those who are drowsy, those who have succumbed to sleep. 'Unvisited' means out of range. 'Endowed with vows' means one accomplished in ascetic qualities. 'Negligence': he speaks referring to drowsiness. 'With a confined mind' means one whose higher mind is obstructed. 'In the cage' means in the body. For the body, on account of being an assemblage of bones bound by sinews, is here called a 'cage.'

Pītavaṇṇāya pana paṭākāya kāyaṃ pariharaṇato, mallayuddhacittakatāya ca “pītamallo”ti paññāto pabbajitvā pītamallatthero nāma jāto. Tīsu rajjesūti paṇḍucoḷagoḷarajjesu. “Sabbamallā sīhaḷadīpe sakkārasammānaṃ labhantī”ti tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ āgamma. Taṃyeva aṅkusaṃ katvāti “rūpādayo ‘mamā’ti na gahetabbā”ti natumhākavaggena pakāsitamatthaṃ attano cittamattahatthino aṅkusaṃ katvā. Pādesu avahantesūti ativelaṃ caṅkamanena akkamituṃ asamatthesu. Jaṇṇukehi caṅkamati “nisinne niddāya avasaro hotī”ti. Byākaritvāti attano vīriyārambhassa saphalatāpavedanamukhena sabrahmacārīnaṃ tattha ussāhaṃ janento aññaṃ byākaritvā. Bhāsitanti vacanaṃ, kassa pana tanti āha “buddhaseṭṭhassa sabbalokaggavādino”ti. “Na tumhāka”ntiādi tassa pavattiākāradassanaṃ. Tayidaṃ me saṅkhārānaṃ accantavūpasamakāraṇanti dassento “aniccā vatā”ti gāthamāhari, tena idānāhaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇe khaṇe bhaṅgasaṅkhātassa rogassa abhāvena arogo parinibbutoti dasseti.

Then, because he went about with a yellow banner and had a mind intent on wrestling, he became known as 'Pītamalla.' After renouncing, he became known as Elder Pītamalla. 'In the three kingdoms' means in the kingdoms of Paṇḍu, Coḷa, and Goḷa. Having come to the island of Tambapaṇṇi, thinking, 'All wrestlers receive honor and respect in the island of Sri Lanka.' 'Making that very goad': that is, taking the meaning revealed in the 'Not Yours' section—'forms and so forth should not be grasped as "mine"'—he fashioned it into a goad for his own mind-elephant. 'When his feet could no longer bear him': being unable to step due to excessive walking. He walked on his knees, thinking, 'There is an opportunity for sleep while sitting.' 'Having declared': inspiring his fellow monks to exertion there by announcing the success of his own energetic striving, he declared final knowledge. 'Spoken' means the words. But whose? He said, 'Of the Buddha, the foremost, the supreme speaker in all the world.' 'Not yours,' and so forth: this shows the manner of that teaching's occurrence. To demonstrate that 'this is the cause for the ultimate calming of my formations,' he brought forth the verse, 'Impermanent, alas...' Thereby he shows: 'I am now free from disease and fully extinguished, due to the absence of that disease known as the momentary disintegration of formations.'

Assāti [M 2.0284] sakkassa. Upapattīti devūpapatti. Puna pākatikāva ahosi sakkabhāveneva upapannattā.

'His' means Sakka's. 'Rebirth' means rebirth as a deva. Again, she became her natural self, having been reborn in the state of Sakka.

Subrahmāti evaṃnāmo. Accharānaṃ nirayūpapattiṃ disvā tato pabhuti satataṃ pavattamānaṃ attano cittutrāsaṃ sandhāyāha “niccaṃ utrastamidaṃ citta”ntiādi. Tattha utrastanti santastaṃ bhītaṃ[P 2.0359]. Ubbigganti saṃviggaṃ. Utrastanti vā saṃviggaṃ. Ubbigganti bhayavasena saha nissayena sañcalitaṃ. Anuppannesūti anāgatesu. Kiccesūti tesu tesu itikattabbesu. “Kicchesū”ti vā pāṭho, dukkhesūti attho, nimittatthe cetaṃ bhummaṃ, bhāvidukkhanimittanti attho. Uppatitesūti uppannesu kiccesūti yojanā. Tadā attano parivārassa uppannaṃ dukkhaṃ sandhāya vadati.

Subrahmā is his name. Having seen the rebirth of the celestial nymphs in hell, from that time onward, referring to the constantly occurring terror in his own mind, he declared, “This mind is always terrified,” and so on. Here, 'terrified' (utrasta) means alarmed, fearful. 'Agitated' (ubbigga) means stirred with spiritual urgency (saṃvigga). Or, 'terrified' means stirred with spiritual urgency. 'Agitated' means shaken by fear together with its basis. 'In things not yet arisen' means in future things. 'In duties' means in those various things that ought to be done. Alternatively, the reading may be 'in difficulties,' meaning in sufferings; this is a locative in the sense of a sign, meaning it is a sign of future suffering. 'When they have arisen' is to be connected with 'when duties have arisen.' At that time, he speaks with reference to the suffering that has arisen for his own retinue.

Bojjhāti bodhito, ariyamaggatoti attho. “Aññatrā”ti ca padaṃ apekkhitvā nissakkavacanaṃ, bodhiṃ ṭhapetvāti attho. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Tapasāti tapokammato, tena maggādhigamassa upāyabhūtaṃ sallekhapaṭipadaṃ dasseti. Indriyasaṃvarāti manacchaṭṭhānaṃ indriyānaṃ saṃvaraṇato[V 2.0264], etena satisaṃvarasīsena sabbampi saṃvarasīlaṃ, lakkhaṇahāranayena vā sabbampi catupārisuddhisīlaṃ dasseti. Sabbanissaggāti sabbassapi nissajjanato sabbakilesappahānato. Kilesesu hi nissaṭṭhesu kammavaṭṭaṃ, vipākavaṭṭañca nissaṭṭhameva hotīti. Sotthinti khemaṃ anupaddavataṃ.

'From enlightenment' means from enlightenment, that is, from the noble path. The word 'except' is used to exclude, meaning 'excluding enlightenment.' The same principle applies to the rest. 'By austerity' means from the act of austerity; by this he shows the practice of effacement as a means to attain the path. 'From restraint of the senses' means from the restraint of the six senses, of which the mind is the sixth. By this he shows all restraint of virtue with restraint by mindfulness as its chief, or, by the method of characteristic and application, all fourfold purified virtue. 'From the relinquishment of all' means from the relinquishing of all, from the abandoning of all defilements. For when defilements are relinquished, the round of kamma and the round of result are also relinquished. 'Well-being' means safety, freedom from misfortune.

Ñāyati nicchayena kamati nibbānaṃ, taṃ vā ñāyati paṭivijjhīyati etenāti ñāyo, ariyamaggoti āha “ñāyo vuccati ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo”ti. Taṇhāvānavirahitattāti taṇhāsaṅkhātavānavivittattā. Taṇhā hi khandhehi khandhaṃ, kammunā phalaṃ, sattehi ca dukkhaṃ vinati saṃsibbatīti “vāna”nti vuccati, tayidaṃ natthi ettha vānaṃ, na vā etasmiṃ adhigate puggalassa vānanti nibbānaṃ, asaṅkhatā dhātu. Parappaccayena vinā paccakkhakaraṇaṃ sacchikiriyāti āha “attapaccakkhatāyā”ti.

One certainly proceeds to Nibbāna by this, or one knows and penetrates it by this—thus it is 'ñāya,' the noble path. Thus it is said, 'ñāya is called the Noble Eightfold Path.' It is devoid of the entanglement of craving—that is, it is separated from the entanglement known as craving. For craving binds together aggregate with aggregate, action with result, and beings with suffering—thus it is called 'entanglement.' Herein, there is no entanglement; nor is there entanglement for the person who has attained this—thus it is Nibbāna, the unconditioned element. Realization is making it directly perceived without dependence on another; thus it is said, 'by direct experience'.

Nanu “visuddhiyā”ti cittavisuddhiyā adhippetattā visuddhiggahaṇenevettha sokasamatikkamādayopi gahitā eva honti, te puna kasmā gahitāti anuyogaṃ sandhāya “tattha kiñcāpī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sāsanayuttikovideti saccapaṭiccasamuppādādilakkhaṇāyaṃ dhammanītiyaṃ cheke. Taṃ tamatthaṃ [P 2.0360][M 2.0285] ñāpetīti ye ye bodhaneyyapuggalā saṅkhepavitthārādivasena yathā yathā bodhetabbā, attano desanāvilāsena bhagavā te te tathā tathā bodhento taṃ tamatthaṃ ñāpeti. Taṃ taṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā dassentoti atthāpattiṃ agaṇento taṃ tamatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā dassento. Na hi sammāsambuddho atthāpattiñāpakādisādhanīyavacanāti. Saṃvattatīti jāyati, hotīti attho. Yasmā anatikkantasokaparidevassa na kadāci cittavisuddhi atthi sokaparidevasamatikkamanamukheneva cittavisuddhiyā ijjhanato, tasmā āha “sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamena hotī”ti. Yasmā pana domanassapaccayehi dukkhadhammehi phuṭṭhaṃ puthujjanaṃ sokādayo abhibhavanti, pariññātesu ca tesu te na honti, tasmā vuttaṃ “sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamo dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamenā”ti. Ñāyassāti aggamaggassa, tatiyamaggassa ca. Tadadhigamena hi yathākkamaṃ dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamo. Sacchikiriyābhisamayasahabhāvīpi itarābhisamayo tadavinābhāvato sacchikiriyābhisamayahetuko viya vutto. Ñāyassādhigamo nibbānassa sacchikiriyāyāti phalañāṇena vā paccakkhakaraṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, “nibbānassa sacchikiriyāyā”ti sampadānavacanañcetaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

But isn’t it that by the term 'purification,' the purification of mind is intended, and thus through the mention of purification, the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, etc., are already included? So why are they mentioned again? In response to this inquiry, 'Though indeed…' and so on is said. Skilled in the proper method of the teaching means expert in this method of Dhamma characterized by the truths, dependent origination, and so on. He makes that meaning known—that is, the Blessed One, through the elegance of his teaching, instructs those individuals who are to be enlightened, whether briefly or in detail, in whatever way is appropriate, thereby revealing that meaning. He makes it clear and shows it—that is, without resorting to implication, he makes that meaning evident and presents it. For the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One does not speak words that require inference or additional means to convey their meaning. 'It comes to be'—that is, it arises, it exists. Because for one who has not transcended sorrow and lamentation, there is never purification of mind, and since the purification of mind succeeds precisely through the transcendence of sorrow and lamentation, it is said, 'It comes to be through the transcendence of sorrow and lamentation.' Moreover, because sorrow and the like overwhelm an ordinary person afflicted by painful mental states arising from causes of distress, and when those are fully understood, they cease, it is stated, 'The transcendence of sorrow and lamentation is the cessation of suffering and distress.' 'Of the path'—that is, of the supreme path and the third path. For through the attainment of that, in due order, suffering and distress cease. The other direct knowledge, though co-existent with realization, is spoken of as if caused by realization because of its inseparability from it. 'The attainment of the path is for the realization of Nibbāna'—this refers to the direct experiencing through fruition-knowledge. And the phrase 'for the realization of Nibbāna' should be understood as a dative of purpose.

Vaṇṇabhaṇananti pasaṃsāvacanaṃ. Tayidaṃ na idheva, atha kho aññatthāpi satthu āciṇṇaṃ evāti [V 2.0265] dassento “yatheva hī”tiādimāha. Tattha ādimhi kalyāṇamādi vā kalyāṇaṃ etassāti ādikalyāṇaṃ. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Atthasampattiyā sātthaṃ. Byañjanasampattiyā sabyañjanaṃ. Sīlādipañcadhammakkhandhapāripūrito, upanetabbassa abhāvato ca kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ. Nirupakkilesato apanetabbassa ca abhāvato parisuddhaṃ. Seṭṭhacariyabhāvato [P 2.0361] sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ, maggabrahmacariyañca vo pakāsessāmīti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.147) vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Ariyavaṃsāti ariyānaṃ buddhādīnaṃ vaṃsā paveṇiyo. Aggaññāti aggāti jānitabbā sabbavaṃsehi seṭṭhabhāvato. Rattaññāti cirarattāti jānitabbā. Vaṃsaññāti buddhādīnaṃ vaṃsāti jānitabbā. Porāṇāti purātanā anadhunātanattā. Asaṅkiṇṇāti avikiṇṇā anapanītā. Asaṅkiṇṇapubbāti “kiṃ imehī”ti ariyehi na apanītapubbā[M 2.0286]. Na saṅkīyantīti idānipi tehi na apanīyanti. Na saṅkīyissantīti anāgatepi tehi na apanīyissanti. Appaṭikuṭṭhā…pe… viññūhīti ye loke viññū samaṇabrāhmaṇā, tehi appaccakkhatā aninditā, agarahitāti attho. “Visuddhiyā”tiādīhīti visuddhiādidīpanehi. Padehīti vākyehi, visuddhiatthatādibhedabhinnehi vā dhammakoṭṭhāsehi. Upaddaveti anatthe. Visuddhinti visujjhanaṃ saṃkilesappahānaṃ. Vācuggatakaraṇaṃ uggaho. Pariyāpuṇanaṃ paricayo. Atthassa hadaye ṭhapanaṃ dhāraṇaṃ. Parivattanaṃ vācanaṃ.

Praise is called 'vaṇṇabhaṇana.' This is not only here but also a practice common to the Teacher elsewhere. To show this, he begins with 'yatheva hī' and so on. Here, 'ādikalyāṇa' means good in the beginning, or that which has a good beginning. The same method applies to the remaining two phrases. It is meaningful ('sātthaṃ') due to the excellence of its meaning. It is eloquent ('sabyañjanaṃ') due to the excellence of its phrasing. It is complete ('kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ') because it is fully endowed with the fivefold aggregate of Dhamma, beginning with morality, and because there is nothing further to add. It is pure ('parisuddhaṃ') because it is free from defilements and there is nothing to remove. It is the holy life of the Dispensation and the holy life of the path, due to its nature as supreme conduct, as he declares, 'I will reveal to you.' This is the summary here; the detailed explanation should be understood in the manner stated in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. 1.147). 'Ariyavaṃsā' means the lineage or tradition of the noble ones, such as the Buddhas. 'Aggaññā' should be understood as 'foremost' because it is supreme among all lineages. 'Rattaññā' should be understood as 'long-standing,' enduring for a long time. 'Vaṃsaññā' should be understood as the lineage of the Buddhas. 'Porāṇā' means 'ancient,' not modern. 'Asaṅkiṇṇā' means 'unmixed,' not removed. 'Asaṅkiṇṇapubbā' means it has never been rejected by the noble ones with the thought, 'What is the use of these?' 'Na saṅkīyanti' means even now they are not rejected by them. 'Na saṅkīyissanti' means they will not be rejected by them in the future. 'Appaṭikuṭṭhā…pe… viññūhī' means they are not rejected, not blamed, or not censured by the wise in the world—ascetics and brahmins. By 'visuddhiyā' and so on is meant by the illuminations of purity and other qualities. By 'padehī' is meant by phrases, or by distinct sections of the Dhamma, differentiated by meanings such as purity. 'Upaddava' means harm. 'Visuddhi' means purification, the abandoning of defilements. `Uggaho` is making it come forth in speech. `Paricayo` is learning thoroughly. `Dhāraṇaṃ` is establishing the meaning in the heart. `Vācanaṃ` is repetition.

Gandhārakoti gandhāradese uppanno. Pahontīti sakkonti. Aniyyānikamaggāti micchāmaggā, micchattaniyatāniyatamaggāpi vā. Suvaṇṇanti kūṭasuvaṇṇampi vuccati. Maṇīti kācamaṇipi, muttāti veḷujāpi, pavāḷanti pallavopi vuccatīti rattajambunadādipadehi te visesitā.

Gandhārako means one born in the Gandhāra country. 'Pahonti' means they are capable. 'Aniyyānikamaggā' refers to the wrong paths, or paths that are fixed or not fixed in wrongness. 'Suvaṇṇa' can also refer to counterfeit gold. 'Maṇi' includes glass gems, 'muttā' includes bamboo-pearls, and 'pavāḷa' can also mean sprouts—these are distinguished by terms like 'red jambunada,' etc.

Na tato heṭṭhāti idhādhippetakāyādīnaṃ vedanādisabhāvattābhāvā, kāyavedanācittavimuttassa tebhūmakadhammassa visuṃ vipallāsavatthantarabhāvena gahitattā ca heṭṭhā gahaṇesu vipallāsavatthūnaṃ aniṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, pañcamassa pana vipallāsavatthuno abhāvā “na uddha”nti āha. Ārammaṇavibhāgena hettha satipaṭṭhānavibhāgoti. Tayo satipaṭṭhānāti satipaṭṭhāna-saddassa [P 2.0362] atthuddhāradassanaṃ, na idha pāḷiyaṃ vuttassa satipaṭṭhāna-saddassa atthadassananti. Ādīsu hi satigocaroti ettha ādi-saddena “phassasamudayā vedanānaṃ samudayo, nāmarūpasamudayā cittassa samudayo, manasikārasamudayā dhammānaṃ samudayo”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.408) “satipaṭṭhānā”ti vuttānaṃ sabhigocarānaṃ pakāsake suttappadese saṅgaṇhāti. Evaṃ “paṭisambhidāpāḷiya”mpi (paṭi. ma. 2.34) avasesapāḷippadesadassanattho [V 2.0266] ādi-saddo daṭṭhabbo. Satiyā paṭṭhānanti satiyā patiṭṭhātabbaṭṭhānaṃ. Dānādīni karontassa rūpādīni satiyā ṭhānaṃ hontīti taṃnivāraṇatthamāha “padhānaṃ ṭhāna”nti. Pa-saddo hi idha “paṇītā dhammā”tiādīsu (dha. saṃ. mātikā 14) viya padhānatthadīpakoti adhippāyo.

There is nothing below it—here, because the intended body, etc., do not have the nature of feeling, etc., and because the phenomena of the three planes of existence, distinct from body, feeling, and mind, are grasped as separate grounds for distortion, the statement refers to the non-establishment of the grounds for distortion in the lower graspings. However, since the fifth ground for distortion is absent, it is said, 'not above.' Here, the division of the foundations of mindfulness is by the division of objects. 'The three foundations of mindfulness'—this is a presentation of the extraction of the meaning of the term 'foundations of mindfulness,' not an exposition of the meaning of the term 'foundations of mindfulness' as used in the Pāli here. For in the phrase 'in the beginnings, the scope of mindfulness,' the word 'beginnings' includes the sutta passage, 'With the arising of contact, there is the arising of feeling; with the arising of name-and-form, there is the arising of mind; with the arising of attention, there is the arising of phenomena' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.408), which illuminates the respective domains of what are stated as 'foundations of mindfulness.' Similarly, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāli (Paṭisambhidāmagga 2.34), the word 'beginning' should be understood as indicating the remaining Pāli passages. 'The establishment of mindfulness'—this is the place where mindfulness should be established. For one engaged in giving and so on, forms, etc., might become the place of mindfulness. To prevent that, it is said, 'The principal place.' Here, the prefix 'pa-' signifies the meaning of predominance, as in 'excellent phenomena' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī Mātikā 14), this being the intention.

Ariyoti ariyaṃ sabbasattaseṭṭhaṃ sammāsambuddhamāha. Etthāti etasmiṃ saḷāyatanavibhaṅgasutte.(Ma. ni. 3.310) suttekadesena hi suttaṃ dasseti. Tattha hi –

'Ariya' refers to the Noble One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, who is the best of all beings. 'Here' means in this Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 3.310); for the sutta is indicated by a portion of the sutta. For there –

“Tayo [M 2.0287] satipaṭṭhānā yadariyo…pe… arahatīti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ. Idha, bhikkhave, satthā sāvakānaṃ dhammaṃ deseti anukampako hitesī anukampaṃ upādāya ‘idaṃ vo hitāya idaṃ vo sukhāyā’ti. Tassa sāvakā na sussūsanti. Na sotaṃ odahanti, na aññā cittaṃ upaṭṭhapenti, vokkamma ca satthu sāsanā vattanti. Tatra, bhikkhave, tathāgato na ceva anattamano hoti, na ca anattamanataṃ paṭisaṃvedeti, anavassuto ca viharati sato sampajāno. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Yadariyo sevati…pe… arahati.

There are three foundations of mindfulness which the noble one cultivates... and is worthy of. This has been said. But with reference to what was it said? Here, monks, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to his disciples out of compassion, desiring their welfare, taking compassion as his ground, thinking: ‘This is for your welfare, this is for your happiness.’ But his disciples do not listen, do not lend ear, do not set their minds on understanding, and they turn away from the Teacher’s instruction. In this case, monks, the Tathāgata is neither displeased nor does he experience displeasure. He dwells unattached, mindful and fully aware. This, monks, is the first foundation of mindfulness which the noble one cultivates... and is worthy of.

Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, satthā…pe...idaṃ vo sukhāyāti[P 2.0363]. Tassa ekacce sāvakā na sussūsanti…pe… na ca vokkamma satthu sāsanā vattanti. Tatra, bhikkhave, tathāgato na ceva anattamano hoti, na ca anattamanataṃ paṭisaṃvedeti, na ca attamano hoti, na ca attamanataṃ paṭisaṃvedeti, anattamanatā ca attamanatā ca tadubhayaṃ abhinivajjetvā upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dutiyaṃ.

Furthermore, monks, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to his disciples out of compassion, desiring their welfare, taking compassion as his ground, thinking: ‘This is for your welfare, this is for your happiness.’ Some of his disciples do not listen, do not lend ear, do not set their minds on understanding, but they do not turn away from the Teacher’s instruction. In that case, monks, the Tathāgata is neither displeased nor does he experience displeasure; nor is he pleased nor does he experience pleasure. Having abandoned both displeasure and pleasure, he dwells equanimous, mindful and fully aware. This, monks, is called the second.

Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave…pe… sukhāyāti, tassa sāvakā sussūsanti…pe… vattanti. Tatra, bhikkhave, tathāgato attamano ceva hoti, attamanatañca paṭisaṃvedeti, anavassuto ca viharati sato sampajāno. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, tatiya”nti (ma. ni. 3.311).

Furthermore, monks, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to his disciples out of compassion, desiring their welfare, taking compassion as his ground, thinking: ‘This is for your welfare, this is for your happiness.’ His disciples listen, lend ear, set their minds on understanding, and they conduct themselves in accordance with the Teacher’s instruction. In that case, monks, the Tathāgata is pleased and experiences pleasure, and he dwells unattached, mindful and fully aware. This, monks, is called the third.

Evaṃ paṭighānunayehi anavassutatā, niccaṃ upaṭṭhitassatitāya tadubhayavītivattatā “satipaṭṭhāna”nti vuttā. Buddhānaṃyeva hi niccaṃ upaṭṭhitassatitā hoti āveṇikadhammabhāvato, na [V 2.0267] paccekabuddhādīnaṃ. Pa-saddo ārambhaṃ joteti, ārambho ca pavattīti katvā āha “pavattayitabbatoti attho”ti. Satiyā karaṇabhūtāya paṭṭhānaṃ paṭṭhapetabbaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Ana-saddo hi bahulaṃvacanena kammatthopi hotīti. Tathāssa kattuatthopi labbhatīti “paṭṭhātīti paṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ. Paṭṭhātīti ettha pa-saddo bhusatthavisiṭṭhaṃ pakkhandanaṃ dīpetīti “okkanditvā pakkhanditvā pattharitvā pavattatīti attho”ti āha. Puna bhāvatthaṃ sati, saddaṃ, paṭṭhānasaddañca [M 2.0288] vaṇṇento “atha vā”tiādimāha, tena purimavikappe sati, saddo, paṭṭhāna-saddo ca kattuatthoti [P 2.0364] viññāyati. Saraṇaṭṭhenāti cirakatassa, cirabhāsitassa ca anussaraṇaṭṭhena. Idanti yaṃ “satiyeva satipaṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ, idaṃ. Idha imasmiṃ suttapadese adhippetaṃ.

Thus, through unafflictedness by aversion and attachment, and by constant established mindfulness, transcending both—this is called ‘satipaṭṭhāna.’ For indeed, the constant established mindfulness of the Buddhas is a unique quality, not so for the Paccekabuddhas and others, because it is a distinctive property of Buddhas. The prefix ‘pa-’ illuminates the beginning, and taking ‘beginning’ as ‘continuation,’ it is said, ‘the meaning is to be set in motion.’ The foundation (paṭṭhāna) is to be established by mindfulness, which serves as the means (karaṇa). The suffix ‘-ana’ (in paṭṭhāna) often denotes action in the objective sense (kammattha) as well. Similarly, its agentive meaning is also found—thus, ‘it is called paṭṭhāna because it establishes.’ Here, the prefix ‘pa-’ indicates vigorous and distinct plunging—hence, ‘the meaning is to plunge in, strive, spread out, and occur,’ it is said. Again, explaining the nominal meaning of ‘sati’ and the word ‘paṭṭhāna,’ it begins with ‘or else.’ Thus, in the previous analysis, the word ‘sati’ and the word ‘paṭṭhāna’ are understood as agentive in meaning. ‘In the sense of recollection’—that is, by the recollection of what was done or spoken long ago. ‘This’ refers to what was said, ‘mindfulness itself is satipaṭṭhāna.’ Here, in this passage of the discourse, this is intended.

Yadi evanti. Yadi sati eva satipaṭṭhānaṃ, sati nāma eko dhammo, evaṃ sante kasmā “satipaṭṭhānā”ti bahuvacananti āha “satibahuttā”tiādi. Yadi bahukā tā satiyo, atha kasmā “maggo”ti ekavacananti yojanā. Maggaṭṭhenāti niyyānaṭṭhena. Niyyāniko hi maggadhammo, teneva niyyānikabhāvena ekattūpagato ekantato nibbānaṃ gacchati, atthikehi ca tadatthaṃ maggīyatīti āha “vuttañheta”nti, attanāva pubbe vuttaṃ paccāharati. Tattha catassopi cetāti kāyānupassanādivasena catubbidhāpi ca etā satiyo. Aparabhāgeti ariyamaggakkhaṇe. Kiccaṃ sādhayamānāti pubbabhāge kāyādīsu subhasaññādividhamanavasena visuṃ visuṃ pavattitvā maggakkhaṇe satiyeva tattha catubbidhassapi vipallāsassa samucchedavasena pahānakiccaṃ sādhayamānā ārammaṇakaraṇavasena nibbānaṃ gacchati. Catukiccasādhaneneva hettha bahuvacananiddeso. Evañca satīti evaṃ maggaṭṭhena ekattaṃ upādāya “maggo”ti ekavacanena, ārammaṇabhedena catubbidhataṃ upādāya “cattāro”ti ca vattabbatāya sati vijjamānattā. Vacanānusandhinā “ekāyano aya”ntiādikā desanā sānusandhikāva, na ananusandhikāti adhippāyo. Vuttamevatthaṃ nidassanena paṭipādetuṃ “mārasenappamaddana”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.224) suttapadaṃ ānetvā “yathā”tiādinā nidassanaṃ saṃsandati. “Tasmā”tiādi nigamanaṃ.

If it is so. If mindfulness itself is the establishment of mindfulness, and mindfulness is a single phenomenon, then why is it expressed in the plural as "satipaṭṭhānā"? It is said, "because of the abundance of mindfulness," and so on. If there are many instances of mindfulness, then why is it referred to in the singular as "the path"? The explanation is: "because of the nature of the path"– meaning the nature of leading out. The path-dhamma is indeed leading out; by this very liberating quality, having attained unity, it definitively goes to Nibbāna; and by those who desire it, it is sought for that purpose—thus it is said, "for this has been said," referring back to what was said by himself earlier. Here, these four—by way of contemplation of the body and so on—are also fourfold mindfulness. In the subsequent phase—that is, at the moment of the noble path—they accomplish their task. In the prior phase, by functioning separately in various ways—such as dispelling the perception of beauty and so on in the body and other objects—at the moment of the path, mindfulness itself accomplishes the task of abandoning, by cutting off the fourfold distortions regarding those objects, and by making Nibbāna its object, it goes to Nibbāna. Thus, the plural designation is due to the accomplishment of four tasks here. And so, this being the case, since it is possible to speak of it in the singular as 'the path' on account of its unity in the sense of path, and as 'four' on account of its fourfold nature due to the diversity of objects, the teaching such as 'this is the one way' is, through this continuity of expression, coherent and not disjointed—this is the intended meaning. To illustrate this point, the sutta passage "the crushing of Māra’s army" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.224) is cited, and the illustration is connected with "just as" and so on. "Therefore," and so on, concludes the discussion.

Visesato kāyo, vedanā ca assādassa kāraṇanti tappahānatthaṃ tesu taṇhāvatthūsu oḷārikasukhumesu asubhadukkhabhāvadassanāni mandatikkhapaññehi taṇhācaritehi sukarānīti tāni tesaṃ “visuddhimaggo”ti vuttāni. Tathā “niccaṃ attā”ti abhinivesavatthutāya diṭṭhiyā visesakāraṇesu cittadhammesu aniccānattatādassanāni sarāgādivasena, saññāphassādivasena, nīvaraṇādivasena ca nātippabhedātippabhedagatesu tesu tappahānatthaṃ mandatikkhapaññānaṃ [P 2.0365] diṭṭhicaritānaṃ sukarānīti tesaṃ tāni “visuddhimaggo”ti vuttāni. Ettha ca [V 2.0268] yathā cittadhammānampi taṇhāya [M 2.0289] vatthubhāvo sambhavati, tathā kāyavedanānampi diṭṭhiyāti satipi nesaṃ catunnampi taṇhādiṭṭhivatthubhāve yo yassā sātisayapaccayo, taṃ dassanatthaṃ visesaggahaṇaṃ katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tikkhapaññasamathayāniko oḷārikārammaṇaṃ pariggaṇhanto tattha aṭṭhatvā jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā uṭṭhāya vedanaṃ pariggaṇhātīti vuttaṃ “oḷārikārammaṇe asaṇṭhahanato”ti. Vipassanāyānikassa pana sukhume citte, dhammesu ca cittaṃ pakkhandatīti cittadhammānupassanānaṃ mandatikkhapaññavipassanāyānikānaṃ visuddhimaggatā vuttā.

The body, in particular, and feeling, as the cause of pleasure, are the bases of craving. To abandon craving, the contemplations of foulness and suffering in these gross and subtle objects of craving are easy for those with weak and sharp wisdom who are prone to craving. Therefore, these are called the "Path of Purification." Similarly, the view that "the self is permanent" is the basis of clinging for views. To abandon this, the contemplations of impermanence and non-self in the mental phenomena that are special causes—whether slightly or thoroughly differentiated according to passion, etc., according to perception, contact, etc., and according to the hindrances, etc.—are easy for those with weak and sharp wisdom who are prone to views. Therefore, these are called the "Path of Purification." Here, just as mental phenomena can serve as a basis for craving, so too can the body and feeling serve as a basis for views. Thus, even though all four (body, feeling, mind, and phenomena) can be objects for craving and views, it should be understood that the emphasis on distinctions is made to show which object is the predominant condition for which defilement. For one with sharp wisdom whose vehicle is serenity, taking a gross object, he dwells on it, attains jhāna, and upon emerging, contemplates feeling. This is what is meant by "because of not settling on a gross object." For one who follows the path of insight, however, the mind inclines toward subtle mind and phenomena. Therefore, the contemplation of mind and phenomena is called the "Path of Purification" for those insight-practitioners with weak and sharp wisdom.

Tesaṃ tatthāti ettha tattha-saddassa “pahānattha”nti etena yojanā. Parato tesaṃ tatthāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Pañca kāmaguṇā savisesā kāye labbhantīti visesena kāyo kāmoghassa vatthu, bhavesu sukhaggahaṇavasena bhavassādo hotīti bhavoghassa vedanā vatthu, santatighanaggahaṇavasena visesato citte attābhiniveso hotīti diṭṭhoghassa cittaṃ vatthu, dhammesu vinibbhogassa dukkarattā, dhammānaṃ dhammamattatāya duppaṭivijjhattā ca sammoho hotīti avijjoghassa dhammā vatthu, tasmā tesu tesaṃ pahānatthaṃ cattārova vuttā.

For them, there: here, the connection of the word "there" is with "for the purpose of abandoning." Furthermore, for them, there: here too, the same method applies. The five strands of sensual pleasure are found in the body with distinction; thus, the body, being particularly suited, is the basis for the flood of sensuality. In states of existence, through grasping at happiness, there is enjoyment of existence; thus, feeling is the basis for the flood of existence. Through grasping the compactness of continuity, there is especially the adherence to self in the mind; thus, the mind is the basis for the flood of views. Because disentangling from phenomena is difficult, and because phenomena, being merely phenomena, are hard to penetrate, delusion arises; thus, phenomena are the basis for the flood of ignorance. Therefore, four are mentioned for the purpose of abandoning them.

Evaṃ kāyādīnaṃ kāmoghādivatthubhāvakathaneneva kāmayogakāmāsavādīnampi vatthubhāvo dīpito hoti oghehi tesaṃ atthato anaññattā. Yadaggena ca kāyo kāmoghādīnaṃ vatthu, tadaggena abhijjhākāyaganthassa vatthu. “Dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo anusetī”ti dukkhadukkhavipariṇāmadukkhasaṅkhāradukkhabhūtā vedanā [P 2.0366] visesena byāpādakāyaganthassa vatthu. Citte niccaggahaṇavasena sassatassa attano sīlena suddhīti ādi parāmasanaṃ hotīti sīlabbataparāmāsassa cittaṃ vatthu. Nāmarūpaparicchedena bhūtaṃ bhūtato apassantassa bhavavibhavadiṭṭhisaṅkhāto idaṃsaccābhiniveso hotīti tassa dhammā vatthu. Kāyassa kāmupādānavatthutā vuttanayāva. Yadaggena hi kāyo kāmoghassa vatthu, tadaggena kāmupādānassapi vatthu atthato abhinnattā. Sukhavedanassādavasena paralokanirapekkho “natthi dinna”ntiādikaṃ (dī. ni. 1.171; ma. ni. 1.445; 2.95, 225; 3.91, 116; saṃ. ni. 3.210; dha. sa. 1221; vibha. 938) parāmāsaṃ uppādetīti diṭṭhupādānassa vedanā vatthu[M 2.0290]. Cittadhammānaṃ itarupādānavatthutā tatiyacatutthaganthayojanāyaṃ vuttanayā eva. Kāyavedanānaṃ chandadosāgativatthutā kāmoghabyāpādakāyaganthayojanāyaṃ vuttanayā eva. Santatighanaggahaṇavasena sarāgādicitte sammoho hotīti mohāgatiyā cittaṃ vatthu. Dhammasabhāvānavabodhe bhayaṃ hotīti bhayāgatiyā dhammā vatthu.

Thus, by explaining the basis of the flood of sensuality and so forth in relation to the body and other things, the basis of the yoke of sensuality, the taint of sensuality, and so on is also illuminated, for in meaning they are not different from the floods. And just as the body is the basis of the flood of sensuality and so forth, so too is it the basis of the body-fetter of covetousness. “The underlying tendency to aversion lies dormant toward painful feeling,” thus painful feeling—whether suffering as pain, suffering as change, or suffering as formations—is especially the basis of the body-fetter of ill will. By grasping the mind as permanent, one clings to the belief that the self is purified by virtue, and so on—thus the mind is the basis of the clinging to rites and rituals. For one who does not see reality as it truly is by discerning name and form, there arises dogmatic adherence to 'this is the truth' in the form of views of existence and non-existence—thus mental phenomena are its basis. The body’s role as the basis of clinging to sensuality is explained in the same way. For just as the body is the basis of the flood of sensuality, so too is it the basis of clinging to sensuality, since their meanings are not distinct. Through delight in pleasant feeling, one becomes heedless of the next world and gives rise to such dogmatic views as “There is no result of giving,” etc.—thus feeling is the basis of clinging to views. The role of mind and mental phenomena as the basis of other clingings is explained in the same way as in the explanation of the third and fourth ties. The role of the body and feelings as the basis of bias due to desire and aversion is explained in the same way as in the explanation of the flood of sensuality and the body-fetter of ill will. By grasping continuity as solid, delusion arises in a mind affected by lust and so on—thus the mind is the basis of bias due to delusion. When one does not comprehend the true nature of phenomena, fear arises—thus mental phenomena are the basis of bias due to fear.

Āhārasamudayā [V 2.0269] kāyassa samudayā, phassasamudayā vedanānaṃ samudayo, (saṃ. ni. 5.408) saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpanti (ma. ni. 3.126; udā. 1; vibha. 225) vacanato kāyādīnaṃ samudayabhūtā kabaḷīkāraphassamanosañcetanāviññāṇāhārā kāyādiparijānanena pariññātā hontīti āha “catubbidhāhārapariññattha”nti. Pakaraṇanayoti nettipakaraṇavasena suttantasaṃvaṇṇanānayo.

With the arising of food, there is the arising of the body; with the arising of contact, there is the arising of feelings; with formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises. According to these statements, those nutriments—physical food, contact, mental volition, and consciousness—which are the source of the arising of the body and so on, are fully understood by comprehending the body and so on. Hence, it is said, “for the purpose of fully understanding the four kinds of nutriment.” The method of the treatise is the approach of explaining the Suttas according to the Nettipakaraṇa.

Saraṇavasenāti kāyādīnaṃ, kusalādidhammānañca upadhāraṇavasena. Saranti gacchanti nibbānaṃ etāyāti satīti imasmiṃ atthe ekatte ekasabhāve nibbāne samosaraṇaṃ samāgamo ekattasamosaraṇaṃ. Etadeva hi dassetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

In the sense of bearing in mind: in the sense of bearing in mind the body and so on, and wholesome and other states. Because they go, proceed to Nibbāna by this, it is therefore called “mindfulness.” In this sense, the confluence, the coming together in the oneness of Nibbāna, which has a single nature, is a confluence into oneness. Indeed, to show this, it is said, “Just as…” and so on.

Ekanibbānapavesahetubhūto [P 2.0367] vā samānatāya eko satipaṭṭhānasabhāvo ekattaṃ, tattha samosaraṇaṃ ekattasamosaraṇaṃ, taṃsabhāgatāva, ekanibbānapavesahetubhāvaṃ pana dassetuṃ “yathā”tiādimāha. Etasmiṃ atthe saraṇekattasamosaraṇāni saheva satipaṭṭhānekabhāvassa kāraṇattena vuttānīti daṭṭhabbāni, purimasmiṃ visuṃ. Saraṇavasenāti vā gamanavasenāti atthe sati tadeva gamanaṃ samosaraṇanti, samosaraṇe vā sati-saddatthavasena avuccamāne dhāraṇatāva satīti sati-saddatthantarābhāvā purimaṃ satibhāvassa kāraṇaṃ, pacchimaṃ ekabhāvassāti nibbānasamosaraṇepi sahitāneva tāni satipaṭṭhānekabhāvassa kāraṇāni vuttāni honti.

Or, oneness is the single nature of the establishments of mindfulness, which, due to their sameness, is the cause for entering the one Nibbāna. The convergence upon that is the convergence into oneness, which is simply its shared nature. Moreover, to show that it is the cause for entering the one Nibbāna, the phrase 'just as,' etc., is stated. In this context, ‘bearing in mind,’ ‘oneness,’ and ‘confluence’ should be understood as being stated together as causes of the single nature of the establishments of mindfulness, whereas in the previous sense they were separate. Or, if the meaning of 'in the sense of remembering' is 'in the sense of going,' then that very going is the confluence. Or, when there is confluence, if the meaning of the word 'sati' is not explicitly stated, then retention alone is mindfulness, since there is no other meaning for the word 'sati.' The former is the cause for the state of mindfulness, the latter for the state of oneness. Thus, even in the convergence upon Nibbāna, those factors are stated together as causes of the single nature of the establishments of mindfulness.

“Cuddasavidhena, navavidhena, soḷasavidhena, pañcavidhenā”ti idaṃ upari pāḷiyaṃ (dī. ni. 2.374) āgatānaṃ ānāpānapabbādīnaṃ vasena vuttaṃ, tesaṃ pana anantarabhedavasena, tadanugatabhedavasena ca bhāvanāya anekavidhatā labbhatiyeva, catūsu disāsu uṭṭhānakabhaṇḍasadisatā kāyānupassanāditaṃtaṃsatipaṭṭhānabhāvanānubhāvassa daṭṭhabbā.

“Fourteen kinds, nine kinds, sixteen kinds, five kinds”—this is stated above in the Pāli text with reference to the sections on mindfulness of breathing and so forth. However, due to their immediate divisions and the divisions that follow them, the development can indeed be achieved in many ways. The power of developing the respective establishments of mindfulness, such as the contemplation of the body, should be seen as similar to the implements of a craftsman laid out in the four directions.

Kathetukamyatāpucchā [M 2.0291] itarāsaṃ pucchānaṃ idha asambhavato, niddesādivasena desetukamyatāya ca tathā vuttattā. “Idhā”ti vuccamānapaṭipattisampādakassa bhikkhuno sannissayadassanaṃ, so cassa sannissayo sāsanato añño natthīti vuttaṃ “idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane”ti. Dhamma…pe… lapanametaṃ tesaṃ attano sammukhābhimukhabhāvakaraṇatthaṃ, tañca dhammassa sakkaccasavanatthaṃ. “Gocare [P 2.0368] bhikkhave caratha sake pettike visaye”tiādi (dī. ni. 3.80; saṃ. ni. 5.372) vacanato bhikkhugocarā ete dhammā, yadidaṃ kāyānupassanādayo. Tattha yasmā kāyānupassanādipaṭipattiyā bhikkhu hoti, tasmā “kāyānupassī [V 2.0270] viharatī”tiādinā bhikkhuṃ dasseti bhikkhumhi taṃniyamatoti āha “paṭipattiyā bhikkhubhāvadassanato”ti. Satthucariyānuvidhāyakattā, sakalasāsanasampaṭiggāhakattā ca sabbappakārāya anusāsaniyā bhājanabhāvo. Tasmiṃ gahiteti bhikkhumhi gahite. Bhikkhuparisāya jeṭṭhabhāvato rājagamanañāyena itarā parisāpi atthato gahitāva hontīti āha “sesā”tiādi. Evaṃ paṭhamaṃ kāraṇaṃ vibhajitvā itarampi vibhajituṃ “yo ca ima”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

The question about the desire to speak arises because other questions are not possible here, and because it is stated thus due to the desire to teach by way of explanation and so on. 'Here' indicates the reliance of the monk who accomplishes the practice being discussed; and since his reliance is none other than the teaching, it is said, ''here' means in this teaching.' Dhamma… This address is for the purpose of making them turn and face him, and also for the sake of listening to the Dhamma with reverence. From the statement, “Monks, wander in your own ancestral domain,” etc., these are the domains of the monks, namely, the contemplation of the body and so on. Here, because one is a monk through the practice of contemplating the body and so on, the text indicates the monk by saying, “dwells contemplating the body,” etc., since that practice is established in a monk—hence, it is said, “by demonstrating the state of being a monk through practice.” Due to following the Teacher’s conduct and being a recipient of the entire teaching, he is a vessel for all kinds of instruction. When he is grasped—that is, when the monk is grasped—the other assemblies are also effectively included by the maxim of the king's journey, due to the seniority of the assembly of monks—hence, it is said, “the rest,” etc. Having thus analyzed the first reason, to analyze the other as well, it is said, 'and whoever this,' etc.

Samaṃ careyyāti kāyādi visamacariyaṃ pahāya kāyādīhi samaṃ careyya. Rāgādivūpasamena santo, indriyadamena danto, catumagganiyāmena niyato, seṭṭhacaritāya brahmacārī, sabbattha kāyadaṇḍādioropanena nidhāya daṇḍaṃ. Ariyabhāve ṭhito so evarūpo bāhitapāpasamitapāpabhinnakilesatāhi “brāhmaṇo, samaṇo, bhikkhū”ti ca veditabbo.

“One should conduct oneself evenly” means that, having abandoned uneven conduct with the body and so on, one should conduct oneself evenly with the body and so on. Calm through the pacification of lust and so on, tamed by the restraint of the senses, disciplined by the restraint of the four paths, a holy-lifer due to excellent conduct, having laid down the rod by abandoning bodily punishment and so on in all respects. Established in the noble state, such a one, with evil dispelled, evil calmed, and defilements shattered, is to be known as “a brahmin, an ascetic, a bhikkhu.”

“Ayañceva kāyo, bahiddhā ca nāmarūpa”ntiādīsu khandhapañcakaṃ, tathā “sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedetī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.271, 287; pārā. 11), “yā tasmiṃ samaye kāyassa passaddhi paṭippassaddhī”tiādīsu ca vedanādayo cetasikā khandhā kāyoti vuccantīti [P 2.0369] tato visesanatthaṃ “kāyeti rūpakāye”ti āha. Kesādīnañca dhammānanti kesādisaññitānaṃ bhūtupādādhammānaṃ. Evaṃ “cayaṭṭho sarīraṭṭho kāyaṭṭho”ti saddanayena kāya-saddaṃ dassetvā idāni niruttinayenapi taṃ dassetuṃ “yathā cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Āyantīti uppajjanti.

In phrases such as “this very body, and externally name-and-form,” the five aggregates are meant. Likewise, in phrases such as “he feels pleasure with the body,” and “whatever tranquility and serenity of the body there is at that time,” the mental aggregates such as feeling are called ‘body.’ To distinguish from that, it is said, “body means the material body.” And “the things beginning with hair,” etc., means the primary and derived elements designated as hair, etc. Thus, having shown the word ‘body’ by the method of its meaning as “the collection, the structure, the heap,” now, to show it also by the method of etymological derivation, it is said, “and as,” etc. “They come” means they arise.

Asammissatoti [M 2.0292] vedanādayopi ettha sitā, ettha paṭibaddhāti kāye vedanādianupassanāpasaṅgepi āpanne tato asammissatoti attho. Samūhavisayatāya cassa kāya-saddassa, samudāyupādānatāya ca asubhākārassa “kāye”ti ekavacanaṃ, tathā ārammaṇādivibhāgena anekabhedabhinnampi cittaṃ cittabhāvasāmaññena ekajjhaṃ gahetvā “citte”ti ekavacanaṃ, vedanā pana sukhādibhedabhinnā visuṃ visuṃ anupassitabbāti dassentena “vedanāsū”ti bahuvacanena vuttā, tatheva ca niddeso pavattito, dhammā ca paropaṇṇāsabhedā, anupassitabbākārena ca anekabhedā evāti tepi bahuvacanavaseneva vuttā.

“Unmixed” means that even though feelings and so on are also based here, connected here, and even when the occasion arises for the contemplation of feelings and so on in the body, the meaning is that it is unmixed from them. Due to the collective nature of the word ‘body,’ and because of the apprehension of the collection in its repulsive aspect, the singular “in the body” is used. Similarly, though the mind is divided into many kinds by distinctions such as object, etc., it is taken together under the general characteristic of ‘mind’ with the singular “in the mind.” But feelings, being divided into pleasure, etc., are to be contemplated separately, hence the plural “in feelings” is used, and the instruction proceeds accordingly. And phenomena, being of over fifty kinds, and also of many kinds in the way they are to be contemplated, are also stated in the plural.

Avayavīgāhasamaññātidhāvanasārādānābhinivesanisedhanatthaṃ kāyaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgehi, tāni ca kesādīhi, kesādike ca bhūtupādāyarūpehi vinibbhuñjanto “tathā na kāye”tiādimāha. Pāsādādinagarāvayavasamūhe [V 2.0271] avayavīvādinopi avayavīgāhaṃ na karonti, “nagaraṃ nāma koci attho atthī”ti pana kesañci samaññātidhāvanaṃ siyāti itthipurisādisamaññātidhāvane nagaranidassanaṃ vuttaṃ. Aṅgapaccaṅgasamūho, kesalomādisamūho, bhūtupādāyasamūho ca yathāvuttasamūho, tabbinimutto kāyopi nāma koci natthi, pageva itthiādayoti āha “kāyo vā itthī vā puriso vā añño vā koci dhammo dissatī”ti. “Koci dhammo”ti iminā sattajīvādiṃ paṭikkhipati, avayavī pana kāyapaṭikkhepeneva paṭikkhittoti. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ kāyādisamaññātidhāvanānīti āha “yathāvuttadhamma…pe… karontī”ti. Tathā tathāti kāyādiākārena.

To negate the grasping of a whole, the over-running of concepts, the taking of a core, and adherence, one analyzes the body into major and minor limbs, and those into hair, etc., and hair, etc., into primary and derived matter. Analyzing thus, one declares, “Thus, not in the body,” and so on. Even proponents of a whole do not grasp a whole when considering the collection of parts of a city, such as a palace. However, for some there might be an over-running of the concept, “There is indeed something called a city.” Thus, the example of a city is given in the context of over-running concepts like “man” or “woman.” A collection of major and minor limbs, a collection of hair of the head, body hair, etc., and a collection of primary and derived matter—these are the collections as described. Apart from these, there is no such thing as a ‘body,’ much less a woman, man, or any other thing. Hence, it is said, “No body, woman, man, or any other thing is seen.” The phrase “any other thing” rejects a being, a life-principle, etc. The whole is rejected by the very rejection of the ‘body.’ If this is so, how then do the over-runnings of concepts like ‘body’ persist? It is answered: “As previously stated… they perform thus.” “Thus, thus”—in the manner of ‘body,’ etc.

Yaṃ [P 2.0370] passatīti yaṃ itthiṃ, purisaṃ vā passati. Nanu cakkhunā itthipurisadassanaṃ natthīti? Saccametaṃ, “itthiṃ passāmi, purisaṃ passāmī”ti pana pavattasaññāya vasena “yaṃ passatī”ti vuttaṃ micchādassanena vā diṭṭhiyā yaṃ passati, na taṃ diṭṭhaṃ taṃ rūpāyatanaṃ na hotīti attho viparītaggāhavasena micchāparikappitarūpattā. Atha vā taṃ kesādibhūtupādāyasamūhasaṅkhātaṃ diṭṭhaṃ na hoti, acakkhuviññāṇaviññeyyattā diṭṭhaṃ vā taṃ na hoti. Yaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, taṃ na passatīti yaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ kesādibhūtupādāyasamūhasaṅkhātaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, taṃ paññācakkhunā bhūtato na passatīti attho. Apassaṃ bajjhateti imaṃ attabhāvaṃ yathābhūtaṃ paññācakkhunā apassanto “etaṃ [M 2.0293] mama, eso hamasmi, eso me attā”ti kilesabandhanena bajjhati.

“What one sees” refers to seeing a woman or a man. But is it not true that there is no seeing of women or men with the eye? That is true. However, the phrase “what one sees” is used by way of the perception that arises, such as “I see a woman, I see a man.” Alternatively, what one sees by way of wrong seeing or wrong view, that is not seen; it is not a form-object, because it is a form wrongly conceived through perverted grasping. Or, that which is reckoned as a collection of primary and derived matter such as hair, etc., is not seen, because it is not knowable by eye-consciousness. Or, what is seen is not seen. “What is seen, that one does not see” means that the form-object, that collection reckoned as primary and derived matter like hair, etc., which is seen, is not seen as it truly is with the eye of wisdom. “Not seeing, one is bound”—not seeing this individual existence as it truly is with the eye of wisdom, one is bound by the bondage of defilements, thinking, “This is mine, this I am, this is my self.”

Na aññadhammānupassīti na aññasabhāvānupassī, asubhādito aññākārānupassī na hotīti attho. “Kiṃ vuttaṃ hotī”tiādinā taṃ evatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ karoti. Pathavīkāyanti kesādikoṭṭhāsaṃ pathaviṃ dhammasamūhattā “kāyo”ti vadati, lakkhaṇapathavimeva vā anekappabhedaṃ sakalasarīragataṃ, pubbāpariyabhāvena ca pavattamānaṃ samūhavasena gahetvā “kāyo”ti vadati. “Āpokāya”ntiādīsupi eseva nayo.

“Not one who contemplates other phenomena” means not one who contemplates other natures; one is not a contemplator of aspects other than the repulsive, etc. This is the meaning. The phrase “What is being said?” and so on, makes that meaning clear. He calls the earth element, the part beginning with hair, a ‘body’ because it is a collection of phenomena. Or, he calls the characteristic earth itself, which is of many kinds, present throughout the entire body, and occurring in a before-and-after sequence, a ‘body’ by taking it as a collection. The same method applies to ‘water-body’ and so on.

Evaṃ gahetabbassāti “ahaṃ mama”nti evaṃ attattaniyabhāvena andhabālehi gahetabbassa.

“Of that which is to be grasped thus” refers to that which is to be grasped by blind fools as ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ in terms of self and what belongs to self.

Idāni sattannaṃ anupassanākārānampi vasena kāyānupassanaṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha aniccato anupassatīti catusamuṭṭhānikaṃ kāyaṃ “anicca”nti anupassati, evaṃ passanto evañcassa aniccākārampi “anupassatī”ti vuccati. Tathābhūtassa cassa niccaggāhassa [P 2.0371] lesopi na hotīti vuttaṃ “no niccato”ti. Tathā hesa “niccasaññaṃ pajahatī”ti [V 2.0272] (paṭi. ma. 3.35) vutto. Ettha ca “aniccato eva anupassatī”ti eva-kāro luttaniddiṭṭhoti tena nivattitamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “no niccato”ti vuttaṃ. Na cettha dukkhato anupassanādinivattanaṃ āsaṅkitabbaṃ paṭiyogīnivattanaparattā eva-kārassa, upari desanāruḷhattā ca tāsaṃ. “Dukkhato anupassatī”tiādīsupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – aniccassa dukkhattā tameva ca kāyaṃ dukkhato anupassati, dukkhassa anattattā anattato anupassati. Yasmā pana yaṃ aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā, na taṃ abhinanditabbaṃ, yañca na abhinanditabbaṃ, na tattha rañjitabbaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “nibbindati, no nandati. Virajjati, no rajjatī”ti. So evaṃ arajjanto rāgaṃ nirodheti, no samudeti samudayaṃ na karotīti attho. Evaṃ paṭipanno ca paṭinissajjati, no ādiyati. Ayañhi aniccādianupassanā tadaṅgavasena saddhiṃ kāyaṃ tannissayakhandhābhisaṅkhārehi kilesānaṃ pariccajanato, saṅkhatadosadassanena tabbiparīte nibbāne tanninnatāya pakkhandanato “pariccāgapaṭinissaggo ceva pakkhandanapaṭinissaggo cā”ti vuccati, tasmā tāya samannāgato bhikkhu vuttanayena kilese pariccajati, nibbāne ca pakkhandati, tathābhūto ca nibbattanavasena kilese [M 2.0294] na ādiyati, nāpi adosadassitāvasena saṅkhatārammaṇaṃ, tena vuttaṃ “paṭinissajjati, no ādiyatī”ti. Idānissa tāhi anupassanāhi yesaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānaṃ hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “aniccato anupassanto niccasaññaṃ pajahatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha niccasaññanti “saṅkhārā niccā”ti evaṃ pavattaṃ viparītasaññaṃ. Diṭṭhicittavipallāsappahānamukheneva saññāvipallāsappahānanti saññāggahaṇaṃ, saññāsīsena vā tesampi [P 2.0372] gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nandinti sappītikataṇhaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Now, to show the contemplation of the body by way of the seven modes of contemplation, the passage begins with “apicā” and so on. Herein, “he contemplates as impermanent” means he contemplates the body, which arises from the four causes, as “impermanent.” Seeing thus, he is also said to ‘contemplate’ the aspect of impermanence. For one who sees thus, not even a trace of the grasp of permanence arises—hence it is said, “not as permanent.” Similarly, it is said, “he abandons the perception of permanence” (Paṭisambhidāmagga 3.35). Here, the word ‘eva’ in ‘he contemplates only as impermanent’ is understood as elided, and ‘not as permanent’ is stated to show the meaning excluded by it. In this context, the exclusion of contemplating as suffering, etc., should not be suspected, because the word ‘eva’ serves to exclude the opposite, and because those aspects are established in the teaching that follows. The same method applies to “he contemplates as suffering” and so on. However, there is this distinction: because what is impermanent is suffering, he contemplates that very body as suffering; and because what is suffering is non-self, he contemplates it as non-self. Furthermore, since what is impermanent, suffering, and non-self should not be delighted in, and in that which should not be delighted in, one should not be impassioned, therefore, it is said, “he becomes disenchanted, not delighted; he becomes dispassionate, not impassioned.” Thus, being dispassionate, he brings lust to cessation and does not arouse it—that is, he does not cause its arising. Practicing in this way, he relinquishes and does not take up. For this contemplation of impermanence, etc., is called ‘relinquishment by abandoning’ and ‘relinquishment by entering,’ because it involves the abandoning of defilements by way of that factor, together with the body and the conditioned formations dependent on it, and because it involves entering Nibbāna, which is opposite to the conditioned, by seeing the fault in the conditioned. Therefore, a bhikkhu endowed with this practice relinquishes defilements in the manner described and enters Nibbāna. Being thus, he does not take up defilements by way of their production, nor does he take up conditioned objects by way of not seeing their fault. Hence, it is said, “he relinquishes and does not take up.” Now, to show which states are abandoned through these contemplations, it is said, “contemplating as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence,” and so on. Herein, “the perception of permanence” refers to the inverted perception that arises as “conditioned things are permanent.” The abandoning of the distortion of perception is by way of abandoning the distortions of view and mind; thus, the mention of perception is to be understood as including them, or their inclusion should be seen with perception as the primary factor. “Delight” refers to craving accompanied by joy. The rest follows the same method as explained.

“Viharatī”ti iminā kāyānupassanāsamaṅgino iriyāpathavihāro vuttoti āha “iriyatī”ti, iriyāpathaṃ pavattetīti attho. Ārammaṇakaraṇavasena abhibyāpanato “tīsu bhavesū”ti vuttaṃ, uppajjanavasena pana kilesā parittabhūmakā evāti. Yadipi kilesānaṃ pahānaṃ ātāpananti taṃ sammādiṭṭhiādīnampi attheva, ātappa-saddo viya pana ātāpasaddo vīriyeyeva niruḷhoti vuttaṃ “vīriyassetaṃ nāma”nti. Atha vā paṭipakkhappahāne sampayuttadhammānaṃ abbhussahanavasena pavattamānassa vīriyassa sātisayaṃ tadātāpananti vīriyameva tathā vuccati, na aññe dhammā. Ātāpīti cāyamīkāro pasaṃsāya, atisayassa vā dīpakoti ātāpīgahaṇena sammappadhānasamaṅgitaṃ dasseti. Sammā, samantato, sāmañca pajānanto sampajāno, asammissato vavatthāne aññadhammānupassitābhāvena sammā aviparītaṃ, sabbākārapajānanena samantato, uparūpari visesāvahabhāvena pavattiyā sāmaṃ pajānantoti attho[V 2.0273]. Yadi paññāya anupassati, kathaṃ satipaṭṭhānatāti āha “na hī”tiādi. Sabbatthikanti sabbattha bhavaṃ sabbattha līne, uddhate ca citte icchitabbattā. Sabbe vā līne, uddhate ca bhāvetabbā bojjhaṅgā atthikā etāyāti sabbatthikā. Satiyā laddhupakārāya eva paññāya ettha yathāvutte kāye kammaṭṭhāniko bhikkhu kāyānupassī viharati. Anto saṅkhepo antoolīyano, kosajjanti attho. Upāyapariggaheti ettha sīlavisodhanādi, gaṇanādi, uggahakosallādi ca upāyo, tabbipariyāyato anupāyo veditabbo. Yasmā ca upaṭṭhitassati yathāvuttaṃ upāyaṃ na pariccajati, anupāyañca na upādiyati, tasmā vuttaṃ “muṭṭhassatī [P 2.0373] …pe… asamattho hotī”ti. Tenāti upāyānupāyānaṃ pariggahaparivajjanesu, pariccāgāpariggahesu ca asamatthabhāvena. Assa yogino.

“He dwells”—by this, the dwelling in the postures of one endowed with contemplation of the body is stated. Hence, it is said, “he moves about,” meaning he engages in a posture. It is said “in the three realms” because of pervading by way of making them objects, but by way of arising, defilements are indeed of a limited sphere. Although the abandoning of defilements is ardor, and that also applies to right view and the like, yet the word ‘ātāpa’ is established only in the sense of energy, just like the word ‘ātappa’; hence it is said, “This is a name for energy.” Alternatively, because energy, when it proceeds with an excess of exertion in abandoning opposing states and associated phenomena, is exceedingly ardent, energy alone is referred to in this way, not other phenomena. The ‘ī’ in the term ‘ātāpī’ (ardent) signifies praise or indicates excellence. The inclusion of ‘ātāpī’ shows that one is endowed with right exertions. ‘Sampajāno’ (clearly comprehending) means knowing rightly, comprehensively, and by oneself. ‘Rightly’ means without perversion, by way of not contemplating other phenomena in the determination of what is unmixed. ‘Comprehensively’ means by knowing in all aspects. ‘By oneself’ means knowing the progression by way of bringing about higher and higher distinctions. If one contemplates with wisdom, how is it the establishment of mindfulness? It is said: “For indeed…” “Universal” (sabbatthika) means being everywhere, because it is desirable everywhere, in sluggish and agitated minds. Or, it means that all the factors of enlightenment that should be developed in sluggish and agitated states are beneficial for this mindfulness, hence ‘universal.’ With wisdom that has received assistance from mindfulness, a monk who has the body as his meditation subject dwells contemplating the body, as described here. “Internally” (anto) means contraction, shrinking back internally, meaning laziness. “He grasps the means” (upāyapariggaheti)—here, the means include purification of virtue, counting, skill in learning, and the like. What is contrary to these should be understood as “non-means.” Because one with established mindfulness does not abandon the means as described nor take up non-means, it is said: “One with forgetful mindfulness… is incapable.” “Therefore” (tena)—due to that yogi's incapacity in grasping and avoiding, and in abandoning and grasping, means and non-means.

Yasmā [M 2.0295] satiyevettha satipaṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmāssa sampayuttadhammā vīriyādayo aṅganti āha “sampayogaṅgañcassa dassetvā”ti. Aṅga-saddo cettha kāraṇapariyāyo daṭṭhabbo. Satiggahaṇeneva cettha samādhissāpi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ tassā samādhikkhandhe saṅgahitattā. Yasmā vā satisīsenāyaṃ desanā. Na hi kevalāya satiyā kilesappahānaṃ sambhavati, nibbānādhigamo vā, nāpi kevalā sati pavattati, tasmāssa jhānadesanāyaṃ savitakkādivacanassa viya sampayogaṅgadassanatāti aṅga-saddassa avayavapariyāyatā daṭṭhabbā. Pahānaṅganti “vivicceva kāmehī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.226; ma. ni. 1.271, 287, 297; saṃ. ni. 2.152; a. ni. 4.123; pārā. 11) viya pahātabbaṅgaṃ dassetuṃ. Yasmā ettha lokiyamaggo adhippeto, na lokuttaramaggo, tasmā pubbabhāgiyameva vinayaṃ dassento “tadaṅgavinayena vā vikkhambhanavinayena vā”ti āha. Tesaṃ dhammānanti vedanādidhammānaṃ. Tesañhi tattha anadhippetattā “atthuddhāranayenetaṃ vutta”nti vuttaṃ. Tatthāti vibhaṅge. Etthāti “loke”ti etasmiṃ pade.

Because mindfulness alone is mentioned here as the establishment of mindfulness, therefore, having shown its associated factors, he says that associated phenomena such as energy, etc., are its factors. Here, the term “factor” should be understood as a synonym for cause. Through the mention of mindfulness, the inclusion of concentration should also be understood, as it is included within the aggregate of concentration. Or, because this teaching is headed by mindfulness. For neither the abandonment of defilements nor the attainment of Nibbāna is possible through mindfulness alone, nor does mindfulness arise alone. Therefore, just as in the teaching on jhāna, the mention of terms like ‘with initial thought,’ etc., shows associated factors, so here the term ‘factor’ should be understood as meaning a constituent part. The phrase “a factor of abandoning” is used to indicate a factor to be abandoned, as in phrases like “quite secluded from sensual pleasures…” Because the mundane path is intended here, not the supramundane path, it is stated to show only the preliminary discipline: “either by the discipline of substitution or by the discipline of suppression.” “Those phenomena” refers to phenomena such as feelings, etc. Since they are not intended there, it is said, “This is stated by way of extracting the meaning.” “There” means in the Vibhaṅga. “Here” refers to the word “loke” (in the world).

Avisesena dvīhipi nīvaraṇappahānaṃ vuttanti katvā puna ekekena vuttaṃ pahānavisesaṃ dassetuṃ “visesenā”ti āha. Atha vā “vineyya nīvaraṇānī”ti avatvā abhijjhādomanassavinayavacanassa payojanaṃ dassento “visesenā”tiādimāha. Kāyānupassanābhāvanāya hi ujuvipaccanīkānaṃ anurodhavirodhādīnaṃ pahānadassanaṃ etassa payojananti. Kāyasampattimūlakassāti rūpabalayobbanārogyādisarīrasampadānimittassa. Vuttavipariyāyato kāyavipattimūlako virodho veditabbo. Kāyabhāvanāyāti kāyānupassanābhāvanāya. Sā hi idha kāyabhāvanāti adhippetā. Subhasukhabhāvādīnanti [P 2.0374] ādi-saddena [V 2.0274] manuññaniccatādisaṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Asubhāsukhabhāvādīnanti ettha pana ādi-saddena amanuññaaniccatādīnaṃ. Tenāti anurodhādippahānavacanena. “Yogānubhāvo hī”tiādi vuttassevatthassa pākaṭakaraṇaṃ. Yogānubhāvo hi bhāvanānubhāvo. Yogasamatthoti yogamanuyuñjituṃ samattho. Purimena hi “anurodhavirodhavippamutto”tiādivacanena bhāvanaṃ anuyuttassa ānisaṃso vutto, dutiyena bhāvanaṃ anuyuñjantassa paṭipatti. Na hi anurodhavirodhādīhi upaddutassa bhāvanā ijjhati.

Having stated the abandonment of the two hindrances without distinction, it is then explained individually to show the particular abandonment; hence the phrase “in particular.” Alternatively, instead of saying “having removed the hindrances,” the purpose of the statement on removing covetousness and ill-will is shown by the phrase “in particular.” For the cultivation of contemplation of the body, the purpose here is to demonstrate the abandonment of attraction and aversion, etc., which are directly contrary. “Rooted in bodily attainment” refers to the sign of physical prosperity, such as form, strength, youth, and health, as the cause. Aversion rooted in bodily deficiency should be understood as the opposite of what has been stated. “By the cultivation of the body” means by the cultivation of contemplation of the body. For that is intended here as “cultivation of the body.” “States of beauty and pleasure, etc.”—the word “etc.” should be taken to include agreeableness, permanence, and so on. “States of ugliness and displeasure, etc.”—here, the word “etc.” includes disagreeableness, impermanence, and the like. “By this” refers to the statement on abandoning attraction, aversion, etc. “The power of practice, etc.”—this clarifies the meaning already stated. For the power of practice is the power of cultivation. “Capable of practice” means capable of engaging in practice. The first statement, beginning with “freed from attraction and aversion,” explains the benefits for one devoted to cultivation, while the second explains the practice for one engaged in cultivation. For cultivation does not succeed when one is afflicted by attraction, aversion, and the like.

Anupassīti [M 2.0296] etthāti “anupassī”ti etasmiṃ pade labbhamānāya anupassanāya anupassanājotanāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ vuttanti evamattho daṭṭhabbo, aññathā “anupassanāyā”ti karaṇavacanaṃ na yujjeyya. Anupassanā eva hi kammaṭṭhānaṃ, na ettha ārammaṇaṃ adhippetaṃ, yujjati vā. Kāyapariharaṇaṃ vuttanti sambandho. Kammaṭṭhānapariharaṇassa cettha atthasiddhattā “kāyapariharaṇa”ntveva vuttaṃ. Kammaṭṭhānikassa hi kāyapariharaṇaṃ yāvadeva kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariharaṇatthanti. Kammaṭṭhānapariharaṇassa vā “ātāpī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.373) vuccamānattā “kāyapariharaṇa”ntveva vuttaṃ. Kāyaggahaṇena vā nāmakāyassāpi gahaṇaṃ, na rūpakāyasseva, teneva kammaṭṭhānapariharaṇampi saṅgahitaṃ hoti, evañca katvā “viharatīti ettha vuttavihārenā”ti etthaggahaṇañca samatthitaṃ hoti “kāyānupassī viharatī”ti vihārassa visesetvā vuttattā. “Ātāpī”tiādi pana saṅkhepato vuttassa kammaṭṭhānapariharaṇassa saha sādhanena vitthāretvā dassanaṃ. Ātāpenāti ātāpaggahaṇena. “Satisampajaññenā”tiādīsupi eseva nayo. Sabbatthakakammaṭṭhānanti buddhānussati, mettā, maraṇassati[P 2.0375], asubhabhāvanā ca. Idañhi catukkaṃ yoginā parihariyamānaṃ “sabbatthakakammaṭṭhāna”nti vuccati, sabbattha kammaṭṭhānānuyogassārakkhabhūtattā satisampajaññabalena avicchinnassa pariharitabbattā satisampajaññaggahaṇena tassa vuttatā vuttā. Satiyā vā samatho vutto tassā samādhikkhandhena saṅgahitattā.

Here, in the word ‘anupassī’ (contemplating), the meditation subject is said to be taught for the sake of the contemplation that is obtained and for the illumination of contemplation; this is how the meaning should be understood. Otherwise, the instrumental case ‘anupassanāya’ (by contemplation) would not be appropriate. For contemplation itself is the meditation subject; the object is not intended here, or it is fitting. The connection is that ‘guarding of the body’ is stated. Since the guarding of the meditation subject is established by the meaning here, it is simply called ‘the guarding of the body.’ For the guarding of the body by one engaged in meditation is solely for the purpose of guarding the meditation subject. Alternatively, because the guarding of the meditation subject is being described by terms like ‘ardent’ (Dī. Ni. 2.373), it is simply called ‘the guarding of the body.’ Or, by the term ‘body,’ the mental body (nāmakāya) is also included, not just the physical body (rūpakāya); thus, the guarding of the meditation subject is also encompassed. And by doing so, the inclusion of ‘he dwells’ in ‘he dwells contemplating the body’ is justified, because the dwelling is specified. The terms ‘ardent,’ etc., however, describe in detail, along with its means, the guarding of the meditation subject that was stated concisely. ‘With ardency’ means by the inclusion of ardency. The same principle applies to ‘with mindfulness and clear comprehension,’ etc. ‘Universal meditation subjects’ are mindfulness of the Buddha, loving-kindness, mindfulness of death, and contemplation of repulsiveness. For this set of four, when practiced by a meditator, is called ‘universal meditation subjects’ because they serve as a protection for the continuous application of meditation everywhere, requiring unbroken guarding through the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension. Thus, by the inclusion of mindfulness and clear comprehension, their being stated is stated. Or, by mindfulness, serenity (samatha) is also stated, as it is encompassed within the aggregate of concentration.

Vibhaṅge(vibha. kāyānupassanāniddese) pana attho vuttoti yojanā. Tenāti saddatthaṃ anādiyitvā bhāvatthasseva vibhajanavasena pavattena vibhaṅgapāṭhena saha. Aṭṭhakathānayoti saddatthassāpi vivaraṇavasena yathārahaṃ vutto atthasaṃvaṇṇanānayo. Yathā saṃsandatīti yathā atthato, adhippāyato ca avilomento aññadatthu saṃsandati sameti, evaṃ veditabbo.

The connection is that the meaning is stated in the Vibhaṅga (in the exposition on the contemplation of the body). This is to be understood along with the Vibhaṅga text, which proceeds by way of analyzing the meaning of the state itself, without taking up the literal meaning. The method of the commentary is the way of elaborating the meaning, which explains even the literal meaning appropriately. 'As it agrees' means: it should be understood as agreeing and harmonizing in terms of meaning and intention, without being in opposition.

Vedanādīnaṃ puna vacaneti ettha nissayapaccayabhāvavasena cittadhammānaṃ vedanāsannissitattā, pañcavokārabhave [V 2.0275] arūpadhammānaṃ rūpapaṭibaddhavuttito ca vedanāya kāyādianupassanāppasaṅgepi āpanne tato asammissato vavatthānaṃ dassanatthaṃ, ghanavinibbhogādidassanatthañca dutiyaṃ vedanāggahaṇaṃ, tena na vedanāyaṃ kāyānupassī, cittadhammānupassī vā, atha kho vedanānupassī [M 2.0297] evāti vedanāsaṅkhāte vatthusmiṃ vedanānupassanākārasseva dassanena asammissato vavatthānaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Tathā “yasmiṃ samaye sukhā vedanā, na tasmiṃ samaye dukkhā, adukkhamasukhā vā vedanā, yasmiṃ vā pana samaye dukkhā, adukkhamasukhā vā vedanā, na tasmiṃ samaye itarā vedanā”ti vedanābhāvasāmaññe avatvā taṃ taṃ vedanaṃ vinibbhujjitvā dassanena ghanavinibbhogo dhuvabhāvaviveko dassito hoti, tena tāsaṃ khaṇamattāvaṭṭhānadassanena aniccatāya[P 2.0376], tato eva dukkhatāya, anattatāya ca dassanaṃ vibhāvitaṃ hoti. Ghanavinibbhogādīti ādi-saddena ayampi attho veditabbo. Ayañhi vedanāyaṃ vedanānupassī eva, na aññadhammānupassī. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā nāma bālo amaṇisabhāvepi udakapubbuḷake maṇiākārānupassī hoti, na evaṃ ayaṃ ṭhitiramaṇīyepi vedayite, pageva itarasmiṃ manuññākārānupassī, atha kho khaṇapabhaṅguratāya, avasavattitāya kilesāsucipaggharaṇatāya ca aniccaanattaasubhākārānupassī, vipariṇāmadukkhatāya, saṅkhāradukkhatāya ca visesato dukkhānupassī yevāti. Evaṃ citta dhammesupi yathārahaṃ punavacane payojanaṃ vattabbaṃ. Lokiyā eva sammasanacārassa adhippetattā. “Kevalaṃ panidhā”tiādinā “idha ettakaṃ veditabba”nti veditabbaparicchedaṃ dasseti. “Esa nayo”ti iminā yathā cittaṃ, dhammā ca anupassitabbā, tathā tāni anupassanto citte cittānupassī, dhammesu dhammānupassīti veditabboti imamatthaṃ atidisati. Dukkhatoti dukkhasabhāvato, dukkhanti anupassitabbāti attho. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo.

Regarding the repetition of terms like 'feeling' here, it is to show the distinction from other objects of contemplation, without admixture, even when the occasion for contemplating the body and so forth in relation to feeling arises. This is because mental states are dependent on feeling by way of the dependence condition, and in the five-constituent existence, formless states occur bound to form. The second mention of 'feeling' is also to show the dissolution of solidity and so on. Thus, it is not that one is a contemplator of the body or mental phenomena in relation to feeling, but rather one is solely a contemplator of feeling. By seeing only the aspect of contemplating feeling in what is termed feeling, the distinctness, without admixture, is shown. Similarly, by stating: "When there is pleasant feeling, there is no painful or neutral feeling at that time; when there is painful or neutral feeling, there is no other feeling at that time," and thus not speaking of the general commonness of feeling but showing each feeling by analyzing it, the dissolution of solidity and the distinction from permanence are revealed. By seeing their existence for only a moment, impermanence is discerned; from that very fact, suffering is discerned; and from that, non-self is discerned. The phrase "dissolution of solidity, etc." should also be understood to include this meaning. For this one is solely a contemplator of feeling, not a contemplator of other phenomena. What is meant? Just as a fool, even when there is no jewel, sees a bubble of water as having the form of a jewel, not so does this one—even when experiencing a stable and delightful feeling, let alone other pleasant appearances. Instead, he contemplates the aspects of impermanence, non-self, and foulness due to their momentary destructibility, uncontrollable nature, and the oozing forth of defilements. Particularly, he contemplates suffering in terms of the suffering of change and the suffering of formations. In the same way, the purpose of repetition should be stated appropriately with regard to mind and phenomena. This is because the worldly practice of comprehension is intended. By the phrase beginning 'But only here,' he shows the limit of what is to be known: 'this much is to be known here.' By 'This is the method,' he extends this meaning: just as mind and phenomena are to be contemplated, so one who contemplates them is to be understood as 'a contemplator of mind in mind' and 'a contemplator of phenomena in phenomena.' 'As suffering' means that because of its nature as suffering, it is to be contemplated as 'suffering.' This same method applies to the remaining two terms.

Yo sukhaṃ dukkhato addāti yo bhikkhu sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vipariṇāmadukkhatāya “dukkhā”ti paññācakkhunā addakkhi. Dukkhaṃ addakkhi sallatoti dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ pīḷājananato, antotudanato, dunnīharaṇato ca sallato addakkhi passi. Adukkhamasukhanti upekkhāvedanaṃ. Santanti sukhadukkhāni viya anoḷārikatāya, paccayavasena vūpasantasabhāvatāya ca santaṃ. Aniccatoti hutvāabhāvato, udayavayavantato, tāvakālikato, niccapaṭipakkhato ca “anicca”nti yo addakkhi. Sa ve sammaddaso [P 2.0377] bhikkhu ekaṃsena, paribyattaṃ vā vedanāya sammāpassanakoti attho.

He who sees happiness as suffering: that monk who, with the eye of wisdom, sees pleasant feeling as 'suffering' due to the suffering of change. He sees suffering as a dart: he sees painful feeling as a dart because it torments, stings within, and is hard to extract. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant: neutral feeling. Peaceful: because, unlike pleasant and painful feelings, it is not coarse, and because its nature is calmed by way of conditions. As impermanent: he who sees it as 'impermanent' because it ceases after arising, because it has rise and fall, because it is temporary, and because it is the opposite of permanence. Truly, that monk is one who sees rightly; the meaning is that he is in every way, or thoroughly, a right-seer of feeling.

Dukkhātipīti [M 2.0298] saṅkhāradukkhatāya dukkhā itipi. Taṃ dukkhasminti sabbaṃ taṃ vedayitaṃ dukkhasmiṃ [V 2.0276] antogadhaṃ pariyāpannaṃ vadāmi saṅkhāradukkhatānativattanato. Sukhadukkhatopi cāti sukhādīnaṃ ṭhitivipariṇāmañāṇasukhatāya, vipariṇāmaṭhitiaññāṇadukkhatāya ca vuttattā tissopi ca sukhato, tissopi ca dukkhato anupassitabbāti attho. Satta anupassanā heṭṭhā pakāsitā eva. Sesanti yathāvuttaṃ sukhādivibhāgato sesaṃ sāmisanirāmisādibhedaṃ vedanānupassanāyaṃ vattabbaṃ.

'It is also suffering' means: it is also suffering due to the suffering of formations. 'In that suffering' means: I say that all that is felt is included and comprised within suffering, because it does not transcend the suffering of formations. And also 'from pleasure and suffering' means: because it is said that knowing the stability and change of pleasure and so on is pleasant, while ignorance of their change and stability is suffering, the meaning is that all three feelings should be contemplated from the perspective of pleasure and also from the perspective of suffering. The seven contemplations have already been explained below. 'The rest' means: as previously stated, the remaining distinctions from the division of pleasure and so forth, such as the sensual and the spiritual, should be discussed in the contemplation of feelings.

Ārammaṇa…pe… bhedānanti rūpādiārammaṇanānattassa nīlāditabbhedassa, chandādiadhipatinānattassa hīnāditabbhedassa, ñāṇajhānādisahajātanānattassa sasaṅkhārikāsaṅkhārikasavitakkāditabbhedassa, kāmāvacarādibhūminānattassa ukkaṭṭhamajjhimāditabbhedassa, kusalādikammanānattassa devagatisaṃvattaniyatāditabbhedassa, kaṇhasukkavipākanānattassa diṭṭhadhammavedanīyatāditabbhedassa, parittabhūmakādikiriyānānattassa tihetukāditabbhedassa vasena anupassitabbanti yojanā. Ādi-saddena savatthukāvatthukādinānattassa puggalattayasādhāraṇāditabbhedassa ca saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Salakkhaṇasāmaññalakkhaṇānanti phusanāditaṃtaṃlakkhaṇānañceva aniccatādisāmaññalakkhaṇānañca vasenāti yojanā. Suññatadhammassāti anattatāsaṅkhātasuññatāsabhāvassa. Yaṃ vibhāvetuṃ abhidhamme“tasmiṃ kho pana samaye dhammā honti, khandhā hontī”tiādinā [P 2.0378] (dha. sa. 121) suññatāvāradesanā pavattā, taṃ pahīnameva pubbe pahīnattā, tasmā tassa tassa puna pahānaṃ na vattabbaṃ.
