Na hi kilesā pahīyamānā ārammaṇavibhāgena pahīyanti anāgatānaṃyeva uppajjanārahānaṃ pahātabbattā, tasmā abhijjhādīnaṃ ekattha pahānaṃ vatvā itarattha na vattabbaṃ evāti imamatthaṃ dasseti “kāmañcetthā”tiādinā. Atha vā maggacittakkhaṇe ekattha pahīnaṃ sabbattha pahīnameva hotīti visuṃ visuṃ pahānaṃ na vattabbaṃ. Maggena hi pahīnāti vattabbataṃ arahanti. Tattha purimāya codanāya nānāpuggalaparihāro, na hi ekassa pahīnaṃ tato aññassa pahīnaṃ nāma hoti. Pacchimāya nānācittakkhaṇikaparihāro. Nānācittakkhaṇeti hi lokiyamaggacittakkhaṇeti adhippāyo. Pubbabhāgamaggo hi idhādhippeto. Lokiyabhāvanāya ca kāye pahīnaṃ na vedanādīsu vikkhambhitaṃ [M 2.0299] hoti. Yadipi nappavatteyya, paṭipakkhabhāvanāya suppahīnattā tattha sā “abhijjhādomanassassa appavattī”ti na vattabbā, tasmā punapi tappahānaṃ vattabbameva. Ekattha pahīnaṃ sesesupi pahīnaṃ hotīti lokuttarasatipaṭṭhānabhāvanaṃ, lokiyabhāvanāya vā sabbattha appavattimattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Pañcapi khandhā upādānakkhandhā loko”ti (vibha. 362, 364, 366) hi vibhaṅgecatūsupi ṭhānesu vuttanti.

“Object… and so on… ‘the distinctions’ means it should be contemplated by way of the diversity of objects such as form and their distinctions as blue, etc.; by way of the diversity of predominances such as desire and their distinctions as inferior, etc.; by way of the diversity of concomitants such as knowledge and jhāna and their distinctions as prompted, unprompted, with initial application, etc.; by way of the diversity of planes such as the sense-sphere and their distinctions as superior, middling, etc.; by way of the diversity of kamma such as wholesome and their distinctions as leading to the deva-realm, etc.; by way of the diversity of results such as dark and bright and their distinctions as to be experienced in this very life, etc.; by way of the diversity of functional consciousness such as that of the limited plane and their distinctions as triple-rooted, etc.—thus is the connection. By the word ‘etc.,’ the diversity of things with and without a basis, etc., and their distinctions as common to the three types of individuals, etc., should be understood. ‘By specific and general characteristics’ means by way of their respective characteristics such as contact, etc., and the general characteristics such as impermanence, etc.—thus is the connection. ‘Of the empty phenomenon’ means of the nature of emptiness, designated as not-self. To clarify this, in the Abhidhamma the discourse on the section on emptiness proceeds, “At that time, there are phenomena, there are aggregates,” etc. (Dhs 121). That which is abandoned has already been abandoned previously; therefore, its abandonment should not be spoken of again and again. For defilements are not abandoned by a division of objects, since only those fit to arise in the future are to be abandoned. Therefore, having spoken of the abandonment of covetousness, etc., in one place, it should not be spoken of elsewhere. This meaning is shown by “Though here one might wish…,” etc. Or, at the moment of path-consciousness, what is abandoned in one place is indeed abandoned everywhere; thus, abandonment should not be spoken of separately for each. For they are worthy of being called ‘abandoned by the path.’ In this regard, the answer to the first objection concerns different individuals, for what is abandoned by one is not thereby abandoned by another. The answer to the latter objection concerns different moments of consciousness. By ‘different moments of consciousness,’ the moments of mundane path-consciousness are intended. For the preliminary-part path is intended here. And through mundane development, what is abandoned in the body is not suppressed in feelings, etc. Even if it were not to arise, because it is well-abandoned by the opposing development, it should not be said there, “This is the non-arising of covetousness and displeasure”; therefore, its abandonment should indeed be spoken of again. That what is abandoned in one place is also abandoned in the others is said with reference to the development of supramundane mindfulness, or, in the case of mundane development, with reference to the mere non-arising everywhere. For in the Vibhaṅga it is said in all four places: “The five aggregates are the aggregates of clinging; they are the world” (Vb 362, 364, 366).

Uddesavāravaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

The Clarification of the Hidden Meaning in the Explanation of the Summary Section.

Kāyānupassanā

Contemplation of the Body

Ānāpānapabbavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on In-and-Out Breathing

374. Ārammaṇavasenāti [V 2.0277] anupassitabbakāyādiārammaṇavasena. Catudhā bhinditvāti uddesavasena catudhā bhinditvā. Tato catubbidhasatipaṭṭhānato ekekaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ [P 2.0379] gahetvā kāyaṃ vibhajantoti pāṭhaseso.

374. ‘By way of object’ means by way of the objects to be contemplated, such as the body. ‘Having divided it into four’ means having divided it into four by way of the summary. Then, from the four kinds of foundations of mindfulness, taking each foundation of mindfulness one by one, the remainder of the text is: ‘they analyze the body.’

Kathañcāti ettha kathanti pakārapucchā, tena niddisiyamāne kāyānupassanāpakāre pucchati. Ca-saddo byatireko, tena uddesavārena apākaṭaṃ niddesavārena vibhāviyamānaṃ visesaṃ joteti. Bāhirakesupi ito ekadesassa sambhavato sabbappakāraggahaṇaṃ kataṃ “sabbappakārakāyānupassanānibbattakassā”ti, tena ye ime ānāpānapabbādivasena āgatā cuddasappakārā, tadantogadhā ca ajjhattādianupassanāppakārā, tathā kāyagatāsatisutte (ma. ni. 3.153) vuttā kesādivaṇṇasaṇṭhānakasiṇārammaṇacatukkajjhānappakārā, lokiyādippakārā ca, te sabbepi anavasesato saṅgaṇhāti. Ime ca pakārā imasmiṃyeva sāsane, na ito bahiddhāti vuttaṃ “sabbappakāra…pe… paṭisedhano cā”ti. Tattha tathābhāvapaṭisedhanoti sabbappakārakāyānupassanānibbattakassa puggalassa aññasāsanassa nissayabhāvapaṭisedhano, etena idha bhikkhaveti ettha idha-saddo antogadhaevasaddatthoti dasseti. Santi hi ekapadānipi avadhāraṇāni yathā “vāyubhakkho”ti. Tenāha “idheva bhikkhave [M 2.0300] samaṇo”tiādi. Paripuṇṇasamaṇappakaraṇadhammo hi so puggalo, yo sabbappakārakāyānupassanānibbattako. Parappavādāti paresaṃ aññatitthiyānaṃ nānappakārā vādā titthāyatanāni.

In ‘And how?’, ‘how’ is a question about the mode. By this, it asks about the modes of contemplating the body that are to be pointed out. The word ‘and’ (ca) indicates a distinction; by it, it illuminates a specific detail that was not apparent in the summary section but is clarified in the exposition section. Because a part of this is possible even for outsiders, the inclusion of all modes is made by the phrase, ‘for one who generates all kinds of contemplation of the body.’ By this, it includes without remainder these fourteen modes that are given by way of the section on in-and-out breathing, etc., and the modes of contemplation such as internal, etc., that are included within them, and likewise the modes of the four jhānas with kasinas of hair, etc., color, and shape as their object, as stated in the Discourse on Mindfulness Directed to the Body (MN 119), as well as the mundane modes, etc. And these modes are found only in this Dispensation, not outside it; thus it is said, ‘all kinds… and also a denial.’ There, ‘denial of being so’ means the denial that a person who generates all kinds of contemplation of the body has any reliance on another Dispensation. By this, it shows that in the phrase ‘here, monks,’ the word ‘here’ contains the meaning of the word ‘only’ (eva). For there are emphatic statements of even a single word, as in ‘wind-eater.’ Therefore, he said, ‘Only here, monks, is there a contemplative,’ etc. For that person who generates all kinds of contemplation of the body is one whose qualities make for a complete contemplative. ‘The doctrines of others’ means the various doctrines and sectarian tenets of others, the adherents of other sects.

Araññādikasseva bhāvanānurūpasenāsanataṃ dassetuṃ “imassahī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Duddamo damathaṃ anupagato goṇo kūṭagoṇo. Dohanakāle yathā thanehi anavasesato khīraṃ na paggharati, evaṃ dohapaṭibandhinī kūṭadhenu. Rūpa-saddādike paṭicca uppajjanakaassādo rūpārammaṇādiraso. Pubbe āciṇṇārammaṇanti pabbajjato pubbe, anādimati vā saṃsāre paricitārammaṇaṃ. Nibandheyyāti [P 2.0380] bandheyya. Satiyāti sammadeva kammaṭṭhānassa sallakkhaṇavasena pavattāya satiyā. Ārammaṇeti kammaṭṭhānārammaṇe. Daḷhanti thiraṃ, yathā satokārissa upacārappanābhedo samādhi ijjhati, tathā thāmagataṃ katvāti attho.

To show that only places such as a forest are lodgings suitable for development, it is said, ‘For this one…,’ etc. A rogue bull is a bull that is hard to tame, that has not been broken. A deceitful cow is a cow that obstructs milking, just as at milking time milk does not flow completely from the udders. The taste for form-objects, etc., is the delight that arises in dependence on forms, sounds, and so on. ‘A previously practiced object’ means an object familiar before going forth or an object frequented in beginningless saṃsāra. ‘Would bind’ means it would bind. ‘With mindfulness’ means with mindfulness that proceeds rightly by way of discerning the characteristics of the meditation subject. ‘On the object’ means on the meditation object. ‘Firmly’ means steadily; the meaning is having made it powerful, so that for one who is mindful, concentration distinguished as access and absorption is accomplished.

Visesādhigamadiṭṭhadhammasukhavihārapadaṭṭhānanti [V 2.0278] sabbesaṃ buddhānaṃ, ekaccānaṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ, buddhasāvakānañca visesādhigamassa aññena kammaṭṭhānena adhigatavisesānaṃ diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārassa padaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ.

It is the basis for the attainment of distinction for all Buddhas, some Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha; and for the pleasant abiding in this very life of those who have attained distinction through another meditation subject.

Vatthuvijjācariyo viya bhagavā yogīnaṃ anurūpanivāsaṭṭhānupadisanato. Bhikkhu dīpisadiso araññe ekako viharitvā paṭipakkhanimmathanavasena icchitatthasādhanato phalamuttamanti sāmaññaphalaṃ sandhāya vadati. Parakkamajavayoggabhūminti bhāvanussāhajavassa yoggakaraṇabhūmibhūtaṃ.

The Blessed One is like a master of site-lore, because he indicates suitable dwelling places for meditators. A monk is like a leopard; dwelling alone in the forest and crushing the opposing forces, he achieves his desired goal. Thus, when speaking of the ‘highest fruit,’ he speaks with reference to the fruits of recluseship. ‘The ground for the speed of striving’ means the ground that is fit for the swiftness of the energy of development.

Addhānavasena pavattānaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ vasena dīghaṃ vā assasanto, ittaravasena pavattānaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ vasena rassaṃ vā assasantoti yojanā. Evaṃ sikkhatoti assāsapassāsānaṃ dīgharassatāpajānanasabbakāyappaṭisaṃvedanaoḷārikoḷārikapaṭippassambhanavasena bhāvanaṃ sikkhato, tathābhūto vā hutvā tisso sikkhā pavattayato. Assāsapassāsanimitteti assāsapassāsasannissayena upaṭṭhitapaṭibhāganimitte. Assāsapassāse pariggaṇhāti rūpamukhena vipassanaṃ abhinivisanto, yo “assāsapassāsakammiko”ti vutto. Jhānaṅgāni pariggaṇhāti arūpamukhena vipassanaṃ abhinivisanto. Vatthu nāma karajakāyo cittacetasikānaṃ pavattiṭṭhānabhāvato. Añño satto vā puggalo vā natthīti visuddhidiṭṭhi “tayidaṃ [M 2.0301] dhammamattaṃ, na ahetukaṃ, nāpi issarādivisamahetukaṃ, atha kho avijjādihetuka”nti addhāttayepi kaṅkhāvitaraṇena vitiṇṇakaṅkho. “Yaṃ [P 2.0381] kiñci bhikkhu rūpa”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 1.361; 2.113; 3.86, 89; paṭi. ma. 1.54) nayena kalāpasammasanavasena tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā. Udayavayānupassanādivasena vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento. Anukkamena maggapaṭipāṭiyā.

One breathes in long by way of the in-and-out breaths that occur over a long duration, or one breathes in short by way of the in-and-out breaths that occur over a short duration—this is the connection. 'Thus one trains' means one trains in the development by way of knowing the length or shortness of the in-and-out breaths, experiencing the whole body, and calming the coarse bodily formations; or, having become thus, one undertakes the three trainings. 'The sign of in-and-out breaths' means the counterpart sign that has arisen in dependence on the in-and-out breaths. 'One comprehends the in-and-out breaths' refers to one directing oneself to insight through the aspect of form, who is called the 'one whose task is the in-and-out breaths.' 'One comprehends the jhāna factors' refers to one directing oneself to insight through the aspect of the formless. The basis is the physical body, because it is the ground for the occurrence of mind and mental factors. 'There is no other being or person'—this is purified view. 'This is merely phenomena, not without cause, nor caused by a disparate cause such as a creator, but rather caused by ignorance, etc.'—thus, having crossed over doubt by overcoming doubt regarding the three periods of time, one is free from doubt. By the method beginning with 'Whatever form, O bhikkhu,' etc. (MN 1.361; 2.113; 3.86, 89; Paṭis I 54), one applies the three characteristics by way of the comprehension of groups. Developing insight by way of the contemplation of arising and passing away, etc. Gradually, according to the order of the path.

“Parassa vā assāsapassāsakāye”ti idaṃ sammasanavāravasenāyaṃ pāḷi pavattāti katvā vuttaṃ, samathavasena pana parassa assāsapassāsakāye appanānimittuppatti eva natthi. Aṭṭhapetvāti antarantarā na ṭhapetvā. Aparāparaṃ sañcaraṇakāloti ajjhattabahiddhādhammesupi nirantaraṃ vā bhāvanāya pavattanakālo kathito. Ekasmiṃ kāle panidaṃ ubhayaṃ na labbhatīti “ajjhattaṃ, bahiddhā”ti ca vuttaṃ idaṃ dhammadvayaṃ ghaṭitaṃ ekasmiṃ kāle ekato ārammaṇabhāvena na labbhati, ekajjhaṃ ālambituṃ na sakkāti attho.

'Or in the body of in-and-out breaths of another'—this Pāli passage is said to have been stated by way of the section on comprehension. However, by way of tranquility, there is indeed no arising of the absorption sign in the body of in-and-out breaths of another. 'Without setting aside' means not setting aside intermittently. 'The time of moving back and forth' refers to the time when the development proceeds continuously on internal and external phenomena. But at one time, this pair is not obtained—thus, 'internally' and 'externally' are mentioned. These two phenomena, combined, are not obtained as an object together at one time; it is not possible to take them as an object simultaneously—this is the meaning.

Samudeti etasmāti samudayo, so eva kāraṇaṭṭhena dhammoti samudayadhammo. Assāsapassāsānaṃ uppattihetu karajakāyādi, tassa anupassanasīlo samudayadhammānupassī, taṃ pana [V 2.0279] samudayadhammaṃ upamāya dassento “yathā nāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha bhastanti ruttiṃ. Gaggaranāḷinti ukkāpanāḷiṃ. Teti karajakāyādike. Yathā assāsapassāsakāyo karajakāyādisambandhī taṃnimittatāya, evaṃ karajakāyādayopi assāsapassāsakāyasambandhino taṃnimittabhāvenāti “samudayadhammā kāyasmi”nti vattabbataṃ labhantīti vuttaṃ “samudaya…pe… vuccatī”ti. Pakativācī vā dhamma-saddo “jātidhammāna”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.131; 3.310; paṭi. ma. 1.33) viyāti kāyassa paccayasamavāye uppajjanakapakatikāyānupassī vā “samudayadhammānupassī”ti vutto. Tenāha “karajakāyañcā”tiādi. Evañca katvā kāyasminti bhummavacanaṃ suṭṭhutaraṃ yujjati.

'It originates from this,' thus it is 'origin.' That itself, being a phenomenon in the sense of a cause, is a 'phenomenon of origination.' The cause for the arising of the in-and-out breaths is the physical body, etc. One who is of the nature of contemplating that is 'one who contemplates phenomena of origination.' But to show that phenomenon of origination by way of a simile, it is said, 'Just as...' and so forth. Therein, 'bellows' means a leather bag. 'The smith's pipe' means the blowing pipe. 'Those' refers to the physical body, etc. Just as the body of in-and-out breaths is connected to the physical body, etc., because it is conditioned by it, so too the physical body, etc., is connected to the body of in-and-out breaths by being its condition. Thus, it becomes appropriate to say 'phenomena of origination in the body,' and so it is said 'origination... etc. ... is called.' Alternatively, the word 'dhamma' denotes nature, as in 'subject to birth,' etc. Thus, one who contemplates the body as having the nature of arising from a conjunction of conditions is called 'one who contemplates phenomena of origination.' Therefore, it is said, 'and the physical body,' etc. And when it is taken thus, the locative case in 'in the body' is very fitting.

Vayadhammānupassīti ettha ahetukattepi vināsassa yesaṃ hetudhammānaṃ [P 2.0382] abhāve yaṃ na hoti, tadabhāvo tassa abhāvassa hetu viya voharīyatīti upacārato karajakāyādiabhāvo assāsapassāsakāyassa vayakāraṇaṃ vutto. Tenāha “yathā bhastāyā”tiādi[M 2.0302]. Ayaṃ tāvettha paṭhamavikappavasena atthavibhāvanā. Dutiyavikappavasena upacārena vināyeva attho veditabbo.

Regarding 'one who contemplates phenomena of passing away': here, although cessation is without a cause, when something does not exist due to the absence of its causal phenomena, that absence is spoken of figuratively as if it were the cause of its absence. Thus, figuratively, the absence of the physical body, etc., is said to be the cause for the passing away of the body of in-and-out breaths. Therefore, it is said, 'Just as with the bellows,' and so forth. This, for now, is the explanation of the meaning by way of the first alternative. By way of the second alternative, the meaning should be understood without any figurative speech.

Ajjhattabahiddhānupassanā viya bhinnavatthuvisayatāya samudayavayadhammānupassanāpi ekakāle na labbhatīti āha “kālena samudayaṃ kālena vayaṃ anupassanto”ti. “Atthi kāyo”ti eva-saddo luttaniddiṭṭhoti “kāyova atthī”ti vatvā avadhāraṇena nivattitaṃ dassento “na satto”tiādimāha. Tassattho – yo rūpādīsu sattavisattatāya, paresañca sajjāpanaṭṭhena, satvaguṇayogato vā “satto”ti parehi parikappito, tassa sattanikāyassa pūraṇato ca cavanupapajjanadhammatāya galanato ca “puggalo”ti, thīyati saṃhaññati ettha gabbhoti “itthī”ti, puri pure bhāge seti pavattatīti “puriso”ti, āhito ahaṃ māno etthāti “attā”ti, attano santakabhāvena “attaniya”nti, paro na hotīti katvā “aha”nti, mama santakanti katvā “mamā”ti, vuttappakāravinimutto aññoti katvā “kocī”ti, tassa santakabhāvena “kassacī”ti, vikappetabbo koci natthi, kevalaṃ “kāyo eva atthī”ti. Dasahipi padehi attattaniyasuññatameva kāyassa vibhāveti. Evanti “kāyova atthī”tiādinā vuttappakārena.

Just as the contemplation of the internal and external is not obtained at one time because they have different objects, so too the contemplation of phenomena of origination and passing away is not obtained at one time. Thus, it is said, 'at one time contemplating origination, at another time contemplating passing away.' In 'There is a body,' the particle 'eva' is indicated as elided. By saying 'Only the body exists,' showing what is excluded by the emphasis, it is said, 'not a being,' and so forth. Its meaning is this: that which is conceived by others as a 'being' (satta) due to being attached to forms, etc., or for the purpose of making others attached, or due to connection with the qualities of a being; or as a 'person' (puggala) because of filling the host of beings, because of having the nature of passing away and being reborn, and because of falling; or as a 'woman' (itthī) because a fetus is established and compacted therein; or as a 'man' (purisa) because he lies or proceeds in the city or in the front part; or as a 'self' (attā) because the conceit 'I' is placed therein; or as 'belonging to self' (attaniya) because of being one’s own possession; or as 'I' (ahaṃ) because of it not being another; or as 'mine' (mama) because of it being my possession; or as 'someone' (koci) because of it being another, distinct from the aforementioned types; or as 'of someone' (kassaci) because of it being the possession of that one—there is no such one to be conceived; there is only the body. Through these ten terms, the emptiness of self and what belongs to self is indeed clarified regarding the body. 'Thus' means in the manner stated, beginning with 'Only the body exists,' and so forth.

Ñāṇapamāṇatthāyāti kāyānupassanāñāṇaṃ paraṃ pamāṇaṃ pāpanatthāya. Satipamāṇatthāyāti kāyapariggāhikaṃ satiṃ pavattanasatiṃ paraṃ pamāṇaṃ pāpanatthāya. Imassa hi vuttanayena “atthi kāyo”ti aparāparuppattivasena paccupaṭṭhitā sati bhiyyoso mattāya tattha ñāṇassa, satiyā ca [V 2.0280] paribrūhanāya hoti. Tenāha “satisampajaññānaṃ vuḍḍhatthāyā”ti. Imissā [P 2.0383] bhāvanāya taṇhādiṭṭhiggāhānaṃ ujupaṭipakkhattā vuttaṃ “taṇhā…pe… viharatī”ti. Tathābhūto ca loke kiñcipi “aha”nti vā “mama”nti vā gahetabbaṃ na passati, kuto gaṇheyyāti āha “na ca kiñcī”tiādi. Evampīti ettha pi-saddo heṭṭhā niddiṭṭhassa tādisassa atthassa abhāvato avuttasamuccayatthoti dassento “upari atthaṃ upādāyā”ti āha yathā “antamaso tiracchānagatāyapi, ayampi pārājiko hotī”ti. (Pārā. 42) evanti pana niddiṭṭhākārassa paccāmasanaṃ nigamanavasena katanti āha “iminā pana…pe… dassetī”ti.

'For the measure of knowledge' means for the purpose of bringing the knowledge of the contemplation of the body to the highest measure. 'For the measure of mindfulness' means for the purpose of bringing the mindfulness that comprehends the body and the mindfulness that sets it in motion to the highest measure. For this one, mindfulness established by way of the successive arising in the stated manner of 'there is a body' is for the abundant increase of knowledge and mindfulness there. Therefore, it is said, 'for the increase of mindfulness and clear comprehension.' Because this development is the direct opposite of the grasping of craving and views, it is said, 'craving... etc. ... he dwells.' And one who has become thus does not see anything in the world that should be grasped as 'I' or 'mine'; whence would he grasp? Thus, it is said, 'and nothing...' and so forth. Regarding 'evampi': here the word 'pi', because of the absence of such a meaning as was indicated previously, is for the purpose of including what has not been said. Showing this, it is said 'with reference to the meaning that follows,' just as 'even in the case of one gone to the animal realm, this too is a pārājika offense' (Pārā. 42). But 'evaṃ' is a review of the indicated manner, made by way of a conclusion; thus, it is said, 'by this... etc. ... he shows.'

Pubbabhāgasatipaṭṭhānassa [M 2.0303] idha adhippetattā vuttaṃ “sati dukkhasacca”nti. Sā pana sati yasmiṃ attabhāve, tassa samuṭṭhāpikā taṇhā, tassāpi samuṭṭhāpikā eva nāma hoti tadabhāve abhāvatoti āha “tassā samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā”ti, yathā “saṅkhārapaccayā”ti (ma. ni. 3.126; udā. 1; vibha. 484). Taṃviññāṇabījataṃsantatisambhūto sabbopi lokiyo viññāṇappabandho “saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ” tveva vuccati suttantanayena. Appavattīti appavattinimittaṃ, ubhinnaṃ appavattiyā nimittabhūtoti attho. Na pavattati etthāti vā appavatti. “Dukkhaparijānano”tiādi ekantato catukiccasādhanavaseneva ariyamaggassa pavattīti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Avuttasiddho hi tassa bhāvanāpaṭivedho. Catusaccavasenāti catusaccakammaṭṭhānavasena. Ussakkitvāti visuddhiparamparāya āruhitvā, bhāvanaṃ upari netvāti attho. Niyyānamukhanti vaṭṭadukkhato nissaraṇūpāyo.

Here, mindfulness is said to be 'the truth of suffering' because the preliminary stage of the establishment of mindfulness is intended. That mindfulness, in whatever individual existence it arises, has craving as its generator; and that craving is also its generator, for without it, there would be no arising. Thus, it is said, 'The prior craving is its generator,' just as in 'With formations as condition, consciousness arises' (M. 3.126; Ud. 1; Vibh. 484). All mundane consciousness, which arises from the seed of that consciousness and the continuous stream, is simply called 'consciousness conditioned by formations' in accordance with the sutta method. 'Non-arising' (appavatti) means the sign of non-arising, being the sign for the non-arising of both. Alternatively, 'appavatti' means 'it does not proceed here.' 'The full understanding of suffering,' and so forth, is stated to show that the noble path operates solely by way of accomplishing the four functions. Indeed, its penetration through development is implicitly understood. 'By way of the four truths' means by way of the meditation subject of the four truths. 'Having striven' (ussakkitvā) means having ascended through the succession of purifications, having led the development further—this is the meaning. 'The gateway to liberation' (niyyānamukha) is the means of escape from the suffering of the round.

Ānāpānapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on in-breathing and out-breathing is concluded.

Iriyāpathapabbavaṇṇanā

The Description of the Postures

375. Iriyāpathavasenāti iriyanaṃ iriyā, kiriyā, idha pana kāyikapayogo [P 2.0384] veditabbo. Iriyānaṃ patho pavattimaggoti iriyāpatho, gamanādivasena pavattā sarīrāvatthā. Gacchanto vā hi satto kāyena kātabbakiriyaṃ karoti ṭhito vā nisinno vā nipanno vāti, tesaṃ iriyāpathānaṃ vasena, iriyāpathavibhāgenāti attho. Puna caparanti puna ca aparaṃ, yathāvuttaānāpānakammaṭṭhānato bhiyyopi aññaṃ kāyānupassanākammaṭṭhānaṃ kathemi, suṇāthāti vā adhippāyo[V 2.0281]. “Gacchanto vā”tiādi gamanādimattajānanassa, gamanādigatavisesajānanassa ca sādhāraṇavacanaṃ, tattha gamanādimattajānanaṃ na idha nādhippetaṃ, gamanādigatavisesajānanaṃ pana adhippetanti taṃ vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “tattha kāma”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Sattūpaladdhinti “satto atthī”ti upaladdhiṃ sattaggāhaṃ. Na pajahati na pariccajati “ahaṃ gacchāmi, mama gamana”nti gāhasabbhāvato. Tato eva attasaññaṃ “atthi attā kārako vedako”ti evaṃ pavattaṃ viparītasaññaṃ [M 2.0304] na ugghāṭeti nāpaneti appaṭipakkhabhāvato, ananubrūhanato vā. Evaṃ bhūtassa cassa kuto kammaṭṭhānādibhāvoti āha “kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā vā na hotī”ti. “Imassa panā”tiādi sukkapakkho, tassa vuttavipariyāyena attho veditabbo. Tameva hi atthaṃ vivarituṃ “idañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

375. 'By way of postures' (iriyāpathavasena) means: the ways of moving (iriyā) are actions (kiriyā); here, however, it should be understood as a bodily activity. The path (patho) of these ways of moving is the way they occur, hence 'posture' (iriyāpatho), referring to the bodily states that occur through walking, etc. For indeed, a being, when walking, performs actions to be done with the body, or when standing, or sitting, or lying down—it is according to these postures (iriyāpathā), meaning by way of the divisions of these bodily movements. 'Furthermore' (puna caparaṃ) means: and further, beyond what has been said about the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing, I will explain yet another meditation subject related to the contemplation of the body—listen, that is the intention. 'When walking' (‘gacchanto vā’) and so forth, is a statement common to both one who merely knows the act of walking, etc., and one who knows the specific characteristics of walking, etc. Here, the mere knowledge of walking is not intended, but rather the detailed knowledge of walking is intended. To clarify this distinction, 'therein' (‘tattha kāma’) and so forth, is stated. 'Perception of a being' (sattūpaladdhi) means the perception or belief, 'there is a being,' i.e., grasping at the notion of a being. One does not abandon or relinquish the thought 'I am walking, this is my walking,' due to the continued existence of such grasping. From this arises the perception of self—'there is a self, a doer, an experiencer'—and this wrong perception is not uprooted or removed because there is no opposing factor, or because this is not thoroughly cultivated. For one in such a state, how can there be the attainment of a meditation subject or the development of the foundations of mindfulness? Hence it is said, 'there is no meditation subject or development of the foundations of mindfulness.' 'But for this one...' (‘imassa pana’) and so forth, refers to the bright side (sukkapakkho), the meaning of which should be understood as the opposite of what was previously stated. To elaborate on this very meaning, 'For here...' (‘idañhi’) and so forth, is said.

Tattha ko gacchatīti sādhanaṃ, kiriyañca avinibbhuttaṃ katvā gamanakiriyāya kattupucchā, sā kattubhāvavisiṭṭhaattapaṭikkhepatthā dhammamattasseva gamanasiddhidassanato. Kassa gamananti tamevatthaṃ pariyāyantarena vadati sādhanaṃ, kiriyañca vinibbhuttaṃ katvā gamanakiriyāya akattusambandhībhāvavibhāvanato. Paṭikkhepatthañhi antonītaṃ katvā ubhayatthaṃ kiṃ-saddo pavatto. Kiṃ kāraṇāti pana paṭikkhittakattukāya [P 2.0385] gamanakiriyāya aviparītakāraṇapucchā. Idañhi gamanaṃ nāma attā manasā saṃyujjati, mano indriyehi, indriyāni attehīti evamādi micchākāraṇavinimuttaanurūpapaccayahetuko dhammānaṃ pavattiākāraviseso. Tenāha “tatthā”tiādi.

Herein, 'Who goes?' is a question about the doer of the act of going, taking the instrument and the action as inseparable. It is intended to reject a self distinguished by being an agent, inasmuch as it shows that the act of going is established by mere phenomena. 'Whose going?' expresses the same meaning in a different way, taking the instrument and the action as separate to clarify the act of going's lack of connection to an agent. For, having made the meaning of rejection implicit, the word 'what' (or 'who') functions in both instances. 'But for what reason?' is a question about the non-perverted cause of the act of going, for which the agent has been rejected. For this 'going' is a particular mode of the arising of phenomena resulting from appropriate conditions and causes that are free from false causes such as 'the self is connected to the mind, the mind to the senses, the senses to the self'. Therefore, it is said, 'Herein,' etc.

Na koci satto vā puggalo vā gacchati dhammamattasseva gamanasiddhito, tabbinimuttassa ca kassaci abhāvato. Idāni dhammamattasseva gamanasiddhiṃ dassetuṃ “cittakiriyāvāyodhātuvipphārenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha cittakiriyā ca sā, vāyodhātuyā vipphāro vipphandanañcāti cittakiriyāvāyodhātuvipphāro, tena. Ettha ca cittakiriyaggahaṇena anindriyabaddhavāyodhātuvipphāraṃ nivatteti, vāyodhātuvipphāraggahaṇena cetanāvacīviññattibhedaṃ cittakiriyaṃ nivatteti, ubhayena pana kāyaviññattiṃ vibhāveti. “Gacchatī”ti vatvā yathā pavattamāne kāye “gacchatī”ti vohāro hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “tasmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tanti gantukāmatāvasena pavattacittaṃ. Vāyaṃ janetīti vāyodhātuadhikaṃ rūpakalāpaṃ uppādeti, adhikatā cettha sāmatthiyato, na pamāṇato. Gamanacittasamuṭṭhitaṃ sahajātarūpakāyassa thambhanasandhāraṇacalanānaṃ paccayabhūtena ākāravisesena pavattamānaṃ vāyodhātuṃ sandhāyāha “vāyo viññattiṃ janetī”ti. Adhippāyasahabhāvī hi vikāro viññatti. Yathāvuttaadhikabhāveneva ca vāyogahaṇaṃ[V 2.0282], na vāyodhātuyā eva janakabhāvato, aññathā viññattiyā [M 2.0305] upādāyarūpabhāvo durupapādo siyā. Purato abhinīhāro puratobhāgena kāyassa pavattanaṃ, yo “abhikkamo”ti vuccati.

No being or person goes; it is merely the accomplishment of the act of moving by phenomena alone, due to the absence of anyone detached from them. Now, to show that the act of moving is accomplished merely by phenomena, it is said: 'by the activity of mind and the vibration of the wind element,' etc. Herein, 'activity of mind' refers to mental action, and 'the vibration of the wind element' refers to agitation—thus, 'the activity of mind and the vibration of the wind element' means by that. Here, the mention of 'mental activity' excludes the vibration of the wind element not bound to the sense faculties, while the mention of 'the wind element's vibration' excludes the kinds of mental activity that are volition and verbal intimation. Together, they clarify bodily intimation. Having stated 'goes,' to explain how the conventional expression 'he goes' arises regarding the moving body, it is said: 'therefore,' etc. Here, 'that' refers to the mind occurring with the desire to go. 'Generates wind' means it produces a cluster of material qualities with an excess of the wind element. This 'excess' refers to capability, not quantity. Referring to the wind element arising from the movement-mind and functioning with a distinctive mode as a condition for stiffening, supporting, and moving the co-nascent material body, he says, 'wind generates intimation.' For the alteration co-arisen with intention is intimation. The mention of 'wind' here is due to its aforementioned heightened role, not because the wind element alone produces it—otherwise, intimation's nature as derived matter would be hard to establish. 'Forward projection' is the moving of the body's front part, which is called 'advancing.'

“Eseva nayo”ti atidesena saṅkhepato vatvā tamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “tatrāpi hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Koṭito paṭṭhāyāti heṭṭhimakoṭito [P 2.0386] paṭṭhāya pādatalato paṭṭhāya. Ussitabhāvoti ubbiddhabhāvo.

'This is the method,' thus stating briefly by way of extension, to explain that meaning, 'therein also,' etc., was said. 'Starting from the end' means starting from the lower end, starting from the sole of the foot. 'The state of being raised up' means the state of being elevated.

Evaṃ pajānatoti evaṃ cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva gamanādi hotīti pajānato. Tassa evaṃ pajānanāya nicchayagamanatthaṃ “evaṃ hotī”ti vicāraṇā vuccati loke yathābhūtaṃ ajānantehi micchābhinivesavasena, lokavohāravasena vā. Atthi panāti attano evaṃ vīmaṃsanavasena pucchāvacanaṃ. Natthīti nicchayavasena sattassa paṭikkhepavacanaṃ. “Yathā panā”tiādi tasseva atthassa upamāya vibhāvanaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyameva.

'One who understands thus': one who understands that movement and so on occur solely through the activity of mind and the vibration of the wind element. For one who understands thus, in order to arrive at certainty, there is an investigation expressed as 'thus it is,' which is spoken of in the world by those who do not know the truth as it is, due to adherence to wrong views or to conventional speech. 'But is there?'—this is a questioning statement for the sake of self-examination. 'There is not'—this is a statement of rejection of a being, based on certainty. 'Just as...'—this is an illustration for clarifying that very meaning, which is easily understood.

Nāvā mālutavegenāti yathā acetanā nāvā vātavegena desantaraṃ yāti, yathā ca acetano tejanaṃ kaṇḍo jiyāvegena desantaraṃ yāti, tathā acetano kāyo vātāhato yathāvuttavāyunā nīto desantaraṃ yātīti evaṃ upamāsaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sace pana koci vadeyya “yathā nāvātejanānaṃ pellakassa purisassa vasena desantaragamanaṃ, evaṃ kāyassāpī”ti, hotu, evaṃ icchito vāyamattho yathā hi nāvātejanānaṃ saṃhatalakkhaṇasseva purisassa vasena gamanaṃ, na asaṃhatalakkhaṇassa, evaṃ kāyassāpīti. Kā no hāni, bhiyyopi dhammamattatāva patiṭṭhaṃ labhati, na purisavādo. Tenāha “yantasuttavasenā”tiādi.

The boat by the force of the wind—just as an insentient boat goes to another place by the force of the wind, and just as an insentient arrow goes to another place by the force of the bowstring, so too the insentient body, struck by the wind, goes to another place carried by the aforementioned wind. Thus, the connection of the simile should be understood. But if someone were to say, 'Just as the movement of a boat or arrow to another place is due to a propelling person, so too is it with the body,' let it be so. This is the intended meaning. For just as the movement of a boat or arrow is due to a person who has the characteristic of being composite, not non-composite, so too is it with the body. What loss is there to us? All the more does the principle of mere phenomena gain a firm footing, not the doctrine of a person. Therefore, he said, 'by means of the machine's string,' and so on.

Tattha payuttanti heṭṭhā vuttanayena gamanādikiriyāvasena paccayehi payojitaṃ. Ṭhātīti tiṭṭhati. Etthāti imasmiṃ loke. Vinā hetupaccayeti gantukāmatācittataṃsamuṭṭhānavāyodhātuādihetupaccayehi vinā. Tiṭṭheti tiṭṭheyya. Vajeti vajeyya gaccheyya ko nāmāti sambandho. Paṭikkhepattho cettha kiṃ-saddoti hetupaccayavirahena ṭhānagamanapaṭikkhepamukhena [M 2.0306] sabbāyapi dhammappavattiyā paccayādhīnavuttitāvibhāvanena attasuññatā viya aniccadukkhatāpi vibhāvitāti daṭṭhabbā.

Therein, 'payuttaṃ' means impelled by conditions in the manner stated previously, by way of actions such as going. 'Ṭhāti' means it stands. 'Ettha' means in this world. 'Vinā hetupaccayehi' means without cause-conditions, such as the mind with the desire to go, the wind element arising therefrom, and so on. 'Tiṭṭheti' means it would stand. 'Vajeti' means it would go or proceed. 'What indeed?' is the connection. Here, the word 'kiṃ' has the meaning of rejection. It should be seen that by rejecting standing and going due to the absence of cause-conditions—thereby demonstrating that the occurrence of all phenomena is dependent on conditions—not-self is made clear, and likewise impermanence and suffering are also made clear.

Paṇihitoti yathā yathā paccayehi pakārehi nihito [P 2.0387] ṭhapito. Sabbasaṅgāhikavacananti sabbesampi [V 2.0283] catunnaṃ iriyāpathānaṃ ekajjhaṃ saṅgaṇhanavacanaṃ, pubbe visuṃ visuṃ iriyāpathānaṃ vuttattā idaṃ nesaṃ ekajjhaṃ gahetvā vacananti attho. Purimanayo vā iriyāpathappadhāno vuttoti tattha kāyo appadhāno anunipphādīti idha kāyaṃ padhānaṃ, apadhānañca iriyāpathaṃ anunipphādiṃ katvā dassetuṃ dutiyanayo vuttoti evampettha dvinnaṃ nayānaṃ viseso veditabbo. Ṭhitoti pavatto.

'Paṇihito' means placed or established in various ways by conditions. 'Sabbasaṅgāhikavacanaṃ' is a term that collectively encompasses all four postures, bringing them together into one statement. Since the postures were previously mentioned separately, this is an expression that gathers them together; that is the meaning. Or, in the previous method, the posture was stated as primary, and thus the body was secondary, a subordinate factor. Here, to show the body as primary and the posture as secondary, a subordinate factor, the second method is stated. In this way, the distinction between the two methods should be understood.

Iriyāpathapariggaṇhanampi iriyāpathavato kāyasseva pariggaṇhanaṃ tassa avatthāvisesabhāvatoti vuttaṃ “iriyāpathapariggaṇhanena kāye kāyānupassī viharatī”ti. Tenevettha rūpakkhandhavaseneva samudayādayo uddhaṭā. Esa nayo sesavāresupi. Ādināti ettha ādi-saddena yathā “taṇhāsamudayā kammasamudayā āhārasamudayā”ti nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ passantopi rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ passatīti ime cattāro ākārā saṅgayhanti, evaṃ “avijjānirodhā”ti ādayopi pañca ākārā saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

The grasping of the postures is also the grasping of the body that has the postures, since a posture is a particular state of the body. As it is said: 'By grasping the postures, one dwells contemplating the body in the body.' Therefore, here, arising and so on are presented solely in terms of the form aggregate. This is the method in the remaining sections as well. By the word 'ādi' here, these four aspects are included: just as one who sees the characteristic of production through 'from the arising of craving, from the arising of kamma, from the arising of nutriment' also sees the arising of the form aggregate. In the same way, it should be seen that five aspects, beginning with 'from the cessation of ignorance,' are also included. The rest is as previously explained.

Iriyāpathapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on Postures is concluded.

Catusampajaññapabbavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on the Four Kinds of Clear Comprehension

376. Catusampajaññavasenāti samantato pakārehi, pakaṭṭhaṃ vā savisesaṃ jānātīti sampajāno, sampajānassa bhāvo sampajaññaṃ, tathāpavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ, hatthavikārādibhedabhinnattā cattāri sampajaññāni samāhaṭāni catusampajaññaṃ, tassa vasena. “Abhikkante”tiādīni sāmaññaphale (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.214; dī. ni. ṭī. 1.214 vākyakhandhepi) vaṇṇitāni, na puna vaṇṇetabbāni, tasmā taṃtaṃsaṃvaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanāpi tattha vihitanayeneva gahetabbā. “Abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī hotī”tiādi vacanato abhikkamādigatacatusampajaññapariggaṇhanena rūpakāyassevettha samudayadhammānupassitādi adhippetoti āha “rūpakkhandhasseva samudayo ca vayo ca [M 2.0307] nīharitabbo”ti. Rūpadhammānaṃyeva hi pavattiākāravisesā abhikkamādayoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

376. 'By means of the fourfold clear comprehension': One who knows in all ways, or excellently and with specifics, is 'sampajāno' (one who clearly comprehends). The state of one who clearly comprehends is 'sampajaññaṃ' (clear comprehension), which is the knowledge that proceeds in such a way. Because they are distinguished by various kinds, such as movements of the hands, the four clear comprehensions are gathered together as 'the fourfold clear comprehension'; the phrase means 'by means of that.' The phrases 'when going forward,' etc., are explained in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta (commentaries), and need not be explained again. Therefore, the clarification of the subtle meaning in their respective commentaries should be understood according to the method established there. According to the statement, 'When going forward, when returning, he acts with clear comprehension,' etc., by grasping the fourfold clear comprehension related to going forward and so on, it is intended here that there is contemplation of the nature of arising, etc., with regard to the form-body itself. Thus, it is said: 'The arising and passing away of the form aggregate alone should be adduced.' For going forward and so on are, in fact, particular modes of the process of material phenomena. The rest is as previously explained.

Catusampajaññapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on the Four Kinds of Clear Comprehension is concluded.

Paṭikkūlamanasikārapabbavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on Attention to the Repulsive

377. Paṭikkūlamanasikāravasenāti [P 2.0388][V 2.0284] jigucchanīyatāya paṭikūlameva paṭikkūlaṃ, yo paṭikkūlasabhāvo paṭikkūlākāro, tassa manasi karaṇavasena. Antarenāpi hi bhāvavācinaṃ saddaṃ bhāvattho viññāyati yathā “paṭassa sukka”nti. Yasmā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.182) vuttaṃ, tasmā tattha, taṃsaṃvaṇṇanāyañca (visuddhi. ṭī. 1.182 ādayo) vuttanayena “imameva kāya”nti ādīnamattho veditabbo.

377. 'By means of attention to the repulsive': The repulsive is so called because it is disgusting. It means by way of directing the mind to that which is repulsive in nature and repulsive in aspect. For even without a word denoting an abstract quality, the meaning of that quality is understood, as in 'the white of the cloth.' Because it is stated in the Visuddhimagga, the meaning of phrases such as 'this very body' should be understood according to the method explained there and in its commentary.

Vatthādīhi pasibbakākārena bandhitvā kataṃ āvāṭanaṃ putoḷi. Nānākārā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne sammissāti ettāvatā nānāvaṇṇānaṃ kesādīnañca upameyyatā. Vibhūtakāloti paṇṇattiṃ samatikkamitvā kesādīnaṃ asubhākārassa upaṭṭhitakālo. Iti-saddassa ākāratthataṃ dassento “eva”nti vatvā taṃ ākāraṃ sarūpato dassento “kesādipariggaṇhanenā”tiādimāha. Kesādisaññitānañhi asucibhāvānaṃ paramaduggandhajegucchapaṭikkūlākārassa samudayato anupassanā idha kāyānupassanāti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

A container made by binding with cloth and other materials in the shape of a sack is a 'putoḷi.' The comparability of the various colors of hair and so on is due to the fact that various kinds are mixed together in one place. 'Vibhūtakālo' is the time when, having transcended concepts, the impure aspect of hair and the like becomes manifest. Showing that the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'aspect,' he says 'evaṃ' (thus), and then, showing that aspect in its own nature, he says, 'by the grasping of hair, etc.' For here, the contemplation of the body is the contemplation of the arising of the utterly foul, extremely malodorous, disgusting, and repulsive aspect of the impure states designated as hair and so on. The rest is as previously explained.

Paṭikkūlamanasikārapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on Attention to the Repulsive is concluded.

Dhātumanasikārapabbavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on Attention to the Elements

378. Dhātumanasikāravasenāti pathavīdhātuādikā catasso dhātuyo ārabbha pavattabhāvanāmanasikāravasena, catudhātuvavatthānavasenāti attho. Dhātumanasikāro, dhātukammaṭṭhānaṃ, catudhātuvavatthānanti hi atthato ekaṃ. Goghātakoti jīvikatthāya gunnaṃ ghātako. Antevāsikoti kammakaraṇavasena tassa samīpavāsī taṃ nissāya jīvanako[M 2.0308]. Vinivijjhitvāti ekasmiṃ ṭhāne aññamaññaṃ vinivijjhitvā. Mahāpathānaṃ vemajjhaṭṭhānasaṅkhāteti catunnaṃ mahāpathānaṃ tāya [P 2.0389] eva vinivijjhanaṭṭhānatāya vemajjhasaṅkhāte. Yasmā te cattāro mahāpathā catūhi disāhi āgantvā tattha samohitā viya honti, tasmā taṃ ṭhānaṃ catumahāpathaṃ, tasmiṃ catumahāpathe. Ṭhita-saddo “ṭhito vā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.263; a. ni. 5.28) ṭhānasaṅkhātairiyāpathasamaṅgitāya, ṭhā-saddassa vā gatinivattiatthatāya aññattha ṭhapetvā gamanaṃ sesairiyāpathasamaṅgitāya [V 2.0285] bodhako, idha pana yathā tathā rūpakāyassa pavattiākārabodhako adhippetoti āha “catunnaṃ iriyāpathānaṃ yena kenaci ākārena ṭhitattā yathā ṭhita”nti. Tattha ākārenāti ṭhānādinā rūpakāyassa pavattiākārena. Ṭhānādayo hi iriyāpathasaṅkhātāya kiriyāya patho pavattimaggoti “iriyāpatho”ti vuccantīti vutto vāyamattho. Yathāṭhitanti yathāpavattaṃ, yathāvuttaṃ ṭhānamevettha paṇidhānanti adhippetanti āha “yathā ṭhitattā ca yathāpaṇihita”nti. “Ṭhita”nti vā kāyassa ṭhānasaṅkhātairiyāpathasamāyogaparidīpanaṃ, “paṇihita”nti tadaññairiyāpathasamāyogaparidīpanaṃ. “Ṭhita”nti vā kāyasaṅkhātānaṃ rūpadhammānaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ khaṇe sakiccavasena avaṭṭhānaparidīpanaṃ, paṇihitanti paccayavasena tehi tehi paccayehi pakārato nihitaṃ paṇihitanti evampettha attho veditabbo. Paccavekkhatīti pati pati avekkhati, ñāṇacakkhunā vinibbhujjitvā visuṃ visuṃ passati.

378. By way of attention to the elements means by way of the attention of the meditation that proceeds in relation to the four elements beginning with the earth element; by way of the determination of the four elements—this is the meaning. For attention to the elements, the elements as a meditation subject, and the determination of the four elements are one in meaning. A cattle butcher is one who kills cattle for a living. A disciple is one who lives near him, living in dependence on him by way of performing work. Having dissected means having dissected them from one another in a single place. At the place known as the middle of the great crossroads means at the place known as the middle because it is the very place where the four great roads intersect. Because those four great roads, coming from the four directions, are as if converged there, therefore that place is a four-great-road-junction; at that four-great-road-junction. The word 'situated' (ṭhita)—as in 'standing or' (Dīgha Nikāya 1.263; Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.28)—indicates being endowed with the posture known as standing, or, because the root 'ṭhā' has the meaning of cessation of motion, it indicates being endowed with the remaining postures, having set aside motion. Here, however, it is intended to indicate the mode of occurrence of the physical body in whatever way, hence it is said: 'because of being situated in whatever manner of the four postures, as it is situated.' Therein, 'by the manner' means by the mode of occurrence of the physical body through standing, etc. For standing and so on are called 'postures' (iriyāpatha) because they are the path, the way of proceeding, for the activity known as posture; this meaning has been stated. 'As it is situated' means as it occurs. As it is said, the very state of being situated is here intended as the placing, hence it is said: 'as it is situated and as it is placed.' Alternatively, 'situated' is an elucidation of the body's connection with the posture known as standing; 'placed' is an elucidation of its connection with the other postures. Alternatively, 'situated' is an elucidation of the momentary subsistence of the material phenomena called 'body', each according to its own function; 'placed' means placed by way of conditions, laid down in various ways by these and those conditions—thus the meaning should be understood here. He reviews means he looks at again and again; having analyzed with the eye of wisdom, he sees separately.

Idāni vuttamevatthaṃ bhāvatthavibhāvanavasena dassetuṃ “yathā goghātakassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha posentassāti maṃsūpacayaparibrūhanāya kuṇḍakabhattakappāsaṭṭhiādīhi saṃvaḍḍhentassa. Vadhitaṃ matanti hiṃsitaṃ hutvā mataṃ. Matanti ca matamattaṃ. Tenevāha “tāvadevā”ti. Gāvīti saññā na antaradhāyatīti yāni aṅgapaccaṅgāni [P 2.0390] yathāsanniviṭṭhāni upādāya gāvīsamaññā matamattāyapi gāviyā tesaṃ taṃsannivesassa avinaṭṭhattā. Vilīyanti bhijjanti vibhujjantīti bīlā, bhāgā va-kārassa ba-kāraṃ, ikārassa ca īkāraṃ katvā. Bīlasoti bīlaṃ bīlaṃ katvā. Vibhajitvāti aṭṭhisaṅghātato maṃsaṃ vivecetvā, tato vā vivecitaṃ maṃsaṃ bhāgaso katvā. Tenevāha “maṃsasaññā pavattatī”ti. Pabbajitassāpi apariggahitakammaṭṭhānassa. Ghanavinibbhoganti santatisamūhakiccaghanānaṃ vinibbhujjanaṃ vivecanaṃ. Dhātuso [M 2.0309] paccavekkhatoti ghanavinibbhogakaraṇena dhātuṃ dhātuṃ pathavīādidhātuṃ visuṃ visuṃ katvā paccavekkhantassa. Sattasaññāti attānudiṭṭhivasena pavattā sattasaññāti vadanti, vohāravasena pavattasattasaññāyapi tadā antaradhānaṃ yuttameva yāthāvato ghanavinibbhogassa sampādanato. Evañhi sati yathāvuttaopammatthena upameyyattho aññadatthu saṃsandati sameti. Tenevāha “dhātuvaseneva cittaṃ santiṭṭhatī”ti. Dakkhoti cheko taṃtaṃsamaññāya kusalo “yathājāte sūnasmiṃ naṅguṭṭhakhuravisāṇādivante aṭṭhimaṃsādiavayavasamudāye avibhatte gāvīsamaññā, na vibhatte. Vibhatte pana aṭṭhimaṃsādiavayavasamaññā”ti jānanato. Catumahāpatho viya catuiriyāpathoti gāviyā ṭhitacatumahāpatho viya kāyassa pavattimaggabhūto catubbidho iriyāpatho yasmā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.305) vitthāritā, tasmā tattha, taṃsaṃvaṇṇanāyañca (visuddhi. ṭī. 1.306) vuttanayena veditabbo. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Now, to show the meaning just stated by way of explaining the state of things, 'just as for a cattle butcher' and so on was said. Therein, 'of one who rears' means of one who raises it with broken rice, rice gruel, cotton seeds, and so on, for the accumulation and increase of its flesh. 'Slaughtered and dead' means having been harmed, it is dead. And 'dead' means merely dead. Therefore it is said, 'just so long.' The perception 'cow' does not disappear, because the designation 'cow' is based on the limbs and parts as they are arranged, and the arrangement of these is not destroyed even when the cow is merely dead. 'They are dissolved, broken up, and divided'—these are pieces (bīlā), parts; the 'v' has been changed to 'b', and the 'i' to 'ī'. 'Piece by piece' means having made it piece by piece. 'Having divided' means having separated the flesh from the collection of bones, or having made that separated flesh into portions. Therefore it is said, 'the perception of flesh arises.' Even for one who has gone forth but has not undertaken a meditation subject. 'The breaking up of the compact' means the analysis, the separation, of the compactness of continuity, collection, and function. 'He reviews element by element' means of one who, by making the breaking up of the compact, reviews each element—the earth element and so on—having made them separate. 'The perception of a being': some say it is the perception of a being that proceeds by way of the view of self. Even the perception of a being that proceeds by way of convention rightly disappears then, because of the accomplishment of the breaking up of the compact in accordance with reality. For when this is so, the meaning of the thing compared truly corresponds and agrees with the meaning of the simile as stated. Therefore it is said, 'the mind becomes established by way of the elements alone.' 'Skillful' means clever, skilled in this and that designation, from knowing that 'in the butcher's shop, when the collection of parts such as bones, flesh, etc., with tail, hooves, horns, etc., is undivided, as it was born, there is the designation "cow", not when it is divided. But when it is divided, there is the designation of the parts such as bones, flesh, etc.' 'As the four great roads, so the four postures' means: just as the four great roads where the cow was situated, so the fourfold posture which is the path of proceeding for the body. Since this is explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga, it should be understood there and in its Subcommentary in the way stated. The rest is as stated.

Dhātumanasikārapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on Attention to the Elements is concluded.

Navasivathikapabbavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on the Nine Charnel Ground Contemplations

379. Sivathikāya [V 2.0286] apaviddhauddhumātakādipaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ odhiso pavattānaṃ kathānaṃ, tadabhidheyyānañca uddhumātakādiasubhabhāgānaṃ sivathikapabbānīti saṅgītikārehi gahitasamaññā[P 2.0391]. Tenāha “sivathikapabbehi vibhajitu”nti. Maritvā ekāhātikkantaṃ ekāhamataṃ. Uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānāti jīvitakkhayato upari maraṇato paraṃ. Samuggatenāti samuṭṭhitena. Uddhumātattāti uddhaṃ uddhaṃ dhumātattā sūnattā. Setarattehi viparibhinnaṃ vimissitaṃ nīlaṃ vinīlaṃ, purimavaṇṇavipariṇāmabhūtaṃ vā nīlaṃ vinīlaṃ. Vinīlameva vinīlakanti ka-kārena padavaḍḍhanaṃ anatthantarato yathā “pītakaṃ lohitaka”nti (dha. sa. 616). Paṭikkūlattāti jigucchanīyattā. Kucchitaṃ vinīlanti vinīlakanti kucchanattho vā ayaṃ ka-kāroti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ yathā “pāpako kittisaddo abbhuggacchatī”ti. (Dī. ni. 3.316; a. ni. 5.213; mahāva. 285) paribhinnaṭṭhānehi kākakaṅkādīhi. Vissandamānapubbanti vissavantapubbaṃ, tahaṃ tahaṃ paggharantapubbanti attho. Tathābhāvanti vissandamānapubbabhāvaṃ.

379. The designation 'charnel ground sections' was adopted by the compilers of the texts for the discourses that proceed by limitation, connected with the bloated, etc., [corpses] cast away in the charnel ground, and for the impure parts, such as the bloated, etc., which are their referents. Therefore, it is said, 'to be analyzed by means of the charnel ground sections'. Having died, that which has passed one day is a one-day-dead [corpse]. 'Beyond the end of life' means above the destruction of life, after death. 'Swollen' means 'risen up'. 'Bloatedness' means being puffed up, being swollen upwards. 'Livid' is blue mixed with white and red, or blue that has become a transformation of its former color. 'Livid' (vinīlaka) is just 'livid' (vinīla); the suffix '-ka' is a word extension without difference in meaning, as in 'yellowish' (pītakaṃ) and 'reddish' (lohitakaṃ). 'Because it is repulsive' means because it is loathsome. Or, to show that this suffix '-ka' has the meaning of contempt, it is said 'contemptibly livid' is 'livid' (vinīlakaṃ), just as it is said, 'An evil reputation arises'. By crows, vultures, and the like, at the places that are torn. 'Oozing with pus' means 'oozing pus'; the meaning is 'trickling pus here and there'. 'The state of being so' means the state of oozing with pus.

So [M 2.0310] bhikkhūti yo “passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍita”nti vutto, so bhikkhu. Upasaṃharati sadisataṃ. “Ayampi kho”tiādi upasaṃharaṇākāradassanaṃ. Āyūti rūpajīvitindriyaṃ, arūpajīvitindriyaṃ panettha viññāṇagatikameva. Usmāti kammajatejo. Evaṃ pūtikasabhāvoyevāti evaṃ ativiya duggandhajegucchapaṭikkūlapūbhikasabhāvo eva, na āyuādīnaṃ avigame viya mattasoti adhippāyo. Ediso bhavissatīti evaṃbhāvīti āha “evaṃ uddhumātādibhedo bhavissatī”ti.

'That monk' is the monk who was spoken of thus: 'he might see a body cast away in a charnel ground'. He applies the similarity. 'This body also...' and so on, is the showing of the mode of application. 'Life' is the material life faculty; here the immaterial life faculty is simply conditioned by consciousness. 'Heat' is the fire element born of kamma. 'Thus, it is of a putrid nature indeed' means it is indeed of an extremely foul, disgusting, repulsive, and putrid nature; the intention is that it is not a mere trifle as when life, etc., has not departed. 'It will be such' means it will be of such a nature; he says, 'It will be of the kind such as bloated, and so on'.

Luñcitvā luñcitvāti uppāṭetvā uppāṭetvā. Sāvasesamaṃsalohitayuttanti sabbaso akhāditattā tahaṃ tahaṃ sesena appāvasesena maṃsalohitena yuttaṃ. “Aññena hatthaṭṭhika”nti avisesena hatthaṭṭhikānaṃ vippakiṇṇatā jotitāti anavasesato tesaṃ vippakiṇṇataṃ dassento “catusaṭṭhibhedampī”tiādimāha[P 2.0392].

‘Having plucked, having plucked’ (luñcitvā luñcitvā) means ‘having uprooted, having uprooted’ (uppāṭetvā uppāṭetvā). ‘With remaining flesh and blood attached’ (sāvasesamaṃsalohitayuttaṃ) means that because it was not eaten completely, it is connected here and there with the little flesh and blood that remains. ‘By another hand bone’ (aññena hatthaṭṭhikaṃ) indicates the scattering of hand bones without distinction; thus, showing their complete scattering, he says, ‘divided into sixty-four parts’ (catusaṭṭhibhedampi) and so on.

Terovassikānīti tirovassaṃ gatāni, tāni pana saṃvaccharaṃ vītivattāni hontīti āha “atikkantasaṃvaccharānī”ti. Purāṇatāya ghanabhāvavigamena vicuṇṇatā idha pūtibhāvoti so yathā hoti, taṃ dassento “abbhokāse”tiādimāha. Terovassikānevāti saṃvaccharamattātikkantāni [V 2.0287] eva. Khajjamānatādivasena dutiyasivathikapabbādīnaṃ vavatthāpitattā vuttaṃ “khajjamānatādīnaṃ vasena yojanā kātabbā”ti.

‘Terovassikāni’ means those that have gone beyond a year (tirovassaṃ gatāni); but since they have passed a year, it is said, ‘those that have exceeded a year’ (atikkantasaṃvaccharāni). Due to their age, their compactness disappears, and they become crumbled—here, this rotten state is called ‘pūtibhāva’. To illustrate how this occurs, it is said, ‘in the open air’ (abbhokāse), and so on. ‘Terovassikāneva’ means those that have exceeded just a year. Because the second and following sections on the charnel ground are established by way of being eaten, etc., it is said, ‘the connection should be made based on being eaten, etc.’ (khajjamānatādīnaṃ vasena yojanā kātabbā).

Navasivathikapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on the Nine Charnel Ground Contemplations is concluded.

Imāneva dveti avadhāraṇena appanākammaṭṭhānaṃ tattha niyameti aññapabbesu tadabhāvato. Yato hi eva-kāro, tato aññattha niyameti, tena pabbadvayassa vipassanākammaṭṭhānatāpi appaṭisiddhā daṭṭhabbā aniccatādidassanato. Saṅkhāresu ādīnavavibhāvanāni sivathikapabbānīti āha “sivathikānaṃ ādīnavānupassanāvasena vuttattā”ti. Iriyāpathapabbādīnaṃ appanāvahatā pākaṭā evāti “sesāni dvādasapī”ti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ panettha atthato avibhattaṃ. Taṃ suviññeyyameva.

By the determination ‘these two alone’ (imāneva dve), the absorption meditation subject is fixed there, because it is absent in the other sections. For where the particle ‘eva’ (alone) is used, it serves to exclude other things; therefore, the two sections should also be understood as not being prohibited from being insight meditation subjects, as they involve seeing impermanence and so on. The charnel ground sections are manifestations of danger in formations; thus, it is said, ‘because they are taught by way of the contemplation of danger in the charnel grounds’ (sivathikānaṃ ādīnavānupassanāvasena vuttattā). The capacity of the sections on postures and so on to lead to absorption is indeed clear; hence, it is said, ‘the remaining twelve as well’ (sesāni dvādasapi). What is not explicitly distinguished here in terms of meaning is easily understood.

Kāyānupassanāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Contemplation of the Body is concluded.

Vedanānupassanāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Contemplation of Feelings

380. Sukhaṃ [M 2.0311] vedananti ettha sukhayatīti sukhā. Sampayuttadhamme, kāyañca laddhassāde karotīti attho. Suṭṭhu vā khādati, khanati vā kāyikaṃ, cetasikañcābādhanti sukhā. “Sukaraṃ okāsadānaṃ etissāti sukhā”ti apare. Vedayati ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavatīti vedanā. Vedayamānoti anubhavamāno. “Kāma”ntiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ iriyāpathapabbe vuttanayameva. Sampajānassa vediyanaṃ sampajānavediyanaṃ.

380. Here, in ‘pleasant feeling,’ ‘pleasant’ (sukhaṃ) is so called because it delights (sukhayati). The meaning is that it makes associated states and the body experience satisfaction. Or, it thoroughly consumes (suṭṭhu khādati) or digs up (khanati) bodily and mental affliction; thus, it is pleasant. Others say, ‘It is called ‘pleasant’ (sukhā) because it is easy to give an opportunity to it’ (sukaraṃ okāsadānaṃ etissā). ‘Feeling’ (vedanā) is so called because it experiences (vedayati), that is, it undergoes the taste of its object. ‘Vedayamāno’ means ‘experiencing’ (anubhavamāno). What is to be said regarding ‘sensual pleasure’ (kāma) and so on is in accordance with the method stated in the section on postures. The experiencing (vediyanaṃ) of one who is fully aware (sampajāna) is ‘clearly comprehended feeling’ (sampajānavediyanaṃ).

Vatthuārammaṇāti rūpādiārammaṇā. Rūpādiārammaṇañhettha vedanāya pavattiṭṭhānatāya “vatthū”ti adhippetaṃ[P 2.0393]. Assāti bhaveyya. Dhammavinimuttassa kattu abhāvato dhammasseva kattubhāvaṃ dassento “vedanāva vedayatī”ti āha. “Vohāramattaṃ hotī”ti etena “sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī”ti idaṃ vohāramattanti dasseti.

‘The basis as object’ (vatthuārammaṇa) means objects such as form, etc. Here, an object such as form, etc., is intended as the ‘basis’ (vatthu) because it is the place of occurrence for feeling. ‘Assa’ means ‘it would be’ (bhaveyya). Since there is no agent apart from phenomena, showing that phenomena themselves are the agent, it is said, ‘feeling itself feels’ (vedanāva vedayati). By ‘it is merely a designation’ (vohāramattaṃ hoti), it is shown that the statement ‘experiencing a pleasant feeling, I feel a pleasant feeling’ (sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmi) is merely a designation.

Nitthunantoti balavato vedanāvegassa nirodhane ādīnavaṃ disvā tassa avasaradānavasena nitthunanto[V 2.0288]. Vegasandhāraṇe hi atimahantaṃ dukkhaṃ uppajjatīti aññampi vikāraṃ uppādeyya, tena thero aparāparaṃ parivattati. Vīriyasamathaṃ yojetvāti adhivāsanavīriyassa adhimattattā tassa hāpanavasena samādhinā samarasatāpādanena vīriyasamathaṃ yojetvā. Saha paṭisambhidāhīti lokuttarapaṭisambhidāhi saha. Ariyamaggakkhaṇe hi paṭisambhidānaṃ asammohavasena adhigamo, atthapaṭisambhidāya pana ārammaṇakaraṇavasenapi. Lokiyānampi vā sati uppattikāle tattha samatthataṃ sandhāyāha “saha paṭisambhidāhī”ti. Samasīsīti vārasamasīsī hutvā, paccavekkhaṇavārassa anantaravāre parinibbāyīti attho.

‘Groaning’ (nitthunanto) means groaning by seeing the danger in suppressing the powerful surge of feeling and thereby giving it an opportunity. For in restraining the surge, very great suffering arises, which might produce another disturbance; for that reason, the elder turns over again and again. ‘He applies the calming of energy’ (vīriyasamathaṃ yojetvā) means applying the calming of energy by reducing the excessive energy of endurance, thereby bringing it into balance with concentration. ‘Together with the discriminations’ (saha paṭisambhidāhi) means together with the supramundane discriminations. For at the moment of the noble path, the discriminations are attained through non-delusion, and in the case of the discrimination of meaning, also by way of taking it as an object. Or, referring to the capability regarding mundane discriminations as well, if they are present at the time of arising, he says, ‘together with the discriminations’. ‘Equal-headed’ (samasīsī) means having become equal-headed in turns; the meaning is that he attains final nibbāna in the turn immediately after the turn of reviewing.

Yathā ca sukhaṃ, evaṃ dukkhanti yathā “sukhaṃ ko vedayatī”tiādinā sampajānavediyanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, evaṃ dukkhampi. Tattha dukkhayatīti dukkhā, sampayuttadhamme, kāyañca pīḷeti vibādhatīti attho. Duṭṭhuṃ vā khādati, khanati kāyikaṃ, cetasikañca sātanti dukkhā. “Dukkaraṃ okāsadānaṃ etissāti dukkhā”ti apare. Arūpakammaṭṭhānanti arūpapariggahaṃ, arūpadhammamukhena vipassanābhinivesananti attho. Na pākaṭaṃ hoti phassassa, cittassa ca avibhūtākārattā. Tenāha “andhakāraṃ viya khāyatī”ti. “Na pākaṭaṃ [P 2.0394] hotī”ti ca [M 2.0312] idaṃ tādise puggale sandhāya vuttaṃ, tesaṃ ādito vedanāva vibhūtatarā hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Evañhi yaṃ vuttaṃ sakkapañhavaṇṇanā dīsu “phasso pākaṭo hoti, viññāṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hotī”ti, (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.359) taṃ avirodhitaṃ hoti. Vedanāvasena kathiyamānaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ pākaṭaṃ hotīti yojanā. “Vedanānaṃ uppattipākaṭatāyā”ti ca idaṃ sukhadukkhavedanānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Tāsañhi pavatti oḷārikā, na itarāya. Tadubhayaggahaṇamukhena vā gahetabbattā itarāyapi pavatti viññūnaṃ pākaṭā evāti “vedanāna”nti avisesaggahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sakkapañhe vuttanayeneva veditabbo, tasmā tattha vattabbo atthaviseso tattha līnatthappakāsaniyaṃ vuttanayeneva gahetabbo.

Just as with pleasant feeling, so too with painful feeling; as it was said with reference to clearly comprehended feeling, beginning with ‘Who feels pleasant feeling?’, so too with painful feeling. Here, ‘painful’ (dukkhā) is so called because it afflicts (dukkhayati); the meaning is that it oppresses and torments associated states and the body. Or, it badly consumes (duṭṭhuṃ khādati) or digs up (khanati) bodily and mental comfort; thus, it is painful. Others say, ‘It is called ‘painful’ (dukkhā) because it is difficult to give an opportunity to it’ (dukkaraṃ okāsadānaṃ etissā). ‘The formless meditation object’ (arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ) means the comprehension of the formless; the meaning is the application to insight through the door of formless phenomena. It is not evident to contact or to the mind due to its indistinct nature. Hence, it is said, ‘It appears like darkness’ (andhakāraṃ viya khāyati). And ‘it is not evident’ (na pākaṭaṃ hoti) is said with reference to such persons for whom, from the start, feeling appears more clearly. Thus, what was stated in the commentary on the Sakka’s Questions and so on—‘Contact is evident, consciousness is evident’—is not contradicted. The connection is that the meditation subject, when discussed by way of feeling, becomes evident. And ‘the evident arising of feelings’ (vedanānaṃ uppattipākaṭatāya) is said with reference to pleasant and painful feelings, for their occurrence is gross, not that of the other. Or, since the other is also to be grasped through the door of grasping those two, its occurrence is also evident to the wise; therefore, ‘feelings’ (vedanānaṃ) should be understood as a non-specific reference. It should be understood in the way explained in the Sakka’s Questions; therefore, the special meaning relevant there should be taken in accordance with the method stated in the Līnatthappakāsanī there.

Pubbe “vatthuṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vedanāva vedayatī”ti vedanāya ārammaṇādhīnavuttitāya ca anattatāya ca pajānanaṃ vuttaṃ, idāni tassā aniccatādipajānanaṃ dassento “ayaṃ aparopi pajānanapariyāyo”ti āha. Yathā ekasmiṃ khaṇe cittadvayassa asambhavo ekajjhaṃ anekantapaccayābhāvato, evaṃ vedanādvayassa visiṭṭhārammaṇavuttito cāti āha “sukhavedanākkhaṇe dukkhāya vedanāya abhāvato”ti. Nidassanamattañcetaṃ tadā upekkhāvedanāyapi abhāvato, tena sukhavedanākkhaṇe bhūtapubbānaṃ itaravedanānaṃ hutvāabhāvapajānanena sukhavedanāyapi hutvā abhāvo ñāto eva hotīti tassā pākaṭabhāvameva dassento “imissā ca [V 2.0289] sukhāya vedanāya ito paṭhamaṃ abhāvato”ti [P 2.0395] āha, eteneva ca tāsampi vedanānaṃ pākaṭabhāvo dassitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenāha “vedanā nāma aniccā adhuvā vipariṇāmadhammā”ti. Aniccaggahaṇena hi vedanānaṃ viddhaṃsanabhāvo dassito viddhaste aniccatāya suviññeyyattā. Adhuvaggahaṇena pākaṭabhāvo tassa asadābhāvitādibhāvanato. Vipariṇāmaggahaṇena dukkhabhāvo tassa aññathattadīpanato, tena sukhāpi vedanā dukkhā, pageva itarāti tissannampi vedanānaṃ dukkhatā dassitā hoti. Iti “yadaniccaṃ dukkhaṃ, taṃ ekantato anattā”ti tīsupi vedanāsu lakkhaṇattayapajānanā jotitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenāha “itiha tattha sampajāno hotī”ti.

Previously, the understanding of feeling's dependence on an object and its nature of non-self was stated by way of 'having made the basis the object, feeling itself feels.' Now, to show the understanding of its impermanence and other characteristics, he says, "This is another way of understanding." Just as the arising of two minds in one moment is impossible due to the absence of multiple distinct conditions at once, so too is it with two feelings because they depend on distinct objects. Hence he says, "At the moment of pleasant feeling, painful feeling is absent." This is merely an illustration, for at that time, neutral feeling is also absent. Thus, by understanding that at the moment of pleasant feeling other feelings which existed in the past are now non-existent, the arising and ceasing of the pleasant feeling itself also becomes known. To highlight its manifest nature, he says, "And before this pleasant feeling, there was an absence." In this way, the manifest nature of those other feelings is also shown, and this should be understood. Therefore he says, "Feelings are impermanent, unstable, and subject to change." By the term "impermanent," the perishable nature of feelings is shown, because when something has perished, its impermanence is easily understood. By the term "unstable," their manifest nature is shown, due to their not always being present. By the term "subject to change," their nature as suffering is revealed, through showing their alteration. Thus, even pleasant feeling is suffering—how much more so the others! In this way, the suffering nature of all three feelings is shown. Thus, it should be understood that the understanding of the three characteristics in all three feelings is illuminated by the principle, "What is impermanent is suffering; that is definitely non-self." Therefore he says, "Thus, one is clearly aware there."

Idāni [M 2.0313] tamatthaṃ suttena (ma. ni. 2.205) sādhetuṃ “vuttampi ceta”ntiādimāha. Tattha neva tasmiṃ samaye dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedetīti tasmiṃ sukhavedanāsamaṅgisamaye neva dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti niruddhattā, anuppannattā ca yathākkamaṃ atītānāgatānaṃ. Paccuppannāya pana asambhavo vutto eva. Sakiccakkhaṇamattāvaṭṭhānato aniccā. Samecca sambhuyya paccayehi katattā saṅkhatā. Vatthārammaṇādipaccayaṃ paṭicca uppannattā paṭiccasamuppannā. Khayavayapalujjananirujjhanapakatitāya khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammāti daṭṭhabbā.

Now, to establish this meaning by means of the sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 2.205), he says, 'And this was said,' and so on. Therein, 'at that time, one does not feel a painful feeling' means that at the time of being endowed with a pleasant feeling, one does not feel a painful feeling, because past and future feelings have ceased and not yet arisen, respectively. As for the present, its impossibility has already been stated. They are impermanent because they endure for only a functional moment. They are conditioned because they are made by causes coming together. They are dependently arisen because they arise in dependence on conditions such as the base and object. They should be understood as having the nature of destruction, vanishing, breaking up, and cessation—hence, they are 'subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.'

Kilesehi āmasitabbato āmisaṃ nāma, pañca kāmaguṇā, ārammaṇakaraṇavasena saha āmisehīti sāmisaṃ. Tenāha “pañcakāmaguṇāmisanissitā”ti.

Because they are to be touched by defilements, they are called 'āmisa.' The five strands of sensual pleasure are āmisa, and because they are together with āmisa in the sense of serving as an object, they are 'sāmisa.' Therefore he says, 'dependent on the āmisa of the five strands of sensual pleasure.'

Ito paranti “atthi vedanā”ti evamādi pāḷiṃ sandhāyāha “kāyānupassanāyaṃ vuttanayamevā”ti.

From here onward, referring to the Pāli text, 'There is feeling,' and so on, he says, 'The method explained in the contemplation of the body is the same here as well.'

Vedanānupassanāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition on the contemplation of feeling is concluded.

Cittānupassanāvaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Contemplation of Mind

381. Sampayogavasena [P 2.0396] pavattamānena saha rāgenāti sarāgaṃ. Tenāha “lobhasahagata”nti. Vītarāganti ettha kāmaṃ sarāgapadapaṭiyoginā vītarāgapadena bhavitabbaṃ, sammasanacārassa pana adhippetattā tebhūmakasseva gahaṇanti “lokiyakusalābyākata”nti vatvā “idaṃ panā”tiādinā tameva [V 2.0290] adhippāyaṃ vivarati. Sesāni dve dosamūlāni, dve mohamūlānīti cattāri akusalacittāni. Tesañhi rāgena sampayogābhāvato nattheva sarāgatā, taṃnimittakatāya pana siyā taṃsahitakāle soti nattheva vītarāgatāpīti dukkhavinimuttatā evettha labbhatīti āha “neva purimapadaṃ na pacchimapadaṃ bhajantī”ti. Yadi evaṃ padesikaṃ pajānanaṃ āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati, dukantarapariyāpannattā tesaṃ. Ye pana “paṭipakkhabhāve agayhamāne sampayogābhāvo evettha pamāṇaṃ ekaccaabyākatānaṃ viyā”ti icchanti, tesaṃ matena sesākusalacittānampi dutiyapadasaṅgaho veditabbo[M 2.0314]. Dutiyadukepi vuttanayena attho veditabbo. Akusalamūlesu saha moheneva vattatīti samohanti āha “vicikicchāsahagatañceva uddhaccasahagatañcā”ti. Yasmā cettha “saheva mohenāti samoha”nti purimapadāvadhāraṇampi labbhatiyeva, tasmā vuttaṃ “yasmā panā”tiādi. Yathā pana atimūḷhatāya pāṭipuggalikanayena savisesamohavantatāya “momūhacitta”nti vattabbato vicikicchāuddhaccasahagatadvayaṃ visesato “samoha”nti vuccati, na tathā sesākusalacittānīti “vaṭṭantiyevā”ti sāsaṅkaṃ vadati. Sampayogavasena thinamiddhena anupatitaṃ anugatanti thinamiddhānupatitaṃ, pañcavidhaṃsasaṅkhārikākusalacittaṃ saṅkucitacittaṃ, saṅkucitacittaṃ nāma ārammaṇe saṅkocanavasena pavattanato. Paccayavisesavasena thāmajātena uddhaccena sahagataṃ saṃsaṭṭhanti uddhaccasahagataṃ, aññathā sabbampi akusalacittaṃ [P 2.0397] uddhaccasahagatamevāti. Pasaṭacittaṃ nāma ārammaṇe savisesaṃ vikkhepavasena visaṭabhāvena pavattanato.

381. Occurring in association with lust is 'sarāgaṃ' (with lust). Therefore he says, 'accompanied by greed.' Here, 'vītarāga' (free from lust) should indeed be the counterpart of the term 'sarāga'; but since the scope of comprehension is intended, it refers only to the three realms, as stated: 'worldly wholesome and indeterminate.' Then, beginning with 'but this...,' he explains that very intention. The remaining two consciousnesses rooted in aversion and two rooted in delusion are four unwholesome consciousnesses. Since these have no association with lust, there is no 'state of being with lust'; but because they are conditioned by it, they might be considered so when associated with it, and thus there is no 'state of being free from lust' either. Therefore, it is said that freedom from this dyad is obtained, and he says, 'they partake of neither the first term nor the latter term.' If this is so, does it lead to partial understanding? It does not, because they are included in another dyad. As for those who hold that 'when the opposing state is not grasped, the absence of association is the measure here, as in the case of some indeterminate states,' according to their opinion, the remaining unwholesome consciousnesses are also included in the second term. In the second dyad, too, the meaning should be understood in the way stated. Among the unwholesome roots, it occurs together with delusion, hence 'samoha' (with delusion). He says, 'accompanied by doubt and accompanied by restlessness.' Here, since 'together with delusion is samoha,' the delimitation of the first term is also obtained. Therefore, it is stated, 'but because,' and so on. Just as, due to extreme delusion, and because individuals with distinct delusion are spoken of as having an 'utterly deluded mind' (momūhacitta), the two types accompanied by doubt and restlessness are specifically called 'samoha,' but not so the other unwholesome consciousnesses; hence, he says with reservation, 'they just occur.' Followed and accompanied by sloth and torpor in association is 'thinamiddhānupatitaṃ' (overtaken by sloth and torpor); the fivefold prompted unwholesome consciousness is 'saṅkucitacitta' (contracted mind). It is called 'contracted mind' because it occurs by way of contracting upon its object. Associated and mixed with restlessness born of strength due to a specific condition is 'uddhaccasahagataṃ' (accompanied by restlessness); otherwise, all unwholesome consciousness would be accompanied by restlessness. 'Pasaṭacitta' (scattered mind) is so named because it occurs by way of scattering, spreading out distinctly upon the object.

Kilesavikkhambhanasamatthatāya vipulaphalatāya ca dīghasantānatāya ca mahantabhāvaṃ gataṃ, mahantehi vā uḷāracchandādīhi gataṃ paṭipannanti mahaggataṃ, taṃ pana rūpārūpabhūmigataṃ tato mahantassa loke abhāvato. Tenāha “rūpārūpāvacara”nti. Tassa cettha paṭiyogī parittaṃ evāti āha “amahaggatanti kāmāvacara”nti. Attānaṃ uttarituṃ samatthehi saha uttarehīti sauttaraṃ. Tappaṭipakkhena anuttaraṃ. Tadubhayaṃ upādāyupādāya veditabbanti āha “sauttaranti kāmāvacarantiādi. Paṭipakkhavikkhambhanasamatthena samādhinā sammadeva āhitaṃ samāhitaṃ. Tenāha “yassā”tiādi. Yassāti yassa cittassa. Yathāvuttena samādhinā na samāhitanti asamāhitaṃ. Tenāha “ubhayasamādhirahita”nti. Tadaṅgavimuttiyā vimuttaṃ, kāmāvacarakusalacittaṃ, vikkhambhanavimuttiyā vimuttaṃ, mahaggatacittanti tadubhayaṃ sandhāyāha “tadaṅgavikkhambhanavimuttīhi vimutta”nti. Yattha tadubhayavimutti natthi, taṃ ubhayavimuttirahitanti gayhamāne lokuttaracittepi siyāsaṅkāti taṃ nivattanatthaṃ “samuccheda…pe… okāsova natthī”ti āha. Okāsabhāvo ca [V 2.0291] sammasanacārassa adhippetattā veditabbo. Yaṃ panettha atthato avibhattaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānameva.

Because it has attained greatness on account of its ability to suppress defilements, the abundance of its fruit, and the length of its continuity, or because it is attained by great ones with lofty aspirations and so on, it is called 'mahaggata' (exalted). And that, having gone to the form and formless spheres, is so called because there is nothing greater than it in the world. Therefore he says, 'belonging to the form and formless spheres.' Here, its counterpart is only the limited, hence he says, 'amahaggata (unexalted) means belonging to the sense-sphere.' With higher states capable of surpassing oneself is 'sauttara' (with a superior). Its opposite is 'anuttara' (unsurpassed). Both should be understood by considering them in relation to their grounds, thus he says: 'sauttara means belonging to the sense-sphere,' and so on. Properly composed by the concentration that is capable of suppressing its opposition is 'samāhita' (concentrated). Therefore he says, 'of which,' and so on. 'Of which' means of which mind. Not composed by the aforementioned concentration is 'asamāhita' (unconcentrated). Therefore he says, 'devoid of both concentrations.' Freed by the liberation by substitution of opposites is wholesome sense-sphere consciousness; freed by the liberation by suppression is exalted consciousness. Referring to both, he says: 'freed by the liberations of substitution and suppression.' Where both liberations are absent, if that which is devoid of both liberations were taken, there might be a doubt that this would include the supramundane consciousness. To dispel that, he says: 'there is no opportunity for eradication... and so on.' The state of opportunity should be understood as intended for the scope of comprehension. Whatever is not analyzed here in terms of meaning is self-evident on account of the method stated previously.

Cittānupassanāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition on the contemplation of mind is concluded.

Dhammānupassanā

Contemplation of Dhamma

Nīvaraṇapabbavaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Hindrances Section

382. Pahātabbādidhammavibhāgadassanavasena [M 2.0315] pañcadhā dhammānupassanā niddiṭṭhāti ayamattho pāḷito eva viññāyatīti tamatthaṃ ulliṅgento “pañcavidhena dhammānupassanaṃ kathetu”nti āha. Yadi evaṃ kasmā nīvaraṇādivaseneva niddiṭṭhanti? Vineyyajjhāsayato.
