Yesañhi [P 2.0398] veneyyānaṃ pahātabbadhammesu paṭhamaṃ nīvaraṇāni vibhāgena vattabbāni, tesaṃ vasenettha bhagavatā paṭhamaṃ nīvaraṇesu dhammānupassanā kathitā. Tathā hi kāyānupassanāpi samathapubbaṅgamā desitā, tato pariññeyyesu khandhesu, āyatanesu ca bhāvetabbesu bojjhaṅgesu, pariññeyyādivibhāgesu saccesu ca uttarā desanā, tasmā cettha samathabhāvanāpi yāvadeva vipassanatthā icchitā. Vipassanāpadhānā, vipassanābahulā ca satipaṭṭhānadesanāti tassā vipassanābhinivesavibhāgena desitabhāvaṃ vibhāvento “apicā”tiādimāha. Tattha khandhāyatanadukkhasaccavasena missakapariggahakathanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Saññāsaṅkhārakkhandhapariggahampīti pi-saddena sakalapañcupādānakkhandhapariggahaṃ sampiṇḍeti itaresaṃ tadantogadhattā.

382. The fivefold contemplation of phenomena has been set forth by way of showing the classification of phenomena to be abandoned, and so forth. This meaning is understood from the Pāli text itself. Pointing out this meaning, he says, 'to teach the fivefold contemplation of phenomena.' If so, why is it set forth specifically in terms of hindrances, and so forth? It is due to the dispositions of those to be trained. For those trainees for whom the hindrances, as phenomena to be abandoned, must first be explained in detail, the Blessed One first taught the contemplation of phenomena concerning the hindrances in accordance with their dispositions. Similarly, the contemplation of the body was also taught with serenity as its precursor. Then followed the further teaching regarding the aggregates and bases to be fully understood, the factors of enlightenment to be developed, and the truths according to the divisions of what is to be fully understood, and so forth. Thus, here too, the development of serenity is desired only to the extent that it serves insight. The teaching on the foundations of mindfulness is one where insight is predominant and insight is abundant. To clarify that it was taught by way of the division of emphasis on insight, he says, 'Moreover...' and so on. Here, the statement of the combined inclusion of aggregates, bases, and the truth of suffering should be understood. The inclusion of the aggregates of perception and formations, too, is compacted by the word 'pi' to include all five aggregates of clinging, since the others are contained within them.

“Kaṇhasukkadhammānaṃ yuganandhatā natthī”ti pajānanakāle abhāvā “abhiṇhasamudācāravasenā”ti vuttaṃ. Saṃvijjamānanti attano santāne upalabbhamānaṃ. Yathāti yenākārena, so pana “kāmacchandassa uppādo hotī”ti vuttattā kāmacchandassa kāraṇākārova, atthato kāraṇamevāti āha “yena kāraṇenā”ti. Ca-saddo vakkhamānatthasamuccayattho.

At the time of knowing that 'there is no yoking together of dark and bright qualities,' due to their absence, it is said 'by way of frequent occurrence.' 'Existing' means being found in one's own continuum. 'How' means 'in which manner'; since it is said 'the arising of sensual desire occurs,' that manner is the causal mode of sensual desire. In meaning, it is indeed the cause—thus it is said 'by which cause.' The word 'ca' serves to collect the meanings that will be stated.

Tatthāti “yathā cā”tiādinā vuttapade. Subhampīti kāmacchandopi. So hi attano gahaṇākārena “subha”nti vutto, tenākārena pavattanakassa aññassa kāmacchandassa nimittattā “nimitta”nti [V 2.0292] ca. Iṭṭhaṃ, iṭṭhākārena vā gayhamānaṃ rūpādi subhārammaṇaṃ. Ākaṅkhitassa hitasukhassa pattiyā anupāyabhūto manasikāro anupāyamanasikāro. Tanti ayonisomanasikāraṃ[P 2.0399]. Tatthāti tasmiṃ sabhāgahetubhūte, ārammaṇabhūte ca duvidhe subhanimitte. Āhāroti paccayo attano phalaṃ āharatīti katvā.

'Therein' refers to the words stated beginning with 'as well as.' 'Beautiful' also refers to sensual desire. For it is called 'beautiful' due to its manner of apprehension, and because it is a sign for another sensual desire that proceeds in that manner, it is also called a 'sign.' A beautiful object, such as a visible form that is desirable or is apprehended in a desirable manner. 'Improper attention' is attention that is not the means for attaining the desired welfare and happiness. 'That' refers to improper attention. 'Therein' refers to that twofold beautiful sign, which is both a homogeneous cause and an object. 'Nutriment' is a condition, so called because it brings forth its own result.

Asubhanti [M 2.0316] asubhajjhānaṃ uttarapadalopena, taṃ pana dasasu aviññāṇakaasubhesu ca kesādīsu saviññāṇakaasubhesu ca pavattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kesādīsu hi saññā “asubhasaññā”ti girimānandasutte (a. ni. 10.60) vuttā. Ettha ca catubbidhassa ayonisomanasikārassa, yonisomanasikārassa ca gahaṇaṃ niravasesadassanatthaṃ katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, tesu pana asubhesu “subha”nti, “asubha”nti ca manasikāro idhādhippeto, tadanukūlattā pana itare pīti.

'Unattractive' refers to the meditation on the unattractive, by elision of the latter word. This should be understood as occurring in the ten unattractive objects without consciousness and in the unattractive objects with consciousness, such as hair. For in the case of hair and so forth, the perception is called 'perception of the unattractive,' as stated in the Girimānanda Sutta (A.N. 10.60). And here, the inclusion of the fourfold improper attention and proper attention should be understood as done for the purpose of showing this exhaustively, without remainder. However, among these unattractive objects, attention as 'beautiful' and as 'unattractive' is what is intended here, but due to their being concordant with that, others are also included.

Ekādasasu asubhesu paṭikkūlākārassa uggaṇhanaṃ, yathā vā tattha uggahanimittaṃ uppajjati, tathā paṭipatti asubhanimittassa uggaho. Upacārappanāvahāya asubhabhāvanāya anuyuñjanā asubhabhāvanānuyogo. “Bhojane mattaññuno mitāhārassa thinamiddhābhibhavābhāvā otāraṃ alabhamāno kāmacchando pahīyatī”ti vadanti, ayameva ca attho niddesepi vuccati. Yo pana bhojanassa paṭikkūlataṃ, tabbipariṇāmassa tadādhārassa tassa ca upanissayabhūtassa ativiya jegucchataṃ, kāyassa ca āhāraṭṭhitikattaṃ sammadeva jānāti, so sabbaso bhojane pamāṇassa jānanena bhojanemattaññū nāma. Tādisassa hi kāmacchando pahīyateva.

In the eleven kinds of unattractive objects, the grasping of the repulsive aspect is the grasping of the sign of the unattractive; or, it is the practice in such a way that the learning sign arises there. Engagement in the development of the unattractive, which leads to access and absorption, is 'engagement in the development of the unattractive.' They say: 'For one who knows moderation in food, who eats moderately, since they are not overcome by sloth and torpor, sensual desire, finding no opportunity, is abandoned.' And this very meaning is also stated in the Niddesa. But one who rightly knows the repulsiveness of food, the extreme loathsomeness of its transformation, its container, and that which is its support, and that the body is sustained by food—such a one, by completely knowing the measure in food, is called 'one who knows moderation in food.' For such a person, sensual desire is indeed abandoned.

Asubhakammikatissatthero dantaṭṭhidassāvī. Pahīnassāti vikkhambhanavasena pahīnassa. Ito paresupi evarūpesu ṭhānesu eseva nayo. Abhidhammapariyāyena (dha. sa. 1159, 1503) sabbopi lobho kāmacchandanīvaraṇanti āha “arahattamaggenā”ti.

The Elder Tissa, the practitioner of the unattractive, was one who saw a tooth-bone. 'Of the abandoned' means of that which is abandoned by way of suppression. In similar instances hereafter, this is the same method. According to the Abhidhammic presentation (Dhs. 1159, 1503), all greed is the hindrance of sensual desire; it is with reference to this that it is said to be abandoned 'by the path of arahantship.'

Paṭighampi purimuppannaṃ paṭighanimittaṃ [P 2.0400] parato uppajjanakassa paṭighassa kāraṇanti katvā.

Regarding ill-will also, the previously arisen sign of ill-will is the cause for the ill-will that arises subsequently.

Mejjati siniyhatīti mitto, hitesī puggalo, tasmiṃ mitte bhavā, mittassa vā esāti mettā, hitesitā, tassā mettāya. Appanāpi upacāropi vaṭṭati sādhāraṇavacanabhāvato. “Cetovimuttī”ti [V 2.0293] vutte appanāva vaṭṭati appanaṃ appattāya paṭipakkhato suṭṭhu muccanassa abhāvato. Tanti yonisomanasikāraṃ. Tatthāti mettāya. Bahulaṃ pavattayatoti bahulīkāravato.

'One is affectionate' (`mejjati`), 'one is fond' (`siniyati`), thus a 'friend' (`mitto`), a person who wishes for one's welfare. That which occurs in a friend, or that which belongs to a friend, is 'loving-kindness' (`mettā`), the state of wishing for another's welfare; the text says 'of that loving-kindness' (`tassā mettāya`). Both absorption and access concentration are suitable, because it is a general term. When 'liberation of mind' is said, only absorption is suitable, because without having attained absorption, there is no proper release from the opposing states. 'That' refers to proper attention. 'Therein' means in loving-kindness. 'Makes it occur frequently' means because of making it abundant.

Sattesu [M 2.0317] mettāyanassa hitūpasaṃhārassa uppādanaṃ pavattanaṃ mettānimittassa uggaho, paṭhamuppanno mettāmanasikāro parato uppajjanakassa kāraṇabhāvato mettāmanasikārova mettānimittaṃ. Kammameva sakaṃ etesanti kammassakā, sattā, tabbhāvo kammassakatā, kammadāyādatā. Dosamettāsu yāthāvato ādīnavānisaṃsānaṃ paṭisaṅkhānaṃ vīmaṃsā idha paṭisaṅkhānaṃ. Mettāvihārikalyāṇamittavantatā idha kalyāṇamittatā. Odissakaanodissakadisāpharaṇānanti (odhisakaanodhisakadisāpharaṇānaṃ ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.115) attaatipiyasahāyamajjhattaverivasena odissakatā, sīmāsambhede kate anodissakatā. Ekādidisāpharaṇavasena disāpharaṇatā mettāya uggahaṇe veditabbā. Vihāraracchāgāmādivasena vā odissakadisāpharaṇaṃ. Vihārādiuddesarahitaṃ puratthimādidisāvasena anodissakadisāpharaṇanti evaṃ dvidhā uggahaṇaṃ sandhāya “odissakaanodissakadisāpharaṇāna”nti vuttaṃ. Uggahoti ca yāva upacārā daṭṭhabbo. Uggahitāya āsevanā bhāvanā. Tattha sabbe sattā, pāṇā, bhūtā, puggalā, attabhāvapariyāpannāti etesaṃ vasena pañcavidhā, ekekasmiṃ averā hontu[P 2.0401], abyāpajjhā, anīghā, sukhī attānaṃ pariharantūti catudhā pavattito vīsatividhā anodissakapharaṇā mettā. Sabbā itthiyo, purisā, ariyā, anariyā, devā, manussā, vinipātikāti sattodhikaraṇavasena pavattā sattavidhā, aṭṭhavīsati vidhā vā, dasahi disāhi disodhikaraṇavasena pavattā dasavidhā, ekekāya vā disāya sattādiitthādiaverādibhedena asītādhikacatusatappabhedā ca odhiso pharaṇā veditabbā.

The production and continuation of loving-kindness towards beings and of applying welfare to them is the grasping of the sign of loving-kindness; the initially arisen attention to loving-kindness, because it is a cause for that which arises subsequently, is itself the sign of loving-kindness. 'Action is their own,' thus they are 'owners of their action' (`kammassakā`), that is, beings; their state is 'ownership of action' (`kammassakatā`), 'heirship to action' (`kammadāyādatā`). Here, 'reflection' is the investigation, the thorough consideration of the dangers and benefits of hatred and loving-kindness as they really are. Here, 'good friendship' is the possession of good friends who dwell in loving-kindness. Regarding 'pervasion in specific and non-specific directions': specific refers to pervasion directed toward those regarded as oneself, a beloved person, a friend, a neutral person, and an enemy, while non-specific refers to pervasion when the boundaries have been broken down. The pervasion of directions is the pervasion in one or more directions, which should be understood in the grasping of loving-kindness. Alternatively, specific directional pervasion is based on a monastery, a road, a village, and so forth. Non-specific directional pervasion is without reference to a monastery, etc., and proceeds by way of the directions such as the east. Thus, with this twofold grasping in mind, it is said 'specific and non-specific directional pervasions.' And 'grasping' should be understood as lasting up to access concentration. The cultivation and development is the practice of what has been grasped. Therein, 'all beings, all living creatures, all entities, all persons, all individuals'—in relation to these five, loving-kindness is fivefold. In each case, 'may they be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from distress, may they live happily'—thus, when applied fourfold, the non-specific pervasion becomes twentyfold. 'All women, all men, all noble ones, all non-noble ones, all devas, all humans, all those in states of deprivation'—in relation to these seven bases, it is sevenfold, or twenty-eightfold. In relation to the ten directions as a basis, it is tenfold. Or, for each direction, by distinctions such as beings, women, etc., and 'free from enmity,' etc., the specific pervasion should be understood as having more than four hundred and eighty divisions.

Yena ayonisomanasikārena aratiādikāni uppajjanti, so aratiādīsu ayonisomanasikāro. Tena nipphādetabbe hi idaṃ bhummaṃ. Esa nayo ito paresupi. Ukkaṇṭhitā pantasenāsanesu, adhikusaladhammesu ca uppajjanabhāvariñcanā. Kāyavinamanāti karajakāyassa virūpenākārena namanā. Līnākāroti saṅkocāpatti.

That improper attention by which discontent and so forth arise, is improper attention in regard to discontent and so forth. For this is a locative case referring to that which is to be produced by it. This is the method in the following cases as well. Restlessness is the abandoning of the state of arising in remote dwellings and in superior wholesome qualities. 'Bodily bending' means the bending of the physical body in a distorted manner. 'A sluggish manner' means the state of contraction.

Kusaladhammapaṭipattiyā paṭṭhapanasabhāvatāya, tappaṭipakkhānaṃ visosanasabhāvatāya ca ārambhadhātuādito pavattavīriyanti āha “paṭhamārambhavīriya”nti. Yasmā paṭhamārambhamattassa kosajjavidhamanaṃ, thāmagamanañca [M 2.0318] natthi, tasmā vuttaṃ “kosajjato nikkhantatāya tato balavatara”nti[V 2.0294]. Yasmā pana aparāparuppattiyā laddhāsevanaṃ uparūpari visesaṃ āvahantaṃ ativiya thāmagatameva hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanato tatopi balavatara”nti.

Because it has the nature of establishing the practice of wholesome states and the nature of drying up their opposites, the energy that proceeds from the element of initiative and so forth is called 'initial energy.' Because mere initial initiative does not dispel laziness nor attain strength, it is said: 'it is stronger than that because of having emerged from laziness.' However, because, having gained cultivation through repeated arising, it brings about higher and higher distinction and becomes exceedingly strong, it is said: 'it is even stronger than that by advancing to successive stages.'

Atibhojane nimittaggāhoti atibhojane thinamiddhassa nimittaggāho[P 2.0402], ettake bhutte taṃ bhojanaṃ thinamiddhassa kāraṇaṃ hoti, ettake na hotīti thinamiddhassa kāraṇākāraṇagāho hotīti attho. Byatirekavasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā “ettake bhutte taṃ bhojanaṃ thinamiddhassa kāraṇaṃ na hotī”ti bhojane mattaññutā ca atthato dassitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenāha “catupañca…pe… na hotī”ti. Divā sūriyālokanti divā gahitanimittaṃ sūriyālokaṃ rattiyaṃ manasi karontassāpīti evamettha attho veditabbo. Dhutaṅgānaṃ vīriyanissitattā vuttaṃ “dhutaṅganissitasappāyakathāyapī”ti.

‘Overeating is taking up a sign’ means taking up the sign of dullness and drowsiness in overeating. This means taking up the cause and non-cause of dullness and drowsiness, in that eating a certain amount of food causes dullness and drowsiness, while eating a certain amount does not. This is stated in terms of exclusion. Therefore, it should be understood that the statement, “eating a certain amount of food does not cause dullness and drowsiness” thus shows, in effect, moderation in eating. Therefore, he said, “Four or five… it does not occur.” ‘Sunlight by day’ means even for one who, having taken up the sign of sunlight by day, attends to it mentally at night; thus is the meaning here to be understood. Because the ascetic practices are based on energy, it is said, “Even in talk that is suitable to those relying on the ascetic practices.”

Kukkuccampi katākatānusocanavasena pavattamānaṃ cetaso avūpasamāvahatāya uddhaccena samānalakkhaṇamevāti “avūpasamo nāma avūpasantākāro, uddhaccakukkuccamevetaṃ atthato”ti vuttaṃ.

Remorse, arising by way of regret over what was done and not done, brings about the mind’s lack of tranquility and thus has the same characteristic as agitation. Therefore, it is said: ‘Lack of tranquility is the unpacified state; in meaning, this is agitation and remorse.’

Bahussutassa ganthato, atthato ca suttādīni vicārentassa tabbahulavihārino atthavedādipaṭilābhasabbhāvato vikkhepo na hotīti, yathāvidhipaṭipattiyā, yathānurūpapatikārappavattiyā ca katākatānusocanañca na hotīti “bāhusaccenapi…pe… uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīyatī”ti āha. Yadaggena bāhusaccena uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīyati, tadaggena paripucchakatāvinayapakataññutāhipi taṃ pahīyatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vuddhasevitā ca vuddhasīlitaṃ āvahatīti cetovūpasamakarattā uddhaccakukkuccappahānakārī vuttā. Vuddhattaṃ pana anapekkhitvā kukkuccavinodakā vinayadharā kalyāṇamittā vuttāti daṭṭhabbā. Vikkhepo ca pabbajitānaṃ yebhuyyena kukkuccahetuko hotīti “kappiyākappiyaparipucchābahulassā”tiādinā vinayanayeneva paripucchakatādayo niddiṭṭhā. Pahīne uddhaccakukkucceti [P 2.0403] niddhāraṇe bhummaṃ. Kukkuccassa domanassasahagatattā anāgāmimaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo vutto.

For the learned one, who frequently examines the texts along with their meaning, distraction does not arise because of the possibility of gaining insight into the meaning and so forth. By practicing according to the proper method and engaging in appropriate remedial actions, there is no regret over what has or has not been done. Thus, it is said, “Even through much learning… agitation and remorse are abandoned.” By that supreme quality of much learning by which agitation and remorse are abandoned, it should be understood that by that same supreme quality, they are also abandoned through questioning, discipline, and gratitude. Associating with elders brings about the conduct of elders, and because it pacifies the mind, it is said to be a cause for abandoning agitation and remorse. However, without regard to seniority, it should be understood that those who dispel remorse are the experts in the discipline and good friends. For the most part, distraction among renunciants arises from remorse; therefore, through the method of the Vinaya, qualities such as questioning are indicated, as in “[one] frequently questioning what is allowable and unallowable.” In the phrase `Pahīne uddhaccakukkucceti`, the locative case is used in the sense of specification. Because remorse is accompanied by displeasure, its non-arising in the future is declared by the path of the non-returner.

Tiṭṭhati [M 2.0319] pavattati etthāti ṭhānīyā vicikicchāya ṭhānīyā vicikicchāṭhānīyā, vicikicchāya kāraṇabhūtā dhammā, tiṭṭhatīti vā ṭhānīyā, vicikicchā ṭhānīyā etissāti vicikicchāṭhānīyā, atthato vicikicchā eva. Sā hi purimuppannā parato uppajjanakavicikicchāya sabhāgahetutāya asādhāraṇaṃ kāraṇaṃ.

‘It stands, it occurs in this,’ hence it is a ground (ṭhānīyā). The ground for doubt is a doubt-ground (vicikicchāṭhānīyā); these are the states that are the cause of doubt. Or, because it stands, it is a ground; doubt has its ground in this, hence it is a doubt-ground. In meaning, it is simply doubt. For that initially arisen doubt is the unique cause for a subsequently arising doubt, due to being a homogeneous cause.

Kusalākusalāti [V 2.0295] kosallasambhūtaṭṭhena kusalā, tappaṭipakkhato akusalā. Ye akusalā, te sāvajjā, asevitabbā, hīnā ca. Ye kusalā, te anavajjā, sevitabbā, paṇītā ca. Kusalā vā hīnehi chandādīhi āraddhā hīnā, paṇītehi paṇītā. Kaṇhāti kāḷakā cittassa apabhassarabhāvakaraṇā. Sukkāti odātā cittassa pabhassarabhāvakaraṇā. Kaṇhābhijātihetuto vā kaṇhā. Sukkābhijātihetuto sukkā. Te eva sappaṭibhāgā. Kaṇhā hi ujuvipaccanīkatāya sukkasappaṭibhāgā, tathā sukkāpi itarehi. Atha vā kaṇhasukkā ca sappaṭibhāgā ca kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgā. Sukhā hi vedanā dukkhāya vedanāya sappaṭibhāgā, dukkhā ca vedanā sukhāya vedanāya sappaṭibhāgāti.

‘Skillful and unskillful’: what is skillful is so by the meaning of arising from skill; what is unskillful is its opposite. Those that are unskillful are blameworthy, not to be practiced, and inferior. Those that are skillful are blameless, to be practiced, and excellent. Or, skillful states, when initiated with inferior desire and so on, are inferior; when initiated with excellent desire and so on, they are excellent. ‘Dark’ refers to what is black, causing the mind to lose its brightness. ‘Bright’ refers to what is white, causing the mind to become bright. Or, they are dark due to a cause of dark origin, and bright due to a cause of bright origin. These are counterparts to each other. For dark, by being directly opposed, is a counterpart to bright, and likewise, bright is a counterpart to the other. Alternatively, `kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgā` means dark and bright, and counterparts. For pleasant feeling is a counterpart to painful feeling, and painful feeling is a counterpart to pleasant feeling.

Kāmaṃ bāhusaccaparipucchakatāhi sabbāpi aṭṭhavatthukā vicikicchā pahīyati, tathāpi ratanattayavicikicchāmūlikā sesavicikicchāti katvā āha “tīṇi ratanāni ārabbhā”ti. Ratanattayaguṇāvabodhe “satthari kaṅkhatī”tiādi (dha. sa. 1008, 1123, 1167, 1241, 1263, 1270; vibha. 915) vicikicchāya asambhavoti. Vinaye pakataññutā “sikkhāya kaṅkhatī”ti vuttāya vicikicchāya pahānaṃ karotīti āha “vinaye ciṇṇavasībhāvassāpī”ti. Okappaniyasaddhāsaṅkhātaadhimokkhabahulassāti [P 2.0404] saddheyyavatthuno anupavisanasaddhāsaṅkhātaadhimokkhena adhimuccanabahulassa, adhimuccanañca adhimokkhuppādanamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ, saddhāya vā ninnapoṇatāadhimutti adhimokkho.

Though all doubt based on the eight grounds is abandoned through much learning and questioning, still, the remaining doubts are rooted in doubt about the Triple Gem. Hence, it is said, “Regarding the three jewels.” When one understands the virtues of the Triple Gem, the arising of doubt such as “Does one doubt the Teacher?” (Dhs 1008, etc.; Vb 915) is impossible. Expertise in the Vinaya causes the abandonment of the doubt expressed as “Does one doubt the training?” Therefore, it is said, “Even for one who has long been practiced and mastered the Vinaya.” ‘One who is abundant in resolution, reckoned as faith that is fit to be believed’ refers to one who is frequently resolved through the resolution reckoned as faith, which is the faith of entering into an object worthy of faith. And resolution should be understood as simply the production of determination. Alternatively, resolution is the inclination and disposition towards faith.

Samudayavayāti samudayavayadhammā. Subhanimittaasubhanimittādīsūti “subhanimittādīsu asubhanimittādīsū”ti ādi-saddo paccekaṃ yojetabbo. Tattha paṭhamena ādi-saddena paṭighanimittādīnaṃ saṅgaho, dutiyenamettācetovimuttiādīnaṃ. Sesamettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ vuttanayameva.

‘Arising and passing away’ means phenomena subject to arising and passing away. ‘Regarding the sign of the beautiful, the sign of the unattractive, etc.’: here, the word ‘etc.’ should be connected to each individually, as ‘the sign of the beautiful, etc.,’ and ‘the sign of the unattractive, etc.’ In this context, the first ‘etc.’ includes the sign of repugnance and so on, while the second includes the liberation of mind through loving-kindness and so on. The rest of what needs to be said here is as was stated before.

Nīvaraṇapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the section on the hindrances is concluded.

Khandhapabbavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Section on the Aggregates

383. Upādānehi [M 2.0320] ārammaṇakaraṇādivasena upādātabbā vā khandhā upādānakkhandhā.

383. The aggregates of clinging are the aggregates that are to be clung to by the clingings by way of making them an object and so on.

Iti [V 2.0296] rūpanti ettha iti-saddo idaṃ-saddena samānatthoti adhippāyenāha “idaṃ rūpa”nti. Tayidaṃ sarūpaggahaṇabhāvato anavasesapariyādānaṃ hotīti āha “ettakaṃ rūpaṃ, na ito paraṃ rūpaṃ atthī”ti. Itīti vā pakāratthe nipāto, tasmā “iti rūpa”nti iminā bhūtupādādivasena yattako rūpassa pabhedo, tena saddhiṃ rūpaṃ anavasesato pariyādiyitvā dasseti. Sabhāvatoti ruppanasabhāvato, cakkhādivaṇṇādisabhāvato ca. Vedanādīsupīti ettha “ayaṃ vedanā, ettakā vedanā, na ito paraṃ vedanā atthīti sabhāvato vedanaṃ pajānātī”tiādinā, sabhāvatoti ca “anubhavanasabhāvato, sātādisabhāvato cā”ti evamādinā yojetabbaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayattā suviññeyyameva.

In ‘Thus is form,’ the word ‘thus’ (iti) has the same meaning as the word ‘this’ (idaṃ), with the intention that it is said, ‘this is form.’ Because this is a complete comprehension of its own nature without remainder, it is said, ‘this much is form, there is no form beyond this.’ Or, the particle ‘iti’ is in the sense of ‘manner’; therefore, by ‘Thus is form,’ form is shown completely and without remainder, along with all its divisions, such as the primary elements and derived form. ‘By its nature’ means by the nature of being afflicted (ruppana), and by the nature of the eye, etc., and visible objects, etc. ‘Similarly for feeling, etc.’: here, it should be connected with phrases such as ‘this is feeling, this much is feeling, there is no feeling beyond this—one understands feeling by its nature,’ and ‘by its nature’ should be connected with phrases such as ‘by the nature of experiencing and by the nature of being pleasant, etc.’ The rest is easily understood, as it has been explained in the stated manner.

Khandhapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the section on the aggregates is concluded.

Āyatanapabbavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Section on the Sense Bases

384. Chasu ajjhattikabāhiresūti “chasu ajjhattikesu chasu bāhiresū”ti “chasū”ti padaṃ paccekaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Kasmā panetāni ubhayāni chaḷeva vuttāni? Chaviññāṇakāyuppattidvārārammaṇavavatthānato. Cakkhuviññāṇavīthiyā pariyāpannassa hi viññāṇakāyassa cakkhāyatanameva uppattidvāraṃ, rūpāyatanameva ca ārammaṇaṃ, tathā itarāni itaresaṃ, chaṭṭhassa pana bhavaṅgamanasaṅkhāto manāyatanekadeso [P 2.0405] uppattidvāraṃ, asādhāraṇañca dhammāyatanaṃ ārammaṇaṃ. Cakkhatīti cakkhu, rūpaṃ assādeti, vibhāveti cāti attho. Suṇātīti sotaṃ. Ghāyatīti ghānaṃ. Jīvitanimittatāya raso jīvitaṃ, taṃ jīvitaṃ avhāyatīti jivhā. Kucchitānaṃ sāsavadhammānaṃ āyo uppattidesoti kāyo. Munāti ārammaṇaṃ vijānātīti mano. Rūpayati vaṇṇavikāraṃ āpajjamānaṃ hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ pakāsetīti rūpaṃ. Sappati attano paccayehi harīyati sotaviññeyyabhāvaṃ gamīyatīti saddo. Gandhayati attano vatthuṃ sūcetīti gandho[M 2.0321]. Rasanti taṃ sattā assādentīti raso. Phusīyatīti phoṭṭhabbaṃ. Attano sabhāvaṃ dhārentīti dhammā. Sabbāni pana āyānaṃ tananādiatthena āyatanāni. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (visuddhi. 2.510, 511, 512; visuddhi. ṭī. 2.510) vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

384. Regarding 'the six internal and external': the word 'six' should be applied separately to 'the six internal' and 'the six external.' But why are both these said to be only six? Because of their classification by the doors and objects for the arising of the six consciousness-bodies. For the consciousness-body included in the eye-consciousness process, the eye-base alone is the door of arising, and the form-base alone is the object. Similarly for the others. As for the sixth, a part of the mind-base, which is called the life-continuum mind, is the door of arising, and the unique mental-object base is the object. The eye (cakkhu) is so called because it sees (cakkhati); the meaning is that it savors and makes clear form. The ear (sota) is so called because it hears (suṇāti). The nose (ghāna) is so called because it smells (ghāyati). The tongue (jivhā) is so called because it relishes (avhāyati) life (jīvitaṃ), being the sign of life. The body (kāya) is so called because it is the origin (āyo) and place of arising for defiled states associated with taints. The mind (mano) is so called because it understands (munāti) the object. Form (rūpa) is so called because it displays (rūpayati) changes in appearance, manifesting its agreeableness to the heart. Sound (sadda) is so called because it moves (sappati), being carried by its conditions, becoming perceptible to the ear-consciousness. Smell (gandha) is so called because it indicates (gandhayati) its own basis. Taste (rasa) is so called because beings enjoy (rasanti) it. Tangibles (phoṭṭhabba) are so called because they are touched (phusīyati). Mental objects (dhammā) are so called because they bear (dhārenti) their own nature. All these are called 'bases' (āyatana) because of their meaning as a source (āya) and of stretching (tanana), and so on. This is a summary here; the detailed explanation should be understood as given in the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhi. 2.510, 511, 512; Visuddhi. ṭī. 2.510).

Cakkhuñca [V 2.0297] pajānātīti (dī. ni. 2.384; ma. ni. 1.117) ettha cakkhu nāma pasādacakkhu, na sasambhāracakkhu, nāpi dibbacakkhuādikanti āha cakkhupasādanti. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “yaṃ cakkhu catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya pasādo”ti. (Dha. sa. 596) ca-saddo vakkhamānatthasamuccayattho. Yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇavasenāti aviparītassa attano rasassa ceva lakkhaṇassa ca vasena, rūpesu āviñchanakiccassa ceva rūpābhighātārahabhūtapasādalakkhaṇassa ca daṭṭhukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtapasādalakkhaṇassa ca vasenāti attho. Atha vā yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇavasenāti yāthāvasarasavasena ceva lakkhaṇavasena ca, yāthāvasarasoti [P 2.0406] ca aviparītasabhāvo veditabbo. So hi rasīyati aviraddhapaṭivedhavasena assādīyati ramīyatīti “raso”ti vuccati, tasmā salakkhaṇavasenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Lakkhaṇavasenāti aniccādisāmaññalakkhaṇavasena.

Regarding 'he understands the eye' (Dī. Ni. 2.384; Ma. Ni. 1.117), here the eye means the sensitive eye, not the physical eye with its components, nor the divine eye and so on—thus it is called eye-sensitivity. This refers to what is stated: 'The eye, which is a sensitivity derived from the four great elements' (Dha. Sa. 596). The particle 'ca' here serves to combine the meanings that are about to be stated. By 'by way of its true essence and characteristic' (yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇavasena) is meant by way of its own unaltered essence and characteristic, and by way of the function of drawing in forms, and by way of the characteristic of being a sensitive element capable of being struck by forms, and by way of the characteristic of being a sensitive element arisen from kamma that is the cause of the desire to see. Alternatively, 'by way of its true essence and characteristic' means both by way of its true essence and by way of its characteristic. And 'true essence' should be understood as its unaltered nature. For it is called 'essence' (rasa) because it is savored, enjoyed, and delighted in by way of unobstructed penetration; therefore, it is said 'by way of its own characteristic.' 'By way of its characteristic' refers to the general characteristics such as impermanence.

“Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇa”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.204, 400; ma. ni. 3.421, 425, 426; saṃ. ni. 2.43, 45; 2.4.60) samuditāniyeva rūpāyatanāni cakkhuviññāṇuppattihetu, na visuṃ visunti imassa atthassa jotanatthaṃ “rūpe cā”ti puthuvacanaggahaṇaṃ, tāya eva ca desanāgatiyā kāmaṃ idhāpi “rūpe ca pajānātī”ti vuttaṃ, rūpabhāvasāmaññena pana sabbaṃ ekajjhaṃ gahetvā bahiddhā catusamuṭṭhānikarūpañcāti ekavacanavasena attho. Sarasalakkhaṇa vasenāti cakkhuviññāṇassa visayabhāvakiccassa vasena ceva cakkhupaṭihananalakkhaṇassa vasena cāti yojetabbaṃ.

In passages such as 'depending on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.204, 400; Majjhima Nikāya 3.421, 425, 426; Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.43, 45; 2.4.60), the form-bases, being collective, are indeed the cause for the arising of eye-consciousness, not individually separate. To clarify this meaning, the plural form 'rūpe ca' is employed. Following that same mode of exposition, here too, even though it is said, 'one understands forms,' yet due to the generality of the nature of form, everything is taken together as one; and externally, the meaning is in the singular, referring to form arisen from the four causes. 'By way of its own essence and characteristic' (sarasalakkhaṇa vasena) should be connected both in terms of its function of being the object of eye-consciousness and in terms of the characteristic of impacting the eye.

Ubhayaṃ paṭiccāti cakkhuṃ upanissayapaccayavasena paccayabhūtaṃ, rūpe ārammaṇādhipatiārammaṇūpanissayavasena paccayabhūte ca paṭicca. Kāmaṃ ayaṃ suttantasaṃvaṇṇanā, nippariyāyakathā nāma abhidhammasannissitā evāti abhidhammanayeneva saṃyojanāni dassento “kāmarāga…pe… avijjāsaṃyojana”nti [M 2.0322] āha. Tattha kāmesu rāgo, kāmo ca so rāgo cāti vā kāmarāgo. So eva bandhanaṭṭhena saṃyojanaṃ. Ayañhi yassa saṃvijjati, taṃ puggalaṃ vaṭṭasmiṃ saṃyojeti bandhati iti dukkhena sattaṃ, bhavādike vā bhavantarādīhi, kammunā vā vipākaṃ saṃyojeti bandhatīti saṃyojanaṃ. Evaṃ paṭighasaṃyojaṃādīnampi yathārahamattho vattabbo. Sarasalakkhaṇavasenāti ettha pana sattassa vaṭṭato anissajjanasaṅkhātassa attano kiccassa ceva yathāvuttabandhanasaṅkhātassa lakkhaṇassa ca vasenāti yojetabbaṃ.

'Depending on both' means depending on the eye, which is a condition by way of the strong dependence condition, and on forms, which are conditions by way of object, dominance, and object-strong dependence condition. Although this is a commentary on a Sutta, this direct teaching is indeed rooted in the Abhidhamma; therefore, following the Abhidhamma method, it shows the fetters by stating, 'sensual desire... up to the ignorance-fetter.' Here, desire for sensual pleasures, or that sensual pleasure which is desire, is sensual desire. That very thing, by its nature of binding, is a fetter. For when this exists in someone, it binds that person to the cycle of existence, thus binding the being with suffering, or binding them to future existences and so on, or binding the result with kamma—thus it is a fetter. Similarly, the meaning of the aversion-fetter and the others should be stated accordingly. 'By way of its own essence and characteristic' (sarasalakkhaṇavasenāti) here should be interpreted as being by way of its own function, which is the non-release of a being from the cycle of existence, and by way of its characteristic, which is binding as previously described.

Bhavassādadiṭṭhissādanivattanatthaṃ [P 2.0407] kāmassādaggahaṇaṃ. Assādayatoti abhiramantassa. Abhinandatoti [V 2.0298] sappītikataṇhāvasena nandantassa. Padadvayenāpi balavato kāmarāgassa paccayabhūtā kāmarāguppatti vuttā. Esa nayo sesesupi. Aniṭṭhārammaṇeti ettha “āpāthagate”ti vibhattivipariṇāmanavasena “āpāthagata”nti padaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Etaṃ ārammaṇanti etaṃ evaṃsukhumaṃ evaṃdubbibhāgaṃ ārammaṇaṃ. “Niccaṃ dhuva”nti idaṃ nidassanamattaṃ. “Ucchijjissati vinassissatīti gaṇhato”ti evamādīnampi saṅgaho icchitabbo. Paṭhamāya sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā anurodhavasena “satto nu kho”ti, itarāya anurodhavasena “sattassa nu kho”ti vicikicchato. Attattaniyādigāhānugatā hi vicikicchā diṭṭhiyā asati abhāvato. Bhavaṃ patthentassāti “īdise sampattibhave yasmā amhākaṃ idaṃ iṭṭhaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ sulabhaṃ jātaṃ, tasmā āyatimpi ediso, ito vā uttaritaro sampattibhavo bhaveyyā”ti bhavaṃ nikāmentassa. Evarūpanti evarūpaṃ rūpaṃ. Taṃsadise hi tabbohāravasenevaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhavati hi taṃsadisesu tabbohāro yathā “sā eva tittirī, tāni eva osadhānī”ti. Usūyatoti usūyaṃ issaṃ uppādayato. Aññassa maccharāyatoti aññena asādhāraṇabhāvakaraṇena macchariyaṃ karoto. Sabbeheva yathāvuttehi navahi saṃyojanehi.

The grasping of sensual pleasures is undertaken for the purpose of abandoning the pleasure in existence and the pleasure in views. 'Delighting in' (assādayato) refers to one who enjoys. 'Rejoicing in' (abhinandato) refers to one who delights with craving accompanied by satisfaction. By these two terms is described the arising of sensual desire that becomes the cause of strong sensual desire. This method applies to the rest as well. Regarding 'undesirable object,' here the word 'āpāthagata' (fallen into the range) should be brought in and connected by altering the inflection. 'This object' refers to this object, which is so subtle and so difficult to distinguish. 'Permanent, stable'—this is merely an illustration. The inclusion of phrases such as 'for one who grasps, "It will be cut off, it will perish,"' and so on, is also intended. For the first identity view, due to adherence, one doubts, 'Is it a being?' For the other, due to adherence, one doubts, 'Does it belong to a being?' For doubt, being accompanied by the grip of self and what belongs to self, does not exist in the absence of the view. 'Longing for existence' refers to one who desires existence, thinking: 'Since in such a fortunate existence this desirable form-object has become easily obtainable for us, therefore in the future too, may there be such an existence, or an even more excellent fortunate existence than this.' 'Of such a kind' refers to such a form. For it is said thus by way of the designation for what is similar to that. Indeed, the designation for what is similar occurs, as in: 'That very partridge, those very herbs.' 'Being jealous' (usūyato) means producing envy and jealousy. 'Being stingy toward another' (aññassa maccharāyato) means acting with stinginess by making something exclusive to oneself. By all nine fetters, as they have been described.

Tañca kāraṇanti subhanimittapaṭighanimittādivibhāgaṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhādirūpārammaṇañceva tajjāyonisomanasikārañcāti [P 2.0408] tassa tassa saṃyojanassa kāraṇaṃ. Avikkhambhitāsamūhatabhūmiladdhuppannaṃ taṃ sandhāya “appahīnaṭṭhena uppannassā”ti vuttaṃ. Vattamānuppannatā samudācāraggahaṇeneva gahitā. Yena kāraṇenāti yena vipassanāsamathabhāvanāsaṅkhātena kāraṇena[M 2.0323]. Tañhi tassa tadaṅgavasena ceva vikkhambhanavasena ca pahānakāraṇaṃ. Issāmacchariyānaṃ apāyagamanīyatāya paṭhamamaggavajjhatā vuttā. Yadi evaṃ “tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā sotāpanno hotī”ti (a. ni. 4.241) suttapadaṃ kathanti? Taṃ suttantapariyāyena vuttaṃ. Yathānulomasāsanā hi suttantadesanā, ayaṃ pana abhidhammanayena saṃvaṇṇanāti nāyaṃ dosoti. Oḷārikassāti thūlassa, yato abhiṇhasamuppattipariyuṭṭhānatibbatāva hoti. Aṇusahagatassāti vuttappakārābhāvena aṇubhāvaṃ sukhumabhāvaṃ gatassa. Uddhaccasaṃyojanassapettha anuppādo vuttoyevāti daṭṭhabbo yathāvuttasaṃyojanehi avinābhāvato. Ekatthatāya sotādīnaṃ sabhāvasarasalakkhaṇavasena pajānanā, tappaccayānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ uppādādipajānanā ca vuttanayeneva veditabbāti dassento “eseva nayo”ti atidisati.

And that cause: the division into the sign of the beautiful and the sign of the repulsive, etc., and the object of desirable or undesirable forms, as well as the unwise attention born from them—this is the cause for each respective fetter. It refers to what has arisen, not having been suppressed or uprooted, and not having attained the ground of abandonment—hence, it is said, 'of what has arisen in the sense of not being abandoned.' The state of being presently arisen is already included by the mention of its manifestation. By what cause? By the cause designated as the development of insight and serenity. For that is indeed the cause for its abandonment both by way of substitution and by way of suppression. Envy and stinginess are said to be overcome by the first path because they lead to states of deprivation. If so, how then is the sutta passage, 'With the destruction of three fetters, one becomes a stream-enterer' (AN 4.241), to be explained? That was stated in accordance with the sutta method. For the sutta teachings are indeed gradual teachings, but this is an exposition according to the Abhidhamma method—thus, there is no fault here. Of the gross: that which is coarse, because it has frequent arising, obsession, and intensity. Of the subtle: that which, due to the absence of the previously described qualities, has gone to a subtle and fine state. It should be understood that the non-arising of the restlessness fetter is stated here as well, since it is inseparable from the aforementioned fetters. To show that the knowing of the eye, etc., as a single thing by way of their intrinsic nature, essential characteristic, and individual characteristic, and the knowing of the arising, etc., of the fetters dependent on them, should be understood in the manner already stated, he makes an extension, saying: 'This is the method.'

Attano vā dhammesūti attano ajjhattikāyatanadhammesu, attano ubhayadhammesu vā. Imasmiṃ pakkhe ajjhattikāyatanapariggaṇhanenāti ajjhattikāyatanapariggaṇhanamukhenāti attho. Evañca [V 2.0299] anavasesato saparasantānesu āyatanānaṃ pariggaho siddho hoti. Parassa [P 2.0409] vā dhammesūti etthāpi eseva nayo. Rūpāyatanassāti aḍḍhekādasappabhedassa rūpasabhāvassa āyatanassa rūpakkhandhe “vuttanayena nīharitabbo”ti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Sesakkhandhesūti vedanāsaññāsaṅkhārakkhandhesu. Vuttanayenāti iminā atidesena rūpakkhandhe “āhārasamudayā”ti viññāṇakkhandhe “nāmarūpasamudayā”ti sesakhandhesu “phassasamudayā”ti imaṃ visesaṃ vibhāveti, itaraṃ pana sabbattha samānanti khandhapabbe viya āyatanapabbepi lokuttaranivattanaṃ pāḷiyaṃ gahitaṃ natthīti vuttaṃ “lokuttaradhammā na gahetabbā”ti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

'In one's own phenomena' means in one's own internal sense-base phenomena, or in one's own phenomena of both kinds. In this case, 'by the inclusion of the internal sense bases' means 'by way of including the internal sense bases.' Thus, the complete inclusion of sense bases in one's own and others' continua is established. The same principle applies here to 'or in others' phenomena.' 'Of the form base' means of the form base, which is of the nature of form, having eleven and a half kinds. It should be brought and connected to the aggregate of form 'in the manner stated.' 'In the remaining aggregates' refers to the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations. 'By the stated method,' through this extension, clarifies this distinction: in the aggregate of form, it is 'arising from nutriment'; in the consciousness aggregate, 'arising from name-and-form'; and in the remaining aggregates, 'arising from contact.' The rest, however, is the same everywhere. Just as in the section on aggregates, the supramundane is not included in the sense-base section of the Pāli text—hence it is stated, 'supramundane phenomena are not to be included.' The rest is in the manner stated.

Āyatanapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on the sense bases is concluded.

Bojjhaṅgapabbavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on the Enlightenment Factors

385. Bujjhanakasattassāti kilesaniddāya paṭibujjhanakasattassa, ariyasaccānaṃ vā paṭivijjhanakasattassa. Aṅgesūti kāraṇesu, avayavesu vā[M 2.0324]. Udayavayañāṇuppattito paṭṭhāya sambodhipaṭipadāyaṃ ṭhito nāma hotīti āha “āraddhavipassakato paṭṭhāya yogāvacaroti sambodhī”ti. Suttantadesanā nāma pariyāyakathā, ayañca satipaṭṭhānadesanā lokiyamaggavasena pavattāti vuttaṃ “yogāvacaroti sambodhī”ti, aññathā “ariyasāvako”ti vadeyya.

385. 'Of a being who awakens' means of a being who awakens from the sleep of defilements, or of a being who penetrates the noble truths. 'In the factors' means in the causes, or in the components. From the arising of the knowledge of arising and passing away, one is said to be established on the path to full enlightenment. Thus it is said: 'Starting from the one who has begun insight, the practitioner is enlightenment.' The exposition of the Suttas is a teaching by way of convention, and this teaching of the foundations of mindfulness proceeds by way of the mundane path—thus it is said: 'the practitioner is enlightenment.' Otherwise, one would say 'noble disciple.'

“Satisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā”ti padassa attho “vicikicchāṭṭhānīyā”ti ettha vuttanayena veditabbo. Tanti yonisomanasikāraṃ. Tatthāti satiyaṃ, nipphādetabbe cetaṃ bhummaṃ.

The meaning of the phrase 'are states that are grounds for the enlightenment factor of mindfulness' should be understood in the same way as explained for 'are states that are grounds for doubt.' That is wise attention. 'Therein' means in mindfulness, and this is a locative case indicating that which is to be accomplished.

Sati ca sampajaññañca satisampajaññaṃ. Atha vā satippadhānaṃ abhikkantādisātthakabhāvapariggaṇhanañāṇaṃ satisampajaññaṃ. Taṃ sabbattha satokārībhāvāvahattā satisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya hoti. Yathā paccanīkadhammappahānaṃ, anurūpadhammasevanā ca anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya hoti, evaṃ satirahitapuggalavivajjanā, satokārīpuggalasevanā, tattha ca yuttappayuttatā satisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya hotīti imamatthaṃ dasseti “satisampajañña”ntiādinā. Tissadattatthero nāma, yo bodhimaṇḍe [P 2.0410] suvaṇṇasalākaṃ gahetvā [V 2.0300] “aṭṭhārasasu bhāsāsu katarabhāsāya dhammaṃ kathemī”ti parisaṃ pavāresi. Abhayattheroti dattābhayattheramāha.

Mindfulness and clear comprehension are 'mindfulness-and-clear-comprehension.' Alternatively, 'mindfulness-and-clear-comprehension' is the knowledge, with mindfulness as primary, that grasps the beneficial nature of going forward and so on. This, because it brings about the state of acting mindfully in all things, leads to the arising of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. Just as abandoning opposing qualities and cultivating suitable qualities lead to the arising of unarisen wholesome states, so too do avoiding persons devoid of mindfulness, associating with mindful persons, and proper application therein, lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. This meaning is shown by 'mindfulness-and-clear-comprehension,' and so on. The elder Tissadatta is the one who, holding a golden stylus at the Bodhi-mandala, invited the assembly, saying, 'In which of the eighteen languages shall I teach the Dhamma?' By 'the elder Abhaya,' he refers to Dattābhayatthera.

Dhammānaṃ, dhammesu vā vicayo dhammavicayo, so eva sambojjhaṅgo, tassa dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa. “Kusalākusalā dhammā”tiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāroti kusalādīnaṃ taṃtaṃsabhāvasarasalakkhaṇaādikassa yāthāvato avabujjhanavasena uppanno ñāṇasampayuttacittuppādo. So hi aviparītamanasikāratāya “yonisomanasikāro”ti vutto, tadābhogatāya āvajjanāpi taggatikā eva, tassa abhiṇhaṃ pavattanaṃ bahulīkāro. Bhiyyobhāvāyāti punappunaṃ bhāvāya. Vepullāyāti vipulabhāvāya. Pāripūriyāti paribrūhanāya.

The investigation of phenomena, or in phenomena, is 'investigation-of-states'; that itself is an enlightenment factor, of that enlightenment factor of investigation-of-states. Regarding what should be said concerning 'wholesome and unwholesome phenomena,' and so on, it is just as has been stated below. Here, 'frequent cultivation of wise attention' means the arising of a consciousness associated with knowledge through understanding, as it actually is, the respective intrinsic nature, essential characteristic, individual characteristic, etc., of wholesome states and so on. This is called 'wise attention' because it is non-perverted attention. Due to its inclination towards that, even the adverting is of the same nature. The frequent occurrence of that is its 'frequent cultivation.' 'For increase' means for repeated cultivation. 'For expansion' means for a state of vastness. 'For fulfillment' means for completion.

Paripucchakatāti pariyogāhetvā pucchakabhāvo. Ācariye payirupāsitvā pañcapi nikāye saha aṭṭhakathāya pariyogāhetvā yaṃ yaṃ tattha gaṇṭhiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ, taṃ taṃ “idaṃ bhante kathaṃ, imassa ko attho”ti khandhāyatanādiatthaṃ [M 2.0325] pucchantassa dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo uppajjati. Tenāha “khandhadhātu…pe… bahulatā”ti. Vatthūnaṃ visadabhāvakaraṇanti ettha cittacetasikānaṃ pavattiṭṭhānabhāvato sarīraṃ, tappaṭibaddhāni cīvarāni ca “vatthūnī”ti adhippetāni, tāni yathā cittassa sukhāvahāni honti, tathā karaṇaṃ tesaṃ visadabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “ajjhattikabāhirāna”ntiādi. Ussannadosanti vātādiussannadosaṃ. Sedamalamakkhitanti sedena ceva jallikāsaṅkhātena sarīramalena ca makkhitaṃ. Ca-saddena aññampi sarīrassa, cittassa ca pīḷāvahaṃ [P 2.0411] saṅgaṇhāti. Senāsanaṃ vāti vā-saddena pattādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Avisade sati, visayabhūte vā. Kathaṃ bhāvanamanuyuttassa tāni visayo? Antarantarā pavattanakacittuppādavasenevaṃ vuttaṃ. Te hi cittuppādā cittekaggatāya aparisuddhabhāvāya saṃvattanti. Cittacetasikesu nissayādipaccayabhūtesu. Ñāṇampīti pi-saddo sampiṇḍanattho, tena na kevalaṃ taṃ vatthuyeva, atha kho tasmiṃ aparisuddhe ñāṇampi aparisuddhaṃ hotīti nissayāparisuddhiyā taṃnissitāparisuddhi viya visayassa aparisuddhatāya visayino aparisuddhiṃ dasseti.

'Questioning' means the state of being a questioner after thorough investigation. For one who has approached a teacher, thoroughly investigated the five Nikāyas along with their commentaries, and asks about whatever has become a knotty point therein—'Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?'—regarding the meaning of the aggregates, sense bases, and so on, the enlightenment factor of investigation-of-states arises. Therefore, it is said: 'frequency regarding aggregates, elements...' and so on. 'Making the bases clear': here, 'bases' is intended to mean the body, as it is the place for the occurrence of mind and mental factors, and the robes connected with it. Making them clear is to make them in such a way that they are pleasant for the mind. Hence, it is said: 'of internal and external,' etc. 'Excessive imbalance' means an excessive imbalance of wind, etc. 'Smeared with sweat and dirt' means smeared with sweat and the bodily grime known as 'jallikā.' The word 'and' includes anything else that afflicts the body and mind. 'Or a dwelling': by the word 'or,' the inclusion of bowls, etc., should be understood. When it is unclear, or when it has become an object. How are they objects for one devoted to development? It is said thus by way of the arising of thought-moments that occur intermittently. For those thought-moments lead to the impurity of mental one-pointedness. In the mind and mental factors, which are support conditions, etc. 'Knowledge too': the word 'too' has the meaning of inclusion. Therefore, it shows the impurity of the subject due to the impurity of the object, just as there is impurity of the dependent due to the impurity of the support. This means that not only that basis, but when that is impure, knowledge too becomes impure.

Samabhāvakaraṇanti kiccato anūnādhikabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Saddheyyavatthusmiṃ paccayavasena adhimokkhakiccassa paṭutarabhāvena, paññāya avisadatāya, vīriyādīnañca sithilatādinā saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti. Tenāha “itarāni mandānī”ti. Tatoti tasmā saddhindriyassa balavabhāvato[V 2.0301], itaresañca mandattā. Kosajjapakkhe patituṃ adatvā sampayuttadhammānaṃ paggaṇhanaṃ anubalappadānaṃ paggaho, paggahova kiccaṃ paggahakiccaṃ, “kātuṃ na sakkotī”ti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Ārammaṇaṃ upagantvā ṭhānaṃ, anissajjanaṃ vā upaṭṭhānaṃ. Vikkhepapaṭikkhepo, yena vā sampayuttā avikkhittā honti, so avikkhepo. Rūpagataṃ viya cakkhunā yena yāthāvato visayasabhāvaṃ passati, taṃ dassanakiccaṃ. Kātuṃ na sakkoti balavatā saddhindriyena abhibhūtattā. Sahajātadhammesu hi indaṭṭhaṃ kārentānaṃ sahapavattamānānaṃ dhammānaṃ ekarasatāvaseneva atthasiddhi, na aññathā. Tasmāti vuttamevatthaṃ kāraṇabhāvena paccāmasati. Tanti saddhindriyaṃ[P 2.0412]. Dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇenāti yassa saddheyyassa vatthuno uḷāratādiguṇe adhimuccanassa sātisayappavattiyā saddhindriyaṃ [M 2.0326] balavaṃ jātaṃ, tassa paccayapaccayuppannatādivibhāgato yāthāvato vīmaṃsanena. Evañhi evaṃdhammatānayena sabhāvasarasato pariggayhamāne savipphāro adhimokkho na hoti “ayaṃ imesaṃ dhammānaṃ sabhāvo”ti parijānanavasena paññābyāpārassa sātisayattā. Dhuriyadhammesu hi yathā saddhāya balavabhāve paññāya mandabhāvo hoti, evaṃ paññāya balavabhāve saddhāya mandabhāvo hotīti. Tena vuttaṃ “taṃ dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena vā, yathā vā manasikaroto balavaṃ jātaṃ, tathā amanasikārena hāpetabba”nti. Tathā amanasikārenāti yenākārena bhāvanaṃ anuyuñjantassa saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ jātaṃ, tenākārena bhāvanāya ananuyuñjanatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Idha duvidhena saddhindriyassa balavabhāvo attano vā paccayavisesena kiccuttariyato, vīriyādīnaṃ vā mandakiccatāya. Tattha paṭhamavikappe hāpanavidhi dassito. Dutiyakappe pana yathā manasi karoto vīriyādīnaṃ mandakiccatāya saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ jātaṃ, tathā amanasikārena, vīriyādīnaṃ paṭukiccabhāvāvahena manasikārena saddhindriyaṃ tehi samarasaṃ karontena hāpetabbaṃ. Iminā nayena sesindriyesupi hāpanavidhi veditabbo.

‘Making equal’ means, by function, making things neither deficient nor excessive. In a matter worthy of faith, due to the predominance of the function of conviction arising from conditions, the lack of clarity in wisdom, and the laxity of energy and the other faculties, the faculty of faith becomes strong. Hence it is said, ‘The others are weak.’ Therefore, because the faculty of faith is strong and the others are weak, it cannot perform the function of exertion, which is the upholding and strengthening of associated states, not allowing them to fall into the side of laziness. The phrase ‘cannot do it’ should be brought and connected here. Approaching an object and establishing oneself there, or non-abandonment, is presence of mind. The counteraction of distraction, or that by which associated states become undistracted, is non-distraction. Just as with the eye one sees the true nature of a visible object, that is the function of seeing. One cannot perform its function because one is overpowered by the strong faculty of faith. For among co-arisen states, the achievement of the goal for those performing the function of a master is accomplished only by their unity of savor as they proceed together, not otherwise. Therefore, this refers back to the meaning just stated as the reason. ‘That’ refers to the faculty of faith. ‘By examining the nature of phenomena’ means by truly investigating, according to the divisions of condition and conditioned arising and so forth, that object of faith in whose excellent qualities, such as sublimity, the faculty of faith has become strong due to the excessive occurrence of conviction. For when the nature of things is grasped according to its true essence in this way, following the law of suchness, conviction does not become excessive, because the activity of wisdom is excessive in fully understanding, ‘This is the nature of these phenomena.’ For among the principal states, just as when faith is strong, wisdom is weak, so too when wisdom is strong, faith is weak. Therefore, it is said, ‘That should be diminished either by examining the nature of phenomena or by not attending to it in the way that made it strong.’ ‘By not attending to it’ means not continuously engaging in the development in the way that made the faculty of faith strong. Here, the strength of the faculty of faith arises in two ways: either through the excellence of its own specific conditions and the superiority of its function, or through the weak functioning of energy and the other faculties. In the first case, the method of diminishing has been shown. In the second case, however, when the faculty of faith has become strong due to the weak functioning of energy and the other faculties by attending in a certain way, it should be diminished by not attending in that way—that is, by attending in a way that brings about the keen functioning of energy and the other faculties, thereby making the faculty of faith equal in savor with them. By this method, the way of diminishing should be understood for the remaining faculties as well.

Vakkalittheravatthūti. So hi āyasmā saddhādhimuttatāya katādhikāro satthu rūpakāyadassanappasuto eva hutvā viharanto satthārā “kiṃ te vakkali iminā pūtikāyena diṭṭhena, yo kho vakkali dhammaṃ passati, so maṃ passatī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 3.87; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.208; dha. pa. aṭṭha. 2.380; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.2.130; dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1007; theragā. aṭṭha. 2.vakkalittheragāthāvaṇṇanā) ovaditvā kammaṭṭhāne niyojitopi taṃ ananuyuñjanto [P 2.0413] paṇāmito attānaṃ vinipātetuṃ papātaṭṭhānaṃ abhiruhi, atha naṃ satthā yathānisinnova obhāsaṃ vissajjanena attānaṃ dassetvā –

‘The story of the Elder Vakkali.’ For that venerable one, having made an aspiration due to his conviction in faith, dwelt constantly devoted to seeing the Teacher's physical body. The Teacher admonished him, saying, ‘What is there for you, Vakkali, in seeing this putrid body? For whoever, Vakkali, sees the Dhamma, sees me,’ and so forth. Although assigned a meditation subject, he did not apply himself to it, and having been dismissed, he climbed to a precipice to throw himself down. Then the Teacher, just as he was seated, showed himself by emitting a radiance—

“Pāmojjabahulo [V 2.0302] bhikkhu, pasanno buddhasāsane;

Adhigacche padaṃ santaṃ, saṅkhārūpasamaṃ sukha”nti. (dha. pa. 381) –

‘The monk, abounding in joy, with serene confidence in the Buddha's teaching, attains the peaceful state, the bliss of the stilling of all formations.’

Gāthaṃ vatvā “ehi vakkalī”ti āha. So tena amateneva abhisitto haṭṭhatuṭṭho hutvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Saddhāya balavabhāvato vipassanāvīthiṃ na otarati, taṃ ñatvā bhagavā tassa indriyasamattapaṭipādanāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ sodhetvā adāsi. So satthārā dinnanaye [M 2.0327] ṭhatvā vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā maggappaṭipāṭiyā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ “vakkalittheravatthu cettha nidassana”nti. Etthāti saddhindriyassa adhimattabhāve sesindriyānaṃ sakiccākaraṇe.

Having recited the verse, he said, ‘Come, Vakkali!’ Then, as if anointed with that nectar, he became joyful and delighted and began insight meditation. Due to the strength of faith, he did not enter the avenue of insight. Knowing this, the Blessed One clarified the meditation subject and gave it to him for the accomplishment of the balance of faculties. Standing firm in the method given by the Teacher, he diligently applied himself to insight and attained arahantship in due course of the path. Therefore, it is said, ‘Here, the story of Venerable Vakkali serves as an illustration.’ Here, this refers to the excessive nature of the faculty of faith and the non-performance of their functions by the remaining faculties.

Itarakiccabhedanti upaṭṭhānādikiccavisesaṃ. Passaddhādīti ādi-saddena samādhiupekkhāsambojjhaṅgānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Hāpetabbanti yathā saddhindriyassa balavabhāvo dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena hāyati, evaṃ vīriyindriyassa adhimattatā passaddhiādibhāvanāya hāyati samādhipakkhiyattā tassā. Tathā hi samādhindriyassa adhimattataṃ kosajjapātato rakkhantī vīriyādibhāvanā viya vīriyindriyassa adhimattataṃ uddhaccapātato rakkhantī ekaṃsato hāpeti. Tena vuttaṃ “passaddhaādibhāvanāya hāpetabba”nti. Soṇattherassa vatthūti sukumārasoṇattherassa vatthu. (Mahāva. 242; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.205) so hi āyasmā satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā sītavane viharanto “mama sarīraṃ sukhumālaṃ, na ca sakkā sukheneva sukhaṃ adhigantuṃ, kilametvāpi samaṇadhammo kātabbo”ti taṃ ṭhānacaṅkamameva adhiṭṭhāya padhānaṃ anuyuñjanto pādatalesu phoṭesu uṭṭhitesupi vedanaṃ ajjhupekkhitvā daḷhaṃ vīriyaṃ karonto accāraddhavīriyatāya visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhi. Satthā tattha gantvā vīṇūpamovādena [P 2.0414] ovaditvā vīriyasamatāyojanavīthiṃ dassento kammaṭṭhānaṃ sodhetvā gijjhakūṭaṃ gato. Theropi satthārā dinnanayena vīriyasamataṃ yojetvā bhāvento vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahatte patiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “soṇattherassa vatthu dassetabba”nti. Sesesupīti satisamādhipaññindriyesupi.

The differentiation of other functions refers to specific duties such as presence of mind, and so forth. ‘Passaddhādīti’—by the word ‘etcetera,’ the inclusion of the enlightenment factors of concentration and equanimity should be understood. ‘Hāpetabbaṃ’—just as the strength of the faculty of faith is diminished through reflection on the nature of phenomena, so too is the excessiveness of the faculty of energy diminished through the development of tranquility and so forth, because tranquility belongs to the side of concentration. For just as the development of energy and so forth protects the excessiveness of the faculty of concentration from falling into laziness, in the same way, the development of tranquility and so forth, protecting the excessiveness of the faculty of energy from falling into restlessness, decidedly diminishes it. Hence it is said, ‘It should be diminished through the development of tranquility, etc.’ ‘The story of Soṇa Thera’—this is the story of the delicate Soṇa Thera. He, the venerable one, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, dwelt in the Cool Grove, thinking, ‘My body is delicate, and it is not possible to attain happiness through happiness alone; even if it is exhausting, the ascetic's practice must be done.’ He resolved to practice walking meditation in that very spot and diligently applied himself to exertion. Though blisters arose on the soles of his feet, he endured the pain and exerted strong energy. However, due to excessive striving, he was unable to achieve any distinction. The Teacher went there and advised him with the simile of the lute, showing the path of balancing energy. After clarifying the meditation subject, he went to Vulture Peak. The elder, standing in the method given by the Teacher, applied balanced energy and, diligently developing insight, became established in arahantship. Hence it is said, ‘The story of Soṇa Thera should be shown.’ ‘In the remaining cases as well’—this applies also to the faculties of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

Samatanti saddhāpaññānaṃ aññamaññaṃ anūnānadhikabhāvaṃ, tathā samādhivīriyānaṃ. Yathā hi saddhāpaññānaṃ visuṃ visuṃ dhuriyadhammabhūtānaṃ kiccato aññamaññaṃ nātivattanaṃ visesato icchitabbaṃ, yato nesaṃ samadhuratāya appanā sampajjati, evaṃ samādhivīriyānaṃ kosajjuddhaccapakkhikānaṃ samarasatāya sati aññamaññūpatthambhanato sampayuttadhammānaṃ antadvayapātābhāvena sammadeva appanā ijjhati. “Balavasaddho”tiādi byatirekamukhena vuttasseva [V 2.0303] atthassa samatthanaṃ. Tassattho yo balavatiyā saddhāya samannāgato avisadañāṇo, so mudhappasanno hoti, na aveccappasanno. Tathā hi avatthusmiṃ pasīdati seyyathāpi titthiyasāvakā. Kerāṭikapakkhanti [M 2.0328] sāṭheyyapakkhaṃ bhajati. Saddhāhīnāya paññāya atidhāvanto “deyyavatthupariccāgena vinā cittuppādamattenapi dānamayaṃ puññaṃ hotī”tiādīni parikappeti hetupatirūpakehi vañcito, evaṃbhūto ca sukkhatakkaviluttacitto paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ nādiyati saññattiṃ na gacchati. Tenāha “bhesajjasamuṭṭhito viya rogo atekiccho hotī”ti. Yathā cettha saddhāpaññānaṃ aññamaññaṃ visamabhāvo na atthāvaho, anatthāvahova, evaṃ, samādhivīriyānaṃ aññamaññaṃ visamabhāvo na atthāvaho, anatthāvahova, tathā na avikkhepāvaho, vikkhepāvahovāti. Kosajjaṃ abhibhavati, tena appanaṃ na pāpuṇātīti adhippāyo. Uddhaccaṃ abhibhavatīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tadubhayanti saddhāpaññādvayaṃ, samādhivīriyadvayañca. Samaṃ kātabbanti samarasaṃ kātabbaṃ[P 2.0415].

'Balance' means the state of faith and wisdom not being deficient or excessive relative to each other, and similarly for concentration and energy. For just as it is especially desirable that faith and wisdom, being distinct leading states, do not surpass each other in function—since their balanced yoke leads to absorption—so too, concentration and energy, which belong to the party of laziness and restlessness, when they are of a single savor, then by their mutual support, the associated states avoid falling into either extreme, and absorption is properly achieved. 'One with strong faith,' etc., is a confirmation of the meaning stated by way of contrast. Its meaning is: one who is endowed with strong faith but whose knowledge is unclear becomes blindly devoted, not convinced through understanding. For such a one has serene confidence in what is not a proper object, just like the disciples of sectarians. 'Takes the side of deceit' means one resorts to the side of craftiness. One who runs ahead with wisdom deficient in faith, thinking, 'Merit consisting of giving arises even by a mere arising of thought without the relinquishing of an object to be given,' and so forth, is deceived by counterfeit reasons. Such a person, with a mind plundered by dry speculation, does not heed the words of the wise and fails to be instructed. Hence it is said, 'Like a disease arising from medicine, it becomes incurable.' Just as here an imbalance between faith and wisdom is not beneficial, but indeed harmful, so too an imbalance between concentration and energy is not beneficial, but indeed harmful, and likewise it does not lead to non-distraction, but to distraction. The meaning is that laziness overpowers, and thereby one does not attain absorption. The same method applies here too when restlessness overpowers. 'Both' refers to the pair of faith and wisdom, and the pair of concentration and energy. 'They should be made equal' means they should be made of equal savor.

Samādhikammikassāti samathakammaṭṭhānikassa. Evanti evaṃ sante, saddhāya thokaṃ balavabhāve satīti attho. Saddahantoti “pathavī pathavīti manasikaraṇamattena kathaṃ jhānuppattī”ti acintetvā “addhā sammāsambuddhena vuttavidhi ijjhissatī”ti saddahanto saddhaṃ janento. Okappentoti ārammaṇaṃ anupavisitvā viya adhimuccanavasena avakappento pakkhandanto. Ekaggatā balavatī vaṭṭati samādhippadhānattā jhānassa. Ubhinnanti samādhipaññānaṃ. Samādhikammikassa samādhino adhimattatāya paññāya adhimattatāpi icchitabbāti āha “samatāyapī”ti, samabhāvenāpīti attho. Appanāti lokiyappanā. Tathā hi “hotiyevā”ti sāsaṅkaṃ vadati. Lokuttarappanā pana tesaṃ samabhāveneva icchitā. Yathāha “samathavipassanaṃ yuganandhaṃ bhāvetī”ti (a. ni. 4.170; paṭi. ma. 2.5).

For one devoted to concentration work: one who is devoted to serenity practice. Thus: in this case, the meaning is, when faith is slightly stronger. One who believes: without pondering, 'How can absorption arise merely by attending to 'earth, earth'?'—instead, believing, 'Surely, the method taught by the Fully Enlightened One will succeed,' and thus generating faith. One who trusts: as if entering the object, deciding upon it with conviction, rushing towards it. Unification becomes strong because of the predominance of concentration in absorption. Of both: of concentration and wisdom. For one devoted to concentration work, since concentration is excessive, an excess of wisdom is also desired; thus it is said, 'also by balance,' meaning also by equality. Absorption: mundane absorption. Indeed, the statement 'it will indeed be' is made with hesitation. However, supramundane absorption is desired by them precisely in equality. As it is said: 'He develops serenity and insight yoked together' (A. Ni. 4.170; Paṭi. Ma. 2.5).

Yadi visesato saddhāpaññānaṃ, samādhivīriyānañca samatāva icchitā, kathaṃ satīti āha “sati pana sabbattha balavatī vaṭṭatī”ti. Sabbatthāti līnuddhaccapakkhikesu pañcasu indriyesu. Uddhaccapakkhikekadese gaṇhanto “saddhāvīriyapaññāna”nti āha. Aññathā pīti ca gahetabbā siyā. Tathā hi “kosajjapakkhikena samādhinā” icceva vuttaṃ, na “passaddhisamādhiupekkhāhī”ti. Sāti sati. Sabbesu rājakammesu niyutto sabbakammiko. Tenāti tena sabbattha icchitabbaṭṭhena kāraṇena. Āha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Sabbattha niyuttā sabbatthikā sabbattha līne, uddhate ca citte icchitabbattā, sabbe [M 2.0329] vā līne, uddhate ca citte bhāvetabbā bojjhaṅgā [V 2.0304] atthikā etāyāti sabbatthikā. Cittanti kusalaṃ cittaṃ. Tassa hi sati paṭisaraṇaṃ [P 2.0416] parāyaṇaṃ appattassa pattiyā anadhigatassa adhigamāya. Tenāha “ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā”tiādi.

If balance of faith and wisdom, and of concentration and energy, is particularly desired, how is mindfulness explained? It is said, 'Mindfulness, however, is always strong and functions everywhere.' 'Everywhere' refers to the five faculties when they are inclined toward sloth or restlessness. When singling out the aspect of restlessness, it mentions 'faith, energy, and wisdom.' Otherwise, joy should also be included. For it is said, 'with concentration inclined toward laziness,' but not 'tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.' Sati means mindfulness. Like a servant engaged in all royal duties, doing all tasks. Therefore, for that reason, because it is desired everywhere. The commentary says: 'Engaged everywhere, 'everywhere-needed,' because it is desired wherever the mind is sluggish or restless, or because all the enlightenment factors to be developed are needed by this mindfulness wherever the mind is sluggish or restless, thus, it is 'everywhere-needed.'' 'Mind' refers to the wholesome mind. For it, mindfulness is the refuge, the ultimate resort—for attaining the unattained and realizing the unrealized. Hence, it is said, 'Its characteristic is guarding,' and so on.

Khandhādibhede anogāḷhapaññānanti pariyattibāhusaccavasenapi khandhāyatanādīsu appatiṭṭhitabuddhīnaṃ. Bahussutasevanā hi sutamayañāṇāvahā. Taruṇavipassanāsamaṅgīpi bhāvanāmayañāṇe ṭhitattā ekaṃsato paññavā eva nāma hotīti āha “samapaññāsa lakkhaṇapariggāhikāya udayabbayapaññāya samannāgatapuggalasevanā”ti. Ñeyyadhammassa gambhīrabhāvavasena tapparicchedakañāṇassa gambhīrabhāvaggahaṇanti āha “gambhīresu khandhādīsu pavattāya gambhīrapaññāyā”ti. Tañhi ñeyyaṃ tādisāya paññāya caritabbato gambhīrañāṇacariyaṃ, tassā vā paññāya tattha pabhedato pavatti gambhīrañāṇacariyā, tassā paccavekkhaṇāti āha “gambhīrapaññāya pabhedapaccavekkhaṇā”ti. Yathā sativepullappatto nāma arahā eva, evaṃ paññāvepullappattotipi so evāti āha “arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūrī hotī”ti. Vīriyādīsupi eseva nayo.

'Of those with wisdom not immersed in the divisions of aggregates, etc.': even for those whose understanding is not firmly established in the aggregates, sense bases, etc., despite extensive learning. For associating with the learned indeed brings about knowledge born of hearing. Even one endowed with recent insight is called 'possessing wisdom in one aspect' because they are established in knowledge born of development. Thus it is said: 'By associating with a person endowed with the wisdom of rise and fall, which comprehends fifty characteristics equally.' Due to the profundity of the knowable phenomena, the wisdom that discerns them is also profound. Thus it is said: 'The wisdom that operates in the profound aggregates, etc., is profound wisdom.' For that knowable must be approached by such wisdom, hence it is the practice of profound knowledge. Or, the unfolding of that wisdom there in various ways is the practice of profound knowledge. Reflecting upon it is called 'the analysis and review of profound wisdom.' Just as one who has attained fullness of mindfulness is called an arahant, so too is one who has attained fullness of wisdom—indeed, that very one. Thus it is said: 'Through the path of arahantship, the perfection of development is achieved.' The same applies to energy, etc.

“Tattaṃ ayokhilaṃ hatthe gamentī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 3.250, 267; a. ni. 3.36) vuttapañcavidhabandhanakammakāraṇā niraye nibbattasattassa yebhuyyena sabbapaṭhamaṃ karontīti, devadūtasuttādīsu tassa ādito vuttattā ca āha “pañcavidhabandhanakammakāraṇato paṭṭhāyā”ti. Sakaṭavahanādikāleti ādi-saddena tadaññamanussehi, tiracchānehi ca vibādhiyamānakālaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. “Ekaṃ buddhantara”nti idaṃ aparāparaṃ petesu eva uppajjanakasattavasena vuttaṃ, ekaccānaṃ vā petānaṃ ekaccatiracchānānaṃ [P 2.0417] viya tathā dīghāyukatāpi siyāti tathā vuttaṃ. Tathā hi “kālo nāgarājā catunnaṃ buddhānaṃ sammukhībhāvaṃ labhitvā ṭhito metteyyassapi bhagavato sammukhībhāvaṃ labhissatī”ti vadanti, yaṃ tassa kappāyukatā vuttā.

By 'Like carrying a red-hot iron ball in the hand,' and so forth (MN 3.250, 267; AN 3.36), is meant the fivefold binding punishment, which they generally inflict first on a being reborn in hell. Since this is stated from the beginning in the Devadūta Sutta and others, it is said, 'starting from the fivefold binding punishment.' The phrase 'at the time of pulling a cart, etc.' includes, by the word 'etc.,' the time when they are harassed by other humans and animals. 'One buddhantara' refers here to beings arising again and again among the departed spirits. Or it could be that some departed spirits, like some animals, have such long lifespans; thus it is said. Indeed, they say, 'The nāga king Kālo, having met four Buddhas, will also meet the Blessed One Metteyya'—for it is said that his lifespan is a kappa.

Ānisaṃsadassāvinoti “vīriyāyatto eva sabbo lokuttaro, lokiyo ca visesādhigamo”ti evaṃ vīriye ānisaṃsadassanasīlassa. Gamanavīthinti sapubbabhāgaṃ nibbānagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ, saha vipassanāya ariyamaggapaṭipāṭi[M 2.0330], sattavisuddhiparamparā vā. Sā hi bhikkhuno vaṭṭaniyyānāya gantabbā paṭipadāti katvā gamanavīthi nāma. Kāyadaḷhībahuloti yathā tathā kāyassa daḷhīkammappasuto. Piṇḍanti raṭṭhapiṇḍaṃ. Paccayadāyakānaṃ attani kārassa attano [V 2.0305] sammāpaṭipattiyā mahapphalabhāvassa karaṇena piṇḍassa bhikkhāya paṭipūjanā piṇḍāpacāyanaṃ.

One who sees the benefit: one who habitually sees the benefit of effort, thinking, 'All supramundane and mundane special attainments are dependent on effort.' The path of progress refers to the path leading to Nibbāna together with its preliminary part, the sequence of the noble path together with insight, or the succession of the seven purifications. For a monk, this is the path to be taken to escape the round of existence, hence it is called the path of progress. One who is much given to strengthening the body: one who is devoted to strengthening the body however possible. Almsfood refers to the alms of the country. Honoring the almsfood means repaying the alms by making the service done by the donors of requisites be of great fruit through one's own right practice.

Nīharantoti pattathavikato nīharanto. Taṃ saddaṃ sutvāti taṃ upāsikāya vacanaṃ attano vasanapaṇṇasāladvāre ṭhitova pañcābhiññatāya dibbasotena sutvā. Manussasampatti, dibbasampatti, nibbānasampattīti imā tisso sampattiyo. Dātuṃ sakkhissasīti “tayi katena dānamayena, veyyāvaccamayena ca puññakammena khettavisesabhāvūpagamanena aparāparaṃ devamanussasampattiyo, ante nibbānasampattiñca dātuṃ sakkhissasī”ti thero attānaṃ pucchati. Sitaṃ karonto vāti “akiccheneva mayā vaṭṭadukkhaṃ samatikkanta”nti paccavekkhaṇāvasāne sañjātapāmojjavasena sitaṃ karonto eva.

He removes: meaning he removes it from the bowl-bag. Having heard that sound: hearing the laywoman’s words while standing at the door of his own leaf-hut, with the divine ear of the five higher knowledges. Human success, divine success, and the success of Nibbāna: these are the three successes. 'Will you be able to give?': the elder asks himself, 'Through the merit of giving and service done by you, by becoming a special field of merit, will you be able to grant again and again divine and human successes, and ultimately the success of Nibbāna?' Making a smile: at the conclusion of reflection, 'I have effortlessly crossed over the suffering of the round,' he makes a smile out of the joy that arises.

Vippaṭipannanti jātidhammakuladhammādilaṅghanena asammāpaṭipannaṃ. Evaṃ yathā asammāpaṭipanno putto tāya eva asammāpaṭipattiyā kulasantānato bāhiro hutvā pitu santikā dāyajjassa na bhāgī, evaṃ. Kusītopi tena kusītabhāvena asammāpaṭipanno [P 2.0418] satthu santikā laddhabbaariyadhanadāyajjassa na bhāgī. Āraddhavīriyova labhati sammāpaṭipajjanato. Uppajjati vīriyasambojjhaṅgoti yojanā, evaṃ sabbattha.

One who has gone astray: one who is not practicing rightly by transgressing the duties of birth, family customs, and so on. Just as a son who has gone astray, due to that very wrong practice, becomes an outsider to the family lineage and does not receive a share of the inheritance from his father, so too, the lazy one, due to that laziness, is not practicing rightly and does not receive a share of the noble wealth of inheritance to be obtained from the Teacher. Only one who has aroused energy attains it, by practicing rightly. The connection is: the energy awakening factor arises—this applies everywhere.

Mahāti sīlādīhi guṇehi mahanto vipulo anaññasādhāraṇo. Taṃ panassa guṇamahattaṃ dasasahassilokadhātukampanena loke pākaṭanti dassento “satthuno hī”tiādimāha.

Great: great with virtues such as morality, vast and incomparable. And to show that his greatness of virtue was made manifest in the world by the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world-system, he said, 'of the Teacher,' and so on.

Yasmā satthusāsane pabbajitassa pabbajjūpagamena sakyaputtassabhāvo sampajāyati, tasmā buddhaputtabhāvaṃ dassento “asambhinnāyā”tiādimāha.

Since the state of being a son of the Sakyan arises for one who has gone forth by the going forth in the Teacher’s dispensation, therefore, to show the state of being a son of the Buddha, he said, 'Unbroken,' and so on.

Alasānaṃ bhāvanāya nāmamattampi ajānantānaṃ kāyadaḷhībahulānaṃ yāvadatthaṃ bhuñjitvā seyyasukhādianuyuñjanakānaṃ tiracchānakathikānaṃ puggalānaṃ dūrato vajjanā kusītapuggalaparivajjanā. “Divasaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāyā”tiādinā [M 2.0331] (ma. ni. 1.423; 3.65; saṃ. ni. 4.120; mahāni. 161) bhāvanāraddhavasena āraddhavīriyānaṃ daḷhaparakkamānaṃ kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamanā āraddhavīriyapuggalasevanā. Tenāha “kucchiṃ pūretvā”tiādi. Visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.64) pana jātimahattapaccavekkhaṇā, sabrahmacārīmahattapaccavekkhaṇāti idaṃ dvayaṃ na gahitaṃ, thinamiddhavinodanatā, sammappadhānapaccavekkhaṇatāti [V 2.0306] idaṃ dvayaṃ gahitaṃ. Tattha ānisaṃsadassāvitāya eva sammappadhānapaccavekkhaṇā gahitā hoti lokiyalokuttaravisesādhigamassa vīriyāyattatādassanabhāvato. Thinamiddhavinodanaṃ tadadhimuttatāya eva gahitaṃ hoti, vīriyuppādane yuttappayuttassa thinamiddhavinodanaṃ atthasiddhameva. Tattha thinamiddhavinodanakusītapuggalaparivajjanaāraddhavīriyapuggalasevana- tadadhimuttatāpaṭipakkhavidhamanapaccayūpasaṃhāravasena, apāyabhayapaccavekkhaṇādayo samuttejanavasena vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa uppādakā daṭṭhabbā.

The avoidance of lazy individuals is the avoidance from afar of persons who do not know even the name of meditation, who are physically robust, who eat to their fill and are devoted to the pleasures of sleep and idle talk. By 'spending the day in walking and sitting meditation,' etc., is meant the association with energetic individuals: approaching from time to time those who are diligent in their practice, who have aroused energy and exert strong effort. Therefore, it is said, 'having filled the belly,' etc. In the Visuddhimagga, however, reflection on the greatness of birth and reflection on the greatness of fellow monastics—these two are not included. But dispelling sloth and torpor and reflection on the right exertions—these two are included. There, reflection on the right exertions is included because it shows the benefits, as it demonstrates that the attainment of both mundane and supramundane distinctions depends on energy. Dispelling sloth and torpor is included because of the inclination toward that; for one who is properly engaged in arousing energy, the dispelling of sloth and torpor is indeed accomplished. In this context, dispelling sloth and torpor, avoiding lazy individuals, associating with the diligent, and being inclined toward that should be seen as arousing the enlightenment factor of energy by way of applying antidotes and removing unfavorable conditions. Reflections such as the fear of the lower realms, etc., should be seen as arousing the energy enlightenment factor by way of inspiration.

Purimuppannā [P 2.0419] pīti parato uppajjanakapītiyā visesakāraṇasabhāgahetubhāvato “pītiyeva pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā”ti vuttā, tassā pana bahuso pavattiyā puthuttaṃ upādāya bahuvacananiddeso. Yathā sā uppajjati, evaṃ paṭipatti tassā uppādakamanasikāro.

The joy that arose previously is said to be ‘the states that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of joy are joy itself,’ because it is a homogeneous cause for the specific cause of the joy that arises later. However, due to its frequent occurrence, taking its multiplicity, the plural is used. Just as that joy arises, so is the practice, the attention that produces it.
