“Buddhānussatī”tiādīsu vattabbaṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.123) vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

What is to be said regarding ‘recollection of the Buddha,’ etc., should be understood in the same way as explained in the Visuddhimagga.

Buddhānussatiyā upacārasamādhiniṭṭhattā vuttaṃ “yāva upacārā”ti. Sakalasarīraṃ pharamānoti pītisamuṭṭhānehi paṇītarūpehi sakalasarīraṃ pharamāno. Dhammaguṇe anussarantassāpi yāva upacārā sakalasarīraṃ pharamāno pītisambojjhaṅgo uppajjatīti yojanā, evaṃ sesaanussatīsu. Pasādanīyasuttantapaccavekkhaṇāyañca yojetabbaṃ tassāpi vimuttāyatanabhāvena taggatikattā. Saṅkhārānaṃ sappadesavūpasamepi nippadesavūpasame viya tathā paññāya pavattito bhāvanāmanasikāro kilesavikkhambhanasamattho hutvā upacārasamādhiṃ āvahanto tathārūpapītisomanassasamannāgato pītisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya hotīti āha “samāpattiyā…pe… paccavekkhantassāpī”ti. Tattha “vikkhambhitā kilesā”ti pāṭho. Te hi na samudācarantīti. Iti-saddo kāraṇattho, yasmā na samudācaranti, tasmā taṃ nesaṃ asamudācāraṃ paccavekkhantassāti yojanā[M 2.0332]. Na hi kilese paccavekkhantassa bojjhaṅguppatti yuttā. Pasādanīyesu ṭhānesu pasādasinehābhāvena thūsasamahadayatā lūkhatā, sā tattha ādaragāravākaraṇena viññāyatīti āha “asakkaccakiriyāya saṃsūcitalūkhabhāve”ti.

Because it is established in access concentration through the recollection of the Buddha, it is said, ‘up to access.’ ‘Permeating the entire body’ means permeating the entire body with refined forms arisen from joy. Even for one recollecting the qualities of the Dhamma, the enlightenment factor of joy arises permeating the entire body up to access concentration—this is the connection. The same applies to the other recollections. And it should also be connected to the reflection on a sutta that inspires confidence, for that too, due to its nature as a basis for liberation, is of that same nature. Even in the calming of formations with a basis, just as in the calming without a basis, the mental application of development, proceeding thus by wisdom, being capable of suppressing defilements, bringing forth access concentration, accompanied by such joy and gladness, becomes a condition for the arising of the enlightenment factor of joy. Hence it is said, ‘in attainment…and even while reviewing.’ Here, the reading is ‘defilements are suppressed.’ For they do not arise. The word ‘iti’ indicates reason: because they do not arise, therefore, for one reviewing their non-arising—this is the connection. Indeed, the arising of the enlightenment factors is not fitting for one who is reviewing defilements. In inspiring situations, the absence of inspiration and affection results in a coarse and dull heart; that is known there through not acting with care and respect—hence it is said, ‘in the state of coarseness indicated by careless action.’

Kāyacittadarathavūpasamalakkhaṇā passaddhi eva yathāvuttabodhiaṅgabhūto passaddhisambojjhaṅgo, tassa passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa evaṃ uppādo hotīti yojanā.

Tranquility, whose characteristic is the calming of bodily and mental agitation, is itself the tranquility enlightenment factor, which is a factor of awakening as stated. The connection is that the arising of that tranquility enlightenment factor occurs thus.

Paṇītabhojanasevanatāti [V 2.0307] paṇītasappāyabhojanaseva natā[P 2.0420]. Utuiriyāpathasukhaggahaṇena sappāyautuiriyāpathaggahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tañhi tividhampi sappāyaṃ seviyamānaṃ kāyassa kallatāpādanavasena cittassa kallataṃ āvahantaṃ duvidhāyapi passaddhiyā kāraṇaṃ hoti. Ahetukaṃ sattesu labbhamānaṃ sukhadukkhanti ayameko anto, issarādivisamahetukanti pana ayaṃ dutiyo. Ete ubho ante anupagamma yathāsakaṃ kammunā hotīti ayaṃ majjhimā paṭipatti. Majjhatto payogo yassa so majjhattapayogo, tassa bhāvo majjhattapayogatā. Ayañhi pahāya sāraddhakāyataṃ passaddhakāyatāya kāraṇaṃ hontī passaddhidvayaṃ āvahati, eteneva sāraddhakāyapuggalaparivajjanapassaddhakāyapuggalasevanānaṃ tadāvahanatā saṃvaṇṇitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

‘The partaking of excellent food’ means the partaking of excellent and suitable food. By 'the taking of pleasant weather and posture' is to be understood the taking of suitable weather and posture. For when this threefold suitability is partaken of, it brings about mental fitness by making the body fit, thus becoming a cause for twofold tranquility. ‘Pleasure and pain arising in beings without a cause’—this is one extreme. ‘And from unequal causes such as a creator, etc.’—this is the second. Avoiding both these extremes, ‘it occurs according to one’s own kamma’—this is the Middle Path. One whose application is balanced has balanced application; the state of that is balanced application. For this, by abandoning bodily rigidity, becomes a cause for bodily tranquility and brings about twofold tranquility. By this, it should be understood that the avoidance of persons with rigid bodies and the association with persons with tranquil bodies are described as bringing about that tranquility.

Yathāsamāhitākārasallakkhaṇavasena gayhamāno purimuppanno samatho eva samathanimittaṃ. Nānārammaṇe paribbhamanena vividhaṃ aggaṃ etassāti byaggo, vikkhepo. Tathā hi so anavaṭṭhānaraso, bhantatāpaccupaṭṭhāno ca vutto, ekaggatābhāvato byaggapaṭipakkhoti abyaggo, samādhi. So eva nimittanti pubbe viya vattabbaṃ. Tenāha “avikkhepaṭṭhena ca abyagganimitta”nti.

The previously arisen tranquility, when grasped by way of discerning its characteristic of being composed, is itself the sign of tranquility. Wandering among various objects, having diversity as its chief quality—this is ‘byagga’ (distracted), which is distraction. For it has been said that its characteristic is instability, and its manifestation is agitation. The opposite of distraction is `abyagga` (undistracted), which is concentration, due to its nature of one-pointedness. That itself is the sign, as should be stated as before. Therefore, he said: ‘and by way of non-distraction, it is the sign of non-distraction.’

Vatthuvisadakiriyā, indriyasamattapaṭipādanā ca paññāvahā vuttā, samādhānāvahāpi tā honti samādhānāvahabhāveneva paññāvahabhāvatoti vuttaṃ “vatthuvisada…pe… veditabbā”ti.

The clarification of the object and the balanced application of the faculties are said to bring wisdom. They also bring concentration, for by their very nature of bringing concentration, they also bring wisdom. Thus it is said: ‘The clarification of the object… should be understood.’

Karaṇabhāvanākosallānaṃ avinābhāvato, rakkhanakosallassa ca taṃmūlakattā “nimittakusalatā nāma kasiṇanimittassa uggahaṇakusalatā” [M 2.0333] icceva vuttaṃ. Kasiṇanimittassāti ca nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Asubhanimittassāpi hi yassa kassaci jhānuppattinimittassa uggahaṇakosallaṃ nimittakusalatā evāti. Atisithilavīriyatādīhīti ādi-saddena paññāpayogamandataṃ[P 2.0421], pamodavekallañca saṅgaṇhāti. Tassa paggaṇhananti tassa līnassa cittassa dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādisamuṭṭhāpanena layāpattito samuddharaṇaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Since skill in developing and skill in guarding are inseparable, and since the latter is rooted in the former, it is said: ‘Skill in the sign is skill in apprehending the kasiṇa sign.’ And ‘the kasiṇa sign’ should be understood as merely an example. For indeed, skill in apprehending the sign—whether it be the sign of foulness or any other sign leading to the arising of jhāna—is called ‘skill in the sign.’ By ‘excessive slackness of energy, etc.,’ the word ‘etc.’ includes dullness in the application of wisdom and lack of joy. ‘Lifting it up’ means rescuing that sluggish mind from sinking by arousing the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor and so on. For this was said by the Blessed One—

“Yasmiñca kho, bhikkhave, samaye līnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, kālo tasmiṃ samaye dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo pītisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Līnaṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ taṃ etehi dhammehi susamuṭṭhāpayaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso parittaṃ aggiṃ ujjālitukāmo assa, so tattha sukkhāni ceva tiṇāni pakkhipeyya, sukkhāni gomayāni [V 2.0308] pakkhipeyya, sukkhāni kaṭṭhāni pakkhipeyya, mukhavātañca dadeyya, na ca paṃsukena okireyya, bhabbo nu kho so puriso parittaṃ aggiṃ ujjālitunti. Evaṃ bhante”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234).

“Monks, at the time when the mind is sluggish, that is the time to cultivate the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, the time to cultivate the enlightenment factor of energy, the time to cultivate the enlightenment factor of rapture. Why is that? A sluggish mind, monks, is easily roused up by these things. Suppose, monks, a man wanted to ignite a small fire. He would place dry grass there, dry cow dung, and dry sticks, blow on it with his mouth, and not sprinkle it with dust. Would that man be able to ignite a small fire?” “Yes, venerable sir.” (Saṃ. Ni. 5.234)

Ettha ca yathāsakaṃ āhāravasena dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādīnaṃ bhāvanāsamuṭṭhāpanāti veditabbā, sā anantaraṃ vibhāvitā eva. Āraddhavīriyatādīhīti ādi-saddena paññāpayogabalavataṃ, pamodubbilāvanañca saṅgaṇhāti. Tassa niggaṇhananti tassa uddhatassa cittassa samādhisambojjhaṅgādisamuṭṭhāpanena uddhatāpattito nisedhanaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā –

Here, it should be understood that the cultivation and arising of the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor and others occurs according to their respective supports, as was explained immediately before. By ‘with aroused energy and so on,’ the word ‘and so on’ includes the strength of the application of wisdom and elation. ‘To restrain it’ means preventing that agitated mind from falling into agitation by arousing the concentration enlightenment factor and others. And this was also stated by the Blessed One—

“Yasmiñca kho, bhikkhave, samaye uddhataṃ cittaṃ hoti, kālo tasmiṃ samaye passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo samādhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Uddhataṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ taṃ etehi dhammehi suvūpasamayaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ nibbāpetukāmo assa, so tattha allāni [P 2.0422] ceva tiṇāni…pe… paṃsukena ca okireyya, bhabbo nu kho so puriso mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ nibbāpetunti. Evaṃ bhante”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234).

“Monks, when the mind is agitated, that is the time to cultivate the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity. Why is that? Because an agitated mind, monks, is easily calmed by these states. Suppose, monks, a man wanted to extinguish a great mass of fire. He would throw wet grass on it… and sprinkle it with dust—would that man be able to extinguish the great mass of fire?” “Yes, venerable sir.” (Saṃ. Ni. 5.234)

Etthāpi [M 2.0334] yathāsakaṃ āhāravasena passaddhisambojjhaṅgādīnaṃ bhāvanāsamuṭṭhāpanāti veditabbā, tattha passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanā vuttā eva. Samādhisambojjhaṅgassa anantaraṃ vakkhati. Paññāpayogamandatāyāti paññābyāpārassa appabhāvena. Yathā hi dānaṃ alobhapadhānaṃ, sīlaṃ adosapadhānaṃ, evaṃ bhāvanā amohapadhānā. Tattha yadā paññā na balavatī hoti, tadā bhāvanā pubbenāparaṃ visesāvahā na hoti, anabhisaṅkhato viya āhāro purisassa yogino cittassa abhiruciṃ na janeti, tena taṃ nirassādaṃ hoti, tathā bhāvanāya sammadeva avīthipaṭipattiyā upasamasukhaṃ na vindati, tenāpi cittaṃ nirassādaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “paññāpayoga…pe… nirassādaṃ hotī”ti. Tassa saṃveguppādanaṃ, pasāduppādanañca tikicchananti taṃ dassento “aṭṭha saṃvegavatthūnī”tiādimāha. Tattha jātijarābyādhimaraṇāni yathārahaṃ sugatiyaṃ, duggatiyañca hontīti tadaññameva pañcavidhabandhanādikhuppipāsādi aññamaññaṃ vibādhanādihetukaṃ apāyadukkhaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, tayidaṃ sabbaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ paccuppannabhavanissitaṃ gahitanti atīte anāgate ca kāle vaṭṭamūlakadukkhāni visuṃ gahitāni. Ye pana sattā āhārūpajīvino, tattha ca uṭṭhānaphalūpajīvino, tesaṃ aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ [V 2.0309] jīvikādukkhaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ saṃvegavatthu gahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati samaye sampahaṃsanāti ayaṃ bhāvanācittassa sampahaṃsitabbasamaye vuttanayena saṃvegajananavasena ceva pasāduppādanavasena ca sammadeva pahaṃsanā, saṃvegajananapubbakapasāduppādanena tosanāti [P 2.0423] attho.

Here too, the development and arising of the enlightenment factors such as tranquility should be understood according to their respective nutriments. In this context, the development of the tranquility enlightenment factor has already been explained. The concentration enlightenment factor will be discussed next. Due to weakness in the application of wisdom—that is, due to the weakness of the activity of wisdom—just as generosity is rooted in non-greed, and virtue in non-hatred, so too is development rooted in non-delusion. When wisdom is not strong, development does not bring successive distinctions; like unseasoned food that fails to delight the mind of a meditator, it becomes joyless. Similarly, through improper practice of development, one does not find the bliss of peace, and so the mind remains joyless. Hence it is said, 'Due to weakness in the application of wisdom... it becomes joyless.' To show that generating a sense of urgency and generating confidence are the remedies for this, the text states, 'The eight grounds for urgency,' etc. Here, birth, aging, sickness, and death occur as appropriate in both good and bad destinies; distinct from these, the suffering of the lower realms—caused by the fivefold bondage, hunger, thirst, and other mutual afflictions—should be understood. All this is taken as dependent on the present existence of those beings, while sufferings rooted in the cycle of rebirth in the past and future are taken separately. As for beings who live by food and depend on the fruits of their efforts, their unique suffering of livelihood is to be understood as the eighth ground for urgency. This is called 'gladdening at the proper time.' This means the proper gladdening of the mind in development at the time it should be gladdened—in the way described, by means of generating a sense of urgency and by means of generating confidence. The meaning is that it is satisfied by the generation of confidence preceded by the generation of urgency.

Sammāpaṭipattiṃ āgammāti līnuddhaccavirahena, samathavīthipaṭipattiyā ca sammā avisamaṃ sammadeva bhāvanāpaṭipattiṃ āgamma. “Alīna”ntiādīsu kosajjapakkhikānaṃ dhammānaṃ anadhimattatāya alīnaṃ, uddhaccapakkhikānaṃ anadhimattatāya anuddhataṃ, paññāpayogasampattiyā, upasamasukhādhigamena ca anirassādaṃ, tato eva ārammaṇe samappavattaṃ samathavīthipaṭipannaṃ. Tattha alīnatāya paggahe, anuddhatatāya niggahe, anirassādatāya sampahaṃsane na byāpāraṃ āpajjati. Alīnānuddhatatā hi ārammaṇe samappavattaṃ, anirassādatāya samathavīthipaṭipannaṃ, samappavattiyā vā alīnaṃ anuddhataṃ. Samathavīthipaṭipattiyā anirassādanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati samaye ajjhupekkhanatāti ayaṃ ajjhupekkhitabbasamaye bhāvanācittassa paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu abyāvaṭatāsaṅkhātaṃ [M 2.0335] paṭipakkhaṃ abhibhuyya pekkhanā vuccati. Paṭipakkhavikkhambhanato, vipassanāya adhiṭṭhānabhāvūpagamanato ca upacārajjhānampi samādhāna kiccanipphattiyā puggalassa samāhitabhāvasādhanaṃ evāti tattha samadhurabhāvenāha “upacāraṃ vā appanaṃ vā”ti.

‘Having entered upon right practice’ means having entered upon the practice of development rightly, without unevenness, and properly, through the absence of sluggishness and restlessness, and by the path of tranquility. In the phrase ‘not sluggish,’ etc., one is not sluggish because the qualities on the side of laziness are not excessive; one is not restless because the qualities on the side of restlessness are not excessive. By the accomplishment of the application of wisdom and by the attainment of the bliss of peace, one is not joyless. Thus, proceeding evenly towards the object, one has entered upon the path of tranquility. Therein, one does not need to be occupied with exertion because of non-sluggishness, with restraint because of non-restlessness, or with gladdening because of non-joylessness. For non-sluggishness and non-restlessness mean proceeding evenly towards the object, and non-joylessness means having entered upon the path of tranquility. Alternatively, proceeding evenly means being neither sluggish nor restless. It should be understood that by the path of tranquility, one is not joyless. This is called ‘equanimity at the proper time.’ This means the act of looking on at the proper time for equanimity, which is characterized by the mind in development not being occupied with exertion, restraint, or gladdening, having overcome the opposing factors. And because of the suppression of opposing factors and its becoming a basis for insight, even access concentration is indeed a means of establishing a person as concentrated through the accomplishment of the task of concentration. Therefore, with an even balance, it is said: ‘access or absorption.’

Upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammāti ettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayānusārena veditabbaṃ. Anurodhavirodhavippahānavasena majjhattabhāvo upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa kāraṇaṃ tasmiṃ sati sijjhanato, asati ca asijjhanato. So ca majjhattabhāvo visayavasena duvidhoti āha “sattamajjhattatā saṅkhāramajjhattatā”ti. Tadubhaye ca virujjhanaṃ passaddhisambojjhaṅgabhāvanāya eva dūrīkatanti anurujjhanasseva pahānavidhiṃ dassetuṃ “sattamajjhattatā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tenāha “sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggalaparivajjanatā”ti. Upekkhāya hi visesato rāgo paṭipakkho. Tathā cāha “upekkhā rāgabahulassa [P 2.0424] visuddhimaggo”ti (visuddhi. 1.267). Dvīhākārehīti kammassakatāpaccavekkhaṇaṃ, attasuññatāpaccavekkhaṇanti imehi dvīhi kāraṇehi. Dvīhevāti avadhāraṇaṃ saṅkhyāsamānatādassanatthaṃ. Saṅkhyā evettha samānā, na saṅkhyeyyaṃ sabbathā samānanti. Assāmikabhāvo anattaniyatā. Sati hi attani tassa kiñcanabhāvena cīvaraṃ, aññaṃ vā kiñci attaniyaṃ nāma siyā, so pana koci natthevāti adhippāyo. Anaddhaniyanti na addhānakkhamaṃ na ciraṭṭhāyi, ittaraṃ aniccanti attho. Tāvakālikanti tasseva vevacanaṃ.

Regarding the factors conducive to the equanimity enlightenment factor, what should be said here is to be understood according to the method stated earlier. The state of neutrality by abandoning attraction and repulsion is the cause of the equanimity enlightenment factor; when that is present, it succeeds, and when absent, it does not succeed. That state of neutrality is twofold by way of object, as stated: ‘neutrality toward beings and neutrality toward formations.’ And the opposition of both of these is removed by the development of the tranquility enlightenment factor. Thus, to show the method of abandoning only adherence, it is said: ‘neutrality toward beings,’ etc. Therefore, it is said: ‘avoiding persons who delight in beings and formations.’ For lust is especially the opposite of equanimity. As it is said: ‘equanimity is the path of purification for one full of lust’ (Visuddhimagga 1.267). ‘In two ways’ refers to these two reasons: reflecting on ownership of deeds and reflecting on selflessness. The emphasis ‘only two’ is to show equality in number. Here, the number is equal, but the countable is not entirely equal in every way. ‘Ownerless’ means not belonging to a self. For if there were a self, something like a robe or anything else would belong to it, but there is no such thing—this is the meaning. ‘Not lasting long’ means not enduring for a long time, not permanent, that is, impermanent—this is the meaning. ‘Temporary’ is a synonym for that.

Mamāyatīti mamattaṃ karoti “mamā”ti taṇhāya pariggayha tiṭṭhati.

‘He makes it mine’ means he makes it his own; he stands grasping it with craving, thinking ‘mine.’

Mamāyantāti [V 2.0310] mānaṃ dabbaṃ karontā.

‘They make it mine’ means they make pride their possession.

Ayaṃ satipaṭṭhānadesanā pubbabhāgamaggavasena desitāti pubbabhāgiyabojjhaṅge sandhāyāha “bojjhaṅgapariggāhikā sati dukkhasacca”nti. Sesaṃ vuttanayattā suviññeyyameva.

This discourse on the establishments of mindfulness is taught in the manner of the preliminary part of the path. Referring to the enlightenment factors that are a preliminary part, he said: ‘Mindfulness that encompasses the enlightenment factors is the truth of suffering.’ The rest is easily understood according to the method stated.

Bojjhaṅgapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on the Enlightenment Factors is concluded.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Recitation Section is concluded.

Catusaccapabbavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Chapter on the Four Truths

386. Yathāsabhāvatoti [M 2.0336] aviparītasabhāvato. Bādhanakkhaṇato yo yo vā sabhāvo yathāsabhāvo, tato, ruppanādi kakkhaḷādisabhāvatoti attho. Janikaṃ samuṭṭhāpikanti pavattalakkhaṇassa dukkhassa janikaṃ nimittalakkhaṇassa samuṭṭhāpikaṃ. Purimataṇhanti yathāpariggahitassa dukkhassa nibbattito puretaraṃ siddhaṃ taṇhaṃ. Siddhe hi kāraṇe tassa phaluppatti. Ayaṃ dukkhasamudayoti pajānātīti yojanā. Ayaṃ dukkhanirodhoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Ubhinnaṃ appavattinti dukkhaṃ, samudayo cāti dvinnaṃ appavattinimittaṃ, tadubhayaṃ na pavatti etāyāti appavatti, asaṅkhatā dhātu. Dukkhaṃ dukkhasaccaṃ [P 2.0425] parijānāti pariññābhisamayavasena paricchindatīti dukkhaparijānano, ariyamaggo, taṃ dukkhaparijānanaṃ. Sesapadadvayepi iminā nayena attho veditabbo.

386. ‘According to its own nature’ means according to its undistorted nature. Whatever nature there is from the characteristic of oppression, that is its own nature; hence, the meaning is from the nature of being afflicted, hardness, and so forth. ‘Generative and productive’ means generative of suffering characterized by occurrence, and productive of that which is characterized as a cause. ‘Former craving’ means the craving established earlier than the arising of suffering as it is grasped. For when the cause is established, its fruit arises. The connection is: ‘He understands: “This is the origin of suffering.”’ Here too, in ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ this is the same method. ‘Non-occurrence of both’ means the condition for the non-occurrence of the two, that is, suffering and its origin; that by which both do not occur is non-occurrence, the unconditioned element. He fully knows suffering, that is, he comprehends the truth of suffering by way of the penetration of full understanding; the one who fully knows suffering is the Noble Path, that is the full knowing of suffering. The meaning in the remaining two phrases should also be understood by this method.

Dukkhasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of Suffering

388. Evaṃ vuttāti evaṃ uddesavasena vuttā. Sabbasattānaṃ pariyādānavacanaṃ byāpanicchāvasena āmeḍitaniddesabhāvato. Sattanikāyeti sattānaṃ nikāye, sattaghaṭe sattasamūheti attho. Devamanussādibhedāsu hi gatīsu bhummadevādikhattiyādihatthiādikhuppipāsikāditaṃtaṃjātivisiṭṭho sattasamūho sattanikāyo. Nippariyāyato khandhānaṃ paṭhamābhinibbatti jātīti katvā “jananaṃ jātī”ti vatvā svāyaṃ uppādavikāro aparinipphanno [V 2.0311] yesu khandhesu icchitabbo, te teneva saddhiṃ dassetuṃ “savikārāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Savikārānanti uppādasaṅkhātena vikārena savikārānaṃ. Jātiādīni hi tīṇi lakkhaṇāni dhammānaṃ vikāravisesāti. “Upasaggamaṇḍitavevacana”nti iminā kevalaṃ upasaggena padavaḍḍhanaṃ katanti dasseti. Anupaviṭṭhākārenāti aṇḍakosaṃ, vatthikosañca ogāhanākārena. Nibbattisaṅkhātenāti āyatanānaṃ pāripūrisaṃsiddhisaṅkhātena.

388. ‘Thus spoken’ means thus stated by way of summary. The statement of encompassing all beings is due to its being an emphatic exposition by way of the desire for pervasion. ‘In the multitude of beings’ means in an assembly of beings, in a collection of beings, in a group of beings. For among the various destinies such as those of devas and humans, a group of beings distinguished by their respective births—such as terrestrial devas, khattiyas, elephants, hungry ghosts, and so forth—is a multitude of beings. Having stated that the first arising of the aggregates is birth in the ultimate sense, and having said ‘birth is the act of being born,’ it is said ‘of those subject to alteration,’ etc., in order to show, together with that, the aggregates in which this alteration of arising, an unaccomplished phenomenon, is to be sought. ‘Of those subject to alteration’ means of those subject to the alteration characterized as arising. For birth and so on are indeed three characteristics that are specific alterations of phenomena. By ‘a synonym adorned with a prefix,’ it is shown that the word is expanded merely by a prefix. ‘In the manner of having entered’ means in the manner of penetrating the eggshell and the womb. ‘Characterized by production’ means characterized by the complete fulfillment and accomplishment of the sense bases.

Atha vā jananaṃ jātīti aparipuṇṇāyatanaṃ jātimāha. Sañjātīti sampuṇṇāyatanaṃ. Sampuṇṇā hi jāti sañjāti. Okkamanaṭṭhena okkantīti aṇḍajajalābujavasena [M 2.0337] jāti. Te hi aṇḍakosaṃ, vatthikosañca okkamantā pavisantā viya paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhanti. Abhinibbattanaṭṭhena abhinibbattīti saṃsedajaopapātikavasena. Te hi pākaṭā eva hutvā nibbattanti. Abhibyattā nibbatti abhinibbatti. “Jananaṃ jātī”tiādi āyatanavasena, yonivasena ca dvīhi dvīhi padehi sabbasatte pariyādiyitvā jātiṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. “Tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ…pe… abhinibbattī”ti sattavasena vuttattā sammutikathā. Pātubhāvoti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho, pakārattho vā, tena “āyatanānaṃ [P 2.0426] paṭilābho”ti imassa padassa saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Ayampi hi paramatthakathāti. Ekavokārabhavādīsūti ekacatupañcavokārabhavesu. Tasmiṃ khandhānaṃ pātubhāve sati. Āyatanānaṃ paṭilābhoti ekacatuvokārabhavesu dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ āyatanānaṃ vasena, sesesu rūpadhātuyaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe uppajjamānānaṃ pañcannaṃ, kāmadhātuyaṃ vikalāvikalindriyānaṃ vasena sattannaṃ, navannaṃ, dasannaṃ, punadasannaṃ, ekādasannañca āyatanānaṃ vasena saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Pātubhavantāneva, na kutoci āgatāni. Paṭiladdhāni nāma honti sattasantānassa tassa saṃvijjamānattā. Āyatanānaṃ paṭilābhoti vā āyatanānaṃ attalābho veditabbo.

Alternatively, ‘birth is the act of being born’ refers to birth with incomplete sense bases. ‘Conception’ refers to complete sense bases. For complete birth is indeed conception. ‘Descent’ in the sense of entering is birth by way of egg-born and womb-born beings. For they take rebirth-linking as if entering and penetrating the eggshell and the womb. ‘Production’ in the sense of manifesting is by way of moisture-born and spontaneously-born beings. For they arise having become clearly visible. Manifest production is ‘production’. ‘Birth is the act of being born,’ etc., is stated to show birth by encompassing all beings with two terms each, by way of sense bases and by way of origin. ‘For those various beings… production’ is a conventional teaching because it is spoken in terms of beings. In ‘appearance,’ the word ‘iti’ has the meaning of ‘and so on’ or the meaning of ‘in this manner.’ By that, the inclusion of the phrase ‘the acquisition of the sense bases’ should be seen. For this too is an ultimate teaching. ‘In the one-constituent existence, etc.’ means in the one-, four-, and five-constituent existences. When there is an appearance of the aggregates in that… ‘The acquisition of the sense bases’—in the one- and four-constituent existences, the inclusion should be seen by way of two sense bases each. In the remaining cases, in the fine-material realm, it should be seen by way of the five that arise at the moment of rebirth-linking. In the sensual realm, depending on whether the faculties are deficient or not, the inclusion should be seen by way of seven, nine, ten, again ten, or eleven sense bases. They appear right there; they have not come from anywhere. They are called ‘acquired’ because of their existence in the continuity of that being. Or, ‘the acquisition of the sense bases’ should be understood as the gaining of their own nature by the sense bases.

389. Sabhāvaniddesoti sarūpaniddeso. Sarūpañhetaṃ jiṇṇatāya, yadidaṃ “jarā”ti, “vayohānīti vā. Jīraṇameva jīraṇatā, jīrantassa vā ākāro tā-saddena vuttoti āha “ākārabhāvaniddeso”ti. Khaṇḍitadantā khaṇḍitā nāma uttarapadalopena. Yassa vikārassa vasena satto “khaṇḍito”ti vuccati, taṃ khaṇḍiccaṃ. Tathā palitāni assa santīti “palito”ti vuccati, taṃ pāliccaṃ. Valittacatāya vā vali taco assāti valittaco.

389. ‘The exposition of its own nature’ means the exposition of its intrinsic nature. For this is its intrinsic nature, that is, of the state of being aged, which is ‘decay’ or ‘loss of youth’. Aging itself is the state of aging, or the characteristic of one who is aging is expressed by the suffix ‘-tā’; hence, he said, ‘the exposition of the characteristic-condition’. ‘Broken-toothed’ is called ‘broken’ by the elision of the latter part of the compound. The alteration on account of which a being is called ‘broken’ is brokenness. Similarly, one is called ‘gray-haired’ because gray hairs are present in him; that is grayness. Or, due to having wrinkled skin, one who has wrinkled skin is ‘wrinkled-skinned’.

Phalūpacārenāti phalavohārena.

‘By way of figurative expression of the fruit’ means by way of the expression of the fruit.

390. Cavanameva [V 2.0312] cavanatā, cavantassa vā ākāro tā-saddena vutto. Khandhā bhijjantīti ekabhavapariyāpannassa khandhasantānassa pariyosānabhūtā khandhā bhijjanti, teneva bhedena nirodhanaṃ adassanaṃ gacchanti, tasmā bhedo antaradhānaṃ maraṇaṃ. Maccumaraṇanti maccusaṅkhātaṃ ekabhavapariyāpannajīvitindriyupacchedabhūtaṃ maraṇaṃ. Tenāha “na khaṇikamaraṇa”nti. “Maccu [M 2.0338] maraṇa”nti samāsaṃ akatvā yo “maccū”ti vuccati bhedo, yañca maraṇaṃ pāṇacāgo, idaṃ vuccati maraṇanti visuṃ sambandho na na yujjati. Kālakiriyāti maraṇakālo, anatikkamanīyattā visesena “kālo”ti vuttoti tassa kiriyā, atthato [P 2.0427] cutikhandhānaṃ bhedappattiyeva, kālassa vā antakassa kiriyāti yā loke vuccati, sā cuti, maraṇanti attho. Ayaṃ sabbāpi sammutikathāva “yaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ sattāna”ntiādinā sattavasena vuttattā. Ayaṃ paramatthakathā paramatthato labbhamānānaṃ ruppanādisabhāvānaṃ dhammānaṃ vinassanajotanābhāvato.

390. Falling away itself is the state of falling away, or the characteristic of one who is falling away, expressed by the suffix ‘-tā’. ‘The aggregates break apart’ means that the aggregates, which are the conclusion of the aggregate-continuum pertaining to a single existence, break apart; and by that very breaking, they go to cessation and non-appearance. Therefore, breaking is disappearance, which is death. ‘Maccu-death’ refers to death designated as Maccu, which is the termination of the life-faculty pertaining to a single existence. Hence, it is said, ‘not momentary death’. If ‘Maccu maraṇa’ is not taken as a compound, then the breaking which is called ‘Maccu’ and the death which is the abandonment of life—this is called death; such a separate connection is not unsuitable. ‘Kālakiriyā’ means the time of death, called ‘time’ especially because it cannot be avoided; its ‘action’ is, in essence, the attainment of the breaking of the aggregates of passing away. Or, it is the action of time, the ender, which action is called passing away, death, in the world. All this is merely conventional speech, since it is stated in terms of beings: ‘that which belongs to these or those beings,’ etc. This is a teaching in the ultimate sense because it illuminates the destruction of phenomena whose intrinsic natures, such as being subject to affliction, are apprehended in the ultimate sense.

Attāti bhavati ettha cittanti attabhāvo, khandhasamūho, tassa nikkhepo nikkhipanaṃ, pātanaṃ vināsoti attho. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃpana “maraṇaṃ pattassā”tiādinā nikkhepahetutāya patanaṃ “nikkhepo”ti phalūpacārena vuttanti dasseti. “Khandhānaṃ bhedo”ti pabandhavasena pavattamānassa dhammasamūhassa vināsajotanāti ekadesato paramatthakathā, “jīvitindriyassa upacchedo”ti panettha na koci vohāraleso pīti āha “jīvitindriyassa upacchedo pana sabbākārato paramatthato maraṇa”nti. Evaṃ santepi yassa khandhabhedassa pavattattā “tisso mato, phusso mato”ti vohāro hoti, so bhedo khandhappabandhassa anupacchinnatāya “sammutimaraṇa”nti vattabbataṃ arahatīti āha “etadeva sammutimaraṇantipi vuccatī”ti. Tenāha “jīvitindriyupacchedameva hī”tiādi. Sabbaso pabandhasamucchedo hi samucchedamaraṇanti.

Individual existence (`attabhāvo`) is so called because the mind (`citta`) exists (`bhavati`) therein (`ettha`); it is the group of aggregates. Its ‘casting away’ means laying down, falling, destruction. The commentary, however, shows that by the phrase ‘of one who has reached death,’ etc., ‘casting away’ is used figuratively for the result, indicating falling as being due to the cause of casting away. ‘The breaking up of the aggregates’ is a teaching in the ultimate sense in one respect, as it illuminates the destruction of the group of phenomena occurring as a continuum. Regarding ‘the cutting off of the life faculty,’ there is not even a trace of conventional expression here; hence, it is said, ‘the cutting off of the life faculty, however, is death in the ultimate sense in every respect’. Even so, because the breaking up of the aggregates occurs, conventional expressions like ‘Tissa has died, Phussa has died’ are used. Since the continuity of the aggregates is not cut off, that breaking up deserves to be called ‘conventional death’; hence, it is said, ‘this itself is also called conventional death’. Therefore, it is stated, ‘for it is only the cutting off of the life faculty…’ etc. For the complete cutting off of the continuity is death by annihilation.

391. Byasanenāti anatthena. “Dhammapaṭisambhidā”tiādīsu (vibha. 721) viya dhamma-saddo hetupariyāyoti āha “dukkhakāraṇenā”ti. Socananti lakkhitabbatāya socanalakkhaṇo. Socitassa socanakassa puggalassa, cittassa vā bhāvo socitabhāvo. Abbhantareti attabhāvassa anto. Attano lūkhasabhāvatāya sosento. Thāmagamanena samantato sosanavasena parisosento.

391. ‘By misfortune’ means by what is not beneficial. As in the Dhammapaṭisambhidā, etc. (Vibh. 721), the word ‘dhamma’ is a synonym for cause; hence, it is said, ‘by the cause of suffering’. ‘Grieving’ is that which has the characteristic of grief, because it is to be characterized as such. The state of being grieved is the state of a person or mind that is grieving. ‘Internally’ means within one’s own being. ‘Drying up’ means drying up due to its own coarse nature. ‘Thoroughly drying up’ means drying up all around by proceeding with force.

392. “Ādissa ādissa devanti paridevanti etenāti ādevo”ti ādevana-saddaṃ katvā assumocanādivikāraṃ āpajjantānaṃ tabbikārāpattiyā [M 2.0339] so saddo kāraṇabhāvena [P 2.0428] vutto. Taṃ [V 2.0313] taṃ vaṇṇanti taṃ taṃ guṇaṃ. Tassevāti ādevaparidevasseva. Bhāvaniddesāti “ādevitattaṃ paridevitatta”nti bhāvaniddesā.

392. Having formed the word ‘lamentation’ (`ādevo`) with the etymology, ‘Pointing to this and that, they lament; they wail exceedingly by means of this, thus it is lamentation,’ that word is stated as the cause for the arising of that manifestation in those who fall into manifestations such as shedding tears. ‘They praise that and that’ means they praise that and that quality. ‘Of that same’ means of that same lamentation and wailing. ‘Exposition of the state’ means the exposition of the state of having lamented and the state of having wailed.

393. Nissayabhūto kāyo etassa atthīti kāyikaṃ. Tenāha “kāyapasādavatthuka”nti. Dukkaraṃ khamanaṃ etassāti dukkhamanaṃ, so eva attho sabhāvoti dukkhamanaṭṭho, tena. Sātavidhuratāya asātaṃ.

393. ‘Bodily’ (`kāyikaṃ`) is so called because it has the body as its support. Hence, it is said, ‘having the bodily sensitivity as its base’. ‘Mental distress’ (`dukkhamanaṃ`) is so called because its endurance is difficult; that very meaning is its intrinsic nature, hence ‘by that which has the meaning of mental distress’. ‘Disagreeable’ is so called because of its being devoid of the agreeable.

394. Cetasi bhavanti cetasikaṃ, taṃ pana yasmā cittena samaṃ pakārehi yuttaṃ, tasmā āha “cittasampayutta”nti.

394. That which occurs in the mind (`cetasi`) is mental (`cetasikaṃ`); and since it is conjoined with the mind in various ways, it is therefore said to be ‘associated with the mind’.

395. Sabbavisayapaṭipattinivāraṇavasena samantato sīdanaṃ saṃsīdanaṃ. Uṭṭhātumpi asakkuṇeyyatākaraṇavasena atibalavaṃ, virūpaṃ vā sīdanaṃ visīdanaṃ. Cittakilamathoti visīdanākārena cittassa parikhedo. Upāyāso, sayaṃ na dukkho dosattā, saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannadhammantarattā vā. Ye pana domanassameva “upāyāso”ti vadeyyuṃ, te “upāyāso tīhi khandhehi ekenāyatanena ekāya dhātuyā sampayutto, ekena khandhena ekenāyatanena ekāya dhātuyā kehici sampayutto”ti (dhātu. 249). Imāya pāḷiyā paṭikkhipitabbā. Upa-saddo bhusatthoti āha “balavataraṃ āyāso upāyāso”ti. Dhammamattatādīpano bhāvaniddeso dhammato aññassa kattuabhāvajotano, asati ca kattari tena kattabbassa, pariggahetabbassa ca abhāvo evāti āha “attattaniyābhāvadīpakābhāvaniddesā”ti.

395. Sinking down all around by way of preventing engagement with all objects is `saṃsīdanaṃ`. A very strong or deformed sinking, by way of causing the inability even to rise, is `visīdanaṃ`. Mental exhaustion is the mind's weariness in the manner of `visīdanaṃ`. Distress (`upāyāso`) is not suffering in itself, because it is aversion, or because it is another phenomenon included in the aggregate of formations. But those who would say that distress is merely sorrow should be refuted by this Pāli passage: ‘Distress is associated with three aggregates, one sense base, and one element; by some, it is associated with one aggregate, one sense base, and one element’ (Dhātuk. 249). The prefix `upa-` has the sense of intensity; hence, it is said, ‘a stronger striving is `upāyāso`’. The exposition of the state, which illuminates the mere nature of phenomena, reveals the absence of a doer apart from the phenomena; and when there is no doer, there is an absence of what is to be done by that doer and of what is to be grasped. Thus it is said to be ‘the exposition of the state that reveals the absence of self and of what belongs to self’.

398. Jātidhammānanti ettha dhamma-saddo pakatipariyāyoti āha “jātisabhāvāna”nti, jāyanapakatikānanti vuttaṃ hoti. Maggabhāvanāya maggabhāvanicchāhetukatā icchitabbāti tādisaṃ icchaṃ nivattento “vinā maggabhāvana”nti āha. Aparo nayo na kho panetanti yametaṃ “aho vata mayaṃ na jātidhammā assāma, na ca vata no jāti āgaccheyyā”ti evaṃ pahīnasamudayesu [P 2.0429] ariyesu vijjamānaṃ ajātidhammattaṃ, parinibbutesu ca vijjamānaṃ jātiyā anāgamanaṃ icchitaṃ, taṃ icchantassāpi maggabhāvanāya vinā appattabbato[M 2.0340], anicchantassāpi bhāvanāya pattabbato na icchāya pattabbaṃ nāma hotīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Vakkhamānatthasampiṇḍanattho pi-saddoti āha “upari sesāni upādāya pi-kāro”ti. Yanti hetuatthe karaṇe paccattavacananti āha “yenapi dhammenā”ti. Hetuattho hi ayaṃ dhamma-saddo[V 2.0314], alabbhaneyyabhāvo ettha hetu veditabbo. Tanti vā icchitassa vatthuno alabbhanaṃ, evamettha “yampīti yenapī”ti vibhattivipallāsena attho vutto. Yadā pana yaṃ-saddo “iccha”nti etaṃ apekkhati, tadā alābhavisiṭṭhā icchā vuttā hoti. Yadā pana “na labhatī”ti etaṃ apekkhati, tadā icchāvisiṭṭho alābho vutto hoti, so pana atthato añño dhammo natthi, tathāpi alabbhaneyyavatthugatā icchāva vuttā hoti. Sabbatthāti “jarādhammāna”ntiādinā āgatesu sabbavāresu.

398. In 'jātidhammānaṃ', the word `dhamma` is a synonym for nature; hence, it is said 'jātisabhāvānaṃ,' which means 'of those whose nature is to be born.' Another interpretation: 'This is not to be obtained by wishing.' That which is desired—namely, the state of not being subject to birth, which exists in the Noble Ones who have abandoned the origin, and the non-recurrence of birth, which exists in those who have attained final Nibbāna, as in 'Oh, that we were not subject to birth, and that birth would not come to us!'—this is not to be attained by wishing. For even one who desires it cannot attain it without the cultivation of the path, and even one who does not desire it can attain it through cultivation. Thus, it is not something to be attained by desire; this is the meaning to be understood here. The word `pi` has the meaning of summarizing what is to be said; hence, it is said, 'the particle `pi` is used with reference to the remaining cases that follow.' The word `yaṃ` is a singular instrumental in the sense of cause; hence, it is said, 'by whatever phenomenon.' Indeed, this word `dhamma` here has the meaning of cause; unattainability should be understood as the cause here. Or, `taṃ` refers to the unattainability of the desired object. Thus, here the meaning of 'yampi' is stated by a change of case as 'yenapi'. However, when the word `yaṃ` refers to 'desire,' then a desire characterized by non-attainment is stated. But when it refers to 'does not obtain,' then a non-attainment characterized by desire is stated. Yet, in essence, this is no other phenomenon; rather, it is the desire directed towards an unattainable object that is stated. 'In all cases' means in all the phrases that follow, such as 'of those subject to aging'.

Samudayasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of Origin

400. Punabbhavakaraṇaṃ punobbhavo uttarapadalopaṃ katvā mano-saddassa viya purimapadassa o-kārantatā daṭṭhabbā. Atha vā sīlanaṭṭhena ika-saddena gamitatthattā kiriyāvācakassa saddassa adassanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ yathā “asūpabhakkhanasīlo asūpiko”ti. Sammohavinodaniyaṃ pana “punabbhavaṃ deti, punabbhavāya saṃvattati, punappunaṃ bhave nibbattetīti ponobbhavikā”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 203) attho vutto so “taddhitā” iti bahuvacananiddesato, vicittattā vā taddhitavuttiyā, abhidhānalakkhaṇattā [P 2.0430] vā taddhitānaṃ tesupi atthesu ponobbhavikasaddasiddhi sambhaveyyāti katvā vutto. Tattha kammunā sahajātā punabbhavaṃ deti, asahajātā kammasahāyabhūtā punabbhavāya saṃvattati, duvidhāpi punappunaṃ bhave nibbattetīti daṭṭhabbā. Nandanaṭṭhena, rañjanaṭṭhena ca nandīrāgo, yo ca nandīrāgo, yā ca taṇhāyanaṭṭhena taṇhā, ubhayametaṃ ekatthaṃ, byañjanameva nānanti taṇhā “nandīrāgena saddhiṃ atthato ekattameva gatā”ti vuttā. Tabbhāvattho hettha saha-saddo “sanidassanā dhammā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. dukamātikā 9) viya. Tasmā nandīrāgasahagatāti nandīrāgabhāvaṃ gatā sabbāsupi avatthāsu nandīrāgabhāvassa apaccakkhāya vattanatoti attho. Rāgasambandhena uppannassāti vuttaṃ. Rūpārūpabhavarāgassa visuṃ vuccamānattā kāmabhave eva bhavapatthanuppatti vuttāti veditabbā.

400. The term punobbhava (rebirth) is to be understood as punabbhavakaraṇa (causing rebirth), with the latter part of the compound elided, and the first word ending in 'o', like mano from mano-sadda. Alternatively, since the meaning is conveyed by the suffix -ika in the sense of 'habit', the absence of a word denoting action should be understood, as in the example 'asūpabhakkhanasīlo' (one who habitually eats without curry) becoming 'asūpiko'. However, in the Sammohavinodanī, the meaning 'it gives rebirth, leads to rebirth, or repeatedly generates existence—hence ponobbhavika (conducive to rebirth)' is stated (Vibhaṅga Aṭṭhakathā 203). This meaning is stated because the derivation of the word ponobbhavika is possible even in these senses, due to the plural designation 'taddhitā' (derivatives), the diverse usage of derivatives, or the characteristic of derivatives to denote meaning. Here, it should be understood that that which is co-arisen with kamma gives rebirth; that which is not co-arisen but acts as a helper to kamma leads to rebirth; both types repeatedly generate existence. Nandīrāga (delight-lust) is so called in the sense of delighting and attaching. Whatever is delight-lust, and whatever is craving (taṇhā) in the sense of thirsting—both of these are one in meaning, only the expression differs. Thus, it is said that craving 'has attained oneness in meaning with delight-lust.' Here, the word saha- in sahagata (accompanied by) has the meaning of 'being of that nature,' as in 'sanidassanā dhammā' (phenomena with manifestation) and so forth (Dhammasaṅgaṇī Dukamātikā 9). Therefore, 'nandīrāgasahagatā' means 'having entered the state of delight-lust,' which is to say, persisting in all circumstances without abandoning the state of delight-lust. It is stated that this arises in connection with lust. Since the lust for form existence and formless existence is mentioned separately, it should be understood that the arising of the aspiration for existence is stated to be specifically in the sensual existence.

Tasmiṃ [M 2.0341] tasmiṃ piyarūpe paṭhamuppattivasena “uppajjatī”ti vuttaṃ, punappunaṃ pavattivasena “nivisatī”ti. Pariyuṭṭhānānusayavasena vā uppattinivesā yojetabbā. Sampattiyanti manussasobhagge, devatte ca. Attano cakkhunti savatthukaṃ cakkhuṃ vadati, sapasādaṃ vā maṃsapiṇḍaṃ. Vippasannaṃ pañcapasādanti parisuddhasuppasannanīlapītalohitakaṇhaodātavaṇṇavantaṃ. Rajatapanāḷikaṃ viya chiddaṃ abbhantare odātattā. Pāmaṅgasuttaṃ viya ālambakaṇṇabaddhaṃ. Tuṅgā uccā dīghā nāsikā tuṅganāsā, evaṃ laddhavohāraṃ attano ghānaṃ. “Laddhavohārā”ti vā pāṭho, tasmiṃ [V 2.0315] sati tuṅgā nāsā yesaṃ te tuṅganāsā, evaṃ laddhavohārā sattā attano ghānanti yojanā [P 2.0431] kātabbā. Jivhaṃ…pe… maññanti vaṇṇasaṇṭhānato, kiccato ca. Kāyaṃ…pe… maññanti ārohapariṇāhasampattiyā. Manaṃ…pe… maññanti atītādiatthacintanasamatthaṃ. Attanā paṭiladdhāni ajjhattañca sarīragandhādīni, bahiddhā ca vilepanagandhādīni. Uppajjamānā uppajjatīti yadā uppajjamānā hoti, tadā ettha uppajjatīti sāmaññena gahitā uppādakiriyā lakkhaṇabhāvena vuttā, visayavisiṭṭhā ca lakkhitabbabhāvena. Na hi sāmaññavisesehi nānattavohāro na hotīti. Uppajjamānāti vā anicchito uppādo hetubhāvena vutto, uppajjatīti nicchito phalabhāvena yadi uppajjamānā hoti, ettha uppajjatīti.

In whatever is pleasing, it is said to 'arise' in the sense of initial origination, and to 'settle' in the sense of repeated occurrence. Alternatively, the arising and settling should be connected in terms of obsessions and underlying tendencies. 'Attainment' refers to human beauty and divine splendor. 'One's own eye' refers to the eye together with its physical base, or the sensitive fleshy part. 'Very clear' means purified, supremely clear, and possessing colors like blue, yellow, red, black, and white. Like a silver tube, the aperture within is white. Like the thread of a head-ornament, it is fastened to the earlobe. A prominent, high, and long nose is called tuṅganāsā (prominent-nosed); thus, one's own nose, which has acquired this conventional usage. Alternatively, the reading may be 'laddhavohārā' (having acquired usage). In that case, the connection should be made as: 'those whose noses are prominent are tuṅganāsā; thus, beings, having acquired this conventional usage, refer to their own nose.' They perceive the tongue... in terms of color, shape, and function. They perceive the body... in terms of the perfection of height and girth. They perceive the mind... as capable of reflecting on past, future, and other matters. 'Obtained by oneself' refers to internal things such as bodily odors, and external things such as perfumes and fragrances. 'Arising, it arises': when it is arising, then it arises here. In this phrase, the act of arising, taken generally, is stated as a characteristic, and the specific object is to be understood as that which is characterized. For there is indeed a conventional distinction between the general and the specific. Alternatively, 'arising' (uppajjamānā) refers to an unintended arising stated as the cause, while 'it arises' (uppajjati) refers to an intended arising stated as the result. That is: if it is arising, it arises here.

Nirodhasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Exposition on the Truth of Cessation.

401. “Sabbāni nibbānavevacanānevā”ti vatvā tamatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “nibbānañhī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha āgammāti nimittaṃ katvā. Nibbānahetuko hi taṇhāya asesavirāganirodho. Khayagamanavasena virajjati. Appavattigamanavasena nirujjhati. Anapekkhatāya cajanavasena, hānivasena vā cajīyati. Puna yathā nappavattati, tathā dūra khipanavasena paṭinissajjīyati. Bandhanabhūtāya mocanavasena muccati. Asaṃkilesavasena na allīyati. Kasmā panetaṃ nibbānaṃ ekameva samānaṃ nānānāmehi vuccatīti? Paṭipakkhanānatāyāti dassento “ekameva hī”tiādimāha. Saṅkhatadhammavidhurasabhāvattā nibbānassa nāmānipi guṇanemittikattā saṅkhatadhammavidhurāneva hontīti vuttaṃ “sabbasaṅkhatānaṃ nāmapaṭipakkhavasenā”ti. Asesaṃ virajjati taṇhā etthāti asesavirāgoti. Esa nayo sesesupi. Ayaṃ pana viseso – natthi etassa uppādo, na [M 2.0342] vā etasmiṃ adhigate puggalassa uppādoti anuppādo, asaṅkhatadhammo. “Appavatta”ntiādīsupi iminā nayena attho veditabbo. Āyūhanaṃ samudayo, tappaṭipakkhavasena anāyūhanaṃ.

401. Having stated, 'All these are indeed synonyms for Nibbāna,' to make that meaning clearer, the passage beginning 'For Nibbāna...' was started. Here, 'āgamma' means 'having taken as a condition.' For the complete fading away and cessation of craving has Nibbāna as its cause. It fades away by way of destruction. It ceases by way of non-occurrence. It is abandoned by way of non-attachment, or by way of relinquishment. It is relinquished by way of casting it far away so that it does not occur again. It is released by way of liberation from what has become a bond. It does not cling by way of non-defilement. But why is this Nibbāna, being one and the same, referred to by many names? To show the diversity of its opposing aspects, it is said, 'For it is one...' Because the nature of Nibbāna is devoid of conditioned phenomena, its names, being indicative of its qualities, are also devoid of conditioned phenomena; thus it is said, 'by way of opposition to the names of all conditioned things.' Craving completely fades away herein; thus, it is 'asesavirāga' (complete fading away). This method applies to the rest as well. This, however, is the distinction: there is no arising of this, nor, when this is attained, is there arising for a person—thus, it is 'anuppādo' (non-arising), an unconditioned phenomenon. The meaning in 'appavatta' (non-occurrence), etc., should also be understood in this way. 'Āyūhana' (compiling) is the origin; its opposite is 'anāyūhana' (non-compiling).

Taṇhā appahīne sati yattha uppajjati, pahāne pana sati tattha [P 2.0432] tatthevassā abhāvo sudassitoti āha “tattheva abhāvaṃ dassetu”nti. Apaññattinti apaññāpanaṃ, “titta alābu atthī”ti vohārābhāvaṃ vā. Tittaalābuvalliyā appavattiṃ icchanto puriso viya ariyamaggo, tassa tassā appavattininnacittassa mūlacchedanaṃ viya maggassa nibbānārammaṇassa taṇhāya pahānaṃ, tadappavatti viya taṇhāya appavattibhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

When craving is not abandoned, it arises wherever it does; but when it is abandoned, its absence is clearly seen right there—thus it is said, 'to show its absence right there.' 'Apaññatti' means non-declaration, or the absence of the convention, 'there is a bitter gourd.' The Noble Path is like a person who desires the non-occurrence of a bitter gourd vine; the abandoning of craving by the path, which has Nibbāna as its object, is like the cutting of the root by that person whose mind is inclined towards the vine's non-occurrence; Nibbāna, which is the state of the non-occurrence of craving, should be seen as like the non-occurrence of that vine.

Dutiyaupamāyaṃ [V 2.0316] dakkhiṇadvāraṃ viya nibbānaṃ, coraghātakā viya maggo. Dakkhiṇadvāre ghātitāpi corā pacchā “aṭaviyaṃ corā ghātitā”ti vuccanti, evaṃ nibbānaṃ āgamma niruddhāpi taṇhā “cakkhādīsu niruddhā”ti vuccati tattha kiccakaraṇābhāvatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Purimā vā upamā maggena niruddhāya “piyarūpasātarūpesu niruddhā”ti vattabbatādassanatthaṃ vuttā, pacchimā nibbānaṃ āgamma niruddhāya “piyarūpasātarūpesu niruddhā”ti vattabbatādassanatthaṃ vuttāti ayaṃ etāsaṃ viseso.

In the second simile, Nibbāna is like the southern gate, and the path is like the executioner of thieves. Although the thieves are executed at the southern gate, they are later said to have been 'executed in the forest.' Similarly, although craving is ceased by means of Nibbāna, it is said to be 'ceased in the eye, etc.,' because it performs no function there. The first simile was stated to show that it can be said of craving ceased by the path that it is 'ceased in pleasant and agreeable forms,' while the latter simile was stated to show that it can be said of craving ceased by means of Nibbāna that it is 'ceased in pleasant and agreeable forms'—this is the distinction between them.

Maggasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Exposition on the Truth of the Path.

402. Aññamaggapaṭikkhepanatthanti titthiyehi parikappitassa maggassa dukkhanirodhagāminipaṭipadābhāvapaṭikkhepanatthaṃ, aññassa vā maggabhāvapaṭikkhepo aññamaggapaṭikkhepo, tadatthaṃ. “Aya”nti pana attano, tesu ca bhikkhūsu ekaccānaṃ paccakkhabhāvato āsannapaccakkhavacanaṃ. Ārakattāti niruttinayena ariyasaddasiddhimāha. Ariyabhāvakarattāti ariyakaraṇo ariyoti uttarapadalopena, puggalassa ariyabhāvakarattā ariyaṃ karotīti vā ariyo, ariyaphalapaṭilābhakarattā vā ariyaṃ phalaṃ labhāpeti janetīti ariyo. Purimena cettha attano kiccavasena, pacchimena phalavasena ariyanāmalābho vuttoti daṭṭhabbo. Catusaccapaṭivedhāvahaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ[P 2.0433], catusaccaṃ vā uddissa pavattaṃ bhāvanākammaṃ yogino sukhavisesānaṃ ṭhānabhūtanti catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ. Purimāni dve saccāni [M 2.0343] vaṭṭaṃ pavattihetubhāvato. Pacchimāni vivaṭṭaṃ nivattitadadhigamupāyabhāvato. Vaṭṭe kammaṭṭhānābhiniveso sarūpato pariggahasabbhāvato. Vivaṭṭe natthi avisayattā, visayatte ca payojanābhāvato. Purimāni dve saccāni uggaṇhitvāti sambandho. Kammaṭṭhānapāḷiyā hi tadatthasallakkhaṇena vācuggatakaraṇaṃ uggaho. Tenāha “vācāya punappunaṃ parivattento”ti. Iṭṭhaṃ kantanti nirodhamaggesu ninnabhāvaṃ dasseti, na abhinandanaṃ, tanninnabhāvoyeva ca tattha kammakaraṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

402. The purpose of rejecting other paths is to refute the path conceived by sectarians, which lacks the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. Alternatively, the rejection of another's status as a path is the rejection of other paths—that is its meaning. 'This' refers to oneself, and for some among those monks, because it is directly experienced, it is a statement of what is immediately apparent. 'Being far' states, according to etymology, the derivation of the word 'noble.' 'Because it makes one noble' means 'making noble' is 'noble'—here, the latter part of the compound is elided; or one is noble because one makes a person noble; or one is noble because one causes the noble fruit to be obtained or generated. Here, it should be understood that the attainment of the name 'noble' is stated, in the first case, in terms of one's own function, and in the latter case, in terms of the fruit. The meditation subject that brings about the penetration of the four truths is the four-truth meditation subject. Alternatively, the meditative action undertaken by a yogi with reference to the four truths is the four-truth meditation subject because it is the basis for special kinds of happiness. The first two truths are the round of existence, as they are the cause of its continuation. The latter two are liberation, as they are the means for its cessation and for the attainment thereof. In the round of existence, there is application to the meditation subject because of the existence of comprehension as to its nature. In liberation, there is none, as it is not an object; and even if it were an object, there would be no purpose. 'Having learned the first two truths'—this is the connection. For in the text on meditation subjects, learning is the verbalization through the marking of its meaning. Hence, it is said, 'reciting it verbally again and again.' 'Pleasing, delightful' indicates an inclination toward cessation and the path, not rejoicing; and that very inclination should be understood as the performance of the work in that context.

Ekapaṭivedhenevāti ekañāṇeneva paṭivijjhanena. Paṭivedho paṭighātābhāvena visaye nissaṅgacārasaṅkhātaṃ nibbijjhanaṃ. Abhisamayo avirajjhitvā visayassa adhigamasaṅkhāto avabodho. “Idaṃ dukkhaṃ, ettakaṃ dukkhaṃ, na ito bhiyyo”ti paricchinditvā jānanameva vuttanayena paṭivedhoti pariññāpaṭivedho, tena. Idañca yathā tasmiṃ ñāṇe pavatte pacchā dukkhassa sarūpādiparicchede sammoho na hoti, tathā pavattiṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ, na pana maggañāṇassa “idaṃ dukkha”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 2.484; 3.104) pavattanato. Pahīnassa [V 2.0317] puna appahātabbatāya pakaṭṭhaṃ hānaṃ cajanaṃ samucchindanaṃ, pahānameva vuttanayena paṭivedhoti pahānapaṭivedho, tena. Ayampi yasmiṃ kilese appahīyamāne maggabhāvanāya na bhavitabbaṃ, asati ca [P 2.0434] maggabhāvanāya yo uppajjeyya, tassa kilesassa paṭighātaṃ karontassa anuppattidhammataṃ āpādentassa ñāṇassa tathāpavattiyaṃ paṭighātābhāvena nissaṅgacāraṃ upādāya evaṃ vutto. Sacchikiriyā paccakkhakaraṇaṃ anussavākāraparivitakkādike muñcitvā sarūpato ārammaṇakaraṇaṃ “idaṃ ta”nti yathāsabhāvato gahaṇaṃ, sā eva vuttanayena paṭivedhoti sacchikiriyāpaṭivedho, tena. Ayaṃ panassa āvaraṇassa asamucchindanato ñāṇaṃ nirodhaṃ ālambituṃ na sakkoti, tassa samucchindanato taṃ sarūpato vibhāventameva pavattatīti evaṃ vutto. Bhāvanā uppādanā, vaḍḍhanā ca. Tattha paṭhamamagge uppādanaṭṭhena, dutiyādīsu vaḍḍhanaṭṭhena, ubhayatthāpi vā ubhayathāpi veditabbaṃ. Paṭhamamaggepi hi yathārahaṃ vuṭṭhānagāminiyaṃ pavattaṃ parijānanādiṃ vaḍḍhento pavattoti vaḍḍhanaṭṭhena bhāvanā sakkā viññātuṃ. Dutiyādīsupi appahīnakilesappahānato, puggalantarabhāvasādhanato ca uppādanaṭṭhena bhāvanā sakkā viññātuṃ, sā eva vuttanayena paṭivedhoti bhāvanāpaṭivedho, tena. Ayampi [M 2.0344] hi yathā ñāṇe pavatte pacchā maggadhammānaṃ sarūpaparicchede sammoho na hoti, tathā pavattimeva gahetvā vutto.

'By a single penetration' means by penetrating with a single knowledge. Penetration is the piercing through, designated as unimpeded movement in the object due to the absence of obstruction. Direct realization is the understanding, designated as the attainment of the object without becoming dispassionate towards it. 'This is suffering, this much suffering, no more than this'—knowing thus after having delimited is, in the stated manner, the penetration of full understanding; by that. And this is said having taken into account the occurrence in such a way that when that knowledge has arisen, there is afterwards no confusion in the delimitation of the nature of suffering, etc.—not, however, from the activity of path-knowledge proceeding as 'this is suffering,' etc. Of what has been abandoned, because it is not to be abandoned again, there is a pre-eminent abandoning, a relinquishing, an eradicating; this abandoning itself is, in the stated manner, the penetration of abandoning; by that. This too is said thus with reference to the unimpeded movement, due to the absence of obstruction, in the occurrence of that knowledge which strikes down and renders unable to arise again a defilement that, if it were not being abandoned, the development of the path could not be, and which, in the absence of the development of the path, would arise. Realization is the making-directly-present, the taking as object in its own nature, having abandoned hearsay, reflection on its appearance, and so on—grasping it according to its true nature as 'this is that.' This itself is, in the stated manner, the penetration of realization; by that. But since its obstruction is not eradicated, this knowledge is unable to take cessation as its object. Because that obstruction is eradicated, it proceeds by making that manifest in its own nature—thus it is said. Development is arising and also increasing. Therein, in the first path, it is by way of arising; in the second and subsequent paths, by way of increasing; or it should be understood in both ways in both cases. For even in the first path, development can be understood by way of increasing, as it proceeds by increasing the full understanding, etc., that occurs in the insight leading to emergence, as is appropriate. In the second and subsequent paths too, development can be understood by way of arising, because of the abandoning of un-abandoned defilements and the accomplishment of the state of another type of person. This itself is, in the stated manner, the penetration of development; by that. For this too is said having taken into account only the occurrence in such a way that when the knowledge has arisen, there is afterwards no confusion in the delimitation of the nature of the path-factors.

Tiṭṭhantu tāva yathādhigatā maggadhammā, yathāpavattesu phaladhammesupi ayaṃ yathādhigatasaccadhammesu viya vigatasammohova hoti. Tenevāha “diṭṭhadhammo pattadhammo viditadhammo pariyogāḷhadhammo”ti (mahāva. 18; dī. ni. 1.299; ma. ni. 2.69) yato sacassa dhammatāsañcoditā yathādhigatasaccadhammālambaniyo maggavīthito parato maggaphalapahīnāvasiṭṭhakilesanibbānānaṃ [P 2.0435] paccavekkhaṇā pavattanti, dukkhasaccammopi sakkāyadiṭṭhiādayo. Ayañca atthavaṇṇanā “pariññābhisamayenā”tiādīsupi vibhāvetabbā. Ekābhisamayena abhisametīti etthāha vitaṇḍavādī “ariyamaggañāṇaṃ catūsu saccesu nānābhisamayavasena kiccakara”nti, so abhidhamme (kathā. 274) odhisokathāya saññāpetabbo. Idāni tameva ekābhisamayaṃ vitthāravasena vibhāvetuṃ “evamassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Pubbabhāge…pe… paṭivedho hotī”ti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu paṭivedho pubbabhāgiyo na hotīti? Saccametaṃ nippariyāyato, idha pana uggahādivasena pavatto avabodho pariyāyato tathā vutto. Paṭivedhanimittattā vā uggahādivasena pavattaṃ dukkhādīsu pubbabhāge ñāṇaṃ “paṭivedho”ti vuttaṃ, na paṭivijjhanasabhāvaṃ. Kiccatoti pubbabhāgehi dukkhādiñāṇehi kātabbakiccassa idha nipphattito, imasseva vā ñāṇassa dukkhādippakāsanakiccato, pariññāditoti attho. Ārammaṇapaṭivedhoti sacchikiriyāpaṭivedhamāha. Sāti paccavekkhaṇā. Idhāti [V 2.0318] imasmiṃ ṭhāne. Uggahādīsu vuccamānesu na vuttā anavasarattā. Adhigame hi sati tassā siyā avasaro.

Let the path-factors as attained stand; even in the fruition-factors as they have occurred, this one is free from delusion, just as with the truth-factors that have been attained. Hence it is said: 'One who has seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, penetrated the Dhamma.' For, impelled by the very nature of the truth, after the path-process which has as its object the truth-factors as attained, the reviewings of the defilements abandoned by the path and fruition, the remaining defilements, and Nibbāna—and also of the truth of suffering, identity view, etc.—occur. And this explanation of the meaning should be made clear also in passages such as 'by the direct realization of full understanding.' Here, a contentious debater says, 'Noble path knowledge performs its function by way of multiple direct realizations in the four truths'; he should be instructed in the Abhidhamma by means of the discussion on limitation. Now, to explain that single direct realization in detail, it is said, 'Thus for him...' Why is it said, 'In the preliminary stage... penetration occurs'? Is it not the case that penetration is not preliminary? This is true in a non-figurative sense, but here the understanding that occurs by way of learning, etc., is figuratively called so. Or, because it is a sign of penetration, the knowledge of suffering, etc., that occurs in the preliminary stage by way of learning, etc., is called 'penetration,' not that it has the nature of piercing through. 'Because of the function' means because the task to be done by the preliminary knowledges of suffering, etc., is accomplished here, or because of this very knowledge's function of illuminating suffering, etc.; this is the meaning of 'through full understanding, etc.' 'Penetration of the object' refers to the penetration of realization. That is reviewing. 'Here' means in this place. When learning, etc., were being spoken of, it was not mentioned, as it was not the occasion. For when there is attainment, there would be an occasion for it.

Taṃyeva hi anavasaraṃ dassetuṃ “imassa cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pubbe pariggahatoti kammaṭṭhānapariggahato pubbe. Uggahādivasena saccānaṃ pariggaṇhanañhi pariggaho. Tathā tāni pariggaṇhanato manasikāradaḷhatāya pubbabhāgiyā dukkhapariññādayo honti yevāti āha “pariggahato paṭṭhāya hotī”ti. Aparabhāgeti maggakkhaṇe. Duddasattāti attano pavattikkhaṇavasena [P 2.0436] pākaṭānipi pakatiñāṇena sabhāvarasato daṭṭhuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā. Gambhīreneva ca bhāvanāñāṇena, tathāpi matthakappattena ariyamaggañāṇeneva yāthāvato passitabbattā gambhīrāni[M 2.0345]. Tenāha “lakkhaṇapaṭivedhato pana ubhayampi gambhīra”nti. Itarāni asaṃkiliṭṭhaasaṃkilesikatāya accantasukhappattāya anuppattibhavatāya, anuppannapubbatāya ca pavattivasena apākaṭattā ca paramagambhīrattā, tathā paramagambhīrañāṇeneva passitabbatāya pakatiñāṇena daṭṭhuṃ na sakkuṇeyyānīti duddasāni. Tenāha “itaresaṃ panā”tiādi. Payogoti kiriyā, vāyāmo vā. Tassa mahantatarassa icchitabbataṃ, dukkarataratañca upamāhi dasseti “bhavaggaggahaṇattha”ntiādinā. Paṭivedhakkhaṇeti ariyassa maggassa catusaccasampaṭivedhakkhaṇe. Ekameva taṃ ñāṇanti dukkhādīsu pariññādikiccasādhanavasena ekameva taṃ maggañāṇaṃ hoti.

Indeed, to show that very lack of occasion, it is said, 'And of this,' and so on. 'From the previous acquisition' means prior to the acquisition of the meditation subject. For the acquisition of the truths is indeed by way of learning, etc. Thus, from acquiring them, due to the firmness of attention, the preliminary aspects such as the full understanding of suffering, etc., certainly do exist. Hence it is said, 'It begins from the acquisition.' 'The latter part' refers to the moment of the path. 'They are hard to see' because even though they are evident by way of their momentary occurrence, they cannot be seen in their intrinsic nature with ordinary knowledge. And they are profound because they are to be seen accurately only by the knowledge of meditative development, and even then, only by the knowledge of the noble path when it has reached its peak. Therefore, it is said, 'But from the penetration of characteristics, both are profound.' The others are hard to see because, being undefiled and non-defiling, having attained ultimate bliss, being a state not yet attained, and not having arisen before, they are unmanifest in their occurrence and extremely profound; and also because they are to be seen only by the most profound knowledge, they cannot be seen by ordinary knowledge. Hence it is said, 'But as for the others,' and so on. 'Effort' means action or exertion. Its greater desirability and greater difficulty are shown by similes such as 'for the purpose of grasping the peak of existence,' and so on. 'The moment of penetration' is the moment when the noble path penetrates the four truths. 'That knowledge is one only' means that that path knowledge is one only, as it accomplishes the functions such as full understanding in relation to suffering and so on.

Imesu tīsu ṭhānesūti imesu viramitabbatāvasena jotitesu tīsu kāmabyāpādavihiṃsāvitakkavatthūsu. Visuṃ visuṃ uppannassa tividhaakusalasaṅkappassa. Padapacchedatoti ettha gatamaggo “pada”nti vuccati, yena ca upāyena kāraṇena kāmavitakko uppajjati, so tassa gatamaggoti tassa pacchedo ghāto padapacchedo, tato padapacchedato. Anuppattidhammatāpādanaṃ anuppattisādhanaṃ, tassa vasena. Maggakiccasādhanena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamāno ekova tividhakiccasādhano kusalasaṅkappo uppajjati. Tividhākusalasaṅkappasamucchedanameva hettha tividhakiccasādhanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Iminā nayena “imesu catūsu ṭhānesū”tiādīsupi attho veditabbo.

‘In these three places’ means in these three bases for sensual, hostile, and harmful thoughts, which are indicated as things to be refrained from. Regarding the individually arisen threefold unwholesome thought. ‘From cutting off the path’: here, the course taken is called ‘pada’; and the means or cause by which a sensual thought arises is its course. The cutting off or destruction of that is ‘padapaccheda’; hence, ‘from cutting off the path.’ Bringing about the state of non-arising is the accomplishment of non-arising; by means of that. Fulfilling the path factor by accomplishing the function of the path, a single wholesome thought arises that accomplishes the threefold function. Here, the accomplishment of the threefold function should be understood as precisely the complete eradication of the threefold unwholesome thought. By this method, the meaning should also be understood in phrases such as 'in these four places.'

Musāvādāveramaṇiādayoti ettha yasmā sikkhāpadavibhaṅge [P 2.0437] (vibha. 703) viraticetanā, sabbe sampayuttadhammā ca sikkhāpadānīti āgatānīti tattha padhānānaṃ viraticetanānaṃ vasena “viratiyopi honti cetanāyopī”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 703) sammohavinodaniyaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā keci “ādi-saddena na kevalaṃ pisuṇavācā veramaṇiādīnaṃyeva saṅgaho, atha kho tādisānaṃ cetanānampi [V 2.0319] saṅgaho”ti vadanti, taṃ pubbabhāgavasena vuccamānattā yujjeyya, musāvādādīhi viramaṇakāle vā viratiyo, subhāsitādivācābhāsanādikāle ca cetanāyo yojetabbā, maggakkhaṇe pana viratiyova icchitabbā cetanānaṃ amaggaṅgattā. Ekassa ñāṇassa dukkhādiñāṇatā viya, ekāya viratiyā musāvādādiviratibhāvo viya ca ekāya cetanāya sammāvācādikiccattayasādhanasabhāvābhāvā sammāvācādibhāvāsiddhito, taṃsiddhiyaṃ aṅgattayatāsiddhito ca.

Here, regarding 'abstinence from false speech, etc.': since in the analysis of the training rules (Vibhaṅga 703) it is stated that the volition of abstinence and all associated states are training rules, and in the Sammohavinodanī (Vibhaṅga Aṭṭhakathā 703) it is said, 'There are both abstinences and volitions,' with reference to the predominant volitions of abstinence, therefore some say that the term 'ādi' (etc.) includes not only abstinence from divisive speech, etc., but also such volitions. This would be reasonable if it were spoken of in terms of the preliminary stage, for abstinences should be associated with the time of abstaining from false speech, etc., and volitions with the time of speaking well-spoken words, etc. At the moment of the path, however, only abstinences are to be accepted, because volitions are not path factors. Just as one knowledge has the nature of being knowledge of suffering, etc., or one abstinence has the nature of being abstinence from false speech, etc., so too, because a single volition lacks the nature to accomplish the three functions of right speech, etc., the state of right speech, etc., is not established; and with its non-establishment, the state of being a threefold factor is not established.

Bhikkhussa [M 2.0346] ājīvahetukaṃ kāyavacīduccaritaṃ nāma ayoniso āhārapariyesanahetukameva siyāti āha “khādanīya…pe… duccarita”nti. Kāyavacīduccaritaggahaṇañca kāyavacīdvāreyeva ājīvapakopo, na manodvāreti dassanatthaṃ. Tenāha “imesuyeva sattasu ṭhānesū”ti.

A monk's wrong conduct of body and speech on account of livelihood would indeed be only on account of an unwise search for food, as stated: 'edibles... wrong conduct.' The inclusion of wrong conduct of body and speech is to show that the corruption of livelihood occurs only through the doors of body and speech, not through the mind door. Therefore, it is said: 'in these seven instances.'

Anuppannānanti asamudācāravasena vā ananubhūtārammaṇavasena vā anuppannānaṃ. Aññathā hi anamatagge saṃsāre anuppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā nāma na santi. Tenāha “ekasmiṃ bhave”tiādi. Yasmiṃ bhave ayaṃ imaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhati, tasmiṃ ekasmiṃ bhave. Janetīti uppādeti. Tādisaṃ chandaṃ kurumāno evaṃ chandaṃ janeti nāma. Vāyāmaṃ karotīti payogaṃ parakkamaṃ karoti. Vīriyaṃ [P 2.0438] pavattetīti kāyikacetasikavīriyaṃ pakārato vatteti. Vīriyena cittaṃ paggahitaṃ karotīti teneva sahajātavīriyena cittaṃ ukkhipento kosajjapātato nisedhanena paggahitaṃ karoti. Padahanaṃ pavattetīti padhānaṃ vīriyaṃ karoti. Paṭipāṭiyā panetāni cattāri padāni āsevanābhāvanābahulīkammasātaccakiriyāhi yojetabbāni.

‘Of the unarisen’ means of those that are unarisen either in the sense of non-manifestation or in the sense of their objects not having been experienced. Otherwise, in the beginningless cycle of existence, there are indeed no evil, unwholesome states that have not arisen. Therefore, it is said, 'in one existence,' etc., meaning in that one existence in which one undertakes this effort. 'Generates' means produces. By forming such a desire, one is said to 'generate desire.' 'Exerts' means makes an application, strives. 'Arouses energy' means sets in motion physical and mental energy in various ways. 'Upholds the mind with energy’ means, by that same co-arisen energy, one lifts up the mind and upholds it by preventing it from falling into laziness. 'Strives' means makes a pre-eminent effort. These four terms, however, should be connected in sequence with the actions of practice, cultivation, making much of, and continuous application.

Uppannapubbānanti sadisavohārena vuttaṃ. Bhavati hi taṃsadisesu tabbohāro yathā “sā eva tittiri, tāni eva osadhānī”ti. Tenāha “idāni tādise”ti. Uppannānanti “anuppannā”ti avattabbataṃ āpannānaṃ. Pahānāyāti pajahanatthāya. Anuppannānaṃ kusalānanti ettha kusalāti uttarimanussadhammā adhippetā, tesañca uppādo nāma adhigamo paṭilābho, tappaṭikkhepena anuppādo appaṭilābhoti āha “appaṭiladdhānaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīna”nti. “Ṭhitiyā vīriyaṃ ārabhatī”ti vutte na khaṇaṭhiti adhippetā tadatthaṃ vīriyārabbhena payojanābhāvato, atha kho pabandhaṭhiti adhippetāti āha “punappunaṃ uppattipabandhavasena ṭhitattha”nti. Sammussanaṃ paṭipakkhadhammavasena adassanamupagamananti tappaṭikkhepena asammussanaṃ asammosoti āha “asammosāyāti avināsanattha”nti. Bhiyyobhāvo punappunaṃ bhavanaṃ, so pana [V 2.0320] uparūpari uppattīti āha “uparibhāvāyā”ti. Vepullaṃ abhiṇhappavattiyā paguṇabalavabhāvāpattīti vuttaṃ “vepullāyāti vipulabhāvāyā”ti, mahantabhāvāyāti attho. Bhāvanāya paripūraṇatthanti jhānādibhāvanāparibrūhanatthaṃ.

‘Of those previously arisen’ is said with reference to a similar designation. For in similar cases, that designation is used, as in 'that very same partridge, those very same herbs.' Therefore, it is said, 'now of such a kind.' ‘Of those arisen’ means of those that have reached a state where they cannot be called 'unarisen.' ‘For abandoning’ means for the purpose of abandoning. ‘Of the unarisen wholesome states’: here, by ‘wholesome’ is meant superhuman states, and their arising means attainment or acquisition. Its opposite, non-arising, means non-acquisition. Thus it is said, 'of those not yet attained, such as the first jhāna, etc.' When it is said, 'he exerts energy for stability,' momentary stability is not intended, for there is no purpose in exerting energy for that. Rather, continuity of stability is intended. Therefore, it is said, 'for the sake of stability by way of a continuous process of arising.' ‘Forgetting’ means disappearance due to opposing states; its opposite, non-forgetting, is non-confusion. Thus it is said, 'for non-confusion, meaning for the sake of non-destruction.' ‘Increase’ is repeated becoming, which is arising again and again, higher and higher. Therefore, it is said, 'for increase.' ‘Fullness’ is the attainment of a proficient and strong state through frequent occurrence; thus it is said, 'for fullness, meaning for an extensive state,' which means for a great state. ‘For the fulfillment of development’ means for the purpose of augmenting the development of jhāna and the like.

Catūsu [M 2.0347] ṭhānesūti anuppannākusalānuppādanādīsu catūsu ṭhānesu. Kiccasādhanavasenāti catubbidhassapi kiccassa [P 2.0439] ekajjhaṃ nipphādanavasena.

‘In four places’ means in the four instances beginning with the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states. ‘By way of accomplishing the function’ means by way of accomplishing the fourfold function all at once.

Jhānāni pubbabhāgepi maggakkhaṇepi nānāti yadipi samādhiupakārakehi abhiniropanānumajjanasampiyāyanabrūhanasantasukhasabhāvehi vitakkādīhi sampayogabhedato bhāvanātisayappavattānaṃ catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ vasena sammāsamādhi vibhatto, tathāpi vāyāmo viya anuppannākusalānuppādanādicatuvāyāmakiccaṃ, sati viya ca asubhāsukhāniccānattesu kāyādīsu subhādisaññāppahānacatusatikiccaṃ, eko samādhi catujhānasamādhikiccaṃ na sādhetīti pubbabhāgepi paṭhamajjhānasamādhi eva maggakkhaṇepi, tathā pubbabhāgepi catutthajjhānasamādhi eva maggakkhaṇe pīti attho. Nānāmaggavasenāti paṭhamamaggādinānāmaggavasena jhānāni nānā. Dutiyādayopi maggā dutiyādīnaṃ jhānānaṃ. Ayaṃ panassāti ettha maggabhāvena catubbidhampi ekattena gahetvā “assā”ti vuttaṃ, assa maggassāti attho. Ayanti pana ayaṃ jhānavasena sabbasadisasabbāsadisekaccasadisatā viseso.

Regarding 'the jhānas are different both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the path': Although right concentration is classified by way of the four jhānas—which arise due to the excellence of development, distinguished by their association with initial application and so on, which are aids to concentration and have the nature of directing, stroking, gladdening, augmenting, peace, and bliss—nevertheless, just as effort cannot accomplish the fourfold task of effort, such as preventing the arising of unarisen unwholesome states, and just as mindfulness cannot accomplish the fourfold task of mindfulness, such as abandoning the perception of beauty and so on in the body and other things which are unattractive, unpleasant, impermanent, and not-self, so too one concentration alone cannot accomplish the task of the four jhānic concentrations. Therefore, the meaning is that in the preliminary stage it is the concentration of the first jhāna, and likewise at the moment of the path; and in the preliminary stage it is the concentration of the fourth jhāna, and likewise at the moment of the path. By 'according to different paths,' the jhānas differ according to the different paths, such as the first path and so on. The second and subsequent paths also belong to the second and subsequent jhānas. Here, regarding 'this of his' (ayaṃ panassa), 'of his' (assa) is stated by taking the fourfold path as one, meaning 'of this path.' And this 'this' (ayaṃ) refers to the distinction of complete similarity, complete dissimilarity, and partial similarity on account of the jhāna.

Pādakajjhānaniyamena hotīti idha pādakajjhānaniyamaṃ dhuraṃ katvā vuttaṃ, yathā cettha, evaṃ sammohavinodaniyampi (vibha. aṭṭha. 205). Aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 350) pana vipassanāniyamo vutto sabbavādāvirodhato, idha pana sammasitajjhānapuggalajjhāsayavādanivattanato pādakajjhānaniyamo vutto. Vipassanāniyamo pana sādhāraṇattā idhāpi na paṭikkhittoti daṭṭhabbo. Aññe ca ācariyavādā parato vakkhamānā vibhajitabbāti yathāvuttameva tāva pādakajjhānaniyamaṃ vibhajanto āha “pādakajjhānaniyamena tāvā”ti. Paṭhamajjhāniko hoti, yasmā āsannapadese vuṭṭhitasamāpatti maggassa [P 2.0440] attano sadisabhāvaṃ karoti bhūmivaṇṇo viya godhāvaṇṇassa. Paripuṇṇāneva hontīti aṭṭha satta ca hontīti attho. Satta honti sammāsaṅkappassa abhāvato. Cha honti pītisambojjhaṅgassa abhāvato. Maggaṅgabojjhaṅgānaṃ sattachabhāvaṃ atidisati “esa nayo”ti. Arūpe catukkapañcakajjhānaṃ…pe… vuttaṃ aṭṭhasāliniyanti adhippāyo. Nanu tattha “arūpe tikacatukkajjhānaṃ uppajjatī”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 350) vuttaṃ[V 2.0321], na “catukkapañcakajjhāna”nti? Saccametaṃ, yesu pana saṃsayo atthi, tesaṃ uppattidassanena[M 2.0348], tena atthato “catukkapañcakajjhānaṃ uppajjatī”ti vuttameva hotīti evamāhāti veditabbaṃ. Samudāyañca apekkhitvā “tañca lokuttaraṃ, na lokiya”nti āha “avayavekattaṃ liṅgasamudāyassa visesakaṃ hotī”ti. Catutthajjhānameva hi tattha lokiyaṃ uppajjati, na catukkaṃ, pañcakaṃ vāti. Ettha kathanti pādakajjhānassa abhāvā kathaṃ daṭṭhabbanti attho. Taṃjhānikāvassa tattha tayo maggā uppajjanti, tajjhānikaṃpaṭhamaphalādiṃ pādakaṃ katvā uparimaggabhāvanāyāti adhippāyo. Tikacatukkajjhānikaṃ pana maggaṃ bhāvetvā tattha uppannassa arūpacatutthajjhānaṃ, tajjhānikaṃ phalañca pādakaṃ katvā uparimaggabhāvanāya aññajhānikāpi uppajjantīti, jhānaṅgādiniyāmikā pubbābhisaṅkhārasamāpattipādakaṃ, na sammasitabbāti phalassāpi pādakatā daṭṭhabbā.

By 'it occurs by the rule of the foundational jhāna,' it is said here, making the rule of the foundational jhāna the principal point; just as it is here, so too in the Sammohavinodanī.
