However, in the Aṭṭhasālinī, the rule of insight is stated because it does not contradict any doctrine, but here, the rule of the foundational jhāna is stated due to turning away from the view based on the individual's disposition regarding the contemplated jhāna. The rule of insight, being common, is not rejected here either, as should be understood. And other teachers' doctrines, which will be explained later, should be distinguished. Thus, analyzing the rule of the foundational jhāna as stated, he says, 'Firstly, by the rule of the foundational jhāna.' One is of the first jhāna because, in the proximate region, the attainment one has emerged from makes the path similar to itself, just as the color of the earth makes the color of a monitor lizard similar. By 'they are fully complete,' it means there are eight and seven. There are seven due to the absence of right resolve. There are six due to the absence of the enlightenment factor of rapture. He extends the sevenfold and sixfold nature of the path factors and enlightenment factors, saying, 'This is the method.' The meaning is that the fourfold and fivefold jhānas in the formless realm... as stated in the Aṭṭhasālinī. But is it not said there, 'In the formless realm, the threefold and fourfold jhānas arise,' not 'the fourfold and fivefold jhānas'? This is true, but for those who have doubt, by showing their arising, it is in effect said, 'The fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise'—this should be understood as the explanation. And with reference to the collection, he says, 'And that is supramundane, not mundane,' because 'the unity of the parts is a qualifier of the aggregate of characteristics.' For there, only the fourth jhāna arises as mundane, not the fourfold or the fivefold. Here, 'how' means how should it be understood, there being an absence of a foundational jhāna? The meaning is that for one belonging to that jhāna, three paths arise there, by making that jhāna's first fruition and so on the foundation for the development of the higher path. But having developed the path belonging to the threefold and fourfold jhānas, and making the formless fourth jhāna that arose there, and its fruition, the foundation for the development of the higher path, other jhānas also arise. The prior volitional formation and the attainment are the foundation that regulates the jhāna factors and so on, and are not to be contemplated; thus, the foundational nature of the fruition should also be understood.

Keci panāti moravāpīmahādattattheraṃ sandhāyāha. Puna kecīti tipiṭakacūḷābhayattheraṃ[P 2.0441]. Tatiyavāre kecīti “pādakajjhānameva niyametī”ti evaṃ vādinaṃ tipiṭakacūḷanāgattherañceva anantaraṃ vutte dve ca there ṭhapetvā itare there sandhāya vadati.

By 'some,' he refers to the elder Moravāpīmahādatta. Again, by 'some,' he refers to the elder Tipiṭakacūḷābhaya. In the third instance, by 'some,' he speaks with reference to the elder Tipiṭakacūḷanāga, who holds the view 'only the foundational jhāna determines,' and, excluding the two elders just mentioned, he speaks with reference to the other elders.

403. Sasantatipariyāpannānaṃ dukkhasamudayānaṃ appavattibhāvena pariggayhamāno nirodhopi sasantatipariyāpanno viya hotīti katvā vuttaṃ “attano vā cattāri saccānī”ti. Parassa vāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tenāha bhagavā “imasmiṃyeva byāmamatte kaḷevare sasaññimhi samanake lokañca paññāpemi, lokasamudayañca paññāpemi, lokanirodhañca paññāpemi, lokanirodhagāminipaṭipadañca paññāpemī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.107; a. ni. 4.45) kathaṃ pana ādikammiko nirodhamaggasaccāni pariggaṇhātīti? Anussavādisiddhamākāraṃ pariggaṇhāti. Evañca katvā lokuttarabojjhaṅge uddissāpi pariggaho na virujjhati. Yathāsambhavatoti sambhavānurūpaṃ, ṭhapetvā nirodhasaccaṃ sesasaccavasena samudayavayāti veditabbāti attho.

403. Because cessation, being grasped as the non-occurrence of suffering and its origin, which are encompassed within one's own continuum, appears as if cessation itself is encompassed within one's own continuum, it is said, 'or one's own four truths.' By 'or another's,' here too the same principle applies. Thus, the Blessed One declared: 'In this very fathom-long body, with its perception and mind, I make known the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world' (Saṃ. Ni. 1.107; A. Ni. 4.45). But how does a beginner grasp the truths of cessation and the path? He grasps them through the method established by hearsay and so on. And having done so, the grasping with reference to the supramundane enlightenment factors is also not contradicted. By 'according to possibility,' it means according to what is possible; the meaning is that, excluding the truth of cessation, the remaining truths are to be understood in terms of arising and vanishing.

Catusaccapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the section on the Four Truths is completed.

Dhammānupassanāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition on the contemplation of phenomena is completed.

404. “Aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ [M 2.0349] samaṃsa”ntiādikā satta sivathikā aṭṭhikakammaṭṭhānatāya itarāsaṃ [V 2.0322] uddhumātakādīnaṃ sabhāvenevāti navannaṃ sivathikānaṃ appanākammaṭṭhānatā vuttā. Dveyevāti ānāpānaṃ, dvattiṃsākāroti imāni dveyeva. Abhinivesoti vipassanābhiniveso, so pana sammasaniyadhammapariggaho. Iriyāpathā, ālokitādayo ca rūpadhammānaṃ avatthāvisesamattatāya na sammasanupagā viññattiādayo viya. Nīvaraṇabojjhaṅgā ādito na pariggahetabbāti [P 2.0442] vuttaṃ “iriyāpatha…pe… na jāyatī”ti. Kesādiapadesena tadupādānadhammā viya iriyāpathādiapadesena tadavatthā rūpadhammā pariggayhanti, nīvaraṇādimukhena ca taṃsampayuttā, taṃnissayadhammāti adhippāyena mahāsivatthero ca iriyāpathādīsupi “abhiniveso jāyatī”ti avoca. “Atthi nu kho me”tiādi pana sabhāvato iriyāpathādīnaṃ ādikammikassa anicchitabhāvadassanaṃ. Apariññāpubbikā hi pariññāti.

404. By 'the skeleton, the chain of bones, with flesh,' and so on, the seven charnel ground meditations are for the bone meditation subject, while the others, such as the bloated corpse and so on, are so by their very nature. Thus, the suitability of the nine charnel ground meditations as meditation subjects for absorption is stated. By 'only two,' these are mindfulness of breathing and the thirty-two parts of the body. By 'application,' it refers to the application of insight, which is the comprehension of phenomena to be contemplated. Postures, gazing and so on, being merely particular states of material phenomena, are not suitable for contemplation, like gestures and so on. The hindrances and enlightenment factors should not be grasped from the beginning, as stated: 'Postures... do not arise.' Just as the phenomena that are their objects of clinging are grasped by means of hair and so on, so too material phenomena that are their states are grasped by means of postures and so on. And by means of hindrances and so on, their associated and dependent phenomena are understood. With this intention, the great elder Mahāsīva also said, 'Application arises even in postures and so on.' However, 'Is there in me...?' and so on, is the beginner's observation of the undesirable nature of postures and so on in their true essence. For full understanding is preceded by initial comprehension.

Kāmaṃ “idha bhikkhave bhikkhū”tiādinā uddesaniddesesu tattha tattha bhikkhuggahaṇaṃ kataṃ taṃpaṭipattiyā bhikkhubhāvadassanatthaṃ, desanā pana sabbasādhāraṇāti dassetuṃ “yo hi koci bhikkhave” icceva vuttaṃ, na bhikkhu yevāti dassento “yo hi koci bhikkhu vā”tiādimāha. Dassanamaggena ñātamariyādaṃ anatikkamitvā jānantī sikhāppattā aggamaggapaññā aññā nāma, tassa phalabhāvato aggaphalaṃ pīti āha “aññāti arahatta”nti.

Although the term 'bhikkhu' is used here and there in the summaries and expositions, such as 'Here, bhikkhus,' and so on, to show the state of being a bhikkhu through that practice, yet to show that the teaching is common to all, it is said, 'whoever, bhikkhus,' and to show that it is not exclusively 'only a bhikkhu,' he says, 'whoever, bhikkhu, or...' The wisdom of the highest path, which has reached the summit, knowing without transgressing the limit known by the path of vision, is called 'aññā.' Because it is the fruit of that, it is also the highest fruit. Therefore, he says, 'aññā is arahantship.'

Appatarepi kāle sāsanassa niyyānikabhāvaṃ dassentoti yojanā. Niyyātentoti nigamento.

The explanation is: showing the quality of leading out of the dispensation even in a shorter time. By 'leads out,' it means the conclusion.

Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

The Clarification of the Hidden Meaning in the Exposition on the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness.

10. Pāyāsirājaññasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Pāyāsi Rājañña Sutta

406. Bhagavatā [P 2.0443][V 2.0323][M 2.0350] evaṃ gahitanāmattāti yojanā. Yasmā rājaputtā loke “kumāro”ti voharīyanti. Ayañca rañño kittimaputto, tasmā āha “rañño…pe… sañjāniṃsū”ti.

406. "Born in the womb of a young woman of a good family," having said this, to show his state of being born from the very beginning, it is said, "and she," and so on. Herein, "she" refers to the young woman of a good family. The word "ca" has the meaning of distinction; thus it highlights the special quality being described. "Family home" means the house of the husband's family. "Sign of pregnancy" means the indication of the established state of the embryo. Even though Visākhā was also included among the families of Sāvatthi residents, to show her prominence there, it is said, "and Visākhā," just as it is said, "The brahmins have come, and Vāsiṭṭha has also come." "Deity" here also refers to that same Suddhāvāsa deity. "Questions" refers to the fifteen questions that begin with, "Monk, monk, this anthill," as found in the Majjhima Nikāya (1.249).

Assāti therassa. Puññāni karonto kappasatasahassaṃ devesu ceva manussesu ca uppajjitvā visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhi indriyānaṃ aparipakkattā. Tatiyadivaseti pabbataṃ āruḷhadivasato tatiye divase.

Assāti: This refers to the Elder. Though he performed meritorious deeds for a hundred thousand aeons, he was unable to bring about any distinction, even after being reborn among gods and humans, due to the immaturity of his faculties. On the third day: on the third day from ascending the mountain.

Tesaṃ sāvakabodhiyā niyatatāya, puññasambhārassa ca sātisayattā vinipātaṃ agantvā ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ…pe… anubhavantānaṃ. Devatāyāti pubbe sahadhammacāriniyā suddhāvāsadevatāya.

For them, destined for disciples' enlightenment, and because of the surpassing accumulation of merit, without going to the lower realms, they experience one Buddha-interval…and so on. The deity: a deity of the Pure Abodes who was formerly a companion in the Dhamma.

“Kuladārikāya kucchimhi uppanno”ti vatvā taṃ evassa uppannabhāvaṃ mūlato paṭṭhāya dassetuṃ “sā cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sāti kuladārikā. Ca-saddo byatirekattho, tena vuccamānaṃ visesaṃ joteti. Kulagharanti patikulagehaṃ. Gabbhanimittanti gabbhassa saṇṭhitabhāvanimittaṃ. Satipi visākhāya ca sāvatthivāsikulapariyāpannatte tassā tattha padhānabhāvadassanatthaṃ “visākhañcā”ti vuttaṃ yathā “brāhmaṇā āgatā vāsiṭṭhopi āgato”ti. Devatāti idhapi sā eva suddhāvāsadevatā. Pañheti “bhikkhu bhikkhu ayaṃ vammiko”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.249) āgate pannarasapañhe.

"Born in the womb of a young woman of a good family," having said this, to show his state of being born from the very beginning, it is said, "and she," and so on. Herein, "she" refers to the young woman of a good family. The word "ca" (and) has the meaning of distinction; thus it highlights the special quality being described. "Family home" means the house of the husband's family. "Sign of pregnancy" means the indication of the established state of the embryo. Even though Visākhā was also included among the families of Sāvatthi residents, to show her prominence there, it is said, "and Visākhā," just as it is said, "The brahmins have come, and Vāsiṭṭha has also come." "Deity" here also refers to that same Suddhāvāsa deity. "Questions" refers to the fifteen questions that begin with, "Monk, monk, this anthill," as found in the Majjhima Nikāya (1.249).

Setabyāti itthiliṅgavasena tassa nagarassa nāmaṃ. Uttarenāti [P 2.0444] ena-saddayogena “setabya”nti upayogavacanaṃ pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Atthavacanena pana uttarasaddaṃ apekkhitvā setabyatoti nissakkappayogo kato. Anabhisittakarājāti khattiyajātiko abhisekaṃ appatto.

Setabyā is the name of that city in the feminine gender. Uttarenāti: Through connection with the word "-ena," "setabya" is used as an expression of location in the Pāli. However, in the explanation of the meaning, with reference to the word "uttara," the ablative usage "setabyato" is employed.

Pāyāsirājaññavatthuvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Story of Pāyāsi Rājañña

407. Diṭṭhiyeva [V 2.0324] diṭṭhigatanti gata-saddena padavaḍḍhanamāha, diṭṭhiyā vā gatamattaṃ [M 2.0351] diṭṭhigataṃ, ayāthāvaggāhitāya gantabbābhāvato diṭṭhiyā gahaṇamattaṃ, kevalo micchābhinivesoti attho, taṃ pana diṭṭhigataṃ tassa ayonisomanasikārādivasena uppajjitvā paṭipakkhasammukhībhāvābhāvato, anurūpāhāralābhato ca samudācārappattaṃ jātanti pāḷiyaṃ “uppannaṃ hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ apadisitvāti tato idhāgacchanakassa, ito tattha gacchanakassa ca apadisanato “tattha tattheva sattānaṃ ucchijjanato”ti evamādi taṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭirūpakaṃ apadisitvā.

407. 'Diṭṭhigata' is simply a view; the word 'gata' is merely a verbal expansion. Or, 'diṭṭhigata' is merely what is gone to by a view. Because it is impossible to proceed by means of what is wrongly grasped, it is merely the grasping of a view; the meaning is simply a wrong conviction. That 'diṭṭhigata,' having arisen due to unwise attention and the like, and because of the absence of confrontation with its counteragent, and due to obtaining suitable nourishment, has become manifest—this is stated in the Pāli as 'has arisen.' 'Pointing out each particular reason' means: pointing out each particular specious reason, such as 'because beings are annihilated right there and then,' by pointing to the absence of anyone coming here from there and of anyone going there from here.

408. Āpannānadhippetatthavisaye ayaṃ purā-saddapayogoti āha “purā…pe… saññāpetīti yāva na saññāpetī”ti.

408. He says that this usage of the word "purā" (before) is in the context of matters not intended by those who have committed an offense: "purā…pe… saññāpeti" means "as long as he does not persuade."

Candimasūriyaupamāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Simile of the Moon and the Sun

411. Yathā candimasūriyā uḷāravipulobhāsatāya aññena obhāsena anabhibhavanīyā, evamayampi paññāobhāsenāti dassento “candima…pe… aññenā”tiādimāha. Ādīhīti ādi-saddena “kittake ṭhāne ete pavattenti, kittakañca ṭhānaṃ nesaṃ ābhā pharatī”ti evamādimpi codanaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Paliveṭhessatīti ābandhissati, anuyuñjissatīti attho. Nibbeṭhetuṃ taṃ vissajjetuṃ. Tasmāti yasmā [P 2.0445] yathāvuttaṃ codanaṃ nibbeṭhetuṃ na sakkoti, tasmā. Attano anicchitaṃ saṅghātanaṃ pakkhaṃ paṭijānanto “parasmiṃ loke, na imasmi”ntiādimāha.

411. Showing that 'Just as the moon and sun, because of their great and vast radiance, cannot be overpowered by other light, so too this one by the light of wisdom,' he said "like the moon…by another," and so on. By "and so on": with the word "ādi," he also includes the challenge such as, "In how many places do these operate, and how far does their radiance extend?" "He will encircle" means he will bind; the meaning is he will cross-examine. "To unravel" means to release it. "Therefore": because he is unable to unravel the aforementioned challenge as stated, therefore. Acknowledging a destructive position undesired by himself, he says, "in the other world, not in this one," and so on.

Kathaṃ panāyaṃ natthikadiṭṭhi “devo”ti paṭijānātīti tattha kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “bhagavā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Devāpi devattabhāveneva ucchijjanti, manussāpi manussattabhāveneva ucchijjantī”ti evaṃ vā assa diṭṭhi, evañca katvā “devā te, na manussā”ti vacanañca na virujjhati. Evaṃ candeti candavimāne, na ca cande vā kathiyante.

But how does this nihilistic view acknowledge 'a god'? To explain the reason for this, 'But the Blessed One…' and so on, was stated. His view might be thus: 'Gods are annihilated through their divine state itself, and humans are annihilated through their human state itself.' This being the case, the statement 'They are gods, not humans' is not contradicted. Similarly, 'moon' refers to the moon mansion, not that the moon itself is being spoken of.

412. Ābādho etesaṃ atthīti ābādhikā. Dukkhaṃ sañjātaṃ etesanti dukkhitā. Saddhāya ayitabbā saddhāyikā, saddhāya pavattiṭṭhānabhūtā. Tenāha “ahaṃ tumhe”tiādi. Paccayo pattiyāyanaṃ etesu atthīti paccayikā.

412. They are afflicted because they have illness. They are suffering because suffering has arisen in them. They are worthy of faith, being a basis for the arising of faith. Therefore, he said, "I [trust] you," and so on. They are trustworthy because reliance and confidence exist in them.

Coraupamāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Simile of the Thief

413. Uddisitvāti [V 2.0325][M 2.0352] upecca dassetvā. Kammakāraṇikasattesūti nerayikānaṃ saṅghātanakasattesu. Kammamevāti tehi tehi nerayikehi katakammameva. Kammakāraṇaṃ karotīti āyūhanānurūpaṃ taṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ karoti, tathā dukkhaṃ uppādetīti attho. Nirayapālāti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho, tena tattha sabbaṃ nirayakaṇḍapāḷiṃ (ma. ni. 3.259) saṅgaṇhāti. Evaṃ suttato (ma. ni. 3.259) nirayapālānaṃ atthibhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni yuttitopi dassetuṃ “manussaloke”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha nerayike niraye pālenti tato niggantuṃ appadānavasena rakkhantīti nirayapālā. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ papañcasūdanīṭīkāyaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

413. 'Uddisitvāti' means 'having approached and shown.' 'Kammakāraṇikasattesūti' refers to the beings who are the agents of kamma, those who strike and crush the hell-beings. 'Kammamevāti' means 'the very action done by those hell-beings.' 'Kammakāraṇaṃ karotīti' means 'it brings about that particular cause in accordance with the accumulation of karma, thus producing suffering'—this is the meaning. 'Nirayapālāti': here, the word 'iti' signifies 'and so on,' thereby encompassing the entire Pāli text of the section on hell (Majjhima Nikāya 3.259). Thus, having shown the existence of hell-guardians from the Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 3.259), now, to show it also from reasoning, 'in the human world' and so forth is stated. Therein, 'hell-guardians' are those who guard the hell-beings in hell, protecting them by not allowing them to escape. What should be said further here is to be taken from the Papañcasūdanī-ṭīkā.

Gūthakūpapurisaupamāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Simile of the Person in the Cesspit

415. Nimmajjathāti [P 2.0446] niravasesato majjatha sodhetha. Taṃ pana tassa tassa gūthassa tathā sodhanaṃ apanayanaṃ hotīti āha “apanethā”ti.

415. 'Nimmajjathāti' means 'cleanse without remainder' or 'purify.' But since that purification of each kind of filth is a removal, it is said, 'apanethā' (remove it).

Asucīti asuddho, so pana yasmā manavaḍḍhanako manoharo na hoti, tasmā āha “amanāpo”ti. Asucisaṅkhātaṃ asucibhāgataṃ attano sabhāvataṃ gato pattoti asucisaṅkhātoti āha “asucikoṭṭhāsabhūto”ti. Duggandhoti duṭṭhagandho aniṭṭhagandho, so pana na yo koci, atha kho pūtigandhoti āha “kuṇapagandho”ti. Jigucchitabbayuttoti hīḷitabbayutto. Paṭikūlo ghānindriyassa paṭikūlarūpo. Ubbādhatīti uparūpari bādhati. Manussānaṃ gandho…pe… bādhati ativiya asucisabhāvattā, asucimhiyeva jātasaṃvaddhanabhāvato, devānañca ghānapasādassa tikkhavisadabhāvato.

'Asucīti' means 'impure'; and because it is not pleasing or delightful to the mind, it is called 'amanāpo' (unpleasant). 'Asucisaṅkhātoti' means it has attained its own nature, which is part of impurity; therefore it is said, 'asucikoṭṭhāsabhūto' (having become a portion of impurity). 'Duggandhoti' means 'foul-smelling,' an 'unpleasant odor'; and it is not just any odor, but rather a putrid odor, hence it is said, 'kuṇapagandho' (the stench of a corpse). 'Jigucchitabbayuttoti' means 'fit to be loathed.' 'Paṭikūlo' means 'repulsive to the olfactory faculty.' 'Ubbādhatīti' means 'it oppresses repeatedly.' The stench of humans... oppresses greatly due to its extremely impure nature, due to being born and nurtured in impurity itself, and it oppresses the gods because of the sharp and clear nature of their olfactory sensitivity.

416. Dūre nibbattā paranimmitavasavattiādayo.

416. 'Born far away' refers to the Paranimmitavasavatti gods and the like.

419. Sundaradhammeti sobhanaguṇe. Sugatisukhanti sugati ceva tappariyāpannaṃ sukhañca.

419. 'Sundaradhammeti' means 'in beautiful qualities.' 'Sugatisukhanti' means 'a good destination and the happiness included therein.'

Gabbhinīupamāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Simile of the Pregnant Woman

420. Puññakammato [M 2.0353] eti uppajjatīti ayo, sukhaṃ. Tappaṭipakkhato anayo, dukkhaṃ[V 2.0326]. Apakkanti na siddhaṃ na niṭṭhānappattaṃ. Na paripācenti na niṭṭhānaṃ pāpenti. Na upacchindanti attavinipātassa sāvajjabhāvato. Āgamentīti udikkhanti. Nibbisanti yassa pana taṃ kammaphalaṃ nibbisanto niyuñjanto, nibbisanti vā nibbesaṃ vetanaṃ paṭikaṅkhanto bhatapuriso yathā.

420. 'Ayo' (gain) is so called because 'it arises from meritorious kamma'; it is happiness. Its opposite is 'anayo' (loss); it is suffering. 'Apakkanti' means 'not accomplished, not brought to completion.' 'Na paripācenti' means 'they do not bring to maturity, they do not bring to completion.' 'Na upacchindanti' means 'they do not cut off,' because of the blameworthy nature of self-destruction. 'Āgamentīti' means 'they await' or 'they expect.' 'Nibbisanti' means 'experiencing that kamma-result, one engages with it'; or, 'they experience' is like a hired man who expects wages.

421. Ubbhinditvāti upasaggena padavaḍḍhanamattanti āha “bhinditvā”ti.

421. 'Ubbhinditvāti': he says this is merely a verbal expansion by means of a prefix, meaning 'bhinditvā' (having broken).

Supinakaupamāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Simile of the Dream

422. “Nikkhamantaṃ vā pavisantaṃ vā jīva”nti idaṃ tassa ajjhāsayavasena vuttaṃ. So hi “sattānaṃ supinadassanakāle [P 2.0447] attabhāvato jīvo bahi nikkhamitvā taṃtaṃārāmarāmaṇeyyakadassanādivasena ito cito ca paribbhamitvā punadeva attabhāvaṃ anupavisatī”ti evaṃ pavattamicchāgāhavipallattacitto. Athassa thero khuddakāya āṇiyā vipulaṃ āṇiṃ nīharanto viya jīvasamaññāmukhena ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ nīharitukāmo “api nu tā tuyhaṃ jīvaṃ passanti pavisantaṃ vā nikkhamantaṃ vā”ti āha. Yattha pana tathārūpā jīvasamaññā, taṃ dassento “cittācāraṃ jīvanti gahetvā āhā”ti vuttaṃ.

422. “Whether going out or entering, it is ‘life’”—this was said according to his inclination. For he, with a mind perverted by wrong grasping, thinks thus: “At the time of seeing dreams, the life of beings goes out from the body and, wandering here and there by way of seeing various delightful parks and so on, eventually re-enters the body.” Then, the elder, wishing to remove the annihilationist view through the designation of ‘life’—just as one pulls out a large peg with a small peg—said, “But do they see your life entering or going out?” And to show where such a designation of ‘life’ applies, it is said, “Taking the movement of the mind as life, he speaks.”

423. Veṭhetvāti vekhadānasaṅkhepena veṭhetvā. Cavanakāleti cavanassa cutiyā pattakāle, na cavamānakāle. Rūpakkhandhamattamevāti katipayarūpadhammasaṅghātamattameva. Utusamuṭṭhānarūpadhammasamūhamattameva hi tadā labbhati, matta-saddo vā visesanivattiattho, tena kammajāditisantatirūpavisesaṃ nivatteti. Appavattā hontīti appavattikā honti, na upalabbhatīti attho. Viññāṇe pana jīvasaññī, tasmā “viññāṇakkhandho gacchatī”ti āha, tattha anupalabbhanatoti adhippāyo.

423. “Veṭhetvā” means “wrapped with a brief covering.” “Cavanakāle” refers to the time when decease is reached, not the moment of deceasing. “Rūpakkhandhamattameva” means “merely an aggregate of a few material phenomena.” Indeed, at that time, only a collection of temperature-originated material phenomena is obtained; or the word “matta” serves to exclude specifics, thereby excluding the specific material continuity produced by kamma, and so on. “Appavattā honti” means “they do not occur,” that is, “they are not found.” However, one has the perception of “life” regarding consciousness; therefore it is said, “the aggregate of consciousness departs.” The intention here is that it is not found.

Santattaayoguḷaupamāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Simile of the Heated Iron Ball

424. Vūpasantatejanti vigatusmaṃ.

424. “Vūpasantatejaṃ” means “whose heat is stilled,” that is, “whose warmth has departed.”

425. Āmatoti ettha ā-saddo āmisa-saddo viya upaḍḍhapariyāyoti āha “addhamato”ti, āmatoti vā īsaṃ darathena [M 2.0354] usmanā yuttamaraṇo marantoti attho. Mīyamāno hi [V 2.0327] avigatusmo hoti, na mato viya vigatusmo. Tenāha “marituṃ āraddho hotī”ti. Tathā [P 2.0448] rūpassa odhunanaṃ nāmassa orato parivattanamevāti āha “orato karothā”ti. Orato kātukāmassa pana saṃparivattanaṃ sandhunanaṃ, taṃ pana parato karaṇanti āha “parato karothā”ti. Paramukhaṃ katassa ito cito parivattanaṃ niddhunananti āha “aparāparaṃ karothā”ti. Indriyāni aparibhinnānīti adhippāyena “tañcāyatanaṃ na paṭisaṃvedetī”ti vuttaṃ.

425. Here, in “āmatoti,” the prefix “ā-” is like the word “āmisa,” meaning “half” or “partial,” hence it is said, “addhamato” (half-dead); or “āmatoti” means “dying, associated with slight fear or warmth”—this is the meaning of “maranto” (dying). Indeed, a dying person is not without warmth, unlike a dead person who is without warmth. Therefore, it is said, “he has begun to die.” Similarly, the shaking of form is just the turning of name inwards; hence it is said, “make it inward.” But for one who wishes to make it inward, the turning around is a shaking; that, however, is making it outward, hence it is said, “make it outward.” For one who has turned their face away, the turning from here to there is a shaking off; hence it is said, “make it back and forth.” The phrase “he does not experience that sense-base” is stated with the intention that the sense-faculties are unimpaired.

Saṅkhadhamaupamāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Simile of the Conch-Blower

426. Saṅkhaṃ dhamati, dhamāpetīti vā saṅkhadhamo. Upalāpetvāti uparūpari saddayogavasena sallāpetvā, saddayuttaṃ katvāti attho. Taṃ pana atthato dhamanamevāti āha “dhamitvā”ti.

426. One who blows the conch, or causes it to be blown, is a conch-blower. “Upalāpetvā” means having caused it to sound repeatedly by means of connection with sound; the meaning is “having made it connected to sound.” But in essence, this is just blowing, hence it is said, “having blown.”

Aggikajaṭilaupamāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Simile of the Fire-Worshipping Ascetic

428. Āhito aggi etassa atthīti aggiko, svāssa aggikabhāvo yasmā aggihutamālāvedisampādanehi ceva indhanadhūmabarihisasappitelūpaharaṇehi balipupphadhūmagandhādiupahārehi ca tassa payirupāsanāya icchito, tasmā vuttaṃ “aggiparicārako”ti. Āyuṃ pāpuṇāpeyyanti yathā cirajīvī hoti, evaṃ āyuṃ pacchimavayaṃ pāpeyyaṃ. Vaḍḍhiṃ gameyyanti sarīrāvayave, guṇāvayave ca phātiṃ pāpeyyaṃ. Araṇī yugaḷanti uttarāraṇī, adharāraṇīti araṇīdvayaṃ.

428. He who has an established fire is an `aggika`; that is his state of being an `aggika`. Since his tending to it is desired through the performance of fire sacrifices, garlands, and altars, and through the presentation of fuel, smoke, barhis grass, ghee, oil, and offerings of bali, flowers, incense, fragrances, and so on, therefore it is said, “a fire-attendant.” “May I attain long life” means: so that I may live long, may I reach the final stage of life. “May I achieve growth” means: may I attain prosperity in bodily constituents and in virtuous qualities. “A pair of araṇis” means the pair of araṇis, namely, the upper araṇi and the lower araṇi.

429. Evanti “bālo pāyāsirājañño”tiādippakārena. Tayāti theraṃ sandhāya vadati. Vuttayuttakāraṇamakkhalakkhaṇenāti vuttayuttakāraṇassa makkhanasabhāvena. Yugaggāhalakkhaṇenāti samadhuraggahaṇalakkhaṇena. Palāsenāti palāsetīti palāso, parassa guṇe uttaritare ḍaṃsitvā viya chaḍḍento attano guṇehi same karotīti [P 2.0449] attho. Samakaraṇaraso hi palāso, tena palāsena.

429. “Thus” means in the manner of “the foolish king Pāyāsi,” and so on. “By you” is said referring to the elder. “By the characteristic of disparaging the stated, proper reason” means by the nature of disparaging the stated, proper reason. “By the characteristic of grasping the yoke” means by the characteristic of grasping the yoke evenly. “By detraction” (palāsena): one who detracts is a detractor (palāso); the meaning is one who, as if biting and casting aside another’s superior qualities, makes them equal with his own qualities. The essence of detraction is indeed to equalize; hence, “by detraction.”

Dvesatthavāhaupamāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Simile of the Two Caravan Leaders

430. Haritakapattanti [M 2.0355] haritabbapattaṃ, appapattanti attho. Tenāha “antamaso”tiādi. Sannaddhadhanukalāpanti ettha kalāpanti tūṇīramāha, tañca sannayhato dhanunā vinā na sannayhatīti āha [V 2.0328] “sannaddhadhanukalāpa”nti. Āsittodakāni vaṭumānīti gamanamaggā ceva taṃtaṃudakamaggā ca sammadeva devena phuṭṭhattā tahaṃ tahaṃ paggharitaudaka sandamānaudakā. Tenāha “paripuṇṇasalilā maggā ca kandarā cā”ti.

430. “Haritakapattaṃ” means a leaf fit to be plucked, the meaning being a tender leaf. Hence it is said, “even,” and so on. Here, in “sannaddhadhanukalāpaṃ,” “kalāpaṃ” means a quiver; and since, for one strapping it on, it is not strapped on without a bow, it is said, “with bow and quiver strapped.” “Āsittodakāni vaṭumāni” means that both the paths for travel and the various watercourses were well touched by the rain god, so that water was dripping and flowing here and there. Hence it is said, “paths and mountain clefts full of water.”

Yathābhatenāti sakaṭesu yathāṭhapitena, yathā “amma ito karohī”ti vutte ṭhapesīti attho karaṇakiriyāya kiriyāsāmaññavācībhāvato. Tasmā yathāropitena, yathāgahitenāti attho vutto.

“Yathābhatena” means as placed in the carts. Just as when one says, “Mother, do it here,” the meaning is “place it,” because the action of “doing” is a general term for action. Therefore, the meaning is said to be “as loaded” or “as taken.”

Akkhadhuttakaupamāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Simile of the Dice Gambler

434. Parājayaguḷanti yena guḷena, yāya salākāya ṭhitāya ca parājayo hoti, taṃ adassanaṃ gamento gilati. Pajjohananti pakārehi juhanakammaṃ. Taṃ pana balidānavasena karīyatīti āha “balikamma”nti.

434. “Parājayaguḷaṃ” means the die by which, or by the peg on which it stands, one loses; causing it not to be seen, he swallows it. “Pajjohanaṃ” means an act of offering with various methods. That, however, is done by way of a bali offering, hence it is said, “a sacrificial act.”

Sāṇabhārikaupamāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Simile of the Bearer of a Load of Hemp

436. Gāmapattanti gāmo eva hutvā āpajjitabbaṃ, suññabhāvena anāvasitabbaṃ. Tenāha “vuṭṭhitagāmapadeso”ti. Gāmapadanti yathā purisassa pādanikkhittaṭṭhānaṃ adhigataparicchedaṃ “pada”nti vuccati, evaṃ gāmavāsīhi āvasitaṭṭhānaṃ adhigatanivutthāgāraṃ “gāmapada”nti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “ayamevattho”ti. Susannaddhoti [P 2.0450] sukhena gahetvā gamanayogyatāvasena suṭṭhu sajjito. Taṃ pana susajjanaṃ suṭṭhu bandhanavasenevāti āha “subaddho”ti.

436. “Gāmapattaṃ” means a place should be reached as a proper village, not one that is uninhabited and empty. Hence it is said, “the area of an established village.” “Gāmapadaṃ”: just as the spot where a person's foot is placed, a defined area, is called a “footprint” (pada), so the place inhabited by villagers, with its established houses, is called a “village-site” (gāmapada). Hence it is said, “this is the very meaning.” “Susannaddho” means well-prepared, in the sense of being suitable to be taken and carried with ease. That good preparation is by way of being well-bound, hence it is said, “well-bound.”

Ayādīnampi lohabhāve satipi loha-saddo sāsane tambalohe niruḷhoti āha “lohanti tambaloha”nti.

Although there is a metallic nature in iron and so on, the word “loha” is established in the Teaching as referring to copper-metal, thus he said, “loha means copper-metal.”

Saraṇagamanavaṇṇanā

Explanation of Going for Refuge

437. Abhiraddhoti [M 2.0356] ārādhitacitto, sāsanassa ārādhitacittatā pasīdanavasenāti āha “abhippasanno”ti. Pañhupaṭṭhānānīti pañhesu upaṭṭhānāni mayā pucchitatthesu tumhākaṃ vissajjanavasena ñāṇupaṭṭhānāni.

437. “Abhiraddho” means one whose mind is pleased. The pleasing of the mind towards the Teaching is by way of confidence, hence he said “fully pleased.” “Pañhupaṭṭhānāni” means presentations in the questions, that is, presentations of knowledge by way of your answers to the matters asked by me.

Yaññakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on Sacrifices

438. Saṅghātanti [V 2.0329] saṃ-saddo padavaḍḍhanamattanti āha “ghāta”nti. Vipākaphalenāti sadisaphalena. Mahapphalo na hoti gavādipāṇaghātena upakkiliṭṭhabhāvato. Guṇānisaṃsenāti uddayaphalena. Ānubhāvajutiyāti paṭipakkhavigamanajanitena sabhāvasaṅkhātena tejena. Na mahājutiko hoti aparisuddhabhāvato. Vipākavipphāratāyāti vipākaphalassa vipulatāya, pāripūriyāti attho. Duṭṭhukhetteti usabhādidosehi dūsitakhette, taṃ pana vappābhāvato asāraṃ hotīti āha “nissārakhette”ti. Dubbhūmeti kucchitabhūmibhāge, svāssa kucchitabhāvo asāratāya vā siyā ninnatādidosavasena vā. Tattha paṭhamo pakkho paṭhamapadena dassitoti itaraṃ dassento “visamabhūmibhāge”ti āha. Daṇḍābhighātādinā chinnabhinnāni. Pūtīnīti gomayalepadānādisukhena asukkhāpitattā pūtibhāvaṃ gatāni. Tāni pana yasmā sāravantāni na honti, tasmā vuttaṃ “nissārānī”ti. Vātātapahatānīti vātena ca ātapena ca vinaṭṭhabījasāmatthiyāni. Tenāha “pariyādinnatejānī”ti. Yaṃ [P 2.0451] yathājātavīhiādigatena taṇḍulena aṅkuruppādanayogyabījasāmatthiyaṃ, taṃ taṇḍulasāro, tassa ādānaṃ gahaṇaṃ tathāuppajjanameva. Etāni pana bījāni na tādisāni khaṇḍādidosavantatāya. Dhārāya khette anuppavesanaṃ nāma vassanameva, taṃ paṭikkhepavasena dassento āha “na sammā vasseyyā”ti. Aṅkuramūlapattādīhīti cettha aṅkurakandādīhi uddhaṃ vuddhiṃ, mūlajaṭādīhi heṭṭhā viruḷhiṃ, pattapupphādīhi samantato ca vepullanti yojanā.

438. The term saṅghāta means that the prefix saṃ- is merely an addition to the word; thus he says, 'ghāta'. The phrase vipākaphalena means by a similar fruit. It does not bear great fruit because it is defiled by the killing of cattle and other beings. The phrase guṇānisaṃsena means by the fruit of prosperity. The phrase ānubhāvajutiyā means by the energy, which is its intrinsic nature, generated from the removal of opposing forces. It is not greatly radiant because it is impure. The phrase vipākavipphāratāya means by the vastness of the fruit of the result; the meaning is completeness. A bad field (duṭṭhukhette) refers to a field spoiled by faults such as bulls, etc. But because it lacks sowing, it is barren—hence it is called 'a barren field' (nissārakhette). Poor soil (dubbhūme) refers to an inferior plot of land, and its inferiority may be due to barrenness or faults like low-lying ground, etc. Here, the first possibility is shown by the first term, and to show the other, it is said, 'on uneven ground' (visamabhūmibhāge). The phrase chinnabhinnāni means cut and broken by sticks and blows, etc. The term pūtīni means rotten, having become putrid from not being well-dried due to being easily smeared with cow-dung and so on. But because they lack essence, it is said, 'devoid of essence' (nissārāni). The phrase vātātapahatāni means struck by wind and sun, that is, the seeds have lost their capacity to sprout due to wind and heat. Hence it is said, 'their potency taken away' (pariyādinnatejāni). The seed-potential capable of producing a sprout, which is found in the grain of naturally grown paddy and so on, is the essence of the grain. Its 'being taken' is simply its arising as such. But these seeds are not like that, due to having faults such as being broken. The entering of a stream into the field is indeed the raining. Showing this by way of negation, he says, 'it would not rain properly' (na sammā vasseyyā). Here, the phrase aṅkuramūlapattādīhi is to be construed as: upward growth by sprouts and bulbs, downward spreading by root-tangles, and fullness all around by leaves and flowers.

Aparūpaghātenāti paresaṃ vibādhanena. Uppannapaccayatoti nibbattitaghāsacchādanādideyyadhammato. Gavādighātenapi hi tattha paṭiggāhakānaṃ ghāso saṅkīyati. “Aparūpaghātitāyā”ti idaṃ sīlavantatāya kāraṇavacanaṃ[M 2.0357]. Guṇātirekanti guṇātirittaṃ, sīlādilokuttaraguṇehi visiṭṭhanti attho. Vipulāti saddhāsampadādivasena uḷārā.

The phrase aparūpaghātena means by not vexing others. The phrase uppannapaccayato means from the gift-item that has been produced, such as fodder, clothing, etc. For even by the killing of cattle, etc., the fodder for the recipients there becomes suspect. The phrase aparūpaghātitāya is a statement of the reason for being virtuous. The term guṇātirekaṃ means surpassing in virtue; the meaning is distinguished by virtues such as morality and supramundane qualities. The term vipulā means magnificent by way of accomplishments such as faith.

Uttaramāṇavavatthuvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Story of the Brahmin Youth Uttara

439. Atha kho tehi sakuṇḍakehi taṇḍulehi siddhaṃbhattaṃ uttaṇḍulameva hotīti āha “uttaṇḍulabhatta”nti. Bilaṅgaṃ vuccati āranālaṃ bilaṅgato nibbattanato, tadeva kañjiyato jātanti kañjiyaṃ, taṃ dutiyaṃ etassāti bilaṅgadutiyaṃ, taṃ “kañjikadutiya”nti ca vuttaṃ. Dhorakānīti dhoviyāni. Yasmā thūlatarānipi “thūlānī”ti vattabbataṃ arahanti, tasmā “thūlāni [V 2.0330] cā”ti vuttaṃ. Guḷadasānīti suttānaṃ thūlatāya, kañjikassa bahalatāya ca piṇḍitadasāni. Tenāha “puñjapuñja…pe… dasānī”ti. Anuddisatīti anu anu katheti.

439. Then, he says 'uttaṇḍulabhatta' because the cooked rice prepared with grains that had bran was in fact rice without bran. Bilaṅga is called āranāla (sour gruel). Because it is produced from bilaṅga, and the same thing, when born from rice-gruel (kañjiya), is called kañjiya. That which has this as a second ingredient is bilaṅgadutiya; it is also called kañjikadutiya. Dhorakāni means to be washed. Because even coarser threads deserve to be called 'coarse' (thūlāni), therefore it is said 'and coarse' (thūlāni cā). Guḷadasāni refers to knotted fringes, formed due to the thickness of the threads and the thickness of the gruel. Hence it is said, 'heaps... fringes' (puñjapuñja…pe… dasāni). Anuddisati means he mentions one by one.

440. Asakkaccanti na sakkaccaṃ anādarakāraṃ, taṃ pana [P 2.0452] kammaphalasaddhāya abhāvena hotīti āha “saddhāvirahita”nti. Acittīkatanti cittīkārapaccupaṭṭhāpanavasena na cittīkataṃ. Tenāha “cittīkāravirahita”ntiādi. Cittīkārarahitaṃ vā acittīkataṃ, yathā kataṃ paresaṃ vimhayāvahaṃ hoti, tathā akataṃ. Cittassa uḷārapaṇītabhāvo pana asakkaccadāneneva bādhito. Apaviddhanti chaḍḍanīyadhammaṃ viya apaviddhaṃ katvā, etena tasmiṃ dāne gāravākaraṇaṃ vadati. Serīsakaṃ nāmāti “serīsaka”nti evaṃ nāmakaṃ. Tucchanti parijanaparicchedavirahato rittaṃ.

440. Asakkaccaṃ means not carefully, an act of disrespect. He says 'saddhāvirahita' (devoid of faith) because this arises from an absence of faith in the fruit of kamma. Acittīkataṃ means not attended to, by way of not establishing attention. Therefore, it is said 'cittīkāravirahita' (devoid of attention) and so on. Or, acittīkataṃ means devoid of attention; it was not done in such a way as to be astonishing to others. But the magnificent and sublime state of mind is obstructed precisely by the careless gift. Apaviddhaṃ means having cast it aside as if it were a thing to be thrown away; by this, he indicates a lack of respect in that giving. Serīsakaṃ nāma means named 'Serīsaka'. Tucchaṃ means empty, devoid of retinue and equipment.

Pāyāsidevaputtavaṇṇanā

Commentary on Pāyāsi, the Son of a Deva

441. Tassānubhāvenāti tassa dānassa ānubhāvena. Sirīsarukkhoti pabhassarakhandhaviṭapasākhāpalāsasampanno manuññadassano dibbo sirīsarukkho. Aṭṭhāsīti phalassa kammasarikkhataṃ dassento vimānadvāre nibbattitvā aṭṭhāsi. Pubbāciṇṇavasenāti purimajātiyaṃ tattha nivāsaparicayanavasena. Na kevalaṃ pubbāciṇṇavaseneva, atha kho utusukhumavasena pīti dassento “tattha kirassa utusukhaṃ hotī”ti āha.

441. Tassānubhāvena means by the power of that gift. Sirīsarukkho means the divine Sirīsa tree, endowed with a radiant trunk, boughs, branches, and foliage, delightful to behold. Aṭṭhāsi means it stood at the palace gate, having arisen there, showing the similarity of the fruit to the action. Pubbāciṇṇavasena means due to previous habituation from familiarity with living there in a past life. Not only due to previous habituation, but also to show that the season was pleasant, it is said, 'for there, it seems, the season was pleasant for him.'

Soti [M 2.0358] uttaro māṇavo. Yadi asakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā pāyāsi tattha nibbatto, pāyāsissa paricārikā sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā kathaṃ tattha nibbattāti āha “pāyāsissa panā”ti. Nikantivasenāti pāyāsimhi sāpekkhāvasena, pubbepi vā tattha nivutthapubbatāya. Disācārikavimānanti ākāsaṭṭhaṃ hutvā disāsu vicaraṇakavimānaṃ, na rukkhapabbatasikharādisambandhaṃ. Vaṭṭaniaṭaviyanti vimānavīthiyanti.

So is the young man Uttara. If Pāyāsi was reborn there by giving a careless gift, how then was Pāyāsi’s female attendant reborn there by giving a careful gift? He said, 'But of Pāyāsi...'. Nikantivasena means by way of longing, that is, with attachment to Pāyāsi, or because of having previously dwelt there. Disācārikavimānaṃ means a celestial mansion that roams the skies, not connected to trees, mountains, or peaks. Vaṭṭaniaṭaviyaṃ means in the paths of the celestial mansion.

Pāyāsirājaññasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

The Clarification of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Pāyāsirājañña Sutta.

Niṭṭhitā ca mahāvaggaṭṭhakathāya līnatthappakāsanā.

Here ends the Clarification of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Mahāvagga.

Mahāvaggaṭīkā niṭṭhitā.

The Subcommentary on the Mahāvagga is concluded.
